Coming off Witcher 3 and Fallout 4, I was looking for another solid game to eat up too much free time. Since I didn't own a PS4, I hadn't been following the advance hype for this game and stumbled across it. Based on reviews and descriptions, we ended up buying a PS4 just to play - and wow, was it worth it.

This game reminds me that you don't need amazing cinematics and cut scenes, fancy fighting sequences, or even top-notch graphics to have a fantastic game. In fact, it really reminds me of the text-based games of long, long ago, since most of the "action" happens in text descriptors. Sure, you can run and fly anywhere in the entire game - and it's huge - but anytime you interact with a computer module or lifeform, the interaction is described in text rather than actually being performed. While this sounds dull, it's surprisingly immersive. We played for about 60 hours in the first week, and have now banned ourselves from playing on weeknights (we're useless at work if we play all night, after all).

This is also the first game that my husband (who loves Battlefield) and I enjoy equally. We trade off playing (with one profile), which is a first for any game we've ever played. It's got an excellent mix of fighting, exploring, gathering, and goal achievement, so it hits all four of the gamer profiles. You can focus on any of the four elements at any time, and ignore anything you don't enjoy. In our case, I do a lot of the exploring, inventory management, and space battles, and my husband poaches Albumen pearls and fights Sentinels (the former has turned out to be our favorite part for some reason).

I'd love to see them add the ability to build structures as bases and storage, since that would encourage even deeper exploration of each star system. I'd also like to see more interactive elements in the environment and with lifeforms, since it actually feels kind of lonely and isolated as you wander the universe. Given how many ships streak across the skies or hang around planets, there should be a lot more activity in the star bases and on planets. But none of that has stopped us from thoroughly enjoying this game.

I've played Civ since way back when it was just "Civilization" (no numbers), and loved every iteration even with their shortcomings. I did skip Civ V based on early terrible reviews, but I see now that it seems to have fixed the problems. So this review will have to compare Civ VI to Civs I-IV, not V. And yes, I kept playing IV off and on since it first came out.

This version has taken a big step forward in a lot of ways, including complexity, resource management, and city customization. It's also introduced some pretty annoying features. First, a few high points for me:

1. City development. The districts add a decent layer of planning to the cities, and make plundering enemies a lot more interesting, too. Being able to buy certain tiles can really help shape a city (literally and figuratively) early on, and district bonuses based on tile features reward a player for thinking ahead. This is a large step forward, and makes city-building a whole lot more interesting.
2. Religion customization. The ability to customize your religion based on how you plan to play a certain game makes a big difference. Some games, I plan to go for culture points, so I'll get the perk to buy Theatre districts with Faith. Or other games I'm aiming for a religion victory, so I'll grab the perk for lower costs to buy apostles and missionaries. Later in the game, government policies can help tweak religion bonuses.
3. Government policies. This version introduces policies, which operate like perks for your government. (And certain Wonders unlock additional policy slots, so they're definitely worth pursuing even if they're not on your desired victory path) The policies really help you adapt your government as the game progresses, and you can pivot quickly to respond to the competition.
4. Spies. The game limits your total number of spies, which really makes you think about how to use them. You can also capture enemy spies (and yours can be captured), so they're effectively out of play until traded back to their civilization. At the end stages of games they make things a lot more interesting, since you have very little to do unless you're in a war or three.
5. Interesting leaders. Leaders are both more varied and more interesting. The civilization perks really require you to change your game style for each game, and each opponent requires different types of behaviors from you. This is a step forward from older versions in a lot of ways (although see the caveat about AIs below).
6. Amusing graphics. This is a really small thing for me, but I do appreciate the little touches like seagulls swarming over fishing boats, doves circling holy sites, or late-stage settlers appearing as Winnebagos. Clever touches are nice to see.

All that said, this game doesn't do away with some of the franchise's biggest weaknesses, and it introduces a couple of new ones.

1. End-game tedium. If you're going for a culture, space, or even religion victory - and you're not at war with anyone - the end game is pretty much still just click-wait-click-wait-click-wait ad nauseum. The "click" is to hit "next turn" and the "wait" is waiting for the other players to take their turns. You're not doing much during your own turn, since all your cities are probably focused on multi-turn projects, your builders have pretty much improved everything, and you've already discovered everything (either through scouts or satellites). There's mild interest if you're spreading religion with your apostles, or tracking down artifacts with an archaeologist, or even telling a spy to steal a Great Work, but mostly it's click-wait-click-wait...
2. It's a looooong wait. I spend far more time waiting for other players to take their turns than I do actually playing my own turn, no matter what performance settings I use. Toward the end of the game, I find myself alt-tabbing to do something else every time I hit "next turn," but it's just as tedious on the first turn as it is on the last. At least older versions of the game didn't bog down this way until the end of the game.
3. Limited AI interactions. Opponents are both more and less interesting to interact with, which is weird. On the one hand, you can have alliances, defensive pacts, trade, friendships, and other levels of interaction. You can complain to them of their spying or converting your cities to their religion. But the interactions are really 2-dimensional, and don't seem to have much nuance. For example, you can be "friends" with, say, China for the entire game, and then build one more Wonder than they have and BOOM, they denounce you. Or you have open borders with someone, which then expire while you have troops near their city (I haven't figured out how close yet), and they get "unfriendly" suddenly because you had troops near their border. Why not give us a grace period to move stuff? Or take into account the 30 turns of friendly relations we just had? This happens even when those troops are in your own territory, even in your own city center, so it's pretty unavoidable.
3. Horrible Civilopedia. In past versions, the Civilopedia was great at actually explaining gameplay and tactics. This time around, it's next to useless. Take Districts, for example. There're a couple of paragraphs with flowery explanation of what they are, and that's it. No explanation why one city needs a population of 21 to build a Spaceport, but another city only needs population 13 (I still don't know). Or what happens if the tile is pillaged (you have to repair it through the production menu). A chart of all the districts and their dependencies would be nice, too, including which Wonders require which types of Districts. And it's not limited to Districts - the first several games I've played I looked up a couple dozen concepts and couldn't find a single helpful answer. It's actually A LOT easier to alt-tab out of the game and search for the answer on the Internet.

There are also some pretty annoying gameplay issues that I hope will be fixed in updates. These are mostly little things that seem fixable, but get in the way for now. For example:
1. The news scroller overlays the middle of the screen and you can't click each news item away. You end up having to wait until they all scroll past to do anything.
2. What's worse, the center-screen news items overlap with a separate scrolling of news on the right side of the screen, so you can't read what just happened to your spy, or who just stole a great work from your city, or whatever.
3. Even WORSE, there's no place to see a history of the news that just scrolled past, so if you miss something, you're on your own.
4. There seems to be a bug that leaves a permanent news item on the right that tells me someone just built Stonehenge, all game, every game (except if I build it first).
5. The news reported by my journalists and "allies" seems suspect. I'm not sure if this is intentional (the Civilopedia is of course useless on this point), to make you question the "news". But as one example, I've been told numerous times that an Ally is preparing military operations against me, when they actually just paid me to be their Ally. Am I supposed to worry they're about to take a giant warmongering penalty for attacking an Ally? But since it's never come to anything, I have no idea what's triggering that "news."
6. The resolution seems to be locked, and the drop-down arrow grayed out to adjust it. No idea why, and I haven't seen an explanation online anywhere. But being able to fix the resolution might fix the news issues, above, besides making the game easier to play overall.
7. Little stuff they did away with: Giving summary of Wonders when you build them. (If it's something that changes how you're playing (like the Wonder gives you more tourist points, so you want to change your policies), you'll have to remember on your own.) The ability to put your units on sentry. Several keyboard shortcuts. The overview report to see all the Leaders' relationships. A clickable city status screen that shows production/food/etc for all cities at once (there is a dumbed down version of this, but I want the old one). There's more, but you get the idea.

Overall, I'm still playing this game for an embarrassingly large number of hours. The franchise is still the gold-standard for turn-based strategy/sim gaming, and the issues I bring up I wouldn't keep me from buying it again. But I'm actually looking forward to updates and new content already, and doubt this version has the staying power for me that even Civ IV had.

Played this ages ago on XBox, and recently bought it for PS4 while I wait for something else worth playing. Like most other PS4 versions of games I've played, the controls on this are great (strong preference for PS4 over XBox in this house). I don't notice many differences in the graphics, but it's been a loooooong time. It's still a visually-stunning game, ambient sounds are excellent, and camera action is very smooth. Load times are very good, especially compared to XBox (used to be able to go get a sandwich on load screens).

If you've never played before, you're in for a treat. Despite playing a couple hundred hours five years ago, I'm discovering dungeons, NPCs, and mini quests I never ran across the first three times I played (and I haven't touched the DLC content yet). The leveling system remains one of the best I've played, with your skills actually improving with use, instead of just pouring points into something unrelated to whatever grinding you've been doing. That means that this time around, I'm forcing myself to use different skills and play as a completely different type of character than my "usual" builds. But since your skill actually improves with use, it feels very organic and natural to learn to play new ways.

The only aspects that haven't aged well in this game would be the NPC appearance and stock phrases. If that guy in Whiterun tells me one more time that "the problem with Skyrim these days is that everyone is obsessed with death," I may have to risk the wrath of the guards and finally firebolt him. But if the shopkeepers' greetings and predictable NPCs are the worst this game has to offer (and they are), it's still one of the best games out there.

I picked up an Assassin's Creed game a few years ago, but just couldn't get into it (could have been the lousy XBox controller getting in the way). But I couldn't go through Horizon: Zero Dawn, Witcher 3, or (especially) Skyrim even one more time, and needed a gaming fix. I'm really, really glad I tried this new Assassin's Creed.

If you're new to the franchise like I was, you may like to know that you don't necessarily need to know any of the lore or backstory to enjoy this game. I did feel (plenty of times) that I could be missing something that would have made the game more immersive, but the characters, voice acting, graphics, and gameplay all contribute to a great experience even without a personal history with the series.

I was half expecting to find that this game was released by the same people behind Horizon: Zero Dawn, because the two games feel a LOT alike. The quest system, story-telling, combat, and character skill development are very similar, although there's enough difference that I didn't feel at all like it was the same game in a different skin - it was just familiar enough to make it easy to pick up.

What I especially like:

1. I find the inventory management to be far better than most games with this level of crafting/collecting. Anyone who's spent ages managing materials and supplies in, say, Skyrim will find this system blissfully simple. You can't craft with the same degree of complexity, but I didn't miss grinding at the forge one little bit.
2. Good combat controls. Once I got used to the slower-than-I-expected response times, the combat is actually very smooth and interesting. It's less about button-mashing than a lot of games, and more about taking on opponents with some degree of strategy. Of course, if you want to just fly through combat with some button-mashing, putting the game in Easy mode will get you there.
3. Great voice acting. The characters' voices and acting don't pull you out of the game like some games can do, although I did have to turn on the subtitles to understand a couple of characters' accents. But I'm really glad they didn't just use a bunch of American-sounding actors (or terrible imitation accents) for a game set entirely in Egypt. The choice to use African (sounding) accents was perfect, IMO.
4. Engaging story. I like a decent story with my hack-and-slash, and this one delivers. One moment early in the game (after you defeat the first big bad guy) was so well done, my husband and I actually reacted like you would to a really good movie. While I did find that the backstory was confusing to get into, I didn't mind the mystery around "what the heck are they talking about?"

My only reservation is that the quests can get repetitive after a while. But this is an issue with all the big, open-world games (less so with Horizon: Zero Dawn, but that game's not really that big a world), so I don't think this game really falls short. So half a star deducted for that.

The other half-star deduction comes from the fact that there's really very little customization of your gameplay, and not a whole lot of replayability. The three skill trees do offer some ability to play your own unique way, but there's not a huge amount of variation available. And once you've gone through the linear story, playing again won't change much even if you change your play style.

I guess Ubisoft knew there's not a lot of replay potential, given the add-on's they've already released. But for a once-through game, this one is polished, fun, and a great introduction to Assassin's Creed (if you need one). Highly recommended.

I installed this with a Pixel XL, which was a tight fit, but it works. Overall, it's a fun little system, but I'm not quite sure it's ready for prime time. Here's how it's gone for me so far, starting from the unboxing to the gameplay:

1. Very giftable packaging. It's a small thing, but presentation does make a difference. I could see kids having a lot of excitement as they unbox this (as an adult, I still got a little thrill out of the lightsaber resting inside when I opened the box).

2. Minimal instructions. What instructions? Actually, there's a little booklet of warranty/safety info with tiny pictures of the components and directions to go to their website to download the app. You can also find it in your favorite app store.

3. Mediocre installation. The app is a huge file, so I'd suggest downloading over WiFi. The installation actually forced a reboot on my phone the first time, and I had to try again. It worked second try, but it was a frustrating 12 minutes, which seems long for installing an app. If you have eager kids waiting, I suggest you send them to get you a drink of something refreshing while you stare at the installation meter.

4. Pretty good setup. The app walks you through each step of the setup, although the steps to get your phone into the headset are less than elegant. Like I said, my Pixel XL was a very tight fit, so I worried I was going to break the plastic tray getting it to work (I didn't). They included different adapters for USB-C, micro USB, and iPhone connections, so you're good to go there.

5. Fit is terrible. This is a pretty heavy headset, and even adjusting the straps six ways to Sunday didn't make it fit any better. It presses very hard on my cheekbones and gives me a pretty good headache and neck ache within about 20 minutes. Anyone with hair longer than a couple inches will probably find that the straps slide and pull the hair a lot, and adjusting the straps after it's on risks catching hair in a most painful way.

6. View screen is awkward. I found that there's a very small sweet spot to stand in to comfortably see everything, and even then I'm frequently craning my neck in awkward angles to get a decent view. There's no visual cue to let you know what the boundaries are, either, so you have to figure it out each time you play.

7. Moderately immersive. As someone else mentioned, you basically see your opponents standing in your room, unless you play in a completely dark space. Then you see them... standing in darkness. This latter is preferable to me, since Darth Maul in my living room isn't exactly the Star Wars experience I was dreaming of. I actually like the Holochess matches the best, since I can basically sit in a tallish chair (a stool works well since it's the right height) and the surroundings don't much matter.

8. Fun games, but just 3. The three games are pretty fun so far, which is good since that's all this thing can do. I'm still trying to get the hang of the light saber action, since it's not really very well calibrated to what's happening in front of you. There seems to be a tiny lag between your movement and the actual action, and it's just so slightly off-center. I've re-centered a bazillion times, but it could be user error. I'll update this review if I figure it out later.

9. Really limited controls and options. I fiddled with buttons on the headset and light saber, but couldn't figure out how to back out and restart. One of the headset buttons takes you to the settings screen with three settings to fiddle with (volume, light saber color, and I forgot the third one), but that's it - no calibration or anything. There's also no way to have more than one profile, so this is purely a one person game unless you don't mind sharing progress.

10. Visuals are okay. It's all pretty fuzzy, not even as crisp as the holochess game you see in the A New Hope. I did expect better graphics.

11. My phone gets HOT. The headset has no venting of any kind and encases your phone in layers of thick plastic. My phone gets almost too hot to touch after 25 minutes of play. I have no interest in burning out my battery, much less my CPU, so I'm seriously reluctant to cram my phone back into this headset to play Holochess.

12. Build quality is fair. Aside from the seriously uncomfortable straps, the headset seems pretty solid. My biggest concern is the flimsy plastic tray that the phone fits into, since I can't see it lasting long with the type of pressure I have to use with it.The light saber has a decent feel, if very, very plastic-y. It's a little small for two-handed use, and little big for one-handed use, but then I've got average adult hands. Might be better for kids two-handed, or a larger adult one-handed.

Overall, it's pretty fun once you get past the installation and setup. If you can deal with the uncomfortable headset and your phone doesn't overheat, you're in for some fun gameplay. But at this price ($200 at this writing), I just can't say it's more than a cute novelty limited to three games.

I haven't played Tropico since the first one came out, so I wasn't sure what to expect from this one. Turns out it's far more fun and involved than other Sims I've played since then, and it sucked away far too many hours the first weekend I got it. PS4 controls are surprisingly intuitive, and actually a lot easier to remember than the old PC version I played before. Graphics are detailed and crisp, music is tolerable (I turned it off after a while - too repetitive), and there are plenty of options for how to play.

I started with the tutorial and scenarios, which were all very well written and which introduced concepts at a good pace. Then I moved over to sandbox mode, which I usually prefer in Sims. I like that you can set your own victory conditions in addition to starting conditions, so you can decide how you want to focus from the get-go. Even playing 10+ sandbox games, the game has continually thrown new challenges at me at different points in the game. Not just the usual natural disasters, like SimCity, but also pirate invasions, invasion by angry Allies (or Axis), or revolutions when I jail/banish/kill too many crime lords or rebels at once.

I've only encountered one bug so far, when my saved game got wiped during a force close. But I suspect that was a PS4 issue and not a Tropico issue, and I'm more careful about closing the application when I put the PS4 to sleep - no more problem.

The only quibble I'd have with this game is that there's so much to it, it's a lot to learn and absorb. But since that's part of what makes it so fun for me, I can't really complain. It's just not a simple game to pick up and play for a couple of hours, then put away for a month - it's much more one of those "I'm sitting down for a serious gaming session and don't intend to shower or eat for the next while" types of games. Highly recommended when you need to zone out for a big chunk of time.

I'm surprised to see so many people find this game different from other AC games, but I jumped into the series late (Origins). This game plays very, very much like Origins, but I'm glad I played that one first. Origins didn't require any AC experience to be instantly engaging, and it introduced the controls and concepts gradually enough to be easy to learn. Odyssey has far, far less explanation of the controls and interface, and it depends a lot on your already understanding the mechanics of AC. I think I would have been utterly confused for a while if I didn't already know about sync points, battle controls, sneaking, etc.

Which would have a been a pity, because the first 10 hours or so of the game are actually just intro to the story. Just when you think "Oh, this is just like Origins, but with more ship battles," you realize there's a whole new layer of gaming with the Sparta/Athens war. You can choose to help either or both sides through various quests, and you have the option of fighting for either side in multiple pitched battles (that are extremely difficult to win, in my experience). THEN you realize that all that stuff isn't even the main story line. I've played for about 30 hours, and just got to the main quest line of [spoiler] hunting down the secret cabal.

Things I really like about this version:
- Bad guys level with you. If you go back to the starter zone, everyone will be your current level, not ridiculously easy. You do run into zones that are far above your level, but once you hit the right level, those zones level up along with you.
- So many options. For any given gaming session, you can either 1) run a bunch of little quests that don't actually feel as horribly repetitive as in Origins, 2) hunt down bad guys for the main quest(s), 3) go fight some pitched battles, 4) explore endlessly (or just run around assassinating people, really), 5) just hunt for resources, 6) sail around and hunt pirates, merchants, etc. The game is actually a little overwhelming in the sheer amount of things to do. Completionists may go crazy.
- Great variety (and dialogue) in quests. Even the mini-quests have good voice acting and amusing dialogue, and most of them feel more interesting and relevant than Origins (or even Horizon).
- Fewer cut scenes to slow down gameplay. Origins had way too many cut scenes (that took forever to load), and it seems the developers decided to put their time to better use for Odyssey.

The only bugs I've encountered are occasional loot containers that are hidden in walls, but otherwise PS4 gameplay has been smooth and error-free. Cut scenes still take a while to load, but it's not as annoying or frequent as Origins. Controls are mostly intuitive, although it sometimes catches me that X (or some other button) sometimes means one thing and sometimes another, and it's not always intuitive why the change. The menus are easy to navigate and don't require too much clicking. What's more, inventory control is super-easy without being utterly dull (and there's no risk of being overburdened!).

If you're new to AC, you might want to consider starting with Origins to get the gameplay and mechanics down first (it plays a lot like Horizon: Zero Dawn, by the way). If you're not sure if you want to dive into this type of game, I'd suggest playing Horizon: Zero Dawn instead, since that one is top-notch in both story and gameplay. I'm a die-hard Skyrim fan, with occasional forays into Shadow of Mordor, Mass Effect, Fallout, Witcher, etc., so if you like those games, you'll probably find quite a bit to like about Odyssey (and Origins). If you're more of a Call of Duty/Battlefield or Tropico/SimCity player, you may find less to like here.

I can't help thinking of this as a "great little game," which doesn't sound all that promising, I know. It plays a lot like a stripped-down version of SimCity (in space), so if that's your genre, this one won't disappoint. Because it's stripped down, it's easy to learn and play through scenarios in short bursts of time. Unlike the larger, more involved games, this one is really well suited to casual, occasional gameplay. But that doesn't mean it's boring, at least not for the first 20 hours (I'm playing in short bursts, so that's all I've played in the month since I got it).

Other details: Controls are intuitive and easy to learn. Graphics are detailed and varied enough to stay interesting. Scenarios are pretty quick and introduce the concepts at a good pace. Menus are intuitive and don't require excess clicking. I haven't encountered any glitches or bugs, either.

I picked this up on a whim for $14, which was a great deal on what is, really, a "great little game." Even if I don't play more than 20 hours, that's a good value for a fun game.

This game was made by control freaks. No wandering around allowed. Follow the leader, NOW!!
The team will run ahead, being immune to bullets, and half the time the fighting is done while you use cover like a normal person.
At frequent intervals the game takes complete control. Suddenly your weapon is disabled so you can button mash for a half hour, trying to get past some stupid hand-to-hand tango.
Don't veer off course or you get the red programmer warning - You're leaving the battlefield! That's geek talk for not being smart enough to sneak around the shooting instead of walking down the middle of the street.
I HATE it when the game takes away my weapons. I hate mashing buttons quickly when just pushing it once would work as well. I hate sequential button pushing that stops the game dead because you didn't do it just right.
These guys also went to that big sale they had for brown and grey paint. Bright colors are for kids, not real life pretend soldier wanna be's.
Another combat game made by people who've never been in the military. Duck you idiots!
I liked Frontlines;fuel of war, Bad Company, Black, Gears of War 2 and 3, Halo 1 and 3.

They should have called it "Crawling Through Weeds Guy", because that's what you do. It goes so far as to punish you for sniping a target! The loud-mouthed, so-called spotter tells you that you screwed up because you shot a guy! Instead, you're supposed to crawl and crawl and crawl and avoid being seen. Of course they won't let you crawl under the buildings unless you find the very specific route that you're supposed to take. And of course every bad guys sees you, even if you're in the bushes, in the shade, and lying flat. "You've set off the alarm!!!" Start again!
One level even has the "save" messed up. You go over a wall-you have to jump just right or you die-and if you go left - no save- if you go right, it saves. Stupid. The penalty for being killed is too severe. You have to go way back and do it again and again until you've memorized every bad guy's position. Not fun.
The whole idea of being a sniper is to shoot from hiding. This is not a sniper game.

Played for ten minutes, which is about how long as it took to load on my PS3. Talk about control freaks. At the beginning you aren't even allowed to move! Once it releases you, you have to follow a bossy, loud-mouthed punk who is supposed to be your partner. The first thing I tried to do was kill him, but control freaks don't allow that. The first time you encounter an enemy you have to - HAVE TO! - use your Crysis stupid thermal vision. Then you have to - HAVE TO! - zoom in and hold your breath before you make the shot. No just lining up the cross hairs and going bang, oh no, you have no choice. The developers DEMAND that you do as they say.
After the first kill you have to follow your "partner". Don't even try to pass him; that's forbidden. He then sets up a shot for you - you aren't allowed to decide. You shoot and suddenly a bunch of guys charge out and kill you. Repeat this five times, put the game back in the box, and go outside and punch a tree.
I am so sick of these games where you have to follow someone around and do as you're told. Then they call it a first person shooter. Get out of my way and let me decide who to shoot and when, including my "partner".

Could have been a good game, but Ubisoft has a guy, like many game makers, whose only job is to remove the fun. The engine is horrible. The A button is for Cover and for Jumping Over Cover and for Moving to New Cover - how could that ever go wrong. You want to duck and hide and it jumps you over the wall and you're dead. You want to run like heck and it ducks and covers. You just want to move from cover and you stick to that spot like glue. It happens again and again and you get killed again and again.
The result is a game that is frustrating instead of challenging and it removes two stars of fun.
When you get killed you sometimes have to rerun a cut scene over and over until you want to through the controller through the tv.
There are a few missions that are pretty good and some that are just plain work. You can only go into buildings that are approved by Ubisoft of course and you have to go down the middle of the street most of the time - no tricky moves or out of bounds wandering allowed - the fun removal guy made sure of that.
If you see it for under $10 then it's not too bad.

This game had lots of potential, which was removed by Namco so that it wouldn't be that much fun. It's pretty, the characters are interesting and the gameplay totally sucks. First of all it's PS3 only, which means bad control setup on a bad controller on a bad gaming system. I say that, having a PS2, Xbox, PS3 and Xbox 360. PS3 means that the character won't rotate half the time - it just refuses to move the camera. It rotates you when you don't want it rotated. The weapons controlls are wrong and not adjustable. The weapons are a joke.
It's climb and fall, start over. You climb exactly where they tell you to - no free choice at all. It's fight endless robots, die, and start over - again and again and again. Ooh look, another giant robot that takes forever to kill.
This game should have been great. If you have enless patience and don't mind repetition and can get it for under $5, then go for it. I like Halo - not 4. I like Gears of War - not Judgement. I like Bad Company 1 & 2. I hate Assasin's Creed and all the other climb and fall games of that type.

Fist of all it's PS3, so it has the usual random rotation problems that all PS3 games have. It's a button masher with endless combinations designed to promote carpel tunnel. You can't adjust the brightness as you can in real games so you can only play at night or with the curtains closed. The dialogue is strictly junior high, but with obcenities thrown in so that no parent would want their kid playing it. You can at least turn off the dialogue, which I did. The main character is a moron. There is really no plot.
The fighting is repetetive. The first female enemy was supposed to be a big battle and she killed Deadpool a bunch of times. Then I just used the square button, pushing it about once a second while looking out the window at the sunny day. She was killed in about 15 seconds with no fancy combos or jumping like a spastic tree frog or even looking at the tv.
I'm on the second chapter and it's already boring.

Grand Theft Auto rewritten. It looked like it was going to be fun, but the control freak developers soon put a stop to that. It's lots and lots of driving around and then you do a 'mission', which is tightly controlled. One mission is to attack another gang. You drive to their location and start shooting - you have to stay right there, no going fifty feet away or the mission fails. You have to fight in three locations and if you fail at two or three you start over again - drive to location one, etc. Boring. Oh yeah, and there are helicopters, gang-bangers with helicopters. I hate helicopters and they have no place in this game.
There's an arcade shooting gallary and if you die you start again. Boring.
If you like driving around and collecting cars and buying businesses, this game is for you. Or you could play Monopoly. If you want exciting combat, forget it. You do get to drive boats and fly planes, which is cool.
The main character is ultra violent and there is no way not to abuse people when stealing cars, etc. Little old ladies get treated as badly as other gang members. Not subtle at all. It is a disappointing game, developed by junior high boys who don't have cars or girlfriends. One day they'll get cars.

I've played to level forty so I can't say it's no fun at all. It's unrealistic in that there are brutes, men who eat steriods three meals a day, who appear to make the gang fights cartoonish and stupid. It's juevenille in it's attitude toward women and sex, although some reviews say it's mature. Being unfit for kids doesn't make it mature.
The driving is fun and the cars handle well. The flying isn't fun because the aircraft are slow and the controls sloppy. The boats are okay, but their is a serious glitch that makes them stutter and almost stall at certain times. Any basic test of the game would have shown that, but they decided to leave it in.
Any time you injure another gang member or cop, you are chased and attacked relentlessly. They always know where you are. Two cops zoom up in a car and you quickly shoot them and then run down alleys and back roads, steal five cars and race accross town. They are right behind you all the way, every single time. There is no subtlety at all. Some cars are very fast and some trucks are slow. Bad guys in a slow truck always keep right behind a fast car. Always.
If you try being a sniper, the people and cars in the distance disappear - another glitch.
You can buy property which earns money. In a town the size of San Fransisco you can buy maybe fifty stores, because fake computer stores are just too expensive to put all over the place. You can go into your stores, but not the other 99% of the buildings. You only earn money by jumping through the game's hoops. I can't swear to it, but I think that you don't earn what your supposed to, due to the game developers being so bad a math and, well, computer stuff.
You can destroy vehicles and kill people, but don't try shooting out a store window because you can't. There are ten year old games in which you can, but not this one. Also tough gang members can't push chairs out of the way or get over a street curb without jumping.
This game has some fun, but it's basically stupid.

If you mis f zero than buy this. It has master controls, awesome art style, awesome hover cars, customization, lots of diff modes and tracks, so much to do. Also it has a doable trophy list if your wondering. No insane ones anyway. 5 stars

With the 3ds and it's weird joystick controls it's kinda hard at 1st but once you get the hang of it this is by far the best 2d metroid ever made. Only reason it's not a five star is because it's not on the switch.

High very high hopes for this game. However it’s very ugly, poor controls, and is very short! Lasts about 3-4 hours, 7-10 if you want 100% complete. If Sega had delayed it for a few months I think this would of been a real gem.
Why make an arcade version then lock out 30$ worth of characters? Was very annoyed that I didn’t get the complete package. Needs to say that on the box.
Animations are a bit stiff but the gameplay is spot on and reminds me of ps1 fighting games. Plenty to to off or online.
It’s great. Only needs 2 things, rumble and the ability to wake up the switch.
If your a fan of ps2 era wrestling games buy it.

Halo Wars is a great real-time strategy game.  I don't care much for the Halo series of games, but I love RTS and there's not many of them for console platforms.  There's good variety created by the six different leaders to play as.  The campaign is great fun to play co-op.  One complaint I have is in the multiplayer ranking system.  It's based on experience points not wins so consequently there's less incentive to work as a team and no disincentives for people quitting early which gets annoying.  Overall though, great game.

I'm so disappointed in this game.  I loved the first Force Unleashed so you know my standards aren't that high to begin with.  All they had to do was make a follow up simple action game in the Star Wars universe and they blew it.  The game seems to drag on forever because even though it's about 12 levels, it's actually 4 huge levels sliced up into smaller pieces so after the 3rd level in the same environment I was just sick of it, then suddenly the game was over and I thought "Really?  I thought I was only half way through this insanely boring and repetitive game.  How could it be over?"  It's so sad how infrequently you get to do something fun like dash through hordes of storm troopers force pushing and throwing them off ledges and stuff like that.  Instead they replaced all the fun from the first one with non-stop mini-boss fights with quick time events over and over and over, maybe the dumbest thing I've ever seen in an action game.  It's a decent story at least, but it's pretty terrible when the best thing about the game is the story scenes between the actual game.

This is one of the best campaigns I've ever played.  Wonderful story, immersive experience, beautiful scenery.  Everything an action game should be.  The multiplayer is fun although doesn't keep me entertained for very long mainly because there's not enough co-op missions and the free-for-all gets monotonous.

This game is just amazing.  It builds on the prior two in the series.  The story draws me in and the environment is immersive.  It adds to its predecessors by having an awesome multiplayer of cat and mouse type games than can be played free for all or in teams.

I was able to play this game for free just for context.  If I had paid more than $5 I would've felt ripped off.  At first it's relaxing and enjoyable.  The environment is beautiful, the combat is simple, the story draws me in... I'm having fun.  After that first hour or so it goes downhill.  The NPC interactions are the dumbest I've ever seen.  The main story is good, but really short, and every side quest feels like like pointless grinding.  To make the grinding worse, the navigation is really frustrating.  There's no minimap and the menu map is useless.  There's a line to follow to your objective which frequently glitches out for no apparent reason.  The ending feels anticlimactic.  There's no replay value.  The co-op is pointless because it's just one person joining another person's game grinding away at the same campaign.  There's also a stupid butler constantly reminding you that there's DLC to buy.  On the bright side, the environment is really beautiful.

This is the saddest disappointment in video gaming history for me. The Battlefield series is the greatest first person shooter experience without a doubt. The Battlefield 4 installment is another great creative achievement in terms of game play, map design, and graphics quality. This is in contrast with EA's epic failure yet again at the basics that I take for granted with other games. The game crashes every few rounds. This is so frustrating that I may just give up for now and try again in a couple months and maybe they'll have patched it by then. The origin client is annoying as it takes over my web browser and changes setting that I have to change back later. Basic menu navigation is confusing, although a minor issue in the grand scheme. Why do I hold on to the foolish hope that EA will learn from past failures and do a better job? Probably because aside from these issues, every game in the Battlefield series, including this one, is amazing.

Update: I'm upping my rating because it seems that the issue with the game crashing has gotten much better. Now it only happens about 1 in 10 rounds instead of 2 in 3 like during the first week. There's a couple more good points. The commander mode has returned, although not quite as good as BF2. You can call in UAVs, cruise missiles, and gunship support; but can't zoom in on the map to spot individual enemies and there's no means for special ops to take out the enemy commander's abilities. The sea warfare is much improved with powerful patrol boats and choppy waves in inclement weather. The destructible environment is great, as advertised, really changing some levels as buildings come down. The graphics are amazing, especially the different optics in vehicles. In short, the game produces an incredible immersive experience, just still a little glitchy with the crashing.

2nd update: One more problem, the game doesn't support my logitech joystick. I read forums with many other people having problems with this. It's calibrated correctly and I was able to test it in another game. I read that there's a couple of complicated workarounds like binding the joystick to keyboard inputs or editing a file certain BF4 file. I may try this eventually, but it's really annoying. Just one more failure on EA's part. On the bright side, the game hasn't crashed on me in quite a while.

Yes, we've all learned to set our expectations low after Modern Warfare 3 and Black Ops 2. Despite that, CoD Ghosts still manages to disappoint.

The pros:
1) As usual with CoD, the basic game mechanics (e.g. shooting, movement) just work right and this shouldn't be discounted, especially when so many other games fail in this area. The game froze a couple of times in the first week, but I think it's a good first week success rate, especially compared to another modern day shooter that was just released.
2) Quick scoping, the dumbest feature to plague past CoD games, is finally gone. I hear that it's not impossible, but it's weakened to the point that I haven't seen anyone using it.

The cons:
1) The maps are stupidly large for 12 person games. This makes it way too convenient for camping.
2) The spawn system is broken. Despite the large maps, I still find myself spawning right next to enemies.
3) It's just not that much fun. I know it sounds like a terribly subjective thing to put on a review, but I don't know how else to say it. It's probably the disappointment of playing this game and wondering why they can't just reproduce the immense fun of earlier CoD games. So I think it's a legitimate criteria that compared to older games this is less fun, so why waste the money. I already did, but I'm definitely not buying the premium package.

The multiplayer is fun, but not really impressive. The most interesting aspect is that it's built around 2 person fire teams. Good level design, lots of cool weapon attachments to unlock. One stupid thing is that when you're killed, your killer lights up with a silhouette visible through walls to facilitate revenge.

The single player campaign is complete garbage. I'm not even sure I can finish it. There's bugs I haven't seen in a while like enemies glitching in and out of cover, spawning in my field of vision, stuff like that.

I liked this controller but the newer ones with the audio jack that allow for third party headsets are way better. If you're wanting to buy a new Xbox One controller get a newer one, it's worth the money.

Comparing it to the original xbox 360 controller however: It takes everything that was good about the 360 controller and improves upon it. It's light weight and micro-usb compatible.

As a fan of Majora's Mask for the Nintendo 64 this remake only takes the base-game and improves upon it. The graphics overhaul is great and the entire game plays fantastically. There's always something to do and the world is very vibrant and alive.

So much game for so little! I'm sure the base game was fun enough but Saints Row IV with all this DLC was just a blast to play. NEGATIVES:

-On the first couple levels, enemies sometimes pop out right in front of you or behind you without even shooting.

-Enemies sometimes run around chaotically without direction.

-Team AI is mediocre throughout the game, you'll be killing the vast majority of the enemies.

-Enemies always yell. You'll always know that enemies are in the area because you'll hear them yelling slogans such as "F*** you GI" & "This is my country" in a stero-typical asian accent.

This happens WAY too much throughout the game.

-Some Enemies take too many hits. 5 bullets from an M-60 or any other gun should be more than enough to put down any VC or NVA soldier but not in this game.

-Directions for completing tasks are too brief. On about every other level, it seems like there are parts where you get stuck because the directions were too brief & you don't know what to do.

-Holding down the B-button to heal your wounds gets really annoying & hurts your thumb. (the developers should have made it so you just press it, not hold it down)

I've died sooo many deaths because of this annoyance!

-Long loading times

-No rewards for beating the game (no cheats, videos, nothing?)

POSITIVES:

-Guns (plenty of awesome firepower)

-Gameplay (for the most part it's usually real good)

-Some levels actually make you feel like your in Nam

-The gun turret parts of the game are really good. You'll be shooting out of a huey & some other helicopter.

-Most levels are well designed

-There are usually enough checkpoints in missions

-The story line is actually decent

-Graphics are pretty good

-Sound is also pretty good

Men of Valor is a good game but it also has it's share of annoyances which can hinder game play.

The main two annoyances being that you have to hold down the B-button when ever you get shot & that enemies take too much damage (usually in the 2nd half of the game)

Over all I would give the game a 7 out of 10.

It would have been nice if there were more game modes for single player.

I picked my copy up for $20 and it was worth it.

I wouldn't have paid more than $25 for it though.

Replay value isn't very high.

I was a huge fan of the first Brother's in Arms (Road to Hill 30) and this sequel (Earned in Blood) lives up to the original and surpasses it!

First, let me get the negatives out of the way...

1. There are some sound issues when firing the weapons. Occasionally in the heat of battle, there will be a delay in sound when firing your weapons. This only occured a few times when I played through the game. (probably like 4 or 5 times....it's no biggy)

2. There is also some slow down (with the frame rate I think), usually when there's a lot of enemies and guns firing all at once. This is probably the most annoying problem in the game but it's not bad enough to affect my score. This problem occured about 6 or 7 times when playing through the game and it only lasts a few seconds....so it's no biggy either.

3. The squad mates aren't as funny in this sequel. No conversations to laugh at :(

Now, the positives...

1. The level design is better and the levels feel bigger

2. The Battles! (The battles this time around are more action packed and feel like actual battles)

3. Better A.I. (The enemies will try to flank you when ever they get the chance and this makes for better, more realistic battles)

4. More of a challenge (the difficulty level has definitely moved up a notch, probably as a result of better enemy A.I. and the inclusion of more enemy tanks and armored vehicles in this game. The germans also use a new artillery gun, the 88mm.)

5. More weapons (there's a little new sub machine gun, "The Greaser" and some other new german gun which the fallshrimjager carry. One version of that gun has a scope and the other version doesn't.

6. More vehicles (the germans can now attack you with half-tracks and even more tanks this time around. One level I went through had 4 enemy tanks! There are even horses in another level. You also get to control a new tank yourself, nick named the "Wolverine."

7. New Skirmish mode adds to the replay value. The skirmish mode objectives are pretty tough and were definitely a challenge for me...even on the easy difficulty setting.

In the skirmish mode, you can also play as the germans which is a cool bonus.

Earned In Blood meets my expectations and surpasses the first game, Road To Hill 30. The 2 glitchy technical problems I mentioned before are forgiveable and don't occur too often, so other than that the game is just about perfect!

If you liked the first Brother's in Arms, then this game is a definite must have.

ORIGINAL REVIEW
There isn't much I can say about this game except that it is incredibly buggy.
Constant game freezes, music glitches, and other bugs have thus far prevented me from actually playing through the game.
Having searched on google, I know there are many others who have experienced these same problems.
I am pretty shocked because I usually expect high quality from Sony, but this time they really dropped the ball by not properly bug testing their game before releasing it. The downloadable patch didn't seem to help with the bugs either. God of War III looks like it would be a fun game, too bad I can't actually play it!

I hope to return this soon and get my money back.
And Sony needs to devote more resources toward quality control in the future.

UPDATED REVIEW
Ok, so I received a different copy of the game after sending the buggy one back and it seems to work fine.
GOW 3 is an incredible game, especially visually. The boss battles and puzzles are truly the highlight of this game.
The main portion of the game, fighting off regular enemies you encounter, does get a bit redundant after a while.
I might play through this game once again, but I doubt I will more than twice. It's one of those games that once you play through the first time you've seen pretty much everything there is to see.

All in all a good game, though I think the series is slightly overrated.

If you're a fan of the Splinter Cell series then you'll probably want to get this. I just finished playing through the first Splinter Cell, and it looked fantastic! Consider that this game was made almost 10 years ago. To my eyes the lighting effects have received a real boost, while the graphics look noticeably better than the old PS2 version I used to play. I'm not sure what some of the reviewers are talking about when they say this isn't in HD. It certainly is on my TV! Granted, the game is old and you can only do so much with visual remastering, so those who were expecting PS3 quality visuals have the bar set a bit too high. Thus far I have not noticed any visual glitches in these games, though some reviewers reported minor choppiness or frame rate issues. The only real downside I noticed, as mentioned by others, is that the cut scenes were not remastered. For me this isn't a major concern because the amazing gameplay is still intact, and that was the main point for me buying this trilogy. Don't really care for online play, so its absence isn't missed by me. Quality wise, I'd say this trilogy is right up there with the remastered ports of God of War I and II on PS3, both of which I also own.

4.5 out of 5.

Not much needs to be said about Metal Gear Solid 2 or 3. They're both amazing games and are in their best form yet with this HD upgrade. I don't regret paying $49.99 to play these two games once again, they're that good!

The major downside to this trilogy would definitely have to be Peace Walker. I just don't "get" this game. It doesn't feel like a Metal Gear Solid game, there really isn't any stealth involved at all, you can't crawl, the menu system is overly complicated and poorly thought out. Enemy A.I. is rather poor too, except when you go up against the enemy vehicles, which replace the boss fights from previous MGS games, and that was another poorly thought out concept! The boss fights were always a staple in the MGS series, and these vehicle fights in Peace Walker don't match up. Although it is cool to face enemy tanks and armored vehicles, these confrontations should not have replaced the boss fights. MGS isn't MGS without boss fights!

Thus far I've managed to play through roughly 5 hours of Peace Walker but I don't plan on completing it because it just didn't hold my interest. As expected, 2 and 3 are fantastic and are still worth the full price of admission.

I never thought I would ever say this about a GTA game, but GTA V gets boring fairly quickly after you've beaten the main story missions. There isn't really anything new in GTA V that hasn't already been done in prior editions. In fact, compared to GTA: San Andreas, GTA V is actually lacking in some areas. The graphics and environment are more realistic and aesthetically pleasing, but other aspects of the game hamper it's replayability, namely the ridiculously zealous police who have near super-human ability and spawn new police helicopters every 5 seconds. Other negative aspects include some of the game physics and vehicle handling. And once again, an almost total lack of building interiors severely limits the scope of the game. There's a casino and race track but they aren't available as properties and no casino games can be played, why not? Why are most of the hobbies and activities incredibly lame? Tennis, golf, and darts, that's it? Why not skate boarding, surfing, hang-gliding, etc?

The main story missions are great for the most part, but it seems like Rockstar is really dropping the ball. GTA 4 and 5 still don't come close to matching the greatness of GTA: San Andreas.

This is probably the best video game I've played in quite a few years.There's not much more I can add to the other great reviews already out there. I'll just say that this game nails down all of its aspects with perfection. The story line is always interesting, the game play is always fun, the environment is a depressingly beautiful post-apocalyptic world, the voice acting is perfect, the cut scenes excellent, etc. The only thing one might find disappointing is the somewhat dark ending, depending on how you look at it. On a positive note, the ending does open the door for a sequel, so let's hope we do get at least one sequel out of this franchise.
