Every year when a Lego game comes out, I rent it and think "You know, this'll be a nice little breezy platformer in a market saturated with war shooters. It'll be a nice escape, and I'll be able to plow through the trophies." And every year when I actually do it, I tell myself, "I'm never playing another Lego game ever again if it's the last thing I do." Yet here I am, again, just having survived the grip of what is Lego Marvel Super Heroes.

The storyline is pretty basic - kind of a mishmash of a lot of the recognized stories from the popular Marvel movies (And the Fantastic Four sequel, but at least they got Galactus right). There's some characters and nods to things that never made it into the films, but not enough for any fanboys to really care. And that's good because games like the Batman Arkham series seem to throw in a little bit too many of those references. It's a bit of a nice balance.

So I basically plowed through the story mode in the spare time I had after work within two days. that brought me to about 20% game completion with having maybe one game freeze. I'm willing to believe that every Lego game I've ever played has been wrought with glitches and game freezes that, with one title, rendered the game unplayable (When I played Lego Indiana Jones 2 on X360, the game froze during an autosave and corrupted my save file, erasing my over 50% completed game). While trying to complete this game 100%:

- One night, I came home and started playing and not within five minutes of playing, the game froze. Right when I had finished one of the many tedious races throughout the game.

- I had markers that had shown up on my game map for items that weren't even there. I had collected two character tokens from the map after completing puzzles, but they remained on my map as if I never received them. This happened after several saves and exits. It wasn't until I was done with the game entirely that they disappeared. A "Stan Lee in Peril" icon appeared on the S.H.I.E.L.D. ship right from the start of the game until I rescued the 50th Stan Lee from that exact location. He hadn't been there up until the end of the game. This lead to me blasting apart the room in hopes of finding him hidden somewhere just to find out I wasted my time. (This also happened when I was playing Lego Harry Potter Years 5-7.)

- As far as glitches in the game outside of map abnormalities and freezing goes, twice did I have to restart a level because the computer AI had broken the game. One level (Near the end of it too), I had to reassemble a group of maybe five characters into an elevator which then took me up to the boss battle (I believe it was with Green Goblin at Doom's hideout). I made sure I collected all the studs I could and, I don't know what happened, but all the AI characters piled into the elevator, the people shifted, and for some reason my feet weren't hitting the buttons that made the elevator work. I tried moving and nothing happened - all I could shake was the camera. I tried punching my way out, nothing. I tried letting it sit and figure itself out, nothing. I had to restart the level from the beginning. Similar incident happened when I was minikit hunting in an underwater level. Jean Grey provided an air bubble that would follow as I walked, making travel underwater not only slow and annoying, but limited by whatever Jean decided to do since I couldn't control her. A sand portal for sandman, where he could just slip in and end up wherever the exit was, was on the ocean floor and lead to a vent system with a minikit inside. I went in there with Sandman, and Jean Grey started walking towards the rock near the vent to try and follow my movements, bringing the air dome with her. I came back out onto the ocean floor, but she was still trying to walk back to where I was, running against a flat wall in the game. I tried hitting her to break her bubble and respawn her, nothing. Tried taking control of her, nothing. Tried going back in and out, nothing. Running circles around her, nothing. That too was right at the end of the level. Even the game is trying to stop you from playing it.

- Button mapping remains a problem. While doing some of the flying races as Iron Man, I was constantly thrown off track due to a poor controller scheme. When driving a car, you can hit R1 to boost, a little factoid they tell you during the loading screen. When flying with a person, like Iron Man, you hit X to lift off the ground, hold X to ascend, hold O to descend, and tap X twice to boost. This lead to me in the middle of a race flying towards a hoop, holding X to go a little higher, not being high enough, holding X again and being BLASTED YARDS AWAY FROM THE HOOP I WANTED TO FLY THROUGH. Why not just make the boost button R1? It's not doing anything! It literally does nothing during flight! I could understand if pressing it made me do a barrel roll or something important, but as it stands it's a dead button with the other functions mapped poorly.

- The Lego games are starting to stagnate. What worked with the Lego Star Wars title has been cut and copied across several other franchises with one or two things added to make it seem new. In Star Wars, Legos could be manipulated with the force. In Lego Indiana Jones, I think they gave that same power to "mystical" characters. In Lego Batman, it was mind control. In Lego Harry Potter, it was the same power of anyone using magic. In Lego Lord of the Rings, it's sorcery. In this, it's telekinesis. I just ended up labeling in my mind the basic Lego game crap - which character blows up silver objects, which character can manipulate blue or purple Legos, which character can melt gold bricks, which character can dig. It's all the same junk reskinned. There was even a few Whac-a-Mole missions I played that I remember being ripped straight from Lego Harry Potter, creature and all. It also contains the obligatory "Reach [x] amount of studs" hidden level in which you play through a more realistic looking Lego sets ("Realistic" meaning you could actually build it at home if you have enough pieces) and smash everything until you get a certain amount of studs. In Lego Star Wars, this was hard, because the level required you to smash exactly everything with nothing missed. In this, I still had some stuff I could've kicked, and I remember the last two games doing the same thing. I somewhat miss the challenge, but altogether I wonder who finds that level fun?

- Another game of Lego characters talking, another game of me getting sick of their dialogue. One mission, while playing in Story Mode (So I couldn't swap out the character), Tony Stark kept walking around his house saying, "Tony Stark: Genius Billionaire Playboy Philanthropist". Over and over and over, almost every twenty seconds or so. I miss the simplicity of the older Lego games, because without having the characters say any words, they expressed so much more and it made the game even more timeless and cute. In this one, they have Nick Fury making pop culture Samuel L. Jackson references. Rating is E 10+ - I wouldn't really expect a lot of kids to know his speech from Pulp Fiction to understand why he screams out "And you will know that I am the DJ when I lay my beats upon you!" It felt somewhat tacky to me, and really out of place in the game.

I left this game, not feeling happy or nostalgic to playing with Legos or reminiscing over great Marvel characters. I left being angry at how years of making these games that they still can't manage to fix basic problems and it seems like the glitchiness just keeps piling up. Then the extra side missions were just so tedious and not very useful.

There's a small saving grace to it. 1.) If the game worked good, it would be an excellent game. As it stands, you would be better off playing Lego Batman 2: DC Super Heroes. Yes, it's one of the newer ones where they talk and it does have its share of problems, but they're not as bad as this title. I remember somewhat enjoying that one, even after being turned off by the characters talking. 2.) Deadpool is hilarious. Any mission you start with a Deadpool intro is worth the time to watch, and his third wall jokes about the downfalls of the game helped me cope with my frustrations with its poor design. At one point, he sarcastically remarks that you're doing a fetch quest for him because "the developers ran out of ideas." He remarks that you were only able to find the item he was missing because a trail of studs walks you right over to exactly where they will be. It was a nice touch to the game and really my fondest memory I'm walking away from it with.

That and I made Iron Man ride a lion. Which was adorable.

To anyone with kids looking to get this title, if you played one Lego game, you've played them all (With the exception of Lego Rock Band, which is actually a solid Rock Band title and I can't recommend enough that you purchase it, especially since it's so cheap these days). Want a Super-Hero, open world game? Get Lego Batman 2. It did it better, it kept it neater, and this thing is a hot mess. To adults looking to play it to unwind, skip it. Don't punish yourself anymore. You don't need to keep playing Lego games just because they keep making them. Buy a real Lego set - it might get frustrating, but it will be so much better for your sanity. To Marvel fanboys looking to buy this - doesn't really matter what I say, because you're still going to get it even if it's only to keep sealed and locked away in a curio cabinet of memorabilia.

I stand at my two stars, and I can't recommend purchasing a copy, no matter who you are.

I really like TellTale Games. I love their Sam & Max entries, their Walking Dead seasons and The Wolf Among Us. I even recently played Puzzle Agent by them and really enjoyed it. They're usually a fun throw back to PC adventure games with either challenging puzzles or deep narratives whose outcomes you control, making their gameplay a unique experience. TellTale Games aren't really so much games as they are interactive stories, and something about that works amazingly well.

But not in this entry.

I really wanted to like this one. I love Jurassic Park (The first movie anyway. I read the books but that was years ago and I don't really remember all that much). Some of it feels so much like the movies that you can kind of tell that they picked up visual cues directly from them - the camera pans, some of the shots of the dinos, etc. As a visual reference, it works pretty well. But gameplay, especially when stacked up against another TellTale series, there's not much to be had.

So story first - it's pretty standard. A group of survivors left after the events of the first Jurassic Park movie are still on the island and need to be rescued, while another group has snuck their way onto the island to retrieve the embryos Nedry was supposed to grab but was unable to. The park's vet ends up saving one of these intruders only to be held hostage while another group of mercenary forces is sent via helicopter to air lift them out. How the game tells the story is another issue. In past and future titles, usually you control one character unless something bad has happened to that character. In The Walking Dead, you control Lee (Until the end and the start of the second season when you control Clementine). In The Wolf Among Us, you're Bigby Wolf. In Sam & Max, you're Sam and usually only play as Max if Sam is indisposed. In Back to the Future, you play as Marty. In this game, you randomly shift between characters it seems. At one point, I found myself controlling the speech branches for the park vet's daughter, and then suddenly I was controlling the speech branches for one of the mercenaries. Some parts of the game transition that fairly well, making you choose different camera angles and such to speak as another character, but there's some times when no effort is put into distinguishing that at all and it makes for a very clumsy narrative.

As far as gameplay, there really isn't any. You normally can't even "move" your character - you can only shift the camera to find things in the landscape to examine and if needed the character will move to that item for closer inspection. Unlike their newer games, there's no element of choice either. In newer titles like Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us, the decisions you make change the outcome of your characters. You can decide who lives and who dies, who is a friend and who is an enemy, and ultimately it changes the ending you receive upon completing the game. Now, older titles like Sam & Max and Back to the Future didn't have this feature either, and that's fine, but they still had some puzzles to solve here and there and there was trial and error between some of it. The gameplay element was still there so the story could kind of take a little bit of a backseat. This one... the only gameplay you really get is a series of quick-time events. (For the uninitiated, a quick-time event [QTE] is when the game will set up a cutscene to deliver more story, only the cutscene will launch into button commands for you to enter on the controller that if missed could lead to a lower score or a "Game Over". The main cause of death in this game is if you didn't press down when the game told you to.) That's the closest thing to any gameplay you receive - being told to press buttons when they randomly pop up across the screen.

To be fair, Walking Dead also did incorporate some quick-time elements into the game, but some of it at least felt avoidable. This gets to be almost like a guided version of Dragon's Lair where if you don't have amazingly quick reflexes or don't know what's coming up, you're dead. It's not the game is hard because of this - it's actually pretty easy - but it's just not any fun and there's nothing really that keeps me invested in the story.

Also, the look of the game is strange. Now that TellTale has been doing more games like Walking Dead and Game of Thrones (Haven't played that one personally because I'm not a big fan of the show), it seems like their art department has been getting much better at being a little bit more realistic. The Jurassic Park game is in this weird limbo for its art direction. Now, if you play their Back To The Future game, that one looks a little bit like this. The characters are a little cartoony, maybe even kind of goofy looking. For Back to the Future, that works. That story had some very light-hearted themes and some honestly goofy moments where being a little cartoonish in its style gave it a bit more punch. This one looks like they tried to make it a bit more realistic than that, and the dinosaurs look fantastic in that regard - don't get me wrong - but the people look a little goofy. They did kind of change the molds from BTTF but it still isn't quite up to the level they're at today and it really takes away from the sort of story the game is trying to tell.

This game is really only going to appeal to people who are really, really into Jurassic Park or who enjoy QTEs. Other than that, this title is kind of bland. I really had hoped for more from it. I remember it being announced and I was excited that TellTale was getting these sort of license deals after I had loved them off of Sam & Max alone. (Oh, they also did a Strong Bad game ala Homestar Runner that was pretty funny and charming. Didn't even think about that until now.) I had been really excited to see where they took this series, but it ended up not really doing anything for me. I look forward to the ongoing future of TellTale Games, but this is definitely a dark mark in an otherwise outstanding record.

I wanna start off by saying I'd recommend this game. I haven't beaten it yet as I've only been able to play it while a friend of mine has doctor appointments, but I feel like I have a very good sense of the game and where it's going. I also haven't played the original Resistance games for PS3 or the one for PSP though I do own them. I would say for the right price, this is a fun title to have for your PSVita.

Why only three stars then? Mostly technical stuff that I can't look past. I'll still play the game, but it's a bit away from a better rating.

First of all, the gameplay - totally linear. Game leads you down a path, you shoot some bad guys, maybe have a boss. It's also done in a weird campaign/not-a-campaign style? I'm not wildly familiar with a campaign element in a game, the closest I've had is with Left 4 Dead where each campaign was playable separately and you could attack any of them in whatever sequence you preferred.This one is brought about in these vignettes where part of the story will close and you'll be treated to a short cutscene where a politician or a news anchor will tell you the situation in the city, how Chimera are everywhere and forces have been employed to combat it, that humans will prevail, etc. Then it cuts you back in the game. Here's a weird thing though - I watched through a cutscene, and then an in-game cinematic leading up to the next part of the game and then I turned my game off. A couple days later, I load the game back up, and I have to sit through the whole pre-rendered cutscene and the in-game cinematic I already watched, totaling I'd like to say about 8 minutes of wasted time I could've spent picking up where I left off. I didn't even get to the next cutscene, but I got pretty far and had to turn my system off again. When I loaded my save that time, I ONCE AGAIN had to watch that pre-rendered cutscene but thankfully after was transported to the part of the game I left off at. I have a feeling anytime there's a cutscene with somebody explaining the situation, it's most likely just a cover-up for the game trying to load its assets and levels, making it seem like you're instantly able to play when in reality you're not. I honestly don't care, I would stare at a progress bar rather than have to watch these same clips over and over anytime I load the game. It makes it feel like before every cutscene, you're being readied for the next "campaign", and with how the game tries to tell its story, the whole campaign system seems a little bit out of its element here.

About the linear qualities of the game I was talking about earlier, that was more so just a warning and not necessarily anything that works against it. A lot of Vita "Versions" of major console games I've played have been the same story, the biggest example coming to mind is Batman: Arkham Origins Blackgate. It's not a bad game, but it definitely sets you in one direction (Though Batman does let you choose in which order). And even that is fun. It reminds me a little bit of rail shooters like House of the Dead, the major difference in this being you do have some free range of your environments where in those games the camera just moves you along into the next room where you have to shoot people. The weapons are fun as well and their little bonuses are great, but the specialty ammo that makes the guns unique and fun is kind of hard to come by. Not to mention that a lot of the secondary functions of your rifles involve interactions with your touch screen, and every so often I'd find myself accidentally brushing against the screen with my thumb and almost sending out a grenade (A few times actually wasting special ammo like that). I gotta give them credit for trying to take advantage of the Vita's touch screen, but it doesn't really give any positive boosts to the game.

The story is interesting though. The actual game look is pretty good. Instructions are a little laxed - I found myself with only a vague idea how to fight at a boss battle only to figure it out and afterwards look it up online to see several people who had the same frustration. The game didn't really communicate well how to take out some of the enemies, but that's fine. Still not really a deal breaker as it was only temporarily frustrating. (If it helps, I've also been playing it on Normal mode, out of the three difficulties of Casual, Normal, and Expert. Those may not be the exact wording in the game for them, but you get what I mean. The game is probably much easier on Casual.) As far as instructions, anytime you pick up a new weapon it plays a small video showing exactly how its special attack works, and that was really helpful.

Another control critique is that there is a "sprint" button to get out of hot situations, but it's for some reason the Down button on the D-Pad? I could understand at least making it the Up button, but it feels very bizarre having it default to being the down button. I haven't really checked to see if there's anyway to change that, and for all I know the Up button might do something in the game later that makes perfect sense - I certainly haven't been using it for much else so far.

Those cutscenes, though - they just pull you out of it. And for some reason, they also look TERRIBLE. Like, it's not like they had a bad art department or anything, it still looks reasonable for the time being, the art looks fine, the animations that play are also good for what they need to convey - but the actual video quality of the cutscenes is ridiculously bad. On some of the scenes I watched, color lines and warping will happen at the top and bottom of the screen. If it's supposed to do that for added effect, it certainly doesn't look like it is, and it doesn't make much sense either way. The color lines and warping make the scenes look almost like they were converted digitally from VHS. There's no other way to describe it, and that makes no sense because this all seems to be happening in 1951. If anything, the scenes should be jumping and skipping, slowing down here and there to imitate a faulty reel projector. Not to mention that these scenes are heavily compressed to where scene of solid color stand out to be artifacted bricks blocking their way in around the illustrations of the scene. Each of those scenes (Before it heads into an in-game cinematic) can't be much more than four minutes. Would encoding these files which are mostly animation in a codec that could've at least been 720p HD without much artifacts present really take up all that much space? I can't imagine it being more than a few MBs.

From what I've played, for an under $20 title, it's a good buy. Would I have payed the full $40 or whatever the original retail price of it was? Hell no. But it's a fun, arcade-y kind of first person shooter and it deserves some love. You should definitely have it in your Vita collection, but don't expect it to be a new favorite. In fact, you might want to buy another game with it just to soften the blow.

I've been a fan of Ninja Turtles for some time now. Granted, I didn't follow them into their newest cartoon incarnation on Nickelodeon (Which this game is based off of - I'm not against it, I've heard great things, I just haven't been interested), and I absolutely hated the recent movie (That older CGI movie TMNT made more sense, and watching the new one has made me really appreciate that one more). Still, I love the concept - teenage turtles using jiujitsu to fight evil aliens and mutants as the unknown protectors of New York. (They're in New York, right? I can't remember if that was ever heavily established anywhere but the movies.) All the while making jokes, having fun, skateboarding, etc. Good times.

This game is reminds you of everything great about Ninja Turtles and delivers on none of it.

The attitudes are all right. The story is okay, I suppose. Common video game practice of "go here, fight a boss, go somewhere else," and the game is set-up like a 3D-modeled 2D sidescrolling platformer, which is what I grew up on and still enjoy playing. But something's off about how it handles. There are several enemies, mostly floating bots with spikes or lasers, that can often get you in a position where you absolutely cannot defend yourself, leaving you open to get hit, occasionally for multiple times. The turtles can seem to do basic attacks forward and sometimes a little bit upward (A boss glitched out and I managed to beat him like that), but there's no diagonal attacks, and sometimes the jump kicks and double jumps don't seem to activate. I tried with multiple controllers and with plugging my controller in - about 20% of the time, something didn't connect when I was pressing the buttons. The same goes for a smoke bomb feature. You're supposed to use it to get around laser barriers by activating the smoke bomb while pressing the direction you're trying to pass. Problem is that several times, it seems to ignore what direction I'm heading. I stopped controlling with the analog stick and moved solely to the D-Pad to make sure it wasn't me just accidentally nudging myself in the wrong direction, but while pressing forward, I'd either be teleported backwards or upwards when I was trying to go forward. I've played through the game twice now - I can say for certain I know how to handle it. It's just the game messing up. Not to mention that when you first get the smoke bombs, you're only allotted to carry three so if you mess up on two of them, you're gonna have to keep spam killing mousers until they FINALLY give you some more smoke bombs. Which has taken me as long as five minutes before. There were also several points where after fighting some enemies up close and then trying to run, my character would simply run in place, letting other enemies with lasers free to shoot me before I could reach them to take them down. Not to mention there being some stuff thrown into the mechanics that is just kind of tricky to get 100% in general. A dash technique is required to break through some windows as well as tight spaces, yet many times when trying to break into those windows, since they're such a small gap, I'll either land above or below the window on the side of the building to where I'll need to double jump again and stick the shot perfectly. More than once, I've tried to break through a window and I'll only be off by a sliver so that in the game I can see and hear glass breaking but my character is still hugging the side of the building. Not to mention that you have basically one button for attack. X is your jump, square is attack, triangle is block, and circle is special item. There's these moves called Shell-kickers you can execute by pressing square three times and then an angle. Sometimes, I'll forget about the angles and just end up pressing square three times, often ducking and attacking or jumping, to where for some reason my character will stop moving and twirl their weapon for about five seconds, leaving me open to attacks I can't block. I think I've been able to break this when it happens by pressing down or up or even triangle, but it happens before I even realize it and then I take damage. What is that move in the game for anyway if it doesn't do anything? Just to punish you if you're not performing Shell-kickers? It's ridiculous.

[EDIT: I'd also like to mention something that I think is a little bit of deceitful advertising. On the back of the box, it shows you driving one of their vehicles - I don't know what it's called, but it looks like a tri-wheel motorcycle with a large shell on top. The truth is that you don't really get to technically drive those at all. Near the very end of the game (When you come back from Dimension X) you unlock that bike as well as a small helicopter. Both of them are merely things you walk over to, press up and X, and then it shows you in them riding to a previous or upcoming part of the map that, honestly, wasn't all that far of a trip, making it a very useless gadget that I barely utilized. Even when I tried to use it, I still ended up way off my mark as they only go to two set places in a cutscene that lasts about eight seconds. Not even any skateboards or sewer surfing in this game. Kinda mad about that.]

The challenge in this game isn't really from its enemies. The bosses are all about the same - just quickly dodge attacks and spam moves or shurikens when you can, cycling turtles for larger health bars. (There is one enemy I had to look up how to kill because I unloaded something like 60 shurikens, countless punches and several health bars to kill it only to find that you need to just kick it two or three times in the head and he's down.) Shredder at the end is even simpler, the bigger challenging being the Foot Clan bots he spawns during battle. Then again, there's a trophy in this game for beating it in under an hour, so I feel like it's designed to be a throwback to the old NES games people like to speedrun. On top of that, the viewing angles suck. So many times I've had to drop down or wall jump up into an unseen area only to have an enemy standing right above/below me where I take a hit, and in the instance of going up, have to start my crawl up all over again and hope I'm luckier as there's no way to scope the area out in advance.

In fact, paying tribute to the NES days seems very vividly apparent from the start of the game. At the start screen, you're treated to a picture of the turtles in a pose that looked very familiar to me - them standing on a large yellow-lighted base, posed in somewhat of a diamond formation fighting Foot bots. The pose is pretty much parallel to the cover art for the old Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles game by Ultra for NES. Then, to add to this homage, in one area of the map, you find yourself underwater briefly, and in the water is what looks like a bomb tied to a small monitor. I don't believe you can interact with it, but down to shapes displayed on the monitor, it is directly lifted from the same TMNT NES game mentioned before in an underwater level where you had to disable bombs on a dam while surrounded by electrified seaweed. Almost had an anxiety attack thinking about the stress of that level from my childhood. The thing is though, that game they're honoring, memorable as it was, was not very good and isn't all that fondly remembered. At least not as much as the Arcade Game (Ported to NES as Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game) or the later Arcade/SNES/XBLA game Turtles in Time. That original NES game was known for having unfair expectations, horrible controls, and a lot of scenarios where the only way to advance was to exploit the game's faults. It's not necessarily a classic of the system or even the best Ninja Turtle video game.

I take it I'm not the only one who was intensely frustrated with this game though. Not only did I find a co-worker who had played it and both him and his kid sincerely hated it, but PlayStation's new trophy rarity rankings show it too. Starting the game by talking to Master Splinter gives you a trophy that on PSN is labeled "Common" by all players who have played the game. EVERY story-related trophy after that one is marked in the category of either "Very" or "Ultra Rare." Like I said, the game isn't even that hard to fight - the main problem is a lot of the backtracking. When your turtle's life bar runs out, you don't "die", but are rather "captured" (Which I think is another tribute to the NES game by Ultra). At that point, you have to find the turtle you lost in a rescue room, labeled with an R on the map. At first, you find out where they're hidden based on blind luck. Pretty soon in the game you get an upgrade that puts a green pinpoint on your map of where a captured turtle was taken, even if you haven't discovered that rescue room yet (The map only shows you what a room is after you've walked inside it). Now, with that mechanic, I would think that the first three rescue rooms closest to me that I find should have a turtle, or the closest ones to where they were captured. Nope. Nope, they're randomly thrown all over the map. I lost all my turtles in Dimension X at one point (See point earlier where I talked about an enemy I didn't know I had to kick in the head.), and when I spawned, my main character was in a rescue room in the middle of the map underground in the sewers. My second turtle was over in an above ground building on the west side of the map in a room I hadn't found yet. My third turtle was in the sewers to the east but still a bit of maze to get to from where I was, and the fourth and final turtle was in a room at the very top of the TCRI building, so I had to backtrack basically through every room of the game I had already played (And by the way, as soon as you leave and re-enter, all enemies except for bosses respawn exactly where they were. So that enemy that killed me in Dimension X? If I kill him, leave the room, and immediately come back - he's there again. It's all random too. I died and ended up in a R room in Dimension X and I didn't want to be there, so my best course of action was to step out and let an enemy kill me again so I'd end up somewhere else. I'm pretty sure it's random, or at least it's a series of alternating patterns, all of which make you traverse the entire game over. Not to mention that if you lose all your turtles, when you come back as the last one you played, you still NEED to get the other three back. It is the most unfair crap I've ever witnessed and just makes me really feel like it's the designers trying to pad out the game by making you kill the same arrangement of enemies in room after room over and over again to kill time and make it seem like you got the full money out of the original MSRP price of $39.99 (I know it's cheaper now, or at least here it is, but this thing doesn't play any different than a $15 download game off the network, and after experiencing it, I think even that's too much. I would really be surprised if the game's assets on the disc even broke 1GB in size).

The rest of it looks sloppy and unfinished, or maybe it's just more of a brilliant homage to older NES games. In every in-game, non-prerendered cutscene, characters mouths aren't even trying to be in synch with their dialog. The mouths just movie up and down as if they're saying "MEP MEP MEP MEP MEP MEP MEP." (YouTube it. Tiger Claw and Leatherhead's appearances stood out the most to me.) A couple levels have some platforms in the background that looked like they could be jumped on in the foreground and weren't, while the reverse of items in the foreground looking like untouchable items in the background were also there.

The game is just unpolished, unresponsive, and worst of all, it isn't fun. It's more of a chore to complete if anything, and the rarity of all the story related trophies is a testament to that. I don't understand how this game has seen so many positive reviews here, as at the time of writing this, it has a about four solid stars. Don't get me wrong, it had potential, but it was all mucked up so horribly. Do not buy this game. Do not waste your time. If you're insanely curious, well, hopefully you have the resources to rent it, but otherwise owning this will be just a gross waste of your money. You would be better off hunting down an NES copy of The Arcade Game and reliving the days when TMNT games were at least fun.

I rented this today... and beat it today. So let me explain how this game works.

This game takes place after the new movie, while not giving us any details of plot from the new movie outside of things shown in the trailers or knowing that the girls saved the city. While they're in Washington getting commended or something, These four other Ghostbusters (I don't know if they establish that they're at a franchise location or the 2016's movie location) when not fawning over the new Ghostbusters achievements take it upon themselves to solve a string of mysterious incidents in New York.

First off, I just want to state that I have absolutely no problem with GB2016. I want to give it a chance, I'm gonna see it when it comes out, my feelings about this game do not come from a place of misplaced hate. However, the story in this game has nothing much to do with anything. It feels like it's based off of a cheap Saturday morning cartoon show rather than a summer blockbuster movie. The line up is two men (One skinny, one big and bearded), two women (One white, one black). None of them have any personality outside of making ghost puns and slime jokes and mentioning how they're good at science. That's all you really need to know about anything this game passes off as story. There's one animated cutscene and throughout the rest of the game, all you get is solid frame "phone calls" (But it has a video monitor, so you know who's calling and because... science?). Then when you beat it, you get... another animated cutscene just to show them celebrating.

The game handles as a top-down shooter/dungeon crawler with twin-stick controls. Move with one stick, aim your weapon with the other. Each character has a special weapon and their proton wand. I chose the girl that had twin proton pistols, but I did notice the big guy has a proton minigun? Most of the enemies require that you wear them down with your special weapon, (You can use your proton wand, I suppose, but it's much easier the other way) and then weaken them with the wand before trapping them. Unless they're just a filler enemy, in which case they simply disappear. There's maybe 20 enemy types in the game I think, there's a gallery showing them all, but in reality there's maybe four - your disposable enemies (Usually flaming skulls or flying books or candles, etc.), zombies (There's three, I think, different zombies, but they all go down fairly easy and move roughly the same way), your minibosses (Usually need to be trapped, take more than two hits to kill, sometimes make you plug away at them for five minutes), and then your bosses (Bigger ghosts, usually have both other tiers of ghosts spawning for them to add difficulty in the form of annoyance), Your PKE meter makes some of the bosses/minibosses appear but in order to find secrets, I just kept it on all the times when I wasn't shooting, which makes you move sooooo slooooow. Also, your weapons don't have ammo, but they do have a cooldown timer. The more often you shoot them, the more heat that builds up. If you don't press the button that relieves the heat, your weapon overheats and is useless for about ten seconds or so.

Every level is the same and incredibly long. There's no level map so you can never see how far you've progressed to the end of the world, but there is a button you can hold to give you a guide to see which path you're supposed to be taking. The guide is helpful because you can also use it to find secret areas, such as if you're in a room that has an open door or a large part of the room that the guide arrow avoids, chances are there's "secrets" there, usually in the form of another ghost fight or more ecto to collect.

You level up your characters by collecting ecto, which gives you upgrade points to where you can make your character more powerful supposedly. I never really noticed much of a difference outside of the "trap mini-game multiplier" that I maxed out and noticed a SLIIIIIGHT difference.

The reason why you shouldn't play this game are as follows:

1.) It's So Tedious and Boring: With every level feeling the exact same, and almost every level having two parts to them that took me about 44 minutes each to explore them the first time, this game is a waste of time. Especially since...

2.) It's Expensive For What You're Getting: As of writing this, Amazon has already marked the game on sale (Maybe it's a Prime thing, but it's showing up $43 or so for me) and the game literally JUST came out. Video games hardly ever go on sale that quickly unless something is really wrong with them. Otherwise, in most other stores, this is a $50 title and it feels like it should have been a $15 download if not even cheaper.

3.) It Barely Has Anything To Do With The New or Old Movie: Outside of the name and weapons, the old movie is completely absent in this game, and the new one is mentioned passively. They are called to bust the ghost "Gertrude" in this mansion, and Gertrude is the ghost shown in the trailers vomiting ectoplasm onto Kristin Wiig. To which the characters say "Not even Erin and Abby could take her down!" Then you go into a sewer because a certain class of apparition was spotted, which, according to one of the Ghostbusters without seeing it, is "just like the one the girls encountered at the concert!" (In the trailers, it shows Patty [Leslie Jones] at a concert with a large gargoyle-like ghost perched on her shoulders.) Sure enough, it's the same ghost as shown in the trailers. Then the last boss is Rowan, which... I've heard a spoiler about that, and his end boss appearance makes no sense because of it. Which is why this would work better in the context of a stupid Saturday morning show, where you can defeat the enemy one day and have him back next week.

4.) It's Painfully Unfunny: I only laughed at some of the dialogue because of how absurd and unfunny it was. And some of it you hear so often. Like a character saying "Oops, you got some slime in your nose!" Like... Do children even find that funny? Because I'd like to give them more credit than that.

5.) For a Next Gen Game, It Looks Terrible: With a such a simple setup and execution, I wouldn't expect frame stuttering and awkward in-level scenes to get glitched up so bad. The PS3/X360 "Ghostbusters: The Video Game" looked better than this. I believe there was even another top-down shooter on those consoles called "Sanctum of Slime" which not only played better (It wasn't great, but it was better) but also looked better.

6.) Even If You're a Trophy Hunter, Forget It: If you're going after the trophies, you're going to need not only a lot of patience but also four controllers. I'll admit, I've played some games just to earn an easy platinum trophy. I beat the game and still don't have 1 character maxed out to level 20, let alone all 4, and I only have one PS4 controller, so to get that trophy would cost me $180 or so.

7.) You Shouldn't Support Junk Like This Anyway: I rented it out of genuine curiosity without seeing any footage, pictures, or trailers. I thought maybe it'd be cheaply produced but still enjoyable. It's not. It looks like it was thrown together last minute, possibly cobbled together off some other game that was repurposed and traded in other villains for Ghostbusters ghosts (For at least three boss fights). You could get a much better game. If you buy stuff like this, it only tells the companies that people will buy this cheaply made stuff at high dollar prices.

No matter what you think about the new Ghostbusters movie or how you feel about the old one, there's nothing for you in this game. Maybe there's a kid out there who likes it, but with its nearly an hour long levels and lack of familiarity, I think it's gonna be something they play once and then forget to trade in until it's practically worthless (more so than usual) at GameStop and such. Keep your money. If you're truly curious, rent it but only do one night. You won't need much more.

I also have some petty gripes with the game:
- the font they use for the menus and loading screens is terrible and looks like something in a party invite template for Microsoft Word.
- To start the game, I had to agree to a massive EULA agreement. I've never had to agree to one of those in a game that didn't have an online mode, and a lot of it had talk about microtransactions. It's like they expected this game to be one thing and ended up compromising and released something utterly different altogether, but kept the same EULA box. It's weird and off-putting.
- The main menu only plays Ray Parker Jr.'s "Ghostbusters." Over and over and over and over and over and over and over...

So, by all means, go see the new Ghostbusters. Looks like it's getting okay reviews, that's good. Just don't play this game. You don't need to, you'll be fine. Nobody else has to play this worthless game. Unless of course you just like throwing your money out the window.

Bought this on clearance in store. For six bucks, I feel like I got my money's worth. It's not terrible, it's just not anything great. It's a tower defense game, which is usually a game you can play strategically, but they pull the strategy away as you can command turrets and heroes yourself, turning it into a third person war shooter. I will also say, my game never froze, but it takes FOREVER to start up the first time you play it. The screen just kept saying "Saving" for maybe a solid five minutes. It's kind of a mess of a somewhat okay idea, but overall not really one I'd recommend rushing out to play.

As a tie-in game, I didn't expect much. And that's pretty much what I got, though I feel there was potential to do so much more with it given the game's assets, and it speaks to the laziness of most movie/television tie-in games.

On the positive side, the game's character models look pretty great. The locations, the people, their facial expressions taken right from the cartoon - even things like Lemongrab's walk cycle is perfectly done in this 3D environment. Being a game based on a cartoon, it shouldn't have to look like a state-of-the-art shooter with realistic detail, but Adventure Time certainly is a hard cartoon to narrow down to one distinctive style. Without making the game crazy and misshapen, it finds a nice balance in the way it looks. On top of that, the cartoon's voice cast is here, and a good deal of the character interactions feel authentic and pulled directly from the show.

Then there's the negatives about the game.

While the story feels like an episode of the show, there's some parts that seem to commit the cardinal sin of almost every tie-in game - endlessly bringing up details from the source material to remind you of other adventures. I don't remember some of the later season episodes all that well of the show, so I don't necessarily remember who Pillowmint Butler is, but even the line of dialogue or two explaining the last time the duo had to deal with him did nothing for me. Even the stuff I do remember didn't add to the story when they explained it. Odds are the people, mostly children, playing this game are paying attention to the show, and with the nature of Adventure Time being kind of fast and loose, even if they don't remember a character being established, I feel like that would work to the game's benefit. The callbacks get so tiresome sometimes. LSP wants to be a singer. Okay, that sounds in tune with her character. Every time you set it up for her to sing, she's still singing the "These Lumps" song from one of the Graybel episodes. You couldn't just make up one or two other lyrics? Most of it isn't even put to music so what's it matter if it's an established song or not?

Then there's just the fixed camera angles and the poor animation. For as good as the character models look, their mouths are never synched with their dialogue. They just flap up and down, or sometimes not at all. I'm also not entirely sure if the run cycle was any faster than the walk cycle, after constantly switching back and forth, I'm not sure if I was moving any faster.

Another positive is I didn't run into all that many glitches. There might have been some slight clipping (Items going through other items), but it wasn't all that noticeable, and then I did break the game at one point by walking into a room before I was supposed to in the last episode. Didn't experience any other freezes though, so overall the play was fairly solid.

There's also not much replayability, and if you're a trophy hunter, it's going to be very annoying if you're not paying attention or following a guide. I didn't realize there was a trophy for finding all the snails until the second act or so of the first episode, so I missed one, maybe two, snails, so I didn't get a trophy for it. You can't replay episodes by themselves, and you have to get all the snails in one playthrough, so to get that one trophy I was missing, I had to replay the game from the start all over again, and being a dialogue-heavy game, I would've really appreciated a button that would've let me skip the speaking portions... which there is not. So it took a few hours just to unlock one more trophy.

For kids though, they'll probably still dig it. It's not really action packed and all the combat sections are exactly the same, but the humor that makes the show great is here and there's a nice quaintness about it. If they like the show, they'll like it enough. It's not all that hard to beat in a day or two, so I don't know if kids will find all that much satisfaction in playing through it more than once. There's also one DLC level available for it, which considering that this game came out as a full-retail release (It's much cheaper now, but when it came out it was $60 or so) I feel like one $5 level would've been better as just an included portion of the game.

It's not the most offensive tie-in game, it's not the worst, but it's not the best and its charm only goes so far. For a $20, it's okay, but you might find yourself reselling it soon after.

I really wanted to like this. I picked it up on Black Friday for $15 and for this version of "America's Favorite Game Shows," I feel like that's all you should pay for a title like this - not a cent more.

Let me get into positives first:

- Wheel of Fortune is actually challenging and gives you long term goals, things you can keep unlocking, the more you play the game. I played it until I had all the trophies, but if there's a game I'd go back and play, it'd be that one.

- There's online play, which is nice to have, but I'll go deeper into that later.

- Jeopardy will let you customize the categories of your game before you play it, so if you only want pop culture questions, no academia, you can do that.

- I imagine if you have kids (I don't), this could be a fun game to play with them if you set up a family game night.

Now, onto everything wrong with it:

Unlike the vastly superior Wheel of Fortune and Jeopardy games that were made for the PS3 by THQ, Ubisoft did not manage to get Alex Trebek, Vanna White, or Pat Sajak's likenesses or voices for these games. Wheel of Fortune at least tried to make it look like the show, but just gave you some generic looking hosts who look nothing like the actual hosts of the game. They also even have some quips they share, but there's only three or so to share so they get old very fast (Like when you solve a puzzle and the host comes up to you and says something like "To be honest, I didn't know how you were gonna pull through that one." Once, I'd find it charming. To hear it twice every game, I got extremely annoyed.

Meanwhile, Jeopardy is just a floating series of screens hosted by the disembodied voice of some woman who never introduces herself. A nitpick I have with her is that they only have her read topics, not answers, and they didn't even seem to record her saying "Player 1/2/3." At the end of every level, it'll say something like "In the lead, we have..." and not even say who it is - it'll just show their avatar.

Wheel of Fortune's controls are also a little janky. There's a strength hold, for if you want to spin the wheel harder (hold X for a stronger spin), but it's hard to gauge. I felt like even when I wasn't holding down for even a second, it was still releasing on a pretty strong spin. Also, there's a contestant customizer, but it's not very diverse. There's basically four guys you can choose from, then you can just change their outfits. One of the shirts you could unlock was a yellow plaid flannel, so I did that, put some glasses on him, and wanted to make him bald so he looked like Anthony Fantano. No bald hair option.

AI competition varies in both games. Wheel of Fortune has random looking AI characters that play against you, but you can at least choose their difficulty from Easy, Medium, and Hard. Hard not only gives harder puzzles, but the AI will be way more correct most of the time, while on easy, they'll just keep asking if there's any Z's in the puzzle. Meanwhile, Jeopardy has no difficulty setting and you always play the same two AI people, Patricia and Robert. They never answer as quick as you can, and they're wrong about half the time. Also Jeopardy, unlike past versions, in this iteration is three answer multiple choice which makes it MUCH easier. Especially if the AI character guesses and chooses wrong. Several questions I would buzz in on and make guesses just based on what sounded right, and usually I was right. Not to mention that with about six puzzles a game in Wheel of Fortune, I don't think I ever saw the same puzzle twice, but I saw a lot of the same categories pop up on Jeopardy. It got to the point where I knew how to clear out entire categories without knowing hardly anything and the topics outside of the game. Not to mention that some of the categories are just insanely easy to begin with.

I believe both games have online play, though I never tried Wheel of Fortune, mainly because I had such a bad experience with Jeopardy. Jeopardy's online play is SO AWFUL. First of all, the Jeopardy game apparently was released digitally sometime in September. This collection was released in October. In December now, barely anyone is playing the game. I never was connected to a classic or quick play game when I searched for one, and when I made my own lobby, I spent forever trying to get someone to join, waiting for forty minutes at one point. Even then, could only find the one person. I spent over an hour in a ranked match lobby trying to get three people. Then when you actually get to play it, the online mode has TERRIBLE lag. In a local game, when I buzz in, it's immediate. I feel it answering right when I meant to answer. In online, I'll hit the button, but the countdown will still keep going for a whole second or more, and THEN it'll say I hit it, or sometimes tell me the other person hit it first and I'll just have to take their word for it as I have no way of checking. Then, say someone leaves during or after the game and you choose to play another round. I was in an online game with another player, and after it, he left. I hit Play Again and another round started up with two AI players. However, the lag was still there. I was still in online mode, even though I had no online competition. My statistics in the game still counted it as a game played online. There's a trophy I got for ten online matches played, and I probably only played four with another actual person.

If you're looking for the challenge that comes with watching Jeopardy on TV, this game is either going to disappoint you or make you feel incredibly smart. At the same time, if you're a child, this game might be right at your skill level. So maybe parents with children will get more out of this game than I did, but I thought that this was the worst Jeopardy I ever played, and a fairly mediocre Wheel of Fortune. The cheaper you can pick this up for, the better.

I had actually purchased this in 2010, but forgot whether or not it was good since I didnt write a review on it. So I played it again. This is not a game that I will play a again. The tombstone puzzles were ok for the first 2-3, but having to piece together ALL tombstones (and there is a lot of them) was just plain ridiculous. On top of that, you had to find four of the same image on each tombstone (such as a pickaxe or bottle). Those were very hard to see.

In order to go to a new building, you had to complete a tombstone. When you go to a building, you need to find 3 flies outside so you can get a hint. Then you have to open the door with the key that you get from each tombstone. Then complete the HOS in order to get the next bag of tombstone pieces. This is the same routine for every single house and every single tombstone. That is the entire game. You dont go walking around from area to area either.

The graphics were "ok", def not the best. The sound/music was good. The HO scenes were ridiculous. Many of the items you cannot even see because it is stuff in a dark part of the area or blends in too much with other objects. Example would be a black bowtie. In one of the HO scenes, that was finally found on an object that was also black. Had to use a hint for that. Some of the house had one extra room where you had to find differences in 2 photos. The photos are all black, white, and tan. Very hard to even see the differences. If you exit the scene before finishing HOS or matching, you had to start the whole scene over. You are only given 2 hints in the beginning, and then once they are used, you have to find 3 flies outside buildings to get 1 hint. If you use the hint in the HOS, it takes 2 long minutes to refill to get 1 hint. So basically you walk in the building with 1, and for the most part walk out with 0 and have to search for flies at the next building. Pretty screwed up way of getting hints and reloading hints.

No adventure or "real" puzzles in this game. Piecing together the tombstone which is much like a jigsaw puzzle is the only type you do in this game. I dont recommend this game. Boring.

Let me start by saying I've never played a Souls game. I'm currently on bed rest so, seeing all the hype surrounding this game, and needing a break from FF Type-0, I downloaded Bloodborne from PSN.

I spent a lot of time in character customization (this is something that I didn't know about until someone posted a screenshot. I thought you were just a game generated generic Hunter!) making my Huntress look properly ruthless then Sat excitedly with the controller in hands as the game loaded...and loaded. Like other reviews said load times are long but oddly enough I don't mind them in this game. The reason? It gives me time to plan out my strategy after I die. Which, as everyone knows, you do. A LOT. There's supposed to be a patch dropping to "fix" the loading.

Once I got into the game I realized there's no tutorial. Or rather, there's no tutorial like we're used to seeing in most games. Pretty much your tutorial is dying and learning from your mistakes. Obviously I'm not a fast learner since it took me forever to figure out certain things but once I did I gave myself a fist bump and kept it moving. Bloodborne doesn't allow pats on the back.

I could gush over the environment but what could I say that others haven't? It's properly atmospheric where you never know what's going to pop up around the corner or be lurking in that dark alleyway waiting for the right moment to hack you to pieces. And I get the sick thrill of coming back, finding the S.O.B who slaughtered me and recovering my Blood Echos.

Fighting is face paced, the weapons/clothing look amazing and I can feel the difference in how each weapon handles. There's always plenty of blood vials to replenish your health. Leveling up is pretty straight forward once you realize you can.

Honestly I'm having fun. Have I wanted to toss my controller? Sure, but what gamer hasn't wanted to do that in other games? I find myself muttering to myself a lot more and a steady stream of curses are banging around in my head but, in the few hours I've played, less than ten I believe, I haven't wanted to give up. Bloodborne is about exploring, about learning from your mistakes, about using the environment to your advantage.

I knew Bloodborne was supposedly hard going in. I just didn't realize how hard...or how rewarded I would feel when I FINALLY saw a trophy pop. It takes my mind off the pain. Bed rest? Who has time for that? I have prey to slaughter!

I read an interview with Sam Raimi that said this game is intended to be a fourth insallment in the series.  It is a total success there. If you are a fan of the movie, get the game. During one of my many ventures to my local game store a year and a half ago, I came across a game called "Syphon Filter". Intrigued, I went ahead and bought it, popped it in my Psone, and to this day, it is one of the best games I have ever played. I have beat the 1st, 2nd and 3rd, and am on my second "pass" through the series. I will then give the "Omega Strain" a go on my PS2 once I am finished with SF3. While I have read no so favorable reviews on OS, I think it would be fair to at least give it a try.

You are "Gabe" Logan, a special operative for a super secret government orginization aptly named "The Agency". Your mission is to find a dangerous chemical stolen by terrorists from a lab and stop them before they destroy the world. You are remotely partnered with Lian Xing, another agent who guides you through your missions and later on in the game is in action on the ground.

You are gradually given an arsenal of weapons as each level moves forward. Among them are: There is the Silenced 9mm handgun, the .45 handgun, the G-18 Pistol-machine Gun, , the HK-5 Pistol Machine Gun, the Shotgun, the Combat Shotgun, the PK-102 Assault Rifle, the M-16 Assault Rifle, and the K3G4 Assault Rifle just to name a few.

In each mission based level, you must accomplish a variety of objectives, and eliminate a tough boss at different intervals. You will use stealth at times, or just face enemies head on. The interesting part about this game is that it really draws you in, and takes some interesting twists and turns as it progresses.

As for gameplay, it is fantastic and addicting. While the levels are challenging and tough at times, they are not overly frustrating or extremely hard. Some levels and missions are easy, and others will take a few times to get through. It will be a bit of a challenge if you play this for the first time, but you won't become overwhelmed as in similar games. As you play it a second and third time,though, you will become familiar with the layout of the levels and more or less breeze through. As an example, I was able to shoot down the chopper on the base tower after 5 tries, as opposed to 30 attempts during my first run through the game over a year ago. You will also attain some "tricks" along the way as well, such as becoming more effective at headshots and so on. I have found that it's the "little" things that get you through this game.

As for game layout and graphics, excellent, IMO for 1999 PS1. Great voice animations and camera angles as well.

While there are many new games out, especially in the wake of the XBOX 360 and PSP releases, I still encourage you to give this masterpiece a try. You won't be disappointed.
