The PS5 is a good system, not great. I own both this and the Series X and I can say that overall the SX is superior as far as interface speed, slightly faster loading times and better graphics on almost all backwards compatibility games. They don't look bad on PS5, games like AC Origins, Odyssey, Crash 4 etc. And they have a nice clarity to them. But they really lack certain textures and the color gamut is very pale in comparison. imo. Now when you're talking exclusives (from PS4) PS5 is the way to go, all the PS4 titles look amazing as they did on PS4/Pro. I think most of these games have received special "treatment" other 3rd party titles have not. And Sony just have the worlds best exclusives bar none.

But until actual titles made just for the PS5 are released, and not for the PS4/Pro. I can't recommend it. Because once you play these games you sit and go, well, now what? So I'd recommend holding onto your pro, since these are scarce anyway, and just wait. The same can be said for the Xbox Series X, but then again games pass just kills it, tons of free games, and if you're more of a 3rd party title person. it's just a no brainer. So the hype isn't that real about the PS5, it is a "good" system, but I think in the future it will be great!! Also all the problems people say they've had or are having with this, I'm not experiencing any. Super quiet, cool and not a single glitch.

Why you may ask, well basically the only reason I've ever owned a Playstation, which I do like a lot is for it's amazing exclusives. No one can argue with it having the best! That being said the PS5 is nothing more than a glorified PS4 Pro, which i own and I'll keep until they don't support it anymore. Speaking of Pros here are the Pros and Cons of the Xbox Series, vs the PS5 and why it's much better imo.

Pros.
12 Teraflops as opposed to 10 tf in the PS5, many think this doesn't make a difference but for overall bandwith and graphical abilities it does make a difference.

Game Pass is just a no brainer, along with my near 300 digital game collection I get over 100 that are free, with a small subscription which blows PS Now out of the water, because it's mostly all streaming (games) anyway.

The graphical differences on PS4 exclusives using backwards compatibility on the PS5 is pathetic compared to the Xbox Series X. The XSX uses better texture filtering, 16x antiostropic filtering on ALL games, including enhancements from the Xbox One X (which is still a great console). So games look better, more colorful and the enhanced games just look out of this world. I tried many on the PS5 I had for a short time and could barely tell any differences. Also it uses Ps4 Pro code for all of it's games. In that case not raising the resolution at ALL on many titles. Which most had hoped for.

You get 3 generations of backwards compatibility on the Series X, which I thought might not be that great and I would want new games, but it's a blast just to test them out to see how much better they look and play. Until Next gen only games arrive. Also speaking of which. The new Sony Exclusives (about 90%) will be on the PS4/Pro as well as Ps5. So what's the point?

So overall the XSX just feels more premium, and looks a lot better. The PS5 is this hideous looking abomination that looks like some new building they just built in Dubai. It would be okay as a decorative piece like a vase or something. But I literally couldn't even stand to look at it sitting with my other consoles. It was immense. No I don't hate playstation but the Ps5 is by far the worst console I think they've ever made. And this could possibly be the best console Xbox/Microsoft ever make. And possibly the last, from what rumors say. So do yourself a favor, don't listen to the hype for PS5, and at this point don't bother. Wait a few years.

Also with the XSX, just like the Xbox One, you can hook up ANY size external HDD to store games (an SSD external is needed to play the enhanced games) but that's no big deal Since the transfer from Ex to SSD is very very fast. With PS5 there are all sorts of issues with storage messing up, not working at all, rebuilding the database etc. Also I think the max is an 8tb hdd, also you can't use it for Media, MKV's, AVI's and such nearly as much as you can on the XSX. Which I also use for Netflix, Primes, Pluto TV, listening to MP3's and downloaded movie files etc.

A couple things I don't like about the Series X, which are very few, is that the controller feels very cheap. The buttons smash in to easily, and it feels as if it could break after long periods of play. I really like the 360 controller (best ever made) and the original Xbox One controller. Which is compatible with the XSX, so if something goes wrong you can always use an old one. And sometimes it does have trouble syncing up right form the start, but that's easily rectified by hitting the button on the console.

Lastly the console is whisper quiet, no issues to speak of. The PS5 I had, did seem a little quirky but not really bad, but I think more people have problems with it, and it does run much hotter. And I noticed the XSX SSD is slightly faster than the PS5's, which i found strange, but awesome at the same time. So I think this time MS may get back the crown they lost after the flop of the XB1. Which they deserve because the 360 was hands down the best console they ever had. Now it looks like the XSX is on it's way up. Maybe even the Series S will help, but imo get this, it's powerful, quiet, nice to look at and will definitely stand the test of time. Very future proof indeed. ENJOY!

I remember debating on whether or not to drop $500 on this back in 2017 when it was getting ready to come out. I decided to get one then and was "slightly" impressed but not overly so. The graphical differences and amount of enhanced games just wasn't there "yet". But once I started seeing the DF videos and what this thing could do and watching comparison videos I was hooked. Played it on a regular Sony 1080p TV for a long time and it looked incredible compared to everything else. With the exception of many Playstation 4 Exclusives which imo no one can come close to. But I use the One X as a 3rd party gaming device and 4K player anyway.

I tried the Series X several times but just can't/couldn't get into the the huge bulky design and it standing up right beside my entertainment center all of the time. And putting it down on it's side just looked plain stupid. Also the differences are miniscule graphically with not much difference in resolution overall. Actually the One X at 4K 30fps runs at slightly higher resolutions at times when the Series X is pushing (trying) to hit 4K 60fps. Though the One X does run some games at 60fps, which are the ones I like. Also on the One X you don't HAVE to play enhanced games at 60fps, you can have the choice. Most S/X games are locked at 60fps. I don't care much for playing AC Origins, Odyssey, Tomb Raider etc at a higher framerate as the aiming accuracy decreases in most 3rd person games. And it's just not necessary. If you're a young person playing COD, Fortnite, PUBG and so on, then the Series X is right up your alley.

I like the design better on the One X, the 4K player seems faster and more stable (not sure why), the 2.1 HDMI isn't compatible with my Sony TV, since it only does 60hz anyway. So no benefit there. And does it really matter if the UI is in 4K? Nah. Also the vapor cooling in the One X (nothing new) is very good and quiet, at least I can hear it and know the fan it working. I don't mind the Series X super silent fan, but I would like to know it's doing its job once and a while. Also I've heard a few horror stories it may be silent but deadly (for the system) at times. ha. And as I said games are basically the same, just lower FPS. And there are NO games out to warrant the purchase of a next gen console as of now imo. And what is out, just well, isn't very good. I think it will be quite a few more years before we get anything to really take advantage of the Series X, so the One X is awesome for me.

Also I like the 1X controller better as it feels more solid overall, and the d-pad is much better. Clicky/noisy, but better. Lastly you can fit quite a few more games on the One X because the games are smaller size and not ALL over 70 to 130gb. A few big ones here and there, but the optimized S/X game sizes are just ridiculous. And with the One X you don't HAVE to have a proprietary drive to run any of your games. So yep, great system, never had any problems with the ones I've had. So I'm good. Also the price is better and it has a much more powerful GPU that the Series S. And I haven't seen any games that "struggle" unless it's from poor optimization. Cyberpunk, anyone? Later.

I wasn't sure what to expect from Infrogames Atari division with their Splashdown release. Much to my suprize, Splashdown is a highly addictive, blast to play. The control is precise, the water effects are amazing, and the racing is very challenging. (It is hard to win, even on easy mode.) The soundtrack has a few good, recognizable songs including Smash Mouth's All-Star. The trick system is somewhat easy to pull off, and as you will find out in the later levels of the game, if you don't pull off tricks, you will not win a race. This really adds to the challenge and replay of the game.
Overall, is this the best looking game on the PS2? No. Does it matter? Not at all!!! The gameplay is so much fun, you will wonder why you didn't quit reading these reviews sooner, and just buyed the game.
Bottomline... Splashdown is a very fun game, and it is the best jetski game for the PS2. If you liked Wave Race 64 on the N64, or Jet Moto on the Playstation, you will love Splashdown.
BUY THIS GAME!!!

Devil May Cry is a little bit Resident Evil, A little bit Castlevania, a little bit of Soul Reaver and a dash of Dynasty Warriors thrown in for good measure. What it all adds up is an excellent action game that you will keep playing for days.
The graphics in Devil May Cry are excellent and the dark setting gives the game an eerie and spooky feel to it. The gameplay is pretty action paced, and upon building your power up, there are a lot of cool attacks that can be performed on the enemies that you face.
Devil May Cry is also quite challenging, and sometimes a tad frustrating as you can only save your progress when you make it to the end of a level. I found that it played a little like a Role Playing Game at times, as I found myself building up my power so that I could go in well armed for when I faced the next boss.
Overall, I enjoyed this game a lot, even during the frustrating periods, it made me pick up the controller and try harder each time I played it. If you are looking for a very fun, action-adventure game with excellent graphics, Devil May Cry is the game for you.
This game will likely appeal to those who like the Resident Evil, Tomb Raider and CastleVania games!! It is definitely one of the best games to hit the PS2 in 2001.
Buy This!!

Jak and Daxter is by far the best Platform game out for any of the next generation systems right now. The gameplay is very similar to that of Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot games. The graphics are excellent, and there is plenty of places to explore, and things to collect. After collecting my first 20 orbs in Jak and Daxter, I must admit that this is one of the coolest games I have played in a while. Wait until you try to get over the lava canyon, or have to catch the fish (you old school gamers may remember the Atari 2600 game Kaboom, its very similar, even though its only for a short time (unless you stink at it ;) )).....this is truly cool stuff!!
The sound is typical Naughty Dog Fair, and doesn't really add to or take away anything from the game. At one point, I could of sworn that it was the same music from Crash Bandicoot.
The saving feature in Jak and Daxter is great, it saves you the frustration of having to restart the level, when you die. This is great because the levels are huge, and it makes the game much easier to play.
Overall, I like this game a lot, its a great looking game, and its a blast to play! I can see Naughty Dog using Jak & Daxter as their next platform game, of which many sequels will be made.

The cinematics are among the best of any PS3 game. Endure the credits for a brief teaser at the end.

The game's environments and music set a slightly eerie mood for the game. The voice acting is top notch - Batman and Joker are the best.

This game ranks in the top ten of my all time favorite video games.
The story telling is good and the twist at the end will catch you totally off guard. I liked the graphic novel style cinematics.
The graphics are spectacular. This game really taps in to the graphics potential of the PS3. The electricity looks very realistic.
The gameplay is solid. I love the freedom of the open world setting. If I want to complete all the side missions before continuing the main storyline...I can. If I would prefer to explore for blast shards and dead drops I have the freedom to do that as well.
The fighting never becomes repetitive or dull. Cole has quite a few spectacular powers. I used them all frequently, never favoring one in particular. The enemy becomes more elite as you progress through the game. So while your powers may have grown, so has the enemies toughness. The boss battles are some of the best I've ever played, and the most fun.
I like the idea of the karma moments. I have only played through as the Hero...but I have spoken to several friends who have played both sides and they have said that the ending is no different regardless of your karma choices. If there has to be a negative about this game, this is it. There is no clear reason why Cole would choose to be evil versus being good. However, Cole's powers are different depending on which karma path you choose.
I highly recommend this game. Any reviewer giving this game low marks is very confused and has a warped fun compass.
High replay value. Buy this game. You will not be disappointed.

Presentation - 10/10

Best PS3 graphics to date. A few oddities here in there but nothing that bogged down the gameplay.

Sound - 10/10
Sound is sound...If I don't get annoyed by the voice acting or an overused phrase I have no complaints. Solid voice acting and sound effects.

Very high replay value. I will be using this game as a benchmark for all future PS3 releases. This game has set the bar high.

If I could give it a 4.5, I would, but alas, Amazon insists on keeping whole stars. Regardless, this game truly blew it out of the water at the time. I fondly look back on playing it in high school and remembering how people who never played games, mostly girls (as I, too, am female), started to get into gaming BECAUSE this game was dictated towards younger, less mature audiences. And, hell, there's Disney characters in it!

The game itself is kind of genius. To combine Squaresoft's popular Final Fantasy characters, new characters of their own such as Sora, Riku (a young Sephiroth look-alike), and Kairi, while ALSO blending in Disney characters seemed destined for failure, but it worked and worked well! Us gamers were overjoyed to see familiar faces, while us Disney dorks jumped for joy upon revisiting our childhood favorites.

The story is centered around a Keyblade master. The Keyblade has chose Sora, our main character, to wield the Keyblade and either save or destroy many worlds. The problem is that some arch-nemesis has begun to let the Darkness and the Heartless seep out into the many worlds of the stars and destroy them. Stars are winking out. Whole worlds are disappearing. Donald and Goofy, two of the more popular Disney characters of all time, join forces with Sora to not only seek out King Mickey, who is attempting to stop the Heartless, while Sora looks for his friends Riku and Kairi after their world disappears. The company must travel from world to world to defeat the Heartless, and seal it with the Keyblade so that the world can be threatened no more.

Each world with the exception of Traverse Town, the first world Sora ends up in, and Destiny Islands, Sora's home world, are Disney worlds. A main gripe is that some of the worlds aren't really what you're going to be expecting. For example, Neverland is hardly Neverland. It's literally Captain Hook's ship and the Clocktower, which, by the way, is in London...not Neverland. The Coliseum, for Herclues' world is just that, a Coliseum, but I do like that there are tournaments you can take part of there so it's forgivable. Understandably, the developers were doing something never done before with a huge blending of games and universes in order to create Kingdom Hearts, and so some of these worlds were not that developed.

Another gripe is that the controls can, at times, be annoying. Jumping onto things is about as erratic as a seizure and many hours were spent overshooting or undershooting targets. While battling, the controls to heal or cast magics can be infuriating as well since it takes a half of a second for an item or a spell to take effect and that can make all of the distance. Why does Sora have to stand still to cast a spell? I just don't get it. BAM!! Sora's dead 'cause he stood still while some nasty boss came flying out of nowhere.

However, this all aside, the game is brilliant. The abilities that are gained, the side-quests, the amount of time spent completing side quests and leveling up are all just so seamless and well thought-out. Summons are a lot of fun, too, since they are Disney characters, too. Though almost all of them are from worlds you don't visit.

The game is easily for all ages. It can be a little hokey for grown adults who aren't into Final Fantasy and Disney, but for kids it's great and for anyone that's into those two categories they'll love to play this.

It's simply a story about not giving up and following your heart and believing in yourself while having fun along the way. All good lessons for us to remember.

To be fair, this game is rather old now, but the in-game graphics are actually still pretty spot on, it's a fun game to play, and was revolutionary for its time. This game inspired more thought towards the Assassins Creed games, and the producers of the game never thought it would be such a hit. However, after the game was played widely and recommended from people who played it to people who did not, they produced more of the Prince of Persia games.

That being said, this is obviously the first of the series, but not the first Prince of Persia game. There were ones that predated it, but aren't worth your spit so don't bother. And they're ancient. However, that is where the death machines come from as it seems highly unlikely that this castle had rotating buzz saws and spiked, spinning columns back in the days of Persian times.

The characters are actually pretty enjoyable. The Prince is an arrogant snot-rag at first, but eventually his snooty, pretentious outlook turns to base sarcasm and then genuine appreciation for the world and people in it, so hey...redemption. His female counterpart-love interest, Farah, is also pretty genuine as she typically talks like an actual person and has a use other than being the "damsel in distress." Both play off of each other well, and once they team up, it's fun to see her helping the Prince.

The gameplay is forgiving, thankfully because of the ability to reverse time, so if the Prince falls an irrevocable death, you can always reverse time and send him careening back up to the ledge he jumped from, safe and sound. And this is super helpful as the majority of the game is puzzle based, attempting to get the Prince to navigate the gigantic palace safely. Only a small amount of the game is actual fighting, and it's pretty repetitive and even gets to be annoying after a certain point.

The story is simple, but intriguing. The Prince must save the world from the sands that have been released from an hourglass by an evil Vizier (I call him Jafar because he looks just like him) who is part of the official governmental party of Farah's homeland. The Prince and her are the only two survivors, other than the Vizier, and they must find the hourglass, return the dagger that started the whole problem to it, and hopefully save the world from being consumed by sand. All the palace workers, guards, creatures, and royalty have been turned into mindless sand beasts keen on killing the Prince and Farah. So, they team up to kick some serious sand.

The ending, for lack of a better term, is pretty lackluster, but again, the developers never intended for it to be such a hit. But with it'\s revolutionary gameplay where the Prince can run up walls, do backflips over sand beasts, and turn back time, the game had a lot going for it.

I am shocked, after nearly ten years after its release, that it is still worthy of a $47 price tag, and that the reviews are so uplifting! The first game was fun, to be sure, but nothing to write home about. This one, the sequel, is not nearly as exciting, and I can't even believe I'm sitting here taking the time to write this.

The story goes that the previous Dark Tower, from the original game, has been destroyed and the evil individual that was there just puffed out of existence. Gnarl, probably the most hilarious part of this game, never gave up searching for a new Overlord, though, and that's where you pick up the story: a cute, tiny, child-Overlord, terrorizing his hometown of Nordberg. You quickly will grow up, become the crummy impersonation of Sauron that we all recognize from the first game, and begin your overlording tasks.

A few things were improved upon from the previous game. Obviously the graphics, though not very notably in game play, the ease of controlling the minion A.I., and that's about it. The storyline is drab. Yes, yes, I understand it's just supposed to be a fun light-hearted game, but does that mean the story has to suffer? Aside from Gnarl's continuous and hilarious commentary, the entertainment factor of this game is at an all time low.

If memory serves me correctly, the original Overlord game was definitely risque with its humor, and this definitely continues to be so, if not more so, in Overlord II.

I don't want to bash it entirely. It's a fun game, has a variety of different puzzles to solve, and ways to approach solving them. The minions are adorable, wear the best hats, and are always a joy to listen to. However, this does not make the basis of a great game. I hardly ever used magic, barely lifted my weapon, and found myself wondering why I was even playing the game. It's easy enough to beat, and really the only frustrating part is when you accidentally set your entire horde of minions on fire or something like that.

If you want something fairly mindless, kind of funny, and if you really like looking at Sauron's backside for 20 hours, go ahead and play it. Otherwise, you may find other things to do with your time...like watch paint dry or washing dishes.

At the time of this review, 2019, the game in questions had been out for five years. It was released right after the first Prince of Persia that kickstarted the time warp trilogy, and frankly isn't exactly the most exciting sequel I've ever played.

The original Prince of Persia game was actually created in 1989, but without the control of time, and it was a pretty crappy game. Fourteen years later, Prince of Persia: Sands of Time came out for PlayStation and it was a hit. The Prince was snarky, arrogant, and sort of adorable while his female sidekick matched him perfectly and wasn't on the screen just to be eye candy. It was a refreshing new take on video games that required the player to puzzle out how to get from one place to another. The Prince is an acrobatic visionary and uses his skills to kick some serious monster butt (rather repeatedly), and avoid hazards like buzzsaws and spikey poles and pits. In addition, he can control time. So, pretty freaking cool.

The sequel, however, is a bit lackluster. It's almost exactly the same game, only no happy, snarky side kick friend and all the women in the game have turned back into eye candy. The only marked improvement was the gameplay itself where the fighting sequences weren't as repetitive, and your abilities expanded. That's not enough, however, to save the game.

The story is alright, at best. The Prince, since he messed around with time, has this shadowy juggernaut after him called the Dahaka. Due to his meddling, the Dahaka wants to consume the Prince and remove him from history. The Prince, of course, doesn't want that to happen. He has lost his snark for an inner brooding that is none-too-fun and the game takes a more angsty approach to the Prince, which is a shame. He works through his emotions by bopping back and forth through the past and the present to keep the Sands of Time from ever being created.

The gameplay, as I said, is better. The combat is smoother, and not as repetitive as the first. The Prince also doesn't consistently say "whoa-oh" at the edge of a fall each time you're within four inches of it. That, alone, has been pleasing. He is controlled easier, and I'm impressed at least in this regard. Though, again, the monsters are rather repetitious, they aren't as annoyingly irritating as in the first game of the trilogy.

The graphics are much the same as the Sands of Time game, and although the landscapes are gorgeous, a newer video gamer will not be impressed by the jagged edges and rough graphics of the Warrior Within. And you only get about three cut scenes away from gameplay during the entire game that effectively attempts to use CGI capabilities.

Overall, not the most impressive game. Fun, yes, and necessary if you want the Prince's storyline, but I wouldn't exalt it into being as groundbreaking as the Sands of Time.

What. A. Piece. Of. Garbage. Look, this game only has 18 ratings on here and most of them are based off of the condition of the game when it arrived upon some unsuspecting, RPG-nuthead's door. I am sure, beyond any doubt, that the CONDITION of the game will be pristine because NOBODY HAS PLAYED IT. And if they have been so foolish enough to play it, I doubt they played it for long...unlike me, the fool, in this scenario.

Let me start by saying I'm a completionist. In other words, I do my damndest to try to do every quest, every side mission, every ounce of the game, if possible. The Last Remnant (The Worst Remnant as my boyfriend and I have come to call it) does not make it easy. Unless you have the guide, which I suckered myself into buying a used copy, you will be wandering around load screens for hours trying to figure out where the side quests are. Even then, the guide is about as useless as toilet paper...wait, considering the Coronavirus crisis now I know exactly what to wipe my ass with; thanks Square Enix! The guide is vague, offers almost no guidance on developing your team of characters, and simply provides advice on where the invisible side quests are and convenient maps (THAT AREN'T ALWAYS ACCURATE, BEE TEE DUBS!). Long story short, I did not complete all the side quests nor did I complete the game. I stopped just shy of the end, and in my frustrations, gave up and watched the ending on YouTube and settled myself in to type this review.

For me to have given up is a loud indicator of just how filled with crap this game has become to me. The gameplay, first of all, is the rockiest thing I've seen since that horrid E.T. game. Maybe that's a bit strong, but I'm aggravated I've spent so much time of my life on this game...so let me have my misery. Each battle will jump and skip and the game can hardly keep up with itself, leaving large swatches of time, cumulatively, where you're waiting for the game to load an outfit... or an action sequence during a battle. With thousands of battles to fight this gets real old real fast. Leveling up in an RPG is tedious as it is, but this? This is downright torture. I would much rather have spent my time drinking a glass shard milkshake than watching the game load the main character's outfit for the 47,000th time. I do enjoy the game's attempt at giving you control of more characters than the average RPG. For example, by the end of the game you can have 18 people making up your little battle-squad, but only a few of them will actually be main characters and you're limited to how many you can have in your group. Still, it's a refreshing new take on turn-based battles, buuuuut...the game attempts to make the battles streamlined with game-chosen actions instead of player-strategic actions. Sounds okay, but it sucks when your five groups (unions) only have four options to choose from and, as a strategic gamer, none of them suit your needs. An example! Your options are: "attack," "use combat arts," "use magic arts," "stay on your toes." What the HELL does "stay on your toes" mean?! Anyway, even though you KNOW you have a healer in that group and you want to heal someone YOU CAN'T! The game didn't give you the option because their HP isn't low enough yet for the game to think it's necessary. After you choose your poorly executed decisions, you're forced to watch your team get eliminated while the game is loading outfits and making useless choices in your stead. And you'd think, oh, well since it's so hands off you can go make yourself a little cup of coffee or something while your characters get eliminated by a giant eyeball in the sky, but nope... the game makes you sit there because you could POSSIBLY hit a button combination when one of your characters is up to bat that'll give you a small, inconsequential boost to your attacks. Yipee... shoot me right the hell now.

The monsters and bosses you fight are incredibly hard, which could also have been a good thing if it wasn't for the game's lag and the handicap of not being able to choose the smartest option in battle. I don't mind a good, hard, you're-gonna-have-to-fight-for-a-long-time-at-this-dude-boss-man-guy. I really don't. Most RPGs have been incredibly "easy" in the last ten years, but a random monster in the woods shouldn't be wiping out your entire team, even with them super strong, like you're nothing. I limped through this game to the very end with my only consolation being that I can take a hammer to the disc when I'm done. That was my motivation, nothing more.

Alright, fine...the gameplay sucks and the battles are a bit too hard. But what of the story? If the story is great, all else can possibly be forgiven. After all, it's the stories we remember the most from RPGs. Yeah, not this one. Several times in the game I wondered what in the world the characters were doing and why and who people were and why, oh why, I was even off doing some mission for a loosely put together plot that seems to have been dreamed up by a bunch of 11-year-olds. It follows the same structure as most RPGs: there's a threat to the world--eliminate the threat. However, for the life of me I couldn't really follow past that point. There was the big baddie who I need to get rid of, sure, but the game attempts to make it very political and involve other side-characters that, in the end, I can't understand why they do what they do. Thanks to everything I've said above, there is, therefore, little connection to the story and the people within and so when someone dies in the storyline or some hardship comes their way I kind of just shrug and hope to all the gods that ever were that I'm a bit closer to the end of this damn game. Which I wasn't. FOR MONTHS. Not very encouraging.

The music is decent, I must say, but not particularly moving; it just wasn't annoying either. Whoever, though, was in charge of the dialogue OUTSIDE of the CGI cut scenes is a genius in hilarity. It's the ONLY redeeming quality worth my attention in this game. Rush, the main character, is a young, naive, male, seemingly ordinary kid and his dialogue matches the personality perfectly. As he meets hundreds of side quest characters, main characters, and the like, his dialogue matches their personalities with ease. The game attempts to be edgy and fun all around but only succeeds in this one aspect. The dialogue falls apart during the CGI scenes and is overly dramatic. It's, clearly, not enough to give this horror show of a game any more than one star. If I could give it a quarter of a star, I would. Sadly, I can't...just like I couldn't choose the right battle options... I'm obviously still not over that. Give me time, and therapy; I'll bounce back.

Overall, the game is a waste of time, money, and effort. I feel particularly bad for the poor people who were forced to work on this. How many hours of THEIR lives did they toil to meet deadlines that were too short only to produce a game that is better used as a skeet for skeet shooting? How many hours of their lives were pumped into a game as pathetically useless as this one? I feel for you, at least in part. I feel cheated and used, drained of my precious life force as if I were a Gelfling in The Dark Crystal. I'm not sure I'll recover, but I can at least take consolation in attaching an M-80 to the disc and blowing it not half to hell, but all the way to hell.

Okay, look, I've been playing Final Fantasy games since I was in middle school, an appalling number of years ago, and they have a VERY comfortable place in my heart of hearts where I love them, they have endeared themselves into my genetic code, and remind me of my childhood. For several decades, FF games and subsequently their players have played and structured these games in much the same fashion. Traditionally, they are turn-based RPGs, there are powerful summons, multitudes of magic, a usually phenomenal storyline overarching multiple side quests and missions that flesh out the world and story even more, and, of course, your main protagonist. However, over the last few years, almost a decade at this point, the world of video games has shifted. Very much gone are the days of turn-based RPGs, which has been gone for a number of years for larger name-brand games, and it seems that many other things are following suit.

FFXV doesn't have traditional summons and magic is more like a concocted (a sometimes irritating process) alchemy grenade that can hurt you and help you. The summons are more like random encounters that you can sometimes chose to use if you happen to see the on-screen prompt. They are powerful, and you have to find them in the world during story or side quest missions, but they are not always readily available, and they often make themselves available during fights you can easily win without their help. Then, suddenly, when you really need a good summon they're nowhere to be found. I suppose linking them to the gods of the world is an easy way to say "they're finnicky and don't always show up because of that," but I'm not buying it. As for magic, it must be created using materials you find in the world along with magic wells that the protagonist can drain from the earth. I'm not a huge fan, and more often than not I didn't use it.

Instead of an expansive amount of characters you can bring in and out of your party, you are stuck with Prince Noctis, the protagonist, and the same three guys: Ignis, Prompto, and Gladiolus. Every so often, yes, you get a guest characters, but it's rare. Thankfully, the main trio of buddies are absolutely delightful. The four pals act just like friends, instead of basically body guards for the Prince. Their banter and conversation and random chit chat in battle is well-rounded and fleshed out fully to allow you the opportunity to get really close with these boys and their antics. Initially irritating characters, Prompto was mine, eventually endear you and worm their ways into your heart. Due to this camaraderie, the game is often described as "four dudes go on a road trip" or, as I like to think of it, the "extended bachelor party."

Along with this, the story is pretty decent as well. It's not some slapdash, thrown together nonsense that has you questioning who in the world people are like the last RPG I played (*cough, cough* The Last Remnant *cough...coughcough*). The game developers and writers kept the story clean, simple, but with enough surprises to keep you going. Other things that are clean are the fighting dynamics, but they are NOT simple. It took me a number of days before my fingers recognized what I needed to do, and if I took a break from playing for a day or two it felt like my fingers forgot everything. The fight system isn't clunky, at all, but it seems like there's way too many buttons to push to just simply fight. Thankfully, there is a wait system to help you figure out your slow, human hands and to target the proper thing you want to target.

Traveling is a bit different as well. There's a car. But you'll learn to love the car, trust me. It's a good car. It's a fun car. But the game is pretty unforgiving when it comes to travel. At night, there are demons, and if they happen to appear in the road the car will stop and you must get out and fight said demons. At first, it's a pain because the demons are too tough, and then it's just straight up annoying because you CAN fight them but it's a waste of time and energy. What's worse is that, as you go through the game, the days get shorter and the nights longer. Even worse, you can't just select an option to wait a number of "in game hours" anywhere for the night to turn back into day. My recommendation? Push through until you get to Altissa, I know the game will tell you four BILLION TIMES that you won't be able to return easily. Don't worry, you can. Get to Altissa, and once you can access the hotel there, select to go back in time, and the night time situation won't be so bad. Also, do as many of the "car missions" as possible to update the Regalia, the name of your sweet ride. Eventually, there will be a mission, which is a pretty tough one, to get a certain kind of headlights...that'll help. Seriously, this is probably the only continually frustrating part of the game. Let me help you; take this advice!

The game is pretty great, and if there are some hangups because it's not a traditional FF, it literally makes the disclaimer before the title screen: "A Final Fantasy for First Timers and Fans." It's true. There are enough things to keep it in the FF category, but also many new things to keep up with the changing view of RPGs and their chemical makeup. Give it a chance, it's pretty great, and allow the sense of change to happen. They basically need to in order to keep the franchise going, and I'm not very mad about it.

As far as I'm concerned, this game is an absolute slammer of perfection. The gameplay is smooth, it's free of glitches or irritating functionality. The interface for leveling and becoming stronger is well thought out and rarely leaves you over or underpowered. The graphics are beautiful, the story is immersive, the voice acting is spot on, and the whole concept's creativity is a slam dunk.

You start off as a young girl named Aloy, who you will continue to play as when the game progresses past the introduction. She is an outcast, living with a fellow outcast named Rost who has become like a father for her. She is motherless, which is nearly as bad as a crime in her Nora tribe. These nomadic people believe in an entity called the All Mother who lives inside of a mountain and their entire basis of religion is matriarchal. Rost, an outcast for an unknown reason (one you can find out later in the game), decided to take her in and raise her. Aloy, at the beginning of the game, is a child who wishes she was part of the Nora tribe and in a fit of upset, running from her emotions, she falls into one of the forbidden places. These are forgotten locations that are the leavings of the Old Ones, namely a technological civilization much like our own that seems to have destroyed itself. Clearly, hundreds of years later, humanity has reasserted itself tribally, but in a world where machines roam the landscape and attack humans more often than not. Inside this forbidden place, Aloy finds a device called a Focus that allows her to "see the unseen." She can see through walls, see the stats of robots, their paths, and can access lost technology. She winds up saving a young man's life so Rost allows her to keep the Focus despite it being forbidden technology. Rost also agrees to teach Aloy all he knows about surviving and fighting so that she can run in the Trials that even outcasts can participate in. If she completes the Trials she is allowed back into the Nora civilization, but if she comes in first she can ask the Matriarchs for one thing: determined to find out where she came from she trains hard and grows up.

Aloy, as a teenager, embarks on the journey of the Trials which winds up having more complicated outcomes. Surviving the ordeal, she insists on discovering the story of the Old Ones, where she came from, who her Mother is, while simultaneously trying to save what world she knows from the metal machines and the corruption that is making them far more dangerous than in years past.

This is definitely a stealth-lovers game. The developers made sure to emphasize that Aloy is simply human and that the machines can definitely easily overwhelm, but with her Focus and patience, she can also learn to easily kill the creatures that roam the landscape. Speaking of landscape, if you're intimate with the Rocky Mountain region you'll find yourself in familiar vistas quite often.

The story itself is completely immersive and addicting while the gameplay remains fun, but this is NOT a game for people who don't like to sneak around and have patience. You will, eventually, be strong enough to be a heavy hitter, but never strong enough to survive a full on onslaught for long. Even at the highest level, 60 with the Frozen Wilds expansion, and the best armor and weapons you will still struggle. You will have to be willing to use bombs, traps, arrows, and your spear equally. Thankfully, this is fairly doable and easy.

Though the game is several years old now, it holds up to the test of time and has easily become one of my favorite modern video games. Pick it up and give it a whirl while you wait to save up your monies for Xbox Series Xs and PS5s.

Since Bethesda is sitting on their butts about making another Elder Scrolls game, I recently picked up Oblivion to play it again. Although it was originally released in 2006 (Chhhhhhhhhrist, I feel old), and the graphics aren't exactly up to par for the 4k TVs and billions of polygons that go into making a blade of grass these days, it still holds up to the challenge of a well-told storyline and a fun game that could be played for months!

Side quests, along with the main story line, are absolutely riveting, enjoyable, and never get too frustrating beyond measure. Tasked with helping to close the Oblivion gates that have sprung up all over Tamriel, the protagonist, you, joins forces with an unlikely bastard son of the late Emperor. Since there was no emperor to rule the seat of Tamriel, the dragonfires were extinguished in Cyrodil (the capital) and the gates of Oblivion (the Elder Scrolls version of Hell) opened to let in all kinds of nasties. Threatening to overrun the human world, the gates must be sealed and the fires relit. Easier said than done, of course!

If you're going to pick up this game now with expectations of it being like Skyrim--don't. This came years before Skyrim was released and although it didn't get nearly half the praise of Skyrim, it's still a great game.
