I will start this review with a disclaimer: I am not a gamer. However I have a teen son who is, and a husband who also enjoys a few hours a week on the X-Box, so I gave this headset to them and asked each of them their opinion (interviewed them independently of one another). This review is an amalgamation of their responses.

Both agree the headset is VERY comfortable. However they both have an issue with the volume control. My son previously used a cheap, $20 headset he got from Walmart. He said the volume control on it is conveniently located so that he can mute very easily. By contrast, the volume control on the SteelSeries headset is located where it plugs into the controller and can be more difficult to get to in a hurry.

My husband said the plug in is complex or reversed. He thinks this is a headset designed for gaming on a PC and adapted for use with the X-Box. As a PC headset, he thinks it would be stellar, but when it was adapted, they didn't quite get the connector "right".

Additionally, my son said at times he has difficulty hearing his friends talk over X-Box live. My husband had a similar complaint although more detailed. He said it is designed to reduce the volume of music when someone talks, but appears to do the opposite. He did wonder if that meant he had it hooked up backwards, but that goes back to the point about the connector being too complex.

Overall, my son gave it a 4 and my husband a 3. Since I can't do half stars, I went with the 3, because after giving his rating, my husband asked about the price. When I told him what it retails for, he definitely said go with the lower rating because at 4x the cost of my son's headset, it should work at least twice as well.

Ever since my son got his first Turtle Beach headset several years ago, that is the only brand he really wants to use. We've tried some cheaper models in the meantime but he always returns to this brand for the following reasons:

Sound: The sound on this headset is exceptional.

Microphone: Wireless chat is easy.

Batteries: The battery life is great.

Accessories: Comes with everything you need.

While not the cheapest headset out there, it is true that "you get what you pay for". For a serious gamer, this is a great headset.

As the title says, this headset is lightweight and comfortable.  The quality of sound is great (to my fairly non-discriminating ears), and the components appear to be high quality.  A great gamer headset with the versatility to be able to be used on different gaming systems as well as with iPod or phone.

In the interest of full disclosure, I am not a gamer. I got this for 16yo teen son who to date is a huge Black Ops and Grand Theft Auto fan. He had not requested Assassin's Creed but knowing it is a popular game and a similar genre, I took the chance and ordered it.

He (and I) is so glad I did! He loves the game and thinks it will quickly become a new favorite series. He likes that there is a lot to do in single player mode offline since our internet is not up to a lot of online gaming. He has been frustrated in the past when a game has little to do unless one is playing online with virtual opponents. Assassin's Creed has online and multi player options but also allows him to play alone and complete many of the tasks/missions without the need to go live.

He likes the characters and story plot and finds the graphics to be well done and fun.

Ever since my son got his first Turtle Beach headset several years ago, it is the only brand he really wants to use. We've tried some alternative/cheaper models but he always returns to this brand for the following reasons:

Sound: The sound quality is excellent.

Microphone: Chat is easy.

Accessories: Comes with everything you need.

Comfort: It is lightweight and fits comfortably over the ears

This is one of the cheaper models Turtle Beach sells and it is true that "you get what you pay for". A serious gamer might prefer one of the higher end models produced by Turtle Beach. My son tends to be hard on equipment and goes through them faster than he should (zero mechanical empathy) so I found this to be a great headset solution for him.

This game sounds neat when you read about it. But the game is virtually unplayable. The biggest problem this game suffers from is its horrible controls. You press a button to attack, and your character swings like he/she is wildly drunk, misses and ends up behind the enemy you are attacking. And since even the weakest enemies in the game can off you in 1-3 hits, this is bad news. You can actually press a button to swing a sword and then fall off a cliff 10 feet away in mid-swing. People tell me "you just don't know how to play it..." but are you telling me I don't know how to press a button? Should I use my toes or something? On top of clumsy handling, your player walks and runs like its in slow-mo, to the point that you want to bring a book to read while you wait for him to walk from one end of a room to another. When you pull up a menu screen, the game screen is no longer visible, yet the game doesn't pause! You can be attacked while trying to equip and use items which isn't a challenge. Its just stupid. I will leave you with a quote from the Angry Video Game Nerd that he used to describe another game, but that I feel sums up this game's downfall to a "T".

"It is totally inexcusable to make a game where the challenge is not in the game itself, but in handicapping the player."
- AVGN

This game looks and handles just fine. Until you lock up with another wrestler. At that moment, a giant picture of a random controller button will appear on the screen and you have to press the same button at the EXACT moment it appears. You have about a 25% chance of success on that, since there are 4 buttons, X,Y,B and A. If you don't win "guess that button", you get reversed and slammed. Doesn't matter how much power you have. So if you can win a match by punching and kicking, you will be in good shape. If you attempt a move, there is a 75% chance it will backfire and you will be counter attacked. There is no rhythm, rhyme or reason to the button thing, its just random. What an incredibly stupid thing to implement into an otherwise perfect example of gameplay. I give it 2 stars just because the roster is awesome. But the game is unplayable.

Even kids wouldn't care for this game for more than an afternoon. I knew it would consist of Olaf collecting snowflakes. That wasn't hard to predict. But there is NO enemies! And NO point to the game! Collect crap if you want to (that does nothing) and just walk through level after boring level. It is at best, an incomplete turd of a game. It looks like it is an unfinished product. Put this garbage on the app store for free. Don't box it up and scam people who loved what was an awesome movie out of thirty bucks. GameMill couldn't program a VCR, much less a good game. Always pay attention to the publisher/developer names. GameMill? GameWho? Guaranteed crap game. Not to say bigger publishers don't put out crap too but this was an obvious dog turd game. Poor Olaf. He didn't deserve this.

This game is not what we were told it was. It was constantly compared to GTA V but it is nowhere near the quality. It reeks of rushed production. Which makes no sense because the street date was much later and then it was pushed up. Hacking? Yeah, you press X to do everything and it just auto-happens. People's personal info? You can't do anything with it. I think they planned for that to have a point and just couldn't program that whole aspect. Hacking isn't even necessary, they just make you play the game their way instead of making use of a perfectly good rifle. Got detected? Game over. Enjoy 10 minutes of loading to get back to a save point and it happens A LOT! Be a vigilante or a criminal? No, you will be a vigilante. Criminal acts will punish you to the point of guaranteed game overs. You don't have a choice. (They said you did..) And here's the kicker: YOU CAN'T PUNCH! YOU CAN'T KICK! AND YOU CAN'T JUMP! Are you serious? Are you really serious Ubisoft? I will back the majority of the reviews on here in saying that all you do in this game is drive around like an idiot and the mechanics stink. If you had put the pre order poster up and it said:"You can't punch, You can't kick, You can't jump... WATCHDOGS...preorder now..." No one would have bought this piece of trash. And not that it matters after all of this input, but the graphics look like steaming manure. This looks like a PS2 game from 2004. Any one who tells you this is a good game is only trying to make themselves feel better for wasting $60 on it and remember, misery loves company. Don't buy this game.

Turtle Beach wrote the book on comfort. Besides having great sound, the ear cups fit all the way over the ears. Even my big 'ol ears. This feels nice and blocks out background sounds. This was all true about the earlier models of Turtle Beach and it is still true with this model. But this has nicer in-line controls and a MLG logo to boot. Love it.

Atlus brings us yet another winner. Love the artwork, love the dungeon mapping. Etrian is a killer franchise with unique weapons, armor and monsters. Skill trees provide lots of character depth and I love the sound and music too. Some think the turn based rpg format is an old & tired genre but not me. And at this level, you get a real quality product.

This is an insult to classic Warhammer. Hit detection is crap, all enemies are the same and matchmaking is broken. Graphics are like PS2 quality. Online only so when it fails (already has) they'll take down the server and the game disc will be useless.

Handles like butt with thumbsticks. Software has to be exited to change to a different game. Menus are a hot mess. And this was delayed? It took you longer than planned to F up a Pacman game and slap it on a disc?

I believe you'll read a lot of bad reviews of this game. The reason is not the game itself, but a situation around it. Pyranha Bites, a developer of Gothic sreies, had to give away the right to make this game after a nasty legal dispute with its former publisher, JoWood. After that PB went to develop a new title, Risen, and JoWood hired a european developer SpellBound to make a next Gothic title, Arcania. Fans of Gothic (and there are a lot of us, mostly in Germany, Russia, and Poland) were pissed beyond measure. From the beginning a lot of people were agains Arcania just because of this reason. They openly wished this game never be published and JoWood go bankrupt. So please perceive this egativity for what it is. I am a Gothic fan, but there are limits, you know. It is not decent to talk crap about the game just to make publisher to loose money, and it is not fair to a very decent game. Some german folks even show up here to write bad reviews. So take it for what they are.
Yes, a lot of elements from Gothic games have been lost, so Arcania is Gothic in title only, but the game itself is quite charming, actually. You will get a big (semi)opened world (each new section of the island opens after you complete the main quiest), but these sections are very big, so you won't feel claustrafobic. The world is great, actually. Beautiful sunrises ans sunsets, very well done architecture (castles are really superb), so you will enjoy just being there. At least I hope you will, because I am enjoying it and want to share. ;)
There are a lot of enemies to slain, of all shapes and sizes, from spiders and goblins to fire golems and demons. There are four difficulty settings to choose from, from very easy, to rather hard. There is a lot of crafting in the game, from weapons to potions and food. A great variety of weapons and armor as well.
The story is good enough, it is not crap by any means, and dialogues, though vary from funny to plain, do a good job of conveing necessary information. And some a real funny and enjoyable. Quests are mostly straiforward, but it does not make them in any way dumb. The compain takes about 25 hours (about 16 hours on main quest and the rest for secondary quests), and for me these were good 25 hours spend in a beautiful new world. Overall, I would say Arcania is worth every cent I paid for it. PC Games and Official XBox Mag give this game 7.6 and 7.5 respectively (good game). I give it 5 stars. Yeah, yeah, it has some flaws (not bugs, but as they say in their reviews, not enough RPG elements and such), but as long as I can totally loose myself in the game, I simply do not care.

I was Ok with the first one, so I did not have either bias, or high expectations. But TW2 demonstrates that the devs can make a very good game if they put enough effort. This game is not really similar to TW1. Not a real open world RPG (you travel through the islands, and unlock different areas according to the story), but in this case it is more of a virtue then a vice. The main story is interesting, to say the least, and a lot of side quests can take a lot of time to finish. They vary greatly, and a lot of them are really good.
The environments are beautiful. This game is set not as much in purely fantasy settings. Savannah area is made in Ancient Egypt settings, with wildly beatufil temples, tombs, and catacombs. The second island is very medieval Japan-like, truly beautiful. Also it is obvuius that the devs used a lot of elements from other games. The swallows area is similar to the Valley of Defilement from Demon's Souls, and Tir Geal area - to the swamps in The Witcher. The end result in TW2 is superb, very atmospheric.
Magic, crafting and alchemy systems are unique, and really cool. Battles are challenging enough, and appearances of monsters and their variety is praiseworthy. Horseriding is fun, and not as difficult as in TW1. Overall, I am extremely glad i bought this game. A great way to spend a month till DA2 release.

This is a great, supremely addictive game. It has a unique artistic and narrative style, with a lot of unique gameplay elements. You can fight as a man (warrior, ranger, mage, priest, or any combination you fancy), fly as a dragon, destroy enemy's fortresses, solve puzzles, uncover a multitude of secrets, and so on. I can't imagine why this game is not very popular. It totally beats any Fable game, and yes, even DA2 (which was not too hard to beat). It shares the same place as DAO on my list, but by different reasons.
Also: for under 40 buck you get about 100 hours total (including add-on). This beats any game on the market.
People, what are you waiting for? To be a dragon for less then $40 - it's like a dream come true. ;)

I bought this game not expecting much. It looked like a budget game, but it looked good enough to try. And I am very glad I did. Yes, it is a simple, old-fashioned game. It has 20 levels/locations, some of them outdoor (fighting and collecting), some - interior (fighting, collecting, and puzzles) and some - underground (mostly puzzles and collecting). Nice combination of activities, a story is nice and kept me interested, with some nice gameplay elements (like tracking and looking for traps and clues). I finished the game twice, and I am sure I'll run through it again in the future. Just do not expect stunning visuals, or any Hollywood-type effects. If you want a AAA title - go for the Witcher 2. But if it is a plain fun you are after - pick this game.

As a lot of people said it is a great game. Stylish, unusual, and very addictive. But it requires to use some thinking, and it punishes any mistakes. In certain respects it is easier then Demon's Souls (gear costs less, for example, 50 souls for a fire bomb comparative with 300, and easier to grind, the first boss is super-easy and goes down much faster comparative to Phalanx), but it is also harder. A cheater's bow strategy is eliminated, it seems ;)
My advice: run to the merchant and buy a spear. It is so much easier then a sword. You can hit while holding block, you know. With a spear you won't have any problems with ordinary enemies.
Buy fire bombs, they are super-cheap.
Also buy a bow with arrows. All these pesky guys throwing bombs from roofs - two-three shots and they are history. Arrows now are also cheap as dirt.
If you are like me, a melee fighter, when fighting demon on a bridge run towards him, as close as possible. Then it is rolling and hitting, till he goes down. Or climb up, jump down on his head hitting him while falling, and then again roll and hit, roll and hit. You might want to raise endurance a bit, if you stamina is not enough.

The title sums it up. This is the best game for me. I have been playing for like 20 years already (yeah, i am that old, 34 and counting ;)), and I am not really too emotional about games anymore. Don't take me wrong, it is my only hobby, and I play a lot. I would say I saw it all already. Skyrim returned me that already nearly forgotten feeling of wonder and owe I had as a teenager. Like the first time I played Gothic 1-2, or M&M games, or Morrowind. By some reason Oblivion did not work for me, but Skyrim worked a miracle. Now I cannot sleep or concentrate on my job, because I am totally under the influence of this digitized drug called TES 5 Skyrim.
It is so addictive it should be illegal, or at least should come with a warning from surgeon general and with a list of crisis hot-line number for addicted players. Shame on you Bethesda for leaving us without emergency psychological care ;)

It is a great game, one of my favorites. It is not as big as Skyrim, obviously (nothing is), but it is in the same league. Open wold game, the world is big enough even without the add-on, and utterly beautiful. It has some multiplayer adventures, but recently a WORLDMERGE mod was released by fans, which brought POTFF and ALL multiplayer maps into the main campaign. So now if you wish, you could play all of it inside the main game, and off-line. It made the game world even bigger, and now you can actually teleport between POTFF, multiplayer maps, and a main campaign.
I want to keep it short, so if you want to know more, read TW2 regular edition reviews.
POTFF is a great and lengthy add-on, takes about 18-20 hours, and adds a new archipelago with multitude of quests. It became available for download some time ago, and now we have a chance to get it on a disk.

Well, I totally agree with GameSpot review (75/100), and only because the game is big. Unfortunately I belong to a a group of RPG gamers who value a good story, great characters, and a living world, and not just good combat.
First of all, the huge net of narrow corridors and wider openings with a gratuitous amount of invisible walls do not make an open world. But it would be not a big deal if a story were good. Well, it is not. It is not too bad either, just very generic and uninspiring.
Second, after playing for 10 hours I still do not give a damn about any event in the game. Probably it is because NPCs are nothing more but answering machines, with zero personalities and any lack of emotions, with dialogues being wooden and boring beyond belief. As if this game has been made by robots, or a kind of computer-generated product, with no humans involved.
Third, man, it is such a rip-off!!! Practically everything was in other games, but made way better. It makes me wonder why, for example, Divinity 2 DKS, which is a similar game in many respects, but with a real personality, really good characters, humor and charm, was not very successful financially, and in the reviews, but KOA is praised left and right.
Combat is good, but without a good story for me it does not matter. May be I am too old already to be happy just with a mindless hack and slash.
Alchemy, crafting, and such are OK, but without a good story is is kinda pointless. Overall KOA is a huge disappointment for me.

I bought this game looking for a new FPS and did I ever get what I was looking for. Admittedly, I'm an FPS junkie, but I also enjoy science fiction RPG's as well. This game successfully balances both - with just a little platforming and puzzle solving to round it out.  I have to say, it took a little getting used to. Once the learning curve had been surmounted though - DAMN GOOD FUN!!! If you appreciate the cyber punk universes of Phillip K. Dick or, more precisely William Gibson, then don't pass this one up.

I was very excited for this monitor. Sadly, like most people that bought it I am experiencing the black screen issue. What happens is that while using it, at totally random intervals, the screen goes black for up to 4 seconds. It's not hard to understand why this is frustrating when you're at a critical point in game play and the screen blacks out just long enough to compromise your situation. However, The truly disappointing part of this problem is that there has been so much noise made about it, and Sony has done little else than repeat to each customer that it's the first time they've heard about the problem. I'm now on my second one (experiencing the same problem as before - which is most people's experience with multiple units) and sending it back to Sony. Lately it seems that Sony has been taking them back for RMA's and somehow fixing the problem with refurbished ones. However, I strongly urge buyers to consider other models; the high defect rate is simply too much of a gamble.

This has been by far my most anticipated game of the year and I'm VERY pleased with the outcome. For Trekkies it lives up to what many of us would expect by including elements of the old canon (like The Gorn), yet weaving them nicely into the new crew. The voice acting is superb and compliments very good graphics to unfold a compelling story. Nothing about it is a 10, but that's ok-nothing is perfect. I'm playing it on PS3 so versions may differ. I also haven't had a chance to play co-op, but I'm really looking forward to it. All in all it is a really great on ramp to next month's movie release and without question (except for some parts of Star Trek Online) the best Star Trek game I've played.

I went into this game simply needing something new to play through over the Labor Day weekend and not expecting a lot given the mediocre reviews I've read. Man oh man was I surprised! Rarely do I feel the need to contradict other reviewers but I have to say - this game was top notch in my opinion. The visuals were superb and at times breathtaking (for instance when you're under the oil refinery rescuing the CIA operative). The voice acting was believable and not over the top. The game's sound was very well layered and added to the realism. The gadgets were helpful and fun. The gameplay was a bit different than what I'm used to but after about a half an hour muscle memory kicked in and I had no trouble with it at all. The one and only problem I had was the camera angle during sprinting. It made sprinting very ineffective. However, sprinting was rarely a must so I was easily able to get past it. Admittedly, I've only played the single player campaign at this point...but loved every second of it.

Very highly recommended!!!

I really loved this series and I was enthralled with this closing chapter. The thing that I seem to be enjoying about it the most is playing with the 3D on just slightly (3 clicks from being completely turned down). It just helps the world pop enough to give it a bit more depth. It's not obnoxiously "3Dish" but a nice way to help carry the story a little bit more effectively. Don't let this one pass you by if you enjoy FPSers and sci-fi.

So. I didn't get mine from Amazon. I waited in the cold at BB. I'm very happy with the purchase save for one small hitch: when I turned it off the first time it got stuck and the little circle just kept spinning. Had to pull the power. It was fine of course, but I was sweat in' there for a second. Other than that, KZ Shadow Fall looks UNBELIEVABLE!!! I know others are having trouble and my heart truly goes out to them. I have high hopes that Sony will remedy all this and we'll get going as a strong community soon.

I just started moving over to Battlefield recently. I kind of needed a break from COD and was stoked to get in on the launch window for a fresh offering. I have to say that what I have been able to play of both single and multiplayer has been terrific. The single player campaign is, in my opinion, world'd better than the all too familiar COD America-is-getting-attacked-again theme. The visuals are stunning and the game play is tight and responsive. Multiplayer is phenomenal and very engaging. With all this said, the crashing is starting to really drive me crazy and I want it resolved NOW!!! You really have to wonder how this kind of thing is let pass onto the community and EA is really starting to make a name for itself in terms of low quality. I have high hopes that they'll get this resolved because there is absolutely a great game underneath all the problems so far.

This is an excellent stealth game. Admittedly, I never played the original but I am enjoying he heck out of this one. I think that if you enjoy stealth games this one will really spark your fancy. It also looks beautiful.
This is a very good game for co-op play. Too hard for single person capaign. I don't think this game was designed for singler players.  I Returned the game.

Terrible controls. Very hard to pick up items. I stood directly over food item, could not pick it up. I had to dance around the item like an idiot before I could pick it up. THEN I had to use trigger two to eat the food. The character movements are 2nd generation. Terrible Terrible Terrible!

At first this game seems like a godsend. It's visually beautiful with nice themed levels and fluid framerate. The audio is about as memorable as it'll ever be for a platformer. I found the controls to be too floaty for this style of platformer one involves plentiful close shaves and relies heavily on timing.

About a few hours in, the game starts to fall apart. The difficulty level becomes absurd and it just gets boring. It isn't overly repetitive, but there's just something that didn't hold my attention. As expected, there isn't much of a story, but neither do its competitors.

I am an adult gamer that has been playing games for years and like to relax while playing platformers. For a game that looks like a Saturday morning cartoon, Rayman becomes outrageously difficult near the end.

Rayman is missing a distinct competitive advantage. The other platforming heavyweights have one. Little Big Planet has its replayability and community while Super Mario has its nostalgia and multiplayer. In one of the oldest genres, it is easy to see how Rayman is overlooked.

I know I am the minority, but this will be my first and only Rayman game. It is a style that I don't appreciate as much as the others.

Let's be honest, the crux of the Final Fantasy games are its stories. FFXIII has to have one of the worst stories of any game I’ve played let alone one that is meant to be a major blockbuster. It is overly confusing and convoluted that no one I talked to has any idea what is going on. Some have even tried writing down plot points into a note pad and are still baffled as to the storyline.

Naturally, a bad story leads to awful characters. This is partly true. A few characters are memorable: Lightning and Fang, a few that just occupy space: Vanille and Sazh, and a few that are completely irritating: Snow and Hope. This volatility is a theme of how this game’s production is. With a series that has brought us Sephiroth and Auron, the characters are generally forgettable.

I know Final Fantasy games can be cutscene heavy, but it almost felt as if you were playing between cutscenes at many times. One of the biggest complaints is its linearity. I personally didn’t find this to be a problem. It does open up slightly in the later parts of the game.

One of XIII’s strengths is that it just feels fluid and polished. The smooth graphics, the quick and stylish UI, and has hands-down the best battling system. For me, this game’s saving grace was its battling system. Battles never felt like a chore and kept me interested in the game despite an awful story.

As a Final Fantasy game, it is a letdown. If viewing in isolation, it is a decent RPG. Despite its many shortcomings, it only took me like a week to get through the 60+ hours of gameplay, a marathon only a few games have warranted.

It was awhile ago I played this game, but remember it being surprisingly good as I wasn't expecting much from the mediocre reviews. It definitely took some notes from the Bioshock playbook especially with the audio logs randomly strewn throughout. It is basically a time-traveling Bioshock and it is definitely good enough to be in the same discussion as Bioshock. The biggest thing I remember is the story. It was one of the better ones this gen. You would enjoy this as well if you liked the Dead Space series.

Just like other atmospheric FPS, you'll probably want to revisit it in a few years, but there isn't much else like a multiplayer that bring substantial value after you've beat it once.

Dead Space 2 gives you a Bioshock feel especially early on. Whereas the Ishimura just gave the feeling of a functional ship, the environments in 2 feel like the sum of their parts. The sense of loss and the confusion of “what the heck happened here?” like Bioshock is present in Dead Space 2.

Games like this can easily fall into a cliché story, but Dead Space 2 does a nice job of being more original than falling into the same story arcs of other horror stories. Nothing is too overplayed: music, enemies popping out of nowhere, etc. This one is much very linear. Might’ve been moreso than the original.

Another negative is that as the game progresses, you’ll figure out what enemies and how many will be coming based on the room layout and size. There’s also the occasional problem with the story where it’s the usual “Oh man! Item A broke down, I’ll go fix Item B, so we can progress.” It is not as noticeable as other games, but it gets tiresome in the later chapters. Despite the linearity, the pace is differentiated by varying elements. You’ll have the usual flying in zero gravity as well as feet on the ground sequences. The game is not too long and not too short.

Like the original, it is completely up to you how you make your way through. This is welcomed freedom. You can upgrade any weapon, or not even use a weapon at all. In fact, the gameplay is basically a carbon copy of the first. Whereas in other games I’d find this a significant issue, I did not mind. I'd give it 4.5 stars, but rounded up to a 5. For a price of around $10, this game is definitely worth picking up.

I’d give it 4.5 stars, which I rounded up to 5. The game was definitely not as I thought it would be. The entire game had a Bioshock-ish feel with its own atmospheric identity, which is its best feat. The set-pieces are varied.

Unfortunately the plot is not nearly as good as it could be, but the execution with the Bioshock-esque recordings etc. make a mediocre plot a better than average one. I think that alone makes it a worthwhile game to play. The past few years games have been way too focused on cutscenes. Luckily, Dishonored does not have many, so I can’t complain about the plot too much. Out of all of these stealth games this generation of games, I think the controls with this one seemed the easiest to use. Naturally, with any of these covert stealth games, the controls can be frustrating and you just want to pry yourself into your TV screen because switching between the powers is sometimes not as quick as one would desire.

The powers are awesome. One thing I really liked is that you can combo them to how you would like to play. Many say that the game does kind of punish you for being what you are, an assassin, which is a valid point. However, it is definitely significantly more difficult to keep the death count low, which is the point. The game length was fine. It promotes exploring. I found though that near the end I was getting tired of it though and just slaughtered everyon

Crysis series single player is what the Halo series should have turned into. In fact, playing the Crysis series for the first time was a lot like what playing Combat Evolved was like for the first time: original story, awesome open set-pieces, refined and fluid gameplay, and solid state-of-the-art graphics. Crysis 3 gives more of the same.

Story is nothing substantial. It is fairly short (depending how you play the game). Took me probably about 8 hours. Graphics are of course the best of the system. They don’t seem nearly as impressive as 2’s however. The set-pieces vary, but some in the latter stages of the game are more impressive than a few early on. In this game, the bigger ones seemed to be the better ones.

The weapon’s look and feel are still the best of any FPS. There are plenty of decent weapons that vary greatly. All pack quite the punch and all are fun to use. Probably the biggest addition is the bow. The bow makes the game significantly better moreso than I could have imagined. It is fun to use a weapon that doesn’t take up suit energy so it really enhances the stealth aspect of the game.

Stealth has the same pitfalls as Far Cry 3. As a game that is supposed to have a huge stealth element, it isn’t always user-friendly. The stealth kills are temperamental perhaps as much as 2’s was, which significantly hampers the fun of the stealth especially if you are trying to flawlessly pass a level. This can actually get pretty frustrating. The other thing is over vigilant enemies. When out of cloaking mode, it will feel as if you are covered in fluorescent orange paint with a “Shoot Me” sign hanging 20 feet above your head. You could be in the bushes and an unaware enemy hundreds of yards away could start shooting at you. This makes stealth more binary than in most similar games. Overall the gameplay is still my favorite among stealth games. It allows for “quick” on the fly stealth and satisfying quick stealth-to-firefight (and vice versa) modes of fighting.

A few other minor complaints are that the vehicle driving is a chore. The controls are way too tight and the PS3 framerate didn’t seem to handle the speed that well. The suit upgrades are not very good this time around. I actually found the first set of upgrades the most useful.

Crysis 3 will could easily warrant another playthrough, but nothing else . It needs a better multiplayer to dethrone its competitors. When accounting for the total value, I give it only 4 stars.

+ Combat System is fun
+ Incredibly fast load times
+ Art style
+ Character upgrade system
+ Battle customization
+ Rewarding exploration
+ Weapon/armor upgrade system
+ Length (took me 35ish hours)
+ Difficulty setting
+ Constant character interactions
+ Worthwhile side missions
+ Decent story
+ Save at anytime

- Story starts off really slow
- Milla’s voice acting is excruciating
- Battle System is overly complex
- Two character choice is more of a gimmick

The biggest complaint is that the game and its story start off extremely slowly. This is also exacerbated by the fact that the story/dungeon ratio is very uneven. The beginning is mostly dungeons and then the story soars about 15 hours in. This can cause doubts about continuing the game and it is well worth it past the 10-hour mark. Add in an overly complex battle system and the game doesn’t seem that great at first.

I want to take time and say that the core of the game is very genius. The only RPG that I’ve made sure that I’ve vigilantly discovered every square inch of dungeons and very few do I habitually traverse back to the towns. The items you find in your travels will help you level up your shops which then upgrade your equipment, items, weapons, etc. Not only does this make more logical sense compared to the usual new-town-better-equipment charade, it provides huge incentive to make money and take time to find these items. You could indeed have an incredibly powerful weapon for the level of your character. These items aren’t few and far between like other RPGs that have a few really hidden chests strewn about. These items are scattered absolutely everywhere, which makes it worthwhile and considerably rewarding. It is almost like following bread-crumbs sometimes where you realize that you just traversed an entire area once you realize it.

This is also the first game where I went out of my way to do side missions. Since the game’s shops allow you to continuously improve your character at your own pace, you can never have enough money for those upgrades. The insanely fast load times make help significantly.

“Dungeons” if you want to even call them that because some of the areas are beautiful and straightforward, which is a refreshing standout as most JRPGS have large, exhausting, and tedious labyrinthine dungeons.

Battle system is overly complex albeit fun. About ten hours in I started to get comfortable enough to begin to understand its intricate details.

It is going to be difficult playing other RPGs because once you’ve played some of the new elements offered in ToX, it is hard to go back.

Tomb Raider is an action-adventure game very similar to Uncharted, but less scripted, more gritty and atmospheric, and more focused on exploration.

Lara Croft is the best female lead I’ve played in a game. She isn’t a female for the sake of being a female and the gameplay is the best suggestion as to why this is such a breath of fresh air. The fluidity of the game is unmatched. She is nimble, quick, graceful, and resourceful all of which explain how she is able to accomplish what she does especially during frenetic firefights and crumbling environments. Using the bow never got dull for one second. The climbing isn’t tiresome or tedious like Uncharted nor does it seem to suffer from too much “convenient ledge syndrome” since the environment is so well integrated.

It feels as if the designers first crafted the island then the rest of the game. It is integrated so well. Games like Uncharted feel like the environments are molded to what is supposed to happen in the game. It’s not like most games where you land in a giant empty room and know there is going to be a huge firefight. Additionally, the graphics are beautiful and the framerate on the PS3 holds very well.

The game’s dark and moody atmosphere is done well and the story is completely unpredictable. This kept me on edge. I really felt the high stakes. The game has a great leveling system. I actually wanted to explore so I could upgrade the weapons. Another positive is the nice menus. Lastly, the game starts off quickly and never lets go.

I have a few complaints. First, the story could have used a better supporting cast. The quick time events are awful and some are the type where they randomly pop out of nowhere and if you don’t hit them then you die. The game could have used a few more hours. It did seem slightly short.

Tomb Raider is one of the biggest surprises and although it has a few minor faults, it is one of my favorite games.

In 1986, Nintendo released a (notoriously difficult) 2D platformer on the NES featuring a charming angel named Pit. Modeled closely after the mythological Cupid, he battled an array of devilish foes while wielding a bow and arrow, ultimately facing his nemesis, Medusa, AKA the "Queen of Darkness." It was a nice concept and supposedly a nice game (I'd never played it myself), but one seemingly destined to be rather short-lived, as it saw no real sequel in a span of 26 years, unless of course you count the 1991 Game Boy follow-up, which didn't receive much attention.

Fast forward to 2008 and Pit suddenly reappears in Super Smash Bros. Brawl, among the most popular and widely known Nintendo franchises. This was surely hinting at a comeback of sorts, and sure enough we finally receive Kid Icarus: Uprising in 2012 (guess the Ice Climbers weren't as lucky).

If you've been paying attention to any gaming magazines, sites or multimedia recently, chances are high you've come across some form of advertisement or promotional material for this game. Arguably one of the most heavily hyped Nintendo games in recent history, and surely the most hyped 3DS game, does Kid Icarus: Uprising live up to its vast array of promises? The short answer is yes, given that the game is undeniably fantastic and in fact arguably one of Nintendo's greatest triumphs ever. This shouldn't necessarily come as a surprise given that its chief developer is the creative mastermind Masahiro Sakurai, creator of iconic pink puffball Kirby and the Super Smash Bros. series. His games are most often innovative and colossally ambitious, but he may have just outdone himself with this one.

Kid Icarus: Uprising offers an obscene amount of content (a trademark of Sakurai), ranging from an expansive 1-Player story mode to elaborate competitive online play, as well as a scattering of mini-games and other little goodies. The 1-Player mode is incredible, featuring stunning, colorful visuals and landscapes throughout a variety of storyline chapters (if you haven't been impressed yet by the 3D capabilities of the 3DS, I guarantee this game will bring you around). You begin each level soaring through the air via a predetermined route (the ascents and dives through gorgeous scenery make for intoxicating aesthetics-and fun), firing attacks at enemies while swerving around to avoid their own. Once again, Pit has teamed up with Lady Palutena, Goddess of Light and ruler of Angel Land (a Nintendo-ified Heaven, more or less. Appropriate, considering the quality of this game) to take on Medusa. The lovely green-haired deity will guide you through various stages and also engage in some entertaining banter with Pit; the dialogue is most often genuinely funny and serious when it needs to be without ever approaching levels of childishly obnoxious or cheesy depravity.

Since Pit (for some unexplained reason) can't fly on his own, Palutena temporarily allows him the power of flight at the beginning of each stage, but once it runs out, you'll come crashing to the ground below. From here, the gameplay switches up and you'll be traversing through corridors and crevices while solving puzzles to reach new areas and battling enemies in the fray with both long range and melee attacks. There is a boss at the end of each stage, and similar to those you might fight in Zelda games, each one has individual weaknesses that may require use of specific techniques or strategies to defeat. You're free to adjust this mode's difficulty to your liking; the so-called "Intensity" scale, ranging between 1 and 10, determines how challenging things will be overall. The game's default is just above 2, and if you want much higher or lower than that you may have to spend hearts (the in-game currency, which can be won in various ways) to make large adjustments. To give you a better idea, extremely low Intensities make for absolute cakewalks, but go too high and I can pretty much guarantee you'll be destroyed in seconds, especially if you have yet to garner much experience. This is a nifty feature, as it allows swift interchange between veteran and newbie players. As you might expect, you'll unlock better goodies and win more hearts if you're daring enough to survive through higher Intensities.

In both the single and multiplayer modes, you'll have a vast array of options to choose from as to which weapon(s) you'd like to duel with. Taking notes from many popular MMOs, Kid Icarus: Uprising offers a massive variety of weapon classes, each of which have individual strengths and weaknesses, some of which handle extremely differently between one another and can completely change gameplay mechanics. There are melee weapons that excel at taking down nearby opponents like Claws, Clubs and Blades, while long-range classes like Bows, Staffs and Cannons can snipe opponents from afar. You'll have the option of experimenting with the weapon of your choice before taking it out on the field, but you'll have to play through the game and win online matches to unlock the most powerful and diverse ones. This isn't to say that anyone will necessarily be at a huge disadvantage starting out, however, as it is possible to master most any weapon available upon practice and recognition of its best accompanying techniques. In addition to differences in power and range, different types of weapons can even have different effects on your opponent or yourself, such as increases in speed or defense or the capability to inflict status conditions such as poison or paralysis, which can further hinder oncoming enemies. The variety of options here is so vast it's staggering, but it's expansive features like this that give online play that huge replay factor.

Speaking of the online play, it is expectedly one of the most appealing and highly addictive aspects of the game. The 3DS and in fact Nintendo in general has tended to downplay the relevance of online capabilities, which is truly unfortunate given that online play seems to be what offers most games their greatest replay value nowadays. Thankfully, the competitive online play in Kid Icarus: Uprising is raucous fun and an expertly executed feature. You can team up with (or duel against) friends or random opponents via either local wireless or online worldwide. The online multiplayer is split into two primary modes, Light VS. Dark and Free-for-All; as you might expect, the latter equates to a straightforward death match in which everyone is out for themselves, while Light VS. Dark is a unique team battle in which each team shares one collective health bar, which progressively depletes as teammates take damage. The player responsible for taking the blow that finishes off the team health transforms into that team's Angel; in this form, they take on the appearance of Pit and are equipped with a random (but usually more powerful) weapon. Once you become the Angel, your best bet is to flee or snipe from afar, because a team loses once their Angel is defeated.

All multiplayer matches make for truly addictive fun, and the fact that there are so many weapon classes to select from can make for an invigoratingly different experience each time. You can win various goodies, such as new weapons, hearts and more, by performing well in online matches. Shockingly, lag is virtually non-existent and the gameplay is unexpectedly fluid amidst such frantic battling. Nitpicks may notice minor framerate changes in particularly chaotic moments, but experiencing a fluid online mode (in 3D) on a handheld console is sheer gaming bliss.

In addition to choosing your diverse weaponry, you'll even have the option of equipping specific "Powers" to your character, or special abilities that can offer assistance to you or hinder enemies in both single and multiplayer modes; these Powers can be used at will but only for a limited number of times per match. You can do things like inflict paralysis or confusion, auto-target nearby foes, perform command jumps, veil your opponents' vision in darkness, create massive cyclones to send nearby foes skyward, and much more. Customizing these Powers to best enhance your strategy or weapon class can set up some devastating scenarios for your opponents. As if this isn't enough, there are also items you can snatch throughout matches and stages, whose effects vary from granting increased strength or abilities to initiating wild super-attacks.

The much debated control scheme is arguably the only thing the average person might complain about in this game, but in all honesty it doesn't exactly deserve the atrocious rap some have given it. To control Pit or your online avatar, you use the Circle Pad to move, dash or sidestep, and the L Button to fire attacks. Pressing and holding L fires continuous shots (better at long range, obviously) while it can be mashed to perform melee combos up close. The stylus is used on the touch screen to dictate the crosshair and aim fire; you can also make quick swishes and sweeps to change the direction you're facing. This might sound wonky at first and yes, admittedly, it's unlikely anyone will be playing this game for long without some kind of solid surface beneath the console. Luckily, Kid Icarus: Uprising comes prepackaged with a free Nintendo 3DS stand, which allows you to prop the 3DS up at a certain height and maintain it at eye level. This not only makes playing the game much easier, but it also greatly decreases the likelihood of losing the top screen's 3D sweet spot. The stand is also frankly very likely to come in handy for other games that make heavy use of the stylus and touch screen. Players will also have the option of customizing various settings, including the control scheme, to their preferences (left-handed players can use buttons as a D-pad, etc.); there is also Circle Pad Pro compatibility. Although the controls will take some getting used to for most players, once you're accustomed you'll be zipping around while maintaining solid control over your character.

It's quite rare that we come across a video game with passion; i.e. one you can tell the developers put a great deal of time, effort and diligent care into. Kid Icarus: Uprising is one such game. It is a beautiful game, plain and simple; with a startlingly impressive variety of modes, content, charming storyline, endearing characters, and that one little thing that tends to matter most-that desire to keep coming back to it again and again-it is an absolute must-have title, and could frankly easily go down as one of Nintendo's all-time classics (which is no small statement). If you own a 3DS and don't have this game, you really should stop reading this review and go experience one of the greatest games available right now.

Mario Tennis Open, the latest installment in Mario's sports spinoff series, is modeled very closely after its GameCube predecessor (which had a Wii rerelease), Mario Power Tennis, but its straightforward, skill-based gameplay recalls the original Mario Tennis 64. It's overall a strong addition to the series, and it makes the intelligent move of offering an online multiplayer mode, which provides a replayability factor never before seen in any Mario sports title aside from Mario Strikers Charged. Unfortunately, however, a handful of substantial setbacks will make many players yearn for what could (and should) have been.

If you've played any previous Mario Tennis title, chances are you'll be familiar with how everything works: you select your favorite Mario character and take him or her out on the court, with the intention of defeating one or two opponents at a match of tennis. You can perform a variety of different types of shots depending on the button you press or panel you tap on the touchscreen; the longer you hold the button or touchscreen panel before releasing, the more of a charge your shot will gain (i.e. it will travel farther and faster). Be cautious when charging, however, because you'll have limited mobility, although you can cancel a charge with the L Button. There are a total of six different shot types (including topspin, slice, lob, and more), each of which have different speeds, spins and bounces. You'll also have the option of pressing the X Button to make a "Simple Shot," which automatically chooses the best shot for you, albeit with weakened power. Just like in real tennis, you'll want to aim and choose your shots wisely to get the ball past your opponent.

You can move your character around the court and aim your shots with the Circle Pad, although a somewhat bizarre new control scheme allows for gyroscope controls in which you get a first-person view and aim the ball by tilting your 3DS in the desired direction (your character moves toward the ball automatically in this mode, which makes for cheap advantages in certain situations but an awkward sense of focus in others). The 3D features automatically shut off for this mode, and the game in fact detects the angle you're holding the 3DS and automatically switches between these two control schemes/angles depending on whether you're holding it downwards or upright; this is honestly obnoxious and highly distracting if you end up making any kind of major movements while playing, but luckily you can shut this feature off in settings.

Throughout each match you'll notice Chance Shot panels, which are circular, multicolored spots that light up in specific areas on the court. Each one represents an opportunity to make a powered-up version of a certain type of shot. Red Fire Flower panels light the ball on fire, making the ball travel extremely quick and push your opponent backward a great deal if they receive it; you'll have to be standing within the panel and input the proper shot command to use these, meaning pressing A in a Fire Flower panel makes for this powered-up topspin. Blue Blooper panels allow for superpowered slices that have a wicked curve, while purple Star panels allow for high-speed flat shots. You'll definitely want to utilize the Chance Shots as often as possible, as they're frequently a key factor in winning matches. Additionally, they are great tools for taking foes by surprise; the panel will light up more brightly as you charge the accompanying shot, which your opponent will likely be preparing for by then. This does not mean, however, that you can't change shots at the last minute and throw them off, which can make for a suspenseful guessing game to keep foes on their toes. Little opportunities for strategic moves like this are a nice touch.

Most of these spinoffs shamelessly abuse the opportunity to highlight the sheer wackiness of Mario's universe; i.e., whether you're swinging a bat, driving a go-kart, or kicking a ball around, if it's happening in a Mario game, you expect that the real focus will be on the random chaos of airborne Koopa shells, lightning bolts, invincibility-granting Stars and other wild items and abilities. Unexpectedly, however, Mario Tennis Open heavily downplays these elements, choosing instead to focus more on pretty simplistic bouts of mostly ordinary tennis. While this does oftentimes allow for a greater implementation of strategy, there's something disappointing about the lack of character-specific individuality or any opportunities to spice things up Mario-style on the court. Mario Power Tennis's Power Shots were occasionally overpowered and came with somewhat distracting cutscene animations, but they gave some great pizzazz and additional reasons to choose specific characters. I was personally hoping they'd return in this installment, but sadly they don't.

This isn't to say the characters all play identically, however; each character has a specific skill set, or more accurately a dominant "trait" that defines their play style. Yoshi and Diddy Kong are based in "Speed," meaning they can swiftly move around the court at a moment's notice, while Donkey Kong and Bowser are "Power" characters, meaning their shots are fast, powerful and slightly more difficult to receive. There are a variety of other traits featuring different strengths, including "Tricky," "Defense," and more. The roster is appreciatively large, featuring pretty much all of Mario's finest, and there are even a good handful of unlockable hidden characters, most of whom are very welcome additions (spoiler: Luma becomes a playable character for the first time!). You also have the option of playing as your own Mii, whose stats become customizable depending on the gear you equip them with (more on that later).

Mario Tennis Open offers a decent variety of modes to explore, although some are better than others and sadly there is no RPG-themed 1-Player mode; instead we get a fairly straightforward Tournament mode in which you play against AI opponents in a series of cups, a la Mario Kart. The Tournaments are alright, but pretty simplistic; you have the option of playing either Singles or Doubles, the latter of which requires you to team up with an AI partner and take on two opponents instead of one in each match. The CPU opponents become progressively more competitive without ever reaching outrageous levels of cheapness; the final cup should give you a real run for your money, but it won't have you pulling your hair out like certain other rage-inducing Mario spinoffs (Strikers, cough). When you beat an Open's final cup, your character will become a Star Character, awarding them a slight boost in power (you'll want to take only Star Characters into highly competitive online matches, FYI).

There's also a series of quirky mini-games in which you play matches under certain conditions or gimmickry. In Ring Shot, you score points by whacking the ball through a series of golden rings that appear sporadically throughout the court, while Ink Showdown pits you up against a single opponent while ink-spitting Piranha Plants distract you in the background. A particularly nice novelty is that presented by Super Mario Tennis, in which you "play" through levels of the original Super Mario Bros. using the ball to smash enemies and collect coins or power-ups. Most difficult of all is Galaxy Rally, in which you must hit the ball to certain spots on the court as portions of it vanish. These games are pretty nifty, but it's unfortunate that they are the only way to unlock most of the hidden goodies. If you're interested in any of the hidden characters or want to collect coins to purchase Mii accessories, the only way to do so is by playing through these mini-games.

The aforementioned accessories include rackets, wristbands, and a variety of other goodies that you can use to deck out your playable Mii character, and its stats will change depending on what you have it wear. There is admittedly a very nice variety of suits, rackets and more to make for pretty nifty customization (I personally favor the Superstar racket and Ice Flower wristbands). Unfortunately, however, the accessories are useless if you're not planning on playing as your Mii, and it's very difficult to understand how exactly the equipment will change your stats, because the information is presented in a series of awkwardly designed pie charts.

The online mode is likely the game's biggest draw and what will keep you coming back for more; you can play either with friends or against random people in a "quick" match or extended series of sets. Unfortunately the developers of Mario Tennis Open did not learn from Kid Icarus Uprising's mistake, as you still cannot play with both friends and random people. The online mode is still pretty addictive, although be warned, the level of competitiveness varies wildly. You'll be able to see monthly leaderboards of the best players, as well as your own Rating, which increases or depletes depending on whether you win or lose matches (you'll also get a medal featuring your opponent's Mii if you beat them).

Overall, the game certainly offers addictive, simple fun, shining particularly in its online and multiplayer modes. The mini-games and customizable accessories are also a very nice touch. Unfortunately, however, the straightforward gameplay can wear thin, particularly throughout the progressively tedious Tournament mode, and the series of small missteps really add up as a whole package. It does ultimately serve its core purpose as a nice handheld version of Mario Tennis featuring a solid online multiplayer, but for some it may end up being little more than a placeholder while we wait on Paper Mario and New Super Mario Bros. 2.

Lollipop Chainsaw is one of those rare games that is a sheer spectacle, defined solely by its intoxicating imagery and firmly established tone. Games of this type, however, commonly tend to encounter that little problem when the gimmick of the shiny surface eventually wears off and the gameplay becomes responsible for reeling in players for the long haul. As most critics have already told many of you, the game is certainly not fantastic, but it really shouldn't be passed up either. Developed by Grasshopper Manufacture as a resulting collaboration of game designer Goichi Suda and filmmaker James Gunn, the game inevitably arrived amidst a sea of comparisons, whether they be Goichi Suda's games (Killer7, Shadows of the Damned, No More Heroes, not to mention his partial involvement in Super Smash Bros. Brawl) or Gunn's movies (Dawn of the Dead, Slither, Super). While this game certainly features dark, twisted undertones echoing both developers' respective creativities, I'll warn everyone beforehand that making too many comparisons to the spectacle that is Lollipop Chainsaw would be unwise. No, this game deserves to be analyzed in its own light, within the "confines" of its own bewildering, nonsensical universe.

In a nutshell, the game is a mish-mash concoction of scantily clad cheerleaders, zombie apocalypse gore, and lots and lots of rainbows and sparkles. It treads a very unique line between bloody hack-and-slash and simplistic childlike glee. If its creative team didn't draw you in, its explosive concept most likely will. The concept is this: blonde, busty, lollipop-loving cheerleader Juliet Starling awakens on the morning of her eighteenth birthday only to discover the beginning of a zombie apocalypse in her town, as hordes of her classmates transform into the undead and roam the city in search of human flesh. Luckily for her, she just so happens to come from a family of professional zombie hunters, something she hasn't yet revealed to her not-so-long-term boyfriend Nick Carlyle. As she heads out to meet up with him this same morning, he's attacked and bitten by one of the zombies. In order to prevent him from becoming a living corpse himself, Juliet severs his body from the neck down and casts a spell to keep him alive as a disembodied head (a nifty trick she picked up via zombie hunting excursions past, surely). Armed with a keychain of her boyfriend's head and an enormous chainsaw adorned with pink hearts, Juliet sets out to defeat the zombies and find out who's behind all this apocalyptic brouhaha.

The combat system is predominantly combo-based, as Juliet strings together various attacks to cripple the undead offenders. Cheerleading-themed pom-pom bashes and kicks make for swift, light attacks that can be quickly strung together to stun enemies, while heavy chainsaw slashes tend to be slower but deal heavier damage. The primary goal is to get zombies "groggy," at which point they'll be temporarily stunned as stars circle their heads, and become much more vulnerable to attack. Pom-pom and cheerleading attacks excel at getting zombies groggy or pushing them back, while chainsaw slashes are usually what finish them off. Each bloody slash of Juliet's chainsaw is accompanied by flurries of sparkles, rainbows, and hearts, a plucky and pretty hilarious contrast to the game's mega-violence. As you proceed through the game, defeat zombies and save citizens from zombie attacks, you'll be awarded gold and platinum coins, the in-game currency which can be used to purchase new combos and attacks, health or strength boosts, and more. You'll also collect various flavors of lollipops throughout the stages; you can hold five maximum at one time, as each one can instantly recover a portion of Juliet's health as needed.

Juliet's chainsaw will eventually become adorned with new equipment and features, allowing her to perform different types of stunts and abilities for hacking up zombies. My personal favorite is the Chainsaw Dash, which allows her to sprint forward at full speed while mowing down zombies in her way, all the while using boost panels to make high jumps across platforms and collect coins and other goodies. You'll also eventually be able to use Nick's head to attack zombies, or even place it on headless zombie bodies to briefly gain control of them. Lollipop Chainsaw's boss battles are generally quite memorable, as punky, wild-haired "zombie rock gods" enter various phases and initiate wild attack patterns.

As Juliet kills zombies, she builds star meter, displayed at the bottom left of the screen. Once it's filled, you can activate Star Soul mode at your leisure, at which point Juliet glows with a rainbowy light, temporarily gaining invincibility and super-strength, set giddily to the soundtrack of Toni Basil's "Mickey." Star Soul mode makes for some of the flashiest, most addictive gameplay offered here-it's a shame the feature is somewhat under-utilized. Another nice feature is "Sparkle Hunting," which activates when Juliet flashily destroys three or more zombies. This triggers a cutscene of Juliet within a glittering background, and you'll be awarded coins depending on how impressive your attack combo was (this also substantially boosts your score/rating). Star Soul mode and Sparkle Hunting oftentimes go hand in hand, as more devastating combos and damage outputs are easier when Star Soul is active.

There are also a variety of options for customization, as you'll over time be able to change Juliet's outfits and even build the soundtrack playlist of your choosing as you play through the stages. The game's spunky soundtrack is among its brightest assets, featuring a cheeky blend of old-school pop, electro-punk and nu-metal. Mindless Self Indulgence, Skrillex, Sleigh Bells, MSTRKRFT, Dead or Alive, Joan Jett, and even 50's pop quartet The Chordettes are just some examples of the vast variety of musical acts you'll be enjoying throughout this game. The soundtrack compliments the extreme irony/silliness of the plot, and helps remind you that Lollipop Chainsaw never once requests to be taken seriously (important to remember, given that certain aspects of the game, particularly the heavy sexualizing of Juliet's character and the accompanying insults hurled her way by other characters, may offend certain players who aren't open to such humor; and be warned, you'll be seeing quite a bit of Juliet's chest and panties).

While this should all sound like a great deal of joyous fun (which it mostly is), Lollipop Chainsaw's missteps can be quite glaring. The nastiest offenders are some of the awkwardly-designed mini-games, which you'll be forced to play through to advance through certain stages. Some of these diversions from the ordinary hack-and-slash gameplay can be fun and add some nice variety, but they're mostly obnoxious buzzkills that harshly stall the momentum. Some examples include weirdly-structured bouts of zombie-themed basketball and baseball, in which you have to destroy zombies in a specific way to score a certain amount of points within a brief time limit, or protect a base runner from oncoming zombies with a chainsaw machinegun that can be awfully hard to aim/control. What ultimately renders these mini-games big stinkers is the fact that you die if you lose, meaning your score and final stage rating can be totally screwed over not because you died at the hands of enemy attacks, but because you lost a wonky mini-game. These really should have been left out and at their worst are totally infuriating.

Additionally, this game is comparatively speaking extremely short; the basic campaign should take most players only between five to eight hours total, and the replay factor can really dwindle from there, since there's no real online play or post-game content. However, the aforementioned end-of-stage ratings are uploaded to national leaderboards, so if you want to get really hardcore you do have the option of competing for the highest scores and see how you rank against other players (or Juliet's dad, the in-game `high score' standard). As previously mentioned, however, these rankings plummet if you die, meaning no matter how many zombies you defeat or goodies you sniff out and unlock, the mini-games can troll you into oblivion. Another of this game's biggest problems is its occasionally terrible camera angling-there's nothing worse than being cornered by hordes of enemies and suddenly having your screen view shift to a random close-up of a wall, which happens far more than it should here. You can manually move the camera, but there are times when you can't, and even when you can the movement tends to be slow, awkward and can be dangerously distracting in intense combat sequences.

Speaking of the combat, although it can make for fluid fun and fantastic visuals, some players may notice that certain chainsaw attacks are slow and clunky, and some animations are required to finish before new attacks can be initiated, which can be a big problem in major zombie hordes. In addition to this, certain powerful combos aren't unlocked until near the game's end, many of which really should've just been available from the start to allow for wider variation from the simple, clunky attacks you'll have to rely on early on (which can ironically make the difficulty level go in reverse as you progressively have more to utilize). This certainly doesn't make or break the game, but it can take more getting used to than some may prefer, depending on personal play styles.

Offsetting many of these flaws is the snappy script and dialogue; regardless of its ups and downs, a big goofy smile will be plastered on most players' faces throughout a vast majority of this game, not only because of the bedazzling aesthetics, but because much of the character banter is genuinely hilarious. Juliet somehow manages to be ditzy and witty all at the same time, while Nick is highly endearing as a wisecracking head; the two will banter continuously throughout the stages, and there's no shortage of random gags. Most of the characters are real gems as well, including Juliet's badass zombie-hunting sisters and the consistently entertaining zombie rock gods. The voice acting is also quite memorable, with Juliet being voiced by the well-known Tara Strong (Rugrats, Powerpuff Girls, Princess Mononoke, Teen Titans) and Michael Rosenbaum (Smallville, It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia, Batman Beyond) as Nick. The storyline, despite its absurdity, also comes together as something surely to develop into a major cult classic (I particularly liked the concept of the universe being split into three realms, and the explanation of the zombies escaping from the "Rotten World").

As I said at the very beginning, this game is indeed a total spectacle, dedicated to blissful fun and entertainment, and that's what has to be understood from the get-go. Its sole purpose is to entertain and bewilder, and that it does very well. This game is designed for laughter and cheap thrills, of which it does offer many. Although it's arguably shorter and occasionally clunkier than it should be, it's such a wild, glitzy ride that it really has to be experienced by most gamers. I'm anticipating a big cult following and a great deal of cosplay inspiration to come. Who knew lollipops and chainsaws were such a nice match?

Although avid Pokemon fans awaiting a 3DS installment (or simply one with 3D models instead of 2D sprites) may have to swallow their disappointment for a bit longer, we have on our hands a truly delightful spinoff to tide us over for the time being. Pokemon Conquest (a Nintendo DS game, playable in 2D on the 3DS, as Nintendo likes to remind everyone) is a highly addictive, deeply strategic RPG modeled closely after the chess-like gameplay of Final Fantasy Tactics. It features a storyline that blends Pokemon-themed fantasy with real-life historical figures from the Sengoku period of feudal Japan (two concepts one wouldn't ordinarily think to mash together). Startlingly, it works very well, and shapes into what is easily the best Pokemon spinoff ever.

You begin the game as an aspiring warrior in the land of Ransei, in which there is a legend of a warlord capable of summoning the legendary Pokemon that created the region by conquering and claiming all 17 of its kingdoms. Throughout this land, each warrior and warlord has the ability to communicate with Pokemon and engage them in battle, but only the Pokemon they have the highest compatibility ("link") with can best serve them in combat. The storyline borrows elements from Koei's Nobunaga's Ambition series (Koei also played a role in the game's development) and peppers them with the collectability factor and addictive battle mechanics of the Pokemon franchise. As you may guess from the storyline, your primary goal is to engage in a series of battles against various kingdoms in an effort to awaken the mysterious creationist Pokemon before the ruthless warlord Nobunaga (the game's primary antagonist, based off of real-life Oda Nobunaga, a major daimyo in the late 16th century) beats you to it.

The combat system is turn-based, like many traditional RPGs, and like the aforementioned Final Fantasy Tactics, you'll spend each turn advancing a certain number of spaces throughout the stage, and must be within range of an opponent in order to inflict damage with attacks. Different Pokemon have different attack and movement ranges, so you'll have to keep this in mind as you progress, since you'll want to advance toward your opponents without leaving yourself within their line of fire whenever possible. Fans of JRPGs such as Fire Emblem and old-school Final Fantasy titles will be fondly familiar with these mechanics, and like those games, battles in Pokemon Conquest can feel a great deal like thoughtfully planned out bouts of chess. Although these types of games can ordinarily turn off gamers who aren't into intense strategy, Pokemon Conquest impressively manages to coax newbies into easily understanding the mechanics all while building upon its array of thoughtful complexity and creative nuances. I myself was largely unfamiliar with this type of battle system and was notably doubtful as to how much I'd enjoy it, but after playing for hours and gaining much deeper understanding, I can wholeheartedly say I'm hooked.

For Pokemaniacs, most of the beloved gameplay elements are retained-there are still type weaknesses and strengths (Fire types still take extra damage from Water type attacks, and so forth), which you'll of course have to consider before sending your team into battle, in addition to character-specific abilities which activate in various scenarios and can be highly useful in specific situations. What adds a nice bit of zest to this is that in addition to the Pokemon having abilities, each warrior (trainer) has his or her own ability as well, which can be used only once per match. This is once again something worth considering in regard to which Pokemon you partner them up with and what teams you place them on, as abilities that increase defense, heal HP or cure status ailments may of course be better suited to certain teams and scenarios than others. You can also once again use items like Potions to heal HP or elemental stones to evolve (yes, Pokemon do evolve in this game, for those wondering). Additionally, warriors themselves evolve ("transform," more accurately) once they've gained strong enough partner links, causing their own abilities and team capacities to improve as well. When Pokemon are a part of a winning battle, and particularly when they land finishing blows to opponents, they don't gain experience points but instead strengthen their link with their trainer, and as their link grows, so does their strength and likelihood of evolving. As previously mentioned, warriors have differing links with different Pokemon, and you'll ideally want to track down the Pokemon that your trainers have 100% (maximum) compatibility with. Pokemon with lower compatibilities can still become powerful, but their strength will max out earlier than desired (a 70% compatibility Quagsire, for example, will stop gaining strength once its trainer link reaches 70, as where one with full compatibility could have continued growing).

Therein lies Pokemon's famous collectability; upon defeating each kingdom, you'll have the option of recruiting certain warriors whose Pokemon you defeated from there (the criteria for recruitment varies, as you may have to defeat certain warriors within an allotted number of turns or fulfill other requirements in order for them to become available to recruit). Each warrior may only be partnered with one Pokemon at a time in-battle, but you can add to their arsenal and switch around which one you'd like them to use (although different warriors have different team capacities, so you may have to let the less compatible ones go eventually). Some warriors are lucky enough to already have a highly compatible Pokemon by their side immediately upon recruitment, but you'll have to seek out something better for most of them. Once a kingdom is conquered, wild Pokemon (in addition to new warriors, or those you may have missed out on recruiting the first time around) will begin appearing inside. These instances will be your primary opportunities to seek out perfect matches for your warriors; a wild Pokemon's compatibility with a warrior will be displayed over their head in battle in the form of a medal; bronze indicates a low compatibility, silver equates to average, and a gold medal means the Pokemon is a great match for that warrior and is capable of a 100% link. You can link warriors with new wild Pokemon by approaching them and choosing the `Link' option, at which point you'll begin a DDR-styled mini-game in which you must press buttons at specific moments to strengthen the link. If you're successful, that Pokemon will belong to that warrior once the battle ends. You'll be able to tell which types of Pokemon to keep an eye out for based on each warrior's elemental specialty, listed in their menu profile; certain warriors favor Electric or Grass types, as where others may specialize in both Ghost and Fire. This doesn't necessarily mean every Pokemon of that type will be a perfect match for them, however, so you'll simply have to explore and experiment (i.e. pay attention to those medals)-trust me when I say 100% links are worth seeking out, because Pokemon with maxed out compatibilities become superbly powerful.

One of the greatest aspects of Pokemon Conquest's battles are their complexity-an ugly word to some gamers, but hear me out: when I say complexity, I mean the vast array of options you have to perform exciting setups, traps and defensive efforts out on the battlefield. Although certain elements of the gameplay may actually initially come off as simplistic, these in reality all come together as a beautifully cohesive whole to make for some of the most addictive, thought-provoking strategy ever presented in a Pokemon spinoff, and arguably any Pokemon game period. While in combat, you'll have to consider your opponent's types in addition to their positions on the field, since if Pokemon are attacked by an opponent they're facing away from, they take additional damage. Certain Pokemon abilities, meanwhile, must also be considered from a positional angle, since Jigglypuff's Lullaby ability can put nearby Pokemon to sleep, while Pansage's Melee ability causes adjacent opponents to randomly take damage. Because of this, you may want to use ranged attacks against specific opponents, or attack/approach them from an angle they may have difficulty retaliating from. Some Pokemon even have attack ranges that could endanger allies, so for example you'll definitely want to keep your Flying types out of your Electric type's potentially wide line of fire.

Adding to all this variety is that not all battles have the same goal; although defeating opponents is never a bad thing, each match has a limited number of turns, during which time you must complete the required goal. You'll sometimes have to claim banners throughout the stage to win, something you must accomplish before your opponent does first.
