This essentially makes for a Pokemon-ified version of capture the flag in which you must protect your own banners while seizing those your opponent has claimed as quickly as you can. There are also different stage hazards in different kingdoms, although they thankfully aren't wildly unpredictable catalysts for random or unfair chaos. No, Pokemon Conquest's stage hazards tie thematically into everything else presented here by being strategy-based first and foremost; one kingdom, for example, features a series of enormous balls placed throughout the field that can be attacked to send them bouncing down that entire row of spaces, doing substantial damage to any Pokemon in its path. Another kingdom, meanwhile, has trenches that can be filled with (or drained of) water each time a nearby button is pressed (stood on), which can once again damage Pokemon in the way. You'll want to utilize these hazards to your advantage whenever you can, while making sure to steer clear of them yourself.

Anyone obsessed with Pokemon knows that, regrettably, some of the coolest and cuddliest monsters are unfortunately ordinarily totally useless in competitive play; this is an issue remedied within Pokemon Conquest, as quite literally any Pokemon can become beastly in combat when paired with the proper warrior. So yes, anyone who's a big fan of the adorable but ordinarily weak Jigglypuff or Minccino is in for quite a treat. In all reality, Pokemon Conquest is such a comprehensive game so jam-packed full of features, it can be quite difficult to fit into one review without rambling. There are even options to delegate specific warriors to specific kingdoms to protect territories from incoming invasions (yes, after conquering so many yourself, you'll have to prepare for counterattacks later in the game), in addition to shopping options to purchase (and create by combination) some of the best items; different warriors have differing Charisma ratings, which affect how well they can exchange with shopkeepers, and you can also feed your Pokemon `Ponigiri' (this game's Poffins, more or less) to increase their strength. The calendar system makes it so that each warrior may perform only one action per month (whether that be mining for gold, shopping for items, engaging in battle or whatever else within different kingdoms), and you may manually proceed to the next month at your leisure; this system may sound wonky on paper but it in fact allows for a unique passage of time within the game and will increase your desire to thoughtfully plan out your course of action.

I have yet to experience a video game that's completely perfect, but Pokemon Conquest's setbacks are so minor that they're only barely worth mentioning. Although its graphical limitations certainly don't prevent it from being a great game, certain sprites or animations can be particularly clunky and pixelated, which may cause nitpickers to wonder what could have been on a more powerful console. Also, moving warriors around to different kingdoms (which you'll have to do fairly often, depending on what types of Pokemon appear and who you'll have to battle inside) can be a bit of a hassle, particularly if you don't remember which warriors are which or what their type specialties are; an option to more easily shift groups around in bulk or display their compatibilities/type specialties on the main screens would have been ideal. Additionally, just like each warrior can only use one Pokemon at a time, each Pokemon can only use one attack at a time, although these attacks change when they evolve, meaning if they're a dual-type, their primary attack type can change as well. This can make things a bit unpredictable and potentially unfavorable when your Dark-based Scraggy suddenly evolves into a Scrafty with a Fighting attack (meaning that Pokemon's strategy and what it can go up against may suddenly change without notice, and you may find yourself without a Dark move to rely on).

I bring the gripes up for the sole purpose of thoroughness; make no mistake, Pokemon Conquest is a fantastic game and should absolutely be owned by every Pokemon lover, in addition to anyone who enjoys RPG/strategy/battle games. Featuring an engaging storyline, incredibly addictive gameplay, wonderful anime-style artwork and the substantial replay value offered by an impressively lengthy 1-player quest in addition to a local wireless multiplayer mode (meaning yes, once you have a decent team formed you can compete with your friends in battle), Pokemon Conquest succeeds in just about every area it can. If there were to ever be a seamless introductory game to the JRPG genre with plentiful opportunity for increased strategizing and complexity, Pokemon Conquest is it. Even if you're not a big fan of the genre, give this one a try and I can almost guarantee you'll gain a newfound love.

A world filled with Disney and Final Fantasy-themed characters was certainly never something anyone asked for, but it's added up to quite the fascinating franchise in the form of Kingdom Hearts, which has always sported a distinct mixture of doe-eyed innocence and encroaching darkness. Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance marks the series' seventh installment overall, and the fifth on a handheld console. While a vast majority of the Kingdom Hearts games have been spinoffs of the primary two (with KH3 being so long delayed), oftentimes featuring storylines of side characters that generally add up to prequels or epilogues, Dream Drop Distance returns to the core storylines of main characters Sora and Riku, although it's never made entirely clear where this particular timeline falls (it is rumored, however, that this game's ending ties directly into KH3, which series director Tetsuya Nomura has supposedly insisted will be the next release). The Kingdom Hearts storyline as a whole is rather convoluted and a bit melodramatic, but very moving and thought-provoking nonetheless. For those initially unfamiliar with the finer details (like myself-this is admittedly the first KH title I've personally played), all you need to know for now is this: best friends Sora and Riku are prompted by the powerful wizard Master Yen Sid (the elderly wizard from Disney's Fantasia) to take the Mark of Mastery Exam in preparation for an approaching threat to multiple worlds. Although they both have already been awarded keyblades, powerful weapons used to correct the balance between light and darkness in the world as needed, they must complete this test before they may be deemed true Keyblade Masters and gain access to the power they'll need for the evil that approaches. This test requires them to enter a series of worlds which were in one timeline destroyed by the Heartless (physical manifestations of darkness, beings devoid of emotion, oftentimes in the guises of Disney and Final Fantasy-themed villains throughout the series) and then restored, but somewhere in between fell into a deep sleep that rendered them incapable of connecting with one another. In an effort to properly "awaken" and interconnect the worlds to restore balance once again, Sora and Riku must unlock the seven Sleeping Keyholes, each of which lies somewhere within a sleeping world.

Early on in this test, the bright-eyed Sora and brooding Riku are separated from one another, hurled into separate versions of the same worlds. This adds up to separate but interconnecting timelines in which different events occur in the same locations/periods, which also ties directly into the gameplay: in KH3D, you'll spend half the time playing as Sora and half the time playing as Riku, each of whom maintains his own separate progression in each world. This is a unique feature that also incorporates the new "Drop" system, which sets off a timer each time you begin adventuring with one of the two heroes. This `timer' comes in the form of the Drop Gauge, which slowly depletes but can reduce or increase quicker depending on what types of items or techniques you use. Once the Drop Gauge hits zero and your time's up, your current character will "Drop," at which point he'll immediately stop whatever it is he's doing and retreat into a sleeping state; then the storyline will switch and you can begin playing as the other character with his own renewed Drop Gauge. This might sound wonky at first but it actually adds an exciting sense of urgency and time progression, encouraging you not to neglect one storyline in favor of the other (they both thankfully tend to remain pretty engaging). You can use items such as Drop-Me-Nots to extend the duration of your Drops, and you can also Drop at will as needed, but keep in mind what you do in one storyline can sometimes affect the other: throughout battles you'll collect Drop Points, which can be used at the end of each Drop to give various boosts to the character you're switching over to, such as increases in attack power, defense, Drop duration and more. You sometimes won't be able to advance to the next section of the world map until you complete a world with both Sora and Riku, so there are many tactical decisions to consider throughout each Drop. My only gripe about this feature is the fact that if you Drop during a boss battle, you'll have to start it over when you Drop back, which can expectedly be really obnoxious, especially for lengthy ones. Because of this I'd recommend keeping watch of your Drop Gauge especially before specific encounters and equipping Drop-Me-Nots as needed.

The combat in KH3D is very fast-paced and exciting, and definitely among the game's brightest highlights. Somewhat like a mish-mash of popular MMOs, Kid Icarus: Uprising and various Legend of Zelda titles, you'll rely on different types of melee weapons (i.e. keyblades) and magic spells to attack enemies from either afar or in the fray. KH3D marks the return of the battle deck, a handy system that allows you to set a customizable series of attacks and abilities for use on the battlefield. You can create separate decks (such as one focused mainly on fire-based attacks, one mainly on healing HP, a balanced mix of everything, etc.) and whip them out from the Pause menu as needed. The deck automatically switches through your magic in the order you select from the deck creation menu as you use each ability; you can also use the D-pad to manually backtrack or swap around mid-combat to particular ones, but each move has a cooldown period you'll have to wait through before a successive use. Expectedly, very powerful/useful abilities have longer cooldowns, so you'll have to consider this when building your decks. There are a vast variety of magic abilities, with spells that can set foes aflame, freeze them, trap them in midair gravity vortexes, home in on them from afar, cure your HP or relieve you of status conditions and much more. Veterans of the series will fondly remember the igniting Firaga, electrifying Thundara and ever-useful Curaga. As you progress through the game you'll earn different and increasingly powerful magic spells for your deck in addition to new keyblades for slashing melee strikes. The X button is used to call forth magic spells from your deck while the A button initiates physical attacks and keyblade combos. With several dozen types of enemies and bosses with varying resistances and weaknesses (as you might expect, water-based foes tend to feel the hurt against electricity and icy enemies don't fancy fire), there's a lot to consider (and enjoy).

An importantly integrated new feature is that of the Dream Eaters, colorful, cuddly critters found commonly as both friends and foes throughout the game. Friendly Dream Eaters are known as Spirits, and they will be absolutely essential to your arsenal in combat. You can create Spirits from Dream Pieces you gather as you battle, and there are a great deal of recipes that make for all types of useful creatures, whether it be an HP-recovering flower or ferocious T-Rex. This adds a very Pokémon-esque element to the game as you level up your Spirits to become stronger and gain new powerful abilities as they fight alongside you in each and every battle. You'll use a Final Fantasy-inspired Ability Link table to progressively unlock new abilities, which will also have direct effects on Sora and Riku. Spirit abilities can in fact come in the form of stat boosts, so using certain Spirits who've gained certain abilities can allow increased resistances to certain attack types or even immunities to certain status conditions. In other words, these little guys can offer both an offensive and defensive edge. They can also unlock brand new magic spells for Sora and Riku to use, in addition to their own attacks to initiate mid-battle. In order to increase a Spirit's Link Points (used to progress through their Ability Link table and gain new abilities), you'll have to play with and feed them, very similar to a Nintendog or a Tamagotchi. You do so by petting them on the touchscreen with your stylus from the pause menu, which is also where you can toss them cakes, cookies and other treats to increase their stats. While it's adorable at first, it becomes tedious as the game progresses, and the fact that it's the only way to push Spirits to their maximum potential becomes pretty obnoxious. Thankfully the Spirits are at least very nice to look at, with quite literally every one sporting colorful, detailed and ultra-cute designs (you'll be very motivated to catch `em all). Be warned, by the way: prevent your Spirit from dying in battle at all costs, because if it does, it reverts back into Dream Pieces. You can recreate it, but it will lose all of its learned abilities and start back at its initial level. Luckily you'll be warned when they're in danger, and you'll have the opportunity to go save them (this also won't be a problem nearly as often as you might think unless you take low level Spirits into intense fights).

One of the greatest features of Spirits is the ability you'll have to "Link" with them; as they fight with you and gain affinity for you (which happens as you battle with them often, play with and feed them), their Link Gauge, which is displayed on the touchscreen, increases. Once it's hit its maximum, you can tap the Spirit's icon to Link with it, which can cause one of two in-battle events depending on who you're playing as. Sora becomes able to initiate a series of super-attacks (or one single powerful one) with the Spirit itself for a certain period, while Riku physically merges with the Spirit and gains one of its abilities himself. If both Link Gauges are full, you can even Link with both of your Spirits at once for an even more devastating Link attack. The Link abilities range from showering the battlefield in damaging light while fully healing your entire party to swishing around with bat wings and initiating lethal dark magic-infused combos. The individual and combo Links vary depending on your Spirits, and it's great fun to experiment with them and their bedazzling visuals.

Another new feature exclusive to KH3D is Flowmotion, a unique ability that allows Sora and Riku to air dash and launch themselves off walls to climb up them, attack enemies, or move very quickly throughout the area. You can also use Flowmotion to swing around poles or slide along grind rails. This is a very welcome addition and should in all honesty become a series staple, as it allows for fantastic maneuverability and thrilling battle sequences. Although it can feel unwieldy at first, once you've practiced a bit you just might start to wonder how you progressed through any game ever without it. Reality Shifts, meanwhile, allow Sora and Riku to enter portals that allow them to bend the rules of time and space; activate one and gameplay will shift to the touchscreen, initiating one of several mini-games (they differ by world) tying into the current theme; cracking codes in Tron: Legacy's Grid will allow you to manipulate surrounding technology, while you can create unhappy comic endings for cartoony baddies in the Country of the Musketeers. Features like this offer some very exciting gameplay changeups throughout.

As KH fans have surely come to expect, you'll progress through a series of Disney-themed worlds featuring familiar scenery, characters and self-contained story arcs (the best of which tie into the central plot). Tron: Legacy and Pinocchio all make for beautiful backdrops, but I was never personally the biggest fan of Hunchback of Notre Dame (although it does make for some well-designed stage terrain and shockingly dark storyline action), and The Three Musketeers was flat out a poor choice (it is overall the dullest, most inane world here). The Fantasia world in particular, however, features an array of intoxicating visual splendor, and the fact that most sound effects are shut off in favor of the warmly familiar musical scores makes for a truly immersive thematic experience. The thrilling, heart-racing, generally epic boss battles at the end of each world are among the game's most memorable highlights, featuring once again a mix of Disney/Square Enix-themed baddies. You'll see some awesome familiar faces in addition to some startling new ones.

Along the lines of flaws, there certainly are a few but thankfully nothing prevents the game from being generally great. For one, the game unfortunately sports a particularly wonky and uncooperative camera that ordinarily has to be manually moved to the direction most people would prefer (a problem I've heard has actually been plaguing most of the series). You can lock on to specific enemies to make focal points easier to keep track of, but occasionally your lock will seemingly cancel at random, which can prove very frustrating in intense boss battles. Additionally, while most of this RPG's platforming is pretty smooth, oddball ticks in stage environments can make for off-kilter interaction, as you may be unable to jump on or Flowmotion across certain things you'd strongly expect to be able to. There are also odd and vaguely sporadic instances of lag after using certain attacks and particularly after blocking attacks; Sora and Riku will sometimes behave as though they are briefly stunned from shielding, particularly after using several successive attacks or when there's a lot going on. Whether this was intentional or not, at its worst your movement will feel clunky in spurts (which can be a total buzzkill in the frantic pace of certain boss fights). Keep in mind, however, that KH3D's strengths so far outshine its weaknesses that very, very few players are likely to walk away sincerely saying they were wholeheartedly dissatisfied with the overall experience.

KH3D as a whole is overall glorious to behold, with beautifully rendered cutscenes featuring spot-on voice acting (much of the star-studded original cast returns) and a generally gorgeous visual style ensuring you're never bored with what you see onscreen. This game really shows what the 3DS is capable of, and what will hopefully be further utilized in the future. Although its storyline strays a bit far from the core plot at times and will definitely confuse newbies, everything comes together during its particularly epic conclusion, as things fluidly segue into what all KH fans have been eagerly waiting for. Whether you're a dedicated longtime fan or a 3DS owner looking for some fast-paced, aesthetically pleasing action, Kingdom Hearts 3D is an absolute must-have.

For a solid decade or so (about 1996 to 2007, to be precise), everyone's favorite turtle-stomping plumber had a rather experimental phase and went on a nice handful of decidedly different adventures. There was the epic Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars that all but redefined what people could expect from a Mario game, and of course Super Mario 64 that did the exact same thing all over again. Although Super Mario Sunshine was released on Nintendo's least commercially successful console and received a rather mixed consumer response, it was a nice divergence in tone, theme, and gameplay, even featuring fully voice acted cutscenes and other major rarities in the franchise. Additionally, I'm sure every platforming addict fondly remembers the more recent Super Mario Galaxy with its gravity-defying planetoids, thrilling intergalactic air rides and cast of endearing new characters. That was about where the Mario Innovation Train came to a screeching halt, however, as pretty much every installment that followed was based almost exclusively on throwback nostalgia and slight expansions of the overly familiar, whether it be New Super Mario Bros. Wii or Super Mario Galaxy 2. The Mario franchise hasn't seen any particularly notable innovations or changeups since 2007's Galaxy, which is a shame given how many new opportunities have arisen technologically and otherwise. New Super Mario Bros. 2, the first 2D Mario platformer on the 3DS, decidedly continues the trend with this bazillionth side-scrolling, Goomba-stomping quest to save Peach from Bowser.

While I understand that a massive portion of Mario's appeal has always been his nostalgia factor (and am absolutely a self-admitted Mario addict myself), I for one am growing tired of Nintendo's recent recurring trend of trying to recapture the 90's glory days in the form of lazy rehashes that feature pitifully low quantities of anything wholeheartedly new. I agree that traditional Mario platformers will never grow old, but a big part of what made them so appealing to begin with was their consistent trailblazing within the genre and even the industry as a whole. The original Super Mario Bros. games were each very different from one another in different ways, and although the big picture remained similar, each installment introduced dramatic shifts in design and gameplay (particularly given the hardware limitations at the time). As of right now, however, I don't feel that there's much difference at all between the New Super Mario Bros. titles, already in their third overall installment (with a fourth on the way, which looks incredibly samey as well). There are differentiations between the level of multiplayer emphasis and one or two new(ish) power-ups, but beyond that it's a patterned sequence of monotony. This is a particularly glaring issue when you realize that the exact same music, sound bites and 3D models are all being routinely reused. The soundtrack of New Super Mario Bros. 2 is ripped directly from previous installments, and veterans will find the desert, plains and title screen themes all too familiar.

The good news is, as it always has been, Mario platforming is pretty much 2D platforming at its very best; players will still be delighted by the intuitively responsive control scheme and whimsical stage design, ideally crafted for exploration and crawling with equally well-designed baddies. You'll still be wall-jumping, ground-pounding and pipe-plunging your way to the princess, and for the most part it's still a great deal of carefree fun, particularly when teaming up with a friend.

As most of you have surely heard by now, the big overarching theme this time around is coin collecting, something that has technically always been a staple in pretty much every Mario game. In this installment, however, it's pushed to the forefront as you'll literally be showered in coins at every corner; enemies cough them up, they spout from pipes and blocks, and there's even a power-up that gives Mario the Midas touch, i.e. the ability to transform the enemies and environments around him into shimmering gold coins. The big supposed goal is to ultimately collect a million of them throughout the course of the game, as you continuously add to your ever-growing coin count while you gather them in each stage. There doesn't seem to be any particular reward for achieving any of this, however, because you'll receive little more than congratulatory screens for each quantitative goal you reach. Additionally, 100 coins still earns you an extra life, and since they're literally everywhere in this game, most players will have hundreds of lives within a matter of hours. This means the once-coveted 1-Up doesn't add up to much of anything, and unless you're truly, truly terrible at this game, it's quite easy to play through the whole campaign without ever once seeing the Game Over screen. This definitely doesn't mean the game itself is a total cakewalk or that you can expect to never die, but it's much less devastating when you have an endless pool of lives to prevent any Game Overs.

Coin Rush is the new mode that utilizes the 3DS's StreetPass feature, allowing you to dash through a series of three randomly selected stages while collecting as many coins as you possibly can. You can share your best times and totals with other 3DS owners, but this all comes off to me like a rather self-contained mini-game (it doesn't affect your in-game progress and I'm not even sure the coins collected in this mode are added to your base total), so I haven't spent much time with it. The big golden coin motif sounds gimmicky because it is, but at its best it adds a nice thematic sheen to the design and gameplay (the golden ring that transforms all enemies and parts of the surrounding environment into sparkling gold is a particularly nice touch).

Many of Mario's most familiar power-ups return in NSMB2, including the Super Mushroom, Fire Flower and Tanooki Leaf, the latter of which finally once again grants the power of flight, a welcome addition to most any game. The shrinking Mini Mushroom and environment-crushing Mega Mushroom also make occasional appearances, but they're unfortunately rarely seen. The only actual "new" power-up is the Gold Flower, which turns Mario's entire body into gold and allows him to hurl enormous golden fireballs that explode on impact, transforming any enemies or blocks in their path into coins. Despite what it looks like, this power-up does not grant invincibility, and Mario is still vulnerable to attacks in this form. This is admittedly a pretty exciting ability, but unfortunately it's a tad under-utilized and only lasts the duration of a level or until Mario gets hit, at which point it vanishes. There is also the pseudo-power-up Golden Block that functions similarly, attaching itself to Mario's head and spouting more and more coins depending on how quickly he's moving.

The multiplayer mode in NSMB2 is fun, albeit less successful than the one featured in New Super Mario Bros. Wii for a handful of reasons. For one, it is limited to two players, both of whom must have a 3DS *and* their own copy of the game to play. The camera is also a bit wonky in this mode, swapping back and forth between a single "focus" character, meaning Mario and Luigi can't go off to explore on their own (ironic, give the separate screens) or even stray too far from the focal character without risking sudden death from traveling too far off-screen. There is no online compatibility (yet another sadly missed opportunity), only local wireless, meaning the person you play with has to be physically near you. The progress can also only be tracked on one player's save file (unless you start an entirely separate one for multiplayer, which can still only be saved to the first player's game), meaning all progress in multiplayer is meaningless for whoever plays as Luigi (the guy just can't get a break). The coins collected, however, are transferable. Although this sounds like a lot of griping, the mode still makes for quite a bit of silly multiplayer madness and is worth trying out, but it's not a defining feature like it was with NSMBW.

The 3D capability of the console is pretty much wholeheartedly wasted on this title, as NSMB2 is easily the worst and weakest use of the feature I have yet to see on the 3DS. It wouldn't be fantastically far-fetched to say this could have probably been a regular DS port. This doesn't mean it looks terrible, but beyond a slight sense of depth between forefront and background, there's little actual 3D to be seen here (and you may flat out prefer to turn the slider completely off to reduce the unfortunate blurring of scenery that occurs otherwise).

New Super Mario Bros. 2 is a quaintly entertaining game, and anyone ravenous for Mario platforming should get a decent fix from it; unfortunately, it doesn't offer anything truly new, and if you were bored with any of the previous New Super Mario titles, steer clear of this one because it's absolutely no different. Although sandy deserts, lava-flowing castles and puzzling ghost houses will always have their charm, here's hoping Nintendo spices things up next time around, because nostalgia can only be stretched so thin.

It's hard to believe it's been a whopping 20 years since the world's most famous pink puffball, Kirby, broke out on the scene. Speaking as someone who's played just about every one of his games ever since, I was delighted to hear that the little guy's birthday was being celebrated with Kirby's Dream Collection, which cherry-picks several of his most commercially successful titles into one package. Given the lackluster disaster that was Nintendo's "acknowledgement" of Mario's 25th anniversary with Super Mario All-Stars: Limited Edition (which was little more than a sloppy port), expectations might be low, but thankfully this collection does its birthday boy right-for the most part.

The collection includes most of Kirby's best-known games; there are the Game Boy titles Kirby's Dream Land and Kirby's Dream Land 2, Kirby's Adventure of the NES, Kirby Super Star and Kirby's Dream Land 3 of the SNES, and Nintendo 64's Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards. If you're among the select few experiencing these games for the first time, you are indeed in for quite a treat, as Kirby games in general offer some of the cutest, most charmingly whimsical platforming experiences available. Kirby's Dream Land 3, Super Star and The Crystal Shards in particular feature Kirby shining his brightest, accentuating his diverse array of awesome abilities as he travels through the colorful, surreal dreamscape that we've all appropriately come to know as Dream Land.

Each of the games can be played holding the Wii Remote sideways, but there is Classic and GameCube Controller compatibility as well. Each game is a to-the-tee port (minus, arguably, Kirby 64, which is rendered at twice the resolution of the original, so keen eyes might notice cleaner, smoother polygons) and plays exactly the same; as veterans remember, classic Kirby gameplay consists of inhaling enemies to copy their abilities and then duking it out using the various powers you gain (ranging from throwing ninja stars to shooting laser beams or simply sweeping a little broom).

Although these only encompass Kirby's first decade of existence (which ironically means Nintendo is ignoring the latter half of the anniversary they're celebrating), there's still much more for Kirby fans to sink their teeth into. Entirely new content is offered in the form of Challenge Stages, a series of time trials based heavily on the gameplay and aesthetic design of Kirby's most recent installment, 2011's Return to Dream Land. Like that game's own Challenge Stages, you'll embark on time-limited missions to defeat as many enemies, collect as many coins and take as little damage as you possibly can while using only one predetermined copy ability per stage. These newly designed Challenge Stages do make for some great fun and in fact present quite a, well, challenge, particularly if you're aiming for a perfect gold medal score. They even added a pseudo-storyline of sorts, reintroducing Return to Dream Land's mysterious alien Magolor as a competitor you'll race throughout the final stages. Although it's not the meatiest of new additions, many collections of this sort don't contain any wholly new content at all, so I appreciate and commend the extra effort.

A lot of the value also comes with the packaging itself: Kirby's Dream Collection is currently only available in its "Special Edition" (which may or may not end up being limited), which includes the game itself as well as a collectible art booklet and soundtrack CD. The booklet is a total fan service delicacy, with each page displaying an array of Kirby artwork, conceptual designs and sketches, screenshots and more. There's even a bestiary of sorts featuring the franchise's most memorable baddies, and several blurbs of informational history denoting Kirby's original conception, plus some seemingly work-in-progress material yet to come. The text is descriptive and the artwork is delightful; Kirby fanatics will definitely treasure this little nugget for years to come. The soundtrack features music directly ripped from the games (nothing is rerecorded or orchestrated, for those wondering), meaning you may or may not have any desire to subject yourself to the relentlessly upbeat, older 8-bit tunes. There are also, however, a small handful of new, Kirby-inspired tracks that do merit an earnest listen, particularly the entertaining "Electro Kirby," a techno mix of memorable Kirby tracks.

Some other goodies include an in-game timeline that allows you to travel through a detailed account of Kirby's history, spanning from his debut in 1992 to his most recent outing on the Wii. In this feature, you'll be able to move Kirby himself along the timeline and physically view the box of each and every one of his games, watch its trailer, read its description, or, if it's included in this collection, jump right into playing it. There is also a wonky but fairly interesting inclusion of random trivia knowledge for each year (you'll be reading little blurbs about Janet Reno and the Olympics amidst all the Kirby games). There are also a few full episodes of the Kirby TV show, Right Back At Ya!, included, which you can view through the interactive timeline section.

Speaking as someone who owned and played every single one of these previous titles, I definitely found some of them to be played out and then some by this point, particularly those that have already been rereleased several times. As truly fantastic as Kirby Super Star was, given that I played it a hundred times over the first time around and then played through the entire thing again on the Nintendo DS rerelease Super Star Ultra, I had little desire to revisit it here. I had also already downloaded the 3DS eShop versions of Kirby's Dream Land and Kirby's Adventure, both of which frankly are much better suited to a handheld console at this point in time. This leads to a bigger overarching issue: this is a collection that, in my opinion, was really meant to be a Nintendo 3DS game. Playing 20 year-old Game Boy games on an HD flatscreen in 2012 feels wonky, particularly when you realize that none of these titles are even the appropriate resolution to be properly displayed on modern TV screens (there is no fit-to-screen mode for any of the classic games, meaning you'll be seeing blocky borders on either side of the screen). This certainly doesn't affect the gameplay experience, but it does make one question if this was really intended for a home console.

Additionally, although the games included are great in their own right, a greater addition of more obscure games such as Dream Course, Kirby's Avalanche, Star Stacker or the Japan-only release KiraKira Kids would've really beefed up the catalogue and made it more worthwhile for already loyal fans (who surely already own the biggest games, either in their original form or as one of their various rereleases on the eShop or Virtual Console). Ignoring all of Kirby's GBA and DS installments was also a bit of a poor choice; Amazing Mirror and Squeak Squad would have been great additions. Also, a big frustration players will be facing is the lack of a return-to-menu option once you start playing one of the classic games; you'll have to return to the main Wii menu and reset the entire game if you want to change games, which can be very annoying if you have the desire to switch games quickly.

So the ultimate question most people will have when it comes to a collection like this: is it worth it? If you're a Kirby newbie and have yet to experience his catalogue of fantastic classic games, the answer is an absolute yes. For tried and true Kirby fanatics who've already played through each and every one, the answer is similar, but a bit more complicated. It really depends on just how much of a Kirby fan you are; speaking as someone who absolutely adores Kirby and didn't actually finish Kirby 64 the first time around (meaning I do actually have a first-time full playthrough to enjoy), I'm pretty satisfied with the purchase, particularly because I'm a sucker for Kirby merchandise (the colorful packaging, detailed art book and comprehensive soundtrack are all delectable goodies) and did get more enjoyment than I was expecting from the all-new Challenge Stages. All in all, if you're a fan of the pink puff, it's hard to go wrong with just $39.99 for this much content, whether you're craving the wholeheartedly new or just want to bask in the warm light of some truly dreamy nostalgia.

The fourth overall release of a series doggedly plagued by monotony, New Super Mario Bros. U is likely to be met with a muddled mix of expectations, particularly given that its predecessor, New Super Mario Bros. 2 on the 3DS, was easily the schlockiest installment yet. The good news is that although NSMBU retains some of the series' trademark setbacks, it is hands down the best New Super Mario Bros. title to date, and in fact presents a blueprint of what the series should have offered from the very beginning.

We all know it by now, the tried and true "storyline" that just won't die: given that Peach is beginning to spend far more of her days in Bowser's Castle than the Mushroom Kingdom, Mario and his pals have got to retrieve her from King Koopa just in time to be kidnapped again for New Super Mario Bros. U2. Like its predecessors, NSMBU is a multiplayer platforming adventure in which players 2 through 4 have the option of playing as Luigi or one of two differently colored Toads, while player 1 must play as Mario. You'll run, jump, stomp and swim through a variety of different worlds while making use of various power-ups and crushing (mostly) familiar baddies.

Although this sounds wholeheartedly identical to NSMB 1 through 3 (and granted, it sometimes is), there are several key factors that amp up the originality and the fun: for one, NSMBU is the first New Super Mario Bros. title to revamp the overworld map, and the results are glorious. Rather than a bland series of numbered, separated worlds and levels with familiar designs, NSMBU presents a beautifully designed and detailed single world map that interconnects on multiple levels via secret exits and other features, very similar to that of the SNES's Super Mario World (each and every stage is even lovingly given its own name). The variety of stage scenery has also been appreciatively expanded-long gone are the days of "forest-desert-lava-repeat" stage sequences. There is now an innovative slew of new environments to explore, including a surreal, watercolor-soaked swamp (inspired by Van Gogh), musty coal mines, seasonal-minded glaciers dotted with enormous Christmas trees and glittering stars, and blissful romps through pink, puffy clouds. NSMBU also borrows Super Mario World's recurring theme of naming worlds after candies and sweets, but pushes it to a delectable new level by incorporating it into stage design (you'll see towering sand dunes that seem slathered in frosting and strawberries in Layer-Cake Desert, as well as acidic liquid that bubbles and fizzes like root beer in Soda Jungle). The overworld map has also become interactive, among the most delightful new features: you'll now occasionally come across Toads and other characters on your way to certain stages who may request something in exchange for a rare item or power-up, while you may have to sneak past an enemy while proceeding or risk challenging them in a bonus stage. You'll encounter baby Yoshis who can join you, and occasionally face a mischievous bunny named Nabbit who will repeatedly steal rare power-ups from Toads (you'll have to chase him through the level he jumps into to retrieve it). Via the Miiverse compatibility, other real-life players from all over the world will appear throughout your map, making exclamations, giving tips and other commentaries about the game. Great touches like these make traversing ordinarily boring world maps much more exciting.

Along the lines of visuals, it is sheer bliss to finally witness a Mario game in glorious HD, and although it clearly doesn't push the Wii U to its limits, this is without question the most beautifully designed 2D Mario game ever. Nuanced details like rainbows, waterfalls and tumbling leaves in the background make most stage scenery a joy to behold. The enemies you'll encounter also come to vivid new life, and there are surprisingly a great variety of entirely new ones, including adorable flying squirrels, snowball-hurling walruses and crafty hermit crabs that could have crawled straight out of Kirby's Dream Land. Along with the aforementioned Nabbit, some of these cutesy and creative new characters I could imagine joining the iconic cast for years to come.

The game also makes fairly inventive use of the Wii U's GamePad by incorporating "Boost Mode," which allows a fifth player (assuming there are already four others using Wii Remotes) to help players out by creating platforms on the touchscreen, stunning enemies and activating other special features. Boost Mode can be activated at any time, which means you can also simply whip the GamePad out during 1-player mode and tap yourself out some platforms if you're having a particularly hard time reaching a certain spot or Star Coin. You can also, should you so desire, play the entire game on the GamePad itself (with normal controls, as Mario), as NSMBU is compatible with remote play. Although this is a great option to have if you share a TV with others or love the thought of playing in bed, keep in mind you'd be missing out on some vibrant HD visuals.

NSMBU also marks the return of the Yoshis, and notably their long-missing baby counterparts (well played, Nintendo). The classic green Yoshis can still flutter jump and gobble up enemies in their way, but the baby Yoshis play a different role than they ever have before. As where full-grown Yoshis are mounted and can be ridden through a stage, baby Yoshis must be manually carried like an item, meaning if you let go of the 1 button you let go of the baby Yoshi and can't use it (this can in all honesty get a bit obnoxious). Unlike the ones found in Super Mario World, the baby Yoshis here don't grow (although you can still feed them enemies); instead, they sport different special abilities depending on their color. Pink Yoshis can inflate to an enormous size and allow you to float, as where yellow Yoshis create bursts of light that illuminate dark rooms and stun enemies, and blue Yoshis blow bubbles that can be used to trap enemies or hopped on as fragile platforms. Each of these abilities are activated by shaking the Wii Remote while holding the baby Yoshi. Curiously, baby Yoshis can travel with you continuously until you lose them in a stage, as where you'll be automatically separated from a full-grown Yoshi once you reach the end of a stage.

The Power-Ups this time around are decent but as with most games in this series, don't present quite enough variety. The Super Mushroom, Fire Flower, Ice Flower and Mini Mushroom all return; the only notable new addition is the Super Acorn, a power-up that essentially transforms Mario and pals into big flying squirrels. At its worst the power-up feels like a wonkier Tanooki Leaf; you unfortunately can't attack with it, but will instead be able to slow your falls by gliding. You'll also gain the ability to air jump and cling to walls. Although there's not exactly a plethora of new choices at first, however, without spoiling anything, I'll just say your arsenal expands as the game goes on. NSMBU also marks the return of stock items (similar to Super Mario Bros. 3), which you'll be able to access from the world map to power yourself up before ever entering a stage.

The game has a rather impressive amount of content, too, and should in fact keep players occupied for much longer than a typical New Super Mario Bros. title. Along with a rather expansive world map with several hidden stages and worlds, the variety of modes is a key contributor to this-in addition to the classic story mode, there are a variety of other modes that successfully switch up the gameplay mechanics and core goals. Challenge Mode lives up to its name, in which you'll traverse through different levels while trying to attain specific goals. These goals cruise through a nice variety of side quests and recurring goodies in the Mario franchise, pushing them to the forefront and making them the focus. There are different goals of reaching a stage's goal within a strict time limit, collecting a specific number of coins or power-ups, making your way to a flagpole without killing an enemy or touching the ground, and even a survival mode in which you have to traverse narrow platforms while having projectiles hurled at you just to see how long you can last. These are unique, innovative divergences from the series' standard gameplay and in fact make for some rather addictive fun. Some of these modes are so enjoyable, in fact, that Nintendo should really incorporate challenges like these into the core story mode next time around; it'd make for some fantastic variety.

Although NSMBU is at its core a success, players particularly weary of the New Super Mario Bros. series and its recurring drawbacks will still find themselves letting out a groan or two. Given how fantastic Mario soundtracks have been in the past and could easily be, why on earth the New Super Mario Bros. series insists on recycling the same tunes in every installment is beyond me. There is some new music to enjoy this time around, but the same ghost house, castle, desert and classic NSMB themes we've been hearing for years reappear yet again. Given how delightful the soundtracks of Mario Galaxy and Super Mario 3D Land were, Nintendo really should know (and do) better. The multiplayer mode is still fun, but also still chaotic and feels built more for trolling each other than working together-intentionally or not, playing with four other people just makes you feel claustrophobic on more difficult stages with a minimal amount of narrow platforms; more serious-minded gamers will have their frustration tested quickly. Although the game looks incredible in comparison to past Mario games, it really only scratches the surface of what the Wii U is capable of and what could have been-I dream of one day traversing through a vividly detailed and beautifully lit Mushroom Kingdom, and I know it is possible at this point in time. Here's hoping the next 3D Mario game takes that step.

All in all, NSMBU is a pretty great game, and unlike many of its predecessors even seems to offer some solid replay value through its various modes and array of secret goodies. You'll be more motivated than usual to collect each and every Star Coin in this game (and the reward is worth it, trust me), and doing so presents quite a challenge; the game itself as a whole is in fact quite a bit more challenging than a typical NSMB game, which is a nice step up given that some previous installments have been plagued by serious simplicity. These new inclusions and features are ultimately an attentive love letter to the veterans, which I'm personally very appreciative of coming from a series that has for too long been built upon vanilla accessibility. In its very best moments, NSMBU reminds us what we loved most about the classic Mario games to begin with, as it recaptures the glitteriest bits of nostalgia while coating it with a new modern sheen and (at last) making it feel fresh all over again. Maybe Super Mario Bros. does have some newness left in it after all.

This little adapter only ads to the fun and extends your playing time longer. I have used this countless times. It has held up to many hours of use with one warning. It seems, that the place where the wire enters the actual adapter that plugs into your cigarette lighter is weak. We haven't had any problems to date but I'd be very careful to not pull it out by the wire (good advice for anything like this) but to pull it out by the adapter piece itself.

Enjoy.

While there are others that can give you more in depth review of this game compared to others similar to this game; let me state this: I love this game.
This game is the reason I bought my DSi XL. And I'm glad I did it.

It is a little bit adventure and a little bit puzzle and a lot of fun. Professor Layton and his side kick Luke are off to solve a mystery. They are searching for the Golden Apple. To do they go visit a town and once they are there; they can't leave until they solve the puzzle.

One of the things I like is that although there are some puzzles you have to solve in order as the story progresses; they are tied to the story. But there are lots and lots of puzzles that are hidden around that you can find and solve anytime you want/can find them. I also like that there is a repository of puzzles that you haven't solved so you can go back and solve them as you have time to mull them over in your head. I also appreciated the hint coins because I often struggle doing these types of games, despite the fact that I completely love them.

There were a large variety of puzzles in this game. Some of the puzzles were word games, logic games, more riddle than puzzle. That is the only way to get the correct answer is to very carefully read the puzzle. Other puzzles are math puzzles. There are spatial puzzles and more. The wide selection ensured that I typically found a puzzle that I was sure to enjoy and sure to be frustrated over in very short order.

The music was very nice and not annoying at all. The graphics were very cartoony - exactly what you might expect when looking at the cover.

Well worth the money.
Enjoy.

This is a great game. It follows the same format of the other games. Professor Layton and Luke must solve the mystery but they are sent ten years into the future in order to solve this mystery. This story plot was my least favorite just because it was so weird. I'd give the plot of the story a four; although overall I give the game a low five. In part it earns the low five because the plot is so wierd; but it also earns a low five because there is much more dialogue and talking that you must click through in order get to the puzzles.

Once again, this has a variety of types of puzzles. There are riddles, word games, math puzzles, spatial puzzles and more. And once again there is a hint system set up in order to help you solve the puzzles. This time though there is a super hint that you can use to help you solve the puzzle. The super hint pretty much gives you the answer although not directly; you would be hard pressed to miss the answer once you have read the superhint. Also, there is an option to make notes and scribble right on the DSi in order to help you solve teh puzzle. And once again, there is a place to go to find the puzzles you didn't solve.

If you like to solve puzzles this is a great game. It is so much more than the seek and find games. You can play this game without playing any other Professor Layton puzzles. It will refer to previous games but you will not need to have played previous games because this one will guide you through the process. (For example; it will teach you about hint coins all over again.)

I think if you have played the other two you will be frustrated by three things: one, many of the puzzles you have not seen but have seen enough like them that you will find many of these are easier to solve. And two, you will have to sit through the teaching process mentioned above before starting the game. Three you will find that there is more talking that you must click through. While this adds to the story, it keeps you from playing the game. Just know that before you start and settle in for a good puzzle.

Well Worth the money.
Enjoy.

This has been my favorite Professor Layton out of the three that I have played to date. Professor Layton and Luke must solve a mystery and this time they are on a train in order to do so.

Once again, if you have played this game previously this is exactly the same set up. You can find puzzles to solve through out the train. You can collect hint coins. you can spend the hint coins in order to get hints that will help you solve the puzzles. There are a wide variety of puzzles from math puzzles to word puzzles to spatial puzzles and more. There are some puzzles you must solve to move forward in the game and there are some puzzles that you don't have to solve or even find to move forward in the game.

You can play this game if you have not played game one. They are not built upon each other. While this game might refer to the other game in dialogue, it is not necessary that you have played the game one first.

Two Frustrations. First you must sit through the whole teaching process that you had to work through the first game. For instance it will teach you about hint coins all over again. This is relatively short and thus not that big of a deal. Second, I often found that I had to travel back and forth through the train over and over again. I'd get to one end of the train only to realize I had gone the wrong way or the next person I needed to talk to was at the other end of the train. I would have liked a faster way to travel through the train by the time I was finished solving this puzzle.

But overall, this game is a great game full of great puzzles with a great plot to keep it moving forward. Completely enjoyable. A favorite of mine.
Enjoy.

I first started playing this game on my computer. I was thrilled to see it for the DS. It is exactly the same as the one I was playing on the computer and now it's portable. Potato bombs, Cherry Bombs, corn shooters and pea shooters and more. I had just as much fun figuring out what each plant did and how it did it best as I did protecting my home from zombies. lost planet got kind of mixed reviews, so i wasn't expecting too much from it. so i was pleasantly surprised that it's actually a very good game. the graphics are impressive, it has a decent story and the shooting action is good and far tighter than that crappy overrated gears of war.. the only thing i don't care for in the shooting is that it has an arrows system inside the crosshairs.. why noob it up any further or complicate the crosshairs? the weapons are great.. everything was great until i got to the first boss. what the hell is with this difficulty? i must have tried to beat him over 5 times. it's not that i'm not up to a challenge.. i like ninja gaiden.. i played a VERY similar boss in timesplitters: future perfect i had to try repeatedly to beat, and did. but this boss is way too hard to be fun. if you're going to make something hard, at least make it so fun you want to keep trying. that's where lost planet fails in my opinion.

this game works on a kind of unique health system.. you go around and pick up these orbs, and they automatically keep running down so you have to pick up more by killing enemies and collecting them. this gives lost planet it's "run and gun" angle, because you can't just hang around and let your (whatever they're called) run down. the problem is, when bosses hit you, they run down your health stuff and so it ends up just functioning like any other health in any other game. nonetheless, lost planet is easily an above average game if you don't get hung up by that boss like i did. it's not that it's OUTSTANDING or highly innovative.. it's just that most games suck and lost planet doesn't.

timesplitters: future perfect is easily one of the best PS2 games and definitely the best FPS i've seen on the system.  it features a great single-player mode, great weapons and aiming.. everything was terrific, addictive and fun, until i reached this puzzle part where you have to figure out how to get two wires to connect through a puzzle.  i had already done this TWICE before!!!!  and it was easy in the other sequences, but then when it asked me to solve two at the same time, and if you're too slow you have to do it over and over and over again... man, that is a huge mistake to make in developing a game.  this goes down in my history with other huge game mistakes such as half-life 2 having too many choppers and max payne including an annoying dream sequence not once, but twice.  if something's annoying the first time, why would it be fun the second time?!?!?!  unfortunately i'm the only gamer who gets mad about crap like this.  after all, timesplitters is a shooter game.  so why the hell would i want to solve annoying PUZZLES if i didn't want to play a PUZZLE GAME?  helllooooooo... this wouldn't have taken much thought for the game-makers to figure out, to leave the puzzles out.  nonetheless a great PS2 game.  it has a bunch of extra modes to play aside from the story, but they weren't very fun to me.  as such, i don't care for the multiplayer mode either.  but as a single player game, there's a good amount of fun here, and it's very rare for me to say that a console FPS (not a PC FPS) is actually good.

black and white 2 has a lot going for it.. fairly unique ideas (at least more unique than the rest of the crap the gaming industry is putting out, though probably not as unique as, say, katamari damacy), a great sense of humor, wonderful graphics..

uh oh, what are we missing here? OH YEAH! great controls and gameplay! two of the most important things in a game! oops! see, black & white 2 is a very "3d" game, and while this looks great, unfortunately it makes it a huge pain to move around between the 10 million camera views. now, other games have been 3d and have been easy to move around in with a default camera view, such as dawn of war. but you won't find that here. here, instead of moving to the sides of the screen to scroll view (DUH, every game has this feature, it's the most obviously easy way to get around an RTS game for years and years), you have to right click and then scroll the screen up, down, left or right. annoying! if you want to click a villager, good luck because with 10 million camera views and depths to choose from, all in 3d, it's hard to target your hand on to the villager.

it's not that i hate this game.. if it had a more simplified camera and controls, i'd probably like it a lot. but i'm not going to spend all my time & energy in a game trying to get to the right camera depth so i can see what's going on and trying to grab things. heck, it makes me want to go grab some console game, where i don't have to deal with this annoying crap.

so if you've played the demo, you might be thinking "cool - a game with some guns, some melee combat, and a dark cool story to go along with it."  unfortunately, the demo is very short and doesn't provide you with a good idea of how bad and boring the game is.  for one thing, the game is way too DARK.  it's not that i'm against darkness in a game, but this is just ridiculous.  i thought doom 3 was the darkest game ever - i stand corrected.  going around from room to room in pitch black is boring.. but not as boring as the melee combat.  block, hit, block, hit.. you can't even hit someone twice in a row or they'll hit you.  yawn.  the sprint function is the most pointless sprint i've ever seen in my life.  your character barely moves faster, and he also can't sprint up stairs (huh??)  it's VERY OBVIOUS the game makers should have made the character move a bit faster all the time.  so you'll be holding down your shift key the whole game for no reason whatsoever.  you're limited to the ammo contained in guns you pick up, so say you pick up a gun with 4 bullets, you use those 4 bullets and then have to pick up another melee weapon.  not a good idea.  i really can't think of much good to say about condemned.  if you want to play a dark game where you shoot things, why not just go play doom 3?  and if you want a good story, why not just go play an adventure game?  skip this one.

wow, this game is bad, and i mean BAD. the graphics are "decent" - the PC king kong graphics are far better. at first it seems like the game may be going somewhere, because the script seems pretty cool, but you quickly find out the shooting is very boring (if you want a good ps2 shooting game, try timesplitters: future perfect). nonetheless i was determined to give this game a fair shot...

too bad it wouldn't let me. i kept going forward and got literally stuck by an invisible wall glitch. the woman said "follow me!" and so i did.. and i couldn't go any further through the invisible wall. oh no! my terribly subpar gaming experience was ruined by a BUG! oh well. king kong for the ps2 is a terrible game, with or without game-ruining bugs.

the PC version is another story. it's a lot more involving and has far superior graphics.

god of war 1 was a semi-fun game that became a lot less fun to me after i ran into a bug, getting trapped in one level. i quit after an hour or so of trying to figure out what the hell to do.

god of war 2 is luckily bug-free. but i had to consult a walkthrough about 5 times and i hate that! what happened to the good old days, when walkthroughs weren't even an option and it didn't matter, because you didn't need them? now more and more games put in incredibly annoying puzzles. well i don't like puzzles. if i wanted puzzles, i could go play a puzzle game. too bad god of war takes the path of half-life 2 - interspersing the fun cool action with lame annoying puzzles.

anyway i solved some of the puzzles, some i looked up online, and by the time i reached a place i didn't know what to do, jumping on a rock that i couldn't get past because of a huge lava pit, i quit this game. god of war 2's strengh is in its action, so why does it insist on putting so many obstacles in the way of getting to the action?? it makes no sense, really.

also i found the flying levels to be mostly a bore. i don't think this game should focus on flying.. it should focus on what it's good at - earthbound action. it's obviously taken a lot of inspiration from ninja gaiden and that's cool, but no way would i rate it as highly as ninja gaiden. unfortunately i'm the only one willing to talk about the negative aspects of this game, because gamers think the graphics are oh-so-kool.. and they are great for a ps2 game, but there are problems.

looking at the screenshots of infernal, it looked like my kind of game, a max payne/hitman kind of style. however, it quickly falls apart not because it's a "bad" game, but simply because it's a mediocre game with no innovation.

first, the good: good graphics. runs well on my older computer/graphics card. shooting mechanics are decent. no auto-target noob crap so that's a definite plus.

the bad: you have to cannibalize corpses (steal their souls, whatever) to gain health and ammo. you have to aim your target at their body, and then wait for this animation (that's too long) to complete to get the goods. while this is cool for about .2 seconds, it quickly becomes old. for god's sake, IT'S 2007!!!!! can't we bring something better into games than that?! you HAVE to raid the corpses because you need the ammo and health. but it's not FUN. it's just a chore. and games are what we do to get our minds AWAY from chores, right??? chores shouldn't be in a game!!!!! one innovation is featured: the "stick to walls for cover" mechanic of gears of war. unfortunately this idea wasn't good in gears of war and it's not good here, either. the cover mechanics of the call of duty series are far more intuitive and fun. the one good thing i can say about it being in this game is to show what a ripoff and lame idea it is in gears of war.

anyway the worst thing about infernal is just that it offers nothing new. run around and kill some guys... ok, that gets old pretty quick. gamespot said it all: "Infernal embraces style over substance, resulting in a dull and repetitive shooting experience."

(this is my review after playing the 360 version and then trying the demo). lost planet is a pretty good game on 360, and while its fun factor can be argued, it's graphical quality cannot. it looks spectacular, and offers a couple of new innovations in gaming that give a breath of fresh air from all the mediocre FPS's.

first of all, let me blow this idea out of the water right now, that playing this game with a mouse and keyboard is more fun. IT'S NOT. it's less fun. i'm a PC gamer and agree that MOST games are more fun with mouse and keyboard. not this one.

second, the graphics looked crappy on my PC, but it's not new or anything. however, it should look better considering the great graphics i get on games like company of heroes and world of warcraft. my FPS was way too low for these kind of graphics. it's very "non-optimized" for PC. it almost seems like an advertisement to buy a new windows vista PC so it will run better! it started out the game in some ridiculously low resolution i didn't even know existed. i have an old monitor and play in 800 x 600, but who uses any less than that?!?! apparently the creators didn't know much about PC gaming.

the port of this game from console to PC was not done well. even in gamespot's full review, they mention how the controls aren't shown on-screen for the PC.. in other words it will say "to enter, press A" or "press B" like the console version, so you have to enter the menu to find which keys to press. are you freakin' kidding me?! the PC is a huge market, and THIS is the amount of respect they give PC gamers?! on one hand, it's kind of a good thing for console games to come to PC, to give people without a 360 a chance to play. however, they should put a little more work into it! some people are worried that the 360-microsoft connection will be the end of good PC gaming, and this game just worries me more. usually games port from PC to console.. and while i would love to be able to play a few games on PC like ninja gaiden, the fact is a lot of innovation happens on PC games, and we don't want to see the end of that by rich lazy microsoft just making games for the 360 and porting them to PC in substandard fashion because it's better for business. maybe they will get better about this over time, but after playing the 360 version, i'd say try this one before you buy it!

This game is very difficult for a game that doesn't take itself seriously. I play it for relaxing fun, but its pretty obvious now that just because it is an RPG with Mario in it and a silly plot doesn't mean that the game will be easy either. I guess I'm just used to playing with the controller, instead of tilting the 3DS for some moves, and not having to make so many sudden movements like in Super Mario RPG for the SNES or even Paper Mario on the N64. For a turn-based RPG, there are too many immediate actions in a battle, I'd rather be able to take my time selecting the opponent, and have the character attack it for me with not too much effort on my part. If I want an action game, I'll play Super Mario 64, Super Mario Bros, Gex, Ninja Gaiden, Max Payne, Doom, or any other action game out there that requires quick input from the player at all times. If you want a completely turn-based RPG for the 3DS, I'd go for Shin Megami Tensei IV or Fire Emblem Awakening if you want something a little more tactical. My two cents.

This is without a doubt one of the greatest games of all time. From the satisfyingly simple controls to the deep storyline this game has to offer, I am impressed with what Square was able to accomplish in it. The game is painted with beautiful, lush environments, and the enemy encounter system is the best one I have seen in any RPG. Instead of guessing what will approach you, you see it on the screen, AND fight the enemy on the screen, which is incredibly impressive for the time! The time travel aspect of the game was extremely well executed, and the fact that taking something as risky as adding in an idea like this came out so well is partially why this game is hailed as among the best of the best. This game also has one of the greatest soundtracks in gaming history, fully utilizing the Sony sound chipset in the SNES. I haven't seen a game that has better utilized the sound chip of the SNES than this one, which sits next to Final Fantasy VI, IV and Breath of Fire as all of those beautifully produced orchestrated music, which is a major accomplishment on the SNES. Overall, if you have a SNES with plenty of cash, or a DS/3DS, a Wii U or a PS3, I highly recommend you buy this timeless classic, you will not regret it!!!

I played this game back in 2005 when GameStop used to carry classic games, and needless to say, the intense frustration of this game is burned into my mind forever. I liked it at first, but when I realized how much better the controls are from Super Castlevania IV to the present games its difficult to look at the first one the same way ever again. The controls are extremely unforgiving, and Simon can plunge into his doom from something as simple as the stairs. Just like the third Castlevania game, you have to be perfect when platforming from block to block and not try to do something as simple as wanting to jump the opposite direction at the last second only to fall into a water pit. This was later remade as Super Castlevania IV for a very, very good reason. It does the first title justice with the far superior controls, and even has a nice bonus of improved graphics, and music, though it was always the controls that bothered me, and  lot of that. If you want a classic Castlevania game without smashing your TV, or having your blood pressure run into unhealthy numbers, please go for the fourth one on the SNES, which is also on the Wii and Wii U eShop. Please avoid the first three games, they will make you bitter!!

When you push the analog stick back, the character just turns around and moves all over the place, and jumping on platforms is painful to say the least. What can I say? This is worth every penny you throw at this compilation! You get both of the Shenmue games without worrying to track down a working Dreamcast, and a working copy of the game! I used to watch my older brother play this way back in 2001, and for its time was incredibly groundbreaking! It has some of the deepest story elements I've ever seen in a game.  While I did not expect any combat at all, because of the unique genre the first game so far is, there are actually fights with the punches and kicks you would see in Virtua Fighter, or in the Yakuza series. This game requires patience, and the ability to enjoy an interesting story that unravels itself as you scour your way down for clues. There may not be much of a map system, but once you get to know the place well enough, and where things are at, it gets easier from there! This is a godsend coming from someone who has tried two different copies of Shenmue on two different Dreamcasts with no scratches on the discs, only to have it crash every 5-10 minutes, not to mention the amazing addition of authentic Japanese voice acting you would not otherwise find in the original American and European releases. Well, did I convince you to play these classics? Go on ahead, play them; you won't be disappointed!!

Where do I start? The game looked promising, but 20 hours later, when I realized that progressing in this game is extremely tedious and annoying, I started to cast more than a couple of doubts towards it. Once you get to a certain point of the game, there are a whole bunch of quests that have level requirements far beyond the level you are, and I don't even think these ridiculous requirements should even be in there in the first place. Even the lowest level of quests you take on are at least a level or two above of the level you are at. Yes, this is an Assassin's Creed game, and stealth is expected, but trying to fit in a bunch of stealth in an attempt to make an RPG really ruined this, as even if you are focused, you will get caught anyways. The loading times after your character gets killed adds insult to injury.

You can expect a loading time of 20-25 seconds after getting killed, and you will get killed a lot in this game, there is just no avoiding that. So, between the fact that you can get killed a lot in the game, the majority of quests being closed down as options due to having to level up because of the minimum level requirements, and equipment requiring you to be a certain level, yeah... You are just much better off playing The Witcher 3, any Elder Scrolls game, or if you still want stealth, an older Assassin's Creed game. I really wanted to like this game, and I thought the premise of it taking place in Greece was very interesting, but unfortunately with all the problems it has, I cannot recommend this to anyone.

Crash Bandicoot was one of my first games for the PS1 once upon a time. It was awesome. Difficult but still awesome. Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back took things to a new level with more fun missions and enemies, as well as some extra moves for Crash. Crash Bandicoot: Warped then skyrocketed the series to new heights that were never reached again by any of the later games (none of which were developed by Naughty Dog, with the exception of Crash Team Racing). Seriously, none of the later games in the series, not even the better ones like Crash Twinsanity or Crash of the Titans, were able to capture the zany magic of Warped or, to a somewhat lesser degree, the first two games.

Now Activision and Vicarious Visions have brought us a remade collection of Naughty Dog’s original Crash Bandicoot trilogy for current gen systems in the form of Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy. Thing is, when this collection released earlier in 2017, I had no plans to get it. As much as I loved the Crash series in my youth, I felt I had outgrown it, so I had traded-in all the games (after having played all of them multiple times throughout the years, mind you). But in the end, I just couldn’t pass up this collection, especially not if this was the first step towards a full on revival of the series (there are already strong rumors circulating that a remake of Crash Team Racing is on the way). Having played the original trilogy extensively, I can confidently say that the N. Sane Trilogy does true justice to its source material. All three games play pretty much exactly the same in the N. Sane Trilogy as they did on the PS1. There are subtle differences though, and a couple of them aren’t great, but they don’t really bring down the experience either.

The first Crash Bandicoot is easily the most challenging (and frustrating) game in the series, just like before. In the original PS1 version, I was never able to collect all of the Gems. In fact, I’m surprised ANYONE was able to without using a cheat code, but some legends say that a certain collection of likely inhuman gamers with endless patience were able to do so. Collecting all the Gems requires breaking all the boxes in all the levels, and you’re actually required to get through certain levels without dying. Probably the worst prerequisite was breaking all the boxes in the bonus levels where you have to reach Dr. Cortex and Dr. N. Brio. You see, in the original Crash Bandicoot, if you died in the bonus levels, then that was it, you had no more chances to go through them without restarting the levels they were set in (and you also couldn’t save your progress). Now in the N. Sane Trilogy, if you fail a bonus level, you can just try again the second you respawn by stepping onto the warp platform that appears to take you to the bonus level. So, getting all the Gems was finally doable for me (still not easy though).

The time trials from the original Warped were also added into this game and into Crash 2, though thankfully they’re not required to get 100% completion in the first two games, they’re just there to provide gamers and trophy hunters with an extra challenge. I liked that because I was simply unable to beat three of the time trials in the first Crash Bandicoot, no matter how hard I tried (damn you, “High Road”). It should also be mentioned that the time trials don’t fit very well with a lot of the levels in the first two games, especially Crash 1. Other slight differences include Papu Papu getting an extra long health bar, as well as hit detection with Papu Papu and Dr. N. Brio being….different than before. Namely, it required more effort to precisely jump on Papu Papu’s head to damage him, and when fighting Dr. N. Brio’s final stage, I vividly recall being able to damage him in the original game simply by jumping towards his head and spin attacking him, but in the N. Sane Trilogy, it wasn’t that straightforward. As for the controls, I was pleasantly surprised to find that they were as precise and responsive as on the PS1. I was concerned that using the PS4 controller’s left stick would make controlling Crash feel too “floaty” or imprecise, but they found a great balance for the control stick’s sensitivity (plus, you can control Crash by using the old school directional buttons instead, should you have the inclination).

The changes included in Crash 2 and Crash: Warped are less prevalent, but that’s because those games were just better overall and didn’t really need many changes to begin with. With Crash 2, the only change worth mentioning is how you access the boss battles. In the PS1 version of the game, once Crash completed a Warp Room, he would have to use the platform in the center to take him to the next Warp Room, but he’d also have to fight the next boss as he made the transition. In the N. Sane Trilogy version of Crash 2, completing a Warp Room unlocks an extra portal that leads straight to the next boss. Incidentally, these extra portals are located in the spots where Crash would have to save his game in the original PS1 version of the game…and the cutscene in the original game where Cortex explains the process of leaving one Warp Room to get to another was cut out of the N. Sane Trilogy. Yeah, I have a very strange and selective eye for certain details. The changes in Warped, well, there aren’t really any except for one that actually affects all three games.

This change is the inclusion of Crash’s sister, Coco, as a fully playable character in all three games. Coco is unlocked in Crash 1 after beating the fourth or fifth level, and she is unlocked after beating the first Warp Rooms in both Crash 2 and Crash: Warped. Coco possesses all the attacks and abilities her brother has, and she is playable in almost every level of all three games except in very specific cases. In Crash 1, Coco is not playable in the warthog-riding levels or the boss battles. Similarly in Crash 2, she is not playable in the levels where you ride Polar, the ones where you use the jetpack, or the boss battles. In Crash: Warped, things are rather different. Coco cannot be used in the levels where you ride the motorcycle or the boss battles (except for Dr. N. Gin), but she is playable both in her own bi-plane levels and in the bi-plane levels that were exclusive to Crash in the original Crash: Warped. Strangely, it doesn’t work the other way around; Crash is not playable in Coco’s bi-plane levels, nor is he playable in the levels where you ride Pura or the jet-ski since they are still exclusive to Coco.
