Not really a big deal, just another one of those weird things I happened to notice.

To sum up, if you loved Crash Bandicoot back in the day, like I clearly did, then the N. Sane Trilogy is most certainly worth getting, especially with the graphical facelift. If you're one of those gamers who are into the seemingly dying breed of platforming video games and have never gotten a chance to play these games, then you owe it to yourselves to play this trilogy. It's basically lots of precision jumping and spin attacking, but it's still very engaging. It’s not a cakewalk, but it’s addicting and fun.

This was a difficult game for me to review and score. Like the title of my review suggests, I had a lot of fun with Monster Hunter: World, but eventually the novelty wore off to the point where I couldn’t even force myself to finish it, and that’s quite unusual for me. When I make the decision to start playing a game, I make it a point to complete it fully, even if it’s not the best game in the world. And while Monster Hunter: World is far from being a bad game, I just couldn’t bring myself to reach the post-game content or even the end of the main campaign. Let’s go into more detail on my experience with this game.

Like with many other gamers out there, Monster Hunter: World is the first Monster Hunter game I’ve played. I’d seen my younger cousins play one of the previous games in the series on the Wii, and while it looked kind of interesting, it didn’t really get my attention. Trying out these games was never really a priority for me, especially given the fact that many of the games in the Monster Hunter series were either never released in the US or were not available on the PlayStation consoles (my go-to consoles). As fellow Amazon reviewer Leohlyon told me, the Monster Hunter games are a very niche series with a very particular type of fan base, and they’re not really for the mainstream type of gamer (which I admittedly am, sort of). Monster Hunter: World was basically the first game in the series to receive such a high-profile release on all major consoles, and the game received very high praise from most. Other gamers I know played and enjoyed the game, and despite the fact that co-op multiplayer was a big part of the game (I prefer single-player), I was told that the game could still be played solo, which is mostly true. The footage I had seen of the game also looked interesting. That coupled with the fact that I could create my own cat companion to fight by my side against giant monsters convinced me to give the game a go. I really got a kick out of creating avatars for both myself and my pet cat and having the two of us kick major monster ass together.

The game’s story sucks, let’s just get that out of the way, though I honestly wasn’t expecting it to be all that great to begin with. It will be obvious even to newcomers from the get-go that the story was not meant to compare to the likes of Metal Gear Solid, God of War, or Mass Effect, especially once they see how all the characters don’t even have proper names and simply go by titles like “Commander”, “Handler”, “Chief Ecologist”, “Excitable A-Lister”, and “Meowscular Chef” (that last one wasn’t a typo, it’s the name of the big, ripped cat who cooks your meals). Thankfully, MHW’s gameplay is great. You can pick between fourteen or so different weapons ranging from more traditional ones like the Sword and Shield, Lance, and Long Sword, to ranged weapons like the Bow and Arrow and Bowgun, to more unusual weapons that can change between different forms or activate status buffs or ailments, like the Charge Blade and Hunting Horn. That’s one aspect of MHW that is certainly not lacking: options. It’s not just the large collection of weapons, but there are so many options when it comes to armor and items. You can acquire weapons and armor sets from all the different monsters you hunt and even from other smaller creatures, as well as herbs and other resources from the wilds that can be used to create health potions and antidotes. There are a few different missions you can go on, like regular hunts, gathering missions where you acquire certain ingredients for food, fishing missions, arena battles, etc.

Let’s go over the combat next. It is extremely varied given the number of different weapon types available (I mainly used the Charge Blade and occasionally used the Great Sword). There is quite the learning curve though, and it’s even more challenging to come to grips with certain weapons due to how the tutorials in the training area are rather basic and don’t go over the more powerful or advanced abilities. Looking up online tutorials on YouTube is highly recommended; I definitely wouldn’t have come to grips with the Charge Blade if I hadn’t watched a video on how to use it properly. Learning how to deal with the different monsters is its own adventure, and there are many types of those big nasties (the monster designs are really cool, I must admit). And there is no shortage of opportunities to hunt monsters, let me tell you. Aside from the main hunts that introduce most of the newer monsters, you can go on investigations to hunt the same monsters again in order to get more materials to forge stronger weapons and armor. This, unfortunately, leads to what made me quit on this game.

There are only so many times I’m willing to hunt the same monsters, and in order to get specific monster parts to forge the weapons and armor I wanted, I had to hunt certain monsters over and over and over again. Which was fine, for the most part, I liked having goals to accomplish, and getting those badass Odogaron and Rathalos armor sets and awesome Anjanath and Diablos weapons after beating the crap out of the tough corresponding monsters was satisfying. But once I reached the higher ranked missions in MHW, my drive for playing the game suddenly took a nosedive. I had spent a considerable amount of time and effort repeatedly killing certain monsters so I could acquire their armor sets and weapons, but once the higher ranked missions began, I found myself fighting stronger versions of monsters I had beaten long ago, meaning I would eventually have to fight stronger versions of Anjanath, Rathalos, Diablos, etc., and not just to advance the main campaign but also to get the stronger versions of their weapons and armor since the ones I had spent so much time acquiring earlier were suddenly obsolete.

I’m no stranger to repetitious elements in video games, in fact, I love repetitive tasks as long as they can manage to be fun and engaging. But the repetitive elements in this game were just too much. I became so tired of the proceedings that I didn’t even want to work my way up to fighting the stronger Elder Dragons (although I did manage to fight and defeat Kirin). And I haven’t even mentioned the even stronger “Tempered” versions of monsters that are so tough that you likely won’t be able to fight them solo. I played a few co-op matches with the previously mentioned Leohlyon, and those were fun, but the damage had been done. I had lost interest in continuing with this game, it was just too much of the same stuff over and over and over and over again. And there was still so much more stuff I hadn’t played, and that’s not even counting the upcoming Iceborne expansion, which is sure to add even more stuff to this game that is already full of fun (and extremely repetitive) content.

I might have stuck with Monster Hunter: World if I didn’t have so many other older and upcoming games to look forward to playing, like Watch Dogs 2, Watch Dogs: Legion, Red Dead Redemption II, Doom Eternal, Ghost of Tsushima, and many others, but there’s only so much time I was willing to dedicate to this game. In the end, Monster Hunter: World just wasn’t for me, but that’s not to say that it’s a bad game. I had a lot of fun with it before the repetition got to me. The Monster Hunter games, as I said before, are rather niche and are simply not for everyone. If you’ve never played these games before and are on the fence about giving Monster Hunter: World a try, then I suggest either watching extensive gameplay first or maybe borrowing or renting it before buying it just in case you are also put off by extremely repetitive gameplay like me.

As a big fan of the Mass Effect Trilogy, I simply had to see where the story was going to go next, despite the less than stellar reception that Mass Effect: Andromeda received when it first released. Based on what I had heard from other people I know who played the game, Andromeda was a flawed but still decent game and wasn’t outright horrible like some reviewers and critics made it out to be. Nevertheless, I wasn’t exactly itching to play the game at the outset, especially considering that it apparently released with a great number of technical issues (the whole “my face is tired” meme comes to mind), so I decided to wait until it was cheaper. I ended up buying the game for about $8, and that is certainly a good price point for this game…in fact, the absolute highest I’d go for Andromeda is $20, and that’s a bit of a generous price point, if I’m being completely honest.

Okay, so first off, Mass Effect: Andromeda begins with a large spacecraft of Milky Way denizens entering the Andromeda galaxy over 600 years after the events of the Mass Effect Trilogy, with the main goal being to find inhabitable worlds where they can begin putting down some roots. Pretty much the minute they arrive in this new galaxy, the poop hits the fan as they end up crashing into some strange dark matter phenomenon that is covering a large portion of the Heleus Cluster that they have entered. Worse yet, the supposedly habitable worlds that they had planned on terraforming were no longer very accommodating due to unknown reasons. Things get even more difficult when the new Milky Way arrivals run into hostile alien lifeforms known as the Kett who seem intent on killing them at all costs. It is then up to you as the Pathfinder to locate some inhabitable worlds for your people to live on before they completely run out of sustainable supplies.

Before I get into the main issue that’s been covered to death in this game already, specifically the technical issues, I want to discuss what I believe to be the game’s main and most prevalent problem: its pacing. Mass Effect: Andromeda is a long game. Not quite Witcher 3 levels of long, but it’s kind of close. Concentrating on the main story and not doing the side missions will shorten the length of time you spend on the game, but the main story itself is still surprisingly long. This wouldn’t be such an issue if the story was better and had more interesting characters. To be clear though, the story and characters aren’t outright bad, in fact, there are some engaging moments spread out in the game, but they are few and far between all the mundane and repetitive fetch quests. Seriously though, just when I thought I was reaching the final leg of this game, that’s when I would get even more missions where I had to do more stuff for my companions or other characters, and this just kept happening to the point where I was asking myself when this game would end.

The number of missions where you will be going back and forth talking to people and fetching things for them with absolutely no combat or even a certain sense of urgency is simply too high. And a lot of these missions end with very little payoff in terms of rewards or how the narrative is affected. Like in the previous Mass Effect games, there are many moments in Andromeda where the Pathfinder must make certain decisions and dialogue choices that (supposedly) will have a lasting effect on how the story unfolds later on, and while this is true to some extent in the final mission, I couldn’t help but feel that most of my decisions had little lasting effects and really only mattered in the moment, although some certainly did affect my standing with my companions. Speaking of, while some of the main characters in this game, including Pathfinder Ryder, are decent enough, none of them can compare to the simply more interesting and memorable characters in the Mass Effect Trilogy.

Now for the technical issues. Apparently, this game had a lot of graphical glitches and just outright poor animations when it first released, but many of them were eventually patched and fixed out. Nevertheless, there were plenty of times when I’d see my companions float in the air and drop down as they were getting out of the Nomad vehicle used to traverse certain planets (we’ll get back to that later), and there were times when Ryder or one of his companions would bend in unnatural positions during moments of dialogue. Other glitches I experienced included me not being able to initiate conversation with certain NPCs in order to advance through a mission, my character phasing through closed doors, enemies disappearing before my very eyes, me shooting an enemy from a distance and managing not to alert other enemies standing nearby, and the screen pausing for a good 2 or 3 seconds as I drove the Nomad through the open-world maps as it loaded the next area I was driving into. The biggest technical issue I encountered was when I slowly sank and then fell through the map while everything around me turned into a dark, purplish haze, but fortunately this was remedied by quitting the game and then starting it up again. So, in my experience, Andromeda has no game-breaking glitches, but it does have a number of other minor yet annoying ones.

But it’s not all doom and gloom with this game. The combat is fun, and the controls for getting around are certainly smoother than those in the previous Mass Effect games. The best example of the better movement has to do with the jump jets that pretty much all the characters in this game have, allowing them to jump high in the air to reach higher areas, hover in the air while shooting enemies, and dodge to avoid attacks. The number of different skills and powers you can unlock for the Pathfinder are quite numerous. Unlike in the previous games where you had to choose a particular class that consisted of one or two collections of skills focusing on Combat, Biotic, and Tech abilities, in Andromeda you can mix and match any type of skills you want to form your own custom builds for the Pathfinder. There are also a number of different types of weapons you can buy and craft for the Pathfinder, namely pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, and sniper rifles, and they can all be upgraded and fitted with mods for extra benefits, like more damage, larger clip sizes, bullet penetration, etc. Other mods can change the type of projectiles your weapons fire, like incendiary ammo, grenades, or lasers. Armor can also be bought and crafted, as well as fitted with additional mods to affect movement and so on.

Speaking of crafting, there are a plethora of materials you can gather by exploring, mining, looting enemies, or buying them at shops so you can use them to craft and upgrade weapons and armor. There’s a lot of resource management in this game, which can seem a bit overwhelming, but it’s not mandatory. I, for example, saved my materials to craft only the select weapons and armor that I found to be most useful. If you wish to gather enough resources to craft and upgrade a bunch of different weapons and armor, then you better be ready for an insane amount of grinding. But I honestly don’t see anyone getting that invested in acquiring every weapon or armor set in the game. As for the exploration in Andromeda, it was actually pretty well done, for the most part. Flying your ship, the Tempest, through the many different solar systems in the Heleus Cluster was normally a nice visual treat. The many planets, stars, and colorful nebulae were sights to behold.

As for when you land on the handful of explorable planets in the game, most of them will give you large open-worlds in which to do missions and battle enemies. While most of these open-world maps are quite large and vast to the point where getting from one mission area to another can feel like an eternity even in the Nomad (unless you use fast travel, but I almost never do since it normally ruins my immersion of the game I’m playing) , I felt it served to make you feel like a new explorer who had to survive in a hostile and dangerous environment. Aside from the enemies, most of the main planets have environmental hazards you have to contend with, like extreme heat, cold, or radiation, that will drain your suit’s life support either slowly or quickly depending on their severity, though the Nomad’s life support is much stronger and will protect you for a longer period of time. This feature of hostile environments makes the Nomad a vital part of your survival rather than just a simple mode of transportation. Unfortunately, unlike the (underrated) Mako and the Hammerhead from Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2, respectively, the Nomad has no weapons, which I felt was a shame since it would have been quite enjoyable to dispatch enemies with some missiles or machine gun fire while driving around in that thing. At least I did get to run over smaller enemies at times, which was satisfying enough. Finally, while we’re on the topic of enemies, I will say that they were mostly fun to fight, though very few battles were especially challenging. In fact, I think I died a mere 6 times total in this game, more or less. Enemy variety was adequate and mostly consisted of different types of humanoid enemies shooting at you, a handful of monster-type enemies, several types of robotic enemies, and one actual boss-type enemy that you fight multiple times mostly in side missions. So, while most enemies weren’t all that challenging, fighting them was still pretty fun given that they normally greatly outnumber you and, therefore, provide you with ample opportunity to test out your fun powers on them.

In the end, I didn’t love Mass Effect: Andromeda, but I didn’t hate it either. It’s an okay game with moments of genuinely exciting gameplay and good storytelling thrown in there that is broken up with boring and drawn out missions that pad the game length way too much to the point where it overstays its welcome. I can really only recommend this game to “space cases” who are truly into the sci-fi space exploration genre. As for everyone else, even other fans of the Mass Effect series, I’d say you should only get this game for a very low price or just skip it altogether since the replay value is quite low, assuming you can stick with it long enough to finish even one playthrough.

There simply aren’t enough games out there focusing on giant robots fighting each other and/or giant monsters, and if you’re a gamer who is looking for just such a game, then this is the one for you. Override: Mech City Brawl is not a well-known game, nor is it the type of game that’s going to win any awards, but it provides plenty of simple, straightforward fun for anyone, kid or adult, looking for a solid 3D beat em’ up fighting game.

There are really only two main modes in this game: Arcade and Versus (though there is a rather limited Training mode as well). In the Arcade mode, you choose between one of 16 playable mechs and go through missions fighting against giant monsters, as well as the occasional mech opponents, that are trying to destroy the Earth. The story is nothing out of this world, but it’s the type of thing you’d expect from a “kill giant monsters using giant robots” narrative (the dialogue changes somewhat depending on which mech you play as, but it’s otherwise the same story for all of them). Aside from the regular story missions scattered throughout the campaign where you always fight set enemies and bosses, most of the regular missions have you fighting through randomized waves of enemies with certain objectives to fulfill, like killing all enemies before a timer runs down to zero, destroying monster nests in order to keep them from spawning too many additional enemies, or defending an important target until another timer runs down to zero. Failing one of these missions will simply lead to you having to play another one with a different collection of objectives to complete. The Versus mode is pretty self-explanatory, you can fight against the CPU, or you can play with or against other players through local or online play.

The different mechs you can play as are quite varied in their designs and abilities. All the mechs are capable of striking enemies with melee attacks both on the ground and in the air, as well as blocking and even countering incoming attacks, but their different abilities make it so that all types of combat styles are catered to. Main “hero mech” Watchbot, for example, can attack enemies up close with a dash attack and immobilize them with an EMP pulse, or he can attack enemies from a distance with his plasma cannons. The heavy bruiser Setesh has no real long-range attacks, but he excels at crushing enemies up close and at medium range with a fiery ground slam and a leaping charge, and he can also use a shield ability that can protect him from the strongest enemy attacks, as well as damage enemies once the shield bursts.

Maestro favors long-range attacks that can damage enemies and cause them to build up heat, which in turn prevents them from using their own special abilities for a time. Then you’ve got the quick and nimble Mya who can avoid enemy attacks and get behind enemies with the Naruto-like “Substitution” ability and take the fight to enemies both up close and at a distance with a dashing slice attack and by throwing shurikens. And when low on health, the mechs are all capable of unleashing powerful Ultimate attacks that can do some serious damage to the opposition, giving the mech who unleashed the attack one last chance to gain the upper hand in a fight they might very well lose otherwise, or the Ultimate attacks might outright destroy all remaining enemies in one fell swoop, assuming they’ve lost enough health beforehand.

The combat in general is well done, with all of the mechs having some weight behind their attacks and movements, which is how it should feel to control a giant robot the size of a skyscraper, but they also don’t feel overly slow or sluggish either. The different maps in which you fight are basically flat and open city areas, many of which have buildings and other structures that will crumble to dust once a mech or monster makes contact with them, although some maps have larger obstructions in certain areas that will require players to maneuver around them and perhaps provide some much needed cover from enemy attacks (especially Ultimate attacks). Extra weapons that randomly appear on the map can be implemented or outright removed to add some extra variety to the combat, and these weapons can be either melee-focused, such as beam swords, sabers, battle axes, or shields, or they can be long-range weapons, like shotguns, mini-guns, flamethrowers, or even grenades.

Completing missions in the campaign or battles online will net you with a plethora of cosmetics for your mechs, like sunglasses, hats, and mustaches, as well as color changes and skins that can greatly change the overall design of your mech. When playing the campaign as your choice of mech, you have some level of customization for your mech’s performance through the use of up to four mods that can be added to your mech after randomly earning them after missions or by using experience points to craft them. These mods can offer certain perks, like increasing the amount of energy (used for abilities and Ultimate attacks) gained from defeating enemies, increasing the speed at which your mech recovers after being knocked down in battle, increasing your attack damage when fighting more than one enemy up close, and many, many more. Furthermore, you can use experience points earned by completing missions to upgrade specific stats for your mechs, namely increasing punch/kick damage, increasing armor, lowering the rate of heat build-up, increasing movement speed, and increasing the damage output of special skills and Ultimate attacks.

I want to quickly mention the option to join with up to three other players in co-op and have the whole party control one mech. I managed to do this once with some friends for a few minutes just to see what it was like, and it was quite interesting and fun in a chaotic way. Trying to figure out how each player’s button inputs would translate to controlling the mech we were piloting while trying to defeat several enemies before a timer runs down to zero was certainly messy but amusing (and while I’m not 100% sure here, I believe this particular co-op feature can only be done through local multiplayer). When playing online, you can fight with or against other players in 2 v.s. 2 or four-player free-for-all matches, though it should be noted that this game did not have a particularly strong online community last time I checked. Personally, I’m fine with that since I’m more of a single-player gamer.

And as far as technical issues go, there were relatively very few I encountered in this game, though they were consistent. When starting a mission in the campaign, as well as when the next wave of enemies is about to spawn, there is a noticeable one or two-second pause that occurs each and every time. It’s not a big deal, but its unwavering consistency is noticeable. Some graphical glitches occur as well at times, but perhaps the most noticeable and annoying technical issue I experienced was when I played through the campaign as one of the DLC mechs called Bellona. The character model of Bellona was basically invisible during all the cutscenes in the campaign. While this doesn’t break the game by any means, it’s a very hard to miss (and personally very annoying) technical issue that should be fixed, though it probably won’t be.

Override: Mech City Brawl is a straightforward game with few bells and whistles, but its combat is fun and surprisingly deep once you figure out how to properly control the mechs and take full advantage of their unique abilities. Those who are looking to play this game mostly for its online component should exercise caution given the apparently very limited online community the game has, but if all you’re looking for is an enjoyable and competent game to kill a couple of hours with every now and then either by playing through the rather fun campaign or playing local co-op or versus matches with some friends or the CPU, then you should be satisfied with this game.

The first Nioh was my introduction to the whole “Souls-like” genre of video gaming. When I first saw a gameplay trailer for Nioh back in 2016 or so, I felt I had to get that game since it looked like a combination of Souls-like gaming and Onimusha, an older Capcom action series of games that focused on samurai, ninja, and Japanese demons. While the story was lacking and, frankly, not very well told, I enjoyed my time with Nioh, despite the high level of difficulty in certain missions (though it is a Team Ninja game, so some frustration was expected). Now comes Nioh 2, a prequel (and semi-sequel) to the original game that takes its best aspects and adds a few improvements to the proceedings…and not much else, really. In its most basic form, Nioh 2 truly is Nioh 1.5. What it does add to the gameplay is mostly positive, but it’s nothing game-changing either. I will say that those who enjoyed the first Nioh should most certainly enjoy Nioh 2, but some might not necessarily like it better.

Personally, I enjoyed Nioh 2 a bit less than the first game overall. First off, much like the first game, Nioh 2 has a “meh” story. It’s actually a bit better than the first game’s story but not by much. Instead of playing as the very bland and forgettable William from the first Nioh, in Nioh 2 you create your own male or female avatar through whom you will be slaying all manner of demons, and as per usual in these types of games, your avatar is mute, so he/she will not be all that interesting or have much of a discernable personality. But this is a Team Ninja title, so that’s par for the course with their games. Team Ninja are also known for their challenging games with very well done combat, and Nioh 2 is certainly just such a game with a wide array of enemies that we get to really mess up by using a surprisingly large number of weaponry, even more than what was available in the first game. The swords, dual swords, axes, spears, kusarigamas (chain sickles), odachis, and tonfas from the first Nioh return in this game (along with the bows, rifles and handcannons as ranged weapons), and the new weapons include hatchets, switchglaives, splitstaffs, and fists (gauntlet weapons). Certainly plenty of different weapon types to cater to all possible playstyles. And sometimes the weapons you find or craft can be either blessed or cursed, which will have negative effects on demon/yokai or human enemies, respectively.

Also returning from the first game are the Guardian Spirits that you can attach to your main character, with each one offering different stat increases, perks, and elemental attributes. One thing that’s changed with Guardian Spirits are how all of them resonate better with your character depending on your build. Since my build focused on Heart, Strength, and Stamina stats more than the other main character attributes, certain Guardian Spirits offered my character more perks that were unlocked as I increased the effectiveness of those specific attributes, while other Guardian Spirits offered extra perks based on a character having higher Skill, Constitution, etc., so I typically avoided those Guardian Spirits since they did little for my character.

Furthermore, each Guardian Spirit is classified as either a Brute, Feral, or Phantom, and depending on which class of Guardian Spirit you have equipped, it will affect your Yokai Shift ability. When using Yokai Shift, you basically turn into a powerful demon that can take on one of three forms: The Brute form (my favorite) turns you into a big, hard-hitting demon with a club, the Feral form turns you into a quicker demon with dual daggers, and the Phantom form turns you into a hovering, ghost-like demon with a sword that you can throw around like a boomerang. While the Yokai Shift doesn’t last all that long, it does offer more versatility compared to the Living Weapon ability in the first Nioh.

Two other new abilities you have access to in Nioh 2 are the Burst Counter and the Yokai Abilities, both of which are powered by the new Anima meter that fills up as you land hits on enemies. The Burst Counter is a quick move that you can perform where you momentarily change into your Yokai Shift form and smack an enemy as they do a Burst Attack. Hitting them at the right time will interrupt the enemy’s attack and take out a huge chunk of their stamina, but getting the timing right for certain attacks can, quite frankly, be a huge pain in the ass. Some enemies have ridiculous Burst Attacks that are too quick to counter or are capable of hitting you even when the enemy starts their attack from very far away. Yokai Abilities are, as they sound, abilities/attacks of yokai that you can use on enemies after attaching Soul Cores to your Guardian Spirit. Getting a Soul Core from a certain enemy lets you use that enemy’s special attack, whether it’s turning into an Onryoki and hitting enemies with its dual ball-and-chains, turning into an Enki and throwing its spear at enemies from a distance, or summoning a Nure-onna and using its paralysis gaze to freeze enemies in place for a few seconds.

One last change in the gameplay has to do with the Dark Realm. Enemy yokai can unleash localized corruption called the Yokai Realm around themselves that drains your ki (stamina) and buffs up the yokai, but in Nioh 2, certain yokai enemies and pretty much all yokai bosses can also summon the Dark Realm, which works like Yokai Realm but covers a much wider area. I was concerned this feature would make enemies feel too overpowered, but fortunately, it was balanced pretty well since the Dark Realm can actually offer the player some advantages along with some disadvantages.

Nioh 2, overall, is noticeably more challenging than its predecessor, and there are several reasons why. Firstly, a lot of the bosses are very tough, whether they’re human or yokai. You actually fight several bosses from the first Nioh in this game, and in almost every case, the returning enemies are tougher than before. This is especially noticeable with human boss enemies that are more resistant to certain attacks, like not being staggered or interrupted by your attacks while they’re in the middle of unleashing an attack of their own on you, or the fact that they get back up almost immediately if you knock them down to the ground, even if you’re hitting them with a finishing move. And some yokai bosses have these absolutely ridiculous abilities and attacks that are almost impossible to avoid. I seriously felt like I got lucky on many occasions when I actually did manage to avoid some of these “super attacks” from yokai bosses.

While bosses and enemies in the first Nioh were certainly challenging, they felt more balanced than the majority of bosses in Nioh 2, who honestly feel the slightest bit cheap on some occasions with these new “buffs” they’ve received, and some bosses were just badly designed, no two ways about it. It sometimes felt like Team Ninja were going out of their way to give every possible advantage to the enemies while making the player character more vulnerable. The fact that the window for dodging enemy attacks seems a half-second smaller than in the first Nioh doesn’t help matters either. And I swear many regular yokai enemies were one or two-shotting me in certain missions while even the bosses weren’t doing that.

Also very much like the first game, Nioh 2 has a hub you go to between missions where you can buy, sell, or craft weapons, armor, items, and so on, as well as a few other options that I quite frankly don’t bother with. I could never really get into or even understand the whole forging process when it comes to making weapons and armor, and that’s fine given that I got so much loot in each mission that I was able to just level up the weapons and armor I liked and then switch them out for something better when I came across it. Honestly, the number of available options and features in both Nioh games is a bit overwhelming, not to mention confusing, but luckily, I was able to get through it just by sticking with what I was comfortable with.

There are a couple other personal issues I have with this game. One has to do with the acquisition of skill points and leveling up. Compared to the amount of grinding you had to do in order to level up in the first Nioh, leveling up in Nioh 2 is a bit less grindy, thankfully. However, gaining skill points to unlock new combos and abilities for weapons, Onmyo magic, and ninja techniques are certainly harder to come by (the locks of hair that you could use in the first Nioh to acquire skill points aren’t nearly as plentiful in this game). The other issue I had with Nioh 2 was that the main campaign was too dragged out, especially after getting the DLCs. I know there’s a certain fan base for Nioh out there that play these games incessantly to the point where they beat the campaign multiple times at all difficulty levels, play the nearly endless Abyss mode, and play online until they’ve reached level 600 or so…and then still keep going. I, on the other hand, am like most gamers and just want to beat the main campaign and as many side missions as possible without learning how to use every single weapon. And even just doing that proved to be a hell of a repetitive ordeal after a while. An intense and action-packed ordeal, to be sure, but still a very dragged out one.

In the end, I enjoyed this game. The combat is second to none, if at times very frustrating and intense (and cheap). I could very well see myself playing the Nioh games again but not for a very, very long time. And the game’s narrative sucks, which helps knock it down a notch. Nevertheless, if you’re a fan of the first Nioh, then Nioh 2 has plenty to offer to make you want to come back to the series. Just don’t expect any groundbreaking changes in the proceedings.

I had some reservations with Immortals: Fenyx Rising when I first heard about it. It initially didn’t impress me all that much, but after watching some extended gameplay footage and early impressions, I became intrigued. It looked like a fun and whimsical good time, an innocent adventure where you fight against mythological monsters in a bright and cartoony world. It reminded me of some of the games I played in my youth, like the Jak and Daxter games. I’ve also always been somewhat of a fan of Greek mythology, and I was rather interested in playing a game where I wasn’t killing all of the gods for a change (that’s right, I’m talking about you, Kratos). After having fully completed everything possible in this game and its three DLCs, I can say with confidence that Immortals: Fenyx Rising is a fun, well made, and fantastical game, but it doesn’t do anything with its story or mission structure to make it an exceptional game that stands out amongst other open-world titles of its ilk. Also, I want to add that I will not be comparing this game to its obvious inspiration, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, since I never played that game.

You are Fenyx, a young man/woman (depending on the player’s choice) who serves as the plucky shield-bearer to a group of warriors. When Fenyx’s ship sinks in a terrible storm, Fenyx washes ashore on the Golden Isle, a land that is filled to the brim with monsters, and furthermore, all the people on the island have been turned to stone, including Fenyx’s brother, Ligyron. Fenyx quickly runs into Hermes, the messenger god, who (sort of) guides him/her towards a quest to help the other gods of Olympos who have been transformed into very different and powerless forms by Typhon, the father of all monsters. And that pretty much ends the most interesting portion of the story. Fenyx basically spends the rest of the game helping the changed gods come to terms with their true selves and be content with who they really are (despite their many, many flaws) so they can be turned back to normal and help bring down Typhon and save the world.

And when Fenyx isn’t doing all that touchy, feely crap, he’s doing favors for the gods, namely fetch quests and killing monsters. At least the interactions between Fenyx and the gods (especially Ares) are kind of funny. Not really laugh out loud funny, but I chuckled a few times at the many jokes and quips the characters throw out (again, especially Ares). In short, don’t expect the story for Immortals: Fenyx Rising to be all that enthralling or interesting, it will likely just make you chuckle with how it mixes modern humor into its ancient Greece setting.

Thankfully, the open world of Immortals: Fenyx Rising has plenty (and I do mean plenty) of stuff for you to do. Firstly, the different regions of the open world are varied and well designed, and they include regions with lots of green hills and forests, war-torn landscapes, industrialized regions with (ancient) heavy machinery, and frozen tundras. And in neither of these regions is there a shortage of enemies for Fenyx to destroy, including cyclopses, gorgons, minotaurs, harpies, cerberi, etc., and all of them have their own unique abilities and attacks, so enemy variety is pretty good. That is until you start fighting the many bosses that you can find scattered around the open world or its dungeons, and aside from a few rare exceptions, most of the bosses are just bigger and stronger versions of regular enemies. And if you’re a completionist like me, then you will be fighting these samey enemies A LOT. Aside from fighting enemies, you’ll mainly be solving puzzles in the form of pulling switches, hitting far away targets with your bow and arrow, moving blocks or rolling balls to activate mechanisms, and the like. Most of these puzzles are in the Vaults of Tartaros, which are subterranean dungeons scattered all over the Golden Isle. Completing these vaults is worth it since they always reward you with more points towards upgrading your stamina, and considering that you use up stamina for gliding, swimming, climbing, sprinting, and using Godly Powers, you’ll want to take every opportunity to increase it.

There will also be many resources that you will be finding out in the open world and in chests that will allow you to upgrade your health, weapons, and armor, which you will also certainly want to do in order to not get killed instantly by high-level enemies. Also, the many mythological challenges you can find in the open world, which consist of shooting a controllable arrow through an obstacle course of loops, getting from one point to another in as short a time as possible by sprinting and gliding, moving tiles around in the right order to form a fresco, etc., reward you with points to upgrade your combat abilities and the previously mentioned Godly Powers. So, while it can be argued that this game has too much to do, at least most of the challenges/activities are worth doing since they offer actually useful rewards.

Going back to the weapons, armor, abilities, and Godly Powers…well, there are a lot of those too. Fenyx’s main weapon classes are swords, axes, and bows, and he will also find helmets and armor sets too, and all these pieces of gear will have their own useful stats, like swords that do more damage when you’re at full health, axes that have a certain chance of doing extra stun damage to enemies, bows and arrows that can occasionally have enemies get struck by lightning if you hit one with a headshot, armor that increases your hit counter by several points as you continue to score hits on enemies without losing your stride or getting damaged yourself (higher hit counts lead to extra damage on enemies), etc.

Each weapon and armor set comes with a number of different skins to earn through accomplishing tasks or finding them in chests (there’s an online store too, but I refuse to buy skins with real money). There are also a lot of skins for your bird sidekick, Phosphor, which all offer different effects for the ability where you summon him to divebomb enemies. Even the number of different mounts/horses you can find and tame is rather high; so high, in fact, that I apparently missed a couple of them even by the time I fully finished the game and had explored almost every nook and cranny of the Golden Isle. By the way, this game really makes you want to explore every nook and cranny in order to find collectibles and activities, especially after using the “Far Sight” ability that lets you go into a zoomed-in first-person perspective to mark missions and collectibles when the cursor hovers over one of them and gives you the cue to mark it.

Let’s finally get to those Godly Powers now. They make Fenyx a real force to be reckoned with, and they include charging into enemies with Athena’s shield (Athena’s Dash), smashing enemies with a huge hammer (Hephaistos’s Hammer), knocking enemies upward with a rising field of spears (Ares’s Wrath), summoning Phosphor to divebomb enemies (as well as turn Fenyx invisible or make use of a clone statue of Fenyx to solve puzzles and even damage enemies), using the Bands of Herakles to lift objects and throw them (also useful for solving puzzles that require the moving of blocks and so on), and using Fenyx’s bow to fire Apollo’s Arrows, which can be controlled mid-flight and guided to specific targets (enemies or switches). The Godly Powers, to me, are great examples on how to properly incorporate special character abilities into a video game. They’re reliable, powerful, easy to use, and don’t require an insane amount of stamina in order to be used (at least not after you start upgrading your stamina). Aside from being able to rely on perks from certain armor sets and weapons to refill some health or stamina, Fenyx has access to upgradeable potions that can be used to restore health and stamina or to increase attack power and defense.

Despite how much content the base Immortals: Fenyx Rising game already has, there are also three story DLCs that further increase the number of things to do and the amount of time you’ll spend on this game, assuming you’re willing to go the distance. Possible story spoilers ahead, so beware with reading the next paragraphs. The first DLC, A New God, has Fenyx on Olympos dealing with a slew of challenges and puzzles, much like the ones in the Vaults of Tartaros, so he can prove himself worthy of joining the gods on Olympos as one of them. So basically, A New God has you doing more of the same type of stuff as you did in the Vaults of Tartaros in the main game. Don’t get me wrong, I commend Ubisoft for being able to come up with so many admittedly clever puzzles for players to challenge themselves with, but jeez, did they have to put so many of them in this game? The first DLC takes it even further by having the majority of challenges and puzzles not revolve around combat. Some challenges do have combat, but they’re few and far between. At least the use of potions is removed in this DLC to make the proceedings a bit more challenging.

The second DLC, Myths of the Eastern Realm, has you take on the role of a young warrior boy named Ku in the realm of Chinese mythology (which I admittedly know a lot less about), and his mission is to assist a couple of his gods to bring balance to his land after chaos is unleashed upon it through a wormhole that has appeared in the sky, bringing forth imbalance and monsters. This DLC is basically a bite-sized version of the main game. The open world is smaller and has a number of challenges like the ones in the main game, some collectibles, and many enemies to fight. Ku’s Godly Powers are reskins of Fenyx’s powers from the main game, only he uses a big axe in place of Hephaistos’s Hammer and a field of swords instead of the spears in Ares’s Wrath, though the other Godly Powers are the same. One key difference with the first two Godly Powers is that they can dish out extra damage and effects when Ku’s hit counter gets high enough by not getting hit and keeping up uninterrupted combos, which encourages a more aggressive style of combat from the player.

The challenges are also reskins of the mythical challenges and Vaults of Tartaros from the main game, as are the enemies. They all represent creatures in Chinese mythology, but they move, fight, and even sound just like the enemies from the main game (with the exception of the final boss). The story for this DLC, also much like the main game, is okay but nothing out of this world. If you’re a super fan of the main Immortals: Fenyx Rising game, then you’ll likely really enjoy the second DLC just for providing more of the same goodness with a different mythological theme.

The third and final DLC, The Lost Gods, changes things up a bit from the previous DLCs. Taking on the role of Ash, a young girl who maintains a temple dedicated to the gods of Olympos, you go on a new adventure given to you by Fenyx, now the God of Unity, and your mission is to reunite the other gods who left Olympos and bring an end to the many natural disasters that have fallen upon the mortal lands since the gods’ departure. While you’ll be fighting the same enemies from the main game (and a couple of newer ones, for good measure) and once again doing favors and running fetch quests for more needy gods, the gameplay has changed to a certain degree. Instead of a large open-world map to traverse, Ash will be journeying through a series of small-ish interconnected islands, which include forested areas, icy regions, scorched and lava-filled landscapes, watery areas, etc. The biggest difference the DLC has from the main game is its isometric overhead camera, similar to that in dungeon-crawler type games, like Hades and Darksiders: Genesis, though you still maintain some control over the camera and can rotate it around a bit, thankfully.

Another big change is with regards to gathering resources and upgrading Ash’s abilities. While Ash’s Heroic Gifts are largely the same as Fenyx’s Godly Powers from the main game (except for Phosphor no longer being used to attack enemies and is instead used by Ash to glide), extra perks can be assigned to the Heroic Gifts and Ash’s other combat and traversal skills by attaching essences to them, which are earned through accomplishing objectives, defeating enemies, opening chests, and the like. Depending on which essences you attach to which skill slots, you can add many different effects to pretty much everything Ash does, and all these effects and perks run on percentages (furthermore, weapons and armor also come with their own set of essence-enhanced perks). Examples include increasing or regenerating health and stamina, stunning enemies, hitting multiple enemies with chain lightning, increasing movement speed, freezing enemies in place (though this also makes enemies invincible for some reason, unlike in the main game), poisoning enemies, increasing critical hit chances and damage, etc.

Just like in the main game, Ash will be doing challenges and going through (thankfully just a handful of) Vaults of Tartaros. Other resources that can be gathered from the environment and by killing enemies are not only used to upgrade Ash’s weapons and gear, but they are also necessary to advance through the adventure and unlock access to the next set of islands by offering them to the gods in exchange for “miracles”, which include activating jump pads, activating gusts of wind to glide through, making platforms appear, and so on. These offerings can be done at altars, which are located in each individual region of the islands. Other actions that can only be done by offering resources to the gods at altars include upgrading Ash’s weapons and abilities, fast traveling, gaining temporary buffs to your abilities, advancing the time of day so resources and enemies respawn, and even saving your game. There are a number of side missions to take part in, and strangely enough, they are necessary in order to unlock some of Ash’s abilities, including her one unique Heroic Gift where she fires a beam of energy from her bow, so they’re normally worth doing in order to max out her combat abilities.

I’ll close with the main flaws of Immortals: Fenyx Rising. As previously mentioned, I find the main flaw of this game to be that it’s unnecessarily bloated and drawn out. While there’s nothing wrong with having lots of things for players to do in a game, it’s better when the different missions and challenges aren’t so similar to the point where you’re doing the same thing over and over and over again. Those who just end up flying through the main campaign might not find the game to be all that drawn out, but completionists like myself will likely feel differently. Other issues I had with the game include the lock-on feature during combat being rather finnicky. I normally preferred using it when fighting one or two enemies, but when fighting multiple enemies at once, it became more of a hindrance since it would typically not lock onto the enemy I was trying to attack.

Late in the game, you go to a snowy mountain region, and navigating this part of the map was quite the pain in the rear due to many portions of the region consisting of cold zones that will drain your stamina and prevent you from climbing too high up any particular cliff, basically forcing you to take very specific routes to your current destination, which was really an annoying limiting factor after spending the majority of the game climbing up any surface and jumping off to glide around whenever I pleased. And twice during The Lost Gods DLC, I had to fight a couple of bosses more than once since I completed certain objectives for missions “out of order”, requiring me to backtrack a bit. And performance-wise, Immortals: Fenyx Rising crashed on me about three times, give or take, which isn’t too bad considering I spent a good 200 hours on this game, and it ran smoothly for the majority of that time. And thankfully, the crashes never made me lose much progress at all since the game auto-saves pretty regularly.

I enjoyed this game quite a bit, but I personally need a game to have a certain level of replayability if I’m going to keep it since I like to revisit my games at some point. And I honestly don’t see myself playing Immortals: Fenyx Rising again. Your mileage may vary though. If you’re like me and would prefer a game not to be too long or bloated with too much of the same content (not to mention have a better story), then I would suggest maybe borrowing or renting this game instead of buying it, or maybe just buy it when it’s $30 or less. Otherwise, if you just want a fun, whimsical, and relatively simple game to kill a bunch of time with, then Immortals: Fenyx Rising should be your type of game. If this game had been a bit shorter and less repetitive, then it might have gotten 5 stars from me, but it will have to settle for 4 stars, which is not bad.

I should start this review with the admission that this is my first FromSoftware game (and likely my last). I’ve never played any of the Souls games or Bloodborne before, though I do have experience with “Souls-like” games, namely the Nioh series from Team Ninja. Yet my time with the rather tough yet fun Nioh games still did not truly prepare me for the level of aggravation and rage I would experience with Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. I’m no pro gamer or one of those masochist gamers who gets off on playing punishingly difficult games, but I’m no slouch or casual gamer either. I’m a competent gamer who likes fun, story-driven adventure games but also enjoys more challenging endeavors, like God of War, Devil May Cry, Ninja Gaiden, the aforementioned Nioh games, etc.

Several of those games made me rage and throw a number of colorful expletives at my tv screen, but none of them had me dreading to pick up my controller again the way Sekiro did for a large portion of my playthrough. Seriously, there were times where I would finish a play session of Sekiro and then come back to it two or three days later with a sense of apprehension similar to what I felt when I was about to take a final exam back in high school. This had me thinking that perhaps Sekiro wasn’t the game for me.

But as hard as it was to continue, I stuck with Sekiro since I really don’t like giving up on games once I’ve committed to playing them. Having finally beaten the damn game, I can safely say that Sekiro is still not the game for me, and I traded that sucker in as soon as I finished it. I cannot imagine any scenario where I would be willing to play through this game again, and I’m someone who likes to replay the games I buy at some point down the line. Having said all that, I’m still glad I forced myself to play through this game since I can now confidently boast that I have beaten a FromSoftware title, and arguably it’s their hardest title to date. The short version of my opinion on Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is that I do find it to be a well-made game overall, and it is not an outright bad game, but it is not my idea of fun.

While finally defeating an enemy/boss that was giving me an exceptionally hard time was very satisfying, this game was just too damn brutal and uncompromising to the point where I just wasn’t having that much fun with it for the majority of my playthrough, and it got to the point where I developed a couple of stress headaches playing this damn game. My beating this game was honestly due more to my stubbornness and commitment to finishing what I started rather than me having any real desire to experience more of the gameplay and seeing how the story (which was okay at best) ends. For more details on what I liked and didn’t like about Sekiro, just read on.

This game’s combat largely revolves around you breaking an enemy’s posture so you can perform an execution-like deathblow on them, which will kill most regular enemies outright, but most bosses require two deathblows before they’re actually dead. While it is possible to kill an enemy just by lowering their health through direct attacks, in most cases it’s not the best strategy to focus on. For one thing, getting a direct hit on even regular enemies to lower their health is quite the undertaking since they’ll block damn near every attack you throw at them; this goes triple for the bosses. The good (sort of) thing about enemies blocking your hits is that it causes their posture to build up, as does blocking and, most importantly, deflecting (parrying) their attacks. An enemy’s posture will break once the associated meter is full. This goes both ways though. Sekiro’s posture will also break if his meter fills up after being hit enough or after blocking or deflecting a bunch of attacks, at which point he’ll be open to further enemy attacks. However, deflecting enemy attacks builds up very little posture for Sekiro, and it has the added benefit of building up an enemy’s posture more than almost any other form of attack; hence, the reason why your deflecting game must be on point at all times…and I do mean at ALL times.

I like making use of what most gamers refer to as “perfect blocks” (parrying) in other games that take advantage of the feature, like in the previously mentioned God of War and Nioh, as well as Ghost of Tsushima. Pulling off a perfect parry in one of those games gives you a great advantage in battle and leaves most enemies open to an immediate follow-up attack that can heavily damage or outright kill them. In Sekiro, the number of deflections and other stuff you’ll have to perform to break the posture of most enemies just once is ridiculously high (again, that goes triple for bosses). Even worse is the fact that the window for deflections is damn tight, and it’s extremely easy to end up performing a regular block or just mistiming it completely and getting smacked instead.

And naturally, the posture and health of bosses in particular far outclass Sekiro’s. Some bosses you can deflect and attack at every opportunity and still get nowhere with filling up their posture since it can empty out very quickly, at which point you must try to hit them when they’re open to bring down their health a bit, which in turn will greatly slow down their posture recovery. I’m sure it should be pretty clear to most of you by now that this game’s combat can be quite grindy. Certain later bosses in particular took me forever to beat since finding an opening to deal health damage was fleeting, and then breaking their posture took some time as well.

Adding more complications to the proceedings is this game’s extremely low margin for error. While enemies and bosses can take a real licking from Sekiro’s attacks, Sekiro himself is quite squishy and can be killed very easily. Even increasing Sekiro’s health and attack power by defeating bosses only makes a slight difference since enemies and bosses become stronger as you progress through the game. Sekiro’s options for attack are also very limited. Using his sword, you can make Sekiro strike enemies with standard attacks, charge attacks, jump attacks, and one of several special techniques that all have their own uses in different types of fights, though only one can be equipped at a time to the assigned buttons. The most advanced special techniques you can unlock are pretty powerful, but they drain Spirit Emblems, which is what is used as “ammo” for Sekiro’s Shinobi Prosthetic. That’s crap, those moves should have operated on a cooldown, but even I know that’s not a gameplay feature in Souls games; not brutal enough, I suppose.

The Shinobi Prosthetic item comes with several unique attachments, like a shuriken launcher, an iron umbrella that provides extra protection and makes deflecting attacks easier, a firecracker launcher that stuns enemies, and more. The thing is that most of the attachments are useful against only very specific enemies and downright useless against most other ones. The flamethrower attachment, for example, can damage most enemies and is supposed to be extra useful at stunning “red-eyed” enemies; in reality, setting enemies on fire does pitiful damage to their health, and there are very few “red-eyed” enemies in the game that would become stunned when hit with fire. The spear attachment lets Sekiro hit enemies with thrust attacks, and it can also be used to tear loose-fitting armor off specific enemies. But I almost never used the spear since, naturally, most enemies block the damn spear thrust, and there were probably three or four enemies in the entire game that had loose-fitting armor for me to tear off them. In most cases, the majority of the Shinobi Prosthetic attachments were just there to keep the combat from getting too stale and samey, but they largely proved to be superfluous, with only the shuriken, iron umbrella, and firecracker attachments proving to be the most consistently useful in most situations.

Furthermore, I tried not to use the Shinobi Prosthetic too much since the Spirit Emblems they use up can run out very easily. And whenever you die, any Spirit Emblems you may have used up beforehand will be gone, so you’d have to go out and farm more by finding other enemies to kill. It didn’t happen to me too many times, but on a few occasions, I had to momentarily refrain from continuing to fight the boss I was currently dealing with to go find more Spirit Emblems, which was annoying. I have to add that I absolutely hated how I spent a decent number of experience points to raise the maximum number of Spirit Emblems I can hold, only to find out that each increase only raises the max number of emblems by one. Freakin’ ONE!

This review is getting to be on the long side, so I’ll go through my last points as quickly as possible. The camera led to several cheap deaths since it goes nucking futs if I get cornered by an enemy, and if an enemy happens to jump over me and I run underneath and past them, my lock-on will suddenly disengage for some reason, and this is not the type of game where you want to fight enemies without being locked on to them. When you die and respawn at an idol (which is where you can rest and refill health items, upgrade, etc.), you lose a certain amount of money and experience points. Unlike in the other Souls games and the Nioh games, you cannot regain any experience or money by going to where you were previously killed, it’s gone for good. There’s a 30% chance you won’t lose anything after respawning at an idol, but those are sh!t odds, and they go down even more if you die too many times to a particular boss or group of enemies.

One other problem I had with this game is that a lot of enemies are just so damn hard to read. They can perform thrust attacks, sweep attacks, and grab attacks, none of which can be blocked normally. You have to avoid them completely, or in the case of thrust attacks, you can deflect them since a regular block won’t do (thank God for the Mikiri Counter). In many cases though, some bosses are so damn hard to read that it’s nearly impossible to tell which of these “perilous attacks” they’re going to hit you with. And I swear that there were times where I completely avoided enemy attacks but got hit by them anyway thanks to some questionable hitboxes. Other times I’ll jump away from an enemy attack, but they’ll still hit me in mid-air since they are capable of tracking you as if they were looking into the future to see exactly where you were going to be in the next second or two.

Despite my many issues with Sekiro, the combat was still engaging and fun(-ish), and it was satisfying to defeat such tough enemies after figuring out how best to deal with their fighting styles and abilities. But when I compare this game to the Nioh series, I can’t help but find those games to be far superior overall. They were punishing too, don’t get me wrong, but the challenge level was (mostly) more reasonable, and there were a number of bosses I was able to defeat in one go, whereas in Sekiro it took me two or more tries to kill 95% of all bosses and mini-bosses. Plus, Nioh’s combat is just way tighter and more fast-paced. Sekiro, despite being a ninja, felt somewhat sluggish compared to the characters you controlled in Nioh, and there was a noticeable half-second pause between button inputs and character actions in Sekiro (you press the attack button, and Sekiro attacks a half second later). In the Nioh games, your character’s actions were immediate and buttery smooth, or at least it felt like they were. I don’t mean to sound like a Nioh fanboy, but I feel those games were just done better and, most importantly, were way more fun; again, the Nioh games pissed me off many times as well, but at least they didn’t demand so damn much from the player while also providing them with such few advantages like Sekiro. There is the option for stealth, but its usefulness is very limited, particularly since you can’t use stealth against most bosses.

In the end, I cannot recommend Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice to most gamers. Naturally, there are plenty of gamers who will and did enjoy this game; it did (somehow) win Game of the Year in 2019 after all. By now, it is well known that gamers with more masochistic mindsets will enjoy playing and replaying this game to kingdom come, but for most others, this is not a game to be taken lightly. Like I mentioned before, I’m no hardcore gamer, nor am I a casual, I’m somewhere in-between. Despite my lack of “hardcore gaming skills”, I still beat this game, and I’m proud that I did. In fact, I actually enjoyed parts of this game after the halfway point where I finally started to “get it”. But the majority of my time with Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice was too consistently frustrating and overbearingly difficult, which greatly lowered its fun factor. If you’re more like me in terms of your “gaming class”, then I suggest you steer clear of this one, it might not be worth it. And if you do decide to give this one a try despite these warnings, then prepare yourselves for a world of hurt.

This game was a breath of fresh air after suffering through the absolutely punishing and unforgiving Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order takes a couple of gameplay-related inspirations from Sekiro but falls mercifully short of providing the same ball-busting experience as that game. Not to say that Jedi: Fallen Order is a breeze to play through, it is somewhat more challenging than the average game, but those who have played actual Souls games or Souls-like games shouldn’t be especially challenged by this one. And that was perfectly fine with me; call me crazy, but I prefer a manageable challenge in my games rather than the type of challenge where it feels like I’m beating my head against a wall.

Jedi: Fallen Order puts you in control of Cal Kestis, a Jedi Padawan who survived Order 66 and has remained in hiding for several years as a scrapper on some backwater planet. After using his Force powers to prevent his friend from falling to his death while on the job, Cal is found by the Jedi-hunting Inquisitors, but he manages to escape with help from new friends who take him on a journey to try to rebuild the fallen order of the Jedi (does the game’s title make sense to you now?). Throughout the adventure, Cal and his friends will visit five planets (not counting two other planets they go to in the prologue and climax) as they try to accomplish their mission. The main gameplay loop consists of Cal battling against Imperial forces and alien lifeforms as he makes his way through each environment. There are also plenty of collectibles to find in the form of cosmetics and “Force Echoes”. The cosmetics are different ponchos and outfits for Cal, as well as paint jobs for his crew’s ship, the Mantis, and his little droid buddy, BD-1. The Force Echoes are auditory glimpses into the past that Cal can sense using the rare Force ability known as Psychometry. And there are also the crates that increase the maximum number of stims (health items) that Cal can carry.

Many of these collectibles can only be acquired after certain points in the main story, so you will have to eventually revisit these planets to access any areas you couldn’t get to before. While the collectibles are optional, it’s worth getting them for the XP they come with so you can acquire Cal’s more powerful upgrades even sooner than if you were just playing through the story and not going off the beaten path. After completing part of the main quest on the second planet, I had the option of either going to the third planet or going back to the first one to explore some newly unlocked areas. Fortunately, I chose the latter, and when I went into one of the first planet’s new areas, I was rewarded with the double-bladed lightsaber, and from that point on I could switch between the single blade and double blade at will (more on the lightsaber combat later).

Exploring these planets and finding the different collectibles is pretty satisfying. The Metroidvania-type of environments encourage revisiting areas as the story progresses and Cal regains the Force abilities he once wielded before he cut himself off from the Force to go into hiding. His main Force abilities include Slow, which lets him slow down enemies and hazards (spinning fan blades and pumping pistons), Push, which can be used to, you guessed it, push back enemies and even return missiles and bombs back at enemies, Pull, which allows Cal to draw enemies and other objects towards him for easy kills or follow up with Push to launch them away or at other enemies, and finally he gains the ability to wall run and double jump. All these abilities can be upgraded after acquiring enough skill points, along with gaining other combat abilities like Cal throwing his lightsaber at enemies or knocking down surrounding enemies by jumping and striking the ground with a Force Push. He’ll also be able to increase his health and Force meter through upgrades and by finding specialized essences hidden in each map. Buying upgrades can be done at meditation circles, where Cal can also save his game and rest, which in familiar Souls-like fashion, heals Cal and refills all his stims with the added effect of respawning all enemies.

Speaking of enemies, the variety is decent but not great. Many of the planets feature just a handful of dangerous wildlife that mostly come in the form of big rats, big spiders/insects, and a few other larger creatures. I was hoping for a somewhat more extensive variety of the bigger and deadlier enemies, but at least the enemies put up a good challenge, even the smaller ones if they manage to gang up on you. The Imperial enemies consist of many different types of Stormtroopers, from the basic footsoldiers in their classic white armor with rifles (and who actually have pretty good aim for a change) to the tougher Purge Troopers armed with electrostaffs and electrobatons that allow them to go toe-to-toe with Cal’s lightsaber. You’ll also take on some Imperial droid enemies and AT-ST walkers. Even Nightbrothers and Undead Nightsisters will appear to challenge the player. Later in the game, Cal will have to deal with somewhat randomized attacks from bounty hunters when he goes to certain areas in planets he has already visited, and even though there are only three types of bounty hunter enemies, they provide pretty consistent challenges (particularly those damn droid bounty hunters).

In a slightly disappointing turn of events, the number of boss fights in this game (not counting the randomized bounty hunters) is rather paltry. Again, Sekiro threw boss after boss after boss at me, so one would think that I’d be fine playing a game that didn’t have a boss waiting for me around every corner, but I still would have liked it if Jedi: Fallen Order had featured a couple more of them. And while most of the bosses weren’t especially challenging, a couple of them were, and they were all enjoyable encounters. One thing I must say that I did not like was this set-piece involving a large monster boss throwing Cal high in the air, and as he fell, I had to “aim” him at the monster as it flies towards or away from Cal so he would grab it and continue the set-piece. If I miss the target by even a hair, then the game goes back a tiny bit and makes me do it again and again until I get it PERFECT, but the game did me no favors with the loosey-goosey controls it gave me during this set-piece. That moment of trial and error just annoyed the hell out of me. Thankfully, the other set-pieces in this game are done much better, like when Cal slides down a giant tree while avoiding blaster fire from an Imperial ship or, my favorite, when he hijacks an AT-AT and uses it to destroy Imperial defense turrets, TIE Fighters, and even other AT-ATs.

Finally, let’s get to the combat already, shall we? It’s great. The developers have actually managed to make a lightsaber feel like a deadly weapon in a video game. From the very outset, Cal’s lightsaber does heavy damage even to bosses. Fortunately, this doesn’t make the combat too easy since things are very well balanced (unlike in Sekiro) with enemies capable of killing Cal quickly if you’re too sloppy. And getting through the defenses of certain enemies, like the Purge Troopers, requires more than just hacking and slashing, you’ll have to deflect their attacks to more easily break through their defenses, and enemies can do the same to Cal if he blocks too much. I especially like how breaking an enemy’s defenses just requires a couple of deflections rather than the hundred or so deflections it takes to break an enemy’s posture in Sekiro. Jedi: Fallen Order has much better balance in that regard, as far as I’m concerned. And I like how Cal feels noticeably more powerful and skilled as you progress through the game, that sense of progression was done very well. I will say though that sometimes it seems like enemies in this game are capable of hitting you even when you dodge them; maybe I just didn’t gel as well with the dodge mechanic in this game as I did with others, but sometimes it felt like the invincibility frames for Cal’s dodge move were off.

There are some annoying but not game-breaking technical issues as well, like long loading screens when you start the game or respawn from a checkpoint. I also experienced some graphical pop-ins and frame-rate stutters in more open areas, and the game even froze a couple of times during battles, though it only lasted a few seconds. As for the story and characters, they’re done well, but I can’t call them exceptional. It’s pretty standard Star Wars fare. The main characters are likeable, if not loveable, and the villains are well done, though they could have used some more camera time. Basically, Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order is a good use of your gaming time if you’re a fan of Star Wars and if you like action-focused games with a sense of adventure, great combat, and Metroidvania-type of exploration.
