So a significant portion of Starhawk isn't available right off the bat. What DO you get here in this package? Unfortunately, not much. And what's here is really uneven. Starhawk is a 3rd person shooter who's uniqueness hinges on the titular (incredibly cool & well-realized) Starhawk, a transforming star fighter in the vein of Robotech's Veritech/Macross' Valkyrie fighters. Which would be totally original on PS3, if it weren't for all the other excellent shooters with transforming robot-planes in them, like Transformers: Fall of Cybertron or A.C.E.-R (Japan import). I mean, there's no region lock on the PS3, so you can grab all sorts of great mecha shooters on the platform from Japan. Transformers FoC though? That is the one that absolutely kills Starhawk for me. I'll get to that later...

So what we have here is a solid 3rd person shooter with an interesting aesthetic; this bizarre 70/30 space western (70% dusty western mining story, 30% space opera). There's no cover system, but who cares - that's worn out at this point anyway. It's solid. There's not really any interesting weaponry - you got your pistol, your machine gun, your rocket launcher, your shotgun, etc. Starhawk differentiates itself by borrowing the "drop structures and items from the sky" mechanic seen in other games like The Outfit or Section 8: Prejudice. It's done... okay, here. Your AI companions are boneheads though, so don't expect them to always take advantage of what you're dropping. And don't expect to always have the energy you need to actually build cool stuff the first time you go through missions. Heck, don't even expect to have many options here - the campaign acts a tutorial, so to make sure you know what each unit does, you can only build the 3 or 4 things each level wants you to use. Lame. By the time it finally opens up, the campaign is literally over - it's VERY short. Build & Battle could've been amazing, but everything is too dumb - it seems the developers were far too eager to get to multiplayer and ignore coding good Artificial Intelligence. It's insane that an action RTS from the early 00's like Battlezone, Urban Assault or Uprising had more interesting "build structures and lead AI friends into battle" mechanics than a game from today. It's a real shame.

Anyway, the rest of the campaign? What are the coolest parts? The parts with the Starhawk, of course. Unfortunately they're few and far between; the emphasis is clearly on the ground-based action, which is pretty forgettable. It's standard modern shooter stuff; you can drop a few turrets and walls, but otherwise, it's like a dumb Halo. Move to the next point with dumb AI buddies, defend something, ride in a hover bike or Warthog (called the "Razorback" here... y'know, another word for Warthog? Very clever) to the next point, repeat.

The thing is, while mostly standard, the Starhawk elevates the campaign so much when it appears! So the few times they DO get it right, it's exhilarating. It's genuinely amazing how it changes the level designs - you'll find yourself flying around these orbital platforms engaged in intense dogfights (fans of Microsoft's similarly-overlooked Crimson Skies will feel right at home), then land at any point, hop out of the Hawk and you realize these tiny platforms (when viewed from the sky) are fully designed gamespaces that accommodate on-foot battles, complete with a detailed, atmospheric interiors. Then you're pushed back out into space to find another Hawk, and take off once again! It absolutely sucks that THESE moments are the ones they DIDN'T focus on, because these moments are one-of-a-kind and by far the best parts of the game. They're some of the best parts of ANY GAME this generation! That's why Starhawk is so disappointing though; because there are a few moments that show off what this COULD'VE been if the focus had been shifted away from boilerplate 3rd person shooting and dumb, repetitive multiplayer modes, and focused back towards what makes this title unique and memorable. There's a little bit of that here, which just highlights how much worse the rest of the package is.

Unlike Transformers Fall of Cybertron - I said I'd get back to that! See, I put off buying Starhawk for a long time because I owned that title already. It's a game with a brilliant, memorable single player campaign and super fun, fully featured multiplayer suite that DOESN'T require an online pass. The on-ground combat is better thanks to more interesting weapons, better mechanics (you can switch if you're aiming over the left or right shoulder in Transformers - you can't in Starhawk here), and the fact that every character in TF doubles as their own transportation. Every multiplayer level also lets you play with a flying character if you want to - something you can't do in all of Starhawk's multiplayer levels (at least going by the "Explore" options). While zooming around as Starscream or whatever isn't as exhilarating as it is screaming around in a Hawk, and feels very different (Starhawk's flying model is MUCH BETTER; Transformers' is much simpler), it's more than good enough. It's such a better package if you're looking for cool transforming robot plane battles and a great 3rd person shooter experience with fantastic multiplayer; I cannot recommend this game when THAT one exists.

When I want multiplayer, I will just fire up Transformers. I'd suggest renting this. Starhawk can be AMAZING though; it's just that those moments are too few and far between. If you love multiplayer though? Who knows; it's probably going to be better for you - until, like I said, the servers go offline and/or the community dies. Then you're sitting on a disc that's incredibly light on content.

If Lightbox is listening, you should've coded some AI bots, you goons. Let people set up games and just play by themselves in these levels with these vehicles and mechanics. That addition would've added potentially thousands of hours of fun to this package. But because there's no thought at all given to giving solo players anything to do besides wander throughout empty multiplayer levels (seriously?), the multiplayer component is honestly just useless for some people like me who won't buy the online pass. And it's useless for EVERYBODY ELSE eventually, when servers get shut down. What's left is 2-4 hours of a campaign that's just plain disappointing. AI bots aren't something that's ridiculous to ask for in a package like this - shooters from the 90's delivered them. Perfect Dark on the N64 had AI bots with different personalities for crissake's! Why can't a major PS3 shooter deliver some bots in this day and age? That's just regressive.

I really liked Sonic & Sega All Stars Racing. Really liked it. It's a quality game - from UK Studio "Sumo Digital", who's worked with Sega before on Outrun 2/2006/Coast-to-Coast. They know their racing games if you look into their history, and it shows off with the Sonic Racing games. These are quality titles that can hang with, and surpass Mario Kart or Modnation Racers in some respects.

I just don't think this is better than the superb first game.

The titular "Transform" mechanic is mostly what's to blame. I mean, it's cool. It just screws up the driving model, and in turn, affects the track design negatively. I think the planes control fine, but drift terribly. Meanwhile, the boats control horribly, but drift is fine on the water - it's weird. So whenever they feel compelled to add a water section to a track because they have this boat mechanic they want to use, it just immediately deflates how well a track is working up to that point (the Billy Hatcher level here). It bums me out. But still, the track design is high quality in general. It's just one disappointment to me in this one.

Next up, we have the actual group of Sega properties here. I just don't think it's as good. One problem with this approach (possibly why Nintendo doesn't attempt a "Nintendo Kart" too) is that it's hard for the art to remain consistent. Hopping from an authentic Sonic stage that looks ripped straight out of Sonic Generations to another House of the Dead stage or Skies of Arcadia just shows that those two completely fail to capture the look and feel of either HotD or Skies of Arcadia. It's very inconsistent, but generally, the brighter, "cartoonier" games work well. NiGHTS into Dreams, Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, Super Monkey Ball, Jet Set Radio and Sonic all work well - everything past there just doesn't. The darker games like House of the Dead are weird inclusions. Shinobi and Golden Axe look weird; they're shooting to evoke Shinobi III from the Genesis with their stage, not either of the 3D Shinobi titles (that's a weird choice), and of course, the 3D doesn't capture the look of a 2D game. Golden Axe looks like neither the classic arcade titles (again, 2D) or the terrible 360 reboot, but it's closer to that. Then you got stuff like Burning Rangers that doesn't like the game they're named after - to be fair, Burning Rangers was released on the Saturn. This is probably the best update they could do to those visuals, but it doesn't really evoke it very well all the same.

It's very inconsistent all over; another thing that annoys me that's inconsistent is the music selection. The first one let you unlock classic Sega tracks and you could select from multiple music tracks for each race track. This one lacks that option, and doesn't have any classic or remastered tracks. It's all remixes, and they're - again (sense a theme here) - not always successful at capturing what made the original music. Like Skies of Arcadia? That doesn't sound AT ALL like the wonderful tunes from the game. I get that you want race music, so they wanted to bump up the tempo or whatever. But it just sounds bland now.

The difficulty spikes from the first game return too. Made worse with a terrible leveling up mechanic that devalues skill-based driving. I don't remember that from the first game. It was annoying before when racers would blast through you in a gold class race when the bronze class is stupid easy and the silver is still a matter of luck really. Now though, it's straight up infuriating when, statistically, someone like Ulala from Space Channel 5 simply CANNOT get ahead of Sonic. The top speed ratings don't support that, but it happens. So that blows.

OH! And Shadow and Alex Kidd no longer have motorcycles, so that blows. You can't do their wheelie tricks to gain speed boosts anymore :(

Technically, it's mostly really good. The racer animations suck, and some racers look AWFUL (Danica Patrick, Vyse from Skies of Arcadia), but generally it's a GREAT looking game. But it takes forever to load things, and you can't install data to speed it up. You'll play a few races, then check the time, and realize hours have passed. That's depressing. Online code works great though - no complaints there. And I bought this in July 2014, but still easily found people to play with online. And a wide range of people. Lost to some unbelievable players, but beat some real loser :) That's healthy. That's good.

The TL;DR version? While the game is generally fantastic, there's too many little things bringing down the game for people who've played the previous one or are big Sega fans. It's not as good, or as fun, as the first one. I think it's got some problems, and whereas the first one was easily better than Mario Kart Wii. But this one is not better than MK8, or Modnation Racers, or probably Little Big Planet Karting (I haven't played that one yet). It's still fine, but it's not as good as it should be. I didn't feel compelled to keep playing it - saw all the tracks, unlocked three extra characters, started getting the reflected tracks, and gave up there. Get this only after you've played those other ones (including the first Sonic/Sega All Stars Racing) that are better than it - that's what I'll say.

Man, what a letdown from LEGO Batman 2 and LEGO Marvel...

LEGO Batman 2 was the first open-world game in the series, followed up by LEGO City Undercover and LEGO Marvel Super Heroes. A design that absolutely freshened up the series thanks to the city of Gotham adding a lot of variety to the game. We had vehicles, and vehicle-focused boss stages and races, platforming challenges up various buildings, and lots of other ways to let people focus on what was great about these games - playing with different character abilities and exploring/discovering new areas & secrets. It also helped shove the less-than-stellar things - the parts that were really unpolished (the fighting) or monotonous (the "puzzles") - into the background. Everything was set for a spectacular LEGO Justice League at the end of that one.

Enter LEGO Batman 3. The game that absolutely should've been LEGO Justice League, and is all the worse for NOT being that game. Make no mistake about it, this is focused mostly on non-Batman characters like Brainiac and the various colored Lantern Corps. It takes place mostly in space and on other planets. There's NO reason Batman should be part of most of this, and it hurts every time they force his being there.

There's a level, called "Europe Against It", that illustrates this point painfully well. In it, Batman is paired with Superman and Wonder Woman in a miniaturized Paris which Brainiac is shrinking. Every "puzzle" involves blocking our heroes' way -- there's only one huge problem here: SUPERMAN AND WONDER WOMAN CAN FLY. Not to mention, Supes and Wonder Woman can SMASH EVERYTHING in their way with SUPER STRENGTH. "Ooh, Brainiac dropped a bus in our way" -- who cares, let them fly over it! "He knocked a bridge out" -- again, let them fly onto land. "For real? He dropped a giant phone booth in our way?" -- LET THEM SMASH THROUGH IT! All of these arbitrary obstacles are there only for Batman! Waiting for Batman to destroy some stuff so that he can make a grapple point so that he can pull down something Superman could've flown over in the first place? That's bad game design, right there.

WHY IS THIS A BATMAN GAME!?! Why is Warner Bros. so scared to put any other hero's name on their merchandise? Ugh - it's beyond frustrating (another great subtitle), because it's what the focus of the game ultimately is. It's like the developers said, "You have well over 100 DC characters with some of the most amazing powers ever to play with; but how can we make players get the biggest loser to the end of the stage in the most lengthy, roundabout way possible?"

They remove the open world and replace it with some small-ish (and generally uninteresting) hub worlds in certain places which is very disappointing. There's no huge, well designed area to explore, having fun taking advantage of powers like flight anymore, y'know? It's just more linear levels to slog through thanks to Batman (and some other losers) bringing the experience down. And make no mistake about it; there's nothing here that isn't the same core experience from the last few LEGO games. Complete with the laundry list of little things that should've been fixed years ago. And could be easily fixed with, like, 2-3 weeks of solid programming at the beginning of production.

- The combat is still messy, with weird auto-aiming getting your guy to glide automatically to the "nearest" - read: usually someone you don't need to hit and is in no way threatening you at this moment - baddie. OR buddy, for that matter - still don't know why it's so prone to making you smash your teammates. To be fair, your A.I. Buddies are still as lazy and dumb as ever, never helping you do basic stuff like smash up items in the environments or collect studs (contributing to the "slog"-like, or monotonous, gameplay)...
- You still take damage during lengthy attack animations that you can't cancel out of (like say, rolling into/pouncing on someone as Cheetah and mauling them). There's still issues with the game logic doing odd things like making a projectile focused character (say, Lex Luthor who shoots with his Kryptonite blaster) get stuck in melee attacks even after you bust up the guy who was closest to you instead of then transitioning to the distance attack for the other guys. All the powers are arbitrarily limited (ex: flying characters have ceilings and invisible walls to box them into areas), some characters are nerfed from the last game (Wonder Woman is no longer invulnerable)...
- The platforming is basic with the same mushy collision as all of these games, and there are still some glitches where triggered events you need to finish stages might not trigger or something like that. Which is always frustrating when you've smashed up everything and can't proceed after an hour or so. Only to come back the next day and see the thing that should've been there last night IS THERE NOW...
- And all the "puzzles" are, once again, solved by smashing everything until you find the thing you need to build, then building it, then switching to the character who needs to use the thing. Yawn. I get it's a game that's inclusive for gamers of all skill types, but jeez louise, you can design some more TYPES of easy "puzzles", y'know?

There is a ton of fan service though - A TON. I mean, seeing obscure characters like Daffy Duck (a.k.a. Duck Dodgers (a.k.a. The Green Loontern - a real character)) is a freakin' treat. And the presentation is great overall; the LEGO humor and fun is here in full effect. The game looks great, and there is ONE core game mechanic that's refined here from the last game - the suit switching. No longer do you need to find the pads to do it. Of course, the Free Play is really great (because you can kick Batman the heck out of the game entirely and play with GOOD characters), and Co-Op is always a blast. But man, all of those don't excuse the core problems. This game could've, AND SHOULD'VE, been a lot better.

==TL;DR
If you're looking forward to playing this after LEGO Batman 2, than wait for it to go down in price to $30 or so. If you played LEGO Marvel or LEGO City, pass it up entirely because you've played better. If you've not played Batman 2, Marvel Super Heroes or City Undercover, you have better LEGO games to play, my friend. This might as well be called "LEGO Missed Opportunity". Here's hoping the LEGO Batman series is over with this one, and Warner Bros. FINALLY finds the confidence to put out a DC product WITHOUT the Batman name on the cover. If 2017 or something brings us a proper LEGO Justice League, THAT game should be great.

But jeez louise. Warner Bros., Traveler's Tales -- fix the buddy A.I. already, please?! They've been sitting around watching the player character fight bad guys, smash stuff up, and collecting studs while NOT participating for a decade now! Since the very first LEGO Star Wars. Refine this stuff already.

Fantastic game overall; if the "Sonic Boom" branding scares you, don't let it. This is one of the best Sonic outings in years.

Sonic Boom is a GORGEOUS 2.5D entry in the series that pulls it's characters and settings from the Sonic Boom branch of the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise. That means it's a sidescroller like classic games, but with 3D graphics - think something like Donkey Kong Country Returns if you haven't heard of the term "2.5D" before. The title incorporates elements from a lot of quality sidescrollers - including world map screens similar to various Mario titles, team based gameplay with unique powers like in The Lost Vikings, expansive maps with hidden paths only accessible with specific skills a la Metroid - and meshes them all with quality Sonic gameplay.

If you just play through the stages as fast as you can, you'll enjoy a Sonic game with great level designs that's a little less precise than the best games in the series, but has a focus on tricks & special moves to engage instead of asking for precision all the time. With the characters' new "electro whip" thingie, they can now swing from grapple points, and with their individual abilities, all the platforming becomes something special. You'll end up pulling off combos like run > jump > swing > air dash > slam down into a zip boost > grind > bounce pad > swing, etc. So the classic-ness of the gameplay, while a little less fast and a little less precise, is actually a lot more engaging and rewarding to play. The game does bring the speed though, it's just metered out a little better than in previous sidescrollers. The camera is also a lot better and more dynamic, with a nice amount of "lead space" (the distance between the front of your character and the edge of the screen) so you actually have enough time to see obstacles coming and AVOID them. Crazy!

The game is a bit of an "adventure" in that you'll need to return to areas with new characters to gain access to different chunks of the levels and collect different doodads. Collecting doodads is important for a few reasons, namely you need them to access new levels (they're locked and require a certain number of emblems - obtained by finishing the stage, finishing it under a certain amount of time, collecting all the crystal shards in the level, etc. - to unlock), and you need blueprints to get Tails to build you upgrades. These upgrades apply to all characters, and include awesome things like destroying enemies by running through them, revealing item locations on the level map, or adding a "Ring Vaccuum" effect to your character so you can grab them by merely getting close to them, instead of having to get through them. A fully powered up character at the end of the game is a big improvement from one at the beginning, so the upgrades are important. Luckily going back into the levels with new characters and using their abilities are really fun. Tails lets you use fans in the level since he can glide, and he also has a toy submarine that lets you access a mini-game to get things too. Knuckles and bust through certain materials and tunnel underground, and Sticks has a boomerang that you can control around in the air - very useful for anything really, but specifically for hitting switches and turning off traps. Our main man Sonic however can air dash, which gives him the ability to reach out of the way areas ("L shaped" moves; air dashing straight up and right, for instance) and bust through blue blocks. You'll see all these "hooks" while making your way through levels, so you're going to WANT to explore further. And with Tails' upgrades, you won't be wandering around aimlessly - you'll see the items on your level map, know where you need to go, and just have to find the way to get there and pick the character who can do it.

The levels are really well designed in general, and - like I said before - gorgeous. This is one game where you'll want to crank the 3D up from time to time, because the depth in the game is really nice. There's a great mix of foreground, mid and background objects and the camera's dynamic; the 3D really makes it look like a diorama with it's mix of depth. All the models & textures look great too - this is one of the nicest looking games on 3DS for sure. It all moves at a smooth clip too. All the worlds are very distinct in aesthetic and feel from one another too. All the levels are built to accommodate both speeding through, with a default "middle track" and exploration, with additional "upper and lower tracks", to every level. So you'll end up exploring above, below and all over your main track on subsequent playthroughs, but it's always off to the side the speedier stuff - it never gets in the way. They're really good level designs that they function so well just racing through or slowing down and taking your time.

Sonic Shattered Crystal is super enjoyable once you come to terms with it's little oddities. Namely how progression works (gotta get those emblems!) and the less-precise-than-other-Sonic-sidescrollers controls (well, that's not true. It's better than Sonic 4 Part 1 and the Sonic Rivals games). It's gorgeous, the elements it adds to Sonic gameplay are fresh and welcome, the way it handles team based skills works beautifully, there's loads of content here, and it's just a blast to play. Highly recommended - but you don't even need to take my word for it. There's a demo for Sonic Boom on the 3DS eShop - just give it a play. This game is rad and deserves a purchase if you enjoy quality sidescrollers and Sonic games. Also, be on the lookout for it's sequel coming up this year: Sonic Boom Fire & Ice. It's from the same developers and looks to be as good as this one while adding in more to the formula.

Fun fact; the developers of this are Sanzaru Games. They're also the studio that makes Sly Cooper for Sony now (Sly Cooper: Thieves in Time for PS3/Vita is freakin' fantastic as well, I should point out). Sony only deals in quality platformers - just look at Jak & Daxter, Ratchet & Clank or Ape Escape - so when Sega gets the makers of Sly Cooper to make a Sonic game, you would figure it would be good, right? Well it is. It's an absolute - baffling - shame that so many outlets refused to cover this and instead focus on the disaster of the console game.

Absolutely as good in quality as an NES dogbone. It feels lighter than I remember, and it's smaller than I remember, but that could be due to... y'know, MOST of my memories of the NES coming from when I was 7 :P

This is a great product that works flawlessly and is super cheap. If you're looking for a good retro controller for an NES or NES Clone console (this worked flawlessly with a RetroN1 and a RetroN3), feel safe ordering one of these!

This Nintendo clone console is probably my favorite that I've yet checked out. It's made me completely forget my old, real-deal Top Loader and Front Loaders (I have two from back in the day), which is good, because I got this to replace those as well as both the N3 I got for my sister and the RetroDuo I got for a cousin.

The build quality & general design of the console is top-notch, so long as you're a fan of Japanese-style gaming hardware from the 90's. It's got some style & color, and is more interested with blending the aesthetic qualities of a high-tech device ("high-tech" for the 80's) with a family friendly toy than trying to look sleek or edgy, and it's beautiful. I MUCH prefer this to the looks of the Generation NEX, for instance, and the boxy, sharp original NES front loader.

The N1 is very compact and light - it's barely bigger than an NES cart, and I'm pretty sure it weighs less! The plastic is solid though, and while lightweight, it doesn't feel cheap. Which is good because you're gonna have to push down on your games to get them to click into the slot; if it were cheaper, it'd probably break after a few times doing this. The controllers too feel light, but solid, and are also compact. For an adult with big hands, this might feel too small - it felt a little too small to me, but also something that I got used to pretty quickly (though I certainly don't have huge hands). Unlike the N3's junk wireless Infrared control pads, these work pretty brilliantly! The circular disc-style dpad is less precise than the traditional cross pattern, but it also feels a lot better than you'd think. All the buttons are really responsive and feel great. Overall, the controllers work really well and you'll totally be fine if you don't have - or don't want to go look for - old NES controllers (though they're compatible here like with other RetroN systems; along with any clone controller, such as the Retro Bit Wired Dogbone controller). Finally - and pretty importantly - the power supply and the A/V cables are things of beauty! Mostly because I've recently seen the old "Power Bricks" and the RF-to-TV hookup -- those old components are gross. I can't imagine how inefficient that Power Brick must be nowadays. That's actually a pretty big reason why I've gotten clone consoles; it's just nicer to have modern components powering these things. And the RetroN1 has simple, reliable, modern parts that work. What more could you ask for?

Finally, I really gotta mention this again: the thing is gorgeous. It's got smoothed/rounded edges to accent it's simple block forms, and the white with red trim just looks fantastic. It just looks really great overall - very much in line with the aesthetics of 80's/90's Japanese game consoles like the Famicom or the PC Engine.

In terms of compatibility, I've not had a problem yet. It's good with all the officially released games I've tested, as well as Reproduction Carts like the English version of Yume Penguin Monogatari and Earthbound Zero. I'm feeling good about getting an English fan translation cart for Capcom's Sweet Home now. The only question mark I guess might be Tengen carts? Hmmm... the ONLY one I own is Gauntlet, so even if it doesn't work, I likely won't care :P And I don't feel like looking for it anyway. Maybe multi-carts too are worth testing, but I don't have ANY. Sorry readers; guess I'm not super thorough with cart checks here.

That aside, the point I'm trying to make is that this thing is quality! It's nice and compact and brilliantly replaces the real-deal Nintendo Entertainment System if you need it for that. Or just want a console that plays old games and are not going to go looking for something so old as an actual Nintendo Entertainment System. It's a real beauty too; a lot more aesthetically pleasing than U.S. machines from back then, that were always darker and angular.

Especially for this price, the RetroN1 is an excellent clone retro console that I would recommend wholeheartedly, so long as you are only looking at a system that plays NES games. If not, you may be better off spending more money on a RetroDuo, a RetroN3 or N5 now, or waiting for the Retro Freak (which plays 11 different consoles' games)

Though there are some frustrating moments, I'm enjoying this install. As others have already mentioned, the graphics are good, and there are many side-missions to help you level up. And once you adjust to (and understand) the combat moves, you'll do well. However, don't expect to take on enemies that are one or two levels above yours as easy as previous AC games, as it'll be like taking a toothpick to fight a bear. But as you level up and get better weapons, and become more and more familiar with your environment(s), you'll enjoy this game for hours and hours.

I purchased these under the Amazon warehouse deals, and I am in no way disappointed.

First of all, when you can buy these virtually new for $100.00 what's not to like? Secondly, I did read all the reviews and decided to purchase anyway as I needed to check out fully wireless headphones for Xbox One firsthand.

Sound: yes, at first they sounded flat, which gave me pause on whether I made a big mistake. But after going to my Xbox settings and turning on the surround, restarting and pairing with my console, WOW! What a difference.

I did notice the slight and very low pitch on the left side of the headset, as others have mentioned, which I believe may be attributed to the Bluetooth connection, but overall you don't really notice or hear it when playing.

I've also read where some said the volume needs to be louder. However, after running the latest update, I simply adjusted the volume and other settings on my computer monitor and now their much louder than when I first tested them out. So perhaps the lower volume is preset by the manufacturer?

Pairing: these pair in seconds just like your controller would.

Comfort: I find these to be pretty comfortable and light; and they don't squeeze your head like it's trying to get orange juice out of you.

Overall, I would rate these as high as I would my fully wireless TB520P's which I use on my PS4. Yes, I have both consoles, so no hater here, just an honest reviewer.

I hae JD2 and JD Summer Party. This is definitely an improvement and not just the same old thing.

The song selections are fun and varied. There will be something that everyone can enjoy. The music choices are highly dancable. The silly ones will have you dancing.

This is also a great motivator for those who are in it for the exercise.

What makes it such an improvement for me though is the level of difficulty of the choreography. In the earlier editions, it seems like the creators focused on making dances that were easy to follow along with. They are perfectly blocked. These are more challenging and so I find them more interesting. I am a dancer and I love following along with these people who use their bodies in such different ways than I do habitually. It is really stretching my imagination. I love it. I think that anyone who likes the previous ones will like this one too. It's worth the money to add it to your gaming collection.

I am not a big gamer, so take that into consideration. I do prefer Role Playing Games (RPG) so other types though. As far as that goes, I think this is the best of its kind. There is so much free will in this game. You will never play the same game twice. The realism is also amazing, both for the quality of graphics and just the type of interactions between characters that can happen. Bears act like bears. Bandits act like bandits. You can sneak away. Everything doesn't indiscriminantly attack you. Like the real world, you have to pay attention to your surroundings. You can fall off a cliff and die. You can be surprised by wild animals. Everything doesn't level up when you do. Some creatures are really weak and some are strong. You have to spend a LOT of time just getting to know yourself and your world, but if you are into RPG, it will be well spent.

The Just Dance:Disney Party is fun, but I think it tries to do too much. It's a great advertising vehicle for Disney because it includes very old song favorites from old classics like Cinderella (1950), new classics like Beauty and the Beast (1991) and new movies like Tangled (2010). They also include songs from their teen sensations like Hannah Montana. Once the kids see the range of products, they will be asking for DVDs from all of them. I see that as a plus and minus.

There are selections with dancing difficulty fit for toddlers and some that are geared to pre-teens, but I also see that as a plus and minus. While your child can grow with it, there are only a few songs that are appropriate for each age group so I can see it getting boring pretty quick. If you have mixed ages, they can all play together though.

I like it. The kids like it. It's clean and wholesome, but they actually like the non-Disney Just Dance titles more.

I thought this would be like Just Dance and wondered why it wasn't a Just Dance Hip Hop product. That's because it's really a distinct product. It's sort of a blend between Just Dance and Zumba, only hip hop style. This one feels more like exercise than dance. It is very repetitive. The choreography is not blocked like Just Dance where when a music phrase repeats, a dance phrase repeats (most of the time). It just feels random. There are 4 game modes. Dance Party rates your best and worst moves and gives you an overall accuracy score. Fortunately, there is a "Power Skooling" mode for practicing moves if you feel self conscious, competitive, or just can't get something. The third mode is the dance battle which is for two or more people. You really are battling in the sense that you are not just trying to do well. You are trying to reduce your opponent's score. The last mode is the dance marathon where you basically dance until you drop. The songs aren't particularly aerobic, so that could be a long time.

The song choices were decent. The graphics were okay. I didn't feel attracted or repelled by either of those, but the "Fun quotient" is just not there the way it is for similar products.

For example, in Black Flag when you are running on a rooftop, you just keep going. In this, you hit each ledge and wobble if you don't time your jumping just right. In Black Flag, if you try to run up a building that has nothing to hang onto, you just drop down where you started. In this, you will jump backward possibly killing yourself. That's incredibly frustrating and the reason I am not giving it 5 stars.

It's fun though. I love that it's historical fiction. I wouldn't recommend it to kids because of the violence and sex, but it could be a jumping off point for educational conversations about the Borgias, Machiavelli and all sorts of history for older kids. I am always up for a learning experience while having fun.

This rifle got 4 stars because I had to tweak it a bit.  Do what I did at your own risk.  If you are an impatient person and / or not mechanically inclined, you may not want to do any modifications.  The first 2 of the 4 things are pretty easy.  First, my experience is you have to be about 10+ feet (yes, I used a tape measure)from the TV in order to get the reticle to line up very closely with the sight on the rifle.  If you are too close, the reticle will not line up properly.  The downside to this is it's harder to see your targets the further back you go.  I recommend as big of a TV as you can afford. I played using my friend's 60" flatscreen LG, and it looks and works great.  I only have a 32" tube TV at home, but it's OK.  As a side note, I actually took the "barrel tube" off of the front of rifle to give it more of the shotgun look.  I'm using it for several of Remington's hunting games as a shotgun.  Second, even with the instructions, the nunchuck can be difficult to put in and take out. My experience was routing the cord thru the left slot on the inside compartment could be a little tricky.  You want to make sure the cord is routed out of the way so the C and Z buttons on the nunchuck engage properly, and also so the nunchuck itself seats properly in the compartment.  You will only need the B, A, and cross buttons for some games, so you might not even install the nunchuck sometimes.  It does give a better feel with it in there, tho.  The next steps get a little more difficult.  I had trouble with the B or trigger button sticking in in the depressed position, so I had to put a stronger spring inside to force the trigger to return further forward after a shot is fired.  So third, you need to take out all the phillips-head screws in the body (don't lose them!), cut thru the 3 stickers on the bottom of the compartments (these stickers show you where to put the controllers), and pull the 2 halves of the rifle apart.  There is a piece of plastic just ahead of the trigger guard.  It is about the size of a medium-sized piece of chewing gum and about the same thickness.  This piece has a bit of glue on it inside, so it's not going to come out easily most likely.  This is a spacer for the 2 halves, most likely so the halves don't cave in when screwed together.  Once the 2 halves are apart, you can see the linkage from the trigger up to the B button on the controller.  Luckily, I think the designers did a pretty good job on this rifle, from a ruggedness/sturdiness point of view.  I just slipped the original spring off the linkage, got a slightly longer and stronger spring, and slipped it on the linkage post, and put it back together.  If you don't have a box of springs (I bought mine from Harbor Freight Tools), your local hardware store can most likely match one up for you.  The spring needs to be strong enough to return the trigger to the forward position (without sticking) after every trigger pull, yet light enough so you don't wear your finger out trying to pull the trigger, so you may have to experiment a bit.  Fourth, I took the ring sight off the front of the barrel while I had the 2 halves apart.  It comes out easily.  If you prefer the ring sight, then leave it on.  I put the 2 halves back together, inserted my controller, and started playing.  It works great now, and I don't forsee and problems into the future.  Alot of work you say?  Of course it was.  What's it worth to you, tho?  I love my hunting games, so it was worth it for me.  I also noticed my scores have increased on every game I've played since my "fix".  Yes, I know I shouldn't have to do this with a gun right out of the box, but I wanted it to work better, and I thot I could fix it.  I'll probably buy another one and tweak it right out of the box.  That way myself and a buddy can play 2-player on these big game shooters.  I chose this rifle over the sniper rifle because the C and Z buttons are on the sides of the frame, not on magazine.  I read several comments about how the magazine-mounted buttons were awkward and made people get sore hands, cramps, etc.  I was playing my shooting games with a Perfect Shot Pistol prior to buying this rifle.  I am more stable using the rifle.  You can use this rifle for any game that uses the B button for the trigger.  With the nunchuck in place, all buttons are accessible on it and the main controller.  So, to recap, this would have gotten 5 stars had I not had to modify it to make it work how I thot it should work.  Hope this helps anyone who is looking to buy a rifle/shotgun.

This is a great game.  The graphics and sound are excellent.  It is really fun.  I would have given it 5 stars, but it's so difficult to get gold medals on each screen, even the very first few screens, in order to earn a new rifle.  There are so many critters coming at you from all different directions, it's mindboggling.  Don't even think of shooting them all--you have to let some get away.  Don't ever miss, either--not even once--after the first few animals.  You get a chain bonus the more animals you shoot without missing--usually over 1000 points each.  You need that to get thru the screens with a bronze medal minimum.  My biggest complaint about this game is the reloading.  In my opinion, it takes forever to reload manually with the A button or automatically letting the game reload for you.  Don't dare pull the trigger too soon when you think you're reloaded, either.  It seems like if you pull the trigger during reloading, the game starts the reload all over again, usually when a ferocious wolf is lunging at your throat, and you end up dead.  I am an avid hunter, and I do not agree with the time and effort it takes to reload the rifles and shotguns in this game compared to the number of animals coming at you all at once.  Someone who likes a challenge will love this game, tho.  See my review of the SureShot Rifle as well.  That's what I'm using to play this game.  Anything else would be pointless, in my opinion.  Precise, controlled shots are a must with this game.  Overall: very good.

This is a target shooter like no other I've ever seen.  There are no human or animal targets to shoot.  Anyone who has a moral problem with shooting animals or real people will appreciate that.  This game is actually a training program.  There's not a lot of hype or fanfare, just hardcore training.  Some of these targets shoot back, by the way--with paintballs, that is.  All scenarios are timed, and all shots are recorded.  As you progress, the scenarios get harder and harder.  Some are almost too hard, in my opinion.  The training scenarios seem very realistic.  Law Enforcement or Military personnel would probably like this.  I've done some training similar to this in real life.  Pretty cool that a person can get a little trigger time inside when it's cold and wet outside.  The higher levels are very hard, in my opinion.  The graphics are a little fuzzy at a distance.  The sound effects are good.  The variation in the scenarios is very good.  Overall:  Very Good.

This is a decent game -- not great, but ok. 3 stars.  Here's why:  First of all, some of the screens are pretty dark.  I know they do this so you'll use the thermal imaging and x-ray vision (both pretty cool), but it takes away from the gameplay, in my opinion, when you can't see the whole screen.  Secondly, I'm using my Sureshot Rifle, so take this in stride, but pushing the C and Z buttons is a little cumbersome, but not too terrible.  I'm going to try this with the WiiZapper, and if it's a lot better, I'll post that on here.  I really think it will be about the same...  The power-up special weapons are a little difficult to use, too.  By comparison, they're much easier to use on my Cabela's Dangerous Hunts 2011 or Remington Grand Slam North America (two excellent games) than this game, but still usable.  It was pretty fun game what I've played so far, but didn't put me on the edge of my seat like the 2 games I mentioned above.  It's an ok buy, tho, for $20.

I give this combo 4.5 stars total: (5) for the bird hunt, and (4) for the fishing game, if you wanna break it down.  I was originally buying just the bird hunt for a friend.  It's really fun, and it is challenging.  I was browsing Amazon, and I saw the two pack, and I said, heck ya, I'll buy the two pack for less money than just the bird hunting game by itself!  The fishing game takes some getting used to, especially using the nunchuck and controller in conjunction.  The bird hunting game is just great, and it gets 5 stars for being able to pick it up and play, sound, graphics, and challenge.  The fishing game gets 4 stars because the controllers are a little testy, the graphics are kinda blocky out to a distance, and for no fault of my own (I think), a couple fish got away from me when I did exactly what the game told me to do -- pull up, left, right, reel faster, etc...  Both games are fun, tho.  I would take the bird hunting game over the fishing game any day, but I'm a shooter, not a fisher.  It was a nice bonus, tho, getting the fishing game in the same pack.  Once I got the hang of reeling in fish, it was "reely" fun. :P

This game gets 3 stars because it's nothing like the quality of Grand Slam North America.  This is more of a kiddy game, in my opinion, than a serious shooter, if there is such a thing.  The graphics are just OK, the sound effects are OK, and the gameplay is choppy.  It's a little unnerving to shoot a target and see coins pop up all over the place, and then only have time to shoot about 5 of them.  The coins popping up was an unnecessary option, in my opinion.  The prizes are pretty easy to win, and you do get rewarded quickly in this game.  If you are waffling between this game or Grand Slam North America, definitely get GSNA.  If you can afford both, then buy both and decide for yourself.  GSNA is hard, I know, but it put me on the edge of my seat trying to get gold medals, and this game doesn't come close to doing that for me.

When I bought this game, I thot I was going to be in a shooting gallery, basically. Turns out this game is more of a big game shooter.  It is a very cool game. I've been using my Top Shot Elite gun that came with Cabela's Dangerous Hunts 2011 (another excellent game--see my review). There are only 2 things so far that I don't like about this game: on screens where you have to pull the trigger and pump the gun a lot, it can get very tiring, especially the bonus screens, and the other think is minor, but there's a load time between every screen. Sure, it's a time to rest if you want, but I'd rather get to the action than to wait every time a screen changes. Compared to Remington's Grand Slam North America (another shameless plug for another great game)there are a LOT fewer animals to shoot, and it seems like the screens only last about 60 seconds, so you need to make every shot count for sure. Another thing I like about this game is the animals seem to react to your shots. For example, you shoot squirrels and coons and possums and birds for bonus points. If there are no bucks to shoot (you only shoot bucks thru the entire game--no does) and you shoot a small bonus target, the does that are on the screen will spook and run right after the shot. I thot that was a pretty cool feature. I haven't finished the game yet, so I don't know if you can earn a semiautomatic shotgun (which would be very cool) by completing more levels. I did see a thing flash on the screen a couple times about unlimited ammo, so it could be an option later on. Overall, the game is very good and very fun. 4 stars.

This is a very good game overall. There are several things I like and several things I don't like about the game. Let's start with the dislikes: You have to do what the game tells you to do, or you can't move on in the storyline. It is very rigid in that sense. I also don't like how when you shoot bad guys, even when you shoot them with a bow and arrow, and they've never fired a shot at you, AND they are carrying guns, most of the time, nobody has any ammo on them when you search the bodies! Or if they do, sometimes they have very little ammo on them. Then, to add insult to injury, kill a couple of infected, and these critters are carrying ammo! It's crazy! I'm sure the game developers did that so you couldn't stockpile too much ammo, but with the "parts" upgrades, you have to earn the ability to carry more ammo, anyway, so it didn't make sense to me. I also don't like how dark the screen is sometimes. I realize if this were an infected apocalypse, most likely there would be times when we would be in the shadows. There's so many dang buttons to push, I sometimes forget which buttons do what, but I'm getting used to it. Now for the likes: I like/love how realistic it is, compared to how it would or could be in the event of an apocalypse. You might have a million guns, and very little ammo. You might have a shortage of supplies in general. Food might be scarce, and we might have to really scrounge to find anything edible. I "like" how some characters are just out for themselves, it seems. I think people will really be like that if an apocalypse ever occurs. None of this cut and dried, good vs. evil. Those people aren't completely bad, but that doesn't mean they wouldn't use a situation to their own advantage to survive, including leaving your character behind or screwing you over, lol. The scenery is amazing. I have seen other landscapes that are very good (Far Cry 3 recently), and this is just as good. I really like how this game makes me think about how to solve a problem to get to the next "level". Because the game "makes" you follow the chapters how it wants you to, you/I know there has to be a solution to get to that next chapter/level. I love the fact that I can find parts and upgrade weapons. The upgrades really do seem to make a tremendous difference (for me) in the game play. Also, the weapons are realistic. We should be able to come up with a rifle, a shotgun, a couple pistols, a bow & arrow, and the striking weapons like the baseball bat, machete, 2x4, and the lead pipe. Oh, that's another gripe, lol, you should not be able to break a lead pipe after killing a couple infected. I can see breaking a ball bat, a 2x4, and maybe the machete, but the lead pipe is a stretch, altho I realize the game must go on, lol. I would have liked to see this game sell for about $40, but even at $60, I believe I got my money's worth. I am 61% thru the game on the easiest level right now, and if I change my mind about the game, good or bad, I will report back here. Definitely buy this game. You won't be sorry.

**UPDATE** 7/21/13 **partial SPOILER at the bottom** I just finished the game on the easiest level yesterday. It's still a great game. It was still pretty hard for me. I can imagine if I decide to play it again that it will be much more difficult to complete on the higher levels. These infected are merciless, lol. They swarmed me and bit my neck with no remorse at all. My best advice, now that I've finished the game once, is to concentrate on maximizing a few key skills, as in maximum health and steady aim, and also to maximize a few key weapons. I prefer the shotgun for close range (with max "clip" capacity), the rifle for long range, and the scoped pistol for all ranges. One thing about that scoped pistol--it's essentially a 1-hit, 1-kill weapon most of the time. The downside to that pistol is the reload time and "clip" capacity. (To be more technical, a "clip" is a stripper clip used to load "magazines", and magazines are what hold the bullets that feed the pistol, rifle, or shotgun, generally. A "gun" is a field gun or large piece of artillery, not something you can hold in your hand.) You military personnel will appreciate that lesson, lol. Anyway...that scoped pistol is the bomb. Unfortunately, by time I got it in the game, I was using my "parts" to develop my rifle and shotgun, and I had already used a LOT of parts on the semi-automatic pistol. You really do have to choose which skills and weapons you want to develop, because there's not enough skill points and weapons upgrades parts to completely upgrade every weapon. As for bombs, they are the equivalent to a proximity grenade. Carry 3 with you at all times whenever possible. They are the single best hand-thrown weapon available, in my opinion. I love the explosive power they have, and they also stay un-exploded until an enemy comes within range. Throughout almost the entire game, there are entirely too many bottles and bricks, lol. I personally found it difficult to want to pick up bottles and bricks when there were multiple enemies in the vicinity. It really was too dangerous with several clickers and runners mucking about. Once 1 of them "sees" you, they are all on you in an instant, so the bricks and bottle have to be very precise if you use them. Bricks and bottles come in very handy, tho, in a burning restaurant, js. One thing that was neat and horrifying all at the same time was switching between the 2 main characters in the last approx. 30% of the game. I will say the scenarios were excellent, and again, probably realistic as to what COULD happen in the event of an apocalypse. **SPOILER** I hated the very end. Maybe that's what the designers were trying to make me feel. I didn't like that Ellie got taken, I got knocked in the head, and that they were going to cut her open. I didn't like having to kill people who were essentially "good" people looking for a cure to save mankind. I didn't like that I earned an assault rifle so close to the end of the game, when I definitely could have used that rifle against the hordes earlier on in the game. I imagine a good player could do just fine without it. I felt like the game ended pretty abruptly after that. I also couldn't tell whether Joel was lying about finding other "immune" subjects, or if Ellie was the only one. Regardless, still a very good game. You should still buy it. :)

I just finished playing this game now. These are the pros and cons.

Pros:
- Solid gameplay. Cover system works fine. Bullet curving and bullet time are fun and easy to use. The game also offers an acceptable amount of variety in gameplay mechanisms.
- Graphics aren't bad. They're not great, but good enough to be a current-gen game.
- Dialogues are good. I never read the comic version, but they give the same feelings with dialogues from the movie (which is good enough for me).
- Bullet cam is killer. It satisfies every time you see a bullet fly into an enemy. It happens randomly, so it's not too much (you could also set the option to 'Cinematic' and makes it happen every time if you'd like).

Cons:
- The game is way too short. I understand that the game was built around a handful of solid mechanisms, but 4-5 hours total is too short.
- More guns, and also grenades, would be greatly appreciated, and they would add a lot of variety to the game.
- Levels are a little too linear and kinda feel alike. The locations change, but they don't affect how you play or how enemies position themselves.
- There are some unlockables, but they're not really that appealing.
- Story could be a little confusing if you never watched the movie. I never read the comic so I couldn't tell how much it follows the comic or not at all.

In Conclusion:
Overall is 3.5 star for me. You don't have to read the comic to enjoy the game, but at least you should watch the movie. Even though the length and replay value of the game don't really deserve its full price, but now that the price dropped, it's worth checking out.

It is a movie game that doesn't suck. If you're a fan of this movie, I recommend you to at least rent it. It's fun to play and it captures the essence of the movie quite well.

This is the review for single player only. I didn't try the online multi-player (I don't know if there's anybody still playing this game online).

Pros:
- Decent 3rd-person shooter.
- Unique environment.
- Now it's cheap.

Cons:
- Story is not so good. It feels like a B-SciFi movie that's trying too hard to be cool or dramatic, but fails.
- No character or weapon upgrade. No interesting unlockable.
- Though the gunplay is alright, but it doesn't last. I had fun for about 2 missions, after that, it gets very repetitive.
- The robot commandeering is a nice touch, but it doesn't help improving the depth of the game much.
- Normal difficulty could turn into a frustrating experience for a player who's not really good at shooting game. Also, the vampiric nature of the game could make it worse since you have to keep getting the thermal energy in order to survive.

In conclusion:
It wouldn't hurt to buy this game, in case you're really curious about it or going to buy Lost Planet 2 and want to complete your collection. Otherwise, just save your money to put it on a better game with more replay value.

Pros:
- Great story. It's kinda remind me of "300". The pacing and the way the story unfolds is right. The performances may be a little weird but I think it's also very entertaining.
- Great production value. Animations are great, not just the combat moves or in-game animations but the performance also. Art direction has a certain appeal. Characters and environment look great. Sound effects and BGM tracks are top-notch. Again, it's like watching a good, highly stylized epic movie, like "300".
- Strong fundamental gameplay. You have combo moves, counter attack, special attacks, and some cool SIXAXIS tricks that you can play with. You get to play 2 characters. The good thing is that the secondary character helps making the game more fun, not dragging it down like many other games.

Cons:
- Learning new combos can become a chore. You'll end up using the same simple sets of moves over and over if you don't want to memorize the more complicated ones. Also, using 3 kinds of attacking and blocking requires some getting-used-to.
- No character upgrade. You unlock new sets of moves as the game progress but that's about it. No weapon or status upgrade of any kind.
- Not much replay value. You can unlock some special feature videos and art gallery, but nothing related to gameplay, except the Hell difficulty.

In Conclusion:
It's a junior version of "God of War" and "300" combined. It certainly has rooms for improvements, but the fundamentals of a good game are already there.
If you could get a good deal on this game, buy it. At least, rent it and give it a try. You'll have fun.

Pros:
- Art direction, graphics, sounds and performances are top-notch.
- Gameplay is great. Combat is fluid. Gadgets are fun to use. Controls are simple and effective. Camera does a decent job both in combat and exploration. The combination between action, stealth, and platforming are well-balanced.
- Collectibles are rewarding. Normally, I don't care much about them. But collectibles in this game help fulfilling the story and also give you XPs needed for upgrades.
- Challenge mode is a nice touch, especially when you can play as The Joker. You can use upgraded equipments and combos in this mode.

Con:
- No 'New Game+' feature means you have to start upgrading from zero if you want to play story mode again. The game doesn't give you a choice on that. If you want to fully upgrade Batman, you gotta get at least 80% of the collectibles.
It's quite a big deal for me because having to explore the island and hunt down all collectibles every time I start a new game is kinda annoying. I just want to sadistically abuse as many enemies as possible right from the start, with my full potential. For a game of only 10-15 hour length, is that too much to ask?

Even though the game lets you free roam the island after the ending to get all collectibles, but without any enemies left and upgrades don't carry over to the new game, what's the point?

Note: This is not a pro or con. The game doesn't progress on a chapter basis, so there's no Chapter Select available either.

In conclusion:
The game is great, but its only flaw is also significant, so I deduct 1 star for the replay value issue.
If you're okay with that, buy it, you'll love the game. If you're not okay with that, rent it first.
Anyway, I'm sure you'll like the game.

I got the game yesterday and I'm up to chapter 4 now. Ninja Gaiden Sigma 2 is the softer and more accessible game than the first Sigma, without losing any elements of fun.

You can select the easy mode, 'Acolyte path', right from the start (without an insult from the producer like the first one, which the easy mode 'Ninja Dog' came with an insulting dialogue from a female ninja, Ayane). Also, the difficulty level of the normal mode got pushed down quite a bit. Normal difficulty doesn't really give you a hard time. You may die a few times in one chapter if you're cheap on healing items, but if not, you could pass a chapter without dying. You gain some amount of health back after finishing off each fight. Some boss fights are just downright easy.

However, it doesn't mean you can beat enemies with button-mashing and your eyes closed. Considerable amount of tactics and quickness are still required. Combos, weapons, spells are getting a few tweaks here and there and they are fun to use. So, fans of the first Sigma shouldn't feel that the game has sacrificed any good thing. Well...at least I don't.

In conclusion:
Anyone who was intimidated by the difficulty of the first Sigma, but still interesting in this game, should definitely pick Sigma 2 up. All the fun is there, while a big chunk of frustration was removed. And when you feel up to the challenge, I recommend you get the first Sigma too.

As for the old Sigma fans, no need to say much, there's a high possibility that they own this game already :)

EDIT:
Now I've found one major flaw. Camera sucks!!! Cheap deaths happen from time to time just because the game force you to use low angle camera and don't allow you to rotate at times. I fought two Tengus (the birdmen in Momiji stage). While I fought one of them, the other one can just swoop in from out of frame and attack me with the unblockable move.

Also, enemies with big body or wings tend to block the camera often.
It's pretty lame to keep dying, not from difficulty of the game, but because of the camera forces me to fight in the angle I'm not comfortable with :P

If I'm not mistaken, I didn't have to fight with camera this much in the first Sigma. So, my overall score of this game has dropped to 4.5 now, due to the serious camera flaw.

I just got the game yesterday. After about 4 hours, the only progress I made so far is just past the tutorial. And I beat Ninja Gaiden Sigma on Normal difficulty for crying out loud!!! This is the game that tutorial stage could kill you!!!

This game is very unforgiving, so casual player be warned. There's no checkpoint and save point. When you die, you start at Nexus (the hub), you dropped all your souls at the place you died and reborn in soul-form, and if you die again, all the souls you dropped are lost. So, you'll most likely go through you first hours getting nowhere.

But, oddly enough, the game keeps you coming back. It's strangely and highly addictive in nature for those who prepared to accept frequent deaths and be patient with it. You'll learn little by little, use less and less time in each fight, and lose less and less health each time.

It's like those NES games (Ninja Gaiden, Megaman, Castlevania, etc.) that you keep dying and dying and dying and dying...and dying until you learn the patterns of enemies and traps by heart. It's frustrating, but satisfying as hell when you finally rise above the challenge.

Even so, I still prefer the game to have difficulty settings or save options for single player. People pay the same money, so they should be able to enjoy the game as they feel comfortable. Developers could reward them differently rather than leaving the casual players out of the circle entirely. And it'd be better for marketing too.

One flaw that I don't see the point why should this happen is that you can't pause the game in single-player. Why !?!? I know that adds realism to the game, but hey... players have to pee sometimes :P

Combat feels responsive and highly TACTICAL. This is by no means a hack-and-slash game, so bashing frenzy won't do you any good here. I'd call the melee combat in this game a fencing simulation. You're no God of War. You're just a person with a sword. You stab them, they die. They stab you, you die. So, be very cautious.

Graphics looks decent enough, not exactly PS3, but more like a PS2.5 game. The game looks better with low brightness, but that makes it harder to see enemies and traps. Though it's understandable that this game is not from a giant team like Square-Enix, but still, I believe they could do better with normal maps and texture details. Also, the character face looks hideous. Making the game looks Western doesn't mean they have to give up the pretty-face trend of the JRPGs. People still love looking at pretty people.

Also, the physics engine is a bit weird here. Pieces are flying around low-gravity-like when props are broken. Enemy corpses are rolling along when you walk over them, and their heads are twitching as if they're listening to iPod while lying dead XD

In conclusion:
I took one star off for the extreme unforgiving nature of the saving system, the lack of choice in difficulty, the no-restroom-break policy, and the less-than-impressive graphics. Other than that, the game is great.

Casual player who doesn't want any frustration should avoid this game at all cost. The game has gained its reputation for being very unforgiving since its first Asian release. You've been warned, and I'm warning you again.

If you can't take it easy when you die once and lose almost all your hours of progress, then DON'T listen to the hype of hardcore players. There's nothing wrong with liking easy games. Because even the greatest game of all eternity doesn't serve its purpose if it doesn't entertain you.

But if you feel up to the challenge, go for it. The game WILL forge you into a real warrior. I'm not there yet. But I'm having a lot of fun dying on the way there. I'm still halfway through Uncharted 2, but all I'm wanting to play now is this game.

First of all, to put this review up as a critical review, I cheated a little by giving this game 3 stars. (Please, don't burn me alive!!! I'll explain now) So, sorry fans, I'm dragging the score down a little.

Actually, this is a solid 4-star game for me. I just want to draw attentions of gamers who are on the fence and still considering about buying this game with an analytical point of view.

Let's start,

GAMEPLAY
Light: The game is everything you'd expected from the creator of Devil May Cry. Fast paced, over-the-top, cool heroine with attitude, cool guns and melee weapons, crazy combos and evasive moves. Combats are satisfying as hell.
The 2-button-attack system makes it simple to do combos. You can either get away with a couple of combos or go crazy and be the martial arts master. A lot of unlockables give the game a good replay value.

Dark: Yeah, it's everything you'd expected from the creator of DMC all right, including the difficulty. Remember that DMC3's difficulty had to be dropped down when they released the special edition, according to complaints from fans. This game is not exactly Ninja Gaiden or Demon's Souls, but it can be punishing at times.

- You can't button-mash your way through the game. Your attacks don't really have a powerful impact or knock-back effect, so enemies counter you all the time. That makes remembering the sets of moves and plan how to execute them in the right moment important.

- Dodging is crucial to your survival, maybe a little too much since you don't have any blocking move. Screw up your dodge once, and the consequence is severe. Health bar can be drained half by one set of 3-hit combo from an enemy.
If you don't hunt down the item that extends your health bar, you'd better excel at dodging. And health recovery items are scarce too.

- Boss battles may need quite specific tactics. You will die and die and die again, get frustrated, curse, cry for your mommy, until you figure out how to fight. If you can endure the gaming-induced anger and frustration, you'll be okay.

- They don't let you customize the button config. I don't understand why. How hard is that? It's an action game. Players should be able to set up the control scheme according to their preferences.

- Check points don't really have very good consistency. Sometimes they are too far apart and it forced you to suffer hordes of enemies and die easily at the boss.

- Loading time of a PS3 version is a little too much. Normally I don't really care, but this one is getting on my nerve quite a bit. The game takes some considerable loading time even when you open up the pause menu or pick up an item. It's not very long each time, but they add up to an annoying amount. I heard that a 360 version doesn't have this issue, so if you also have a 360, I recommend that one.

STORY & CINEMATIC
Light: Story doesn't make much sense at first. But as the game progresses, it will unfold and you'll understand more and more. There are some cool cinematic cut-scenes. Actors' performances are over-the-top, but since the story doesn't take itself too seriously, that turn out to be quite hilarious and fit for the game atmosphere.

Dark: Story doesn't give you any 'wow' moment, just a typical Light VS Dark stuff. And it looks like the developer didn't finish all the cut-scenes in time. They put in a lot of film-strip animatics with just character poses and voice-overs where there should be fully animated cut-scenes. Doing so gave a weird result, consistency wise.

- The overly-sexualized characteristic of this game might pluck some feminists' nerves. With the amount of butt, crotch, and boobs shots in this game, it's too much to be sexy. While I myself found it hilarious and I'm willing to bet that those animators must have done their serious research from porno and strip club, feminists with no sense of humor would find this game greatly offensive (since, to them, everything that guys think sexy is objectifying women)

VISUALS & SOUNDS
Light: Character designs are good, very unique. They cleverly made angels look threatening and ugly while they still look like angels. Environments and props are intricate. Effects are lush and abundance. I'm not gonna go deep about models and textures since I'm playing this game on a very old TV. Soundtrack is a little bit on the weird side. They pick 'Fly Me to The Moon' and pop-jazz mix songs for battle BGMs. They go well with the atmosphere of the game though.

Dark: Yes, effects are lush and abundance. But that turns into the downside as well. With all the razzle-dazzle going on the screen at the same time, dodging the attacks of 3 or 4 enemies becomes deadly. Effects can be very distracting and lead you to cheap death. Many times my mind just went blank and helplessly keep mashing the buttons just because I was overwhelmed by the visuals. Oftentimes after the fight ended, I had no idea what the hell I just did.

- You'll also fight with camera quite a bit. Mostly it does a decent job, but it twists into weird and undesirable angles at times and big enemies can completely block the view of your character. In those epic boss fights, they were so epic that your character sometimes shrunk down to about no bigger than half an inch. Playing this game for a long time can make your eyes filled with tears, but not of joy.

IN CONCLUSION
Despite some rough edges, it's good-looking, fun to play, and has a good replay value. Critics giving it 5-star or 40 out of 40 maybe a bit of a stretch. Nevertheless, the game is worth its full price, especially for Devil May Cry fans.

Button-masher and casual gamer beware, by the way. Under the sexy guise, Bayonetta is a younger sister of Ninja Gaiden, and she's a real feisty one. You're not gonna pass this game with one hand on something else. If you can't satisfy her, she'll punish you hard.

FF XIII is by no means a bad game. However, it's not exactly an heir to the throne either. New good stuff were added, but the old legacies which helped FF series gripped the heart of their fans were still lost.
Here we go...

PROS:
- Battle System is fun. It starts off slow and seems boring, even a bit clunky, at first. But you'll get more and more comfortable with the system as you proceed. It also gets deeper as you start facing tougher enemies. You can't win the fight without strategic thinking and being quick on the execution. Many fights seem impossible, until you grasp the right strategy.

Many complains about not being able to control all the team members. That doesn't bother me much since the AI is quite reliable, and the Active Time Battle in this one is quite a bit too rushing to put in commands for everyone anyway. Paradigm system works as effectively as the Gambit system in FF XII, and it's simpler to set up.

- Item and skill upgrading systems are similar to that of FF X. They're not revolutionary, but not at all bad.

- Art direction and graphics are, of course, impressive as ever. Soundtracks, though not imressive and not much of a romance in the melodies, get the job done.

CONS:
- The game forces you to endure an endless limbo of boredom during the first long hours, and that's critical. The game makes you switching back and forth between all the two-man teams of the 6 characters who got separated. I understand that it's a form of story telling. But 20-30 hours of very limited strategies and fighting hordes after hordes of weaklings seems like eternity. It picks up the pace greatly after the reunion of all characters. But for those with low tolerance, the first hours is more than enough to make them throw away the game.

- Being unable to control other team members or removing of the MP system might get on your nerve at first, though not a big deal and you'll get over it eventually. But what really frustrated me is that the death of the team leader alone decides the fate of the whole team. It means, in the tough fights, your only option for the team leader is the characters with high strength, not the mages. And since tough fights do come along quite often later in the game, you'll find yourself using the same set of characters over and over. Trying new combinations might spoil the fun rather than improving it.

- Story telling is less than impressive. It's not exactly sucky, but definitely not good. Character development hardly occurs. Though it's not as bad as FF XII, but you don't really care about the characters either.

Now the unforgiveable part. The developers did quite a good job creating an interesting world. BUT, sadly, they took the lazy way out of a story telling hassle by putting them in the glossary and notes. I'm talking about the descriptions of the locales, background stories, and even many crucial points of the main story line that would help players to understand. It wouldn't be a big deal if this was a PS1 game, but it's not.

Story telling and soundtrack of FF series have gone down the dangerous path since Hironobu Sakaguchi and Nobuo Uematsu left Square-Enix after FF X. The developers that took over the projects had done terrible jobs so far. And I'm certain that it's a fatal blow to the heart of FF fans.

...We dropped the controller when Aerith was stabbed in FF VII, from that moment on, revenge on Sephiroth was personal...
...We smiled with the two-generation romances of Rinoa and Squall and his father and her mother in FF VIII...
...We shed the tears with Yuna when Tidus faded away in FF X, and were happy to see their reunion in FF X-2 (even though FF X-2's gameplay sucked)
All other FFs also had their moments of emotional grip. And those moments are what set FF apart from other JRPGs.

But since FF XII, they focused too much on the gameplay. You could still go on for a 100 hours on quests and leveling up. I don't say that it's a bad thing to be creative on the gameplay. But those moments are no more. The stories and characters in FF XII and XIII are... bland. And spending 50-80 hours taking in a story of the boring or annoying characters is not a happy time for FF fans.

If SE's teams won't develop their story telling skill to be at least on par with the old members who left for Mistwalker, this franchise might someday die a tragic death or transform into something entirely different, and lesser.

- Dialogues in FF XIII are cheesy. Voice acting of Vanille is unbearable.

IN CONCLUSION:
3.5 stars from me. (I can't believe I give an FF less than 4 stars. Sad but true)

FF XIII feels a lot similar to FF X. Better in the esthetic department (of course, it's a generation apart), different and fresh in the gameplay department, but a lot lesser in the story department. The game itself is not a bad RPG, but considering all the series' landmarks that are lost, it's not a good FF.

Die-hard fans, like me, might find it to be reasonably fun and a bit dissapointing at the same time. I got my money's worth nonetheless.

But if I want my friends to love FF, I won't recommend this one as their first game in the series. At least not until the price dropped.

A pretty solid GBA release. Is better than the previous Legacy of Goku games. In this one you play as a selection of Z-fighters through the Buu Saga. ALl in all pretty fun with some neat RPG elements.

This game is actually pretty amazing. Kirby of course, almost never disappoints. take all of your favorite SNES, GBA, and NES parts of Kirby, add some more Kirby's and you have basically one of the best handheld side-scrollers ever made.

This game is a fantastic open world action adventure game.

There are a number of great things about this game. You can play straight through the story and enjoy it, or you can use this as a pick up and play game, cause a little chaos and come back later. Fall damage is basically non-existent and the grappling hook system is so fun allowing you to easily exit any situation it makes the game just feel good. While it is lacking on realism, this is more of a traditional lets blow things up in an interesting way kind of game.

You do what you want, whenever and wherever you want. It has HUGE numbers of collectables for those who enjoy that and also has tons of trophies that are not simply given to you like in others games.

It has a perfect difficulty. If you attack a village you will easily complete it. If you attacked a huge military base, you might just die.

The map is absolutely huge. This game is easily one of the gems of the PS3.

The big cons are somewhat poor voice acting and a story that lacks just a little bit.

Budokai 2 is a pretty solid game all in all. While gamers today might be getting dragged down by the new DBZ games, this one is a solid old classic. While game does not define the genre, or even the series for that matter it does offer a fresh beautifully cell-shaded fighting game - something the Gamecube arguably could have used more of.
