No Mans Sky suffers from what I would call some bad business decisions on the part of Hello Games (the creators). Somewhere along the way they decided to sign across the dotted line with Sony for what can be described as preferential treatment of the Playstation platform. In exchange Sony would take care of the marketing for the game which as we know costs a lot of $$$'s.

The issue is that his ended up being bad for consumers. Hello Games talked a big game early in the development cycle and really painted a beautiful picture of what their vision was for the game. As pressure mounted over the past year to push the game out the door, they became tight lipped, ambiguous, standoff-ish. The marketing and overall anticipation for this game completely bubbled over into absurdity, and the developer made a few tepid attempts to temper down expectations. Communication with consumers was absolutely botched, and a game was pushed out that had no right to charge $60 for, and most consumers were in the dark until it was too late.

This almost feels like a bait and switch, but I understand the developers had to stay quiet as they were under the thumb with the corporation they signed the contract with.

At this stage, No Man's Sky is a very buggy indie game that has had much of it's initial promise stripped away in order to get a game out out the door. It's not the game we were told about, but it's the start of a game that needed another year in the oven.

For those who don't already know, the gameplay is No Man's Sky at this moment is fighting with inventory, take snapshots of mr potato head creatures where parts just get swapped around, refueling EVERYTHING all the time, flying a spaceship that's mostly on autopilot and dying to pirates. There's planets that all orbit each other extremely closely but don't seem to be orbiting their suns properly. Forget any other space phenomena outside of very uninspiring black holes. Ring planets? Nothing we've seen. Gas giants? no. Red dwarfs? no. Neutron Stars? no. Our actual REAL galaxy we call the milky way is 100x more exciting than the quintillions of samey planets generated in No Man's Sky's fictional scifi universe. Much more work needed to be done on the mechanics of the game, and much work effort should have gone into the variety of systems we encountered, even if we couldn't land on the objects they could have made great scenery.

I wonder what would have become of No Man's Sky if Sean Murray and his team decided to take their idea to kickstarter, and talk to the players directly. Worked with the players, set proper expectations, received real feedback on their development process and actually put out an early access that people knew was early access and then continued to work on their technology until something of quality was released.

As of now we're being told by the creators that we get free DLC for life. This a way to pretend they are doing us all a favor but they are just finishing the game they originally promised. Don't buy unless you enjoy spending $60 to be a beta tester for an incompetent indie studio and their corporate overlord. Wait for the $20 sale in a year.

I can definitely say and without hesitation that Jedi: Fallen Order is in fact a video game. A micro-transaction sale window did not pop at the title screen, there was no online social features or loot boxes I could observe, and video gaming was had in my opening hours. Button presses, story stuff, jumping from platforms, maps, combat, exploring. Things happened.

After an Uncharted 2-like sequence alluding to the amazing train chase from stated game, I'm thrust into a lush green planet with animals to discover, a map to look at and things to do. I decide to tell BD-1 to take a hike because I in fact am doing my own thing. Buzz off I say. Lo and behold a discover a damp dark cave and I light it up with my saber. Moments later out of the corner of my eye I discover outline of the galaxy's largest toad. Oggdo Bogdo he is called. Tales of his prowess is told across the parsec. Oggdo Bogdo the king of one-shotting newb Jedi. There was a moment after my 15th death, with palms sweaty and moms spaghetti, I questioned my own sanity. "EA greenlit this game?" I muttered in disbelief.

If you're a Star Wars fan, I would buy this game with the acknowledgement it needs a few weeks of patches, however if you're not a Star Wars fan, I would purchase this game because it's in fact a game and EA doesn't really do games anymore. If enough people buy games, perhaps more massive publishers will decide to greenlight more games again. Games where you put in a disc, and there's just the game and you play it. Everything there is, is the game. No spinning wheels, no casino bloops and beeps, no opened ended social features designed to encourage micro-transactions, no gating satisfaction behind a paywall.

Consider this game if you like Rise of the Tomb Raider, Uncharted 2, Bloodborne (on training wheels) and Star Wars.

I purchased this game for the Xbox 360 without any idea what to really expect other than a shooter.  As a shooter it's a mediocre game, and there are a lot of better titles out there.  As an overall game though, it's a fun title.  The graphics and controls can be a bit clunky, but are still good.  The AI is usually decent, but sometimes will have a complete meltdown which can be frustrating or disappointing.  The story progression and the characters are excellent.  What makes this game is the choices you can make and the results of those actions.  Do you try to do X, or save person Y, or try to figure out alternative Z.  All of the main characters in the game you can attempt to become friends or enemies with, ally with them or betray them, let them live or kill them (or let them get killed).  The RPG elements are a split of perks for performing certain actions or accomplishments, and a selection of skills and specialties to suit your play style. Alpha Protocol is substantially longer game than a normal shooter.  The multiple endings are also a nice touch even though they are all lackluster in their execution.  Overall I enjoyed this game, and I'm really glad I ended up picking it up.  I would suggest giving it a try.

Just Dance 2 is better than any regular 'dance mat' game, because you are actually dancing!

The amount of songs is 50+ when you include the downloadable songs(need Internet connection and Wii Points). I won't list them, because some people already have, but some of my favorites are "Move Your Feet" by Junior Senior, "Sway(Quien Sera)" by The Marine Band, "Soul Bossa Nova" by Quincy Jones and Orchestra, and "Katti Kalandal" by Bollywood. The variety is great! Lyrics are shown when they are available, but they can be turned off. I have gotten 10,000+ points on at least 8-10 of the songs.

NOTE: THE 1st AND 3rd WIIMOTES ARE REPRESENTED BY THE WOMAN DANCERS WHEN PLAYING A "Duet" SONG, JUST AN FYI FOR GUYS!

Choreography is good, and the dancers know their stuff! If a dance drags on too much for you, there is a shorter version of EACH song. In the right hand corner of the Song Screen( Just Dance mode, maybe Just Sweat mode too), there is a timer that displays the song's time. You can switch between short and long versions with the Wiimote's 'minus' button. It isn't terribly hard to follow along to the dances, and you get the hang of it pretty easily. The pictogram man at the bottom lets you know what is coming next, and it is fairly clear.

Downloading songs is a good option. That adds about 10-12 more songs to the already large selection list. These include "Pump Up the Volume", "Come On Eileen", and "American Boy". The songs cost 300 Wii Points each, about $3. It also includes a free download song, Katy Perry's "Firework".

The different dance modes aren't superb, but I do like Dance Battle. 4-8 players sign in and you choose teams. Instead of picking a song, it randomizes it for you. You can choose the "Joker" button, but only once per round. Otherwise, gameplay is the same. At the end of each round, the scores are tallied. The rounds can go at least over 5. Just Sweat is the same as the Just Dance mode, but only one person plays, and a meter on the right shows you how much "sweat" you are working up. This helps you earn Sweat Points, to keep track of on a graph. There are three programs: Easy(1 song), Tough(3 songs), and Intense(6 songs).

Overall, Just Dance 2 is awesome! Now, what songs should be on Just Dance 3...???

UPDATE: Another new FREE download song is out, "Here Comes the Hotsteppers" by The Hit Crew!

Summary: An quick review for the Wii version of Disney Infinity.

Essential points:

- Play Sets only support 1-player gaming; Toy Box supports 2 players

- No concrete information on online support for the Wii version

- One hexagon Power Disc comes with the Starter Pack

- Buying the Sidekick or Villain packs (counterparts for the 3 included characters) is the cheapest way to get more figurines for 2-player co-op.

- Each character is confined to their Play Set when not in Toy Box
- For example, Sulley cannot play in the Pirates/Caribbean Set, Jack Sparrow cannot
play in The Incredibles Set

Controls: Disney Infinity is fairly easy to pick up, but I would advise reading the manual, because this game uses all Wii remote buttons in different ways. Nunchucks are required to play this game, so be prepared. Most controls are standard, so there is not so much of a learning curve here.

Play Set Gameplay: Each Play Set involves completing a plethora of missions (6-10 hours) that help you level up characters, buy special vehicles and weapons, and earn Spins in the Disney Infinity Vault. Some missions are harder than others, but they are fun to complete.

Toy Box Gameplay: Mentioned previously, Spins allow the player to receive items in the Disney Infinity Vault that fill their Toy Box worlds (Block packs, Creativi-Toys, and Landmarks). Those Spins can be earned through Play Set missions and other activities. Toy Box is a really fun experience, and I will certainly have a blast making game 'levels' for my family to win.

Online Play: First off, the Wii is nearly seven years old, so the Internet capabilities are limited. It does not have an option to link to my Disney ID, and I do not see an option to play with others. For now, I would not count on online gaming for the Wii version.

Power Discs: There are three types of discs: Toy Box Toys, Toy Box Themes, and Character Powers. The only way to re-theme a Toy Box world is to collect a Theme disc, FYI. We received "Carl's Cane" (Up) in our pack.

Audio and Video: The audio part of the game seems a little lacking, and not as rich, but the music is dead on. One of the songs makes me feel like I am in Disney World, and 'Metroville' from The Incredibles is fast-paced and jazzy. The graphics were also less than desired, but that's expected from the non-HD Wii.

Overall: This game gets a B+ from me after six hours of gameplay. The Toy Box component is a little more advanced, so that's a good chance for the parent to jump in (wink, wink). The Play Sets are freeplay for the most part, and missions are completed on your own time. Disney hit a triple with this game.

Thanks for reading my review. I may be able to help with any questions, so feel free to ask.

After two weeks, my impressions of NSMBU are in. This game crushes NSMBWii by a landslide, and I don't see how anyone could say different.

Gameplay: There wasn't any need for Nintendo to branch out from a successful system, so I'm glad they kept everything the same [that's what I bought SM3DW ;)]. The baby Yoshis are a great addition, and I love the P-nut powerup. The controls are easy to learn, and there is nothing complicated about them.

Levels: These have the same layouts as before, but new mechanics and enemies. I enjoyed the refresh, and some of the new levels are really fun (especially the 2nd level in a secret world...). I didn't really get a "Gee, did that level before" feeling from this game, which other reviewers were complaining about. The levels are slightly longer than before, as well; some are more difficult than others. I enjoyed the game, and have not quite finished it yet.

Boost Mode: This is great for the days when I want to "help out" fellow players. It's definitely more complicated than it seems, and there were some miscues in the beginning. But, I'm pleased with the "4 ½ player".

Overall, I have enjoyed NSMBU a ton, and haven't really gotten to the bonuses yet, so this should keep me occupied for a couple months...

This is a short and concise version of NSMBU, and I actually like it more. Played this after the young one went to bed, because this game is way more hectic than its older brother.

Nabbit: If I have one thing to say, Nabbit rocks. I was stealing mushrooms left and right, and left my fellow players in the dust. There's nothing like running through Piranha plants. Plus, those "stolen" powerups are converted to 1-ups at the end of each level, so I don't have to worry about jumping to the elusive top of the flag.

Gameplay: The added "hops" of each character is handy, but that lost traction can burn you in tight spots. But, that's part of the fun. The levels are shorter, and I like that aspect. It's easier to jump in for "one more level before bed", than NSMBU, and definitely faster than Super Mario 3D World.

Levels: These are redone levels of NSMBU, but they still felt different. In fact, they weren't completely recognizable as the counterparts of their longer cousins, so props to Nintendo. Some of them are "kill levels", but I think those are the best types. Overall, after a few hard ones, the game is not too difficult. We got to World Three in one night. Oh, don't even try Boost Mode on this game for really fun party nights.

NSLU was a shining moment for Nintendo this year. I love everything about it, and can't wait to finish it.

Tomodachi life is more than just a combination of Animal Crossing and The Sims, it's a game that mocks you and your family in friends in the most friendly of ways. Each mii you add has their own
totally unique personality, with events of all sorts occurring at random to ensure you never put your 3DS down. The game feels like very much an experimental game, and yet it feels very refined, possibly due to the fact that the previous entry in the series was not introduced outside of the Japanese market, and although this game is built for everyone, it has a distinct Japanese charm that sets it apart from slightly-similar "free" smart-phone apps that have no soul.

The game revolves around an island, and the Mii's you decide to add to that island. Don't be afraid to add as many as possible, the more the merrier! My game includes random celebrities, game developers, politicians, family members and significant others, and the results are whacky and hilarious. Overall it's the type of game that will hook you for hours at a time. There's much tomodachi life has to offer even to the non-gamer, and is sure to bring a smile to those watching.

So then, why the 3-star rating? The game is almost a decade old at this point. This game can be picked up for the 360/PS3 for 5-15$ at most game shops nowadays depending on whether you get the GOTY edition PS4/Xbox One (special editions) have been on sale for 20-30$.

If you're interested in buying this title. I think the main qualifiers are:

Do you think the mobile version is worth twice as much more than the Special Edition(30$)? Three times more than the 360/PS3 versions (15$)?

I suppose if you think it's worth it, then by all means, buy it. The motion controls are kind of fun, and the Zelda-themed gear is cool. I just don't know if it's worth 60$....

This is the game that makes Uncharted the great franchise it is. After finally getting around to beating the first game, I had this impression that Uncharted is good, but expected something more. Finally I got around to the sequel Among Thieves. This game improved on all core gameplay issues I had with the first all while delivering once again an even better story.

In terms of the combat, while the controls can still be a little wonky at times, Naughty Dog certainly improved upon them. I found the firefights weren't as tedious and honestly fun. What my gripe about the first game is is that the gameplay itself is not particularly fun. The story and characters essentially carry that game. This game improves upon the shooting sections, but adds more platforming sections, puzzles, and crazy action sequences to the game which the first game lacks. It makes for an ultimately fun game. The train section is just epic and the fight through the city on the rooftops is fun. However, while the game does add more of this, it still could have used more crazy sections like the train in particularly. It was definitely the most memorable action sequence of the game.

Now Uncharted is a game notably known for its story. Among Thieves once again finds Nathan Drake seemingly done with the treasure hunting business only to be lured back into it by old associates on a quest to find yet another lost city, but this time it is Shambala. This takes Drake on a quest around SE Asia and particularly the Himalayas region. This simply provides for a beautiful backdrop to this game and man does it look beautiful. The story itself is excellent. The villains are better than that of the first game, but the main antagonist is still just a throw away villain, typical power hungry guy.

To sum it up, Uncharted 2 is the game that makes this franchise great. It improves upon the gameplay aspects of the first game and delivers a fun experience. The story is great and the main cast of characters are great. Awesome game.

This is one of the freshest games I have played in some time. One of the few things I have like about this generation of gaming are the games that have been a throwback to a gaming era some 15-20 years ago. When first person shooters like Doom were just there to give you high octane, fun gameplay and 3D platformers like Ratchet and Clank a long with Jak and Daxter rained supreme with there fun platforming mechanics and shooting. Now we've seen the return of Doom and not to mention Wolfenstein. For platformers, we got Sunset Overdrive, Ratchet & Clank made a return, and now we have Recore which embodies all that was good about the platforming shooters from 15-20 years ago. As someone who grew up playing the Jak and Daxter trilogy, Recore felt right at home.

I'd like to keep this short though. To summarize,the story and characters are interesting. Your robot companions are fun and cute. The gameplay is top notch. However, the game does have technical issues. While it is nothing to stop me from playing, they are certainly there. Then there is the famous loading time problem as well. Now one complaint coming up is the backtracking later in the game. To advance into certain areas or dungeons you need to have a certain number of 'prismatic cores' to advance. Now I personally don't see this as a problem. This is a very common mechanic in the old school platformers that this game is a throwback too. However, I understand where people not overly familiar with this mechanic will take issue especially with the load time problem as well. It is a mechanic you just don't see anymore so I feel people playing a game like Recore for the first time, will hate the backtracking.

At the end of it all, I really find myself enjoying this game. I look forward to completing it and getting as much done in the game as possible. If you grew up on the platforming shooters of the late 90s and early 2000s, you'll probably enjoy this game. For newcomers to the genre, be warned.The game certainly starts off on a great note, but the backtracking can certainly get to you. Though I do think there something for you to enjoy from this game no matter what. Recore is just a fun, cute, and interesting throwback to a time when 3D platformers were supreme.

The Forza racing game franchise in the last few years has become king of the genre. Yet I feel the Horizon series is what put it on the pinnacle. The first one blended a fun arcade racer with the great mechanics of the Forza Motorsport franchise which provided for a fun, yet grounded arcade racer. Horizon 2 improved on its predecessor in every facet with it's beautiful open world of Southern Europe, the openness of the world itself, the showcases, cars, and all around fun. It made you wonder what else could they possibly do to improve going into the inevitable third Horizon game and Playground Games knocked it out of the park.

With Horizon 3, you are the boss of the festival. The campaign has you working your way around the Australian map looking to expand and make the Horizon festival even bigger. What sets Horizon 3 a part from its predecessor is the sheer amount of customization you have now. You have a select number of character avatars to choose from and can even pick a name or nickname you'd like to be called. It seems Playground took some pointers from Fallout 4 on this matter if you catch my meaning, but made it even better. Being referred to by my own name in a game just makes for a more personalized experience and that is what Horizon 3 is about. You making the festival your own. Even to the point where you can design the races themselves with the blueprint system.

From a gameplay standpoint, you know what to expect for anyone familiar with the previous games or the Forza franchise itself. Just an awesome all around racing experience. The driving mechanics are on point as usual and all the other aspects from weather effects add even more. One thing I love about Forza is that each of the two versions, Motorsport and Horizon tend to build on each other's strengths. I personally like how Horizon 3 has incorporated more of the weather effects from Forza 6 with the puddles and such on the raceways. The Australia setting itself is beautiful and extremely diverse from cool beaches, the desert outback, urban area, and jungle which just adds to the experience.

Now since this is the ultimate edition, for anyone who is just a die hard Forza fan, it is totally worth it. Especially if you can get it with the prime discount. With it you get the car pass and VIP. For a casual Forza player, just get the standard edition especially since the car pass always goes on sale for cheap down the road. VIP I always have found to be worth it and is best gotten early to take advantage of the bonuses. All in all a decent package and the steel book case is very nice. You just can't beat it with that prime discount though so kudos to Amazon.

So in the end of all this excitement, Horizon 3 once again keeps Forza at the top of the racing genre. This game is hands down the racing game of the year and is even deserving of some overall consensus game of the year awards as well. It truly deserves it. Fantastic game. Bravo Playground Gamaes, Bravo.

While I have only put two hours into the Aqua portion of the game, just based on the overall package, this game warrants five stars. I have already played DDD on the 3DS and it is easily one of the best games in the series. Definitely top four. I really look forward to playing through this game again on a console and TV screen compared to the 3DS. It should definitely be a much better experience gameplay wise. The narrative while confusing, is enjoyable. This is also one of only a couple of KH games where you get to play as Riku, who is one of my favorite characters and is also fun to play as. The big highlight of Chain of Memories for example was the Riku story mode, and same goes for DDD. The combat itself is fun too and for those wondering about boss fights and difficulty, its a KH game so there is always a couple fights that will frustrate you. All in all DDD is a great game and worth playing for any KH fan.

Now in regards to the Aqua portion of the game, this is essentially the prologue to KHIII and pretty much the MGSV Ground Zeroes of Kingdom Hearts. The game is meant to connect to the story of Birth By Sleep to KHIII and of course the ending of DDD for those who have already beaten it. Yet it is also here to show us what we can expect graphically and gameplay wise from KHIII. The game is running on Unreal Engine 4 and you can definitely see a huge graphical difference between the KH games of past and now. From a gameplay standpoint, its a combination of Birth by Sleep and KHII. The magic gauge is the same as KHII, same goes for the d-pad menu, and the quick menu to easily use your magic and potions. It also uses the gauge thing from Birth by Sleep where you can hold R1 to lock on to a target and shoot a burst of magic or energy at it. All in all the combat is fluid and quick. Controlling Aqua is very fun and moving around each combat area feels right. The magic spells feel really powerful and are cool to use. The game also starts you off with an Aqua who is already at level 50 and the four magic spells are already in their third -aga form which is necessary since this is a keyblade master after all, so I like this touch Square Enix put here. One of my worries about the Aqua portion was that it could potentially be rather short. Yet with two hours put into it, those worries are being simmered down. Square Enix put in these things called up objectives where you need to do specific tasks, some combat related, boss fight related (these are especially missable), and story related. These essentially give the player more things to do. If I finish the the main story with 5+ hours put into it and still some objectives to do then the game is worth it in my opinion. Doing these objectives of course awards you with items you can decorate Aqua with. This is a new system for KH, one where we can actually dress up our character, that I hope makes its way into KHIII. It allows the player to add their twist to the character and just gives you more options and customization. So far I have enjoyed my experience in the Aqua portion and it just makes me more excited for KHIII, it gives me hope Square Enix can pull this off.

Now the package comes with an addition movie that I guess gives you the story of this desktop KH that came out in the last year or so. From my understanding it takes place even before the Birth by Sleep and I assume in incremental to the overall story especially in regards to KHIII where games like Birth by Sleep, Chain of Memories, and DDD are now very significant to the story. I like that Square took this approach so that these games are more than just spin offs, but are essential as well.

Overall, this is a great package. I picked up the Limited Edition which comes with two pins. It was the same price as the standard so hey, why not? The pins are pretty cool looking too for anyone wondering. Now the big question for some, is it worth the $60? Unless you are a die hard KH fan, then I'd say no. Though worth is subjective. If you base worth around hours you can get out of a game and you don't tend to rush through games, you can easily get 30-40 hours out of this whole package, which some $60 releases fail to do. That being said this game is certainly worth owning at some point for anyone who likes Kingdom Hearts. It is essentially the prologue to KHIII, highlights the gameplay mechanics we can probably see in KHIII, and has one of the best games in the KH franchise which is Dream Drop Distance. A game perhaps not worth it for some now, but worth it eventually.

The Order 1886 is one of a number of controversial releases the PS4 has had exclusive wise. Though not as bad as No Man's Sky. What made the game controversial was its short story, casual gameplay segments what with the QTE boss fights and other sections, and not much replay value.

Yet is this a bad game? No. I liked it myself as the four star Amazon review would describe it. That being said, I only just recently got it when I was able to nab it for $5. At that point, how could anyone pass that up? So then my great adventure through 6-7 narrative of the Order 1886 began and as I said previously, I like it.

This game is essentially what Uncharted would have been if it went fill on cinematic and had very little gameplay segments. As someone who mainly plays on Xbox, I almost felt at times this could have been the Playstation's very own Gears of War. It is a third person cover based shooter and any Gear player will feel right at home. The shooting sections albeit simple and not tedious, I still enjoyed. The guns were fun to shoot and I wish the game had more power weapons like the thermite gun and the tesla gun. Those were fun to use and the game could've used more. The gameplay is there, it just could've used more. Like many have noted, this game is short and definitely could have used a longer story and perhaps some additional side modes or a wave based co-op mode. This game could have been Playstation's Gears of War.

Now for the story, its great. The characters are cool, the world is cool, and its beautiful. This game a long with Uncharted 4 are two of the best looking games this generation. For the narrative, you play as Grayson or Sir Galahad, a Knight of the Order (essentially the knights of round table) who under her majesty protect from the world from all that is evil, particularly from the monstrous half breeds which in this game are lycans (werewolves) and vampires. Galahad eventually catches wind of a conspiracy and he works to unravel it. The story is great and leaves the door open for a sequel which I would like to see happen. The game is also atmospheric and does a great job putting you in late 1800s London with a mix of steampunk. The game is dark and you really feel a part of the world.

That being said, The Order: 1886 is good game. It had a good narrative, beautiful world, and I particularly like the cinematic nature. You couldn't really tell the difference between gameplay segments and cutscenes, thats how graphically good this game was. Yet it was short and gameplay segments were few and quick to get through. The game could have used a longer story and perhaps some additional modes. A co-op horde type mode would have been solid. Thus there is some potential here and Ready At Dawn certainly seems poised to do a sequel, the ball is essentially in Sony's court now.

Mass Effect Andromeda is a game that as we all know has been received fairly mixed. People either love it, are iffy on it, or just hate it. For myself, I am thoroughly enjoying my experience with Andromeda. I absolutely adore the original Mass Effect trilogy with my boy Commander Shepard and have been more than satisfied with Andromeda. Now in regards to the game itself, Andromeda really does act as a fresh new start for the Mass Effect franchise. From my understanding, Bioware Montreal were the particular developers who made Andromeda and are essentially rookies. For them, the best direction to take Mass Effect was to take it somewhere new, Andromeda. Whether you agree or not, I find the best way to appreciate Andromeda is to try to ignore the OT and look at the game as its own thing. Treat Andromeda as Andromeda. If anything I recommend comparing the game to ME1 and not the entire trilogy. Andromeda essentially establishes a whole new universe within the Mass Effect universe and may not come to its full potential until its sequel just like in the OT with ME2. For many of the characters in Andromeda, the reason they joined the Initiative was for a fresh start, the same can be said for the game. Andromeda kisses goodbye to the Milky Way. Goodbye to the characters we all loved. The worlds, the Citadel, and everything else. The characters in Andromeda have said goodbye to their old home and while I will now and then return back to the OT, I am ready to move on as well. Andromeda has done that for me extremely well.

Now that I've gotten all the sentimental stuff out of the way, let's dig into the game. Andromeda takes place 600 years in the future in the Andromeda galaxy. Some of the top Milky Way races (Humans, Asari, Salarian, Krogan, and Turians) have come together under the Andromeda Initiative to become pioneers, leave the Milky Way, and settle Andromeda. The game follows the protagonist of either male or female Ryder, the Pathfinder. Just like other Bioware games this character can be customized or a default character. The main mission of the Pathfinder is to lead the effort in discovering new planets, making them viable, and then establishing outposts. The story itself seems like it'll be pretty good. I've put about 15 hours into the game and am liking where the story is heading and its kept me entertained. Now what also makes a story is the characters. The ones you'll be spending the most time with is your crew on the Tempest which is your personal ship. This crew consists of the 6 squad members you have to pick from and a few other characters like the pilot for example. They are all fairly likable and I enjoy the banter in between them just like in previous Mass Effect games. Being aboard the Tempest with this crew makes me feel right at home in the Mass Effect universe once again.

When it comes to gameplay, Andromeda is kind of similar to the first Mass Effect. It doesn't just establish a new world in Andromeda, but sort of brings back the great RPG elements from ME1, that the other two sort of lacked with a little extra. The game now has a crafting mechanic where you can make weapons, armor, mods, and things for the new vehicle the Nomad. Just like in ME1 we see the return of being able to land on planets, explore them, do side quests on them, and mine for materials. Now I've seen some complaints about not being able to land on every planet in the game. Here is my simple reason why we can't: not every planet is going to be hospitable. That being said, I'm glad this feature has returned. I just wish you could launch mining probes on all the other planets you can't visit though like in ME2. Now when it comes to picking your squad this is where the game has another problem. In ME1, ME2, ME3, and nearly all Dragon Age games, you could somewhat customize your squad members' loadouts. In Andromeda, this feature is absent and it kind of sucks. I don't mind not being able to customize their armor, but I'd like to at least equip them with some good weapons. You can still pick which skills you want for them, but for this I usually just auto-level them.This feature should've been in the game, same goes for the mining probe. The game also sees the return of the co-op mode from Mass Effect 3. Its pretty much the same thing and is pretty fun, but a bit more challenging with enemies being more aggressive and having to adapt to the new combat system which I will remark on shorty. The co-op mode allows you to unlock in game rewards and items for the SP similar to how playing it in ME3 impacted the story. You have these Apex missions where you send squads on timed missions or in some cases do the mission in the co-op mode which is pretty cool.

Now for combat itself, the game is still a third person shooter, but it is no longer a grounded cover shooter and this I like. With the addition of the jump jet, the player can now jump and boost around the battlefield. Its kind of like playing Halo 5 as a third person shooter. The firefights are more aggressive and feel a lot more fast paced now. It has also in particular made playing as a biotic a lot more fun. I just remember instances in the OT when you would see the biotic ability characters doing cool stuff in cut scenes, now you get to do that cool stuff. Now that you can move around a lot more, certain classes that I never really used in the previous trilogy, I'm using now since I feel their true potential has been unleashed. One new addition though is that you're not tied down to a particular class or profile as the game calls it. Through a certain mechanic that the story will explain to you, you can now change your class as you go through the game and I think even in the middle of firefights. This definitely gives the player more freedom with the gameplay and this was a nice new addition. Its cool being able to switch from soldier to biotic to engineer at a whim and experiment and use the different abilities. The combat in this is definitely a lot of fun and perhaps even better than the ME2 and ME3 combat, but it takes some practice to get good with it.

Well that is all I have to really see about Andromeda at the core. Its a great, but flawed game with some technical issues. As most of us know, there are the complaints about the animations which I will agree on. There is definitely moments in cut scenes or dialogue where thinks look a bit weird. Also there are times where the game will transition out of a scene and it'll be a bit odd. Then there is the issues of certain features like squad loadouts and probe mining that should be in the game. Yet despite all this, I have still enjoyed this game immensely. Its a new start for Mass Effect, a new cast of enjoyable characters, and a whole new world of lore that is being created. The game is a clean slate for this franchise and there is a good foundation to work from here. The game still feels like Mass Effect and for that I am happy.

I wouldn’t call myself a hardcore Pokémon fan, but definitely consider myself a fan. I’ve played nearly every generation so far except 2, 4, and 7, but will get around to doing so. Sword is imo one of my favorites in the franchise. The game itself ran well for me. I had a fun time playing it and I think the new Pokémon from the Galar region were for the most part well designed. The game at its core is still the same old Pokémon. You catch Pokémon, battle trainers, compete against gyms, save the world, and become champion.

Graphically, the game looks really good. The Galar region was one of my favorites to adventure across. One thing I particular liked with this game was big wild areas where Pokémon an abundance of Pokémon ran free for you to catch or battle. Plus I liked how the tall grass functioned where you could slowly sneak through it, see the Pokémon, and if you ran through it, startled unseen Pokémon. I thought this was a cool change. I was playing through Yellow on the 3DS prior to this game and I definitely do not miss how the tall grass worked in previous games. Another new feature is “dynamax” and “gigantamax”. This essentially replaces mega evolution and I think it’s much better. Mega evolution was too OP and while dynamaxing can be, it’s only available in certain battles, but it’s a very cool feature and certain Pokémon even take on a new appearance if capable of gigantamaxing.

Now obviously one of the cons to newer Pokémon games is they’re easier. While I agree with this, it’s not a dealbreaker. I like EXP share, I like that HMs are no more. While these things have certainly made battles easier, it’s made the games much more convenient and less of a grind to play.

All in all, this was another enjoyable Pokémon experience for me and I’d put Sword up there as one of my favorites in the franchise and I look forward to the two expansions.

As a longtime fan of the series I can't help but feel as though something was lost in translation with Breath of the Wild. Gone are the handcrafted dungeons and boss fights. Gone is the charming narrative.

My biggest issues with Breath of the Wild are the weapon fragility and it's narrative. It was marketed on player freedom, yet it contradicts this by breaking weapons you enjoy using in an attempt to force you to experiment. If you have to 'force' a player to experiment, that's bad game design. New things should be compelling enough on their own to cause the player to experiment on their own. This system also undermined any sense of discovery that would have otherwise came from opening a treasure chest. It also causes you to horde weapons and ultimately avoiding combat all together.

More traditional dungeons have been replaced with 150 shrines and 4 divine beasts. The problem is that the shrines end up becoming repetitive, while the divine beasts are utterly forgettable. These end up feeling a bit like they were copy/pasted throughout the world. This extends to the boss battles as well where it's hard to distinguish between the various incarnations of Ganon.

In terms of it's narrative the game is a step back from the likes of Skyward Sword, Twilight Princess and Windwaker. Part of the problem is that the game is set 100 years after Hyrule fell to ruin. There are no real stakes in the game. I couldn't help feeling like I would rather have been playing during the events of 100 years past. They really want us to care about the champions but none of them get enough screen time to where you feel you have a good sense of their character. Not like Midna in Twilight Princess.

Perhaps even more insulting is the inclusion of 999 korok seeds. This is the kind of stuff you would expect in an Ubisoft open world game. Not something from Nintendo. There is a lot of quantity but not all of it is 'quality'.

If your going into this game expecting an engaging story like we had with Twilight Princess? You won't get that here. By all means, try it. You may enjoy the game, unfortunately I was left feeling a bit...underwhelmed.

What's better than the best game of 2015? Being able to play the best game of 2015 wherever and whenever you please. What CD Projekt Red and Sabre Interactive have accomplished here is nothing short of amazing. You get an expansive open world that can last you well over 200 hours. Concessions were obviously made to get it running on Switch hardware but the experience doesn't feel compromised. You get the base game, all dlc, and both equally excellent expansions "Hearts of Stone" and "Blood and Wine" all on one 32gb cart. For $60? You get your money's worth and more. Certainly more for the same price you might pay for lesser games. To top it off? You get some small goodies like a foldable map and stickers in the box that the game comes in.

If you thought that it couldn't get better? You should know that the game recently was updated to allow for further tweaking of visual fidelity and it looks even better as a result. Not only that? But they added "Cloud save functionality between Steam and GOG Galaxy." So if you already own the Switcher on PC? You can now play it on your big rig at home, sync your save to the Switch and continue your adventure on the go.

This is how you treat your fans.

I remember when Final Fantasy 7 skipped the N64 and would cement Sony as a rival to Nintendo for years to come. This was in large part due to the limitations of cartridges at the time. It's surreal then that we not only see FF7 come to a Nintendo platform but on a cartridge no less, with a remastered version of FFVIII to boot.

This appears to be the same multilingual version that is still sold on PlayAsia which is where I attained a copy from.

Both games have gameplay boosters like the ability to turn off random encounters, speed up the game and power your characters up.

FF7 looks nice and clean and I would say it's a better version than the PS1/Vita and of course you can take it with you on a screen that isn't as small as the Vita. FF8's remaster is nice, but perhaps doesn't go far enough. The new models look great. But background environments didn't see much in the way of enhancements.

My other gripe is the cover. It's fairly underwhelming and I feel something more could have been done. I made a custom cover of my own for that reason.

This is a great pickup for any fans looking to experience a piece of history. And it's also a great entry point for newcomers.

Final Fantasy VII remake is a solid first entry in this episodic release. It deftly walks the line between homage to the original while also offering its own spin. What once was a 5-hour segment in the original has been expanded to 40-50 hours depending on how much you engage with side content. Some times the sense of padding can arise. Some sidequests for instance feel a bit long in the tooth, but they do offer some slight character development for ancillary NPCs. In the latter part of the game, you get a number of sidequests that have you return to previously visited areas. These could have felt like more of a chore than they were. They have fortunately been designed in such a way so as to overlap and allow you to complete a few of them at the same time.

Combat in Remake is a hybrid of sorts drawing from both turn-based games of the past and action games of the present. You can't simply button mash your way to victory. A lot of your success comes down to exploiting the weaknesses of enemies and coming up with different Materia combinations. For those that want a more traditional feel? Tactical mode temporarily pauses combat allowing you to issue individual commands to different party members. Due to the way enemies aggro your active party member? It encourages you to swap characters frequently which helps you get into a satisfying rhythm as you react to the battle unfolding around you.

The standout of this remake is easily the characters. All of the characters here are presented with such care. They are further aided by a likable cast of voice actors that accentuate their personalities. Characters like Biggs, Wedge, and Jessie feel fully fleshed out and become immediately likable.

I do not want to spoil anything but go into the game with an open mind. It is not a 1 to 1 remake, but it did leave me interested to see where they go with the next installment.

Reading some other reviews I have noticed people expressed that they have felt deceived or that Square is a bunch of con artists. I realize not everyone closely follows games media. However, I do think it's worth noting that from the moment Square announced the remake? They made their intention clear that this would be episodic and that this first installment would just be covering up through Midgar. I say this as someone that was also initially skeptical of this episodic approach. It's also worth noting that if you look at the back of the box of both the deluxe edition and even the standard packaging? It says "The story of this first, standalone game in the FFVII Remake project covers up to the party's escape from Midgar and goes deeper into the events occurring in the city than the original Final Fantasy VII."

I understand the desire to have it all in one game. However, having played the game to completion, I can honestly say I don't feel cheated. There are 40-50 hours of solid content here (Counting sidequests and optional content) with good character development backed by excellent voice acting. The game offers an extra layer of challenge in hard mode for those looking to get a platinum trophy. Many of the boss fights even introduce different mechanics on the hard mode that will be sure to keep you on your toes and test you.

I have been in the process of rounding out my collection of gameboy titles and picking up titles I am missing. The renewed/refreshed games have thus far worked well. I put this in a Gameboy Advance SP (also renewed) and the game works like a charm and boots up without any issue. With the Gamboy Color or a GBA? Metroid II has a bit of a nice touch in that it has a colorized palette!

Hades on Switch is a great addition to the library. It's a rogue like that has great visuals, lore, characters, and yes even voice acting with an impressive amount of dialogue. Prepare to die...a lot. But death isn't the setback it is in other games. Each run you get just that bit more powerful and are able to progress a bit further each time. You feel the progress you make. What's even more astounding is that the characters react to your failures and successes. It all feels incredibly organic and unscripted which is impressive.

This is one well worth adding to your library even if you perhaps aren't a fan of rogue likes or never tried them before.
You get a number of cases for your carts. They aren't as good as official cases nor do they fit as tight. But they do the job that is they keep the dirt and other foreign material out of your carts.
Great case for the Vita. It is padded inside and is sure to keep the system safe from scratches.

WCW STINKS. At least that's what most WWF, ECW, and other wrestling fans believe, and from the looks of this game, they're right. The only fun thing about this game is the 4-man battle royal. Everything else, the character designs, the entrances, the bizarre physics of contact (I punch while you're a mile away; you feel it) just smell worse than... Santa after a rowdy elf party. Stay away from this game... it gets one star for the battle royal, and the other for just booting up when you turn it on. Go buy Tony Hawk's Pro Skater.

In all my years of gaming, I can truly say FINALLY that Sega has a good shooting/Doom/whatever game. The problem is you can't really aim that well without getting shot about fifty times. The multiplayer is average; online-capability would've been sweet. All in all, the graphics are, like any other Dreamcast game worth its salt, breathtaking. The sounds are nice, with explosions and speaking roles (not too bad voice acting, if I might add) however, the gameplay tends to wear thin and becomes stale after about three weeks. But thy'll be the best spent three weeks of your life. Get it. Now.

FF7... if you've ever played this game, the words send shivers of delight down your spine. Squaresoft really outdid themselves with this one. The world's in trouble thanks to a large corporation (Shinra) who is, basically, sucking the planet dry of its natural resources. Bummer. That's where Cloud, Barrett, and Tifa (oh, yeah, there's this girl named Aeris... hint: be nice to her at al times) come in, equipped with HUGE swords, a Gun-Arm (gotta get me one of those), and snazzy magic spells and fighting combos. The game is a marvel to play, and is clearly addictive. The gameplay is perfect, with tight controls which respond perfectly, an intuitive Materia (Magic) sysetm, and some kick ... bosses. ...

Lock your doors. Your windows. Kick your family outta the house. Including your pet hamster. You're gonna want all the time in the world with this bad boy. Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 is the best ... skateboarding game I've ever witnessed. Ever. Ever ever. The fun, addictive gameplay will leave you trying to make sick combos for major points all hours of the day. It's got the best skaters, the best places to skate, the best tricks, the best shoes... everything is great! You can even create yourself into the game and see if you can hang with Mr. Hawk. ASIDE FROM SEGA'S VIRTUA TENNIS, THIS IS THE MOST FUN GAME OUT THERE. Get it now.
(My rating system is now out of five stars. Sorry for any confusion.) Graphics - 4.5 outta 5. - they're good, but still kinda blocky. Sound - 5 - the music rocks. period. Control - 5 - If you mess up, you can be sure of one thing: it was your own stupid fault. Fun-ocity - 5 - OOOOOOOHHHHHHHH, yeeeeaaaahhh!!!

We waited for years. Played through hundreds of hours of such stinkers as the Nintendo 64 version of Superman .... Batman, the X-Men, the (shudder) Fantastic Four, even Spider-Man; nobody seemed to do them any justice. Our childhood heroes were being destroyed by an evil even worse than Lex Luthor, Magneto, or the Green Goblin and Carnage combined... bad games. ( Well, except for X-Men 2 for Genesis a few years back. That ROCKED!) That is, until now.
Activision, the wizards <gods?> behind Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, did this game, Spider-Man, and I have to say it is un-...-believable. Never, NEVER has ol' web-head been represented so well. Johnny Cochrahan couldn't represent somebody this good. Anything Spidey can do in the comic, you can now achieve. Web swinging. Anywhere. In NEW YORK CITY. THIS is cool. You can literally get lost in the levels; this is not usually a good thing, but here, oh, baby, it is. The graphics are good as they seem to be pushing the PlayStation to the max. However, the game falls a little short of my expectations.
The controls are tight, so controlling Spidey is a snap; but, as in every third-person game, there is one fatal flaw: the ... camera! You can literally fall to your death because of this thing. Especially in boss fights. It just seems to wanna say, " ... you, I'm going over here." But don't worry, this only happens rarely, and in the later levels. Which brings me to my next complaint. The game is simply too short. 6 levels, even though huge, still add up to just 6. And that's simply too few for a game this good. The fighting interface is inventive, allowing you to do like Spidey and use the webs as weapons, but after a while it becomes the same old punch-punch-punch-guy-falls-down thing.
RATINGS (1-5) Graphics: 4.5 they're scrum-diddley-upmtious Sound: 5 Come on, it's even got the old T.V. song! Control: 3.5 this is what kills the game. ... camera. fun-ocity: 4.5 it's short, but it's really good!
Total: 4 stars. You'll like it. Buy it. Trust me.

Many gamers know the words "Metal Gear" to be associated of the truly innovative NES title released some ten or eleven years ago. Truly revolutionary for that time, it was the only action game that didn't allow you to just go running around looking for fights; otherwise the same thing that would happen in real life to a one-man army would happen to you in the game. It made you think. Few games do this, and that's what makes this game, no, this franchise, so great.
MGS follows te never-ending story of one Solid Snake, a one-man army working to stop terrorists from an organization named FOX-HOUND from launching a nuclear warhead from a killing machine named <gasp!> Metal Gear. Although this game may seem too hard for even a seasoned gamer, that's because they're approching the game the wrong way. You can't expect to go the whole game without getting caught by a guard or without not quite knowing what to do. That's where this game's real beauty kicks in.
The cut-scenes, taken right from the in-game engine, work flawlessly with gameplay to give the feeling of playing a movie more than a game. The player MUST use stealth tactics, or he/she won't survive the first level, which is (believe it or not) the easiest one. The game gets progressively harder, but you never get discouraged enough to just give up. It keeps bringing you back for more. There are weapons a-plenty, and just because you won't be using them much (if you're smart,) you better get anything you can. <hint: chaff grenades are REALLY handy against certain bosses, like Ninja and Vulcan Raven's tank.> If you don't like using your head, you won't like this game. One last tip: the CODEC system used to communicate with others is a valuable too against bosses. Use it whenever you don't know what to do.
RATINGS (1-5) Graphics: 5- truly remarkable. You can even see Snake's breath when it's cold in a certain area! Sound: 5- all the sounds are in there, and the noise you make also affects whether you get caught or not. Control: 5- superb. Snake handles like a well-oiled... something. Some innovative ways to use both controller ports by Konami, as well.. (wait 'til you fight Psycho Mantis; you'll find out.) Funocity: 5- DID YOU EXPECT ANYTHING ELSE?!?
OVERALL: 5 out of 5- it's just too good to deserve anything else. Be sure to pick this one up if you haven't already.

You may have seen my consumer report on this item. Well, here's the review. By the time you read this, Smackdown!2: Know Your Role will have been released and is probably sitting in your hands right now. You then already know the joy. SM!2 uses the same game engine and ideas from SmackDown! 1. Season mode, special referee... all the original modes are there, along with some new ones: ladder matches(oh joy), Heel-in-a-Cell (oh rapture!), TLc (you'll figure out what it means), Casket matches, basically any match you could ever imagine the WWF doing is here.
The graphics have been polished nicely, while keeping the arcade feel that drove away a few gamers last time around. The sound has improved, with real entrance themes along with VOICE-OVERS (yeah, you heard me) from all of the over 50 WWF superstars included in the game, such as Rikishi(BOO!), Kurt Angle(oh, it's true,),the Rock, and... dare-I-say-it, Too Cool. My only gripe with the characters is the fact that Stone Cold Steve Austin, arguably one of the WWF's biggest stars, is a HIDDEN CHARACTER! That's right, spunky, you gotta unlock him. Even though it isn't that hard to do so, (play season mode, make it to Backlash, win your match, he's unlocked) it's still a little weird. Just hope it's not like last year; you didn't unlock the characters themselves, just the ability to CREATE them. That was one of the earlier game's biggest flaws. Control is tight, but you can only do a small number of moves, unlike No Mercy for the N64, with over 50 moves per character, so you'll end up using the same moves over and over. Not too good for creativity, even with the new matches.
RATINGS (out of 5) Graphics: 5- for the last PlayStation WWF game, it's purty. Sound: 5- good. all the whacks, music, and attitude are there. Control: 4- tight, responsive, but also repetitive. Funocity: 4.5- not the best, but it's close.
OVERALL: 4 out of 5- the arcadey feel detracts from the fun and replay value, but you'll have fun while it lasts. A pretty good game.
(and for those who question the validity of this review, I got the game from Electronics Boutique in Alton. there's your proof that I played it.)

All good things come to an end. However, it doesn't look like the Final Fantasy steamroller is gonna stop anytime soon. The last FF game for the original PlayStation is a truly stellar one.
The story revolves around a pirate/thespian who kidnaps a princess (go figure) who actually WANTS to be captured, a knight of the royal family who follows the princess Garnet everywhere, and a black mage which looks a little like Orko from the old He-Man cartoons. All the goodies are here: MPs, spells, summons (YES!), and of course, more monsters than you could shake a stick at. If you've played and enjoyed the other games in this series, you'll get to like this one immediately. The newest additions include doing away with Save Points (you gotta find a Mog to save your progress. If you don't know what a Mog is, shame on you.)
The other changes include the return of the Limit Break meter (called the "trance" meter here) and the all-new ATE (Active Time Event) where you can see what two or more different characters are doing at the exact same time as you. Your choices in the game influence these characters later on. Cool, huh? Okay, let's do the usual run-down:
Graphics -5 stars- the best on PlayStation, especially with the CG cutscenes. Sweet magic attacks.
Sound- 5 stars- everything's there, including some music from FF 7 & 8. Gotta love it.
Control- 5 stars- let's face it: the controls are always the same, but it's a good thing here.
Fun-ocity- 5 stars- Oh yeah, you're gonna like this one. Plan on losing touch with a few loved ones (like your family, boyfriend/girlfriend, family pet) before you're done with this one.
OVERALL: 5 Stars. For the FINAL Final Fantasy for PlayStation 1, what a way to go. Pick this one up if you are a fan of games in particular.

I was super excited to find this was delivered a day early. That excitement was quickly erased when I opened the box to find a bent and dented unit, and NO CHARGER. I read the product description and the only thing that was stated was:

"May be missing one of the following: manual, cover art, or packaging. Bonus downloadable content may have already been redeemed."

When you buy a product, unless specified it doesn't, it's just a given that it's supposed to come with a cable to run it.

The bend and dents in the unit were over the cartridge port, so in order for me even insert a game I had to use foam and a knife to gently try to pry it open enough to get a game to slide in there. Not like it matters. Won't be able to play the game until I get a charger.

Do yourself a favor and spend the extra $5-10 on a quality higher than "acceptable" that also comes with a charger. It's been a long time since I've had such a bad purchase on Amazon. I guess I'll stick to more trusted sellers in the future. The photo I took is after I bent it back up a bit. Should've taken a photo first.

I have been waiting for a Metroid game like this for a very very long time. Even if it is a remake and remaster of an old Gameboy title, it did the series justice. This game provided a good challenge at times and hours of exploration. It even has the charm of roping you back in for another play through, or getting you to want to explore every area and get every last power up. Music track was alright, but not the best the series has offered. Graphics for a 3DS were great. Controls varied but overall were great. After playing this and seeing what they were capable of, I would love to see some of the other older titles receive the same treatment.

This is a must have item for any 3DS owner.

Every time a version of this game comes out, I buy it. Every time, the story is just as good as before. The benefit of the switch version means end game I could grind out those post game quests and level up when I had time on the go.

This is essentially the PS3 quality port for anyone wondering. But still amazing. A must have for RPG fans on the Nintendo switch.

Initially while playing I wondered if there was anything more than each character’s story. Near the end of each character’s story arc I started seeing the dots connect. It wasn’t until I beat the final boss that I discovered the true boss of the game was the optional super boss and that the little bits of back story and details were drip fed to you through each character’s arc. This super boss story line ties all of the characters together as if fate really did have an ultimate plan.

One of the best JRPG games I’ve ever played in my 34 years. Amazing stories. Amazing battle mechanics that make you plan and rethink your strategies. Get creative with the job mixings.

And man. The music?! There were times I would just let the music in an area play so I could lay and enjoy it.

Finally! A console pokemon game with a battle system that isn't milking the tit of Pokemon Go! The story was as good as you'd expect a Pokemon game story to get. Actually, in my opinion it was the second-best story (after X/Y). This game contains many quality of life improvements. It is now easier to fill your Pokedex as long as you want to pursue that. Leveling pokemon isn't hard at all. You get experience share from the beginning, and all of the raids drop experience candy that you can use on any pokemon. Super helpful if you got a pokemon and you just want to evolve it for the dex entry. Pop it an XL Exp candy and boom. Instant levels. The Pokedex event makes recommendations to you with 1-3 pokemon you can catch right then to fill out the dex, and shows you where you might find them. The daily weather system adds a lot of dynamics to the game, making it possible to only catch certain pokemon in that kind of weather.

But the best part of the experience is the Gym challenge. For the first time do you really feel like you are a pro taking on a league. Battles in a stadium. Walking out onto the turf. Fans cheering. Customizable trading cards. Epic music. This is the Pokemon game we all have been waiting for.

Final Fantasy VII on the PlayStation was the Final Fantasy that got me into RPGs. From here, I went on to play every Final Fantasy title released. I've purchased the original FFVII whenever a port to a console was done. It was the game that made me care about stories in video games. Before that, Mario, Pokemon, Zelda... the story existed but it wasn't deep. When I played FFVII, my mind was opened to what kind of medium a video game could be. It could be the deep story from a book, the visuals and music from a movie... but I was engaged and able to control my character and move through that story.

Since then, story has always been one of the most important factors in whether or not I love a game. I never cared for Kingdom Hearts because I felt the story telling did not flow smoothly (I am not even sure the creators know exactly what is going on....). Hell, even Final Fantasy XIII (and the two sequels) had such a convoluted story that it detracted from my overall experience with the game, leaving a bad impression of the game.

For a while, Square-Enix tried to milk the Final Fantasy VII cash cow for everything it was worth. A movie, a couple of prequels, a couple of sequels for the supporting cast of the main game... But I saw what they were trying to do. They wanted to expand the universe to a game that made so many of us realize what a video game's story was capable of. Many people hated the spin off games. I didn't "hate" them. I just didn't hold them to the same standard as their inspirational source. I personally loved Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII. I cried at the end. I did my final art piece in college of the main hero for the piece that showed when I received my diploma.

So I understand truly how important story is. And how important it is to preserve what makes something great.

As I played through Final Fantasy VII Remake, I was overcome with the feeling of nostalgia. But because of the rewrite to the story, I felt like I was playing the game for the first time all over again. I was suddenly a 13 year old boy, sitting on my bedroom floor, wide-eyes glued to the tv again. The over-arcing story is the same, but because of the additions to the story, and expansion to the smaller arcs, enough was changed that it kept me on the edge of my seat wondering what was going to happen (even though I knew the destination, I didn't exactly know the path to get there).

Final Fantasy VII Remake has done something that not many can accomplish. It's a game that gives old fans that nostalgia, but also delivers the same experience that a new fan would get. It delivers both wrapped in a visually stunning, deep and moderately paced packaged.

This remake is about 40 hours long in story. The source material only covers the first 4-5 hours of the original game. So they had to stretch that 4-5 hours by ten times. Naturally, there was a need to add additional story and side quests. New sections. New characters. They aren't limited by 90's hardware and storage anymore. They can finally do a story that's deeper and still true to it's source.

Don't let those bad reviews out there detour you from playing. If you're an original fan, take off the rose-colored glasses, sit down and take it all in. Experience it all again like it was the first time. It's ok to appreciate both original and remake. And remember, it's a remake. Not an ultra HD remaster. As an artist if I decided to remake an art piece I did previously, you bet I would change a few things after having a long time to look at it and see it for what it could be.

Many people know this already, but in case you don't, this is a time-limited release. That means it won't be available for long. The digital version of this game on the Nintendo e-shop is also time-limited. After the deadline, they will be pulling it off the shop. So grab this physical copy while you can! It will be a nice showcase on your game shelf. For the price, getting 3 amazing Mario games in one package, all of which have been updated to look "better" on an HD TV. Mario 64 still has the worst camera ever, but nostalgia and challenge are there. Sunshine and Galaxy look amazing and smooth. The main menu of the game also has the ability to listen to each game's soundtrack.

I remember when Pokémon first came out. And at the time it was revolutionary in game design. However, that formula didn't ever seem to grow with the gaming industry. Minor enhancements to each new installment weren't enough to give me the same sense of wonder and excitement. Every new title felt like the same title before it, with new Pokémon names. There was never any real challenge to the games either. Then they came out with Pokémon Sword and Shield, and for the first time in a very long time I felt recaptured. I wondered "Where will they go next?" Pokémon BDSP felt like a cheap remake cash grab (and the game was shipped unfinished essentially). But then came this game. And I understood why they wanted to bring Diamond and Pearl back to the modern era (still a cheaply made cash grab).

Pokémon Arceus introduced to us a wide open world where we had to actually hunt down Pokémon at various times and weather patterns. It introduced survival mechanics found in Zelda: Breath of the Wild, which made the adventure feel even more alive. And there was challenge here too. Because it wasn't something Pokémon fans had already experienced 1000s of hours before and mastered. It was new. It was fresh.

That's not to say this game doesn't have its short comings. But they are FAR less than previous games. People complain about the art style. I don't hate it. It matches the art style of the aesthetics they were going for. What I am thinking is more along the lines of the actual "bosses" of the game. There should have been more of them. The trainer battles are NEARLY non-existent. And to some that's a breath of fresh air. But this is Pokémon. The only trainer battles that spring to mind when I think back to my time playing are the 3 bandits that try to jump you in the wild if you enter their area. Over and over and over. Just those three. Having more flavor could've made the world seem a bit more dangerous. Perhaps if they added other types of trainers that only appeared to jump you at certain times of day or during certain weather effects. Things that really caught you off guard.

But overall, I was happy with all of the other changes. I liked that the Pokédex had it's own quests for each Pokémon entry. I like that you could swap out moves without the need for a special NPC. I loved coming across a mossy boulder in the forest, and seeing suddenly my Eevee wanted to evolve. The world of Pokémon has potential to feel alive and dangerous and this game really took a running leap towards that.

If this is a preview of the formula for games to come, count me back into the franchise. Let's just hope it's not another 25 years before they decide to do better.

Fractured but Whole is not a game you play for its mechanics, but to take part in the South Park universe (so for those with no interest in this, you can safely pass on this entirely). With this in mind, it starts off beautifully, but unfortunately quickly fizzles due to slow tempo as you poke around the town, house to house, with not much going on. The good news is it consistently has brilliant, funny moments that bring it back, but not enough to make me want to keep playing. With all that said though, for those who REALLY like the show, this could very well be a 4 to 5 star game for you. But even then, a lot of the jokes used get recycled over and over and really start to fall flat after 10 or so hours of game play.

With so many great RPGs out at the moment and considering the $60 price tag, I just think this game is okay, but would still recommend to a dedicated South Park fan.

I prefer "normal" controllers to the Switch Joycons, but the cost of 4 Wireless Pros was too much. I think these PDP Wired one are a good compromise for my guests. My friends and I can enjoy Mario Kart (and soon Smash) for a few hours without JoyCons for a reasonable price.
But if you're shopping for a controller for yourself, or you're more serious and/or competitive with your gaming, then definitely look elsewhere!
