Note: This controller is a bit different to the PDP Wired Pro Mario/Luigi model in that it has turbo buttons, but not programmable shoulder buttons.

New to the Crew series, but do enjoy light-hearted racers and have had good experience with past Ubisoft titles. I was pretty shocked how poorly this game looks and handles for its AAA asking price.

Right off the bat, the cut-scenes are some of the worst I've ever seen: bland textures, awkward motions, and bad voice acting that doesn't even come close to matching the models' mouths. Not a very good first impression. But whatever, as long as the racing is good, right? Well that was a letdown too. Controls felt stiff and awkward and the physics just felt off. Top all this off with the mandatory Ubisoft account and the "must be online" to play requirements, and you have a very mediocre game.

Worth checking out for the racing diehards when this thing drops to $30, but a huge pass for anyone else.

First off, this case is really large, so pay attention to the pictures to make sure that okay with you. While being large isn't necessarily a bad thing, I do feel like they don't really utilize the space very well. That being said though, the case has wonderful vibrant colors, is made of nice, sturdy material, and holds the DS well.

Assassin's Creed Origins gave me some hope that Ubisoft was going to give its franchise the time and attention it deserved to deliver unique and solid titles again, but Odyssey is proof positive that's not the case. Terrible design decisions to encourage spending real money, bugs, and repetitive gameplay is more than enough reasons to let people know they can pass on this and play any of the other great open world games that has come out recently.
I'm so sick of the mindless busy work, micro transactions, and multiple price point versions of these AAA games that are too shallow to justify it.

At its core, for Honor is pretty fun game. The battle mechanic is easy to learn and felt just tactical enough to be interesting. As someone who is burned out on FPS's, it's nice to see developers try something different. The single player experience is short, but fun; and to be honest, with so many companies ignoring single player completely, it’s nice it's there at all. The main focus of the game, multiplayer, is also pretty fun, but I could see it getting old after a while.

I remember this game absolutely struggling a few years back, so it's nice to see devs that are trying to improve the game as best as possible. Microtransactions are still cancer, and despite lowering the cost, I still think are ridiculously expensive for a game I paid full price for. Nothing kills the enjoyment of a game faster than seeing XP boosts and the like for real money.

Overall, I think at $60, this bundle is just "okay". The game shows at lot more promise than other Ubisoft titles I reviewed, but just like their other titles, the greed really gets in the way of what could be an awesome game.

Starlink is a creative, brilliant, and fun game. The RPG elements are really in-depth and the gameplay is a lot of fun. Oh, and couch Co-oP; more games need this! The only thing holding me back from recommending this to everyone is the extra purchases needed to get the most out of it. For those that think the price is worth it for the toys alone, this is not an issue for you, and by all means check this game out. For those that don't like the toys, there are digital purchases available, but the thought of paying money for extra weapons and ships is not very appealing to most. But worth mentioning: One, the prices on many of the components are half what they used to be, so that might tip the scale for you. And two, you can still complete the game without buying anything extra; it will just be a more limited experience.

One final note: the Switch version includes StarFox content for free, so think about getting this version if you can.

This game is one of the greatest Murder Mystery type games I've played. Well, it's not really a Murder Mystery, it's a platform shooter, but it wants to pretend it's this big, epic Movie, with lots of mystery and intrigue.

Which, really, it sure could be!

But, why did it have to be a game?

Let me add a little history here. The only other Metal Gear Solid game I had ever played was the first. For all of about 5 minutes. These kinds of games really aren't my "style", but I had to know what all the hype was about at the time. I didn't play the other two games, but I loved the gameplay in this one.

When you get to play, that is! Sure, you start out being able to move around. You roll under a truck and go find a gun, running away from these really freaky robot creatures. And then you get to the narrative and the in-between videos and... they just don't stop! By the time I was 8 hours into the game, I had realized I had only played the actual GAME part of this "game" for less than half that time. Hideo is an incredibly eloquent man, and refuses to just allow Metal Gear Solid to be an awesome game, it has to have an epically long epic to go with it. The most evil part of this, is that in order to get the bonus face masks in the game, you HAVE TO listen to the entire in-betweens (when Snake and co. are sitting in their hideaway and talking about the things going on in that part of the game) and ram into people at specific parts. Yes, you can skip those narratives, but then you miss out on awesome bonus stuff!

But overall, it's a great game. It does get you into the moment, and I personally find the bosses (girls who have been transformed into monsters) to be sufficiently creepy and awesome. It has a great story line, so long as you don't mind not playing the game part of the game for over an hour at a time.

Not to mention the loading screens... which go on for upwards of 30 minutes each. Though it does make for a good snack break.

Hori makes some really great screen protectors. They're my personal favorite, as far as tactile feedback and appearance goes (they don't change the visibility of the screen in any way and still feel like the original surface).

This has been the only one I've been disappointed with, and that's only because one side refuses to stay down completely. There's a line about 1/16th of an inch wide on the left side that refuses to lay flush. :/ The rest of it is great (other than the tiny spot at the bottom where I caught some dust in it, user error).

Got this bag for my husband. He loves it, it's a very high quality bag. I love Hori's line of products. Everything from their bags to their screen protectors, I've never had anything that was just plain terrible. Even the smallest detail on this, the little coin zipper pulls, are excellent quality.
I love Hori's screen protectors. I use them for every gaming product that I own. I wish they made tablet screen protectors too. :c

You get free games when you have the PSPlus membership, which is pretty sweet, but then you have to keep the PSPlus membership and be online in order to play those games. Ugh.

Wait until Black Friday to get this and you'll get a good deal every year.

You can play multiplayer with someone playing on a Wii U!

My SO and I are able to play this together thanks to that function. Being of the glasses nation, the setup of the screen on the 3DS version really bothered me, but with the Wii U I can utilize my massive LCD TV or even play on the Wii U's gamepad while we watch a movie. Makes for a really fun evening.

Gets a little repetitive once you get to the point where you have to grind before being able to take the next quest or hunt the next baddie, but mix this up with a little Mariokart 8 and you're all set. Plus you get to hang out with cute kitty people and dress up a little piggy!

"You're a Pomeranian living in a post-nuclear Japan. All humans are eradicated, and you have to fight against deer, crocodiles, lions, and cheetahs!"

My first response to this was, "A Pomeranian against a lion? You're kidding, right? That sounds like the stupidest game ever. How on earth could that be fun?"

I don't know how they did it, but they made that concept into the greatest game. I can play this for hours without getting bored. You can play as several different kinds of animals; from Pomeranians to bears, goats to giraffes, Akitas to zebras. Each time you complete the main mission on one animal, it opens a new animal, making the replayability of this game almost everlasting.

The longest I've managed to live out my generations so far is 76 years. I think it was on the Beagle.

The only negative I have is that I wish it had more diverse music, rather than the two or three tracks that it has. After a couple hours it starts to drone on and I end up needing to take a break - if it weren't for the music, I'd probably be naughty and play it all night.

If you like silly games like Katamari Damacy, I'd definitely recommend this one.

Oh god. I'm very sad that I spent 6 bucks on this game. This game looks like it should be in Early Access, not a fully-fledged game.

I mean, the UI isn't even formatted correctly. It makes me cry every time I have to look at it. There's parts of the UI that hide, and the tutorial mode will still highlight the button even though it's not there, because the idiots who programmed it wouldn't know how to program their way out of a paper bag.

I managed to get a town profitable once, and wasn't able to reproduce the results, even on a similar landscape.

It's still better than the new SimCity, though.

To be completely honest, I like this guitar better than either first party guitar that comes with Rock Band or Guitar Hero 3. I haven't used the one from the new Guitar Hero, but the FrontMan reigns superior over the older 2.

I will admit that it's larger than the other guitars. It helps if your hand is bigger for it. It personally doesn't affect me, as my hands are large enough to handle it appropriately.

One thing that I noticed with this guitar is, unlike another reviewer mentioned, it actually drops FEWER notes than the Guitar Hero 3 Les Paul. Occasionally I would drop a note while holding it for a while on the Les Paul, or miss one note in a long rapid stream of single notes/chords, but with this guitar I feel like the timing is superior to that one. I can play through the intro to Holiday in Cambodia much better now than I am able to with the Red Octane guitar.

Overall I feel like I generally don't trust third-party products in terms of game controllers, by Nyko has really hit a home run with this one...

Shadow of the Colossus has to be one of the most intriguing games I've ever played. Scratch that, it is the MOST intriguing game.

This can be a good thing or a bad thing, varying from one individual to the next. However, in my case, the artistic nature of this game, alongside its "narrative", if you can call it that, is enough to call it the best game I've ever played on the Playstation 2 console.

I truly do not wish to spoil any of this game, because every moment must be appreciated to the fullest. The game focuses around a silent hero, with little information being presented about him. Through the course of the game, you come to appreciate his motivation, but your task is essentially to destroy 16 Colossi. (plural of Colossus, for those who don't know) These beasts are like nothing you've seen in any video game before, ever. The concept is the same across all of them--find a way to scale them, and then use your sword to destroy them by attacking their very visible but not always so accessible weak spots, in the form of white glowing glyphs around the creatures' bodies.

This task sounds easier than it is--the first of the colossi is simple enough, but as you progress, the difficulty as well as the scale of the creatures increase, and the challenge of figuring out how to approach each colossus is just as tricky as the task of implementing your plan is. I don't want to say any more, but the feeling of beating a colossus after challenging bouts, deaths, or utter confusion is one of great joy.

The game is very nontraditional in the sense that there are really no other characters in it. It is just essentially you and your loyal horse, Agro. Many have said it before, but I to this day I have not seen better animations than in this game, especially for the horse. Some get discouraged by the controls, but it actually feels like it has weight and mass to it, like a real horse. Additionally, controlling the protagonist can be tricky at first, but it feels very good after you adjust to it--it's a very different game from any other you've likely played, to say the least.

The visuals are very impressive for the PS2 era of games. I was at first very frustrated by the framerate, which admittedly does skip on occasion, but after I started to look at the level of detail in yourself, your horse, and the world around you, you really appreciate how much this game accomplished for its time. The fur on the colossi is incredible, for a PS2 game, and though the graphics aren't on par with the current generation of consoles, this is the next best thing, in my opinion.

Some find it very tough to "get into" this game. There are no real interactions, except between you and your horse, for the most part. Most of the story is not spelled out for you--instead it is "understood". By this I mean that you as the player need to fill in the majority of it--the story is unclear for the very reason that it does not need to be specific to have an impact on the player's emotions. There is a wonderful landscape and beautiful terrain to cross, which does take some time, so make sure you look around as you ride. There is a "hint" button to find the next colossus, which is essentially holding your sword up and allowing reflected light to lead you to it. Traversing the landscapes is something to appreciate, not something the developers wanted to torture you with, so remember to keep that in mind as you move in the game world.

One thing to keep in mind is that Shadow of the Colossus is a VERY UNIQUE game. It is NOT for everyone. If you're looking for a hack-n-slash adventure game, you may prefer Zelda. If you're looking for deep character development through interactions with NPCs, find a Final Fantasy. But if you want a deep game, which takes some thought to really appreciate, this may be for you. This is one of the only games I would ever consider calling "art" in the traditional sense, and I say that for a reason.

I hope you all enjoy my favorite PS2 game based on this recommendation.

Bionic Commando was a game I really looked forward to for a while. It has a lot of potential, since it essentially looks like a fast-paced, action-packed version of Spiderman 2. I say this because web-swinging was revolutionary in Spiderman 2, so it's the best comparison I can make.

I was sorely let down with the gameplay in Bionic Commando, however. First off, the controls took a while to get used to. Nothing was quite fluid enough to enjoy for quite some time, and even after I got the hang of things, I wasn't really enjoying it the way I expected to. Just expect to die. A lot. I'm a seasoned gamer, I play my systems every day, and I love a challenge, dating back to Contra on the NES. But this game wasn't challenging, it was irritating. Things just don't work the way you want them to at most times.

I would imagine if I played this game for about a month every single day for at least an hour or two, I might be more comfortable with it. However, I'm not willing to invest 60 hours of "work" in trying to enjoy a video game. I respect those who have overcome this barrier, but if I'm paying for a video game to entertain me, it should entertain me out of the box, in my opinion. Learning curves are okay, but this game simply was not FUN in playing it--and I did try to enjoy it for many hours.

Overall, the 3D rejuvenation of Bionic Commando is hardly rejuvenating at all. It leads to a great deal of frustration, because swinging and combat just don't control well enough in 3D space. The game was great in 2D, but in 3D a better team needs to work on the controls to make this one shine. It has the potential, but just doesn't deliver.

So, I've owned SOCOM Confrontation since "day 1". I pre-ordered it with the headset, played the beta, and received it in the mail within the first few days of launch. When the game launched, it was nearly unplayable. It was awful and didn't work well at all. Considering this game is ONLINE ONLY (stop reading here if you're looking for a single player experience!) the networked gameplay needs to be very solid.

I was a big SOCOM fan in the PS2 days, so I kept playing, though not every day, in hopes that the game would improve. Finally, a little under a year later, we have (more or less) the game we were promised.

This is not quite the same as the original PS2-era SOCOM games, since it was made by another developer. (Zipper made the originals; Slant Six makes Confrontation) Still, the game is a quality affair, most definitely. There are two factions in this game, each of which can be customized to your liking. You can choose different clothing, different camouflage patterns, and different weight/armor levels. Heavier means you might take a few more shots, but lighter will allow you to sprint to key locations on maps that little bit faster, which could make the difference. The weapons you bring into battle also affect your weight/speed balance, so choose wisely for your play style. The two factions have different weapon selections at their disposal, which may also afford different play style opportunities.

There is no shortage of guns in this iteration of the SOCOM franchise. You will find a healthy supply of rifles, submachine guns, shotguns, light machine guns, sniper rifles, and pistols in this game, as well as a good slew of secondary items (grenades of different varieties, claymores, RPGs, etc.) to really fine tune your play style well.

The game controls well, and motion controls may be disabled at any time if you prefer, or can be used by holding an activation button (much like push-to-talk chat systems) to enable the motion sensor. I modified the sensitivity and was able to find a sweet spot to use for myself.

The gameplay is good, but can be unforgiving at times. It doesn't take much to be shot down--this is a much more realistic game than many others, so your health does not regenerate, and you really need to use proper tactics to ensure your own survival. If you get into a clan, you'll have some great teamwork potential as well. Since the game includes a bluetooth headset, there's not much excuse for not being able to communicate with your team, but more on that later. The different game modes work well, though there is nothing that really stands out from the rest of the online shooters out there.

Perhaps most important to this game is communication. That's made much easier by the fact that most players opted to buy the bundle with a bluetooth headset. This headset is of great quality, featuring a mute button which allows the classic "baby crying" and "Mom! Meatloaf! Now!" moments to be minimized. One of the biggest flaws with online gaming on the PS3 (in my experience) is lack of communication, and since the majority of players seem to have purchased the bundle, it's quite a positive leap for PSN gaming.

In conclusion, the patches since the game's launch have really improved the gameplay, offering better controls, better networking/game matching, and overall a better experience. Voice communication is better in this game than any other PS3 game online, and customization allows for a wide variety of play styles to bring online. And for those deciding between the game alone, and the bundle, keep in mind that the headset launched at $50 and the bundle at $60, whereas the game alone launched at $40. If you consider the value of the bundle, you'll see the clear advantage. This bluetooth headset is better than the other 4 I've used (I do all the electronics shopping for my family, so the only quality sets I haven't used are the Aliph Jawbones--if you have one of those the choice is yours to make) There is also a downloadable version of this game on PSN, allowing for gameplay without a disc, which might be nice for some out there as well.

P.S.-The next patch is said to offer free DLC to the SOCOM community, though I don't know the details of it.

Honestly, I think that this case is GOOD OVERALL. It's not perfect, but it is good.

It has a very sturdy, solid feel to it. I am willing to carry my PSP around in a bag with this, whereas without I would only carry it in my pockets, so I know it's not shifting around. With that said, I still wouldn't pack it away in a bag that might get thrown around or roughed up--it's definitely not made of steel.

Everyone seems to think that this case doesn't fit the Go. I personally like the way it fits for the most part because it's very SNUG. It fits tightly so that NOTHING SHIFTS AROUND when it's in the case. That is a feature that some people seem to think may damage the product, but in fact, it actually just makes it that much more secure. It was a tight squeeze but at no point did I feel like I would be damaging anything to apply slight pressure. I pulled the brackets outward slightly as I pushed the system downward into place, and it was quite painless. The case is so snug in fact that the sliding mechanism feels like it has some resistance. You may not like this, but in my opinion the inside of the case material is VERY soft, and is not likely to scratch the shiny plastic at all.

The outer material has a nice leathery feel to it as well. The Go with the case on still fits in my pocket, so it's nice and thin, despite how solid it feels. And again, it does feel quite solid due to its snug fit. (like a glove)

When using this case, most buttons around the exterior rim of the Go are accessible--L/R, Wifi, Power/Hold, as well as the multipurpose port and the headphone jack. The volume/brightness/mute buttons will be inaccessible when closed. (and effectively inaccessible when the case is open and the screen is slid upward exposing the controls, as your fingers may not fit to reach them) I don't feel comfortable pressing the volume/brightness/mute buttons with the case and screen both in the "open" position, as I feel like my fingers push the screen forward just slightly--something I'm not willing to do. Thankfully I don't need to use volume controls very much, but if you're using it for music and have a very wide dynamic range in your music, it might be an issue.

Opening the case, you can opt to either let the front flap dangle around the back of the unit, or use the velcro clasp to secure it to the reverse side of the case. This is how the unit is designed to stand (with the velcro flipped around on the back side of the case) but I find that it stands a bit too vertically for my liking, so a cool potential feature doesn't really play out too well in that situation. In my experience the case gets in the way if you're trying to hand-hold it while the flap is secured to the rear via the velcro.

The only other issues I have with it are relatively minor--one is that the right side clasp actually covers up the PSP Go's battery light--so if you're charging your PSP Go in the case, you may not be able to see when the light turns green indicating a full charge. Additionally, I don't really like the use of velcro for the clasp, but it's not obnoxiously used, so I'll excuse it for that.

Overall, I personally think that if you want a sturdy case, this is a good product. There are definitely drawbacks to it, but most of the drawbacks don't actually AFFECT me, personally, so I do not regret purchasing it. I will likely buy a set of screen protectors as well, so that when I REMOVE the Go from the case I still feel that the screen is protected. If you're worried about breaking your Go, just be cautiously firm when placing it in and taking it out of the case. It's definitely not as bad as some have made it seem, as long as you apply pressure to the whole system, and not just the screen or controls, when inserting it/removing it.

This case is a two-zipper side-open case. So if you're holding the case like you would hold the PSP when gaming, the zipper threads go from the top center, around the left side (when the case's logo is oriented properly), to the bottom center. Two zippers mean you can zip in either direction, based on preference--not that I care much, but I suppose someone might, if listening to the music and using headphones with it. (though you can't access any buttons easily in there...)

The material is very nice, and VERY well padded. I read a review once where someone said they'd be willing to drop the thing 4-5 feet and not worry due to the casing. I thought to myself "what the hell is wrong with that guy?!?" But now, I know what he meant. (Note, I still won't DO it, but I'm fairly confident it would survive without a scratch, based on how thick the padding is--hence why it's HUGE and not pocket-sized in this pouch)

The outside of the pouch has an extra flap, where you can put a memory card, or if small enough, headphones, or something like that. My headphones fit, but they're Shure earbuds, and the extension cable makes it a bit of a tight fit. I'm likely to carry them in their own case (Shure headphones come with their own zipper case as well) since I have it already, and as of right now I have no use for the extra flap on the outside of the Go's soft pouch. It also doesn't close up, but it's a pretty tight flap, so I doubt anything would fall out easily unless you really toss it around. It also isn't as padded, so it might be a concern if you carry your memory cards around without their plastic cases. (I don't know anyone who does that though) I suppose if you had any reason, you could also carry something like a USB flash drive. But I'm sure you're all clever enough to figure out how to use this flap!

Overall I'm really happy with this case as well. It likely wouldn't be my "every day" case, but if I plan on traveling, it could definitely have its place. Even in my laptop bag which I bring to work daily, it seems worthwhile to put it in here. If I accidentally flip it upside down and the laptop winds up on top of the Go, I'm not concerned at all. The hard case would also probably be fine in this situation, but since I have a bumpy car ride, the repeated impacts would make me want the security blanket that is the soft pouch.

The PSPGo is a point of controversy for gamers. The general consensus is that it is a flop, and undeserving of the price of admission. There are a small percentage of users who disagree. I fall somewhere in between.

It is necessary to go into detail to fully explain the portable console, so I apologize in advance for the lengthy upcoming review.

Design-wise, I am a big fan of the PSPGo. I am an adult male with somewhat large hands. Many complain about the smaller size cramping the hands. I actually felt cramped on the original PSP, and for me this isn't any worse. The analog is in a slightly different position relative to where it was on the other PSP models. I think this is an improvement, in general. My hands are still cramped, but I have found slightly more comfort with the PSPGo after adjusting how I position my hands to hold the system. Many will find it more cramping, but I think it was about the same. Children may welcome the smaller grip, but I'm not sure about that.

The screen. A sliding screen means the screen stays exposed even when the main controls are concealed. This doesn't serve too much purpose to me. There are a couple of games that use the shoulder buttons exclusively, and you can use the shoulder buttons while listening to music, but this is not a major factor. With that said, the screen is somewhat smaller than the older PSP models. While it provides an advantage in terms of portability of the device, it means...a smaller screen size. I wish I could say it doesn't make a difference, or isn't noticeable, but I'd be lying. The screen is attractive, but it's simply a bit on the small side. However, I like being able to more comfortably fit the PSPGo in my pocket, which I can't say about the larger models.

The face buttons are clicky and responsive. They all feel nice. The two shoulder buttons are a tiny bit squishy, but not terribly so. I wish they were a bit firmer, but I can live with what they are without any issues.

Bluetooth is an added feature to this model of the PSP, as well. This means support for audio over bluetooth. I was hoping to be able to use my Android phone as a bluetooth modem for the PSPGo. However, I was never able to set this up properly (ever). I tried many, many times, and was always unsuccessful. It kind of frustrated me, and I am still disappointed, although again, it's not a dealbreaker.

One nice little feature on the PSPGo is that you can now pause any game at any time. You can only do this for one game at a time, and pausing a new game forces you to overwrite the previous paused game state. It's quite a handy feature, since sometimes portable gaming sessions get cut short, for various reasons.

The major departure from the PSP, however, is the complete lack of UMD support in any form. UMD is the traditional physical format of PSP games (and media). 16GB on-board memory replaces the UMD slot, and is used to store downloaded content to the PSPGo (this can be expanded with a proprietary Sony memory card). This means if you're upgrading from a prior PSP to the PSPGo, you won't be able to pop in an old disc and just play. Instead you'll need to repurchase the game from the PlayStation Network Store. This means you will spend a lot if replacing a large library of games. This is the biggest gripe most people have with the PSPGo. Sony never offered a trade-in/download program to help users replace their UMD's. Additionally, the price of downloaded games is generally the same as purchasing physical discs from a retailer, for a brand new game at the time of release. However, many "new" games (i.e. non-used) will drop in price, whereas game downloads tend to remain at a higher price, even after discounted. There is no guarantee either way, but that tends to be the case. People who like collecting discs, manuals, and boxes will often be disappointed that the same money will often go toward a less satisfying purchase. Additionally, there are fewer places to purchase PSN downlaods from: Amazon.com now has a store for that, and the PlayStation Network Store is the only other option. This means sales are going to be more limited as compared to having many retail options competing for your business.

Overall, the PSPGo is a great little system...for SOME people. For others, it is a horrible misstep from Sony. I wish I could give you a better answer than that. I didn't own a PSP before, so I like my PSPGo. I don't have the issue many had with abandoning an old UMD library. I like the size, despite the issues I have with the screen size. The controls are cramped, but in my opinion no worse than the original PSP or other portable gaming systems.

I own a PlayStation Move. I was an early adopter, and honestly, while the technology is solid, the games being produced are the same as Wii games.

Enter The Fight: Lights Out. If it wasn't for this game, I would probably sell my PS Move used to someone else. First, let's get out of the way the fact that you need two PlayStation Move controllers to play The Fight, plus the PlayStation Eye camera. It's quite the investment.

This game winds up not only being the most fun I could have with the Move controller, but possibly the best workout I could get, as well. For me, there was a pretty big learning curve playing this game. You need to stand in the right position, and try not to move from that position as you play--stepping forward, backward, or side to side causes your punches to go out of alignment (your position relative to the camera has changed, so your punch angle and direction will change in game). A simple button press recalibrates your position, but after some practice, it becomes easier to stay in one place.

When you first get the game, you are plunged into a tutorial fight. Honestly, I played for about an hour, and was completely inept and unable to complete this first "gimme" fight, on the first night I played the game. I came back at it the next day (optionally--you can skip it next time you start the game up) and was able to beat it easily. I am extremely happy I put a little more time into it. I now absolutely love The Fight.

Throwing punches...throws punches. Your arm will be reflected on screen very close to where it is in real life. Blocking is done by holding your hands in front of your face. Danny Trejo boldly (in an entertaining, over the top manner) tells you how to perform these and other moves in the tutorial and when learning new "dirty moves". Head tracking allows you to duck and lean to avoid punches. I have found the head tracking relies heavily on having decent lighting. You may need to experiment with your position relative to the camera and light sources of the room. You will also need a good amount of space to play this game--the recommendation is ~6-8 feet I think. You'll do better if you have more space, but I have played with around 5 feet without major issue. The setup is what makes or breaks the game. If you're not flexible in terms of moving the camera, yourself, or lighting sources, you may want to see if you can borrow or rent this game first.

Playing the game does increase in difficulty as you progress through the story mode. Enemies get harder. Better at blocking, harder hitting, and overall more difficult. You learn moves as you progress through the games, which are scripted and activated by holding the Move trigger and performing a gesture with one or both controllers. Relying on these helps in a pinch, but real fun comes from learning to play without these dirty hits.

In addition to the championship/story mode, there are training games. Training consists of various activities you might find in training a boxer--heavy bag, speed bag, sparring, etc. The game tracks the number of calories you burn, approximately, in training and story mode, allowing you to use the game as a fitness tool. (Finally a fitness game that's not strictly a "fitness game"!) They have added several more training activities since the game launched, making it a bit more varied. It is possible to "cheat" at some of these games, but there is little reason to do so--you'd only be cheating yourself, really.

Finally, there is online play. However, it is hardly the main feature of the game. Ultimately, The Fight is best viewed from the perspective of a single player game. At least, from my point of view. The multiplayer is a nice addition, but the bulk of the game is single player.

Ultimately, I completely recommend this game for anyone who has a PlayStation Move, as long as you're willing to sweat a little bit, and as long as you're willing to take some time to set up your gaming environment for this game. You will need light, you will need space, and you will need 2 Move controllers and a PlayStation Eye. If you have these things, and can find the "sweet spot" in your setup, this could be the best motion game you've ever played. It's deep enough to provide extra play time. It's got training mode in which you can simply exercise using the game as a tool. It's got a lot of value for what it is.

Not only did the sixth installment to the Resident Evil/Biohazard franchise undermine longtime fans view of the series, but also it hindered Capcom’s relevance among the survival horror genre of video gaming. Fans, like myself, just wanted that “good ‘ol” Resident Evil feeling and most importantly, something scary even if it meant moving onto different franchises completely. Well, I’m proud to say that Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was definitely the shock-to-life entry the franchise needed. And, wow, it truly is a shocker.

RE7 presents significant changes to gameplay that is both classic and fresh for the series:
First person Perspective.
This technically isn’t the first RE-based game to use this camera angle, but this is the first mainline entry to do it correctly. Somehow the horror atmosphere feels more personal when viewing decrepit environments and watching monstrosities or infected residents stalk directly towards you. The first person perspective helps draw in the immersion that the Baker Estate is conveying adequately. This decision was obviously met with criticisms among fans and non-fans, where the majority thought Capcom was “ripping off” other indie horror titles such as Outlast and Amnesia. I can assure you when playing it, it feels like an original idea from Capcom. Viewing everything in first person also helps intensify the stellar sound design RE7. While there is a severe lack of soundtrack music, your eyes and ears will be working together to perceive RE7’s amazing environment ambience.

Returning to its “Roots.”
RE7 is not the action packed horror adventure where the main hero is performing ridiculous feats after the player performs numerous QTE prompts. This is literally opening a door and searching around the environment for clues so you can progress further into the Mansion estate. Some doors require a certain themed key, or require certain puzzle solving after you backtracked for particular items for close examination. The inventory screen is simple and makes combining and examining items an ease. You also have to decide what to take with you and what to leave in inventory boxes since your character can’t hold everything. Supplies such as healing and weapon items are not in bountiful quantities at the Baker Estate, where the phrase “make every shot count” is constantly prevalent. Moving around and aiming in first person definitely feels slower or sluggish compared to the faster pace of the previous two entries. However, this was intentional as Capcom wanted to bring back the “you are vulnerable” vibe the RE series once had. Controlling the main character in RE7 was never difficult in this newer perspective. On easy and normal difficulties, RE7 does utilize a checkpoint system for some scripted encounters or “boss fights.” However, to literally save your game progress, you will need to find a safe room and use a tape recorder. On Madhouse difficulty, you can only save if you find cassette tapes which harken back to the old typewriter days of classic Resident Evil.

The Bakers.
This is probably my favorite change that RE7 presents. The effort that Capcom put into the main antagonists help convey that this story feels more personal or grounded. In RE7, you don’t play as a super cop/anti Bio-terrorist operative who mows down hordes of mindless monsters and stops an evil corporation’s schemes. In RE7, you play as a normal person trying to escape an insane family that constantly stalk and ridicule you. While there are scripted moments and boss encounters you cannot avoid, the threat the Baker family impose actually feels terrifying. There are even multiple situational events that can occur when encountering just one of them. Jack, the father, is arguably the most memorable of the bunch. He’s a snarky son-of-a-gun who offers southern wit while bursting through walls or throwing you around a room. The technicality of Jack brought back unsettling moments of Nemesis from the third RE game that I didn’t know I actually missed. Marguerite, the mother, is a shrill lady that isn’t afraid to share what she thinks of you. She’s also a “creature feature” who literally provides the term, nightmare fuel. Lucas, the son, is a crafty scoundrel who is actually the less scary of the bunch. He provides the death room or murder puzzles that fans of the Saw movies will feel right at home with. It’s not just the Bakers you have to worry about, there is also the molded, which serve as the “grunts” to the Baker Estate just like how the Zombies were for the Spencer Mansion in RE1. They feel like a combination of the black ooze monsters of RE 5 and the regenerators of RE4. While their details grotesque enough in first person, they aren’t as memorable as encountering the Bakers. I guess Capcom thought there needed be some gun fodder that aren’t literally zombie-clichéd versions of the Baker’s victims. There is an explanation for them, but I felt they weren’t entirely needed since the bakers steal the show every time.

VR.
I regretfully don’t have any first impressions on this feature. I’m still uncertain if I want to spend the hefty price to gamble on Sony’s support promises for this peripheral. However, I’ve watched and read numerous opinions about playing RE7 with PSVR, and they all sound positive. In fact, some state that RE7 SHOULD be played with VR because Capcom actually put effort into the mode.
While the main concept changes are not original and genre defining like Resident Evil 4, RE7 pulled these off so well. If you are unfamiliar with the franchise, you will not be hindered at all with how things play out in RE7. While it has a classic feeling, it’s the most departed from the franchise for all the right reason. I wasn’t sure if I would like this setting since I’m not a fan of grindhouse and cult horror movies like Texas Chainsaw Massacre. However, I am a fan of the Evil Dead, which RE7 captures that horror feeling perfectly during its opening segment. This game surprised the hell out of me and it was hard to take breaks from it. The big difference from the other first person horror games, like Alien Isolation, is that RE7 actually feels like a Resident Evil game. It’s first person, but it feels like the old RE games I played on the original PlayStation.

For some, the game is considered short where one could finish their first play through in about 9-12 hours. However, older RE games are usually not long and provide plenty of opportunities for reward unlocks depending on how fast you complete them. RE7 has been so good that I will definitely replay it on Madhouse Difficulty and try to find everything I missed the first time. It’s exciting to hear people are use the word “scary” when talking about Resident Evil again.

In its current state, Fallout 76 is nothing but a mess. One could spend hours replaying the same explore, loot, and craft gameplay loop that was very prevalent in Fallout 4. However, the lack of engaging narrative with the zero NPCs and the uncertainty to erratic behavior from human players starts to overshadow the survival experience. The game is better with friends, as Bethesda will claim. You'll have to expect bugs and the occasional server issues taking place when trying to form a party. There is a story, but it's nothing more than just recorded holotapes, written notes, and computer terminals spread around the wasteland. Some of these are well written and acted out. It's just a shame that this is the only way the story can be delivered when you have your friends or other players talking over them, ruining any sort of immersion. Todd Howard claimed that VATS does in fact work for a multiplayer Fallout game. It "does work" but it's nothing special at all. There is zero RPG mechanics when utilizing it. It's only beneficial purpose is to get an aimbot-like attack on smaller ground enemies. Somehow, the building of settlements or structures were made worse here with the new controls. To this day, I'm still unsure if you can remap controls to accommodate which will leave many PC players frustrated. If there is one good thing about FO76 is that the world environment displays the most effort from Bethesda. The rest of the game's textures and animations are literally asset ripped from Fallout 4, but its the sprawling biome diversity of post apocalyptic West Virginia that actually entices.

The Fallout fan in me still has a sliver of hope that Bethesda might pull this out of the trench it dug, but a part of me wants them to live there for awhile to understand they cannot get away with this business practice anymore. I might pay $10-$15 to explore West Virginia for a couple of hours later on, but even that feels like a detriment to my free time. There are plenty of other games or game modes out that deserve more attention. Hell, there are even older games that are a better time sink.

I was leaning on near 6/10 or 3/5 stars during the earlier parts of Anthem with and without friends. I did find some enjoyment within the design of the game. I commend Bioware for actually wanting to present a story and world building unlike Bungie's severe lack of for the Destiny franchise. I enjoyed the flying and shooting mechanics the most. It was easy to pick up a controller or put my hands on the keys and traverse Bastion. I experienced some rough edges within the game's design and saw areas that have potential for improvement later on since this is a games as an online service mentality.... then I got to a particular mission involving a checklist of various activities to progress through the story. I attempted to retain some enthusiasm by playing the game again with some friends past that section (like the available stronghold), but I couldn't go on anymore solo.

This game was such a detriment to my free time that ignoring Anthem in favor of watching the 2019 Oscars felt more fun. I ended up not wanting to sit at my PC, wait for the game to load, do the EXACT same mission structure again, and then only to receive the EXACT same loot as I've received for the past 16 hours. I played Anthem through Origin's Premier Access $15/month subscription platform, and two days into it, I was already unsubscribing before finishing the main story. It took Bioware 6 years to put this together, and it was honestly all in vain. The greatness this game could provide is just buried too deep under malicious practices and just overall bland game design.

Arguably, this game is 5/10 (or 2.5/5 stars), but I could definitely see how somebody could hate this game for the 4/10 (2/5 stars) area. Do not, I repeat do not buy this game for full price. Any full 5 star ratings on this site are people in denial. I had my opinions about Destiny 1 when it launched, but it was a farcry compared to how Anthem launched. Another online service shot in the dark with EA now contemplating Bioware's future. It may get better, but this IP needed a few more months, or arguably another year to incubate. Such a waste of time.

First off, was the wait worth it for Death Stranding? Was it worth receiving close to nothing on specific game details until the literal week of embargo? Is this game literally worth experiencing?

In hind sight, it's a yes and no to those questions. I had this pre-ordered since February 2017 and was excited as more gameplay details surfaced since then. But once I received my copy and began playing, I immediately saw how this is one of the most divisive games to come to the end of the PlayStation 4's life cycle. The back of the box should have a disclaimer stating "This game WILL NOT be for Everyone." There were so many dumb and tedious moments within this game where I understand people checking out early or later within it. Even when the game gets close to what we are used to from Kojima Productions (innovated combat and stealth), it literally falls flat on it's face. This game is literally something akin to Elite Dangerous but instead of piloting a space ship delivering cargo, you are piloting Norman Reedus over rugged terrain.

Thankfully Hideo Kojima's take on presenting his literal wild ideas come to digital life is what makes this title stand out. Even if I was to attempt to describe what the player experiences within the cut-scenes of Death Stranding, I couldn't ever do it justice. It could take hours regardless of how non subtle Kojima can be with his themes and references. The literal carrot-on-a-stick for Death Stranding is the story itself, even though it feels like you have to literally drag it behind you for a large portion. Yes, there are some REALLY stupid dialogue moments, and I came very close to wanting to eject my PS4 disc. But almost immediately (and thankfully) the amazing performances from the voice and mo-cap cast outshine those indulgent Kojima annoyances. I wanted to know more about Mads Mikkelson's character. I wanted to construct that zip-line path to Hearman. I wanted to punch Higg's smug attitude with a piece of cargo. I wanted to attempt to figure out what the hell was going on!

If you stick with it, the ending of Death Stranding is worth the cinematic journey. Never has a game made me literally cry let alone actually feel something this close to it before (Not even The Last of Us's prologue). As pretentious as that sounds (kind of like a certain game developer), it's the honest truth. Unfortunately, I have zero gumption to ever want to play this again..until maybe a decade later. The game felt like it took A LOT of me, and I honestly don't want to squander the impact of it. Death Stranding is at least worth experiencing, but that is all dependent on the player's patience. I've read reports about how Kojima's team intended that to be the case of the protagonists journey. It was supposed to start off difficult and slow, then it transcends into a visual and emotional tour-de-force for gaming. Yes, Death Stranding is a literal "video games as works of art title." It's just a shame the overall gameplay moments don't live up to that standard.

I'll get the first important issue out of the way. The Combat/ATB mechanics and straight to the point nature of the Materia system is to celebrated here. Finally after so many years of Square's weird struggle to make combat encounters accommodate towards current HD graphics and action heavy set pieces, Square finally did it. Combat is both fun to engage in every time and has some well thought out depth to it. Besides just determining which stance or ability to have characters like Cloud or Tifa perform, you can also decide which specific magic via Materia to unleash upon enemies. This game has honestly been the closest to actual Final Fantasy since maybe...FFXII? It's all thanks to this tactical slo-mo menu mode through the Active Time Battle (ATB) charges. The combat and progressions systems makes both FFXV's combat look insanely shallow and something like Xenoblade Chronicles 2's still insanely convoluted. These fundamental systems in RPGS (or JRPGS) should always be easy to understand, something to master/experiment with, and above all fun to play. FFVII: Remake was exactly that for me.

Also, I can not express enough how much more enjoyable it was being able to switch party members on the fly with literally just a button press while in combat. You can make tactical and situational decisions, and be able to change up combat itself every-time. Much like in the Original game, Materia is once again straight to the point and easy to understand. Equip/insert it, you can use it. And just like in the original, there are support materias where you can change up how an abilities or magic perform. For example, have lighting hit all enemies, or make a party member auto follow up with a specific spell. Worried about not having a full ATB charge when you start battle, there is a materia for that. Need help gaining ATB when blocking or dodging? There is a materia for that. And yes, just like FFXII, there are summons and they ARE MAGNIFICENT to use here and actually occur MUCH more frequent. While not something you can always use for normal combat situations, when available, they actually have utility to them...unlike FFXV.

I'm not going to go into super detail about the story because I rather not create or add to the already beating horse that is the internet complaint session. I will agree that with a lot of reviews (the more sane ones) that 95% of this game is purely awesome. It's awesome for fans of the original 1997 game, and for those who are finally experiencing a version of FFVII's world. Unfortunately Square created some narrative pacing problems with the dungeon like areas and some boss fights by adding too much padding. Side quests mostly felt flat or nothing too exciting. Though areas like the Shinra VR and Wall Market Colessum do stand out as fun extra activities. It's for these reasons that I can't give the game a perfect 5 star or 101/10 rating.

But because of the combat, characters, and music, I agree 100% that this game is more deserving of a very high 4/5 or 9/10. I put in 47 hours into one playthrough of this game, and I already want to replay one chapter in particular and be sure to obtain a summon materia I missed out on. So the ultimate answer to the question everybody has: "was it worth the wait and the $60? Of course it was. Yes, an originally 6 hour section has been blown up to about 30-40+ hours, and has caveats to beloved narrative from 1997. However, I'll argue that most of the "faithful" reinventions to characters and their story arcs have never been better here. Cloud, Barrett, Tifa, and especially Aerith have been dramatically improved and provided so much character depth that I didn't know it was possible before. A particular chapter 9 had me at an all time high of not only appreciating the obvious hard work from Tetsuya Nomura and team's long years of hard work, but also appreciation for the original game as well. Yes, I agree the ending 2ish hours will be a divisive issue until the second part of this Remake project has been announced. But know that I personally thought it was fine, and also made me even more curious about what's to come...whenever that will be from Square-Enix.

I can't help but state any review that just "claims" this is nothing more than a cash grab and only "10%" of a game, that have been drinking too much of the Mako. People, this is a full on FF release, as Square stated it was to be. It has a definitive beginning, middle, and end, you'll be wishing you had more time to spend with beloved characters before heading to the Shinra HQ to face whatever destiny has in store for our beloved characters. Don't ignore this title because of some body played a tiny bit then thought to review it for attention on here. Please, play it and enjoy the ride.

Resident Evil 3 (2020) is such a pretty looking game in such a short underwhelming package. Usually you replay RE titles because you loved the initial experience and you want to master it...here, you replay it simply JUST to get more game time out of it for the price paid. In its current and apparently final state, it is not worth above the $20USD price tag at all. No matter how much somebody pours they're opinion on why they think this product deserves a perfect 5-star rating on Amazon, don't believe it. The game has some genuine good parts to the RE-formula that was remade from RE2 (2019). Like the dodge mechanic, I love the inclusion...but that's it. This game was designed as DLC for RE 2 (2019) and it clearly shows. And as usual, Capcom got greedy here. I do really like this version of Jill and Carlos, but it's too bad the actual good moments are over WAY TOO FAST. It's a trimmed down version of the beloved PS1 game that is missing the heart and soul of original experience. Instead of authentic Survival horror dread, you get cheap spectacle.

"But what about Project Resistance as part of the package? Surely it's worth the initial asking price for that, right?" Sorry, but nobody sane really cares about multiplayer in a RE game unless it's designed to be like playing a campaign setting or it's Horde/Mercenaries mode. The tacked on (also made by a completely different team) 4v1 mode really isn't anything special. It reminds me of anytime the Metal Gear Solid games have a MP mode implemented. Sure, the idea could be fun on paper, but something essential is missing to the formula where you just end up ignoring the mode altogether. The funny part is Capcom knew people were more interested with just the single player portion of this package that Project Resistance is thankfully a separate install (at least on Steam). Also, it has micro-transactions via loot boxes with a XP grind per character. It'll stay uninstalled indefinitely for me at least.

This stick is absolutely incredible. The aluminum casing is very solid and sturdy. Probably the most sturdy case I've come across and I've tried just about every commercial stick out there. The surface has a lot of room for your hands which I really like, and the surface is actually slightly angled, which makes a huge difference for me. This is one of the best features of the stick in my opinion. The case also has two large cutouts on the bottom which are used as “handles”. Thank you Victrix…this is the second best feature.

The stick and buttons are Sanwa, with 8 black OBSF buttons and a JLF stick. But this JLF has a detachable top similar to Phreakmods Linq. It is in fact the Linq II and is very handy for removing the stick and storing in the bottom compartment. It also comes with a little rubber “cap” to cover the hole where your lever was, but one thing to note, there's no where to store the cap. I wedge it behind the included hex wrench in the bottom compartment.

Speaking of the bottom, the door to access the innards is there. Flip the stick over, and you get access to the buttons, wiring, PCB Board and the stick. It’s all very neatly put together with nice braided coverings on the wires (in Victrix signature purple). Buttons can be replaced and the stick as well. Note. There’s not a whole lot of room in here, and if you want to install a different stick, then you may not be able to. The spacing around the plate for the stick is very tight. So if you want to put in a different lever, this is not the stick for you. Buttons can be replaced easily enough, but the vewlix layout is tighter than say a Noir one (which is true for any sticks using the vewlix layout).

As far as replacing buttons, that’s what I did. As much as I love Sanwa buttons, one thing to note about this case. It’s loud. Much louder than any other stick. The tapping of the Sanwas are amplified greatly over a TE2, Obsidian, Panthera, RAP, Fighting Edge etc. It’s quite noticeable compared to those. I tried some 2nd Gen Silent Sanwas and they were great, muffling the sound a lot but keeping the classic feel. Then I also tried some Gamerfinger Silvers. These are also great. I decided to leave them in and I’m quite happy with them after using them for a couple weeks.

The stick has a touchpad button function(not a touchpad), as well as buttons for L3, R3 which you set up in the button bar above the layout. It also lets you control the LED lighting which glows from the sides of the stick, similar to the Qanba Obsidian, but with every color and light option you can think of. It’s a nice touch (though completely gratuitous and I’d take a version without the lighting for a lower MSRP). You can also turn it off.

The cord. A purple colored USB C able wrapped in braiding allows you to connect to the PS4 and is completely replaceable with any other normal USB C cable. This alone makes it highly desirable for me. My Razer Panthera is missing a cable which Razer cannot even provide since they changed the wiring on the Pro cable that comes with it. There’s die cast metal cord wraps on the top of the case so you can neatly wrap your cable up instead of wrapping it around the case like you see people do at tourneys. Very handy. With the handles too? Awesome.

Price is steep being such a premium constructed product, but after using it for a couple of weeks…I have to say that this is my favorite stick ever and replaces my favorite Obsidian as my primary travel stick of choice. If you can afford it and don't care about chaging the lever itself, it's fantastic.

Those of you looking for a wired fight pad for fighting games should look at this Power A pad. First, you can see that it has the classic Sega Saturn pad shape which was known in its day as the pad to have for fighters. Slightly thicker, and boasting removable face-plates for customization, it still feels like the Saturn pad. The D-Pad, like the original Saturn is a circular one that is very loose and allows you to do motions for fighters very easily. If you’ve only used a DualShock or Nintendo Cross D-Pad, be prepared to wonder why more D-pads aren’t like this. It is smooth, and circular motions are sublime.

The face buttons are good feeling buttons and of course, have a six button layout Street Fighter Style. If you’re playing a 4 button fighter like Tekken, these do not get in the way. Shoulder buttons are in the same place as the original Saturn pad, and are extremely light and easy to press. Some might argue too sensitive. They are a bit touchy, and require way less pressure than the Saturn one, so it is in fact easy to accidentally press them. Not sure why they made the shoulders that sensitive.

The pad is wired only and comes with a nice long braided Micro USB cable (I was hoping for USB C) that fits into a channel to help prevent cord bending. Weight of the pad is light, but it doesn’t feel cheap…it feels perfect for me. I had several people at numerous FGC local events I put on try the pad out and most of the people who tried it liked it. The ones familiar with the Saturn pad or the Hori Fighting Commander especially liked it. It’s a good fight pad, with the only adjustment I would like to see is slightly more pressure to activate shoulder buttons. While this didn't interfere with my own play, I could see it affecting other people, so I will knock off a star for that.

I love to look at gaming headsets since there are so many out there.  There are good ones, and there are bad ones.  This is a good one.  It is not perfect, but at this price point, don't expect super high quality audio and perfect mids.  What we have here is a good entry level headset with a decent microphone for chat.  It would work fine for your kids playing Fortnite.  The build quality is decent, comprised mostly of plastic of course, but it doesn't feel too bad.  The look is okay, and doesn't scream "gamer" like so many other ones do now.  I like that.  The cans have 40mm drivers which sound okay, probably better than you would expect at this price point.  You won't be using these with your phone to listen to Ariana Grande's latest (but you could), but for most games, you will be fine.  Bass is okay, mids and highs are serviceable.  Worked great in Apex Legends and Destiny 2 as well as Resident Evil 3 Remake and the Vanquich/Bayonetta Remasters.  Tested on PS4 through the DS4 and through a Victrix Pro Fight Stick on Street Fighter V.  Sonically, for the price this isn't half bad at all.  Chat with the mic was fine too, but you won't mistake these for Astros.  Just remember these are entry level cans with a mic and it then makes sense.  The one thing that bothered me teh most, and it's pretty much an issue with any set of wired headsets under $50 is that you have two separate wires to each cup.  I prefer one cable, but that is usually reserved for a higher price point these.  All in all, I give it a solid 4 out of 5 based on what it is.  It's not better than Sony Golds, or a bunch of higher priced Hyper X cans, but again, look at the price.

These Micro USB cables are good. Using them for connecting Dual Shock 4s to PS4s and also for charging various devices. The quality of the cable itself is sturdy and the connectors have held up over the past few weeks of constant plugging and unplugging on both the micro USB side and the USB A side. These work for data as well as charging. I haven't had any issues with these and the blue coloring for PS is a nice touch.

With the PS5 now beginning to take center stage as well as USB C becoming more and more prevalent, there isn't a better time to get discounted micro USB cables for your legacy devices. I've noticed they have been dropping since more and more USB C stuff has come out. My SteelSeries Artic 7p also still takes Micro-USB and I use this to charge that too.

These USB C cables are good.  Using them for connecting DualSense controllers to PS5 and also for charging various devices.  The quality of the cable itself is sturdy and I  have used them to charge my Xperia Phone too.  Also, a voice recorder and a battery pack.  No issues with anything.  I have also connected my phone to my car's Android Auto with them, my laptop, etc.  That worked out great and all works well.  Charging seems to be pretty good with my phone, these charge just as well and at the same speed as my Sony provided ones.  I have had some USB C cables from other places  not pass through data but these seem fine.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite is a game that had so many hopes as finally being “The One”. While there have been countless games over the years attempting to capture the feel and sound of James Cameron’s take on the Alien franchise, few have given the series any justice. The previous Aliens: Colonial Marines game by Gearbox did a lot of harm towards fans with an abysmal experience. Enter Aliens: Fireteam Elite. It sounds like it might be a mobile game, but there’s more here than you would expect.

It’s not perfect by any means. It’s not a AAA title in terms of design, graphics or story. But…it has fast fluid control, good shooting feel, and isn’t that janky (PS5 version at least). The story is mostly throwaway taking place 23 years after the vents of Ripley and company. Aliens are now known to exist in several parts of the galaxy and you and up to two pals of yours are here to clean them up. You can match with online co-op friends or have the game assign two androids (Alpha and Beta) to back you up. There are twelve mission to tackle, whether by yourself and the Android buds or with friends or randos online, the game is quite fun and rather tough. The missions are no cakewalk and waves upon waves of Aliens will do everything in their power to make sure you don’t leave alive.

It’s a good thing you have a choice of 4 classes (a fifth later) to play as including the standard soldier(Gunner), a Heavy Weapons (Demolisher), a Medic (Doc) and a Technician (can place turrets). All have their own arsenal of weapons and abilities that do make them feel different when playing as. The Demolisher has access to the famed Smartguns of the franchise which auto tracks targets and have high ammo capacities whereas the Technician only has a handgun and a close quarters weapon (shotgun or submachine gun) but has shock grenades and the ability to place a smart auto firing turret down for peace through superior firepower.

The sound of the Smartguns and Pulse rifles have that distinct sound you love and isn’t just one short clip on a loop which some games have done. There are many weapons to unlock and discover as well as attachments for your guns that enhance their magazine capacities, handling, range etc. In a budget title, this is welcome.

Online play was good from the few times I have tried it though I did experience a sound drop out on one occasion which fixed itself in about 15 secs. I played this while on PS5 Beta 3.1 for what it’s worth. Load times on PS5 are very quick as you would imagine, though if matchmaking with people on PS4 you will have to wait for them. The game on PS5 runs at a very smooth framerate and graphics are more than great enough. Playing by yourself with the AI androids can be tough since they do not seem to be as capable the further you get into the story missions. It’s probably better played with human players if you can. In-between mission you can explore your home base ship the Endeavor and purchase weapons and upgrades, consumable items like turrets and recon drones, and get some lore/story from the ship’s crew. These NPCs don’t move their mouths when talking to you (budget game) but it’s not a huge deal as this game was almost half the cost of most new titles.

If you are a fan of the series, you can say that while far from perfect, this satisfies the itch of wanting to be in that universe blasting xenos. If you aren’t then you can subtract a star and know that this is a challenging 3rd person shooter that delivers what many fans wanted. It’s a fun game especially with some friends.

This is a decent headset for gaming. It's lightweight, and had a decent sound for gunfire, explosions, the running of your opponents behind your back and to the sides and yes even the music. The cable plugs into a controller and you got a nice immersive headset with a semi decent mic. It won't win any awards from your friends but they won't be asking you what you said either. It's more than serviceable.

Sound is not too bassy or bright. Decent mids and things sound well enough for a budget headset. I'll be using this as a headset that can be used in fighting game tournaments by people who don't bring their own (once we can have them again). Tested on a PS4 Pro Dualshock 4 and a PS5 Dualsense with Apex Legends, Street Fighter V, Kena: Bridge of Spirits, Aliens: Fireteam Elite, Life Is Strange: True Colors, Returnal, and Deathloop.
