Here's the deal. At $20 or more this game is simply not worth it. Sorry, it's true. On the other hand, if you pay $3.99 like I did on a sale day, it is an amazing value!

This is NOT a building game. This is not Simcity. You can only build transportation related stuff. No buildings, no anything else. If you lay down roads, buildings will pop up, expanding city population and by extension the number of people who use your transportation systems thereby making you more money. Otherwise, you're laying down metro rails, tram rails, bus routes, ferry routes, etc.

It actually is pretty fun for a while. I enjoyed it. It seems to have a multiplayer feature which appears to be completely useless. The campaign gives 12 scenarios to complete. Most are about expanding coverage or hitting a certain company value. Once you figure out that all you have to do is lay down a metro route or two and the cash comes flying in, the rest gets pretty easy. Still it's pretty fun for a while to play with. It does get old after a while but I didn't hit that until I was about done with the campaigns anyway and was close to done with the game.

So if you can pick it up for under $10, it's a good deal and you'll get your money's worth from it.

Maybe I'm too harsh because I'm used to good games that are well put together like GTA, Hitman, Arkham City, etc., but I really wanted to give this game 1 star. The only reason I didn't was because it is a really neat concept and I liked the idea of it. I think this game has a couple things going for it. First, its 3rd person rather than a 1st person game. Most zombie games are 1st person shooters and personally I don't care for those. Second, it's not all hack and slash. You gather resources and manage people so there's a little more strategy to it. I also liked the realistic elements such as stamina conservation.

Unfortunately for me the game was practically unplayable. The graphics were just absolute crap. They looked like something you would find on a video game from 2001. I'm fairly sure the graphics were comparable to GTA III, which were amazing in 2001 are flat, unrealistic and static in 2014. Controls are all over the place. This was where I had my biggest issue. The controls were very loose so entering doorways or trying to do anything that required any amount of precision was extremely frustrating. Even turning my mouse sensitivity all the way down, the slightest mouse movement sent the camera all over the place. At first I thought it was just a matter of getting used to the controls, so I played with it for quite a while, but the controls never improved for me.

As much as I would say the idea of resource gathering and management is a good thing, I would also say its a bad thing. It gets very repetitive so you go from one building to another repeating the same thing over and over. Kill the zombies, search area A and B, take whatever is there, move to the next one. After a while it gets a little boring. I think part of what makes it worse is the time it takes to do searches while you sit there just holding the E key. This is a tough thing to review because on the one hand, the realism of taking time to quietly search for resources is a positive thing, but between the crappy graphics, the difficult controls and the fact that many buildings and areas are just copied out multiple times so each one looks exactly like the last, it just gets old pretty quick.

I'm usually pretty good when it comes to picking games, I rarely pick bad ones and I was on the fence about this one after reading reviews and seeing the screenshots. My instinct told me to pass but when it came up for sale for $7, I decided to take a chance on it anyway, why not? What this taught me is that I really should listen to my instincts about games. Its possible that I'm being too harsh or too quick to judge because I didn't get very far in the game. It just got too frustrating just trying to navigate and crudeness of the graphics just drove me crazy after a while. I'd love to see an amazing 3rd person zombie game with some resource and personnel management, this one was certainly on the right track, but it just wasn't executed well.

So I wrote a long review of this game, but came back to edit after playing 25 games. It kills me to say this, but this game sucks. There is a comeback engine in the game that is maddening, frustrating, and makes the game little to no fun to play. Basically, if you score, plan on the opponent scoring as well. I've had games up 5-0, 4-0, and 3-0 going into the third, invariably the opponent will go into "God Mode" and become unstoppable. I've had opponents do the following:
1. Skate through 4 defensemen, score over the goalie's pad even with the goalie having the angle
2. Take a terrible shot, the kind you don't even take in hope of rebound, that the goalie doesn't see until the last second, despite a lack of a screen
3. Get poke checked only to do a 180 degree turn from the waist to grab the puck and take a shot that goes in from the high slot, again with no screen
4. Dump the puck from the rear blueline on the PK, only to bounce on net and become too hot to handle for my goalie
5. The piece de resistance; a poke check from a tied up face off that sneaks five hole despite being slow enough for my grandmother to handle

Every time these improbable things happen, and they happen with regularity, I am winning. Mind you, none of these things happen if the game is scoreless, or you are losing, only if you are up. It has gotten to the point where my wife said "you don't even celebrate scoring goals any more" and I don't because they will score to match you and keep it close. I went into the season stats to find data to prove this, and it is there. My goalie is leading the league in wins, but is 55th in Save Percentage and 49th in Goals Against Average. The only reason this can be possible is because they always match me nearly goal for goal.

I should have known better after buying Madden 12. Thing is NHL 12 was so fun, I played that game like it was going out of style, and while goalies would let in the occasional softy in NHL 12, they are Patrick Roy compared to the goalies in NHL 14. I can't believe I was so optimistic with an EA title. Please God, let this company go out of business forever.

Resident evil village, to nobody's surprise, continues the formula that was well established in re7. Trying to give no spoilers, you reassumed the role of Ethan, trying to track down his daughter who is abducted by Chris Redfield.

BLUF: Beautiful, subtle, with 0-60 gameplay that can easily turn from a tranquil ride through the woods into a panicked fight for your life in just a few heartbeats, Elden Ring has just the right amount of everything. Graphics: Words fail. Even on a PS4, words fail. This is one of those games that truly moves the bar for what you believe to be possible.

Story: There are some bumps. The story, in true Souls fashion, is mostly hidden in the softer details, in the description of items and the rare, precious few conversations with NPC's. And while the overall story is generally understood, that makes some of the elements even more... peculiar.

Gameplay: Dark Souls 3 on steroids. The inclusion of the horse adds another layer to the symphony of gameplay, but otherwise, the majority of the structure is unchanged. However, you best learn to love the horse quickly, as you will be brutally punished in encounters that require the horse but give no clue whatsoever that its critically important.

This is the only crack in the finish. Souls games have always been hard. Brutally, unforgivingly hard, but they've never been cruel. This feels cruel. If you truly want to experience this for yourself, without the slightest assistance, you're truly doomed until well past the 40 hour mark. XP is so pathetically doled out after even a few hours, that without cheap cheese and tricks to get the whopping amount you need for even a single level, this feels like a tedious, grinding drag, as you may need to grind twenty or thirty levels to use a new weapon. With a cheap work around, that can take an hour or two. Without the inside scope, it could easily take hours or even days.

Hades is a roguelike randomly generated dungeon crawler where you attempt to escape the underworld. That simple descriptor can barely do justice to a setup that appears so bland and uninspired, that you quickly realize it is an astounding multi-layer cake that becomes more incredible the more you cut into it.

Lets start with the story. Its fed in paltry sips, but you get more than a few sips on every loop. Every character knows something, and you know things even you the player don't know, but they don't have a heart to heart lore dump almost anywhere. Story kinks are everywhere, and even the sidebar character interactions are intriguing and engaging, from the court musician waiting for the return of their muse, to the god of death throwing a tantrum over his best friend trying to leave him behind and one up him.

The graphics are lush and the sound is at least decent. I will admit reluctantly that it starts to feel a bit cookie cutter after a while, but thats more due to you being stuck in the first world so much that it definitely feels like old hat after a while. The fields of Elysium are beautiful, but you'll definitely loath the tombs of Tartarus quickly.

Combat is the meat and bones. Everything snaps together like an intricate puzzle. There are six main weapons, and more can not be said without drifting into spoilers. Suffice to say, theres no "bad" or "best" weapon, as each has a pro and con, and the game even entices you to play ones that you haven't by attaching carrots to them.

One thing thats simply incredible is the feeling of scarcity. If you play long enough, you'll open everything, but you constantly hit with decision points that feel like sophies choice. You need everything, you want everything, but you are faced with crippling decisions. Do you focus on powers for the run your on, or gems and skill points that'll last for every loop, but don't have as much impact? Do you go for a power that appears worthless because you've never tried it, or stick with something you know works but isnt very good? Do you accept a curse knowing the payout off is worth it, but also knowing you might be cursed during a boss fight?

The only nit, and this is from scouring it for something to needle, is the fact that combat can become to compressed. With all the flashing effects and certain weapons needing you to be up close and personal, you can quickly find yourself overwhelmed by something barely out of few, hidden by an aura effect or explosive flashes. Separate from that, there are a few points where you can over look something because the glimmer of the background is indistinguishable from the glimmer of an item you desperately need to interact with. Particularly with fishing. Yes, you fish the rivers of the underworld.

BLUF: While theres a story thatll keep you guessing from the very beginning, basically all of the meat and potatoes of what made batman games good has been replaced with grind. Grind and grind and grind. Then grind some more.

Graphics shockingly havent improved from Arkham Knight. While theres more sprites, theres so much grey on gray that you cant really appreciate it. Your HQ is vibrant and alive, but thats basically it.

Story: Story and voice are where this makes a significant improvement. You knew from the moment you turned on any Arkham game several of the main highlights. The Knight is Jason Todd. The Jokers never really gone while Mark Hamill has breath in his body. The Jokers always the main villain or the surprise twist villain. All of that would be wrong in this case. Regardless, you know several high points. Not in this case. Batmans dead. with a capital D.

Gameplay: This is where the game nosedives into the ground. 60-70% of the game now is grinding combat. This would be okay if it went somewhere. Anywhere. But it never does. You're not building on a side quest. Theres no plot. Beat up a group of thugs. Then do it again. And again. And four more times. Then fifteen more. Then twenty more. And you're forced to. The game basically requires it, as you have to level up. Gone are riddler trophies. Gone are actual investigations. You'll see the same body lying in front of the same crate of beers against the same trash can with the same burn on their hand twice in the same night.

So much of this is so generic and tone deaf its just jaw dropping. Combats worse. Now you dodge and weave, and dodge and weave. Which would make sense, but countering was a big part of Batman games.

You'd think the various characters would actually have strengths and weaknesses? Nope!. They're all basically skins on the same bland vanilla move set. Theres differences in appearance and a handful of under the hood modifications, but again, its all generic.

And somehow everything in Gotham has fallen apart in a matter of minutes. Gordons dead, and the entire GCPD suddenly is hankering to fill you full of holes. Forget helping cops or EMS.

A hollow empty world that doesn't give the same feel as any Arkham game and somehow has less in it. Combat watered down and washed out. Four characters that might as well be one with different hats. Generic RPG shoehorned in to pad length. Pretty disappointing.

But I will give props on story. Story is bewildering and novel, and you'll never see the next act.

Man... what a treat Puppeteer is. Sony apparently cares passionately about games and their customers, because to pull something like this off cannot be easy. It must've been an enormous risk to create such a game, one that's based on a character nobody's heard of, and one with such an incredibly quirky (and at times downright weird) storyline. It's not exactly easy to market something like that. Fortunately they did it, because Puppeteer is simply one of the most wondrous works of art I've ever seen in video-game format. This is a piece of pure and unadulterated imagination, crafted with such care and integrity, and not motivated entirely by the desire to just take your money. Sony wants to make "art" believe it or not, art that is remembered and cherished by those that are brave enough to experience it. This game surprises and delights to an absurd degree, and the experience is sure to be nothing short of sweet for anyone who gives it a chance.

Puppeteer tells the wacky story about a puppet who must save a moon kingdom from the stygian, Moonbear King. What ensues is some tremendous platforming that operates on fairly simple mechanics, most of which are dictated by an important item you acquire early on, known as "Calibris." This is a magical pair of scissors that you'll use to reach high places and attack enemies. What makes the use of this item so fun and unique is the way in which you travel with it: you'll be cutting through paper, webs, bad guys, etc, sometimes at very high speeds.

The game though, for the most part, is a slow burn. You can't run very fast or jump all that high, and there isn't a whole lot of variety to your attacks. But you won't care because you'll be having so much fun with everything else that Puppeteer has to offer. There is just so much beauty and detail to behold in every frame, and the game knows how to change things up by throwing you a vehicle to commandeer occasionally. The boss fights are also a major reward and surprisingly epic for a platformer, boasting some of the game's greatest moments.

We should be grateful that developers are still daring to bring us something as detailed and intelligent as Puppeteer. Its originality is refreshing in an age riddled with the same old shooters and sequels. Paradoxically, the game's power lies within its innocence, its charming simplicity, its tendency to daydream and surf the threads of imagination at random. Prepare to smile... a lot.

Not quite an interactive movie, but not your standard video game either. The emphasis in this experience comes down to one major thing: story. And what a fascinating and deeply suspenseful story it is. Jodie has a unique psychic ability: she is linked with a spirit named, Aiden. This duality makes for a fantastic and stimulating gameplay dynamic. You have to learn two very different control styles simultaneously, and at first the controls for Aiden may feel a tad weird. This partnership also lends to some excellent cooperative play. I had some friends over this past weekend and we had a great time digging deeper into the story together.

Something I think that is being sadly overlooked about this game is just how monumental the graphics are. There are chapters that left my friends and I dumbfounded; we could hardly continue playing because we were so busy gawking at the eye candy. One notable chapter takes place in the rain, and there were moments that I thought were going to be a video, until I realized that Jodie was standing still and waiting for me to step in and control her. Her movements are incredibly smooth as you make her walk, while the lighting is simply serene and surfaces glow beautifully with moisture. The textures look thick and layered, i.e., real.

So you're worried that you'll get bored? You want constant action? The chances of you being bored by this game are contingent on all the other games you've played and enjoyed. Were they shooters? Or did they involve story? I'm not here to judge, and I won't bother asserting which gaming style is more rewarding than the other; we all know that that's just opinion. What I will say is that if you love movies, and you also love story-driven video games, then you will simply admire Beyond. The narrative is suspenseful from the very beginning, and it will effectively pique the interest of any curious gamer who enjoys piecing a good story together. And guess what? It is not something you just sit back and watch. I was actually very pleasantly surprised by how much I was involved as a gamer. You near-constantly control Jodie or Aiden, and even when you don't, your actions and/or decisions play a prominent role in your experience.

I'd also like to mention that this is a significant improvement over Heavy Rain, if anything just because the pacing feels perfectly executed here. There is constantly something going on, and you'll find yourself perpetually more and more curious. You will be desperate to understand it all, and this is part of how Beyond maintains tension throughout the experience so consistently.

So if you can get over the fact that this is anything but a sandbox action-shooter (and why would've you expected that in the first place? c'mon), then you will swoon while playing Beyond: Two Souls. 9/10.

Killzone is a technical marvel of sorts. It’s sublime. The philosopher, Edmund Burke, described the “sublime” as the feeling of awe one experiences when faced with something that is both beautiful and terrifying, something that instills fear and uncertainty due to how little we may comprehend its being. You feel simultaneously infinitesimal and enormous in the presence of the sublime. There are moments in Killzone that left me breathless, where I couldn’t help but just stare. I’m grateful to report that video games, at last, have taken their rightful place next to the great mediums of expression: literature, architecture, music, film, etc. Advancements in technology, coupled with a passion for creative gaming experiences, is the formula that will jettison this age into an era where games will be respected for what they essentially are: works of art.

95% of your experience playing Killzone will be the most s***-inducing excitement you've ever felt playing a video game. I award it a perfect score for three main things: the mind-bogglingly gorgeous visuals, how fun it is to play, and its sound design.

Two friends and I devoured nearly half of it on the Saturday night after the PS4 was released, and we were so thoroughly hooked that we could hardly eat the pizza we'd just ordered. We were that stunned. It's the sort of game where you will stop “playing,” and instead just simply look around so you can analyze the world that's been created, just for you. Prepare to be inundated with a stunning level of detail. This is a very handsome game. A friend of mine, who is a developer, was able to expound on a panoply of technical terms: I learned about volumetric lighting, blooming, bump mapping, specular lighting, and ambient occlusion, to name a few. Before Killzone, my interest in video games merely tiptoed in the minutiae of design; now my level of appreciation has been galvanized by sincere wonderment.

The story, though, is just ok, and there are two moments where I got a little frustrated. The ending will polarize gamers: I was personally underwhelmed. But as I said earlier, my love for this game is more concerned with the fun I had playing it, the visuals, and the sound design. And why has nobody mentioned that last detail yet? This is both the best looking AND best sounding game I've personally ever played. Make sure your speakers are cranked, and prepare for sonic bliss. I’d love to see the keyboard and program that were used to make the soundtrack. Some of the songs are surprisingly catchy; occasionally I would just stop and listen to the music.

Killzone isn't flawless, God knows it tries; but where it's good, it's simply brilliant. Above all, this game is a statement about what is to come, and I’m extremely excited to see what developers do next with PS4 exclusives. Anyone who is passionate and fascinated by video games needs to experience this game, at least for its technical aspects. It’s thrilling to know you’re a part of history, that you are one of the first gamers to experience this exciting shift into next-gen technology.

Dark Souls II is one of the most imaginative games I've ever played. It's a reminder of those precious moments that stimulated our childhood with so much wonder and adventure, that incredible sense of discovery that accompanied each new experience: our first tree house, our first trip through a neighbor's backyard, our first best friend. This is a brand of creativity that is rare on consoles, but one that your inner child will instantly recognize.

Dark Souls II is a massive whirlwind of bone-rattling terror and excitement, and it is riddled with moments of adrenaline-pumping ecstasy of the most epic caliber. Truly, no other game has got my heart pumping this fast, nor has any other filled me with such a deep sense of accomplishment. It is patterned with a surfeit of jaw-dropping moments, one after another; sometimes I could hardly play the game because I felt so wonderstruck, consumed with the purest and most debilitating sense of awe.

This is also one of the most intimidating games I've ever played, but that is just merely another part of its allure. Yes, it is hard, and you will fail repeatedly, sometimes on a terrifyingly grand scale. You will lose everything. But—and this is an astronomically huge but—you will most assuredly succeed, and you will rarely feel frustrated. This game is meant to be experienced online: you will battle with other players, sometimes for their benefit, other times for your own, and you will also fight against them.

The multiplayer dynamics are deeply nuanced, and the game's universe will begin to take on a startlingly organic feel because of this. Nothing is set, nothing is certain: help other players, or invade them if you wish. Think you're right at the cusp of victory? Think again, because this game will throw you curve balls out of pockets of space you never thought existed.

The Dark Souls experience (and Demon Souls for that matter) is definitely an acquired taste, one that will not suit your palate after just a couple hours of play. You need to get comfortable with its RPG elements, and this, for me at least, was initially difficult. This aspect of the game just felt dull at first. Once I began to understand how it worked—that is, the specific use of items and myriad upgrades—I then fell comfortably into its cradle of chaos, and was en route to becoming the biggest badass in the universe.

The Dark Souls games aren't inaccessible just for the sake of being difficult though. The developers weren't merely interested in pissing off players. Instead, what we have here is some first-class gaming; and games, like anything else, acquire a stratified presence when they're imbued with this much possibility, complexity, and freedom. Wine, cigars, movies, albums, games—the best of these all take a little time to get used to before the participant can fully enjoy their treasures, and Dark Souls is an exemplary case of this phenomenon.

You will be filled with wonder. You will be more freaked out and intimidated than you've ever been playing a game. Ultimately though, you will prevail, and you will experience the greatest sense of reward a game could ever provide.

A very worthy entry in the Shin Megami Tensei series. After 77 hours of game play I was able to finish the game with the neutral ending. This entry has improved in many ways over it's predecessor SMT III: Nocturne. Which happens to be my favorite game of all time. SMT IV has a well done story, very unique, and very likeable law and chaos heroes as well as the heroine who stays by your side. I felt like SMT IV was more of a throwback to SMT I and II. With a first person turn based battle system and the return of swords and guns. Which all work very well. Exploring at first was kind of boring as for whatever reason you start with menu based exploration like persona 3 portable. This changes after about 8 hours or so. Here it introduces a quest system which is very nice for fighting extra bosses and just for giving you more things to do in a pretty big world. The main story starts out slow, but I didn't really mind. If you are an veteran SMT player you should find this game pretty easy, simply being familiar with how everything works. I do feel like the battle system is much too streamlined, it actually tells you what enemies are weak to, repel, and immune to right before you use your attacks which made everything even easier during random encounters. The amount of demons this game has is insane! Huge variety with many opportunities to form the perfect party. Demon fusing is better than it's ever been. Finally we can hand pick our skills while fusing! It's been a long time coming, but a much needed change. Things I didn't like was the simplistic design of boss battles. All you had to do was find the boss's elemental weakness and spam it until they die. More thought should've been put in besides just that. SMT III had very tricky and memorable boss battles that were very well designed especially on hard mode. Also the dungeon design was very simplistic. No puzzles in dungeons to solve at all until the VERY end unlike SMT III, with very tricky and memorable dungeons through out the entire game.
Overall though I love this game and can't wait another decade for SMT V.

I have played ME on three different platforms as of the release of this package, and am very happy with the content of this release overall. Potential buyers, however, should be aware of some issues that mar an otherwise excellent package:

-I have to say I am disappointed with the PS3 version of the original ME--a real selling point for PS3 owners who missed out on the first one (after I am sure a pitched battle ensued with Microsoft to get the rights). Texture issues, long load times, issues with dialog synching up with animations, occasional frame rate drops, hangups (during combat!). ME 1 is a glitchy mess--some of these issues exist with the original versions, but I would have expected them fixed for this compilation. They are glaring compared to ME2 and ME3 (and really any modern game released in the last five years). You can hear the disc straining to catch up at times, which is simply frustrating.

-The packaging flat out sucks. Card stock slip cases with plastic inserts for the discs that for some reason fit a little too snugly to make it easy to take it out and replace it without damaging it. This is not going to last for years to come, that's for sure. I would hate to see what used copies are going to look like for this thing.

-DLC inconsistencies: different versions have different DLCs, which personally annoys me. You will have to do your homework to see which DLC comes with which version, but it is not consistent across the board. If you are looking for a "complete experience," you won't find it here. You still gotta pay EA to play.

But for the price point--$59.00--you are getting each game for $20. Gamestop has jacked up ME1 alone up to $25, so it is really a bargain. Couple in the DLC's value, and you really make out well with this collection. You will just have to suspend your expectations for ME1. I would say get it, it would make a great gift or entry for newbies to this series (or folks looking for a single-package collection, like me).
Believe the hype--this is a worthy entry to console co-op games as of late, and is a much better version of D3 than the PC version.  It IS NOT D2--know that on the front end.  That is all.

Reviews (particularly IGN's scathing coverage) touted this game's release as a complete failure; bugs, poor graphics, incomplete ideas, too many players (in an MMO?) and not enough character advancement to show progress all marred what should have been this generation's precursor to Destiny (can't wait for that one, either). The important (and largely forgotten) thing to remember is that with an online game of this nature, players are going to find a plethora of issues and broken gameplay as they play and patches are the solution. That's just where we are with gaming, for better or worse (I'd like to think for better personally).

With the majority of the patches applied--particular fixing gameplay balance and leveling issues--Defiance is a playable, unique experience that satisfies in customization, co-operative play, and a decent storyline. Since this is a bit of a late review, I will highlight a couple of the interesting things I have found while playing and why I would recommend this to console owners looking for something a little off the beaten path.

Customization
With the EGO system (Defiance's answer to leveling) you receive points that are spent on abilities and perks, allowing you to make whatever kind of hero you want in this game around four major powers. Want to be super-fast with the ability to whack baddies in the back of the head for bonuses? Got it. Interested in a stealthy character focused on critical strikes? Yes. Want to make copies of your self to baffle your enemies and reap bonuses to attack for them being a moving target? You guessed it. Builds are the key to enjoying this game, and though a major complaint is that over time a player will essentially have access to all the powers in the game, it's still fun to develop over the grid and make the kind of player you want to play. Me? I have a stealth-based, Pistol-wielding outlaw that gets loads of bonuses for silent kills, sneak attacks, and ambushes. You will also gain proficiency in the weapons and items you use, so that plays into the Build you are trying to make as you play, so it all adds to your overall experience in a very good way.

Co-Operative Play
This is my absolute favorite part of this game. The game gives you all the standard options to have structured cooperative play, parties, and instanced missions for groups to tackle. What I am most impressed about is the organic cooperation that happens in missions and Arkfalls (group-based assaults on single targets, loads of enemies, great drops). Any time you take on a mission, you will inevitably encounter other players trying to complete it as well, and you begin to earn XP together while accomplishing the goals of the mission. This is great and requires NO COMMUNICATION if you use common sense and cover each other, hit the objectives, take out the bigger baddies or mobs as needed. It works, and works VERY well and that I really enjoy. It is somewhat entertaining to see players working hard at an Arkfall, take it down, collect their (individual) loot, then take off in whatever vehicles they rode in on (which disappear when you dismount for their protection). In short, this is probably my favorite part of the game. You can walk up on just about any situation and get right involved helping other players out (or being helped). Don't forget to Res other players if you see them drop (there is a trophy for it).

There are a great number of other reviews out there that go into more depth. By all means check them out if you are curious about some of the more technical aspects. The graphics still aren't very good, but I have noticed a lot of interesting shadows and light sources at work as you move around and that's pretty neat. I do wish that the weapon modification system was explained just a little bit more, as early on you end up with a lot of stuff and it isn't evident what is useful and what is garbage so early on (I scrapped my shield!).

Plenty of players, decent price point now (and some DLC already out and on the way). I would say go for it. That's all.

I have been avidly watching this game as a great summer stop-gap for Dragon Age: Inquisition, Dying Light, and Destiny (all set to come out this fall for PS3/PS4, respectively). Since the pickings are getting slimmer and slimmer for PS3, this kind of game definitely gets my attention as a fan of games like The Witcher, Dragon Knight Saga, Dragon's Dogma, Dark Souls, and other action-based RPGs. I feel like this is worth your time and money, ultimately, with some caveats that must be discussed so you know what you are getting into on the front end. It's a good game and a great offering from smaller developer.

Pros:

Customization

-Character creation: This has taken some negativity because there aren't a lot of options, but you can choose your main character to be male or female and choose their face and hair. It's not Skyrim's algorithm of choices, but I still appreciate that they gave you some choices. I am very pleased that the developers added both genders, too. That's forward thinking that needs to be in more games.

-Crafting system: EVERY piece of equipment can be customized, from pommels and guards on your swords, daggers, axes, and hammers, to greaves, gauntlets, chest plates, pauldrons, the whole nine. All these have remarkable detail and they show up in the cut scenes with your character as well as in the game itself; for awhile I ran around with a cleaver-style weapon with no guard just because I could. It's a small thing, but a NICE touch.

-Item creation: You can create traps, crossbow bolts, potions, and other goodies throughout the game. The main character is an explosives expert, so it makes sense that you could do this in between fights and in your down time, no crafting table or merchant needed.

Combat

Combat Layout: If you played Mars: War Logs, then you already know the system (and if you haven't, give that game a try at $10 from PSN); you have a main attack, a group attack, a guard break, block, and pressing one of the shoulder buttons gives you a radial to access items and slow down the action. What is slightly different here is that holding down the other shoulder button lets you access hotkeys, like your magic, crossbow, and traps. You can also switch weapon styles in real time, going from the Warrior stance (two handed weapons) to Ranger stance (twin short swords) with ease, though there is a realistic delay in switching weapons. Watch out for that.
-Combat depth: Running and and attacking like crazy will most likely get you killed. You do have to watch your enemies' patterns and choose the right stance going in. You can sneak up on enemies and backstab and there is a charged power attack for each weapon type that is pretty satisfying. My favorite attack is the flying knee. It just looks neat.

Companions & The Demon

Ally, Deserter, or Something More: So far I have three at my disposal, with varying back stories, combat styles which you can adjust like in the old Fallout games through conversations, and different motivations. Depending on your choices your companions will follow, challenge, or flat out abandon you in the game as you decide responses and your overall alignment. I understand that you can romance them, too, but I haven't got that far yet.

-The Demon: Early on you are possessed by a Demon who gives you access to some pretty awesome magic powers (like lighting your sword with flame). The story that the demon brings is interesting and hints and a very rich game world and history. As you play, the influence of the demon and how much you allow them to give you power will determine your ending and companions, which is just cool. Clearly they paid some attention to games like Mass Effect and I feel it pays off by giving you a sense of choice and direction.

Cons:

Graphics

-Character models: The characters look pretty good overall with good lighting and detail; main characters have a ton of detail, facial expressions, unique items and models. A number of the mercenaries look very similar, which makes some sense thematically, but still can be confusing.

-Environments: The environments, while FULL of stuff to see and check out, have some odd textures and don't quite look right. Also, during the daytime in the day/night cycle the lighting is too bright. The games' scenes really look the best at night, with nice fire reflections and your own character's light source (a white light with some nice particle effects when you turn it on or off). Shadow effects, particularly light through trees on the characters, function well enough but are jagged (PS3 limitations).

Vulcan

Protagonist: The main character is all over the place, sometimes pretty callous, other times trying to be funny and failing entirely, and other times flat out threatening in cut scenes. You can tailor your responses somewhat, but the base character is kind of a cocky jerk. I am hoping that in the story this will be a part of the adventure, ultimately deciding who he is.

Overall

Summary: I feel good about this purchase for a number of reasons. The developer has made two other games whose ideas have made their way into this one and you can really see that they are only getting better at what they do; you don't get to see that -often outside of AAA titles and larger developers. Check out some of Focus Interactive's other offerings, Of Orcs and Men and Mars: War Logs if you are curious or on the fence, as a number of ideas and the general controls, menus, and powers will be very similar in how you interact with them. This helped me immensely and is telling of how they are improving with each release as developers.

I would love to see what they have next in this rather rich game world. I enjoy a new take on fantasy, particularly dark fantasy by European developers (The Witcher); I think they have a different set of sensibilities that makes their offerings very interesting and worth your time.

The story is interesting and I want to see how it plays out. The concept of an old world being dominated by these Ice Lords and their undead army and how it affects the people of the game is fascinating and I am curious to see who will survive, stay with our party, leave us entirely, and ultimately make my choice as to how I fit into all of it. The story becomes one of how fighting a losing war affects individuals and what they are willing to do to defend their way of life.

I further enjoy whacking everything I can with different weapons just to see what happens. It is satisfying in a way that finding the perfect sword in Dark Souls can be, and the customization is an added plus.

Try it out.

We just got an Xbox One thanks to the Fallout 4 trailer release last week (how's that for a killer app, right?) and I was looking for something to play until then. Could be a long wait. Thanks to this piece of software, Xbox One owners (and Windows 8.1) get the same kind of experience folks have been having for awhile while with Little Big Planet on Playstation systems. I'm going to keep it short, and go into detail below: I LOVE this game, HATE the microtransactions. See below:

LOVE:
-Great world design software: intuitive, easy to navigate, great pre-rendered assets. You can really create a world in about 20 minutes, maybe even shorter with the biome feature (which lets you "paint" in scenery essentially).
-Brains system: EVERY object has a programmable brain, and the game comes with a good amount of common brains you can use.
-Kode system: dumb name, great idea: using tiles, you can create "When/Do" statements that the game will run for you (essentially If/Thens). With a few tutorials, I had a level where you could switch characters on the fly, see their health and damage, and pick up items in the world. If you use a little patience here, you can easily learn how this works, and the game's tutorial will have you doing this on a basic level in now time.
-The sharing: I have played some demos, full games, worlds just to run around, seen some amazing content from users. Best part, I don't have Xbox Live and STILL get access to play others' creations and share my own.

HATE:
-Microtransactions: Want to edit someone else's level? That's going to cost you. Want to download the "premium" levels the designers of this title made with the software? Going to cost you. Want more face/hair/body designs? Nickling and diming you all the way. I HATE that part of the game. Luckily there are enough assets to feel pretty good about the game without buying anything but this Starter Pack (with codes for three or four packs of content). Microsoft has got to stop this nonsense.

This is a great way to learn some coding, create a few fun things, and walk around in some other peoples' heads for awhile. For $20, I think it's well worth it. I've spent more and done less with it. Also of note is the ridiculous amount of achievements you get, both in game and for your system, resulting in some nice background art for that drab X1 dashboard. Give it a go, my creations are under the name AccountRecreate, and I would love to play yours, too (seriously).

Let me be honest and up front - I bought a refurbed Wii-U from Nintendo directly to play this game. After the disappointment in Nintendo's development practices and sheer stupidity with the Wii (The Operation Rainfall games really left a bad taste, look those up if you don't know that story), I wrote off the Wii U and focused on PC gaming until last year's Super Mario Maker came out. I told my wife, they make one more killer app, we might need to give them another try. Here it is, the sendoff for the Wii U, Breath of the Wild. I'm now around 10 hours in and have a lot to say that I think you might appreciate about this game.

The Good:
-Open World: This game is a dream-come-true for me, an idea that formed when I played Shadow of the Colossus back in college. Why couldn't they make that kind of game an open world RPG? Breath of the Wild does it superbly. Many games say "If you can see it, you can go to it;" this game delivers that promise and then some. Bear in mind that it's not always easy to traverse - there are climbs, sheer drops, weather, and other factors to manage to get to that amazing vista you want to check out or up that castle to see what's there, but you can do it. And you should, it's amazing and the game rewards you for exploring it. Most of my time is simply spent saying "that looks neat, let's go check it out." And off we go, for another couple of hours of unfettered adventure. This reminds me of the promise of games like The Elder Scrolls and Fallout series, actually brought to completion. I love this feature and would recommend on this alone.
-Story: It's dark, post-apocalyptic, but still retains the features that make a real Zelda game. And the way the game is designed you can pretty much experience it in any order you want just by going off the beaten path. The more you learn about this game's backstory and how the world became what Link wakes up to is fascinating and makes his discoveries in it our discoveries, and that's an amazing feat.
-NO HAND HOLDING: Japanese games over the years have really started to grind my gears in terms of just how long you spend staring at tutorials and expositions to get you into the game world and interacting with the systems. None of that here. Even your first guide in the game tells you at one point to "trust your judgment" when locating some spots on the map, which has few markers other than places you find. This is not a Ubisoft game where somehow you know every location of every place and encounter. Nintendo is giving you the player a huge amount of trust that you will find your way and have a good time while doing it, with is HUGE for this company on many levels.
-Risk/Reward and Challenge: I died seven separate times while playing in one two-hour session, from seven separate things. I jumped into a frigid lake and froze to death. I got shot by a laser and died. I got hit by a giant rock and died. And numerous times misjudged an enemy and died. The difference between this game and the rage-quit inducing Dark Souls series, by contrast, is that every one of these deaths were my fault and could be avoided (no spamming or failing to grind enough here). Every challenge has that cycle of risk reward - do you take on the enemy encampment to raid their treasure boxes or avoid it and live to fight another day? That's all up to you.
-Crafting: Lots of it in the form of food, potions, and elixirs. Reminds me vaguely of Monster Hunter here, but much more friendly. You can combine ingredients to make a wide range of status buffs (resistance to cold and increased speed or stamina, for example, very handy when you head into certain mountainous areas). What's great here is that the game hints at what works together, rather than give you all the answers. Experiment and see what works for you.
-Weapons and Armor: So. Many. Weapons. Sure, most of them are disposable with different durabilities, but there are a number of classes of weapons that all perform differently for different situations, and have the ability to charge attack for massive damage and a neat animation for each weapon class. Anything from Link's classic sword and shield combo, to spears, axes, hammers, clubs, and many types of bows and arrows, all at your disposal. I beat an enemy with a skeletal arm in a pinch. You read that right.

The Bad:
-The Graphics/Performance: My ONLY complaint really, is that this game is UGLY on my 1080p television, with jagged edges and issues with the shadows. Add to that some wild dips in FPS at times and you really are looking at a game that could have used just a little more polish or the ability to turn off shadows. Reports show that even on the switch it has issues on TVs. Both systems, though, change things up when you play from the handheld side. On Wii-U, it's a drastic change; softer lines, more blended shadows, and overall a smoother experience. I hope Nintendo continues to patch this game and eventually we see the drops in FPS diminish a bit, but for now it is noticeable. Truly this is what takes this game from 5 to 4 for me, but clearly not a deal-breaker.

All in all, this was an excellent purchase for me and I highly recommend you try this game out. I bought and now support the Wii U quite a bit more for it, totally worth the cost while Nintendo modifies the switch a few times to get everything right. If you're a current Wii U owner, even better for you. Play this game. Simple.

The next generation of gaming is here! I have been excited to get my hands on this console since the moment it was announced. The console is beautiful, the controller is top notch, and the Kinect seals the deal.

Ill start off by saying I got the 'Day One' edition. It includes a black box (part matte and part glossy to mimic the console itself), the included controller is Black with a dark chrome dpad and has 'Day One 2013' etched with matching dark chrome. Finally it also unlocks a 'Day One' achievement. There really wasn't too much included but since it was the same price as a standard edition they were fun inclusions.

Some say the console is big, bulky, and looks like a VCR but I couldn't disagree anymore. It is larger than the slim Xbox 360, but not unbearably so. I doubt anyone will have an issue putting the One in their entertain shelf. The two tone glossy/matte finish looks slick and unique along with the chrome touch of the BluRay slot and eject button gives the console an unbeatable design. Vents on the top and rear help eliminate the risk of overheating the early Xbox 360s were famous for. On the front you'll see a chrome Xbox logo for the power button and glows when the console is on. The glowing logo is not distracting in any way and looks great when lit up. As for ports the One has the right amount. On the left side you'll find a USB port for easily charging a controller, on the rear you find a non-standard port for the Kinect, two more USB ports, another non-standard power input port, LAN port, IR blaster (which sadly isn't included), Optical audio out, a HDMI out, and surprisingly an HDMI in (Which I'll talk about more in a little bit). With just the right amount of ports, a great design, and sleek color scheme I couldn't find any issues when the Console itself.

Moving onto the Kinect it features the Glossy theme from the Xbox One console. While smaller then the original Kinect its still large enough to take up a noticeable presence. I mounted mine on top of my TV and sometimes its hard not to notice it. Like the console it features a glowing Xbox logo on the right side when on, and a semi-transparent camera lens on the left. There is also a small bar underneath that houses the multiple microphones. The kinect can easily mount on top mounts using a standard tripod screw so unlike the original Kinect you won't have an issue finding a mount to fit with your home theater. My issues with the Kinect are the rather short cable and the IR lights. The cable does have a decent length, but I can see it being an issue for people that keep the console a fair distant from their TV. Finally the IR lights the Kinect uses for depth recording is in the visible range. I had no troubles seeing the three red lights emitting from the center of the Kinect. It both distracting at times and annoying. Really it the red that clashes with the rest of the consoles that bothers me. The black with white/chrome accents don't mesh well with the red IR lights.

Next up is the controller. Simply put, its the best controller I have ever used. Refining the Xbox 360 was no easy matter I'm sure, but Microsoft pulled it off. My fingers fit snugly and comfortably around the wider triggers, my thumbs grip onto the thumbstick, the clicky Dpad improves greatly from the mushy Dpad of the 360 design, and the raised Xbox guide button means no more accidental presses. My only complaints are cosmetic. I don't understand why Microsoft moved from the well know 'Start' and 'Back' buttons to the odd 'View' and 'list' buttons. Worse than that these new buttons aren't even labeled with words, just an odd three lines for 'List' and two squares representing 'View'. Finally just like the Kinect the controller features two IR leds near the top that are in the visible range and distracting/annoying. Still that being said the One controller is still the controller to beat.

Finally software. Right out of the boxed its needed an update to work, which I expected but I'm sure there will be a handful of people that will not. After about 45 minutes to an hour I was finally booted in the new home screen. Clearly inspired from Microsoft's new universal software design its both visually minimalistic and modern but can still be deep and complex at times. Visually is you see lots of solid colors with white logos and text, but through this simplicity I found myself quickly jumping in and out of settings, apps, and games with ease. It was both easy to spot the next app or game you wanted to get to and easy to go from one home screen to another. With the ability to pin my most used apps and games to the home screen and keep the apps I was never going to use out of sight helped make the home screen a personal place, and at the same time stick with a general design language that I appreciate. But the real star of the show is the Kinect. What once took several button presses and lists now takes a single sentence. The ability to quickly snap Netflix alongside he game I was playing was amazing. Every time I said Xbox On and watch the logo on the console light up made me smile even after the 50th time. There are a few annoyances though. Not every app and menu is Kinect compatible. For example when searching for a tv or movie title in Netflix the kinect offer no help in the search screen. It also requires exact phrases and words. It really needs a natural language filter that you can find from Google Now or Apples Siri. Learning the phrases Kinect seem outdated and confusing these days.

All in all the One is the definition of Next gen for me. Its no longer just about gaming, but about entertainment and new ways the interact with whats happening on screen, I'm excited about the potential the One has and very happy with its current capabilities.

This incentivized you to play and participate in the challenges in order to progress through the game.

The entire game has changed now. It is less like a campaign and more like an arcarde style game now. Basically any tournaments you enroll in doesn't reward you with a car. If there is no reward for completing races it takes away the thrill of winning the races and the incentive to get first place. I thought this was extremely stupid for them to do. You can win cars by completing mission challenges as well as license courses but it's not the same, because you can't progress in either of these areas until you beat the entire list of challenges and earn the car. It's not like everything is unlocked and if you can't beat some of the events you just skip them, the game forces you to have to beat everything which makes it not fun if you're struggling to beat a challenge.

Finally the customization aspect of the car, from mods to paint to decals is all gone now, it just doesn't feel like the gran turismo I grew up with, it just feels like you're driving around in pointless circles and it's just not fun anymore.

1. One would most definitely be noise. How noisy would the newer model be
2. Wi-Fi built in
3. Does it run cooler or faster
4. Is it really `slim' or just shorter
5. Is there a slot loading disc drive

And the digital audio port was a bonus, not having to have an adapter to get audio to my Onkyo receiver. Having only pass-thru, the port made it easier to not have to go through my HDTV which is finicky about digital out.

In the first week or so owning this model, I couldn't be happier. I got rid of my Wi-Fi adapter, my digital audio adapter and have it all in a nice sexy package.

* The cross-fade switch has only 3 settings, but has a lot of "play" in-between those settings, and the flimsiness
of the switch made moving between the 3 settings difficult sometimes
* While there are options to play with 2 DJ Hero turntable controllers (only one included), or one turntable and one
guitar controller (not included), the game play seems very single player focused.
* The controller requires you to have a surface to set it upon to use, but only the more expensive Renegade edition
comes with a stand

Overall, the product seems to cater to a very niche audience with both the style of music offered and the unique controller. I have liked the Guitar Hero and Rock Band games because they are great for parties. Everyone can participate and we can all manage to find a song or two we enjoy. This game's appeal is too narrow for my typical party group and does not seem very conducive to larger group play. If a friend and I were very much into the DJ scene I think we might be about to enjoy a little joint play, however that is not my circumstance.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a return to the excellent form that was Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory...almost. For the most part, SC: Blacklist does a good job of balancing stealthy sneaking and frenetic action.  What I find most jarring are the arcade-y aspects that play out like mini-games, but they can be overlooked easily enough. The open environments are nice, and allow for multiple approaches to achieving mission objectives. The game's story feels weak, like a generic action movie plot, but it accomplishes what it needs to. I had more fun with Splinter Cell: Blacklist than I expected to have, and it was fun to be super-spy-ninja, Sam Fisher, again. I recommend this game for anyone looking for modern stealth action, or who has fond memories of Chaos Theory.

First of all, I will state that I am not a big fan of these one-ear styles.  I get that it's so you can hear what's going on around you while playing, but it seriously messes with my immersion.  The sound quality on this is mediocre at best and I was never able to get it up loud enough to really be usable to me.  It looked nice, so I had high hopes, but unfortunately looks really seem to be all it has to offer.

This is a perfect example of a transitional game that should have only released on the latest consoles.  The amazing things that Rockst*r managed to accomplish on the previous generation with GTA5 are only emphasized when you play a game like Watchdogs which tries to occupy the same gaming niche. Watchdogs on PS3 chugs along in its unoptimized and adequate way, and tries to tell an uninspired and adequate story.  It isn't a terrible game, but compared to how it plays on current gen and PC it is a chore to slog through.  If you are particularly interested in some aspect of Watchdogs I would recommend that you play it on PS4, XBox One, or PC. If you don't own any of those platforms you shouldn't lose any sleep about giving this title a pass.

Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed games have been very hit-or-miss for me. I particularly enjoyed the recently released Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag, and perhaps because of how much I enjoyed where Black Flag took the franchise I find myself disappointed with Assassin's Creed Unity.  I'm a bit of a history buff, and I was very excited by the idea of running around in revolutionary France, but the execution of this game leaves a lot to be desired. It feels like the game design of Unity took no cues from the successes of Black Flag. Technically the game has a lot of bugs and frame-rate drops, but that could be forgiven if the story and setting were well executed. Unfortunately, the story is not great and the setting feels hollow, and that is a terrible shame because there should be innumerable interesting story threads to explore in revolutionary Paris. Unity feels like a re-skin and re-tread of what has come before. Aside from graphical improvements, I would believe that Black Flag was a sequel to Unity, and not the other way around. This isn't a terrible game, and fun can be had playing it, but I am disappointed by what Assassin's Creed Unity delivered compared to what it promised to deliver.
