When you get down to it, the ultimate barometer for a game is whether or not it’s fun. Is the game hard to put down? Is there enough content to keep you entertained for a sufficient amount of time? In all three cases, Shadowverse get a resounding YES. That’s not to say that the game is without its flaws. The biggest problem I found was the plot getting in the way of playing the card game. I’d want to get back to card battling but you have to take long breaks to let the plot continue.

One of the measurements I use for the quality of a game is whether or not I’m playing for the fun of it or playing it just to collect items and meet achievements. In Shadowverse, you get some reward regardless of whether you win or lose and there sure as heck is a huge collecting element to the game. However, for me, the game is fun just for the sake of playing. Even if there were no rewards, the card battling would still be fun. The collecting element only adds to the game. The real fun is facing off against a new opponent who wallops you. Then it’s time to adjust your deck for another round. You can just play with the premade decks, but I love to tweak.

There are eight different classes of cards as well as generic cards that can be placed in any class of deck. With a total of 600 cards in the game, that means there’s probably in the neighborhood of 60 to 70 cards per class with the rest being generic. There are 40 cards in a deck and a maximum of 3 cards of one type so there are a lot of chances for huge variations. Each of the card classes have a very strong and obvious theme that you can exploit. You start with premade decks that you can then modify. What I would do is remove all the generic cards from a deck and then over time determine which cards really didn’t work and replace them with something better.

As much as the plot can often get in the way of card battling, it is good for slowly ramping up the difficulty through the story. It also forces you to spend significant amounts of time with different deck classes, which is pretty cool. There are loads of side quests for someone like me who loves to explore as much of a game as possible. If you’re trying to get 40+ hours out of a game you should easily find it here and this is the kind of game that has endless replayability. Shadowverse has an 82 on Metacritic which to me is a low score. It might not be the slickest, most polished game on the Switch, but it makes up for that in shear fun. This is definitely one of the hardest games for me to pull myself away from.

Decades ago, I used to LOVE tactical shooters like the original Ghost Recon and Rainbow Six. Run and gun is cool and all, but I prefer the slower paced, more realistic shooters. I prefer shooters where there is a set number of enemies, and you need to strategize and think logistically. Sniper Elite has the advantage of being generations ahead of the shooters I used to enjoy, and the graphics are light years ahead. So, is this game the answer to my dreams? Yes and no.

This is a game that requires a lot of patience early on and a lot of practice. When I started the first level, I was getting frustrated as hell. I was being detected almost immediately and once I was spotted the enemies were ruthless. I may be a Sniper Elite, but the enemies could fire at a near equal distance with pinpoint accuracy. I was getting mowed down by enemies I couldn’t spot and even when I knew where an enemy was, I would get disoriented for a moment when I looked down my sniper scope which was plenty of time for the enemy to take me out. When the enemy got close, I had even more problems as I fumbled around trying to switch weapons and awkwardly target the enemy. All in all, I was dying a whole lot and thinking this game absolutely deserved it’s 79 Metacritic score.

After completing several more (long) levels I returned to the first level and found it SIGNIFICANTLY easier. Basically, I had partially overcome the somewhat significant learning curve. You need to be able to quickly read and understand the information being given to you, particularly regarding the alert levels of the enemy. You need to be able to swap between the binoculars and sniper scope quickly and increase or decrease the magnification to avoid being disoriented. When everything works, this is a fantastic shooter. Besides sniping, there are many moments of run and gun in the vein of some of the older Call of Duty and Medal of Honor games and you even get a lot of stealth elements. The further I got into the game, the more I was enjoying it.

There are definitely some issues with the game. In some cases, I can be right on top of an enemy, unloading bullets and they simply refuse to die. I guess it’s just the occasional bad luck of constantly missing every vital organ. After emptying my clip, I need to reload which gives the enemy more than enough time to dispatch me. The enemies also seem to be able to hit me at seemingly impossible angles. I figure, if I can’t see the enemy around a corner, they shouldn’t be able to see me. There is a very steep learning curve for a third person shooter and I like that. I find games that you can master in a few hours to be boring and in ES4 I feel like I am constantly improving and learning new things as I play. It took awhile but I even started using traps to kill the enemies and landmines to take out tanks.

My guess is that a lot of reviewers only scratch the surface of the game when they write their reviews which may account for the 79 Metacritic score. The truth is that the weaknesses of the game are very apparent from the get go, and the strengths of the game become more apparent the further you get into it. Some of the best games out there have serious problems because the developers reach so high. Games like Skyrim and Snowrunner have massive bugs in the games but were also incredibly fun to play. Sniper Elite’s biggest issue is the sometimes frustrating controls but I chalk that up as the price for such a complex control scheme and it does get better with practice. Overall, I really enjoyed this game and would put it among the best third person shooters I’ve ever played.

Blazblue: Central Fiction is part of my continuing quest to find a 2D fighter that can rekindle the feelings I had playing the 2D Street Fighter games back in the 90’s. Blazblue: CF was released in arcades in Japan in 2015 and got a home console release in 2016, then arriving on the Switch in 2019 so the game isn’t exactly fresh and new. This is my third attempt at enjoying a 2D fighting on the Switch following Under Night In-Birth and Blade Strangers. I wasn’t that impressed by the other two but Blazblue: CF seemed to be regarded more highly than the others, so my hopes were up a little. Is this the fighter to finally win me over? Mmmm, no.

Let me get straight to my issue with this game as well as the other 2D fighters and, quite frankly, the older Street Fighter games. When I start a new fighting game, I generally start out by button mashing and as time goes on, I start discovering certain moves that I can exploit and spam to victory. The goal is that over time I can use the tutorials to learn the subtle mechanics of the game and become a complete fighter. The intention is to get to the point where intelligently fighting is more effective than just using the same couple of basic moves over and over again. To get over that hump, you need to know the moves and master the timing until it becomes second nature and therein lies the problem.

Here is just one example of the difficulty I have. In Blazblue: CF, you can defend against a throw by pulling back on the joystick while pressing A+B+C (yes, the buttons in the tutorial are different from the actual Switch buttons). When I attempted this in tutorial, I KNEW a throw was coming and the game even gave me an additional visual cue and I STILL couldn’t pull it off. The other problem was that pushing A+B+C (X+Y+A) at the same time is rather awkward so in order to integrate this technique into the game I would need to be able to anticipate that my opponent was going to throw me, quickly get my fingers into and awkward position and nail the timing just to stop a single throw. The game would also train you in very long and complex series of button combinations and joystick sweeps that I simply could not do. I had the exact same issues with the other 2D fighters I played with.

Maybe other players are just better than I am at learning the mechanics of the game. My gaming skills aren’t bad, and I’ve mastered complex games of other genres. I could simply devote my life to this game and suppose over time would master it, but would I have fun doing it. My biggest litmus test for any game is to ask how hard it is to put down. In the case of Blazblue: CF it was very easy. In fact, I kept return to the previous game I had been playing, Sniper Elite 4. Most of the time, I was going through Blazblue: CF’s massive 40 hour story and it’s really not that riveting. There are 24 characters in this game and the story is squeezing them all in. The tutorial is ok, but nothing special and there is way too much extraneous dialogue that I end up skipping through.

I also struggled with this game a lot more than other 2D fighters and it wasn’t uncommon for me to lose in the first round, which only added to my frustration. I certainly couldn’t experiment with refining my skills if I often lose even when spamming the easiest moves. If I can only perform more elaborate moves 20% of the time or less in practice, I sure as heck can’t integrate them into my fighting repertoire. My final verdict is that fighting games just aren’t for me. I love so many different game genres, but I’ve come to the conclusion that fighting games have lost their appeal due to the fact that I simply don’t feel like they’ve evolved. I just tire of the games long before I come close to mastering them. This might be a game that appeals to true fans of 2D fighting but my boredom came on very fast.

WRC 9 is a pure racing simulator and WOW is it twitchy. The moment I started racing, the car was continuously a half second away from fishtailing and spinning out. The tiniest little error and the car would start wobbling and shaking and it was nearly impossible to straighten out unless I slow the car down significantly. What’s even more fun is that the tracks are so narrow that the margin of error is practically nil so prepare to spend a lot of time off the track and/or spinning out. The secret for me is to drive REALLY slow. I end up dead last, but I still put-up better times then when I drive the least bit aggressively. Put your blinkers on because in this racing game, it’s time to drive like granny.

I made three changes in the game to help me out. I turned on the traction control, I set the difficulty to easiest, and I changed the accelerator from ZL to right stick forward. It’s always a problem in driving games on the Switch (and previous Nintendo games) because the shoulder buttons are digital, and a gas pedal would technically be analog. The right stick forward acts as a far more realistic gas pedal and actually feels more comfortable than the ZL button. Did all these changes pull me out of last place? Nope. I did better but was still way behind the second to last place driver.

So, the question is, is this just an exceptionally challenging racer or is it a lousy port with broken mechanics. I’ve never driven in a real rally race, but I’m going to assume it isn’t like controlling an elephant on roller skates. If this is intended to be a realistic racer, I would have to say it fails miserably because the cars drive as if they have zero grip to the road. My time is WAY behind any other racer gaining me a loss of reputation and morale (stats in the game). After a short period of time, my morale was buried at the minimum so at least I didn’t have to watch it go down anymore. It is a negative fun factor. I’ve been playing racing games since Pole Position, so I have decades of experience and I’ve never played such a controller smashingly impossible racing game. I’d also say that I’ve put enough time into the game that if I haven’t moved out of last place at this point, I probably never will.

The game gets hit a lot for the graphics, but I didn’t think they were that bad. I do like racers where you not only move horizontally around a track but also vertically up a mountain and we have those kinds of races here. There is quite a bit of detail, and I don’t recall any pop up issues. The rough, desert tracks look pretty cool, but they are so damn narrow. Again, the car is such a bear to control that it is practically impossible to stay on the track and when you have rocks and slopes all around, a wreck feels inevitable. Just a teensy bit towards the edge of the track and your car will hit a rock and flip or slide off the edge.

WRC 9 has a 64 on Metacritic with a 4.8 User Score but this is on just a small number of reviews. I’ve seen low scores on other driving games including Snowrunner, which had a 75 and was one of the greatest driving games I have ever played. Gear.Club 2 received very similar scores to WRC 9, but I found the game entirely playable and quite a bit of fun. As one user wrote on Metacritic about WRC 9, the game is basically unplayable. There are nearly 800 reviews for the game on Amazon but almost all are for the Playstation which might be playable. Only two written reviews are for the Switch and of those only one put in some actual effort. This review gave the game 1 star and basically mirrored my own experience saying that the game is nigh on unplayable.

This is the worst game I’ve played on the Switch, and it’s a shame because it’s clear a lot of work went into it. It could have been an enjoyable racing game, but the gameplay absolutely botched. I would battle it out for first place in Gear.Club 2. I 100 percented many of the regions in the extremely challenging Snowrunner but I don’t believe I’ll ever complete a rally in WRC 9 where I don’t come in last place. It’s literally that impossible to play. The 64 Metacritic score is WAY too high. One reviewer gave it an 80 and claimed it was a near perfect racer. Unless this guy is freakishly talented at video games, I think he’s out of his mind. Avoid this game like the plague.

My review is going to exclusively talk about Dark Stalkers because that is the sole reason I bought this collection. I used to play the original Darkstalker, released in 1994, back in college and over the next three years a total of five Darkstalker games were released in the arcades and that was it. Although five games were released in a technical sense, the final two games were just modifications of Vampire Savior: World of Darkness. I didn’t realize when I bought this collection that two of the three most recent games were almost indistinguishable.

Darkstalkers is really fascinating. There are comics and figures and statues and animations. Even up until today, new Darkstalker collectables are still being created. There just aren’t any new games since 1997. The closest Capcom came to a new game was in 2013, but it was still just an HD version of Vampire Hunter and Vampire Savior. Given that the Darkstalker series lasted just 3 years, it’s not surprising that the graphics and the gameplay evolved very little in that short period. There were only a handful or so of new characters added in the sequel games, but the characters are so iconic that not much else was needed.

I’ve done a ton of research on Darkstalkers since buying this game and have discovered a whole new respect for the series. Darkstalkers set the standard for diverse characters. Not only are their appearances diverse but their gameplay style is radically different. Each character controls in an entirely unique manner and it goes way beyond just move set. The differences are astounding, and it really is one of the main strengths of the game. For example, if you back dash with Anakaris when he’s at the edge of the screen he will teleport to the other side of the screen. He is the only character that does that, and ALL the characters have little quirks and sometimes very large quirks. Once you establish the rules of the game, you’ll suddenly find a character that breaks a rule. I love that sort of thing. There are also a TON of game mechanics and moves that started with Darkstalkers. This is really a groundbreaking series.

I’ve played many of the highest rated fighting games on the Switch including Blazblue, Under Night and Blade Strangers and I’m continually underwhelmed. One of the big problems is that it feels as if the developers constantly strive to expand the complexity as if they are being developed exclusively for tournament level players. I find myself unable to pull off many of the simpler combos in training modes and there’s not a chance in hell I can perform some of the dozen plus button combinations that often require precise timing. Fighting games is just one genre of game I enjoy but these games feel like they’re designed only for dedicated fighting fans. Darkstalkers is FAR more accessible to the casual fighting game fan then these recent fighting games. I also find the series more forgiving than the Street Fighter games from this era.

It’s generally recognized the Darkstalkers peaked with Darkstalkers 3 and I would agree with that. Not only were the games groundbreaking for their time but they have also stood the test of time. I honestly enjoyed the Darkstalker games more than the fighting games released in the last decade. For various reasons, I haven’t played the heavy hitters like Street Fighter V, Mortal Kombat 11 or Smash Brothers but I really enjoyed Darkstalkers and I really enjoy all the lore. I ended up watching the four part Darkstalkers OVA and read the two hardcover Darkstalkers books. I had a heck of a time reliving these old games and they remain a joy to play.

This is just an initial reactions coming from someone who uses controllers a LOT but does not consider himself an expert. For example, I would have no use for storing button mappings because I’m just not that in to tailoring my control scheme. My current controller of choice is the first party Nintendo Pro Controller. I’ve always stuck with first party controllers because for Nintendo systems, they’ve always been the highest quality controllers. Thus far I’ve only used this controller for one game, Snowrunner, and it’s worked great.

The 8bitdo controller has a very similar weight to the Pro Controller and is just slightly smaller. Both controllers feel about equally solid. The buttons are laid out slightly differently with the + and – buttons more centered. It took me a little bit to get used to the buttons not being exactly where I expected but no big deal.

I was really angry when the Switch came out and wasn’t compatible with the rather expensive Wii U Pro Controllers. I now have three lovely Wii U controllers sitting in a box in my basement. You can buy a third-party dongle to make it work but it’s not particularly cheap. I’m hoping that since the 8bitdo controller isn’t technically tied to any one system that it will continue to work on whatever Nintendo’s next system is.

I’m only using this for the Nintendo Switch and there are some features that really serve no purpose for the Switch. I believe the last time Nintendo used analog shoulder buttons was on the Gamecube and analog buttons are incredibly useful for driving games. The 8bitdo has analog shoulder buttons but since the Switch doesn’t support analog they simply act as mushy digital buttons. The buttons certainly didn’t act as analog when I played Snowrunner but later I’ll try it on WRC 9 which does allow you to map the accelerator to the thumb stick to act as an analog accelerator. I suspect it wont work with the shoulder buttons regardless of whether or not they are analog. I appreciate that 8bitdo made a controller for multiple systems but for a system like the Switch a straight digital shoulder button would have been better since they don’t support analog. If my wishes get answered the next Nintendo system will support analog buttons.

There are P1 and P2 buttons that look pretty neat. They would be pressed using your middle finger but since Switch doesn’t support these buttons, they serve no purpose. (Actually, I saw a video implying that you can remap the buttons to use P1 and P2 so if you prefer their placement, it sounds like you can use them). Overall, I’d say the playing experience between the 8bitdo controller and Nintendo Pro Controller is pretty much the same. There are some differences under the hood such as how the thumbsticks are designed but I forget I’m using the 8bitdo controller because they feel so similar. I do like the idea of third party developers lighting a fire under Nintendo. Not that their controllers aren’t already fantastic but I competition can only breed more innovation.

I’m leaning more and more towards Metacritic being a near worthless resource for determining the quality of games. Wreckfest is the 8th highest rated racing game on the Switch, which puts it in the top 10 percent but the 79 rating isn’t exactly amazing. Of the realist racing games on the Switch, Wreckfest is actually number one and I’d say that it’s probably now taken its place as my favorite racing game on the system. My previous favorite was Gear.Club Unlimited 2 which has an even more unfair score of 57. My least favorite is the entirely unplayable WRC 9 with a lousy, yet still way too high 64.

Here are the things I don’t love about the game. The menuing system is pretty clumsy and unintuitive. All the cars are unlicensed, and in the garage they look like something from the N64. I couldn’t really understand how the upgrades worked. Some were free and some cost credits and I wasn’t sure if they would open up for free later if I reached a certain level. The upgrades also seemed to have nearly no effect. They might raise the acceleration a tiny amount, but no other stats appeared to be affected. The Armor will increase the durability of your car but at the expense of acceleration and cornering.

The strength of the game is the fun factor and isn’t that what’s it’s all about. It’s about racing to the finish line while battling for position and it truly is a battle. Cars will ram into each other aggressively and with realistic physics you can spin cars around or send them into the wall. These aren’t silly exaggerated physics as in Burnout. The cars also accumulate damage throughout the race so you can see how much a car is banged up. Too much damage and your car might become an undrivable wreck. You might even acquire a when you bump into another racer. The realistic physics can also work against you as you might get spun around near the end of the race, killing your placement. If you’re in a multi-race series, you can always retry individual races if you don’t like where you finished.

There are a variety of different modes on the game but the one I really love is the demolition derby. Who doesn’t love driving in an enclosed area, smashing cars as hard as possible? Even in race mode, it can be very satisfying to ram another driver. Even though the collisions are far less spectacular than in Burnout, I found them much more satisfying because they feel real, and you don’t have that stupid slowdown to accentuate the impact. There is the sound of impact, grinding metal, smashing glass and you can feel the impact. After the collision, you can see the resultant damage to each vehicle. It all feels so good.

I had a massive amount of fun with this game. The races can get absolute crazy, and I won’t deny that it can be very frustrating when the finish line is in site, and someone spins you out, but such is life when you have real world physics. The physics are slightly exaggerated but this isn’t a simulator and it’s close enough. There is a bit of a lack of cars compared to other racers and the upgrading is so miniscule as to be almost pointless. There are also not a ton of tracks, but I’m cool with that because I think it helps so that the player isn’t overwhelmed. It’s a good thing to know tracks well to being able to anticipate turns. This game isn’t just turns and straightaways, it’s also up and down and it can be a challenge knowing what turns are coming up. Overall, this is easily one of the best racers I’ve ever played and there is real joy in playing far beyond just advancing and upgrading. I highly recommend the game.

I’m old enough to have played Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles in the arcades as well as the sequel, Turtles in Time. I’d always play with a friend and have fond memories of the experience. I’ve seen multiple reviewers claim that Shredder’s Revenge is the greatest side scrolling beat ‘em up of all time. The question is whether or not side scrolling beat ‘em ups are even worth it on the home console in this day and age.

When I first played this game, it was online with a friend and someone else at the house and we had a blast. It brought back all those old feelings of nostalgia playing in the arcades. It’s definitely an advancement over the arcade version in terms of graphics but still has a very retro feel and it’s not pushing the capabilities of the Switch. After awhile I asked my buddy over the phone how many levels there were and he told me 16. That is a LONG game for a beat ‘em up and I was starting to get tired. Finally, we finished off Shredder and the closing credits ran. At this point I’m faced with the same problem I have with other beat ‘em ups. Now what?

In the 80’s and 90’s, beat ‘em ups were ubiquitous because they were basically cutting edge. We would simply play the same levels over and over again. My friend and I played Story mode a few days later but it’s 90% the same as Arcade mode. I unlocked Casey Jones and that was pretty much it. It’s basically the same feeling I had with Streets of Rage 4 although SoR4 had more unlockables. I’ve put about 2 or 3 hours into Shredder’s Revenge, and I really don’t have a burning desire to jump into it again. There are tons of achievements, but I really don’t like playing for achievements rather than the sheer fun of playing.

I think I have to just face facts that what I loved when I was younger just doesn’t really appeal to me anymore. It’s the same with Shoot ‘em up games. I used to play them all the time when I was a kid and might still toss in a quarter or two at the arcade, but they are extremely shallow for a home experience. They are fun for maybe one or two run throughs but then you’ve seen pretty much everything. There are many games on the Switch that I’ve put 40 or more hours into as compared to a few hours on a Beat ‘em up or Shoot ‘em up.

I think Shredder’s Revenge would have been better if there were a handful of unlockable characters rather than one and maybe some branching in the arcade mode. I might literally avoid playing arcade mode because I don’t feel like slogging through 16 levels in one sitting with a friend. If the game had branching, it could have the same levels or more but not be so long on a single playthrough. The gameplay was fine but nothing spectacular. I wouldn’t put it above SoR4 or a game like Fight ‘N Rage. I figure this game will get set aside and every once in a while I may pop it in and play a little bit with a friend online. Not sure if that was worth $35 for me.

However, it is just so fun running around a 1920's post-apocalyptic setting trying to find out what the heck is happening. The graphics are pretty good for its generation and they definitely mix things up constantly, so it always feels like you are progressing into new territory.

These are fantastic games - I've been hooked since I received them about a month ago and haven't stopped playing! The storyline and universe are intriguing, and the gameplay and graphics improve over time (I'm currently in ME2). If you enjoy choose-your-own-adventure stories with consequences, space, and shooters, this game is definitely for you!

This game completely grabbed my attention a couple years ago, so much so that I bought my PS4. The graphics are incredible and unique, the gameplay is straightforward, but challenging, and the story is dystopian, but original and thought-provoking. I'd give it more stars if possible!

This game will make you think and engage you on a different level than most games can achieve. The gameplay makes you use every part of the controller and make split-second decisions that will affect the lives of your characters in profound ways. I would give this game 3.5 stars (if you're a guy...probably add another star...). If you enjoy RPGs in general, Qoga will definitely suck you in after playing for a couple hours. If you have ever played a PC Japanese dating sim (I mean strictly dating sim game..not RPG), you will know what to expect as far as the interaction between the characters. (Boy sticks by girl to the ends of the earth, girl is very wimpy and fragile, etc). This is not A+ quality storytelling or dialogue. But if you like being able to make decisions and see different outcomes, Ar Tonelico Qoga will deliver.

Oh yeah, one other thing that irritated me...your AI controlled party members are not always bright. They can die often by standing in one spot taking damage instead of properly guarding themselves. They will also push enemies that are nearby your Reyvateil further into her circle....quickly killing her... I played this tonight after I received the game in the mail. Overall it is very addicting to see the storyline progress and I like the way you can affect the outcomes. There are supposedly 8 endings. But if you go for the different endings and two different girls, you will obviously have a lot of replay value. Catherine has many funny moments and everyone can relate to the relationship issues in here. The puzzles are CHALLENGING which is what I like. There were times when I was very frustrated screaming at the TV, and a few had me redoing them for over half an hour because I couldn't solve them correctly. People who get frustrated easily will probably not enjoy this game. The stages actually require you to think and use your brain. I wish there were more games like this. If you get stuck, it's better to just restart from the checkpoint or do something differently because there aren't infinite ways to solve each puzzle. You're either doing it right or wrong. Bottom line Catherine is UNIQUE and one of the best PS3 games I've played in a while. I rarely buy a full price game freshly released but this was definitely worth my money.

I don't know what this game is like for the other two platforms, but on Xbox, it's a tad confusing. The game gets away with this by giving you control of three characters at once and dividing the characters up into four different teams--Team Sonic, Team Dark, Team Rose, and Team Chaotix. Each team member has his or her own strengths, and your abilities as a team change depending on which character you have set as the team leader. The inclusion of the four different teams, however, seems a bit pointless since the game is virtually identical for all four of the teams, save for some different story elements in between levels. To be blunt, no one cares about these peripheral characters that Sonic Team seems hell-bent on pushing on gamers. People play Sonic games to play as Sonic the Hedgehog.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from a problematic, finicky camera, occasionally spastic controls, and some bad clipping. The level designs are pretty straightforward, though you'll occasionally find portions that aren't entirely intuitive. Moreover, it's likely that you'll find yourself plummeting into a bottomless nothing without any idea of what you did wrong more than once. This is a rental, for sure.

Sometimes I can play a game for hours and not even notice if it's repetitive or not. Grabbed By The Ghoulies was one of those games that I just couldn't get into. It's a haunted mansion romp that looks and sounds really impressive, but it's ultimately marred by repetitive, overly simple punch-and-kick gameplay that's compounded by the game's lack of length.
The gameplay in Grabbed by the Ghoulies is deliberately simple. The left stick moves Cooper, and the right stick controls Cooper's attacks.. fairly simple. While Grabbed by the Ghoulies may present itself quite well, the dull gameplay that hides behind the great graphics and sound really hurts the experience. The game's short length makes it perfect for rental, as most anyone should be able to blaze through the game and see many of its unlockable items within a day or two.

Being a huge fan of XSN Golf for Xbox, I decided to try Tiger Woods' game because of all the rave reviews I've heard. I was so disappointed. The controls are rather difficult and hard to master. Tiger Woods PGA Tour 2004 is not that much different from last year's Tiger. The analog swing is unchanged, letting you control the power and direction of your shot with a back-and-forward motion on the analog stick.
One of the big new additions to Tiger Woods 2004 is the "game face" feature that allows you to create your own pro golfer with a rather painstaking level of detail. This player creation mode lets you define virtually every aspect of your player's appearance. For some idea as to how extensive it is, there are 18 different attributes that can be modified in terms of facial structure alone, not including facial hair, eye color, skin tone, and what your golfer's teeth might look like. Truly, the level of character customization offered by the game face feature is unparalleled.
The only nagging issue with the Tiger Woods games that EA has yet to address seriously is the game's soundtrack. For the past two years, EA has been assembling seemingly random collections of contemporary licensed songs and calling them soundtracks.

Unlike many game sequels, this one has improved. The only thing that really hasn't changed are the graphics. In this edition, you get a ton of new weapons and you can upgrade them at certain vendors. You even get to upgrade your ship by adding on shields, guns and other mods. What makes this game fun is that there are several mini games within the main game.

For example, you must win a Hoverboard race before you're given a map for the next planet. I think this will be frustrating to many gamers and may cause some to pass on the game entirely. It was frustrating to me because this wasn't a requirement in the previous game.

Overall, I'd recommend picking up this game. It's a fun, relaxed game that you don't need to take seriously.

Katamari Damacy is far and away one of the strangest, most original games to come along in years. The gameplay concept, the visual style, the soundtrack, even the backstory are all conceived and executed with such a unique flavor that, when presented as a whole, it's difficult not to be drawn in by all the weird little idiosyncrasies. It's not a complex game, nor is it especially challenging, or long.

Using the analog sticks exclusively, you'll roll the katamari around with tanklike controls. Pushing both sticks up moves the katamari forward, pushing both sticks down moves it backward, and pushing one stick up and one stick down will cause it to turn. There are a few other tricks, such as moving both sticks up and down really fast to gain a quick boost, or pushing in on both sticks to hop on the other side of the katamari and quickly change directions--but this is basically all you'll need to know in order to control it. However, controlling it well is a more nuanced thing. The shapes of the things you collect will affect the overall shape of your katamari, thus affecting how it actually rolls. So, if you roll over a bunch of pencils or a ladder or some carrots, it can make your going a bit more challenging.

What started as a quirky, interesting use of Mario and all his iconic friends on the N64 has turned into an annual bash, which is now in its sixth year. On the surface, Mario Party 6 seems to offer some of the biggest fundamental changes the series has ever seen. But this is really just a fresh coat of paint on an old building. As always, Mario Party 6 is modeled after a board game, of sorts. Much of the other changes that Mario Party 6 makes to the Mario Party formula are largely superficial.

Whether you've worn out your last copy of Mario Party or are just looking for a light, accessible multiplayer experience, number six is a fine pick. Alternately, if you have yet to be charmed by previous Mario Party games, this one isn't likely to change your opinion of the series.

Forza Motorsport is a stylish and challenging game that is easily one of the best racers on the Xbox, if not the best. There are more than 230 cars from 60 manufacturers and a track list that, if not extensive, at least features a nice mix of tight street courses, real race tracks from all over the world, and challenging fictional environments. If you don't have the slightest clue about entry points into turns or when to step on the brakes, Forza has a handy "suggested line" feature that is one of the slickest innovations in racing games to come along in a long time.

Forza places a huge emphasis on every car's individuality through features such as the rarity rating and powerful customization tools, which let you paint your car and/or add a massive number of vinyls and decals, creating, with a little patience, a car that will be unique and unlike any others. That individuality can be further celebrated by pitting your car against other players' cars online. The fun doesn't stop there, however, as Forza also lets you buy and sell cars in online trading sessions with friends and strangers alike. By setting up a "buy and sell" session, you can browse the collections of up to eight other players who agree to enter the lobby with you.

Forza may well be remembered as a title that, through its mix of challenge and control, introduced an entirely new set of fans to the beauty and power of driving games.

We Love Katamari unapologetically revels in its own extraneousness. The setup for this latest session of clump-rolling is that the people of Earth had become downright obsessed with the enigmatic King and his katamaris. Eagerly, they show their affection for King and katamari by making all sorts of requests for demonstrations of the katamari's power, and by generally feeding the King's ego with many, many compliments. The King, being ever the crowd-pleaser, is always happy to oblige the affectionate earthlings, and so he puts the Prince (and this time, his many, many cousins) to work, demanding even bigger and more exciting katamaris than ever before.

We Love Katamari is basically just a big, happy love letter to the fans that contributed to the first game's success. Namco clearly had no intention of mucking up a winning formula, and as such, it has created a sequel that delivers more of the same fetchingly enjoyable gameplay and whimsical humor that made Katamari Damacy so much fun. Undeniably, We Love Katamari lacks the consummate originality of the first game, but for most, the lack of originality won't be a hindrance. And anybody who played and enjoyed Katamari Damacy will feel right at home with the sequel.
