The biggest knock here is that you MUST be online to play it. I don't completely understand why a single player campaign requires online play, but there you go. That means that if the Ubisoft servers are down, the disc is useless... likewise, in a few years, if the servers aren't around, this disc will be useless.

As others have mentioned, the online multiplayer is fun, but there is no effort to match similarly leveled characters. So expect to be in deathmatch with someone who will kill you in two or three blows, over and over again. I suspect this will push people away from deathmatch, which will in turn make the environment not so robust, consisting of the same 'regulars' rather than bot experienced and casual players. That seems a shame.

That said, the single player campaign is fun. The combat system here is good, as other have described. You have three sectors to both block and atack - top, right and left. The right thumbstick in conjunction with L1 determine which sector you are focusing on. Before an enemy strikes, there is a red flash showing which sector they are attacking, allowing you to block if you are quick enough. On top of that, each faction has a small roster of special attacks and moves of which any two can be equipped to be used only once, or once between slow recharges. For example, you might be able to land blows through another fighter's defense. You might throw a smoke bomb to cloud their vision, etc. It adds nice variety to the combat system. Still, that's about it - so if you want to fight and block with swords while managing special attacks, this title would work for you. I felt that the system was robust enough for an afternoon, but it didn't really hook me. The single player campaign is over in a few afternoons, and after that you are back to the online component, thrown into a match with a potentially much higher level opponent. So I could see this getting old in a few weeks. Still in all, the single player was fun and modestly challenging (on normal difficulty) despite being so relatively short.

Bear in mind that online is absolutely required. I wonder why this would be, and certainly hope it does not point to a future trend in console gaming. Online play is a lot of fun, but make it a choice of the individual player. We don't want to be dependent on your servers after buying a physical disc.

While this game is good, I am not so crazy about so much of it requiring an online component. I am also not a fan of in game purchases, especially not after buying the full version of a game application. It feels a little 'cheap', pardon the pun.

The main single player campaign is fun, but not something that will draw you back over and over again - you run several fairly short, tactical style missions to save a hostage, disarm a bomb, kill terrorists, etc. None of these are very large maps, instead relying on the tactical aspect to make them interesting. They are fun, but honestly, after a half hour or so, they get a little tiring... there is no story mode, your character does not progress or gain any new abilities (each mission features a different character, actually), and the environments do not change to a significant degree. Warehouse, office building, airplane - you get the picture. While there is certainly appeal to playing a game for just a short while, I'm not sure it is worth the price.

The online component is a little more interesting. I prefer terrorist attack, in which you and a squad of online players rescue a hostage from a clutch of AI terrorists. I like it because it's really co-op; nobody can wait for you to snipe you, for example - all of the players are working together towards a common goal. This is fun, but again, each mission is very short, and don't seem all that worth replaying once finished.

Squad combat occurs with different unlockable characters. Some specialize in offense and others in defence - but to be honest, I didn't care so much that I wanted to play enough or spend the money to unlock them all.

Fundamentally, these online components require the Rainbow Siege servers to be up. Which is great for the time being, but say five or six years in the future, will this still be playable? I feel like games that require online servers have built in obsolescence written all over them.

As harsh as all this was, the game is fun, especially in short bursts. The design is tight, and the tactics are engaging. For now, the online component is good too. It's just that none of it seems engaging enough to bring a player back for any significant amount of time. I'd say wait for this to come down in price, and be sure you have Playstation Plus to get the most out of it.

This is a surprisingly fun game - while it is not particularly original in either gameplay or design, what it does it does well - namely, operating a special forces team taking out drug cartel members and giving a sense that anything could go wrong in an instant.

The mechanics are pretty simple. You can walk or commandeer a vehicle - trucks, cars, helicopters, and you go to locations marked on your map (think Far Cry 3 or 4) to complete a story mission, acquire new gear or loot, or question a local for more info. There are also 'protect the flag' missions, recon missions, and full on attack missions.

Because it's an open world, you can set up strategies for attack. What makes the game fun is that very often, after planning an attack and taking time to get everything in position, after starting things go way off the rails, turning a plan into a seat of the pants slugfest that truly feels uncontrollable and highly chaotic.

All in all, recommended, especially if your are partial to open world games. If you take your time with this, it will take you a long, long time to finish. Of course, if you jump straight to story missions it will go by more quickly, but still last for at least 40 hours or so.

There are a few nitpicks - locals don't notice a truck full of camo-wearing American soldiers, there are few spotty controls (until you get used to them), the aerial vehicles do not control very well, and in the beginning some of the situations can get overwhelming before snuffing your life out pretty quickly. Still, with the excellent team member AI and ability to plan assaults on grimy drug gangs, the good far outweighs the questionable.

... I think you'll like this game as well.

I am very impressed with what was done with the franchise in this title. Basically, you have an open world with missions on the map that can be done in any order (although some will advance the story), or you can travel and look for people or missions to interact with independently. There are also boat battles and nautical missions, allowing great flexibility for the player. Think Witcher 3 without magic spells, and adding boats.

I have seen criticism for microtransactions; they are available through a nested window, but are not at all necessary if you are willing to play the game and grind a bit. I mention the menu microtransactions because if you don't open that menu, you wouldn't know they are available - no unaccessible rooms or chests without a fee, for example. No lootboxes, either. You can play the game completely without any of them - they are simply for folks who do not want to grind or optimise their character (although if you play a game like this, why anyone would want to shortcut the process is honestly beyond me).

There is a bit of grinding. And traversing the world can take some time - still, that doesn't bother me at all. I play open world games for the experience, so time spent exploring or discovering side missions is a good thing.

There is also a Far Cry mechanic here which includes taking down settlements and forts. If you enjoy going up against a small army with a combination of stealth and force, this game has it in spades. The flexibility to approach these is wide open, and subject to the player's creativity. I loved playing one area where I would hide on a cliff, and when the chiefs of the fort I was sieging followed me, I would kick them off and kill them instantly - I still smile remembering that (hearing their screams as they fell to their death). Also, these missions scale as your character levels up, so you will never be able to plow through them. This keeps the game fun.

There is also a mercenary mechanic ala [[ASIN:B00WOK8YX4 Shadow of Mordor]] where you will be hunted across the world depending on your actions and be confronted by specially skilled soldiers or have to hunt down whoever placed the bounty. Awesome!

This is a very detailed world with many layers of gameplay. You can choose to be good or evil, and develop your character skills across several lines - combat or stealth, for example. Each skill you choose as you level up will also make a difference to gameplay, showing how carefully this was developed. Quick tip: Get the Spartan Kick skill first, as it will make a big difference as you play, as well making you smile every time you kick someone off a high tower.

Also, decisions you make will change the game going forward , and change it beyond dialogue choices. It great to see this, as it bodes well for replayability.

Highly recommended if you like open world RPG games with real time combat elements. You're going to spend a long time here, and it will not get boring.

I did enjoy For Honor, as it has a deep combat system that is surprisingly robust. This title does have a few flaws, however, which keep it from being a must-buy. It requires an internet connection, along with an active Ubisoft account. That gives it a shelf life - there might be a time the Ubisoft servers are out or down, and this game will no longer run. That remains true even for the single player campaign, which makes no sense to me. Why should a connection to be required when playing a single player, non networked game?

This brings me to the second knock: microtransactions. Here we go again - if you play this online (fighting other people), unless you pay to unlock highly powered weapons and overprotective armor, you will be killed again and again and again. Why pay for a full version of anything if you then must shell out to get a playable experience? This sort of predatory software has to stop. Chicken and egg, I suppose, since so many people seem to pay for upgrades. Can't we all make this money grabbing behavior stop once and for all?

Back to the game itself, this upgrade brings Breach mode as well as four new characters to the game. All must be downloaded via an included code and are not on the base game disc, so what you are getting here is the regular version with a download code. There is a claim that textures have been enhanced, but I could not see much of a difference between Marching Fire and the standard edition (I am not playing on a 4K screen, to be fair). There is no update to the single player campaign. With four new characters I thought we might get four new solo adventures, but no go. If you have the original For Honor and are enjoyed the single player campaign, you get the exact same one here. Too bad this was not updated.

All that aside, the combat system is very well designed. If you are new to the series, this is the one to get. If you have the original For Honor and want Marching Fire, best to purchase the upgrade as a download and not rebuy this.

This is a good headset for the price, but it is sized very small, and it is very basic. There is no mute function on the microphone - according to the manual, to mute the mic you just push it up, away from your mouth. There is a volume knob on the side of the headphone, but it doesn't get very loud, and again, there is no mute for it should that be a requirement.

That said, it is plug and play, it does work as it should, and it reasonably priced. If you are an adult, though, think twice about this as it might be uncomfortable after a few minutes due to it being hard plastic and sized small.

Everybody knows that movie/game tie-ins don't have a good reputation, but this year I was surprised and delighted by offerings like Green Lantern: Rise of the Manhunters (which, in my opinion, looks great and plays fun, albeit repetitive, and actually ended up being one of my favorite games so far in 2011), and the reviews of Captain America: Super Soldier have been generally good that I decided to purchase it in hopes it might delight me in the way Rise of the Manhunters did. In some ways it did, in others it didn't.

First off, I wasn't as initially interested in this game because, quite honestly, I only ever heard things here and there about Captain America and had little interest in his character, whereas I am a major Green Lantern fan. The game looks great, but on my plasma it lacked the polish and flash Manhunters had. Captain moves awkwardly and very clunky (he can't really run and he climbs ladders so slow it's almost laughable), and the camera angles have the similar annoyance factor that I found in Batman (which, while a huge Batman fan, is a game that didn't really appeal to me due to the camera angles and gave me headaches).

Super Soldier kicks off right off the bat on the war front and takes off (literally) when you jump from a plane and land in a vast castle in Nazi Germany where the enemy has taken hold. Like last year's amazing Prince of Persia: Forgotten Sands title, this game takes place in just one location, ie. this castle. I love the slow motion takedowns (reminiscent of the aforementioned Batman), but found that Captain's punching abilities lacked fluidity and seemed clunky, at times even robotic. Using his infamous shield is a lot of fun because it can take down so many at once, which actually turned into my main way to take down enemy. Platforming also plays an important role in this game, and it can be quite fun to loop-dee-loop around beams a la Persia's Prince or Uncharted's Nathan Drake, but it too lacks the same level of satisfaction or grace; the screaming "Leap!" can get tiresome too as it appears, due to awkward camera angles, that it's there in order avoid missing a leap around a corner.

Overall, Captain America: Super Soldier is one of those games that defies the stereotypical "bad movie-game tie-in", just like Green Lantern: Rise of the Manhunters (which, in my opinion, was better). It's fun simply for fun's sake. It's not going to be winning any awards, but it's definitely one of the best Marvel movie-game tie-ins to date.

Halo is a classic in the gaming industry. Like Gone With the Wind is to movies. Classics, whatever they may be, are basically essential goods that have influenced their respective realms and have achieved iconic status. But the problem with classics is that despite the acclaim and general reverence they eventually show their age, pretty badily too.

Take Gone With the Wind again: The acting is relatively bad in most parts and compared to modern day it's almost pathetic. Halo, which is one of my all-time favorite series, has a similar problem. Graphically, it's gotten a MAJOR overall (it's not the extra pixels that most HD collections get, ie. Ico & Shadows of the Colossus - it's completely redesigned) thanks to 343 Industries, and it's definitely cool to switch to what the game originally looked like (if not to see how far we've come graphically in a decade but also for nostalgic reasons), but the game play is archaic (at least to me...) in comparison to the fluidity of the modern day. That said, the graphics are great, but nothing close to, say, the recently released Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception - 343 definitely impresses with their prowess in this department, but it doesn't jump off the screen and amazes you (overall, I found the graphics pleasant, but perhaps expected more from all I saw and heard about in trailers); still, it's by far the best HD reworking of any dated game to date and 343 deserves a pat on the back.

Halo Anniversary is a great title to pick up for many reasons. The new graphics are amazing, as is the ability to go from the original to the flashy new skin. I encountered a few glitchy spots, and the character faces are almost unrecognizable in their new form, but the pros far, far, FAR outweigh the cons. Halo: Combat Evolved was never my favorite Halo game (Halo 2 warrants that due to its great story line, excluding the cliffhanger ending), but Microsoft gives us a true Christmas treat here.

I love gaming, but I never really got into the whole Call of Duty franchise. I prefer series in the vein of God of War, Halo or Uncharted, games that are more action and adventure based than shoot-'em-uppers. But the hype -and trailers- surrounding CODMW3's release had me eager to try my hand at launch, and I finally gave in. Consensus? I'm glad I did.

I was instantly impressed with the controls, game play and the graphics. I've read some reviews that say the graphics aren't superb, but compared to a lot of the games that came out this year they're pretty realistic in my opinion. They have a more "real" quality, unlike Uncharted 3, a game I love but that has a glossy, computer animated movie-like quality, whereas this game is going more for succinct in its attempt to appear as if in real life. MW3 impressed me particularly with its intensity to feel, again, "real," and it really gives you the feeling you're in a real war (as close as a game has in my experience). Ok, so facial animations are a bit hokey, and definitely not the best out there, but character movement is really what makes this game feel so genuine in my opinion. Running and taking cover is brilliant, and enemy AI is particularly strong (as is the comrade AI-they actually take out quite a few themselves, something that can't be said for many shooters out there).

So what's disappointing? To me, it was the confusion in shooting enemies. Not the shooting part itself, that's been made quite easy with the help of targeting, but sometimes it feels like you just run in and shoot anything that moves, which resulted in me shooting a few of my fellow comrades and having to restart at the last checkpoint since the game doesn't allow that; yes, I can tell who's on my team when the name appears on top, but that -at least in my case- didn't happen a couple times, hence some of my comrades went down in a blaze of my glory. Not a big deal, of course, but I think that could have been improved. Don't hate me-remember, this is my first COD experience!

Overall, CODMW3 is a great, highly enjoyable and very intense first person shooter. The game definitely deserves its sales because it impresses on many levels, and rarely disappoints.

I should start off this review by saying Gears 3 is my first Gears title and, after completing it, it most definitely won't be my last.  I also should add I'm a huge sci-fi shooter fan (since the Halo days, or at least the beginning of Halo days since Halo 4 is right around the corner), so Gears of War 3 is right down my alley, and yet I didn't leave the game after I beat it with the same sense of awe and wonder I felt after Halo 1-3.  Gears 3 is certainly good, one of the best looking games on the Xbox 360 and the ending boss and cutscene really cemented my appreciation for this title, but the gameplay and controls felt clunky, almost as if they were themselves grinding away and heavily burdened like the characters' suits.  The charging/run feature was odd to me, since you hunker down in a crouch and the screen becomes slightly warped - and there doesn't seem to be an exact direction except in a very general sense when you try to run one way or the other.  The voice acting is atrocious most of the time, save for the always amazing Claudia Black (who has a somewhat limited role in comparison to that of her Chloe counterpart in Uncharted 2).  The story itself is equally typical save-the-world-from-infestation schlock and unique, and -as I previously mentioned- the ending left me with appreciation, but, again, not in the same way other sci-fi shooters have (under-appreciated Lost Planet 2, one of my faves of 2010, included).  Overall, I recommend picking up a copy of Gears of War 3 as obviously it's a good game that diehard Gears fans love, but for a newbie like me perhaps a Gears 4 will merit whether I love it or leave it.

First off, since its release last spring, Journey is and has been, by far, the best game I've played all year (I highly doubt Halo 4 will be able to change my mind about that).  In fact, it's one of the Top 3 gaming experiences IN MY LIFE.  It is, in short, an amazing achievement in gaming and art in general, a moving experience that lives on well past this relatively short game has been completed.  Its simplicity and haunting sense of loneliness is something that is incomparable nowadays.  This IS what gaming should be about.  Don't get me wrong, I love series like God of War, Uncharted and Halo, but Journey stands all on its own.  thatgamecompany's two other jewels (Flower and Flow) are equally mesmerizing and unique, albeit nothing quite grabs at the heartstrings like Journey.  Overall, if you didn't get the game on the Playstation Network, THIS IS A MUST.

So first thing's first - Asura's Wrath isn't exactly the traditional video game, but that doesn't stop it from being a walloping good time.  I personally LOVED the game, from start to finish, and the little mini-games (after getting a hang of them - the publishers shouldn't have blended everything in so well because, at times, it's hard to see what you're supposed to press at that exact moment).  The cutscenes were gorgeous and provided an entertaining, albeit over-the-top performance that I'd expected from an anime style title.  The action is terrific, but some aspects - particularly playing as Yasha - got to be a bit tiresome after a few levels simply because Yasha lacks the power that Asura possesses, so it was more dodge-hit-dodge than pummel.  Overall, I highly recommend Asura's Wrath to anyone interested in a game that's chock full of action and who enjoy plenty of storytelling cutscenes like myself.

I've been a longtime fan of Halo (Halo 2 being my favorite of the trilogy, until now).  Needless to say, after seeing the announcement of Halo 4 at E3 2011 and helping put on an event during E3 2012 for Halo 4, I was more than a little excited to say the least for the game.  That, and nervous as many Halo fanatics were after Bungie left Microsoft to pursue other ventures and 343 Industries took over.  Is Halo 4 a dud?  Certainly not.  In actuality, it's one of the best games in the series (again, the story line of Halo 2 is so nostalgic it's hard to surpass), if not the best thus far.  Graphics are terrific, the voice acting is the best of any of the series thus far (Cortana shows emotion this time around, something she lacked in my opinion except for sounding ever much like a "sidekick") and the story delves into the emotional side of Master Chief and Cortana.  Did I get a little teary eyed at the end?  Oh yeah, and I'm not afraid to admit it.  Halo 4 possesses everything that made Halo, well, Halo in the first place, but 343 took it and ran with it even further, becoming much more serious and dark in nature.  In the end, it's arguably the best game in the Halo series and promises much for the future.  In two words: GET IT.

The new Tomb Raider is a gem.  No, seriously.  Being a longtime God of War fan, Ascension was more important for me to start playing than this (even though I was hyped up about both), but Tomb Raider's effortless controls, intriguing story line, terrific voice acting and perfect combination of action-adventure and horror elements sucked me in and I found myself coming back to Lara Croft over Kratos more and more.  That's not to say this game is perfect, as I found it frustrating sometimes to which direction or what needed to be done next, but nearly everything other element - gameplay, controls, story, etc. - were, to me, near flawless.  People have been comparing this latest Tomb Raider to Uncharted and, yes, in many ways there are similarities, but that could've been said about Uncharted back in the day when it was a newbie and Lara Croft had been a name renowned in the video game industry almost a decade prior.  The survival aspects of this game really hooked me, although I died more than I'd like to admit sometimes when a sudden QTE happened that required an immediate button to survive (partly my fault, I'll admit).  There were moments galore when I was completely immersed in Lara's story and situation and where I found myself with my jaw on the floor or audibly saying exclamations of some sort (or, more frequently, cussing up a storm).  Overall, longtime fans and new fans have a lot to love with Tomb Raider 2013 and I highly recommend it to all gamers.

This bundle is one of the best one's I've purchased for the Wii- this bundle includes The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword, gold Wii Remote Plus, and an audio CD with Zelda music. Since I've already reviewed the game itself (which is wonderful, see my Skyward Sword review for more details), I'll just concentrate on the other items. The gold Wii Remote Plus works exactly the same as other Wii Remote Plus devices, so the function remains the same. The only difference is the color and the Hylian crest logo on the remote, it also includes a white Wii Remote jacket. The audio CD is great too- it includes music from the Zelda Symphony Orchestra, doing full-blown orchestral renditions of well-known Zelda theme songs from previous games like Ocarina of Time and The Wind Waker. This entire bundle comes in a gold box with Skyward Sword art on the front and back, it looks great displayed on a bookshelf. Overall, I would highly recommend this bundle if you can still get your hands on it!

I was pleasantly surprised by Pokemon White Version 2. I was expecting the game to be more of an expansion game to Pokemon White, instead of a full-blown, full-content Pokemon game. The game plays out extremely well, with a few added graphics enhancements to Pokemon White. The number of Pokemon is overwhelming in the game, as well as the number of areas and cities to explore. The story line is also cool, it picks up 2 years after the events of Pokemon White, so you get to see a lot of the old characters return. I could go on about every detail in this game, but suffice it to say that all features in this game work extremely well and are really fun to play. I would recommend this game to any fan of the Pokemon franchise!

Halo 4 is a great installment in the Halo franchise. The campaign is great and challenging, and the multiplayer is even better. The multiplayer environment has its bugs (as to be expected from such a big game) like dropping or freezing during a match, but it isn't frequent enough that it is a huge deal. My favorite feature by far is the Spartan Ops feature. This feature runs you through additional gameplay and storylines while set in the multiplayer environment, i.e. respawning after a time limit and allowing you to change your load outs after deaths. The best part is that you can increase or decrease the difficulty level, all while gaining XP points to add to your multiplayer profile. Overall, I'd say this would be one of my favorite Halo games for Xbox 360, I would recommend this to anybody.

I purchased this silicone jacket after doing a lot of research on Gamepad cases--this is the best one I've found by far! The silicone is a few millimeters thick, and allows access to every button and port on the Gamepad. The most important feature I was looking for was an open port at the bottom to allow docking in the charging dock; this jacket was one of the few that actually has this feature! The Gamepad fits perfectly in the dock with this jacket on. This jacket is well made by PDP--there is only one little section of silicone at the top that doesn't fit flush against the Gamepad, but it isn't a problem. I would recommend this to anyone looking for simple protection for the Gamepad; it's well made and is at a great price on Amazon!

This Wii U Precision Screen Filter is great, it fits my Wii U Gamepad perfectly and was a breeze to install. The video on this product's page does a better job showing the installation than the included paper instructions. Once installed there were no air bubbles, and my finger and stylus respond to everything on screen just as if it wasn't there. I would recommend this to anyone looking for a screen protector for their Wii U Gamepad.

UbiSoft has yet again released a killer (no pun intended) Assassin's Creed game for the franchise. This game has a cool storyline, excellent controls, beautiful graphics, and an awesome open world. This is the first Assassin's Creed game where I feel like the game is a true open world--as the protagonist Edward Kenway you can completely stop playing the main story and pillage and plunder the Caribbean at your will. The game map is massive, with plenty of side quests and hidden secrets to keep you entertained for hours. The story feels short, but was most likely intentional to allow the player room to explore the map at their own will. I would highly recommend this game, even if you aren't acquainted with previous games in the series, I give this game 5 stars!

Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary is a great throwback to the first Halo game for the original Xbox. This game is an updated, high-definition version of that very game; all game elements, story, and levels remain unchanged, but graphics and music have been remastered. The updated graphics and new, orchestral music are awesome to experience, especially if you owned and played the original Halo like I did. The game even features a function to change the gameplay to the old graphics and music while in game (just press the Back button). The multiplayer in the game is fun as well, although it is not as heavily trafficked as newer titles like Halo 4. If you played the original Halo on the original Xbox, this game is a must-have. Even if you haven't played the original, it is still a great installment in the Halo game franchise.

This Xbox Live 12 month subscription card worked perfectly as described--it extends your Xbox Live Gold membership by 12 months. I chose to have the physical card shipped to me (as opposed to ordering a digital code), it shipped fast and worked as soon as I entered the scratch-off code on the back. I would recommend this to anyone looking to extend their Live membership.

Anyone looking to start a Nintendo Entertainment System collection is going to want this game. The Donkey Kong Classics NES cartridge has both Donkey Kong AND Donkey Kong Jr, so only hardcore collectors are going to want to get the more expensive black box Donkey Kong cartridge and the black box Donkey Kong Jr cartridge.

Donkey Kong and Donkey Kong Jr hardly need any in-depth description, they are both two of the most popular video games of all time. I find Donkey Kong to be the tougher of the two games, but after a few boards Donkey Kong Jr is also extremely difficult. Both games, even after all these years, are still extremely addictive, challenging, and extraordinarily fun to play.

Both games ported over very well to the NES from their arcade counter parts. Visuals, sound, and control are all satisfactory. There are only a couple of minor complaints. Like many old NES games, your high score is erased as soon as you reset or shut off the game, so it is incumbent on the player to catalog high scores themselves. Also, just like the black box NES cartridge of Donkey Kong, the game is still missing the "cement factory" (or "pie factory") stage. This is a problem that really should have been rectified with the Donkey Kong Classics version. It would have been really great if Donkey Kong III had been included on the cartridge. Also, there's no Donkey Kong Jr Math on the cartridge, but that game is unimportant to the Donkey Kong series anyway.

Aside from these minor complaints, this is still a fantastic cartridge with two great video games. As I get older, I find myself more satisfied with classic video games like Ms. Pac Man and the Donkey Kong games due to their simplicity, and I am less interested with investing large chunks of time into games that meant to be more immersive.

Donkey Kong Classics is very much an essential cartridge for any NES gamer or collector. The price range is in the middle of $10-$20. At $14, this cartridge is an outright steal.

Ecco the Dolphin has some pretty unique elements. While most retrogamers are more familiar with the Sega Genesis version, the video game was released on a few other systems. Truthfully, the Sega Genesis version is very much inferior to the Sega CD version. On the Sega Genesis, the music and the visuals are a bit grainy and uninteresting. On the Sega CD though, Ecco the Dolphin's music is extraordinary and the colors very nice and bright.

The video game itself is a very difficult labyrinth. The controls will take some getting used, and some of the mechanics required to solve labyrinths are very unintuitive, such as how to use the "star-rings". There are over 25 levels with a few variations in design, such as Atlantis, Icy waters, etc. The levels themselves are quite lengthy and difficult to navigate, and only a gamer committed to finishing the game will progress. Thankfully, there is a password system as well as unlimited lives, so the challenge is reasonable.

The labyrinth aspect is done pretty well, and the uniqueness of the game is held in high regard by retrogamers. The biggest complaint about the game is that many gamers will get frustrated and bored. It's just not a game with universal appeal despite being a fairly interesting video game experience.

The Sega Genesis version can be had for $10-$15, and I think this one is a "pass". However, the Sega CD version is also about $15 for the disc only (be wary of the condition of the disc, though), and is really the way the game was intended to be played with gorgeous music, sound, and visuals. I am aware that few retrogamers own a Sega CD, but thankfully it is still a pretty cheap buy ($50-$75) for an older video game system that didn't sell well.

For a video gamer that is hellbent on experiencing Ecco The Dolphin, I recommend the Sega CD version instead.

Yo Noid might be Capcom's most bizarre idea for a video game. Of all the fast food company mascots, the forgotten Domino's Pizza mascot "The Noid" was a strange one, and it is certainly amusing to see The Noid get a video game on the Nintendo Entertainment System from Capcom.

The game itself checks all the right boxes. Yo Noid is a very playable platforming video game, the music and sound are good, the visuals are really nice, controls are tight and fluid, even the levels are interesting. In some levels, the Noid is skateboarding, other levels the Noid uses a silly helicopter-backpack, and there's a pizza challenge mini-game at the end of each level. It should be a recipe for a great NES game, right?

Well....the game is a little too long and too tough. I'm ok with one-hit deaths in a video game, but the levels need to be shorter for that to be a fair challenge. Instead, the levels are quite long with many hazards and enemies. The Noid has a short-range yo-yo attack but can also use screen-clearing attacks. Even with the screen-clearing attacks though, the length of the levels makes this game a slog. The only way to progress through the long levels is to move at a slow and cautious pace to avoid one-hit deaths. Also, the pizza challenge minigame at the end of each stage slows the game down considerably, and probably should have only been at the end of every few stages.

It's a long and difficult game, and while I wouldn't recommend it for fair-weather 8-bit NES gamers, I definitely think this game is worth your time if you are a platforming veteran looking for a challenging video game. The price range is $10-$20, and for $12 I think this is a pretty good bargain.

Any Super Nintendo gamer on a tight budget will enjoy this game. Street Fighter II is the quintessential tournament fighter video game, and provides hours of high quality gameplay for one or two players.

Street Fighter II has very attractive visuals and music which will be familiar to anyone well acquainted with Capcom's video games. The controls are very responsive, and...with the exception of Zangieff...the special moves are intuitive and simple to figure out and execute in the heat of battle. The player will select a fighter and travel around the world to defeat the other fighters and win the circuit. Some of the later fighters can be difficult to adjust to and defeat, so there is a reasonable challenge and learning curve involved.

When it comes to the Street Fighter II games...namely Street Fighter II, Street Fighter II Turbo, and Super Street Fighter II The New Challengers...there is a pretty silly debate over which version is the superior. All 3 have virtually identical mechanics, the only major difference of note is the number of selectable characters and the ability to tinker with the speed of the fighters. For Street Fighter II, the player is limited to the 8 main characters and unable to play as any of the 4 boss characters. As for the speed, some retrogamers consider the speed option to be mandatory but I never mess with it. Street Fighter II's speed is fine the way it is.

The price of the game can be somewhat difficult to determine since many sellers don't seem to understand the value of the game. Street Fighter II sold very well and is considered outdated compared to the two other Street Fighter II sequels, so the price should be cheap. I see Street Fighter II on Super Nintendo listed anywhere from $7-$35, but the game is truthfully only valued at the low-end. For a Super Nintendo gamer on a tight budget, Street Fighter II can easily be found and purchased for about $9, which is a bargain for such a fun game.

For gamers willing to spend a little extra cash though, I recommend forgoing both Street Fighter II and Street Fighter II Turbo and going straight for Super Street Fighter II The New Challengers. The game regularly sells for $20 and although is virtually identical to it's predecessors in visuals, music, and control, the game does feature 8 more playable characters compared to Street Fighter II. All three of the Street Fighter II games are a bargain, it only makes sense to get the best bargain game possible.

The Super Mario Brothers/Duck Hunt/World Class Track Meet 3-in-1 cartridge was the pack-in game for the Nintendo Entertainment System Deluxe bundle. The NES Deluxe bundle was quite the package, and came included with two NES controllers, the Zapper light gun, and the Power Pad. Most gamers that got the Nintendo Entertainment System got the bundle with two NES controllers and the Zapper gun with the Super Mario Brothers/Duck Hunt double cartridge as the pack-in game.

I don't think I need to go into detail describing the games. Super Mario Brothers is one of the most well-known video games of all time, and provides countless hours of fun classic one or 2-player platforming action. Duck Hunt is a pretty simple arcade-style Zapper game, and while most gamers grew pretty bored with the repetitive gameplay, the Zapper works extremely well with this game and is really fun to use. World Class Track Meet, on the other hand, is the weakest game on the 3-in-1 cartridge, and doesn't utilize the potential for fun on the Power Pad (Short Order/Eggsplode would have been better).

One point of note is that this cartridge obviously requires a functioning Zapper and a Power Pad in order to play Duck Hunt and World Class Track Meet. Moreover, modern television sets are incompatible with the Zapper, so you will need an old CRT box-style television set if you want to play Duck Hunt.

Even if you don't have a Zapper, Power Pad, or CRT television, I still recommend this cartridge to any Nintendo gamer looking to start a collection. Getting a cartridge that only has Super Mario Brothers costs between $10-$20, but both the Super Mario Brothers/Duck Hunt cartridge AND the Super Mario Brothers/Duck Hunt/World Class Track Meet are in the $5-$10 range.

It's a no-brainer, the 3-in-1 cartridge is the most bang for your buck even if you just want Super Mario Brothers.

Admittedly, I'm not a big fan of "run 'n gun" video games, but I can still be fair in a review. Contra III The Alien Wars on Super Nintendo was a bit of a letdown for me.

Like Contra and Super C on the NES, Contra III has really user-friendly controls that work extremely well. The visuals are very nice looking, the sound is definitely improved. There's also some very welcome new mechanics, such as using vehicles, climbing, bombs that can clear the screen of enemies, and the ability to store a weapon type. All in all, Contra III made some quality improvements from the previous NES Contra games.

Then there's the complaints. Specifically, the overhead stages are often discussed as being the weakest part of Contra III, and many players have remarked that it spoils an otherwise good game. I tend to agree, the overhead stages are very different from the overhead stages of Super C and maybe a little too ambitious. To put it bluntly, it is weird-looking, disorienting, and crummy.

Then there's the difficulty, a staple of the Contra video games. Contra III has difficulty setting, but even on the lower difficulties this game is brutal. I'm not very good at run 'n gun games in general, but of the first three Contra games I find this one to be far too punishing. Only run 'n gun fanatics or players looking for a serious challenge are going to relish Contra III.

The price range is pretty wide on Contra III The Alien Wars, anywhere from $30-$50. For $30 I think this is a good buy. Personally I think Sunset Riders is the best run 'n gun video game on the Super Nintendo, but unfortunately Sunset Riders' price range is $65-$100. Contra III The Alien Wars may not be as good as Sunset Riders, but it's certainly more affordable.

Rygar has aged surprisingly well over the years. I don't recall much fanfare for Rygar during the heyday of the NES, this was very much a video game that went under the radar. Even in 2020, Rygar tends to be overlooked for the more popular NES games like the Castlevanias, the MegaMans, etc.

It's too bad because Rygar is excellent. It is an adventure quest style platformer with RPG elements. The world to explore strikes a nice balance of being not too big but also not too small. The level-up system is a little confusing at first, but it isn't nearly as bizarre as Kid Icarus. The controls are extremely user-friendly and intuitive, making for a very fun video game experience. The power-ups, such as the grappling hook and the zipline, are very interesting and serve the proper function of allowing the player to explore the rest of the world. With regard to the gameplay, Rygar is definitely a high quality NES video game. The visual and the music are also really well done, and the story is held in high regard by retrogamers.

There are a handful of complaints, though. Just like Metroid, many gamers often complain about the lack of an in-game map system. However, Rygar (again, just like Metroid) included a map in the game's instruction manual, so I don't consider the lack of an in-game map system to be a proper complaint. Due to the "adventure quest" style of gameplay, Rygar would have benefited from a password system. Instead, the player must learn the whole game start to finish. It's not nearly as lengthy as The Legend of Zelda or Metroid, but a password system would have been nice.

The best news about Rygar is that it is a very affordable game. Currently, a copy of Rygar sells on the low end of a $9-$17 price range. For an NES gamer on a budget, Rygar is an bargain at $12 or so.

I don't see the point in describing the gameplay of Tetris. It is one of the most innovative and original video games ever made. The idea of the game is both brilliant and incredibly simple at the same time.

The official licensed NES copy of Tetris is a pretty familiar and faithful port. There are three different music tunes for the player to choose from, or the player can choose to have no music (but keep the sound effects). The player can also choose which speed the blocks fall at the start. As the player clears more and more lines and racks up points, the level will increase and the blocks will fall faster.

Tetris is definitely a mandatory video game, and I confess myself surprised that it wasn't included pre-loaded onto the NES Classic Mini. Nevertheless, the game falls into a very wide price range running anywhere from $9-$35. I tend to think that $13 is a reasonable price because there are plenty of copies in circulation.

A word of caution: Tetris is VERY addictive...in my opinion, it is the most addictive video game of all time. It's not difficult for even a fairweather video game player to get sucked into Tetris for hours at a time. Play sparingly to avoid the feverish "Tetris Effect", which results in seeing blocks lining up EVERYWHERE, even as you try to get sleep. It sounds silly and harmless, but it is quite a stressful symptom that takes a couple days to abate.

"Bring us the girl, and wipe away the debt."

You are Booker DeWitt, a former Pinkerton agent sent to the floating city of Columbia in 1912. Your task is to find a
mysterious girl named Elizabeth and return her to New York unharmed. Seems easy enough, right? Wrong. During your journey in Columbia, you'll really question your motives and learn more about who Elizabeth really is, and why these people want her so badly. I won't spoil anything, but the story of Bioshock Infinite is fantastic, and you'll really grow to love these characters. The ending is truly satisfying, and it doesn't leave any questions unanswered.

The visuals in Bioshock Infinite are amazing, and they really help to suck you into this immersive world. As you're shot up into the sky and see Columbia for the first time, you'll be left in awe at this gorgeous place. Many people roam around the city, filled with cheer. But you'll soon come to realize what a horrible place Columbia really is. Its people hate foreigners of any kind, hurting or even killing any person that isn't white (provided they aren't already being forced to work in the factories). The citizens of Columbia worship the Founding Fathers, and are wholeheartedly devoted to their fanatical leader, Father Comstock. At one point in the game you'll even see people revering a statue of John Wilkes Booth! Some foreigners, tired of the discrimination and abuse of their races, make up the Vox Populi ("voice of the people" in Latin), a ragtag group of common people who lead a civil war against the ultranationalist Founders, who blindly defend the Prophet. DeWitt is caught in the middle of all this, and doesn't want any part of it. Booker is a very cynical and reserved fellow, one who doesn't care much for the people of Columbia. But that all changes when he finds Elizabeth, an intelligent, optimistic young girl who has been locked up in a tower for all of her life. She tries to bring out the best in Booker, who has had a dark and troubled past. You'll quickly find that Elizabeth has an astonishing ability; she can open up tears in the environment, objects or weapons brought in from another dimension. These really change combat, as you can have Elizabeth conjure up some cover, a shotgun, or health kits and nearly any point. She'll also toss you ammo, coins, or salts (your fuel for using Vigors) at just the right time during combat. All of these don't make the game too easy, though: you'll find quite a challenge in Columbia on some of the higher difficulties.

One of the best new additions to Infinite was the Sky-Line system. With the push of a button, your character can use his awesome Sky-Hook to attach onto a Sky-Line and travel around Columbia in a fun and easy way. The controls on the Sky-Line are extremely intuitive, and you'll quickly learn your way around the sky. You can also use these to get an edge during combat, whether you slow down and do some precision aiming, go by your enemies in quick and lethal assaults, or even drop right onto them with a Sky-Line Strike. You can also use your Sky-Hook to perform brutal executions on your enemies when their health is low enough, and I'm sure you gore lovers out there will get some fun out of this.

There are many weapons available in Bioshock Infinite: this is a very good thing, but one of my major gripes with the game are that you can only carry two at once. This really limits some of your strategies during the game, and it can be quite frustrating if you keep on dying during a tough fight just because you didn't have the best tools for the job at hand. There are eight Vigors in total for you to use, and some of these are pretty cool. However, I didn't really use them that often: I played on Medium difficulty, and rarely ever needed to use them. That may not be the case for the higher difficulties, but so far for me, they haven't been all that useful so far. Many vending machines are scattered throughout Columbia, where you can buy health, salts, ammo, gun upgrades, vigors, and vigor upgrades. Money can be found all throughout Columbia, and I've noticed that enemies' bodies drop many more items than in the original Bioshock. When you die in Bioshock Infinite, there isn't really that much of a punishment: you simply lose some money, regain a bit of health and ammo, and respawn a few paces away from where you died. Your enemies regenerate a bit of health, too. There are 80 Voxophones (audio journal entries) and 37 Kinetoscopes (brief silent films) hidden throughout Columbia, and locating these will reveal much of the backstory, giving you a deeper understanding of Columbia. Bioshock Infinite is mildly difficult: I'm a decent gamer with a lot of FPS's under my belt, and I didn;t have a lot of trouble on Medium difficulty. Sure, there were some challenging bits, but nothing way too frustrating. However, for the ultra-hardcore gamers, there's 1999 Mode, a new difficulty level unlocked after your first completion of the game (or with a special code activated at the main menu). In this mode, you're severely punished when you die, enemies are much more lethal than before, items are scarce, and you don't take nearly as much damage as normal. I've heard that this is insanely difficult, and I'm sure that you hardcore gamers will get a kick out of it.

Overall, Bioshock Infinite is a fantastic game. The characters, visuals, voice acting, gameplay, and story are amazing, and it's a fun and perilous journey through Columbia. There are a few gripes that I have with the game, but in the end, they don't really detract from the overall experience that much. If you buy one game a year, then this should definitely be a consideration. If you're a huge singleplayer fan like me, then this should be right up your alley. Even if you're a more multiplayer-oriented player, then you should still give it a try! I promise you that it will be worth your while. I hope that this helped, and thanks for reading!

This game is awesome! It makes you feel just like you're in the Wild West. With superb voice acting, entertaining gameplay, and a wide variety of things to do, this is s steal for the price. Undead Nightmare and Multiplayer are good too, but the main single-player is really the main attraction here.

RDR takes place in 1911, near the US border states. You are John Marston, a former outlaw turned bounty hunter when the government takes and threatens his family. He is sent to hunt down some of his former gang members, and along the way he tries to find a new, better life for himself. The story of RDR is epic, and you really begin to love its characters. On your journey through the West, you'll meet many interesting people, and their personalities are really brought to life. The cutscenes in this game are excellent, and are a joy to watch. The story pays homage to many Western movies, and you'll feel like you're in one of them! The ending is very satisfying, one of the best I've seen in a game.

RDR is a third-person shooter, so you'll always be looking at your character's body. Many period-accurate guns can be used throughout the game, including Pistols, Revolvers, Rifles/Repeaters, Shotguns, Throwable Weapons (like Tomahawks or Fire Bottles), and Sniper Rifles. You auto-aim to characters, animals, or objects by pulling the left trigger, and you can choose how easy you want the targeting to be in the main menu. Hunting plays a large role in RDR, and many animals roam throughout the land. After you kill an animal, you can skin it and sell its body parts at a store, where you can use that money to buy new weapons, ammo, maps, horse, etc. Horses play an extremely large role in this game, as your trusty steed will take you many places around the map. Many are available, and it'll be well-worth the reward when you buy the best ones. The world feels very realistic in RDR, and new surprises are around every corner. You might see a woman in peril, a stagecoach being robbed, or two lawmen chasing an outlaw. It's up to you what to do in these situations, and you have a Fame and Honor meter that is constantly updated throughout the game. Your fame will increase with everything you do, whether it's good or bad. Honor can go up or down any time, so it's up to you whether you want to play as a shining knight or a total scumbag.

I personally haven't played too much of Undead Nightmare or the multiplayer, but from what I've done, it seems very fun. For just around $20, this Game of the Year Edition is a steal! It includes the oridinal RDR, Undead Nightmare, and Multiplayer. It also has all of the DLC packs already included! If you don't have Xbox LIVE, this is a great way to get the DLC. And if you do, and if this is your first time playing, it will simply save you a lot of money! I'd recommend this game to ANY videogame fan, whether you're into the shooter genre or not.

Napoleon: Total War is a great game, and is a lot of fun. It improves greatly upon the previous installment in the Total War series (Empire) in terms of combat, and there;s a vast array of units for you to train and command! The tried-and-true, easy-to-learn, hard to master Total War battles are back, and they've been improved a lot! Napoleon's campaigns are very fun, as well as his historical battles against the coalitions. Each campaign (especially the European one!) is very grand, with a very wide area for you to play around in. You can choose to command your troops directly in a battle or Auto-Resolve it if your odds are good. And if you have friends online, then you can even invite one to play as the enemy in a drop-in battle, right in the middle of the campaign! You can also play Campaigns online with your friends, whether it's cooperatively or competitively. The Campaigns of the Coalition are very entertaining as well (although really hard sometimes!). You take control of Great Britain, Russia, Prussia, or Austria and take up arms against the great French leader. All of the Campaigns provide an interesting and varied experience, and it's really a challenge if you bump up the difficulty. The customizable battles are back, and are still as fun as ever! You have full control over which nation you play as, which units, if AI will be allied with or fighting against you, maps, funds, times of day, weather, etc. It just feels so epic to have a 4v4 match on a giant map and watch the battle unfold! You can also join and create multiplayer lobbies (public and private), and it's really easy to connect with your friends (and make new ones!) through Steam. I know that it's received a lot of criticism from its users, but I personally haven't had any issues with it whatsoever. For less than $20, this is a complete steal! If you're interested in the Napoleonic era, like RTS games, want to try one out, or just like PC games in general, then I highly recommend that you buy Napoleon: Total War.

My first Assassin's Creed was AC3. It was highly enjoyable for me, although I didn't pay a whole lot of attention to the story. I hated the bits where I had to play as Desmond, and some of the missions felt extremely linear (especially the ones where you need to assassinate someone). However, I loved the gameplay, and it was a refreshing change from the typical FPS gameplay that I had been used to. After completing the game and doing most of the side missions, I was looking for more Assassin's Creed. Fortunately, AC2 became free to download on Xbox Live! Once I started the game, I was immediately hooked. Sure, it was a big change coming from 3, but it is just so much fun to play! You play as Ezio Auditore, a young Italian man living in the city of Firenze/Florence. Soon after the game starts, your father and two brothers are publicly executed. You grab your father's gear and seek revenge on the men who did this to your family. I won't spoil anything else, (heck, I haven't even finished the entire story yet!) but I can tell you that the story is amazing. The cutscenes are very cool and entertaining, the characters are very interesting (particularly Ezio and Leonardo da Vinci!), and the atmosphere feels great. There are a few cities that you can travel to in the game, including Florence, Tuscany, and Venice. All three cities are very cool, and are packed full of stuff to see, do, and collect. Treasure chests are scattered across the towns, and it's very rewarding to find and loot these. You can do missions where you beat up an unfaithful husband, take on an assassination contract, find and traverse through secret Assassin tombs (one of the best parts of the game!), and take over Templar strongholds. You can also purchase weapons and armor, unlock new capes for your character, or customize the color of your outfit. It's all very cool, and you really get immersed in this huge world. And then there's Monteriggioni, the small villa owned by your uncle Mario (pay attention to the first cutscene with him!). You soon find yourself there, and you're put in charge of renovating and upgrading the villa. There are many shops to be renovated, and it's extremely rewarding to do so. Every 20 minutes, you receive a specific amount of income in your villa's chest. This amount drastically improves the more and more you upgrade the buildings in your villa, and it becomes very easy to make money after all the shops are upgraded. While this is extremely satisfying, it also serves as a bit of a con to this game. In the early game, weapons and armor seem very expensive, and money is a whole lot harder to come by. But once you upgrade your entire villa, you don't need to worry about being low on money anymore. I've fully upgraded mine, and I'm making nearly 12,000 Florins every 20 minutes! The game notifies you whenever money is deposited to your villa's chest, so you can just fast travel there in between missions to collect your income. When you upgrade shops in your villa (such as the Doctor, Blacksmith, Painter, Tailor, etc.), you also receive a small discount on all items purchased from that shop. The gameplay in AC2 is immensely fun, and the wide variety of weapons provides for an interesting, near-RPG like experience. You can be stealthy and use the Hidden Blade (probably the most badass weapon in the series), wield a dagger, or charge in on horseback whilst swinging your warhammer. While you're being pursued by enemies, there are many places to hide. You can walk with a large crowd, hide in a bale of hay, or sit on a bench to evade your pursuers. You build up Notoriety whenever you kill guards, and the more notorious you are, the faster guards will detect and attack you. You can decrease your notoriety by tearing down posters, bribing town criers, or finding and killing a corrupt public official. Travel in this game is very easy, and you'll want (but not necessarily need) to utilize the fast travel stations later in the game, when it can take you around 10-20 minutes to ride somewhere. It just costs around 100-200 Florins to travel around the map, and this becomes extremely handy when your missions will be spanning many different cities. You can also mount up on your trusty steed if you're outside a city (you cannot call a new horse nor ride one inside a city, unfortunately), and this makes exploring much faster. Highly elevated viewpoints are also scattered throughout the map, and when you Synchronize with them, more details of the map are revealed. It's pretty much a necessity to Synchronize with all of the viewpoints when you're in a new city, and it's very fun to do so. The parkour in AC2 is great for the most part, but sometimes a bad camera angle or accidental button push can kill you. This is only annoying in a high-risk situation, such as in an Assassin's Tomb (where great precision and patience are required to navigate the course) or when you're pursuing an enemy on the rooftops. Overall, AC2 is an excellent game, and I'd buy it for full price if I needed to. The atmosphere, gameplay, and story are all excellent, and you'll be having fun for many hours on end with this game. I'd recommend this game to fans of the Assassin's Creed series, history buffs, or gamers looking for a change of pace. I hope this helped, and thanks for reading!

Battle of Forli:

In the original game, sequences 12 and 13 were 'corrupted' in the Animus, rendering them unplayable. They were later released as paid DLC. I personally think that it was really stupid of Ubisoft to do this. While this part of the storyline isn't strictly necessary to understand the story, they are very important for full enjoyment of the game. However, I recommend you either get both or neither. If you only get the first one or second one, a lot of stuff wont make sense. Anyway, on to the reviews for both of these. The Battle of Forli is a very fun sequence, and most of it (obviously) involves you defending the town of Forli. It takes about 20-30 minutes to complete, and it's very fun all the way. There isn't much stealth in this (being a battle and all), but the huge skirmishes were very enjoyable. I was glad that they had a sequence take place in Romagna/Forli, because it was barely featured in the main storyline (you pretty much get there and then leave for another city in the story). If you're a big fan of large-scale swordplay, then you'll heartily enjoy this DLC.

Bonfire of the Vanities:

This sequence was great as well! While the last one was a straight-up battle, this one features a lot more variety. It mostly features you running around Florence and killing 9 lieutenants of an evil man who has come to power there. Each lieutenant is different, and you'll be forced to use some strategy for some of them (for some, you can just run up and murder them, but for others, you have to remain undetected or you'll be desynchronized). It was great to go back to Florence again, and more of the city is opened up then before. It was very fun to do all of these, and it took me around 45 minutes to an hour to complete this. If you love the iconic assassinations that this series is known for, and you want to run around Florence again, then you'll really enjoy this DLC.

I just finished the story today, and it was AWESOME! Once again, I highly recommend this game to you.

This game picks up right where 2 left off. Ezio has returned to Rome, and has to deal with the Borgias' corrupt regime. Some cool new characters are added in, and all the ones we know and love from 2 are brought back. The story is great, and the ending will leave you in awe. As the series is known for, the cutscenes, dialogue, and visuals are awesome. The gameplay is much more streamlined than 2, and it's been greatly improved upon. Many tools are available for you to use during combat, and many different strategies can be used. Renovating shops and famous landmarks increases the income of the city, which is deposited in a bank every 20 minutes. You can then collect this money however you please! It's kind of hard to get a lot of money in the beginning of the game, but after you renovate many shops and collect a lot of your income, money doesn't become an issue anymore! The gameplay is much more streamlined than 2, and it's been greatly improved upon. Many tools are available for you to use during combat, and many different strategies can be used. Rome is a big city to roam around in, and there's many things to see and do. These include: clearing out Borgia towers scattered throughout the city (allowing you to renovate buildings in that district), getting Assassination contracts, completing challenges for different guilds, recruiting your own Assassins, ranking them up and calling them during combat, flashback missions, etc. You'll spend a lot of time on this game if you're willing to, and the game does a good job of making sure that there's always something entertaining to do while playing.

Although many great additions have been made to the game, it's still essentially the same gameplay from 2, only faster and more streamlined. I have to admit that 2 did some things better, such as the hidden hideout missions. The main missions in this game now have an optional objective, and it is required of you to complete all of them in order to achieve 100% sync. While some may see this as a positive, I don't really like the addition. If you're big con completing the game, it really restricts the open style of gameplay that we've grown to love in the series. It doesn't matter if you've spent 10 hours unlocking the best weapon in the game, you can't use it if you want to achieve full sync in some missions. Sure, they're completely optional, but it's still kind of annoying. You can replay memories if you want to go back and achieve full sync, however. Playing as Desmond was pretty entertaining in the game, although I've always found the story of his ancestors far more interesting. You only HAVE to play as him at the beginning and end of the game, it's completely optional otherwise.

Overall, this an awesome game! It took a spectacular game, Assassin's Creed 2, and greatly improved upon it! While some may say that this is just a money grab by Ubisoft, I heartily disagree. You can tell that they worked hard on this game, especially with the visuals, gameplay, story, and atmosphere. I highly recommend this game to anyone, although I strongly urge you to play Assassin's Creed 2 first if you care about the story at all. Hope this helped!

STORY:

The game takes place many years after the events of Brotherhood, and Ezio is now in his early 50s. He is still as potent of an Assassin as ever, though, and the intro to the game is excellent. You soon find yourself in Constantinople, now occupied by the Ottomans. There's a power struggle between the contenders for the Sultanate, and you meet with a few cool historical figures on your journey. It wraps up the story of Ezio, and brings in many new characters into the game. At the same time, Desmond is still in the Animus immediately after the events of the previous game, trapped on an island within it. His mind is in pieces, and it's up to you to put them back together. The story, cutscenes, dialogue, and background are excellent as always, and you'll really start to grow on some of the new characters you meet. The ending is great, and it leaves you both satisfied with this one and looking forward to the next game.

GAMEPLAY:

To make a long story short, gameplay is essentially the same as within Assassin's Creed Brotherhood. Sure, a few new additions have been made, such as the new Hookblade (which allows you to free-run much faster), Master Assassin missions, and a Tower Defense mechanic, but nothing is really too groundbreaking. Some may see this as a negative, but since I absolutely loved Brotherhood, it's fine with me. You do a few side missions as Altair, the main Assassin of the first game in the series. The missions, while few and brief, are very cool, and chronicle Altair's life after the events of the first game. One big change in this game is how Notoriety works. It's called Templar Awareness now, and it increases whenever you're seen committing a crime. However, you aren't recognized by guards more easily if your Notoriety is higher. They react in the same way to your actions, regardless of your Notoriety level; they won't notice or bother you until you murder someone or something. Once your Notoriety reaches its peak level, the Templars become aware of the Assassins' presence in the city. They'll then attack one of your Assassin dens (which are the same as the Borgia towers from the last game), and you are required to defend your den from the Templars. As always, you can lower your Notoriety by bribing heralds or killing corrupt public officials. Bomb crafting has been added to the game as well, and it's a very detailed and complex system. Many materials can be collected and used to craft bombs that damage, distract, or blind enemies. It is a cool mechanic, but I never found myself in a situation where I absolutely NEEDED to use a bomb. In fact, that's how many of the things are in the game; it's easy to avoid them if you want to, but you'll be more rewarded if you take the time to invest in them. The visuals are stunning as usual in the game, and Constantinople is a nice change from the Italian cities that we've become so accustomed to. The city is noticeably smaller than the cities in the previous games, but it never feels too cramped. There's plenty of side missions to do, and many of these are surprisingly entertaining!

OVERALL:

This game is awesome! The gameplay is essentially the same as Brotherhood's, and the story is one of the stronger in the series. Although some additions have been made to the game, some of them seem pointless and out of place. For the price, it's a steal, and I recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the Assassin's Creed games. However, if you haven't played any yet, then I strongly recommend starting right from the beginning. It's fine to start on 2 as well, though. Hope this helped!

Much has already been said about this game, so I'll keep this pretty short. The story is fantastic, and it's one of the few games where you really enjoy watching the cutscenes! The world looks absolutely beautiful, and the voice acting is superb. The gameplay is awesome, too! It's very easy to pick up, and it's well worth the effort to improve your character. Hunting is some of the best I've found in a videogame, and Rockstar really nailed the atmosphere here. The landscapes, the guns, the wildlife, everything seems just in its right place! There's so many things to do, some planned, some done on the spur of the moment, so you'll definitely play for at least 20 hours on just one playthrough! In addition to this superb singleplayer (which is the primary focus of the game), there's Multiplayer and Undead Nightmare! This pack also comes with all the DLC preloaded already. I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone, regardless of if you're an open world fan or not! The gameplay is pretty similar to GTA, so fans of that will adjust really quickly. And for the price, it's a total steal! If you're looking for an epic open-world game with a superb story, memorable characters, fun gameplay, an interactive and expansive world, and a vast multiplayer, then this game is for you!

Grand Theft Auto 5 most certainly lives up to its astounding hype and sets yet another boundary for open-world gaming. Grand Theft Auto over the years has garnered a tremendous amount of praise (and controversy) as the pinnacle of open-world gaming today. With its excellent story, characters, gameplay, and variety of things to do, GTA 5 will most indefinitely provide an enjoyable experience for any mature gamer.

Grand Theft Auto 5's story is amazing, and matches, sometimes even surpasses, the quality of many of the finest Hollywood films. I won't go into too much detail, but the decision to have 3 main characters in the story served it very well, and the narrative is greatly enhanced by this trio. Each character is different in his own way, in nearly everything, from his motivations to his skills. As with any good open-world game, your decisions have a major impact on the story and you can really see that easily. The voice acting for all the characters is superb, and the dialogue is some of the finest that I've heard in a videogame. It keeps the game entertaining and interesting the whole way through, and you can be assured that there's many laugh-out-loud moments to be had. The entire story, along with its colorful cast of characters and vibrant dialogue, serves as a great social commentary on the America of today, and really provokes your thought.

The gameplay of Grand Theft Auto 5 is fantastic, and is fun as the day is long. There's an astounding number of things that you can buy and do, ranging from purchasing a tank on the internet to playing darts at your local bar. All of these activities are presented to you in one way or another across the length of the storyline, and whether or not you choose to do many of these is entirely up to you. There's surely something here for everyone, and many of the unstructured things you can do are mostly the most fun. The gameplay, while very complex, is extremely easy to pick up, even for a relatively inexperienced newcomer to this genre as I was. Using your skills to make money, find stores, and buy things is extremely rewarding. Part of how much you'll enjoy this game is how much you're willing to work and immerse yourself in this world. If you're the type of person who just plays through the main missions and then quits, you'll still have a lot of fun with this game, but not anywhere near how much someone who takes their time to collect things, do the side missions, and just simply explore will. The game world is huge, and it will take you a very long time to explore all of it and discover all its secrets (if you're an avid Rockstar gamer, then here's some perspective: the map of GTA 5 is bigger than the maps of Red Dead Redemption, San Andreas, and GTA 4 combined, with some room still left to spare). As with any game as large as this, there are inevitably some bugs, but most of these are very hard to notice or very menial. However, there have been a few cases of game-breaking bugs. To give you an idea of how many things there are to do in this game, keep this in mind: I've played for over 40 hours total, and I'm barely above 75% done with game completion.

GTA Online is an ambitious, humongous addition to this already-great game. In short, you can do anything in online that you can do in singleplayer, but with up to 16 friends at once. The entire map is available online, and new additional content is constantly being put out for free. Multiplayer will provide many more hours of entertainment and shenanigans to you, and the experience is enhanced so much more if you're playing with a few friends.

In conclusion, Grand Theft Auto 5 is an exceptional game, and it's worth every penny. The singleplayer, with its excellent story, characters, and variety of things to do, along with the extensive multiplayer, will provide many, many hours of quality gameplay and entertainment for you. If you're a mature gamer who is willing to work hard, explore, and have fun, then this game is for you.

I've played this DJ game in on an arcade machine and I really like it. When I played the demo, I absolutely loved it. So I went ahead and purchased the full game. Here's the problem:

1). The demo had 5 or 6 songs (I'm sorry I don't remember the exact number because I deleted it after I got the full game.) and most of them are really nice English songs, including rock and rap I've never heard of. When I got the full game, I realized the VAST MAJORITY are Korean songs. The demo songs are still in the full game, but what I'm trying to say is the demo was definitely not a fair representation of the full game. I honestly I felt like I've been cheated into buying the full game. This is borderline fraud. They picked the only 5% English songs in the full game into the demo to suck you into buying the remaining 95% Korean songs. But if you like K-pop, this wouldn't be an issue for you then.

2). The difficulty level. The demo's difficulty was perfect. It was challenging but after a few tries, I really got the hang of it. The full game has a RIDICULOUS difficulty level. I'm a dedicated gamer myself for decades and I understand challenges make the game more fun, but let me explain why I hate this one. In most other music games, there's a health bar and every time you press the wrong note or off key, you lose a bit of health. But in this one, you can lose the entire bar 3 seconds into the song if you press the wrong note. Or even if you can keep up for a while, a small simple mistake can cause you to die and the song will stop right away when it's just about to get to the best part. I find that very irritating and too harsh.

Other than the two problems I mentioned I above, the game was overall ok. The graphics are especially good. If you don't mind spend 5 hours trying to play through one Korean song, then I guess you will like this one.

i liked the second one the best because i felt more connected with the characters overall and loved to help gain their loyalties. i felt the third had limitations and mostly focused on going to the citadel... a lot. every time i was playing, i felt like the game should have been called: MASS EFFECT: CITADEL EXPLORATION SIMULATOR. i was frustrated with it and wanted to move on.

This is the first time I've been able to play mario kart with friends with the screen split 4 ways and actually retain good graphics and frame rate and isn't that what Mario Kart is all about?  Sitting on the couch, shooting a turtle shell at your best friend, right before they cross the finish line.  Sure the one player mode isn't deep.  And it is in other racing games like Gran Turismo?  What do people expect?  The one player version of racing games is pretty formulaic.  You race in a series of multi-race cups and unlock stuff if you win.  Sure, Diddy Kong Racing back in the day (still have it on N64) was a bit more inventive but I played it recently and it's not that different.  And I just don't understand why reviewers aren't dinging Gran Turismo or PGR for following that same formula iteration after iteration.  The tracks are absolutely gorgeous and entertaining.  There is a lot more verticality in this game which I have found gets me leaning over in my seat.  The amount of weapons/boost and their power seems fairly appropriate, still perhaps a bit too strong.  The anti-gravity effects are a fun, if minor, addition.  This is clearly the best Mario Kart to date.  Finally in high definition and with good enough graphics to split screen four ways and maintain a good picture and decent framrate.  Unless you just don't like Mario Kart (and hey, that's fine), I can't imagine why this isn't a 10/10.  I will say I can't comment on battle mode.  It's just not my thing and I've never liked it.  It's like your playing Mario Kart without the race which is just removing the best level of excitement in my mind (you know, sticking to your buddy with a shell in his posterior right before he crossed the finish line).  Also, I have not tried the game on-line so I can't review that aspect.

However, there are also so really cool things in the game. The voice acting again is great. Graphics don't seem quite as sharp as Swap Force to me but are still very good.
