First-person shooters are usually not focused on story. Games like Call of Duty are more focused on action than an interesting storyline. Who cares if you can't remember why you're hunting down a terrorist, because THEY JUST DROPPED A NUKE!!!!! I'm not saying that Call of Duty is bad - I'm just saying its story is forgetable. This is where Homefront comes in. This game has a much bigger focus on story than many other shooter franchises, putting players in the middle of a Korean occupation of the US. Does this shooter succeed in its goal, or is it just another bland shooter?

Homefront's campaign starts off with one of the most emotional openings I've seen in quite a while, showing players the true brutality of the savage Korean occupation. Seeing people being beaten on the streets, while a baby is crying over his parent's dead bodies is truly unsettling. Soon after the introduction, you are a member of the Resistance, fighting back against a superior force. Writer John Milius (Apocalypse Now, Red Dawn) has created one of the most emotional stories in video games, and I actually felt like I was about to cry in a few spots. My only complaint about the story (and trust me, this is the only one) is the main character. He never talks, and you have no idea what he's thinking. Giving him a voice and mind would have helped the story quite a bit. But, considering how great the rest of the story is, this is a very minor complaint.

While the story of Homefront is really quite excellent, the gameplay never quite reaches that standard. Don't get me wrong - the gameplay is not bad, it's just slightly repetitive. This game definitely gets the basics of first-person shooters down, however. Shooting feels satisfying, and the action is almost always non-stop. One thing I like about the game is that the game doesn't throw thousands of explosions at your face every ten seconds. The game is more about action-packed gun-fights instead of non-stop explosions. The game has just the appropiate amount of action - there's always a lot of it, but it doesn't get over the top.

However, back to my complaint about the gameplay - it just gets a bit repetitive. While the locations are diverse, the game just doesn't have quite enough variety. The first four chapters are basically just "shoot all enemies, then proceed to shoot more in a different area." While the remote controlled tank you can control in the game (nicknamed "Goliath") shakes things up a bit, the game is still slightly repetitive as a whole.

Luckily, the last three chapters (sneaking your way through a camp, defending a convoy in a helicopter, and taking part in a full-on assault of the Golden Gate bridge) are much more fun that the first four chapters. The variety here is a lot better, and it makes me wonder why it wasn't like this in the beginning of the campaign. In particular, the Golden Gate bridge siege is one of the most memorable moments I've experienced in first-person shooters.

Overall, the campaign was very good in Homefront. While the beginning of the campaign was repetitive, the later parts of the game make up for it. The emotional story was something new and refreshing that I have never experienced in a first-person shooter. A sequel, being developed by Crytek, has also been announced, and is coming for 2014. While that's a long way off, I can't wait to see how the story continues from this game, considering the massive cliffhangar ending of this one.

Once you have beaten the campaign, there is also a multiplayer mode. This mode is a fantastic alternative from bigger franchises, and features a slew of unlockable weapons, gear, and perks. Vehicular combat is also a big focus here, and the remote-controlled drones are also deadly. The maps are very well designed, and the game is also very balanced. One complaint that I have with the game is that there aren't that many maps and modes. There are a total of seven maps, and while these maps are well designed, I think that there could have been more. However, the biggest disappointment is that there are only two game modes - Team Deathmatch and Ground Control. While both of these modes are fantastic fun, I think that there could have been just a few more modes of play.

However, these complaints are minor due to one simple fact - Homefront multiplayer is a blast. The tight gunplay from the campaign transitions well onto the multiplayer battlefield, and the leveling system is fantastic, with perks, weapons, and drones waiting to be unlocked. Also a great feature is that the game's two game modes (TDM and Ground Control) both appeal to two different types of people. Those who want more of a straight-forward, CoD-like experience should pick TDM, while Ground Control is very similar to Battlefield's Conquest mode. People wanting more of a tactical experience should play Ground Control.

However, one of the best parts of Homefront's multiplayer is the Battle Points system. The Battle Points system is where things get interesting. See, when you capture objectives and kill enemy players, you gain battle points. These battle points can be spent in-game on drones and vehicles. Whether you want to spend your points as soon as you get them or save up your points for the bigger and more powerful vehicles and drones is up to you. Either way, most matches begin with foot soldiers and small drones, and end with attack helicopters and battle tanks. All multiplayer matches don't feel like minor skirmishes - they feel like all-out war, mostly due to the 32-player count, but also due to the massive amount of vehicles and drones on the screen at once.

Overall, the multiplayer matches of Homefront are some of the most fun I've had in a first-person shooter. Homefront has earned its place among the ranks of Call of Duty and Battlefield, and anyone looking for a good time couldn't go wrong with this game.

As for Homefront's overall presentation, the graphics are pretty good. Textures look really good, and the framerate holds up no matter what's happening onscreen. However, the graphics aren't quite as good as its competitors. For instance, there is some aliasing issues in the game, as well as a blurry texture here and there. However, Homefront is still a very good looking shooter, despite these issues.

Now, on to easily one of the best things about this game - the audio. The voice acting here is Hollywood caliber, with the characters delivering emotional lines without things getting too cheesy. The sound effects are also some of the best I've heard, with the fantastic gunfire and explosion sound effects making it feel like you're in a real war. However, none of these componets come close to the quality of the soundtrack. The main theme is so good that I have to listen to the two minute long song at the main menu before I even start playing. The soundtrack fits the game really well, and its so good that I actually went on to iTunes and downloaded the song to my iPod. It's just that stunning.

As for how long you will be playing this game, let me just come out and say it - a pretty long while. While the campaign is pretty short, and really only worth 1-2 playthroughs, the multiplayer features a pretty in-depth level cap of 75. There is no prestiging like in Call of Duty, but the game is still a blast to play, even when there is no more to unlock.

Overall, this game is fantastic. The campaign is emotional, the multiplayer is fantastic, and the game will last you a long while. While I wish the campaign was less repetitive, the game is still a very good choice for someone tired of the more popular shooter franchises.

If there's one genre that needed a boost on Sony's handheld, it's FPS's. Ever since the system launched, the system has had a very low reputation in terms of shooters. Ever since the release of the system I have played a lot of FPS games on it, in hopes of finding a game that is as good as a console shooter. Does Medal of Honor Heroes succeed at bringing a good FPS to the system? Not quite - but it came really close.

The reason why this game isn't quite as good as console FPS's is because it lacks polish in story. The story is non-existent, and your teammates are all look-alike US soldiers that shout things like "INFANTRY!" and "GRENADE!" While this makes the game a bit more realistic, your teammates never have any lines of dialogue other than these shouts. While you could blame the lack of story on system limitations, I can't see how hard it would be to add in a coherent plotline to your Nazi killing.

Once you get over the lack of story, the gameplay is the first thing you'll notice. First of all, the controls are much better than any other shooter controls for the system. Like other shooters on this system, you aim with the face buttons, and reload, crouch, and pick up items using the D-pad. This control scheme is actually done well in this game, however, and it takes little time to get used to them. As for the gameplay itself - it's a blast. Each mission is action-packed and chaotic, with tons of Nazis on-screen at once. Also a plus is the AI. The enemies in this game will try and flush you out of cover with grenades, and will kill you if you are rusty in your tactics. I highly recommend playing on normal or hard. There is little challenge on easy, and normal and hard bump up the challenge considerably, forcing you to think more about your strategies in combat.

There are multiple types of missions in the game, most of them objective-based. In one mission, you have a primary objective, and multiple secondary objectives to tackle. Most of the secondary objectives consist of collecting an item, but the real thrill is in the primary objectives. Whether you're struggling to capture control points throughout the map or assassinating Nazi generals, you are constantly getting shot at by a dozen Nazis at once. The chaos of every battle is stunning for the system, and the game handles it with no framerate drops or slowdown.

The graphics of MoH Heroes are simply stunning. Heroes is simply the best looking game on the system, with detailed environments and impressive looking explosions and effects. There are little to no graphical glitches, and the game runs at a smooth 30 frames per second. The audio is also impressive. The music is simply fantastic, with the main theme being one of the best songs in any WW2 video game ever. However, there is a strange lack of music in the actual gameplay. Some nice orchestral music would have made the game more immersive. Also, as I mentioned before, your teammates randomly shout out things during battle. It does make battle a bit more realistic, but there could have been some actual lines for your teammates to say.

The game will not last you forever, but it certainly has some great value. Having bought this game for $10 on PSN, the value here was outstanding. However, one of the main reasons I got this game was to experience 32-person multiplayer warfare. Yes - 32 players. However, I was saddened to realize that EA shut down the servers for the game before I got it. I was excited to play the online, but sadly, it is now impossible.

However, there is some local multiplayer options available, so if you have some friends with PSPs and a copy of this game, you can battle it out in multiplayer this way. Also, there is a Skirmish mode, in which the game pits you versus other enemies in a free-for-all. This mode is great, and is also great practice for those getting used to the controls. I must also point out that the maps are fantastic. Each map has different sniping spots and choke points, and they keep things intense.

Overall, Medal of Honor Heroes is simply the best FPS on the system. The game has great gameplay and graphics, and there is a lot of content for players to sift through. While the campaign may be a bit short, the game has plenty of other things to keep players busy, whether it's the Skirmish mode or the local multiplayer options. While it is disappointing that EA shut down the online servers, but the game is still a lot of fun.

I wasn't sure what to expect from this game. There hadn't been much advertisement or news about the game prior to release. However, being a fan of both the first Ghost Warrior and of Sniper Elite V2, I figured there wasn't much to lose. Luckily, I wasn't disappointed. The game is a fluid, cinematic, and exciting sniping experience, and a big improvement over the first game.

The story puts you in the shoes of Cole "Sandman" Anderson, a highly trained (you guessed it) sniper tasked with preventing a highly dangerous bio-weapon from falling into the wrong hands. However, things go haywire rather quickly, and it's up to Cole to secure the bio-weapon at all costs.

Now, this may sound like the typical "save the world" plot told in many other military shooters before, and in a couple of ways, it is. However, without spoiling anything, there are a number of plot twists that had me completely surprised, and I was actually wanting to beat the game to see how it ended. While it may not be the absolute best story I've ever seen, it is MUCH better than the plot of the first, and still had me hooked.

As for the gameplay, things play out much like the first game. The realistic bullet ballistics from the first game return. You still sneak through enemy camps, hiding in foilage with the help of your trusty ghillie suit, and eventually reach an overwatch position where you either guide your teammates from point A to point B, or eliminate an enemy of importance. However, there is much more emphasis on stealth this time around. Even when you're in an overwatch position guiding your teammates, you have to be stealthy about it, eliminating enemies when their buddies have their backs turned. New tactics, such as shooting out lights to hide dead bodies and shooting oil tanks to distract enemies also keep things fresh. Also, if you miss a shot, the enemies will be alerted, and will eliminate your squad, so you have to aim carefully.

The plays much better than the first for a number of reasons. First of all, the issues with getting stuck on the environment have been mostly fixed. Stealth kills have been added, where you pull out a knife and silently eliminate enemies from the shadows. There are some parts of the game that shake things up a bit. In one instance you're deep within enemy territory with nothing but a pistol with four bullets in it. In another, you're in the middle of a park with snipers in almost every building around you. Moments like these keep the game from getting stale too quicky.

However, I still have a few complaints. My biggest complaint is the missions where you're with a spotter. The spotter is pretty much a godsend. He marks nearly every enemy in the area with a target over their head, and tells you exactly what order to eliminate them in, and when to do it. However, these missions are WAY too easy, and the only way you'll die in these is if you miss a shot. This is also a problem in the overwatch missions, because your squad marks every single enemy they see, including snipers that are over a kilometer away. Sure, while this is how snipers in real life operate, I still think that it has an effect on the game as a whole. It would have helped if there had been a spotter mission like in the first game, where you were the spotter and you had to actually search for the enemies for your sniper to eliminate.

However, this is not a game-breaking issue. There are also missions where you are separated from your spotter, and you have to mark enemies for yourself. These missions give you a "do whatever you want" mentality, which means you can eliminate enemies in whatever order you want. While the environments you're traversing are still pretty linear, these missions are still a refreshing change of pace from "shoot this enemy, then that one," missions.

I also felt it was worth noting that the infamous bullet cam returns. While it is kind of cool, it is nowhere as bloody as it was in the first. As a matter of fact, there was barely any noticeable blood. The animations of the enemies while getting hit by the bullet are also stiff and unnatural. Granted, the backflips from the first game weren't that realistic either, but at least it was sadistically satisfying. In this game, the bullet cam is nowhere near as awesome than it was in the original. However, it is far from a game-breaker.

The graphics are MUCH better than the first game, with beautiful environments, great character models, and realistic animations. This is not that surprising, considering that the game runs on CryEngine 3. While it admittedly doesn't look as good as, say, Crysis 3, it still looks pretty good. However, in the multiplayer (which i'll get to in a second), the graphics take a bit of a hit. There are a lot of flickering textures and aliasing issues to be had, and while it doesn't look terrible, it still doesn't compare to the great looking campaign.

The audio is fantastic, with great voice acting adding to the immersion in the game's plot. Even better is the soundtrack. The main theme is stunning, with some admirable music during actual gameplay. The sound effects are great as well, with the sound of an unsilenced XM5000 shot having the appropriate oomph.

The campaign will take up to five hours to beat. While this isn't that long, the game is fun enough that I actually played through it three times. The surprisingly good story, combined with the realistic sniping, varied environments, and polished stealth made for a memorable sniping experience.

However, this is not all. There is also a multiplayer mode based on (you guessed it) sniping. If you enjoyed the multiplayer in the original Ghost Warrior (which I did very much) then you will be impressed by the improvements in gameplay. The best part of the multiplayer is the map design. The maps are focused on sniping, with the maps each having multiple convenient sniping spots. However, don't expect this to be an exciting, Call of Duty-like experience. It takes patience to be a real-life sniper, and it shows in the multiplayer. You may go through a 20-minute match only getting five kills. As I stated, it takes patience. When you finally see an enemy hiding in a bush, and you blow his face off with an Intervention, it is incredibly satisfying. PS: Look out for people online. They have a tendency to run across the map to your team's side and pick you off one by one, which can be extremely annoying.

However, there is one absolutely glaring flaw. There is only ONE mode (Team Deathmatch), with TWO maps (Resort and Sarajevo Downtown). I can't see how City Interactive couldn't have made a few more maps than that, especially with the numerous delays. However, there is supposedly some free multiplayer DLC coming out soon, adding a Deathmatch game mode and two new maps. I don't know if this is a mere rumor, or if it's true, but we'll have to wait and see. For now, I still think that the multiplayer in the original Ghost Warrior is better, simply because there is way more modes and maps included.

Overall, the game is a great game. The cinematic campaign is memorable, fun, and has a great story. The multiplayer may be severely lacking on content, but it still manages to deliver with addictive and satisfying sniping gameplay. Overall, well worth the $40 price tag.

Originally, Resident Evil games were scary and tense survival horror games. Whether you were exploring an abandoned mansion, an eerie police department, or the streets of Raccoon City, the games had zombies, creatures, and even a huge, 8-foot tall guy in a trench-coat and a rocket launcher. However, ever since RE4, the series has been changing from a survival horror game to an all-out action game. Some people, once loyal fans of the series, have abandoned the series entirely, claiming it no longer had any scares. While this is definitely true, I am not a part of this group. I, as an action fan myself, can safely say that Resident Evil 5 is a fantastic game.

The story takes place in Africa. Classic RE character Chris Redfield, and his partner, newcomer Sheva Alomar, are both members of the B.S.A.A., a global organization created to prevent bio-terrorist attacks. Chris and Sheva are there to investigate bio-terrorist activity. As you can imagine, things go horribly wrong. Chris and Sheva are attacked by a new type of creature, the Majini. The duo must figure out what is behind the outbreak, and how to stop them.

The story, while pretty good, is a bit lacking compared to other entries in the series. While there are classic characters that return in the game, the games plot is still a bit too simple compared to other entries in the series, where there was a lot of backstory and characters with different agendas. In this game, the story basically boils down to "go to Africa, stop the outbreak."

Before I get into the gameplay, it is important to note that this game was designed as a co-op game. You can play this game by yourself, but by doing so, you miss out on a lot of the fun that you get when you play in co-op mode. While the AI partner is okay, she isn't quite intelligent enough to hold her own against a horde of Majini. On top of that, she needs to be revived when downed, you are forced to heal her when she's hurt, and she will waste the precious ammo that you give her. While its not bad, you are doing yourself a disservice by playing by yourself.

Any negatives about the game in single-player are completely blown away when you play the game with a friend. This is a game where cooperation and skill are required to survive. The feeling of working together against the enemies you face by cooperating with your partner is incredibly fun, and makes the game an absolute blast to play through.

There are many weapons in the game, and all of them can be upgraded with the money you earn. While some upgrades don't really make any sense (you can get a triple-barrel shotgun that has a ten-bullet clip) but they are definitely worth the investment. You can also buy infinite ammo by saving up the points you earn. However, infinite ammo takes away a lot of the tension that makes the game so much fun. The feeling of getting chased down by a Majini with a chainsaw with no ammo left, only to be saved by your buddy is an exhilarating experience. A lot of that tension is lost when you can simply blast away at the chainsaw Majini without any fear of running out of ammo. Luckily, infinite ammo is optional, so I would recommend not buying it.

The game is about 7-10 hours long. While this is short compared to the length of RE4, the co-op adds enough replay value to it that I was playing through it many times with my friend just to find every treasure, get every BSAA emblem, and find all of the weapons. There is also the infamous "Mercenaries" mode that is unlocked after beating the game. This mode pits you against hordes of Majini in an arcade-style, score-based mini-game. While this mode is mostly just a slight diversion from the main game, there are extra characters to unlock, as well as a slew of maps to play on. The mode also supports co-op.

The graphics in RE5 are nothing short of stunning. Amazing lighting effects, detailed environments, and great creature designs are just the tip of the iceberg in the graphics department. The audio is also fantastic, with great voice acting (with the exception of Irving... just wait until you hear his voice), awesome sound effects, as well as great music.

Overall, Resident Evil 5 is a fantastic game. With addictive gameplay, stunning graphics and a lot of replay value, the game is nowhere near as bad as people say it is. If you're looking for a Resident Evil game that will scare you like RE1 or RE2, go replay one of those classics, or try out Dead Space, which is an absolutely terrifying game. However, if you want a co-op game that features amazing graphics and fantastic action, Resident Evil 5 is right up your alley.

DLC

With the Gold Edition, you get all of the DLC for the game along with the game itself. I will go over each of the DLC packs individually.

Versus mode is exactly what it sounds like - you have to kill other players, as well as the usual assortment of Majini. I thought this mode would be bland and forgettable, but it is actually quite fun if you get three other friends together. There are two modes - Slayers and Survivors. Slayers is basically four-person competitive Mercenaries. You get points for killing Majini, and while you can still shoot other players, I found this mode more fun when you are working together with your teammates, but still trying to get a better score than them. Survivors is just straight-up deathmatch. You only get points for killing other players, and there are weapons littered around the level to pick up. I found Slayers to be the preferable mode, but Survivors is still fun. There are also team variations of these two modes, but I prefer the free-for-all modes.

Lost In Nightmares is, in my opinion, the best DLC the game has to offer. In this DLC, You are in Spencer's estate, which is a mansion modeled after the one in the Arklay Mountains that you explored in the first Resident Evil. This means that the first half of this DLC is extremely familiar. However, the creatures that chase you in the mansion are much more terrifying than any zombie. That's right - this DLC can actually be pretty scary and tense. There are also small little details around the mansion that are references to the first Resident Evil, such as a diary in which a lab worker describes his transformation into a creature ("itchy and scratchy") and a segment where Jill must play the Moonlight Sonata to open a door for Chris to enter.

However, once you enter the basement of the mansion, things get different. In the last part of the expansion, you and your partner lose all of your weapons, and must use traps to kill the creatures to collect emblems to open a door. The part of the DLC is easily the best, because it forces cooperation between you and your buddy to collect the cranks, lift the spiked ceiling, and have your partner lure the creature to the trap and kill him. Overall, this expansion is the best of the bonus content.

*SPOILERS AHEAD*

The other major DLC pack is Desperate Escape, where Jill Valentine and Josh Stone must escape the Tricell facility that Chris and Sheva blasted their way through in the main campaign.

This DLC, unlike Lost in Nightmares, is action-packed, just like the main campaign. There are explosions, gunfire, hordes Majini - you get the idea. There isn't as much to talk about in this DLC, unlike Lost in Nightmares, so I'll be brief. This DLC is pretty good, but a bit too similar to the main campaign for my tastes. I much preferred the unique feel of Lost in Nightmares. However, it is still pretty fun, but it is nowhere near as solid as the other DLC.

Finally, there is Mercenaries Reunion, which is basically Mercenaries mode, but with different characters. It may just be me, but there also seems to be more Majini than there were in the standard Mercenaries mode. Again, it may just be me. All the new characters are awesome, especially characters like Barry Burton, with his sniper rifle, handgun, and revolver, and Chris Redfield's "warrior" outfit, which comes packed with a handgun, rifle, and an amazing shotgun. There are no new maps in Mercenaries Reunion, unfortunately, but Mercenaries Reunion is still a great mode that's even better with a friend.

Overall, the DLC for the game is extremely fun. Even fans of the older Resident Evil games should try out Lost in Nightmares, as it is extremely fun and terrifying. If you already have RE5, then you should buy the DLC separately. However, if you haven't played RE5, then this is the edition to get.

Games like Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row get most of the attention, but this game (which originally was part of the True Crime series, to be named True Crime: Hong Kong, was canceled and the rights picked up by Square Enix, and rebranded Sleeping Dogs) is an incredible amount of fun to play in its own right.

The main character, Wei Shen, comes over from the US to help the cops, and it turns into a very twisted, awesome story in which lines are crossed and friends end up being betrayed (or killed). The ending of the Triad storyline, especially, is incredibly satisfying, which I won't spoil but is great :)

The "story" is made up of the aformentioned Triad storylines and as well as the Cop storyline (Triad shows up as Green on your map, Cop ones are blue). No mission is truly impossible or controller smashing difficult (something that Grand Theft Auto IV definitely can't claim), but some are challenging enough where if you do not obtain the upgrades from the health shrines (increases your max health) or increase your face meter (which bestows buffs/benefits to Wei) that you CAN die if you're reckless.

For those "trophy hunters" out there, this is also a VERY easy platinum, the only frustrating part is obtaining the Gold for the "Pure Gold" trophy, as it requires you to win $1M gambling, and only one cockfight will give you the ability to bet enough to do this, and it's COMPLETELY RANDOM. Meaning, you better save before each attempt. It took me 2 hours of grinding before I finally achieved enough wins to earn the $1M. Everything else (relatively speaking) is a piece of cake.

I really could not find a reason to drop a star on this game at all. In over 30 hours of gameplay, it never froze my PS3 once. I cannot say that, honestly, about any other PS3 game I have played (for comparison, Fallout 3 and New Vegas, Skyrim and Borderlands 2 have all done it more then 5 times each). The game rarely stutters or slows. The radio stations are nice and varies. The combat is fluid and adds a lot of room for improvisation. Maybe the only gripe (if I had bought this brand new) is the story parts end up being a little short, so if that's all you are playing it for, that might disappoint you a bit. If you intend to do everything, you will definitely get your money's worth especially at the current price point ($14.99 or less).

Finally, the language is DEFINITELY bad in this game (Including words that Grand Theft Auto V didn't use, and I thought THAT game was bad enough). If that's something that's a turn off, then I'd look elsewhere. The game definitely lives up to its mature rating on the box.

All of the Resistance games together tell a great story, however you will only be able to experience 1/2 of the equation.

As of this week, Sony shut down the online servers for all 3 Resistance games, meaning:
- You cannot access online multiplayer for any of the titles
- All the associated trophies for online multiplayer are unobtainable, meaning the Platinum for Resistance 1, 2 and 3 are now no longer obtainable.

If you're good with having the single player campaigns only (which clock in at about 8-15 hours each), even then I would not pay the $35 being asked (FOR SURE) and even the $25 I have seen on the Warehouse Deals.

So Buyer BEWARE...you are NOT getting 3 full games. You're getting 3 full single player campaigns and no multiplayer.

First of all, full disclosure: I've never heard of One Piece outside of games offered on PSN and had never played one until One Piece Unlimited World.

This game is, in a word, NUTS! If you don't know anything about One Piece you have no idea what's going on.
Secondly, definitely heed the "Teen" title on this game, right away you're seeing a very well drawn woman in scant clothing with big tatas...it might make your teen go ga-ga but it's definitely age inappropriate below that (as well as some of the dialog in the game).

The actual "Game" borrows action components from others before it (a little Dynasty Warriors here, a little Naruto there, Kingdom Hearts, etc). This doesn't mean it's not fun to play, far from it! It's easy to pick up and learn.

Expect the main story to run 20-25 hours and then you have Colisseum mode which allows you to unlock more goodies. Finally, as others have said, you can cook, fish etc. with your friends online.

One Piece is definitely out there, but it's also refreshing in a COD/Battlefield rehash world. And I see this easily being a collectors item (read: poor selling in the US) so it might be one of those games you buy two of; one to play and one to keep sealed.

I had only dabbled about an hour in Saints Row II and Saints Row: The Third before starting Saints Row IV (by comparison, I probably wasted a good 40-60 hours in GTA: Vice City and GTA V). I got it free through Playstation Plus.

And...wow. What a game. One that doesn't take itself or anything seriously...at all.

The plot is pretty simple: The Saints run the US. Then the aliens invade, wipe Earth off the map, and you end up in a virtual version of Steelport from Saints Row: The Third (So when people are saying "Saints Row 3.5", that's pretty much why).

The main protagonist, Zinyak, is wonderfully voice acted and proves a good villian to the Saints attempt to bring him down.

The side missions are very important, not only giving you upgrade versions of your homies, but unlock both weapon and superpower upgrades and give needed "cache" (cash) and experience.

There is also great incentive to get to level 50, as that makes all ammo unlimited. This allows you to choose the weapons you love the most and not have to worry about anything but kicking Zin butt.

All the superpowers are cool, and you really won't be driving a car much, once you unlock the Unlimited Super Sprint and the Glide/Wall climbing abilities, you'll be doing that all over Steelport.

This game is an incredible amount of fun, and the language is right there on par with any Grand Theft Auto game, so it's not something to really let your 10 year old play (not to mention, the various "romancing" options between the President and the other Saints, which I will not spoil as they are hilarious enough on their own).

If you didn't get this through PS+, it's at a price point ($12-15 used, and the National Treasure Edition, which gives you ALL 50 (!!!) pieces of DLC for $29.99) where it's well worth every penny of that and more.

If you're sick of GTA and want a different take, this game comes heavily recommended, as I'm sure someone is working on Saints Row 5 that will likely be in a new location (Steelport in SR: The Third and then simulated (blown up) in SR:4...seems to me like they are going in a different direction).

I played through all of Diablo III on the PS3 and, alas, didn't have my Diablo III copy on PS3 as I was going to get the update for my PS4, so sadly, long story short, I couldn't import my PS3 save to my PS4.

TDRL: You MUST have a copy of Diablo III on the PS3 to import your save to the PS4 (Unless you previously did this to Battle.net when you owned the game). You have been warned!

So I started a new character (Crusader, which is the new add under the Reaper of Souls expansion) and started from the beginning. I'm through Act I and will update this review as I keep progressing.

What has stood out for me so far:
- Absolutely no loading screens or lag. It's amazing it has taken video games this long to get so seamless, and man, is Diablo III seamless. Once it's loaded, that's it. No "now loading" to be had.
- The gameplay is just as tight and refined as Diablo III on PS3, just looks a HECK of a lot prettier and runs butter smooth with no lag whatsoever. I did see a couple weird instances where the enemy's name would appear but the actual "enemy" was about a second late, but it's very minor and has zero effect on the gameplay itself.
- You not only get a free piece of gear with the game, but you also get another one if you link your PSN account to your Battle.net account. Sweet!
- The company line from Blizzard is that you'd see a piece of legendary gear every hour of gametime, maybe it's because I started over and am on Normal, but in 4 hours I haven't seen one. I've gotten a few Rare items. Your experience may vary.
- The "Reaper of Souls" only adds the one character and one more Act. So it's really not all that, truth to be told, unless you're REALLY into Diablo in which case at the end game (Level 60+ there ARE a ton of things to do, the Paragon system, the varies dungeons that randomly develop once you're inside and throw insane groups at you, just like with WoW, Blizzard is trying to get the competitive co-op gameplay in with Diablo as well.
- For my money, it's absolutely the best use of the touchpad of any game released for the PS4 to day. VERY intuitive. It frees up all the face/shoulder buttons to be used for skills and let's the player push the touchpad to bring up the inventory. Well done, Blizzard!
- Oh, and the Dodge button (circle). What a lifesaver that baby is!

All in all, it's the definitive version of Diablo III and when you consider there are 6 characters, if you intend to take them all to 60 and beyond (kinda like I did with Borderlands 2, a game I put well north of 200 hours into all told), it's a great value at $59.99 and instantly slots as one of the best games of the PS4, if not just a shade below TLOU: Remastered in terms of PS3 to PS4 ports. Buy with confidence and get to killing some demons :)

After the mess that was the Final Fantasy XIII series (some would say, a series ending detour but that's a bit harsh), and with Square working on Final Fantasy XV, which is showing much promise, we have Final Fantasy Type-0 HD to fill the void.

For the uninitiated, Final Fantasy Type-0 was a game only released overseas, and was supposed to be brought to the US but for many reasons was never released (probably the biggest of which is projected sales). Let's get this out of the way, straight up: This game doesn't even come close to pushing the graphical ability of next gen consoles. There are parts of this game that look like a PSP game, so if you're expected Bloodborne level graphics you'll in for a rude awakening.

Next, in 2015 some of the things this game does are simply unacceptable. The camera, wonky and possessed. The inventory screens are clunky. At a shop, there's no up or down arrow to tell you if this item will make your character more or less powerful. The English voice acting is atrocious (stick to the Japanese to get the true feeling, MUCH superior).

So why did I give this 4 stars? It's Final Fantasy going in a different direction. This is the most action-oriented FF released since another PSP Game (Crisis Core), but it's WAY deeper than that. You have 12 different characters to choose from and any 3 can be in battle at the same time (you control one, the AI controls 2). If one gets KO, one of you remaining characters joins in. The key to this is, once they are KO'd, they are out of the game until the mission is over. So, let's say you have a mission where you need a ranged character to take out ranged enemies. If you're not careful and all your ranged characters are KO'd, those ranged enemies will slaughter you. It makes each battle have weight to it, unlike the whole "Phoenix Down/Characters restored after battle" feel of other FF games.

And this game isn't your fathers FF in another way: It's violent. The first 10 minutes of this game will shake you to the core and I won't spoil it, needless to say you aren't seeing this in another FF game, more than likely. And it's good for the franchise.

In between missions you have more options on what to do with your time. You have a certain number of days/hours between them, and every action you take decreases this time. Do you go out and do random encounters? Do you talk to other characters? Do you take classes and level up? One thing is for sure: Make the WRONG choices and you might end up having to replay earlier missions because your level won't be high enough to advance.

In short, many people are buying Type-0 as a $60 demo for the first 2 hours for Final Fantast XV. But you're not just getting a game you should turn around and trade for $37 on Amazon. You're getting a nice, in-depth experience and look at new ideas that could just help revitalize this series, after it's gone stale and nearly dead in the water the past several years. And that's a great thing.

So far I've managed to play through the first area of the game, and that's doing every side-quest and location.

I've never played a Witcher game before but give me an open world RPG and I'm a sucker.

I'll try to stick to bullet points rather than write an opus:
Graphics: Incredible but, of course, pop-in still hasn't be solved. There was one cut-scene where a tree was popping through the wall of a log cabin. That must have been one strong Spruce.

Sound: Equally amazing. The music when you are in the open world is great and the voice-acting is top-notch, not just limited to the main characters but the NPC's as well.

Gameplay: This is where, I suppose, you could cut a 1/2 star or so. It can get a little clumsy, especially getting mounted/unmounted and jumping/dodging. On anything outside of the easiest difficulty, if you try and run into a pack you will get slaughtered. So there is a pinch of "Souls" here though by no means am I comparing this to that bundle of frustration in any way.

Interface: You could dock a 1/2 star here too. Skyrim's inventory=magical. Witcher's inventory: OMG why??? The PS4 is not a PC. And that's what this seems set up for is PC (click on what you want, etc). For the Gods I hope they patch this or do something different.

Replayability: Are you serious? This is looking at 200+ hours and there are 30-40 more coming if you have the season pass. If this isn't enough for you, IDK what to say. Maybe get a life? LOL

Overall: This game, for me, is miles better than Dragon Age: Inquisition and should hold the PS4 RPG crown until Fallout 4 or the next Skyrim comes along.

You know, Gamefly *IS* overpriced, but it's times like this I'm eternally grateful for that service.

I got this 2 days after release as it was at the top of my Q. I put the game in, and, all I can say is it was massively disappointing.

While I wasn't expecting Skyrim on PS4 level graphics, most of them look like a very early gen PS3 game.

I DID expect to be able to stay online more than a few minutes, instead of getting kicked out of the server.
In fact, it took me a full HOUR just to get online (While the statement "You are #1 in the queue, estimated wait is 1 minute" just stayed there and mocked me).
When I got there, it's simply a broken game. Even trying to use my own markers, I constantly got lost going from quest to quest. That is, IF the person I needed to talk to or turn in even existed. Which would mean...restarting the game.

Drobot is a Tech Skylander.  He is basically a mechanical dragon that can shoot lasers and spinning razors.  In the game, Drobot can be extremely powerful after upgrading Drobot's lasers, so he has a lot of potential in-game.  Before buying this version, note that there is another option available: the Series 2 edition.  This version does not light up and it does not have the Lightcore "flash bomb" effect that damages all on-screen enemies the first time it is activated.  However, it does have a Wow Pow upgrade available, which adds a bonus effect to the character's attacks.  I would recommend the Series 2 version unless it is significantly more expensive than this one.

The game Skylanders: Giants is basically a game where you play as different characters through a series of chapters that eventually create the entire plot of the game.  The character you play as depends on the figure you decide to activate.  In this case, it's Hot Head, a Fire Giant.  Like other Skylanders, he becomes playable in the game and unlocks some bonus material (such as a Heroic Challenge mini-game and the opportunity to unlock rooms available only to Fire Skylanders).  He's a fun character to play as, and the toy is high-quality.  I'd recommend it if you're looking for a gift to someone who plays the game or you want to add to your own collection.

The Classic Controller is modeled after the game controllers from earlier Nintendo systems, such as the Nintendo GameCube or the Nintendo 64.  It connects to your Wii Remote in the place of the Nunchuk Remote.  This remote can be used to play Virtual Console games (classic games from decades before that have been re-released for the Wii), and it can also play select Wii/Wii U games.  I originally bought this controller to play two Virtual Console games I bought (Super Metroid and Super Mario 64), and it has worked excellently.

I'd like to give this product one star because it's really annoying to play against in player vs. player mode, but that really means it deserves a good rating.  Zoo Lou is a pretty interesting Skylander.  His abilities come from summoning animals, like a flock of birds to fly toward the enemy, a boar to ride, and a wolf to fight and find food.  These are pretty good skills; while the boar is kind of uninteresting in my opinion, the wolf finds food, which is very useful for both story and player vs. player mode, and the bird is a good attack all-around.

Free Ranger.  A ninja chicken that channels the power of the wind.  Kind of weird, undoubtedly, but pretty fun to play.  His gameplay on its own is average, but as a Swap Skylander with spinning powers, Free Ranger can unlock special Swap Zone challenges for bonus content in SWAP Force.  He can also "swap" halves with other swappable Skylanders to create new Skylander combinations with different ability sets.

To fully use all the content available in Trap Team, you will need 8 Trap Masters (large Skylanders with impressive crystal weapons) and 9 Traps (crystal figures used to hold bonus characters). You get 1 Trap Master and 2 Traps from the Starter Pack, so you'll need 7 Masters and 7 Traps (1 from each of the remaining elements). This means you'll be spending about $140 (minimum; estimating $15 per Trap Master and $5 per Trap, not counting any tax or shipping costs). That's a lot of money.
However, that's only if you plan to spend the money on all the content. If you just want an extra Trap to play a few bonus characters, that's fine too. The Air Trap does exactly what it's supposed to do; it holds Air Element villains. Whether you want to spend a few dollars on a single Trap, or you want to go all-in and get everything, this Air Trap is definitely a nice piece.

Shroomboom is pretty fun to play in the Skylanders games.  He's a giant mushroom who uses a slingshot to shoot spores or himself at his enemies, and he can also summon a ring of mushrooms around himself.  It can feel kind of repetitive if you play him a lot, but don't get me wrong - he's still a lot of fun overall and is pretty useful through the games.  One issue though, is that he's a core Skylander who doesn't really bring any special qualities to let him unlock special features in the game, so you might want to consider getting something like a Trap Master or Giant if you're looking to buy Skylanders.

Enigma's actually a really cool Skylander.  Of course, the idea of a spectral wizard is nothing new, but that doesn't make them any less cool.  Enigma's playstyle involves invisibility and casting laser spells, both of which sound pretty cool.  As a Skylander, his figurine is also interesting: his colors fade until his feet and the bottom of his cape become transparent, and the hood of his cloak is actually empty, really making him feel like a ghost.  Anyway, he feels like one of the more serious Skylanders, as opposed to some of the characters who feel more like comic relief or gag figures, both in-game and as a toy.

I bought this for my then four-year-old nephew. Since I'm a gamer, he's always wanted to play the games I play, such as Super Mario, but doesn't know how. So after Googling about video games that are suitable for preschoolers, I stumbled on this. He also loves Diego, so that was a plus.

Go Diego Go Safari Rescue is a good, introductory game for little, newbie gamers. Diego's voice is the same as the series. The storyline is linear and simple: Diego needs to rescue the elephants from the evil sorceress, and he helps the safari animals he encounters on his journey. The story isn't scary and very child-friendly. I haven't heard my nieces or nephew ( they've all played the game lol and they were all under the age of five at the time ) tell me that they got scared while playing it. Additionally, Diego doesn't "die" or fall off an edge, which saves kids from ample frustration.

You don't need the nunchuk for this game which was favorable. All your child has to do is tilt the Wiimote, while holding it horizontally using both hands, in order to prompt Diego to walk/run, and the 2 button is to jump. That's it. You also get an on-screen prompt image of doing certain moves using the wiimote. The moves are uncomplicated and very simple, such as shaking the Wiimote back and forth in order to shake a tree. There are several types of moves which should entertain your kid and get their upper body moving.

My nephew loved the rescue pack mini games - you get to choose from different items (such as a zip line) in order to aid you through your journey. It was fun seeing him maneuver the wiimote and choose the correct item. You also get to choose the correct animal that Diego is helping, so your child gets to learn the names of the different animals which I found pretty neat.

As an adult, I found this game very repetitive and boring like Candy Land, but my nephew liked this game a lot. I have also bought Go Diego Go Great Dinosaur Rescue, Dora Saves the Crystal Kingdom, and Dora Saves the Snow Princess. The format, level design for each one of them was the same as Go Diego Go Safari Rescue, and I have regretted buying them. So for example instead of Diego sliding down a muddy cliff using a board, Dora gets to ice skate. This is a good game, but if you decide to buy it, then don't buy the rest.

I believe kids above the age of 5 or 6 will get bored from it. Right now my nephew is six and he stopped playing with it several months ago because he'd much rather play Lego video games. This game is a good game for preschoolers and to introduce them to the world of gaming, but in my opinion, its appeal will only last a year or two. I hope you find this review helpful in basing your purchase decision.

After finishing Dead Space 1, I eagerly borrowed Dead Space 2 from a friend in order to play it (and now I'm definitely going to buy a copy). I loved the first part, so I couldn't believe that I'd love the second part more than the first! I love horror games and scaring myself silly, and nowadays survival horror games are few and far between. So, this game is absolutely amazing! It's a combination of survival horror and action, similar to Resident Evil 4. I wish there were more games like this.

I found Dead Space 2 less scary than the first part, but it's atmospheric nonetheless. In Dead Space 1, Issac had to roam through tight, dark corridors, so the scare factor was RELENTLESS. Dead Space 2 is still very scary, but it's slightly more open spaced than its predecessor. The new monsters such as "The Sprawl." A pack of screaming monsters which resemble children terrified me! Once they get ahold of you, it's hard to free yourself.

In Dead Space 2, the graphics are more polished and outstanding! Unlike the first part, Issac can now speak. The voice acting was excellent. I wasn't a fan of the holographic map in Dead Space 1, so I was delighted to find out that it was replaced. Instead of consulting the map for the Bench, Store, Save Stations, you can find out by pressing R3. You get different colored lights for each one. I found this feature very convenient.

Another difference was that you can now re-fill your health bar by pressing the O button. In Dead Space 1, while I was in the middle of battling (and whimpering LOL) the army of Necromorphs, I had to open my inventory in order to re-fill my depleted health. So in those precious seconds, Issac usually got his behind mauled. So I'm thankful that the producers fine-tuned this feature.

Additionally, the producers have fine-tuned the zero gravity area by enabling Issac to fly instead of jumping to other platforms (like in Dead Space 1). So getting to other platforms is swifter and fun!

I also noticed that the Stasis module duration doesn't last long in Dead Space 2 as opposed to 1. It could be my imagination, but you could solve it by upgrading your stasis at the Bench.

Another nice feature is that the game provides you with claws (from the dead Necromorphs) and sharp-looking objects that resemble a spear in order to attack the enemies. It's a great way to save ammunition. However, I'm what you can call trigger-happy so despite my efforts, I end up shooting blindly (especially when I'm flustered and petrified :p).

Last but not least, the annoying asteroid-shooting mini game is gone in Dead Space 2! I can't tell you how many times I've died during that horrible mini-game (which just increased my frustration). I'm sure I'm not the only one who's relieved to know it wasn't featured again in this game.

The game starts with Issac running away from a mob of Necromorphs while strapped in a strait jacket. Swell, right? When I was running away with my heart in my throat, I just knew that this was the start of an impending doom for poor little me. The producers have outdone themselves with this game. It deserves to be owned by every gamer who loves survival horror or just to play a fantastic game. Everything ranging from the graphics to the controls is simply splendid. It goes without saying that I highly recommend this game. I advise you to play Dead Space 1 first in order to understand and follow the story. I hope you enjoy playing this game as much as I did!

I bought this screen protector for my newly purchased Wii U gamepad. After an extensive research and via the reviews here at Amazon.com, I decided to purchase Hori. It's supposed to be Nintendo licensed and the best on the market. I haven't used my gamepad except to adjust the settings. So I followed the instructions carefully on how to apply the screen protector and even checked out a YouTube video and it was very easy to apply even to someone like me who is not dexterous. There were a few air bubbles but I was able to smooth them out except for one because the screen protector I received had a dent. So the air bubble was trapped under it. (I asked Amazon for a replacement so that's not the reason for my one star review. )

The main reason for my poor star rating is simply because the gamepad became absolutely unresponsive. At first I thought it was odd since my gamepad was working beautifully. Whenever I tried to access the game or press any icon on the screen, it wouldn't respond at all or it would become wonky and the homepage would jerk from side to side. I recalled another reviewer for the 3DS's Hori screen protector saying that her/his touchscreen was non-responsive after using it.
So I decided to take it off and the second I took it off my gamepad became responsive again. I don't recommend this screen protector at all. I loved its easy application, but it was pointless since it rendered my gamepad unresponsive. What a complete waste of money.

UPDATE:

So I received my replacement for the damaged one, and after applying it, my touch screen has become responsive. As I've originally said, the air bubbles could be smoothed out and its application is as easy as ABC. Do I recommend this product? Not really- since it's packaging is awful, it's almost like gambling your money away. Many people have complained about its packaging, and I agree. Plus, it doesn't seem to be a reliable product since it made my touch screen go wonky. Another issue I have is that it does not cover the entire screen so that means that dust could creep into its parameters. If you have cash to burn or don't mind buying two of these filters just in case one of them is damaged, then I say go for it.

When I purchased my 3DS XL, one of the first few games I got was this. After reading the reviews, I decided to try it. It didn't disappoint.

This is such a fun, charming, and creative game. The music is also very engaging. You play as Maxwell, and you must collect starites by creating objects. The sky is the limit. You type up the words and then presto, an object is formed. For example: You need to eradicate the dinosaurs without the use of weaponry or asteroids. Sometimes you're required to think outside the box. It's really fun to play with the words, especially with the game's massive vocabulary. There is a caveat: sometimes there are certain objects that do not fit. This game is child-friendly, so profane images aren't accepted by the game's data bank. I read a review where a person tried to create phallic images and was disappointed when the game didn't do that.

You receive a tutorial at the beginning in order to get you attuned with the controls and basic gameplay. You can either use the stylus or D-pad to move Maxwell.

I am a right-brained person, and consider myself creative. So this game appealed to me very much. It may look kiddish and the graphics aren't all that polished, but I think if you are in touch with your creative side and love solving puzzles, you will love this game, regardless of your age. I wished it was more open world. (Scribblenauts Unlimited is a sandbox mode.)

This game is suitable for people ages 5 - 100. It requires reading and spelling. (If you spell the word wrong, the game gives you the correct spelling.) It's a "fun" way to teach kids how to read and write. I find it very educational for a video game.

I bought this for my 3DS XL. While I'm not wildly crazy about it, I am content with it. It's easy to put on your device. I have small, feminine hands with slender fingers, so the grip was comfortable. I can remove the stylus with ease. The reason I didn't give it five stars is because it seems to me that it doesn't fit the device as snugly as it should. Plus, every time I have to remove/ put in a game, I have to lift the flap from behind because it seems to overlap it. That's my personal opinion. However, don't let it dissuade you from buying it. As I've previously said, I am happy with it and its texture is smooth and soft. It makes gaming on it very comfortable.

I caved and bought the basic Wii U solely for this LEGO title. I am a huge LEGO fan and have played all of the available titles on my PS3. So when I found out that Lego City was a Wii U exclusive, I was bummed.

I grew up playing Nintendo since the late 80s. So I am a Nintendo gal. That said, when I purchased the Wii, I never got used to the Wii mote and the nunchuk. I like the traditional controller. So when they announced the release of this console, I initially decided against buying it, since I thought that the Wii U gamepad was too gimmicky. It turns out I was wrong. Massively wrong.

LEGO City Undercover showcases the gamepad's features. So far, I'm only in chapter 5, but its features are the following (if I discover any more features, I'll edit this review): a. can scan for hidden collectibles and suspects (which is addicting - I found myself scanning the environment instead of embarking on my mission).

b. shows you the City's gargantuan map

c. Listen to audio conversations

d. Engage in video chats with your colleagues, etc.

The gamepad is very interactive, and I'm loving it so far! (On that note: the battery drains fast, so keep the charger next to you while playing.)

Lego City Undercover is probably the BEST outta all the titles. It was worth every cent. Its environment is amazingly colossal! It's much, much, much bigger than the Lord of the Rings and Batman 2. I knew prior to purchasing it that the City is huge, but I honestly didn't expect it to be this vast! I found myself exploring the areas. The view was simply spectacular as I was standing atop a bridge. It's so obvious that the producers put a lot of thought and detail into this game. Kudos to them.

I wish that Lego City Undercover is a two-player game. My six-year-old nephew and I always play the LEGO games together, so I'm disappointed that it isn't available for this title.

There is a lot of driving in this game (and since I am not a big fan of driving vehicles in any video game, I mentally groaned). My six-year-old nephew tried driving and then handed the controller to me (as if his aunt could do a better job lol). I ended up running over pedestrians and smashing into everything. The game thankfully doesn't penalize you for your accidents. The driving is MUCH better than Indiana Jones 2, but it is still a bit of a chore. (That said, I am getting the hang of it.) Luckily, I learned that you could hail a cab and you could be driven to your destination. So I can't complain much.

Another teeny tiny gripe: I occasionally found out that I can't rotate the camera (using the right analog stick) 360 degrees.

Also, the loading time is very long. Too long by any standard. Personally, I don't mind waiting, since the game makes up for it.

Despite my minor gripes, I gave it a five star. I love this game so much and I'm still early in the game. The graphics are simply stunning. The dialogue is funny and witty! It's the ideal game for the whole family. I can tell right off the bat that its replayability factor is high. You can unlock many disguises throughout your playthrough. For example: A miner's outfit, a robber's outfit, etc. I love the "special effects" when Chase McCain gets suspended in mid-air while driving, a la Hollywood. I also love the martial arts. Instead of mashing your button while in attack mode, you can do certain techniques. It's fun.

If you're a Lego fan, then I recommend that you buy it. If you haven't played any Lego title before, then this game comes highly recommended from me. If you want to play with another person, then I suggest you pick up The Lord of the Rings (since it has an offline co-op mode). I can't tell you how many times my six year-old nephew made me play it with him. There came a time when I actually hid it from him.

Plants vs Zombies is an amazing tower defense game which has taken the gaming world by storm. This game has humorous, cartoonish animation and mild violence.

Your job is to stop the army of the undead from entering your home and eating your brains by soiling your lawn with plants. Each plant has its strengths and weaknesses; offensive and defensive mechanisms. The gameplay is very simple, yet challenging (but not impossible to defeat). There's no single right way of playing this game, since each person has a different strategy that works for him/her.

As a person whose heart palpitates at the sight of zombies (and sometimes I squeeze my eyes shut - LOL - I'm no warrior) while playing Resident Evil and the Walking Dead, I simply loved the zombies in this game. They've got style! They range from cheerleading zombies to zombies donning a ducky flotation device. You can't help but love 'em. After completing each level, you receive "sinister" letters from the colorful undead.

After playing this highly addictive game on my android, I just had to get it a PS3 version. At first, I was skeptical as to how well it's going to translate onto the big-screen. However, I threw caution to the wind and decided to buy it.

Truthfully, I expected it to be a lot harder to play it here than on my android. It isn't as easy as playing it on my android/tablet, but it isn't as hard as I thought it would be. (I used my Dual Shock controller.) You collect the sun and coins by moving the analog stick over them. So you needn't to press any buttons. You plant by scrolling through your list of plants (L1 & R1) and then pressing X. While with the android version you just tap on the selected plant, the PS3 version requires you to scroll through the plants. This was a bit of a chore, since this game requires quick-thinking/action.

I played this game with my six-year-old nephew and it was a blast playing co-op. You get a lot of things in done in half the time. Unlike the android/tablet version, you don't get any access to coin packages (which was a shame). By level 2-4, you receive the Almanac book. By level 3-4, you get Crazy Dave's car keys and you could buy stuff.

Unlike Survival Mode and other mini games, you don't need to finish the Adventure Mode in order to play the Versus Mode. (And if memory serves me right, it gets unlocked right after finishing level 1.) The Versus mode is a two player game where you either play as Team Zombies or Team Plants.

If you're on the fence about buying the console version, then I say go for it. It's worth owning, especially for the leaderboards, co-op mode, and versus mode.

First off, this game will be released in parts. From what I’ve read, it will be 3, possibly 4 parts. Most likely each game will be $60. SE has done this in the past but with those games, each part was pretty much a full game (FF13 had 3 parts and FF10 had 2 parts for example). The developers were saying that they can’t release it all in one game bc it’s too big but if each part is 35 hours and there’s 3 parts, that’s 105 hours. I went through FF13 and completed about 80% of the entire game (100% main story plus most side quests) and I finished it in 112 hours. Not sure why ps3 discs and console can handle big games but ps4 discs and consoles can’t? Something doesn’t add up.

Combat: a lot like FF15. Action based, blocking, hacking with some abilities or magic used in between. Sometimes gets dull but boss fights are fun. It’s not turn based Like the original or FF9 and not actual turn based like FF13.

Story: good story, but 90% linear. It’s very similar to FF13 in the regard that it’s very linear but FF13 was a long game, (about 60-80 hours with some open world), so to me, the linear-ness was justified. Unfortunately, FF7 isn’t as long as you can finish it in 30-35 hours easily. It’s disappointing bc If it’s 3 parts, we’ll end up paying $180 for what will ultimately take 100 hours to beat. The story itself is enticing and very good, like the original. There’s really not much for side quests until you get to certain parts of the game that tells you that you should help people and then people give you side quests. It’s not like most RPGs where you can switch between main and side quests anytime.

Overall opinion: I gave it a 4/5 but if I could I’d go 3.5/5. It’s a solid game and it’s very nice to be able to play as these beloved characters like we all did years ago. It being in parts is annoying and makes it feel like a cash grab. Hopefully they give a discount for the other parts instead of full price. Either way, good game but I’m not sure if it’s worth it. I’d wait until it’s about $30 or $40 and then get it.

I like to only play the very best games, because I have other things to do in my life. RDR2 is one of the best games ever made and a must play. You will enjoy riding your horse through all the wilderness. There's regular areas with lots of pine trees. There's snowy, wintery mountain areas. And there's some hot, swampy areas. I remember not being the biggest fan of this when it was new, but after giving it a shot, it is genuinely a good game. The biggest problems with it is the fatalities are butchered, but when you consider the inclusion of 70 fighters, it makes sense. The next biggest issue is Motaro, there's not really much of an excuse for that, there may have been problems with him as a fighter but they could've cut him out completely instead. I remember being terrified of the Wii version as well because the idea of motion controls and Mortal Kombat is a nauseating idea. Thankfully they did not do that, it plays with a normal controller like a normal video game should. I would call the Wii version the definitive/best version as it includes Khameleon and Wii U support meaning you can play it in a better visual quality than the Xbox or PS2. The Konquest mode is really good, it plays like a watered down beat em up instead of an open world tutorial like Deception. You play as one character the entire time, so you get plenty of time to learn and practise. The characters moveset is super user friendly and easy to handle unlike Shujinko in Deception. It's super easy to complete and unlock everything, the Konquest mode is fairly short, but still super fun. The only issue with Konquest on Wii is unskippable cutscenes while the PS2 version allows you to skip them. The rest of the game is standard MK, everyone gets two fighting styles: With weapon/Without weapon. It has a lot of fanservice to the entire series, including levels from MK5, MK6, MK3, so on. I would say it's one of the best games on the Wii and worth a go if you've ever had doubts about it.

I always had issues playing GH 1-3 and never understood why people liked them, plus I play Bass guitar so the first three limit my ability to play that as well. The slider can act as a whammy bar for sustain notes, or like the bottom row of buttons used in Rock Band Guitars for solos (they are purple framed notes, you can use the slider or regular buttons to hit them). However 10 years later I'm having a bit of issues and I don't know if it's the game or the fact that I've upgraded my TV since initial release, but the timing window seems, too generous. So if there is a string of notes, you kind of need to break rhythm in order to hit the needs because the timing window is 20 seconds wide. This wasn't only the case, but it's an issue I have now, hopefully you don't encounter this because I do think it's a great game.

There's dialogue scenes between each level which I didn't mind but I wouldn't blame you at all if that wasn't your thing. The first and last one are the longest, while the middle ones can be done in about 5 minutes. The levels are pretty beefy, so I'd only recommend doing one at a time just so you don't exhaust yourself. That's about it though. It's fun, super simple, better than I thought it would be. Despite the idea that it was marketed as "buy the game or else no NMH3" that's not the truth at all. It was worded that way just so people wouldn't skim over it. Despite the trashy marketing, it's perfectly fine and costs half as much as most modern games anyway.
