I've been playing Pokemon since the first games came to the US, but I've only actually beaten three or four of them. Red, Sun (only because I forced myself to), maybe one other, and now this. And yes, I own just about all of them. For me, they become real slogs the closer I get to the end, so I generally get to the Elite 4 and then lose interest. There are too many Pokemon to catch, too much grinding to do, and then there's the prospect of an entire new region to explore in the post-game. It's just not appealing to me.

Enter this game. There are still a number of things that need improving, but I'll start with what I like.

-Fewer Pokemon. I've been saying for years that they need to stop adding more Pokemon and was pleasantly surprised when they actually cut back on the number for this game. I realize many people are complaining about it, but it was absolutely the right call. Right off the bat, there are tons of great Pokemon to choose from. They all feel relatively balanced, so my choice is just personal preference. On top of that, removing many of my default choices has forced me to pick an almost entirely different team. And I'm glad I did, there are so many Pokemon I have ignored over the years.

-The wild area is pretty cool. You can just roam around to different areas (or fly to them if you want), pick up items, fight Pokemon, join raids... it's just a really neat addition. It's also fun when you are online and can see other players roaming around, kind of like Dark Souls in that regard.

-The story is finally the right length for me. Seems like you could get through it in about 20 hours or so (maybe less), so it never feels like it's dragging on.

-Raid battles with friends are tons of fun and the rewards are excellent. It's much more fun to grind out levels when you're working cooperatively with others. Since experience is granted via candies, you can divide it up however you want. And you get TRs (the new limited-use TMs, since HMs are completely gone now) and other goodies. I suspect raids will be the main draw in the post-game.

-While I'm not that into the Dynamax thing on the whole, I do like that they got rid of all the mega evolutions and other nonsense they've had in recent games.

And a lot of quality of life things that just get rid of the tedium of flying all over and remembering where things are:
-Love being able to access the PC from anywhere. Additionally, any time you heal at a Pokemon Center, the Pokemon in your PC heal, too. So much simpler.
-Move deleter/rememberer/name rater in every Pokemon Center!
-Healing automatically after certain major battles so I don't have to waste time going back to the Pokemon Center.
-Camping so I don't have to waste time going to a Pokemon Center.
-Items to let you change natures and abilities in the post-game so I don't have to waste time trying to catch 5 of the same 1% chance Pokemon just to get the right one.

With all that said, there are a number of things that need some improvement:

-The network connection bits in general. By default, the game loads you into local wireless communication. This means that the entire system is disconnected from the internet. You can't even look at your friends list without changing the connection mode. If I want to play with friends that aren't in the room with me, I have to manually tell the game to connect to the internet. That's fine, but any time I go back to the home menu or put the console to sleep, the game disconnects me and I have to manually reconnect again. On top of that, the battery drains incredibly quickly because of the way the game uses the connection. Like twice as fast as any other game, it's insane. Finally, sometimes my friend will post that he's opening a raid but it just doesn't show up on my end for some unknown reason. Either he has to restart it or I have to reconnect. It's irritating. Lots of work to be done on the networking front.

-While I like the wild area now, I think they toss you into it a little too soon (or at least have it a little too open too soon). I spent a while just wondering around before the first gym because it felt like I had to explore everything before I moved on. It got to be a little overwhelming - too many places to go, too many Pokemon to choose from. And by the time I moved on, I was a bit overleveled. I really think this could have been done better.

-Dynamax generally. I have never been a fan of gimmick mechanics, but this one especially is quite useless. It gives you a couple new moves and more HP. I suppose they added it because people would've complained if wild raid Pokemon were the only ones who could use it, but... on that front, I am not a fan of the shield mechanic employed by raids. I don't necessarily mind that they put up shields, but I hate that it happens at set HP points and, more annoyingly, that any damage beyond that fixed point is simply negated. It's really frustrating. Maybe if the damage had been reduced by a percentage instead it wouldn't feel so cheap.

-Having to walk around "cliffs" that are ankle height. Like... come on, really? Surely we can move on from the old mechanics.

So, in summary, the game feels like a breath of fresh air. Gen 2 was probably the last time I thought the game was new and interesting, but this has reigniting that excitement for me. I really hope the fix some of the negatives and improve on the positives for future entries in the series.

There's a lot that appeals to me about this game, so I'll start there:
-I love the art. It's just awesome.
-It's a "metroidvania" and I generally enjoy those.
-It has an interesting story.
-It's challenging (not always in a good way, though, more on that below).

But there are really just a handful of things that really hold it back for me. It seems to me like it takes a lot of queues from Dark Souls 1 without really learning from the various upgrades the genre has had since then. This makes it a very frustrating game at times and not for good reasons.
-It adopts the overused mechanic of giving you an in-game reason why you respawn... but not why everything else does, too. On top of that, when you die, you can't just go get your stuff (money and ability to fill your soul meter completely) back, you have to kill your ghost first. It's not exactly challenging to do, but... that's kinda my point. It's only ever annoying, it doesn't actually add anything to the game. This is probably why Sekiro abandoned that.
-When you die, you respawn at the last bench you rested at. If you press a button to get off the bench before your character has fully finished his waking up animation, nothing happens until you let go and press the button again. Not a big deal until you've died 20 times to the same boss and your yelling "just get off the stupid bench!" at your TV.
-Speaking of, the controls just... don't respond sometimes. Like if you hit heal and hold it but you started it at a certain point in your jump, it just gets ignored until you let go and press it again (by which time you've probably taken more damage). Same with the crystal dash. So it just feels like the game is dropping inputs.
-I do not like the boss fights at all. Not once did I beat a boss and feel like it was because of my own skill. This completely robs me of the satisfaction of overcoming the challenge. Most of them are just frustrating with way too much going on at once for me to keep up with. I just don't have the reaction times. The game badly needs difficulty options. I'm perfectly capable of dealing with the platforming challenges, but when you start adding in bullet hell boss fights... it's just not fun anymore.
-Healing takes forever and you have to be stationary (ie vulnerable) while doing it. It makes healing all but impossible in boss fights. I'm glad to see they've improved this for Silksong.
-Contact damage. I get that it's somewhat necessary for the platforming aspects of the game, but it just doesn't feel good. Especially in a boss fight touching a stunned boss (that can't even move) deals damage or standing between its legs and not actually touching it at all does damage. They really need to rethink that, it just feels bad.
-When taking damage, you freeze in place for a brief bit. For me, this frequently led to me falling to my death immediately after. At least give me an option to turn this off (like in Katana Zero).
-The benches are too far apart. Having to trudge back to a boss is not challenging, it's just annoying. Just let me fight the boss without dealing with two rooms of nonsense, please. Or at least provide a shortcut for the next time.

So, basically, there's a lot about the game that I like and want to like more, but a lot of just bad decisions have left a really sour taste in my mouth. And this is coming from someone who has beaten all bosses in DS1, Bloodborne, and Sekiro (several times in most cases). Hopefully Silksong is better.

I have used this (the Tournament Edition) for about 15-20 hours now, mostly playing Monster Hunter World. I have another 100 hours in that game that was mostly played with an Elite Series 2. I have to say that neither controller is perfect, but my overall preference is the Wolverine. I will say that I do have larger hands than some (roughly 7.5" from wrist to fingertip), so those with smaller hands might have a different experience.

Overall comfort: The Wolverine matches the basic design of the official XB1 controller very closely. However, it's a bit lighter that the standard XB1 controller and quite a bit lighter than the Elite 2 (but not as light as a DualShock 4). Although a lot of people seem to think that heavier means more premium, I prefer the lighter weight of this controller. However, for general comfort, I think the Elite 2 is still better. Having the controller completely wrapped in the grippy, rubbery material feels a lot nicer than just the grips on the back of the Wolverine. The grip portion of the Wolverine is also a little thicker toward the bottom than a standard XB1 controller and this has caused some discomfort for the pinky of my left hand, though as I have used it more, this has lessened. It seems that gripping the controller more loosely helps, but it did require some retraining to find the right grip. Finally, the taper to the shoulder buttons at the top of the controller is more steep on the Wolverine so it's not as comfortable to tap the bumpers as a standard XB1 controller. None of these issues are dealbreakers for me as they are really relatively minor.

Thumbsticks: Everyone is concerned about stick drift these days, so I'll start there. These thumbsticks are not 100% perfect, but then again, I only own one controller for any system that has perfect thumbsticks and that is the Switch Pro Controller. Using a gamepad tester, these sticks "drift" out to about 7.5% or less. This is better than any other XB1 controller I own, including the Elite 2, and is about on par with my DualShock 4s. What this means to me is that I'd set the inner deadzone to 10% and have no issues. To me, that's very good. We'll see how they hold up over time, but after 15-20 hours of use, that's where they are at. In terms of feel, they have about the same tension as a standard XB1 controller. I would prefer a higher tension and find it odd that Razer doesn't have adjustable tension since they had that way back on the 360, but I can live with these sticks. The grips are nice but not exceptional. The actual motion of the sticks is smooth. The controller also has antifriction rings which adds some smoothness at the extremes, but they are not as smooth as an Elite 2, probably because the shafts aren't metal. Finally, the actual shaft itself is thicker than most other controllers. I'm not sure why Razer did this, but I understand it to be an intentional decision. However, that makes me cautious about replacing the sticks with aftermarket ones. Maybe it would be fine, but I'll probably leave them alone for now. The stock sticks do feel a little thinner and cheaper than even a standard XB1 controller when they smack against the sides, but they are otherwise fine.

Face buttons: These will probably be the biggest point of contention for most people. The standard XB1 controller (and most controllers) use a rubber membrane design. It's cheap and easy to manufacture and generally feels good. However, official XB1 controllers use a bad contact pad design, so if the hole around a button is slightly too big, it's possible to push the button down at a slight angle and not close the circuit, meaning the button press is not registered. All of my official XB1 controllers have this to some extent, but my Elite 2 is the worst (despite costing the most). The Wolverine, by contrast, uses Razer's Omron mechanical switches for the facebuttons. It's weird at first, but provides a very satisfying click and feel when pressed. You KNOW when the button is pressed, which makes it so that I know the game is dropping my inputs and not the controller just not registering them (looking at you, Elite 2). I really like them overall, but I have two minor gripes. The first is that they are a bit too stiff for my taste. They are about on par with, say, the Switch Pro Controller, but definitely stiffer than my Elite 2 or DualShock 4. My second issue is that I think there's too much travel before the actual button click. I'd prefer a more shallow button press. I expected the buttons to feel more like the d-pad does, but instead they are really more like a mouse click as everyone says. For most people, they will be just fine, but the stiffness and travel distance could be an issue for button mashers (like speedrunners) as I don't think it's possible to mash the buttons as quickly as you can with a membrane button.

D-pad: It's a little stiff for my taste, but it seems to be breaking in a bit with use, so hopefully that changes over time. In particular, the down button seems more stiff than the other directions and less consistent in the overall feel. It's hard to describe, but sometimes it feels fine and other times it feels really stiff. Stiffness aside, my other issue is that the separated button design makes it harder to press diagonals. As long as I'm a bit more intentional about my button presses, this hasn't been much of an issue in practice so far (tested in Mega Man 2 making sure I could shoot the metal blade in all directions), but I definitely have to think about it more than I would with, say, a DualShock 4. Still, overall it's a pretty decent d-pad. I like that the buttons aren't as tall as a standard XB1 d-pad, so it's more comfortable to roll my thumb from one direction to another.

Bumpers and triggers: The bumpers are fine, but as mentioned in the comfort section, I think having the outside edge be more rounded would have made them nicer to use. They also don't give as much tactile feedback as the standard XB1 controller, so in the heat of the moment, I don't feel the click as much so I'm not as certain if the button was pressed. For the triggers, in general they are fine. Something about them feels less nice than the standard XB1 triggers, but they aren't bad by any means. If I had one gripe, it's that it seems like my right trigger has to fully bottom out to register 100% actuation whereas the left trigger registers 100% slightly before bottoming out. Both work in their full range and I probably wouldn't have even noticed if I hadn't checked with a testing utility, but it's still odd. One thing I do love is the hair triggers. I thought I'd love the hair triggers on the Elite 2, but the trigger stop is so solid that it just doesn't not feel good. It's like slamming into a wall and it just feels wrong. By contrast, these trigger stops have a slight amount of give, so they feel more like pressing a button. I love them. And in case you were worried, when you activate the trigger stop, the controller switches it to a digital input, so you'll never miss a button press just because the trigger throw distance is shorter. If you are curious, on the Elite 2 your three options are full throw, shortened throw (which still registers the full 0-100% range, just over a shorter distance), and digital (which just registers 0 or 100% like a button). On the Wolverine, it registers 0-10%, then skips to 100%. So it's technically not a fully digital button at that point, but it works perfectly and feels great.

Extra buttons: Probably the biggest reason to get a premium controller. The M1 and M2 buttons are up top between the triggers and bumpers. For someone like me, I would almost rather use these than the bumpers because they are in such a convenient location, but for someone with smaller hands, they might be almost unusable. I definitely have adjusted my grip to hold the controller higher up to get the most of them, though. They have a very clicky feel similar to the face buttons. The "paddles" are pretty nice as well, but with the way I have been gripping this controller, I wish they were just a little farther out. They also required a little getting used to; on the Elite 2, I actuate the paddles with a sort of squeezing motion, pulling them toward the grips of the controller to press them; with the Wolverine, it feels like I have to press them straight in toward the body of the controller to properly actuate them. However, they work well and I have no major complaints.

Software: Most places list this as using Synapse, but it doesn't (at least not anymore). It uses the "Razer Wolverine for Xbox" app, which is separate from the usual Razer Synapse software. While it's a little annoying to have a separate utility, the app is a universal Windows program, meaning it will install on both Xbox and Windows 10 PCs. Not only that, but as far as I can tell, it also syncs your settings, so if you use it on your Xbox and your PC, all your profiles will be there with both. It's really easy to use, though some aspects aren't as snappy as I might like. You also are limited to reassigning the M buttons. While these can be assigned to replicate any other button on the controller, you cannot remap the standard buttons (for example, if you wanted to swap A and B, you can't). This is a controller aimed at tournament use, so I imagine that keeps it tournament legal. Still, something to keep in mind if that's a feature you want. Overall, then, the software is easy to use but there aren't a lot of things you can do with it other than remap the M buttons and change the lighting.

Other: The start, select, and guide buttons (or whatever they are called) feel weird. They seem to have a long throw and stiffness that feels off. Not a big issue as these buttons are used frequently and the design of them means I certainly won't press them accidentally, it's just different. Also, for anyone who is worried about this sort of thing, the controller is smart enough to know that you shouldn't be able to press opposite directions on the d-pad at the same time even if you assign a direction to one of the extra buttons. For example, if I assign left and right to the M1 and M2 buttons, even though I am now physically able to press left and right at the same time, the controller will only send the first button I pressed. Being able to press both at the same time probably breaks tournament rules and it definitely breaks some older games, so it's good to see they accounted for that.

Final thoughts and summary: I chose the Tournament Edition over the Ultimate Edition because of the paddle placement and now that I've had my hands on it, I don't regret that at all. As mentioned above, I actually wish the paddles were a little farther out; I definitely don't want them closer to the middle like on the Ultimate. I also figured I'd prefer this d-pad, though, having not tried the Ultimate, I can't say for certain. But what I would love to see next from Razer is a controller that combines the best of both controllers as well as a few small tweaks. I'd lke the metal, swappable thumbsticks from the Ultimate, but otherwise the rest of the controller could just be the Tournament Edition. Add a second set of paddles, make the d-pad and face buttons a bit less stiff, and round the corners for the bumpers and this would be a killer controller. With that all said, it's absolutely a more reliable controller than the Elite 2, so if you're looking for something to upgrade to and don't mind losing wireless functionality, the Wolverine Tournament Edition is an awesome controller.

As someone who 95% of the time has no need of analog triggers, I would really have liked for this to have digital triggers. However, I know that analog triggers appeal to a wider audience. 8bitdo has been doing a really great job with their controllers lately with some notable improvements over previous models. For example, I have had an SN30 Pro (not the Pro+) for a while now and it was generally pretty good except that the d-pad registered diagonals when it really shouldn't. I also noticed that the analog sticks were a bit strange when used on PC - they would snap to the cardinal directions and the movement was more of a square than a circle. The d-pad issue I fixed with a bit of tape, but it wasn't until I finally bothered to update the firmware that I noticed that the thumbstick issues have long since been resolved. But enough about that controller, here is what's great about the SN30 Pro+.

Pros:
-The d-pad is pretty much perfect right out of the box this time, at least for the controller I got. Diagonals only register when I want them to.
-The thumbsticks are great. They are very similar to the sticks on a DualShock 4 - not quite convex, but not quite concave, either. The tension is also similar to a DS4, which is how I like it. There was a bit of roughness when moving the thumbsticks along the edge of the hole, but I just took the front off and lightly sanded it to get rid of that.
-It feels almost exactly like a DualShock 4, but also like an SNES controller at the same time. The grips and analog triggers are practically identical, but obviously the d-pad is spot-on for an SNES controller and the spacing of the face buttons (ABXY) are a little wider like an SNES controller.
-The buttons are all nice and snappy, but not quite as stiff as they are on my SN30 Pro.
-No stick drift. Technically they center at like 0.000002 instead of just 0, but in practice they are the same thing. The SN30 Pro does this, too, so I suspect it's something 8bitdo is doing that makes that happen.
-I really like the ergonomics. It's light and the grips aren't too thick, so it's very comfortable to use for long periods of time.
-The rechargeable battery can be removed and you can use AA batteries instead.

Cons:
-Personally, I would have preferred to have digital triggers. I can understand that they probably wanted to appeal to more people, but I have very little need for analog triggers and if I had to pick one or the other, I'd choose digital every time.
-I would have liked a headset jack. I know it's primarily marketed as a Switch controller, but I use it primarily with PC and it would have been nice to have there.
-The included cable is too short to be of any use except for charging.
-The first time you use the thumbsticks after turning the controller on, no matter how much or how little you move them they will snap to 100% movement. Not physically, just in terms of how the software/console/game reads the input. They work fine after that. It's odd, but easily remedied by just moving them even once before you start playing.

I highly recommend this controller for anyone, but especially for people who really like the feel of a DualShock 4 and want a similar controller for the Switch or for PC.

As a word of caution for this review, I was never able to get into Monster Hunter pre-World. It was obtuse, complicated, and I never had anyone to show me how it's supposed to work. Heck, I didn't even get into World until someone showed me how it's supposed to go. Now I have over 600 hours in it, making it my most played game ever, so... yeah. The point is that if you are reading this as someone who is a long-time fan of the series, my opinions may not mean much to you. Having said that, I've also seen people complaining (probably a loud minority) about various improvements the game has made and I think it's important to address those, too. This review is mostly going to focus on what the changes are and what I like and don't like about them; my overall view after about 60 hours is that I really, really love the game, but I do have a list of improvements I'd like to see at some point.

The objective of Rise seems to be to generally take the feel of World but iterate and improve on it while also bringing back some of what people liked about previous games. As a result, if you are an old school Monster Hunter fan and just hated World, you probably won't like this game, either. But if you liked World and just thought there were some things that could be improved, you'll probably love Rise after you give it a chance. Essentially, the combat feels almost identical to World, but they took out the clutch claw and put in the wirebug. This allows for some neat combat moves and gives some extra mobility, especially for the slower weapons that can now just zip toward the monster. The most useful part of the wirebug, in my opinion, is that you can zip away from the monster after you get hit. This gets you out of the way, sheathes your weapon, and puts you back on your feet so you can heal. Conversely, you can also zip back toward the monster, but you have to be careful with that or you'll just get smacked again (so that helps balance it).

Another improvement over World is multiplayer. While I have mixed feelings about splitting single- and multiplayer, there aren't any escort quests or mid-quest cutscenes anymore, so every multiplayer quest can be started together with your friends instead of waiting, exiting, and rejoining. Hooray! The downside of splitting the quests is that you can't do everything with your friends anymore, but the upshot is that each has a different purpose. The village (singleplayer) quests are noticeably easier and are only low rank, so it seems that they are intended as something of a training ground where you can get used to new weapons, get some money, or just generally have something to do when your friends aren't around. Hub (multiplayer) quests are harder, even if you play solo, and feel more like the intended/standard difficulty. High rank is restricted to the hub, as are certain monsters, so it's clear that this is meant to be the "real" game. If you've read reviews complaining about the game being too easy or too short, it's likely that they didn't venture into the hub much.

Eating at the Canteen is also changed. In World, your food could give you attack or defense buffs in addition to other skill buffs, but now it only buffs your health and stamina. You choose the food based on what skill buffs you would like, but you don't get any attack or defense buffs (unless you choose certain food that gives you that buff skill). Instead, they added spiribirds, endemic life that you collect out in the field. You can ignore them, collect a few of them, or wander around collecting them all until you max out your stats. This changes the dynamic of the hunt a bit as you can't just do everything in town, but overall I'd say it's just different, not better or worse. The canteen overall is definitely improved, though, as it's really easy to tell what skills you're getting instead of having to mix and match weird assortments of foods to get things. And yes, hot and cool drinks are gone. Good riddance.

The Hunter's Notes have gotten an overhaul and for the first time will give you the actual hitzone values for raw and elemental damage. Status is relegated to a bar chart of sorts, but it is still divided up between initial proc and subsequent procs, so it's significantly easier to tell what you're actually looking at than ever before. For example, I can look at the notes for one monster and see that they have low raw hitzones but decent elemental hitzones and bring a weapon that favors element over raw; conversely, if they have high raw hitzones and crap elemental hitzones, I can bring a weapon that favors raw instead. On a related subject, you also don't have to gather footprints and snot and the like anymore. This is more like pre-World games where you'd just kind of wander around trying to find the monster, but now you at least start with a question mark on your map that gives you an idea where to look. Some might say this makes it too easy, but it's really not that different from previous games, especially after you've hunted the monster a few times. You also unlock all the notes (aside from drops) after the first kill/capture of a monster, so that's nice.

Speaking of the numbers game, it feels like some of the damage bloat is gone. We still don't get to see motion values for the various moves, but they've gone with attack values that seem more directly comparable. For example, every Magnamalo weapon has the same raw attack value (I think), so while it's still true that the greatsword will do more damage per hit than, say, dual blades, it feels like you can look at the two and say that yes, these are on the same tier in terms of DPS. It used to be that the greatsword attack value might read 1200+ while dual blades would be in the 300s, so comparisons were pretty meaningless.

There are a number of things I would like to see changed, some of which are regressions of improvements World made. Maybe that's a symptom of still having two development teams even though there aren't really portable consoles anymore, so here's to hoping they just combine the teams moving forward. First and most importantly, while this might be the most accessible Monster Hunter yet, it is still far from easy for a newcomer to get into. Tutorials are buried in walls of text and even then they don't explain everything very well (if at all). On top of that, while the wirebug is pretty neat, it has also added a lot of complication to the controls (especially since the controls for it are different with ranged weapons), so it's probably harder than ever just to learn how to play. Monster Hunter has a long way to go when it comes to making these games newbie friendly.

Most of the rest of my complaints are nitpicks, but they start to grate on you over time. I can't rearrange my item pouch from the equipment box, so I have to exit the box and go to the start menu to rearrange items. This was not the case in World, so... what gives? You also can't arrange the item bar separately from the item pouch nor can you remove fixed items from your item bar, so that's a bit annoying. When departing on a multiplayer quest, there's no warning that you are about to leave people behind if they didn't mark themselves ready, so it just kicks them from the quest instead and they have to wait and then rejoin. And for those for whom visual stimuli are an issue, 4-player hunts can have an awful lot going on that makes it really hard to see what's going on or even where you or the monster are. Individually, these are small things, but when so many other games don't have these problems, you just have to wonder why they still can't get them right after all these years.

In conclusion, the game is excellent and improves upon the formula in a lot of ways. There are a few minor gripes that I hope Capcom addresses, but I think they're on the right track. And for those worried that the game is "too short," keep in mind that Monster Hunter games are more of a service than a game and we're already getting more content (the first of many updates!) in a few weeks, so I expect that I'll have hundreds of hours invested in this game by the time I'm done.

I never really liked the PlayStation controller up until the DualShock 4. While at first I thought the symmetrical thumbsticks would be annoying, I got used to them and never found them to be problematic. However, that controller still had some problems, namely a poorly designed USB connection and some strange thumbstick quirks when using it on PC.

Enter the DualSense. This controller adds a TON of welcome new features. It uses USB-C now. The buttons have all been slightly revised and all feel great (and area also the quietest I've ever used on any controller). The thumbsticks now have anti-friction rings standard. The adaptive triggers are simply amazing, though you really have to try them to understand. And the "HD rumble," while really not essential, is also quite nice. On top of that, it has less input lag and more accurate thumbsticks. On paper, then, it's a DS4 that works better and has a bunch of nice new features to boot.

But there are a number of issues that were either introduced or just left unresolved. First, it's thicker, bigger, and heavier than the DS4. This also means that the distance to the thumbsticks is a bit greater and for me, it's just enough to make the controller physically painful to use (unless the game uses the d-pad, in which case it's quite nice). Second, while the adaptive triggers are excellent, the default feel of the triggers is pretty much the same and I still don't really like it that much. They are also just underutilized and I really think there should be a way to set them manually to mimic short-throw triggers. Third, while the anti-friction rings are nice and smooth, the shaft of the stick still contacts a sharp angle on the ring, meaning you'll still wear down the stick much quicker than you really should. Maybe someone else will make replacements with rounded edges? And finally, the battery life is really pretty bad compared to most other controllers out there.

I would really like to see two things from Sony (though I doubt either will happen): a version of the controller with asymmetrical thumbsticks and/or better support for PS4-compatible controllers (and potentially other 3rd party controllers generally) in PS5 games. As it is, as much as I love my PS5 and as much as I want to use the DualSense, my physical limitations make it so that I basically can't play PS5 games because I can't use the controller without causing pain. And with no other controllers available that support PS5 games... I'm just out of luck for now.

Having said all that, if you don't have hand/wrist issues and can use the controller without pain, it truly is a very nice controller. With a couple tweaks, though, it could be just about perfect.

As a caveat, I will say that I only just received the controller and cannot speak to the long-term durability. I know that has been an issue with past Scuf controllers, but from what I've seen online and what I see in front of me, I can't see anything about this that makes it seem less durable than any standard Xbox controller. If that changes with time, I will update my review. With that said, I think this is the best Xbox controller available. It's a little overpriced and there are some thing that could be better, but I'm still giving it 5 stars simply because they have done so much right that even Microsoft can't figure out that I really think it's worth commending them for it. TL;DR version of this review: if you are looking for a fancy controller, buy this one. Let's start with...

The thumbsticks. Maybe I just lucked out, but mine are as perfect as I have ever seen on any Xbox controller. On the Xbox One, every one of my controllers had sticks that didn't center properly. That is, they might "settle" at 7% up and 2% right. When people talk about drift, this is primarily what causes it. Fortunately, Microsoft mostly fixed that with the new Series controllers and on all three I have, the sticks center more or less in the actual center. However, they are still a bit loose and can still settle a bit off center. Not these. The Scuf sticks are as close to perfectly centered as I have seen. This will change over time as it does for all controllers, of course, but it's nice that they at least start correct. The actual sticks themselves are really nice, too, though I notice they use a lighter, thinner plastic than the standard controllers. Part of me thinks that is to save costs, but I also wonder if this was an intentional choice because a lot of people have theorized that the heavier metal sticks on the Elite Series 2 cause the thumbsticks to wear out faster. Having lighter, thinner plastic should mean less momentum and more accurate recentering, so it could very well be intentional. The anti-friction rings are also very smooth, so overall the sticks are a real joy to use. If for some reason you don't like the included thumbsticks, you can just swap them out for standard ones, though, having used these, I cannot imagine why you would want to (except if there is a particular color you want).

The face buttons are basically just the same as the standard ones, so they are a bit taller than those on the Elite Series 2 but otherwise perform as you'd expect. HOWEVER, and this is a big but, they actually work! Every single Elite Series 2 I have used (5-6 of them by now) has had an A button that does not register reliably, particularly when pressed at certain angles. Xbox One controllers also had this issue, though Series controllers seem to have mostly resolved it (despite not actually addressing the underlying cause). So I am happy to report that I am unable to cause any of the face buttons to not register when pressed. Having a controller that actually functions reliably is reason enough to buy it over the Elite Series 2, but fortunately there are more reasons to love it. UPDATE: after using it more, I did find an angle at which the A button doesn't register (down and to the left on mine), but it's not as bad as the Elite controllers I've tried and about on par with every other Series controller. It's a bummer, but it's not any worse than a standard controller, so I guess I'm neutral on this point.

The d-pad is now magnetic and can be easily swapped (without even removing the faceplate) between the new hybrid design and the standard design, though the standard one still has the visible circle around it. Otherwise, it's clicky and functions just like the standard d-pad, so no issues there. Still, it's nice to have the option. The new hybrid d-pad is, in my opinion, superior to the circle one on the Elite Series 2, so the options here are an improvement over that controller.

There's nothing particularly special about the bumpers, but, unlike all of my official Series controllers, Scuf seems to have actually bothered to acoustically match the two of them so they sound the same. It's a welcome attention to detail.

The paddles are a bit of a mixed bag. Like the bumpers, they at least have a consistent sound profile, or rather the two outer ones sound the same and the two inner ones sound the same (but different from the outer ones so you can tell which you pressed). The outer ones aren't exactly where I would like them to be, but that's a bit subjective (depending on hand size in particular) and overall they are easy enough to use without getting in the way. The inner ones are a little awkward, though. It seems like they are intended to be pressed by flicking your finger out, but they are a little too stiff to really do that with. Maybe I will get used to them over time, but I think I would have preferred paddles where the outer ones are and then another pair farther down where my ring fingers can actuate them instead of these. Regardless, they aren't really paddles anymore as much as they are just buttons, so I don't foresee them breaking any time soon.

Finally, the most unique aspect of this controller are the triggers. Hair triggers are nothing new, but Scuf has finally done what I always though they should be and made it so you have either full analog triggers or hair triggers that actuate actual buttons. On the Elite Series 2, you have full movement, which has a bit of a squishy feel when bottoming out; half pull, which feels obnoxiously stiff when bottoming out and I really can't think of any reason to use this option anyway; and super short throw, which has a nice amount of travel but is still entirely too stiff when bottoming out. Scuf have eliminated the pointless middle option and instead given us either a full analog trigger or an actual button that feels like a button. My only gripe is that I wish there was just a tiny bit more travel when using the hair trigger mode so that you could more easily feel that you pressed it, but otherwise it's nearly perfect. One other nitpick is that it's easy to swap from analog to digital triggers with the switches on the back, but it's a lot harder to swap back from digital to analog mode. I'm not sure if that was on purpose, but it does make swapping back and forth on the fly a bit annoying.

So all in all, an absolutely fantastic controller. Outside of my minor gripes, I would like to see Scuf make a few other changes that don't directly have anything to do with the controller itself. First, it should really be $180 to better compete with the Elite Series 2. Yeah, you still wouldn't get a case or as many accessories, but the controller is just so much better that I don't really care (plus the case is the only accessory I would actually use). Second, they really need more color options and more consistent color choices between parts (like why can I make the sticks light grey but not the d-pad?). Long story short, this controller is what the Elite Series 2 should have been all along. If you can justify the cost, buy it.

For a while, I was mostly gaming with either the Sennheiser HD560s or PC38x, but after picking up the IE300 and really enjoying them for gaming, I wanted something closed back. Unfortunately, most headsets sound awful, are cheaply made and uncomfortable, and often just don't fit my huge head (all of SteelSeries's previous offerings fit that last one). I had my doubts, but the reviews were good, so I sucked it up and paid the hefty price tag to try out the Arctis Nova Pro. I'm glad I did.

In terms of sound profile, this seems to try to adhere to the Harman target and it seems to do a pretty good job. The bass is slightly boosted but not boomy or bloated; the mids are generally well handled, though probably not Sennheiser quality; and the highs are bright but never harsh. Some people might want more bass (which you can do with the DAC), but I think the default sound is just about ideal for both gaming and music. It's possible that there is less detail than in a truly audiophile headphone, but it still compares favorably to other headphones in the <$300 range and is genuinely impressive for something marketed for gaming. It's the closest a headset has come to being an audiophile product, at least outside of the PC38x.

It also has really impressive imaging. Using something like Dolby Atmos for Headphones, I'm able to hear where sounds are around me with near pinpoint accuracy. I won't go so far as to use a cliche and say I have a competitive advantage, but it's accurate and precise. Any faults will be yours, not the headset's.

So the sound is great, possibly best in class for a closed headset, but if I can't or don't want to wear it, that doesn't really matter. Fortunately, I am happy to report that this headset fits my enormous head with room to spare. Finally! It's also relatively light weight and the headband design is so good that you won't even feel it on the top of your head. The ear cups are deep enough to not bother me, though people with very large ears are likely to find that the tips of their ears touch the sides. The ear pads are also very comfortable, but I really wish they had gone with a breathable mesh instead of leather as the leather does get a little warm and sticks to my skin. I considered marking it down to 4 stars, but I feel like it's overall still closer to 5. Maybe they can offer replacement pads later? Overall, though, the clamping force is relatively light and the headset is incredibly comfortable even for large heads.

The mic is decent enough, though lacking in low end. I haven't messed with the software, but I think you can handle that there, so it's not a dealbreaker. I do like that it retracts completely and the mute button is silent when muting and unmuting, so that's another win.

Finally, let's talk about the included DAC. On the one hand, I wish they offered a version that was just the headset without a DAC as the headset is still excellent without it and it would lower the cost. On the other hand, it's actually a very nice DAC. There's no audible noise, it has a lot of handy features on it, and unlike most DACs, you can get one that works with Xbox. That means you can have the same sound settings with the same headset on all platforms and that's really nice. So sure, I didn't NEED the DAC, but it's a nice one and I'm happy to have it.

So, the elephant in the room. Is it worth $250? Considering the quality of the headset and the included DAC, yes. I can understand that the price is tough to stomach, but they really are making it worth it. This is probably the best headset available now.
