Dark Souls, much like its glorious predecessor Demon's Souls, is an incredibly rich, nuanced, and ultimately fun game that hides behind an extremely dark, sharp exterior. Everything in the game exists to get you killed. Quite literally any single foe can kill you at whatever level you are, particularly if you get sloppy or just have the bad luck of getting knocked off a platform, triple teamed, or just stabbed in the back. But by the same token, if you learn from your missteps, plan ahead, and become proficient at certain playing styles or tactics, you can go very far even with a level 1 character. The game rewards patience, persistence, and varying your tactics. A seemingly insurmountable problem is usually only that way because you are trying to tackle it the wrong way; if a dragon has taken over a bridge, see if there is another way past. If an armored boar is patrolling a hallway, perhaps there is a way to get the drop on him. Paying attention to your surroundings and always watching your back is the the best way to at least minimize deaths.

Ahh, death. Dark Souls will kill you, over and over. There are no multiple save files or re-dos (unless you cheese out and do a hard quit, which usually doesn't work anyway). When you die, you respawn at a nearby campfire, in a "hollow"/undead form and absent all the soul money you may have built up from killing enemies. If you can make it back to the place where you died, you can recover souls and Humanity, but if not it is lost forever. And since you likely died in a new area where you were meeting new foes, it can often be challenging to get back safely to where you were. However, this dynamic is not quite as punishing as it seems. First of all, everyone dies in Dark Souls, all the time. Indeed, you will often encounter bloodstains you can activate to get a glimpse of the last few moments of the life of someone else playing online. Near campfires, you will often see the ghostly apparitions of other online players as they struggle with the same challenges you face. And if you are lucky, you can even find glowing white symbols that let you summon usually helpful online allies to battle foes with you (you can also be invaded by online enemy players if you are in Human form). This creates an odd sense of camraderie despite the fact that most areas consist of just you against the world, because regardless of how frustrating and/or embarrasing your latest death was, pretty soon you will see a replay of someone else experiencing something even worse.

Second, death can actually be a tactic. Your character will keep anything you manage to pick up before you die, aside from souls/Humanity. This means if you are already Hollow from an earlier death and have little soul wealth, dying really doesn't do anything to you. Suicide runs into dangerous territory can be a great way to collect rare items and equipment and jumpstart your character, trigger switches, or simply scout the area a few times to get a sense of where all the enemies congregate before you commit to actually battling them.

Dark Souls is also an extremely detailed and layered game. Beyond the amazing 3-D environment, which is riddled with hidden passageways, shortcuts, and elaborate zones, there is an extensive interplay between the NPCs you run into, the loot you can find, and even the boss monsters. Missing a chat with a wandering NPC or even failing to kill them at the right time can cause you to miss a piece of loot forever, and many items are either extremely obscure or can only be upgraded by certain items. Playing Dark Souls in many ways resembles trying to play a scavenger hunt orchestrated by a lunatic while many of the other contestants are also trying to kill you. At the same time, triumphing over those odds brings a kind of gratification that you will not find in any other game. In addition, many tactics that work against computer enemies may be ineffective against human invaders, and vice-versa. It may well take you several "practice" characters and some time with a good walkthrough to figure out what play style you prefer and what items you need to pick up. But the great cruelty of Dark Souls is also its greatest asset: just as you can be killed by anyone on a bad day, you can kill anyone on a good day. Don't let the daunting foes and overpowered player killer invaders stop you from experiencing one of the best games the PS3 has ever seen. I promise you, you won't remember the deaths, but you will remember the victories.

Oh, Xcom. How I want to love you. I grew up on the original XCom and played it to death, and still consider it one of the best games of all time. To say I was keyed up for this updated reinvention/sequel was to put it mildly. Indeed, much of the game mechanics are the same, including various developments for your home base, research trees, character level and equipment upgrading, and even the UFO interceptor fights. But what should have been the central strength of the game -- the turn based strategic combat -- is its most glaring weakness.

In the original XCom, you could with some degree of effectiveness ensure that your characters were extremely unlikely to get shot, by strategic use of cover. The ability to hide out of line of fire behind trees, rocks, or walls ensured that weapons fire would at a minimum have to penetrate that cover before it could hit you, or be fired blind with low hit probabilities. In XCom: Enemy Unknown, all that seems to matter is hit percentages. In other words, hiding behind even huge rocks, vehicles, or other forms of obstruction simply reduces the chances of that character getting hit, but even then not significantly. Do you enjoy watching an alien fire a plasma rifle through 2 walls and then the side of an 18 wheeler trailer in order to hit your otherwise invisible character? Do you like the idea of a group of aliens being able, in a single unbroken turn, to sprint out into the open and unload their weapons halfway across the map at one of your characters who is hidden on the other side of an entire hill, and hit your player effortlessly every time? Is your idea of fun reloading your game every 5 minutes for hours on end just so you can keep moving different characters in sequential order and hope that something gets shaken up in the game's random number generator such that for one additional precious turn nobody gets shot through a wall from halfway across the map? Then XCom: Enemy Unknown is for you.

Contrary to other reports, XCom: Enemy Unknown is not a hard game. I've platinumed Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, I know what a hard game is. XCom: Enemy Unknown does not require you to learn new skills or tactics, learn from your mistakes, or overcome challenges. Instead, all you are doing is fighting a random number generator that favors the home (alien) team, and reloading over and over and over until you finally get to go back and do the fun stuff like horsing around with your headquarters. Strategy is actually a hindrance; no amount of covered movements and careful player positioning can change the fact that a random alien can just flat out shoot you right through a brick wall as if you're standing right next to them. Honest to god, one of the best ways I've found to win missions is to literally have every single player but one stay in permanent "overwatch" right where they are standing when you load up the ground combat map, and have a single expendable rookie run around drawing fire so your troops can engage in counterbattery attacks. Hiding doesn't matter. Cover doesn't matter (and often is harmful, as vehicles can explode in a single turn if set on fire even by your own attacks through them). All that matters is brute force firepower at the start of each turn, so you kill them through all the solid environmental "cover" before they do it to you. That's it.

It's a truly sad thing when you have all this fun designing and upgrading your base, researching and crafting your new gear, getting your satellites up, defending your planet, and then realize that oh god I have to do another one of these stupid ground missions where unless I reload each turn a dozen times all my Colonel level supersoldiers in robotic exosuits are still coming back in body bags. How they screwed this up I'll never understand.

Mass Effect: Andromeda is a difficult game to categorize. I had avoided spoilers prior to release so had almost no expectations and certainly no awareness of the controversies about some of its designers and its ham-fisted blundering in the social media space. So I came to this game almost as free of bias as one can get these days. In short, some parts of ME:A are as good as anything I've experienced in the series. And some are far worse.

Positives: Level design is often creative and involves clever three dimensional puzzles and loot finding. If you enjoy scavenging, you are often rewarded by loot chests hidden well off the beaten path. The open world areas are also typically true to form, and in fact can change over time as your alterations to the environment allow you to enter previously irradiated or hazardous areas. Improvements to the land rover dramatically increase its initial handling, and you and your combat team will similarly increase in power and showy effectiveness as your skills and gear improve. Trying the multiplayer missions is also a great way to practice your combat skills early as well as become familiar with many of the game's enemies, and you can earn gear and loot that carries over into the single player mode.

Negatives: The character graphics are as bad as you've heard. Maybe even worse. Most planets and zones are fine, but non-combat areas where you have to do a lot of talking are poor. Facial expressions vary from vacant to idiotic, and are worse than what you'd see on games from 10 years ago. I recently played Borderlands 2 on the PS4 and random NPCs in Sanctuary actually have better voice-mouth movement calibrations than in Andromeda. There are tons of basic character movement errors like running nearly sideways while going up stairs, getting stuck in random objects, and people that seem to shatter their own spines when turning around to talk to you. Nobody blinks. I have a clip of 6 npcs staring at my character in which nobody blinks, ever. It is genuinely creepy.

Unfortunately, combat is also often glitchy and frustrating. Enemies can hit you through solid "cover," and often use moves that are broken. One of the worst occurs in multiplayer in which certain "mini-boss" style monsters can one hit you through walls or from some distance away, instantly killing you with no possibility of revive and usually ruining the mission. You have to learn what the windup on those moves looks like and jump away if they start to us it, even if they are in a different room and not even facing your direction. Otherwise you die. Weapons are also often unpredictable, in a way that makes it hard to know if they are coded that way or buggy. Sniper rifles often fire low, particularly if the target is in cover, and shotguns often send pellets everywhere but at the target. Grenades bounce off walls and fall through the floor or go sailing up into space. Multiplayer also allows you to send NPC "strike teams" on missions that run while you are doing something else or offline, but these are likewise glitchy. Teams routinely fail missions with 90%+ success likelihoods -- my record is a level 20 team using the best gear that failed four (4) 94% success rate missions in a row -- which gave them permanent negative traits. Truly stupid.

The ultimate impression I have is that the game was broken up into different development areas by the designers. Some coding teams did their parts of the game extremely well, and others were terrible and seemingly didn't even beta test their own work. If you can stick to the areas that the competent programmers worked on, and ignore the places the B team was involved, you can enjoy this game. But you will have to work at it.

I purchased this game based on the Castlevania/Dark Souls hype without any prior exposure or spoilers, and so far have been entertained but often frustrated by its glitchy mechanisms. At core it shares a lot of similarities with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, a fantastic game that still retains a loyal following many years after its release way back on PS1. But unfortunately it is nowhere near as polished, which is particularly confusing given how many years it has been since SOTN. For example, one of Dead Cell's more interesting features is randomized dungeons, a concept imported from the vast history of "roguelikes" known for their replayability. But Dead Cell's randomization is so glitchy that it actually makes the game less replayable. For example, on my very first game, the starting area right outside the cell consisted of nothing but a long straight corridor with (pointless) warp locations at each end. The corridor ended in nothing but a long upwards vertical space, requiring a very high jump that my starting character could not clear. After endless attempts to discover some sort of hidden triple jump object Mario-style, or some sort of secret exit from the area, I had to restart the playthrough via the menu, generating a new map and causing various NPCs to update. It's a bad look when your game literally dead ends out of the box.

The Dark Souls aspect of the game is found in its death = advancement concept, whereby your inevitable deaths still can advance the plot or unlock other aspects of your equipment or NPCs. But unlike Dark Souls (or SOTN) you do not retain items on death, and have to rely on a grindy process of unlocking various features through the use of "cell" currency so that your next restart is slightly less punishing. You can also use the roll command to evade attacks similar to Dark Souls, although it functions oddly in a 2D platformer and tends to launch you into space or cause greater confusion with its sometimes unreliable invincibility frames. For example, I was able to clear long SOTN-esque spike pits by just rolling through them, but could not do the same with certain pendulum traps or enemy AOE attacks. In the end, you tend to find yourself just jumping or ducking past dangers like old school platforming. In addition, deaths can often be unfair even when dealing with known risks, including enemy attacks that go through obstacles or enemies that somehow break out of combos or status effects before they should. There's even a curse status where you die with any type of hit, which can effectively force you to try to play through long stretches using only a bow or ranged skill given the unpredictable AI and hitboxes of a number of the enemies.

I still have hope that Dead Cells will grow on me in its own way, rather than as a cludgy amalgamation of various other games. It has some clever ideas and some interesting areas to explore for sure. But never knowing whether you are stuck because of an intricate map puzzle or because the game didn't actually create a viable exit for the area is sure to be only more frustrating as time goes on.

Virtua Fighter 4 evolution has done the near impossible, make one of the best fighting games of all time even better.  There is still all the depth and enjoyment of the original, while adding two more characters and the next level of Kumite mode, Quest mode!  This mode is a challenging ongoing game where you make your name in every arcade in Tokyo, eventually getting to the center Arena, to become the best Virtua Fight in Japan.  Yes, it is a bit tacky, but that is not what is important.  Customizable characters get even better as a new array of items is found.  You can also get new fighting modes in the central arena, like balance and a mode where you take extra damage when you hit the floor.  The fighting moves have always been, and still are, incredibly complex and deep.  This is one of the only games I have seen that includes evasion, counterattacks, throw evades, and rolls that allow you to avoid ground attacks.  It takes a while to master, but once you get it, it is a very deep and ingenious control system.  The reviewer that gave two stars seems to be what most people are that dont like VF4: impatient.  He claims that it is too easy in quest mode, but by the time you progress throughout Tokyo, you begin to fight some fighters that are modeled after real people that are among the best VF players in the world.  They also lack the patience to go to practice sessions and explore the numerous moves available to them.  The only regretable thing to VF4 Evolution is the lack of training your own A.I., which is included in the original.  Most VF4 fans can compensate by just whipping out their old copies.  If you are new to the series and you want to play the A.I. training version, then I suggest that you buy VF4 and VF4 Evolution, they are only $20 each and are both well worth it.  Overall, I would say that VF4 Evolution is a wonderful game that makes other fighting games, with the exception of Soul Caliber 2, look just plain silly.  VF4 Evolution, in my opinion could even top the prowess of SC2.  Buy this, or at least rent it, you will not regret it.

I have played many of the recent fighting games, including VF4, VF4 Evolution, Soul Calibur 2, Tekken Tag, Tekken 3, and this game, Tekken 4.  While all have their specific qualities that stand out from the rest, I would have to rank this one last.  Despite an astonishingly large array of characters, with 10 of them being unlockable, I only found 2 to be fluent enough in style to match with the characters or Virtua Fighter 4 or Soul Caliber 2.  Those characters were Yoshimitsu and Christie.  While the others are clunky, the AI gives you back the advantage by being sub-par, although sometimes they like to throw in several cheap shots if you are one hit away from victory.  The graphics are average, but the music is very cheesy, and instantly goes to a specific chord when someone is defeated, no matter how awkward it may sound.  One the plus side, Tekken 4 has a bevy of modes, including an arcade mode, a mode that is essentially the Tekken Tournament, a survival mode, and a mode where you fight hordes of minions with your fighting skills.  The difficulty curve is not too intense as to blow you away, and you can unlock most of the character's endings with relative ease, some seriousm, and some surprisingly comedic.  I managed to unlock the majority of the endings within a five day rental, and I suggest that you rent it as well.  Despite it being worth playing, purchasing it unless you are a true Tekken fan or you truly enjoy the game, is a waste of money.

Tony Hawk's Underground(THUG) is a brand new innovation in a series, that despite having 5 games in a sport that stays relatively similar from year to year, has innovated every time. THUG is no different. Although the same elements exist from THPS 4, there is a new twist(Before you read the rest of this review, know that I am not a gigantic violent video game freak, I am just talking about innovations to the THPS series, and read the entire review so you can understand my point). Without the names of several superstars burdening the main character, he or she can be seen breaking the law. Now believe me, this is in no way a GTA kind of crime spree, it is all in good taste in an attempt to do something that is meaningful to the story, unlike the gratuitus violence in several games today. With this freedom, the THPS crew has the ability to completely innovate the plot making it much deeper with a great story to boot. There are some minor polishing effects that THUG could use however. Once again the music selection is a little under par, but this is not a problem. The difficulty curve for some missions is also steep, but fortunately you can skip the majority of these missions if it is too hard for you and come back to it later when you feel you can tackle it. Finally, some goals can be a chore, but they are few and far between so you will not have to worry about it.
Pros:
Great Story(Especially for a sports game)
Innovative THPS game
Fluid movements, as usual
Most goals are fun and not too hard
Cons:
Some goals can be lame or difficult
Soundtrack could use some polishing
The verdict:
This is a great game that is worth a rental at least and for most people a purchase. The minor criminal activity is nothing like GTA or The Getaway and is all in good intent. Play this game at least once, you won't regret it.

This game got the gold award from EGM and high ratings from every game magazine out there.  It even recieve Game of the Year honors from EGM over KOTOR and Mario Kart: Double Dash!!  So why is it sitting on the shelves of game stores, collecting dust?  The game's only drawbacks are a lousy save system, and sometimes(not always) cheesy sound effects.  In the game, you unlock the sands of time, and steal the dagger of time.  This ends up sending you on a quest to undo the mistake you have made and you encounter many foes along the way.  The graphics are flawless, even on a PS2, the fighting system is great, the controls are almost an afterthought, you dont even have to think about which button you need to press, and the puzzles are enthralling.  Do not let the low sales fool you, this is a great game on the verge of being deemed a "failure" in a business world that relies on sales.  Do not let such a greatgreat game go the way of many other underrated games such as Ico, Kya: Dark Lineage, and Beyond Good and Evil.  Buy it and you will not regret it.

Over the last 3 years, there have been a bevy of fighters abound. Currently, however the main contenders are the Virtua Fighter and the Soul Calibur Series with Mortal Kombat and Tekken's dissapointing showings putting them just out of the bubble, though that could change with a good future release. Anyway, I have played both Virtua Fighter 4 and VF4 Evolution as well as Soul Calibur 2, and while Soul Calibur 2 is the best weapons fighterin its class(though to be fair there arent very many weapons fighters), Virtua Fighter 4 Evolution takes the cake. Now for the features of Soul Calibur:
Characters: 9/10(simply because I have no need for Heihachi in a weapons fighter, 10/10 for Xbox and GC)VF4:10/10
Controls: 9/10(Clunky as you get used to them but easilly adapted when you get the hang of it) VF4 9/10(same reason)
Moves: 10/10(Perfect combinations of easy and difficult moves with a simple yet complex system) VF4: 10/10
Special Mode(overall): 10/10 (Slightly edges out VF4's quest mode because the weapons you acquire effect you in combat) VF4:9/10
Special Mode system: 8/10 (while some of the fights are fun and innovative, like one in a windy area where you have to knock your opponent off a windmill, it can be a pain going through the dungeons, fighting drone after drone, while gaining back minimal hitpoints to sustain you from some of the massive attacks, unrewarding ranking system with no real base) VF4:9/10(easier to sustain, many fighting modes, relatively easy to unlock things, good ranking system, can always take a break but still be able to fight new people, very long)
Replay Value: I decided not to count the replay value, because in fighting games that is hard to judge but I would mark them about even.
Graphics: 10/10 (superb, easy to move around in, great environments) VF4: 10/10 (similarly flawless)
The winner: Virtua Fighter 4/VF4 Evolution! Both franchises will hopefully be making admirable fighting games down the road and both games are worth getting but VF4 slightly edges out SC2 to take the prize. Though this did not effect my decision in any way, as a bonus, Virtua Fighter 4 and Virua Fighter 4 Evolution both are only $19.99 while SC2 is $37.95. Simply put, if you are strapped for cash and can only afford one, get Virtua Fighter 4 Evolution, but if you can spend a little money, then get both of these masterfully rendered fighting games. I've been a fan of the Gran Turismo series since the first game stormed onto the original PlayStation and gave us all a realistic console simulation experience the likes of which no one had ever seen before. Since then, each new release has had its share of ups and downs, and it's always been the case of two steps forward, one step back. Overall the series continues to progress, but this release is no different - while there are some great new improvements, there are some disappointments as well. But it is still a Gran Turismo game through and through, and if you're expecting anything other than a demanding and time consuming driving simulation, look elsewhere. This is not Burnout or Need for Speed.

Here's how I'd break things down.

Two steps forward:

* There is a LOT to do in this game. I've been playing it for about two weeks straight and I'm maybe 20% done with it - and the further you go, the harder (and more time consuming) the events get. There are also a lot of different types of events this time around - in addition to the standard leveled racing events as in past GT games, there are now themed "special events" and even seasonal events. The license tests are still there but are not required. The new B-spec mode lets you control an AI driver. There is a full online racing mode.

* The presentation is still the classiest around, from the menu music to the graphics to the car models to the tracks. Everything is just tasteful looking, tasteful sounding and beautiful. It's almost jarring to be so used to hearing Guns N Roses or something fire up in most racing games, and then to launch GT5 and hear some smooth lounge music or classical guitar sounds instead. The car models *all* look really good, premium or not - it's generally hard to tell the difference. (The premium models all have cockpit views, can take damage and can accept more visual upgrades, which are the most obvious differences.)

* Pretty much every facet of the game has been beefed up since GT4. Car sounds are now very distinctive - you can finally tell a Ferrari from a Prius! The graphics are now native 1080p. There are a lot more upgrades available to your car, though some of them are not immediately obvious (they're split among two areas, one for mechanical and one for cosmetic or aero upgrades). There are more tracks. There are more cars. There's visible damage (such as it is).

Now for the "one step back":

* Damage modeling, which was hyped pretty heavily and is a feature a lot of us have been asking for, is a joke. They almost may as well have not even bothered. Even on the cars that have it, you can slam head-on into a wall at 200mph and maybe you'll scratch the paint a little bit. Do this three or four times and maybe your bumper will start to sag a little. There is no setting to make this more realistic, either; this is just the way it is. This means that it's still possible to win races by using your opponents like pinball flippers in turns. There is no penalty for doing so.

* The graphics look very nice but I'm not getting the same "uncanny valley" feeling that some people are. They still have a somewhat cartoony look, although they're very smooth for the most part. Also, car shadows have not been improved at all over GT4; they still have very bad aliasing that kind of ruins the effect of the initial start fly-around, and of some of the replays.

* B-spec mode is an interesting diversion but should not make up 1/3 of the game as it does. You need to complete all the same races as A-spec mode (racing yourself) in B-spec mode to complete the game, and some of these are very long. During that time, you're just sitting there and watching.

* The AI is supposed to be better (they say this with every release) but I see no evidence of it. AI cars don't really race among themselves but basically keep to a strict racing line. Hilariously, in the Ferrari challenge I actually forced the car behind me to stop at one point - instead of going around, all the cars behind *him* politely stopped too!

* There is a *lengthy* install that only seems to marginally cut down on the ridiculously long load times. I don't mind some time to load courses, but there are load times to do *anything* in the game. Some of them actually aren't really that long, but when you need to wait 4-5 seconds every time you even change screens, it starts to get very annoying. And that's *after* doing the optional install!

* As in past games in the series, events often have opponent cars that make the race unwinnable given the restrictions and the cars available to you at that point. The only solution is to back out of the race and try again until you randomly don't get those cars racing against you.

Overall, I'd say it's pretty much what I expected, knowing the pedigree and the history of the series. A ton of cars, realistic physics, nice sound, nice graphics, a lot to do; but bad AI, bad damage modeling, and some technical annoyances. Yep, it's another Gran Turismo game!

I've been playing Railroad Tycoon games since the beginning, and the second and third games in the series are still among my top 5 favorites of all time. I had high hopes for Sid Meier's Railroads, the "spiritual successor" to those games from the man who created the original.

But honestly, what this game actually is is a sequel to the original Railroad Tycoon. Sid Meier's gone back to his roots, alright - to the point that he's almost ignoring all the good things that made it into RT2 and RT3. Railroads is much simpler than either RT2 or RT3, and it brings back some of the conventions from the first game, like signals and stations with multiple tracks (IIRC, RT2 and 3 allowed just one or two tracks in stations, whereas the original would let you create mammoth 12 track terminals if you wanted).

Railroads is a lot more about just creating a rail system and watching it run than RT2/3 were. Those games were basically economic simulations with the railroad serving as the economic engine. Railroads is, instead, more of a virtual toy train layout. There is an economy, and obviously you have to connect resources to cities that need them in order to generate profit. And if you opt to play against competitors, you need to do this before they do. But it's not nearly as fleshed out or realistic as it was in RT2/3. For example, goods don't move themselves (you don't need to compete against other forms of transport) - they will wait forever for a train and production will simply stop if an industry is full up. This means both that there's not much impetus for you to provide reliable service (in RT3, if you didn't move the goods, they'd move themselves and leave the scraps for you) and there's also no real way to make money on industry unless you (or a competing railroad) have linked it up. In RT3, industries could make money even if you were nowhere near them, meaning the harder scenarios could be won by buying industries all over the map. In Railroads, all you can do is build more connections and run more trains (and then you can buy those industries that you've linked up).

The money does pile up pretty quickly because there are fewer ways to make it; the economy has been rebalanced to only account for your trains. In previous games, the early going could be a real struggle and some scenarios could be a real slog to the end unless you took advantage of the whole in-game economy. But even the most complex scenarios in Railroads can be finished in a few hours. The pace is actually pretty blistering, and I play on 1/2 speed most of the time because otherwise the decades will literally just pass you by and you can easily miss your objectives just because you can't click fast enough.

It's not all bad, and the game is still fun to play. But even some of the positives have their downsides. For example, laying track is now generally much easier than in previous RT games - you almost don't need to think about it (and this is one thing that was *really* tedious in RT2, and improved but not great in RT3). On the other hand, the automatic signaling and pathfinding can be a real pain, especially when you try to go for multi-track ops. I'm playing a scenario right now where one corridor is so busy that I need three tracks, and I need switches between each track in each direction. Every switch gets a signal. Get three or four trains running through this area and they will take really weird paths to their destination (switching over all three tracks for no reason) which of course blocks all the signals and then no one can pass. So you end up needing to think about your track laying after all, and trying to be really efficient so that trains don't go wandering into other trains' paths. (The first RT, IIRC, had directional signals, which would be a big help here. You can't just have all trains running in one direction on one track, and the other on a second track.)

Also, unless I'm missing something, there is no "undo" button. You can sell your track back if you make a mistake, but not for full value.

AI competition is also kind of weird, in that it's much improved over previous games in some ways and much worse in others. In my last scenario, I was getting beaten soundly by one competitor who had bought out our third competitor and locked up all shares of both that company and his own. He was also pulling away from me in terms of revenue. So all I did was stop, wait a few in-game years until I had some money saved up, and then I somehow bought his company out from under him for far less than his company value - even though he was the only shareholder and was hugely profitable! On the plus side for the AI, he *was* beating me legitimately before that.

The interface has a lot of "quirks" and/or just poor design. A couple examples: you can't upgrade all of your engines at once - you need to do it one at a time with about 3 clicks each. You can't clearly see what the load a train is carrying is worth. There's always a major discrepancy between the amount of cargo waiting at a station on the map screen vs. that same cargo when you actually go to fill out a train consist. The train and station lists are both nightmarishly laid out - there was obviously an attempt to simplify them but when you have a lot of each, you can't see *any* real detail at a glance, you need to click into each one. This makes it impossible to quickly compare things. RT2/3 displayed all pertinent info in the list itself, so if a train was running 100% empty or a station had 50 tons of goods just sitting there, you could see it with one quick glance through the list.

Even with all its faults, though, it's still a fun game to play and one I'm looking forward to getting back to as I write this review. Maybe it's just the concept itself, of building an empire while watching a bunch of trains run around. It's kind of hard to really mess that up badly enough that the game would be unplayably bad (though I'm sure a lesser game designer could). But still, I expected more. Honestly, I'd go back to playing RT3 if it was actually playable on Windows 7. (I still don't know why it isn't!)

I buy maybe one basketball game every 5 years... it's one of those sports I'm not a huge fan of in real life, but I love to play it myself and I do like video game representations of it. I'd read about how realistic this game was so thought I'd give it a shot. But I'm about ready to trade it in after just a few days of play.

Here's the problem in a nutshell: the AI is cheap. *Really* cheap. It cheats. Incessantly. I don't mean you'll be playing against a good team with star players and one of them makes a great move and you say "welp, he *is* a star player, that's his job." I'm talking about total scrubs - including centers! - shooting 3 pointers consistently with defenders right in their face, and not only making them, but swishing them. I'm talking about when a "good" team is playing a "bad" team and the "bad" team has been beating the pants off the "good" team all game long and is up by 10 points with 2 minutes left, you can almost guarantee the "good" team's about to go on a 12 point run to close out the game.

It's almost like the game has its own idea of what the basketball world order is supposed to be, and it will do whatever it has to do to preserve that. If a team is "supposed" to win, it will win about 90% of the time, regardless of how well you're playing as a human player. If you're shooting 60% from the field, the AI will shoot 70%. If you're making 90% of your free throws, the AI will make 95%. It really takes almost all the fun out of the game if you're playing single player.

You can sit back and coach instead, which is something I like to do, but the game's really not as well fleshed out in that area as I wish it was, and the interface is cumbersome. There's no easy way, for example, to tell who's the best stealer on your team. When you look at the roster or lineups, you only get a generic "perimeter defense" attribute, and it's presented as a letter grade rather than a number. Obviously, there are fewer gradations between A and F than there are between 100 and 50. And again, if there is an actual "steal" stat, I can't find it.

A lot of people have talked about the presentation, and it *is* a lot like watching an actual game on TV. But here's the problem: I'm not watching a game, I'm playing one. NBA 2K12 simulates all the *boring* parts of a TV broadcast, from the random chatter among the commentators that has nothing to do with what's going on in the game to the long "free throw routines" that every player in real life has. You can turn the latter off (it's really about the same as watching a batter in baseball take his practice swings before every pitch), but there are a lot of things that you can't.

For example, after every quarter ends, you'll be presented with highlights from another game. You can skip it, but you need to wait for it to load, then press X, then wait for something else to load, then press X again. Then you need to wait for your game to re-load, then press X to skip the part of the game where your guys are just standing around waiting for the game to re-start while the cheerleaders dance to the arena music (which you can't turn off - even if you explicitly *do* turn it off in the menu!). It's maddening. There is no "quick play" option that I've found, where you can just keep playing until the end of the game with no interruptions, without waiting for the ref to pick up and hand you the ball after every stoppage, etc. It would be like a baseball game constantly making you watch the guy standing in the on-deck circle, not allowing you to skip it when the batboy runs out to pick up a loose ball, then forcing you to sit through highlights of other games after every half inning.

It's a shame because the basic gameplay mechanic is solid, and the graphics are good. I can't imagine what more you could want from a basketball game that isn't in here; there are a lot of plays to choose from, the pace is pretty realistic, the players move like you'd expect from real life, etc. It's just too bad the cheap AI and maddening presentation basically ruin it.

Games like this are hard to find nowadays. But if you're a fan of Locomotion, Transport Tycoon or games of that ilk that are all about taking people from point A to point B as efficiently and economically as possible, this is the latest in that genre. Given its obviously low budget and inherent limitations, it feels surprisingly polished and modern. And it's as addictive as any of its predecessors.

This game is based in Europe and takes place from around the 1920's to the present day. The general goal is to build up mass transit systems using buses, trams (light rail), metros (subways), water taxis/ferries and helicopters(??). There are several scenarios, one for each city in the game, though they basically all come down to the same thing - just build the most efficient transit system possible.

The graphics are very detailed and realistic, and it's obvious how much care went into them. People walk around realistically and actually walk on and off your vehicles (they don't just appear and disappear), planes take off and land at airports (and they look like real planes), long distance trains arrive and depart from train stations (and they look like real trains), traffic moves mostly like you'd expect, with jams in busy areas. The cities do feel alive, and when stations and stops on my lines start to get really crowded, I find myself actually feeling bad for all the little people standing there waiting endlessly. It's fun to actually just sit there watching as any new vehicles you add slowly start to pick up the slack and empty those platforms or sidewalks.

Of course, the really addictive thing about any game like this is connecting people with where they want to go, and this game is no exception. For example, getting people from their homes to their places of work, getting people from airports and train stations to hotels, etc. This game simulates those realistic routings very well, as it does transfers. If a passenger needs to go from their home to the department store, and you only have a bus, a subway and then another bus set up to take them on that route, then that's what they'll do - as long as they don't need to walk too far in between stops. This means you can set up feeders into your main lines and create major transfer points, just like in real life.

There are some annoyances and limitations. The biggest is that, unlike real life and previous games in this genre, your transit system doesn't really affect the city itself. Nothing ever gets built that isn't preordained to get built at some pre-determined time. This makes everything less satisfying, because all you're really doing is just trying to carry as many people as possible, not helping build a city.

Time also moves very slowly (you can speed it up, but it doesn't really matter), and even playing each scenario for several hours, I only ever make it a couple of years in game time, meaning I'm stuck using the same vehicles most of the time. In most scenarios, you'll be lucky if one or two new vehicles (total, among all types) are introduced before you finish the scenario. And usually, the newest vehicle in any category is clearly the best, so there's no real incentive to mix vehicles in your fleet. Railroad Tycoon II this is not.

There are also a few play balance issues. The first scenario I found extremely difficult, and only won through trial and error experimentation in how sleazily I could run my business without getting run out of town. (Turns out yes, people will still ride your buses even if they have to pay $15 for a ride, and your employees will not all quit if you pay them a salary of $1!) Subsequent scenarios start out difficult too but end up almost impossibly easy once you have enough money to build some effective metro lines. The metro is like a miracle of science and economics in this game - it's your ticket to riches. The trick is just getting over that hump to where you can afford to set up some good lines, but then you've got it made.

And finally, I'm increasingly convinced there's a memory leak of some kind in the game, and I can't find a patch to fix it (the developer web site refers customers back to the site they downloaded the game from, but I don't see a patch on Amazon). Loading a game - regardless of how far in I am - starts out a smooth experience. But even if I do nothing but pan around for a while, after 15 minutes or so everything is crawling. I don't have the most powerful graphics card, but I don't see why everything should be smooth initially and then quickly degrade when I haven't even done anything. This is consistent and repeatable. Luckily, the degradation seems to level off after a while, and it'll stop at "choppy but playable". It almost seems like the game initially loads only the part of the city you're looking at, but as you're panning around it loads more and more without ever dumping anything *out* of memory. Eventually, it's loaded everything and then it stops getting worse, but sticks at a degraded performance level.

Overall, though, this is a fun game that I can just sit there and watch and get enjoyment out of. If you're that same type of person (and not everybody is), give it a shot.

I love this thing, and I've owned various Genesises (Genesi?) continuously since 1990. I mean the system and its games are legendary, so any handheld that could play them even remotely well would be a winner. Sega themselves had a "portable" Genesis called the Nomad that was huge, could only play one game at a time (and since they were home carts, they stuck out the top) and got about 2 hours of battery life out of six non-rechargeable AA's, and people these days are nuts for it - go look up the prices it commands on Ebay.

Well this thing plays 39 Genesis games out of the box and lets you load however many others you want via SD card that you can just leave in it permanently. And yes, I have gotten the SD card to work - you just need to follow the instructions. Make a folder called "Game" and put your *bin* files in it - they need to be real bin files, not just some other format you've renamed. You can use a utility like SBWin to convert them if need be. Not every game works, but in my experience about 80% do if you just follow the instructions... and that's still many hundreds of games, a large number of which are amazing games that still hold up today as some of the best 2D gaming on any system ever.

One of the problems with emulated systems like this is that there are people that expect perfection. Well, the system's not perfect - so what? It doesn't play 100% of all Genesis games, its sound is a little scratchy if you play it too loud, and in some cases the emulation is not perfect even if the game is playable. (Though often it *is* perfect; most of my games play just as well on this system as they do on a real Genesis.)

You're still getting a portable system that's about 1/4 the size and an 1/8 the weight of the Nomad, has a really nice backlit screen, a rechargeable battery(!), and controls that feel and work really well, and it also happens to play a large number of great Genesis games. What the heck is there to complain about? You will easily get more than enough entertainment out of this thing to justify the price, especially when you remember that you literally need to pay *nothing* after your initial purchase. This isn't like a modern system where you need to keep buying games. You buy this thing and you're set. Maybe you'll need to pay 8 bucks for an SD card if you don't have a spare one lying around. It's an amazing value considering the time you'll spend playing even just the games it comes with.

This is my third recent VR headset. I also have a PSVR and an original Oculus Rift, so I have some basis for comparison.

I wanted this because it's both a standalone headset *and* it can now connect to your PC via Oculus Link, which gives it all the same functionality as the Rift. So it's a clear upgrade in that sense; it just does more than the Rift, being that it can also be used (with its own dedicated apps and games) without the PC, and even when running PC games it does not require external sensors. Since all the wires the other VR systems require are my big pet peeve about VR in general, I thought the Quest would be the perfect solution.

And if this is your first experience with VR, definitely prepare to be blown away. Modern VR just in general is almost a life-changing experience, and the Quest is no different. The graphics are to the point where it's easy to immerse yourself in the content. The Quest has a little higher resolution than the Rift and a little lower refresh rate; overall it's kind of a wash IMO. It looks pretty similar to me. But both look great overall.

Compared to the PSVR, both are obviously higher quality in terms of the image, although PSVR holds its own and is still more than good enough to immerse yourself in. PSVR also has better lenses than either the Rift or the Quest, both of which have obvious "god rays", where the light bounces around and reflects off the inside of the lenses. I had hoped the Quest would fix this issue, but it hasn't. Its lenses do look a little different than the Rift - the light rays are kind of evenly distributed rather than all concentrated in the middle as on the Rift, but there's just as much of it. PSVR doesn't have this at all.

There are two medium-sized caveats with the Quest:

1) It's uncomfortable! Oculus is going backwards on this. The Rift was comfortable *enough*, but not very much so... I expected the Quest to be an improvement after 4 or so years of extra development. This is a really big issue for VR - it has to be comfortable. And the Quest is just not. It's extremely front-heavy, for one thing, and its head strap seems somehow even less well designed than the Rift's (which was already kind of hacky, with velcro and whatnot). It's meant to go down further on the back of your head and grab the entire circumference of your skull, but in practice it just slides forward no matter what I do. And when it slides forward, it presses really hard on your face.

There are accessories you can get to alleviate this, which makes it clear too that it's a real issue (if it weren't, companies wouldn't be profiting from it). But that's an extra expense, and something I'm going to have to use trial and error with some of these products to fix.

If you're wondering, the PSVR is very comfortable and it's supposedly the "low end" option these days, but I can wear it for hours without even thinking about it. It doesn't press against your face at all. The Quest I can wear for maybe 30 minutes before it's unbearable. Other VR companies need to just copy Sony - they've got it right.

2) It's missing any sort of headphones. Again, you can fix this by buying something extra - you can either use regular earbuds (though the cord will probably get in the way) or you can buy special earbuds just for the Quest with short cords. But I feel like this is a major omission - VR just doesn't feel right when listening through speakers. It takes you out of the immersive world. This reeks of cost-cutting - the Rift had some pretty good headphones attached directly to it. The PSVR at least came with a set of special earbuds with the right length asymmetrical cord (I eventually upgraded to something more like the Rift has, headphones attached to the headset side rails, but it at least came with *something* so you didn't need to spend extra money right off the bat).

I'm sure I'm getting more critical as someone who's on his third VR headset. But that's the thing - VR should be maturing, and while the Quest is awesome for being standalone *and* PC linkable, in other important ways it's a regression, with extra purchases required to fix its issues. I just expect better at this point, and we all should. These systems are not inexpensive, nor are they new tech anymore. And Oculus is not some tiny little indie company; they are owned by Facebook. (Oh, also? They *really* want you to log in with Facebook now. I tried logging in with just my email address, but they linked my email address with my Facebook account and logged me in with Facebook anyway. You have to manually unlink your account, but you will "lose access to certain functions" if you do so.)

Still, I'm probably going to end up selling my Rift simply because it doesn't do as much as the Quest. I'll bite the bullet and buy what I need to buy to bring the Quest up to standard (I've already ordered Quest-specific earbuds; some sort of comfort solution will come next). Once I do that, I think I'll be happier with it than with the Rift, especially because I can finally get rid of the rat's nest of cables going to my PC (HDMI and three sensor cables), and only connect the Quest when I need to in order to play PC-based games. That was the original goal; I just thought the out of the box experience would get me there, and it didn't.

At least at the time I bought this (mid 2019), this was one of the very few Switch Lite-specific cases available in the United States, and one of maybe two that's actually officially licensed. (I like having logos on my handheld system cases.) It fits the system pretty well and doesn't add a whole lot of bulk, though obviously this is not the most svelte of handhelds to begin with.

There's a licensed case in Japan that actually conforms to the system's contours, so it's a *very* tight fit. This is not that. This is the standard zipped up semi-hard cloth pouch type thing that's become common in the US. And at the time of my purchase and this writing, it was only available in white. So, ok. Not my favorite color for a case, which by nature is designed to protect a system from the elements.. meaning it's likely to get dirty very quickly.

But all that said, it protects the system pretty well, is nicely padded and all that. And props to the designers for including the little spandex slot for the zipper pull when you close the case, so the zipper pull isn't just hanging out and flopping around. Seriously, that's my pet peeve with a lot of cases, and this one at least solves that.

Overall I'd probably like something a little more stylish and maybe more form fitting, but this'll do for now, and it is the official US case.

I admit that I went back and forth on my rating for this case... I think it's maybe just a little bit too much form over function. It's actually a beautiful case, as are all the ones in this series (they make them with several different designs, though I just wanted the basic Switch logo on mine), and it's metal, so it feels premium.

But I find myself wanting a case for my case. I don't want this case itself to be damaged, and it seems quite fragile both from what I've read in other reviews and just from what I see and feel from it. Metal may not really be the best case material; it can easily dent and scratch permanently. I actually try not to take it out too much so mine hasn't become damaged (yet), but the design lends itself to wanting to avoid that. It's probably like having a new car; you try hard to avoid that first scratch, but once you get it, you stop caring so much and the floodgates open.

There's also a bit more of a gap between the sides of the system and the sides of the case than I'd like; it doesn't hold the Switch in place all that securely.

I think this is more of a really great long-term storage solution, or maybe something to impress your friends with (you honestly *will* get comments on how nice of a case it is) than it is a really functional protection device for walking around with your Switch. For that, you might want something uglier, but less prone to visible damage.
