I was browsing Amazon on "Black Friday" after not having worked in retail for two years now, and I came across this guitar for Guitar Hero.  I own Guitar Hero 3, Aerosmith, and World Tour so I thought I would do my friends a favor and pick up this second guitar for the $13 it was selling for.  I completed my transaction and the confirmation screen showed another of the same for $7 including shipping.  I purchased it and canceled my first order and now have been enjoying this guitar for several weeks.  It feels better and the buttons are more rounded than the Aerosmith guitar.  Even at the $15 price this is a worthwhile purchase that feels very reliable.

Since I purchased an iPod Touch roughly two years ago I have been using the InvisibleSHIELD products by ZAGG on my small portable devices. The protection they offer is great, and I find their products to be durable and not to scratch like generic products. With that said there are two small issues I have with this product on this device. First and most noticeably is the slight distortion it adds to the display, most noticeably when the stereoscopic 3D is enabled. Let me first assure anyone reading this that I applied the product myself and that there are no bubbles, or dirt between the film and the screen. The image has roughly a dozen points on the screen where the colors are distorted possibly from bending the light as a magnifying glass preventing the pixels to be seen by one eye from displaying correctly. This imperfection is tolerable and preferable to risking a scratched screen.

The second issue is a 3DS design issue that Nintendo should correct, but ZAGG could proactively correct. With or without a screen protector the lower screen contacts the upper screen when closed. This leaves two vertical marks across the upper screen. These marks go away with time, but when present intensifies the first problem I mentioned above. To prevent this from occurring at all two short rubber nubs can be placed on the upper screen to contact to the sides of the lower screen. I made this change on mine, using the rubber feet of an old router, and now the 3DS closes without issue and no marks are made on the upper screen.

I purchased this for our Wii U GamePad after typically buying the ZAGG Invisible shield products and not wanting to spend that much but have a good screen protector.  HORI is world renown for their superior joysticks and arcade quality products.  I took a chance on their screen protector and do not regret it at all.  After cleaning the screen and blowing off some small pieces of dust I applied the protector.  It went on very easily and as described had no air bubbles.  I used the included cloth to press the protector against the screen and with quite a bit of use the protector still looks brand new.  It's actually difficult to tell that it is even there.  Highly recommended.

So my title describes this adapter very well, though the adapter is actually quite good.  At first when I tried it out by connecting it into a Wii remote and then plugging in a controller, the cursor was slowly moving toward the top of the screen.  I simply unplugged the adapter (leaving the controller attached) and plugged it back in again.  Usually this is a common problem when the joystick is offcenter when the controller is connected, but this time that wasn't the case.  Despite this connect and reconnect, it hasn't happened since.  The responsiveness despite going from a controller, through the adapter, through the wii remote and back to the Wii U is still very precise and responsive.  I was very impressed.  Because the adapter is emulating a classic controller, the start button does need to be pressed twice quickly to function as a typical "START" button press.  Pressing and holding the same button for several seconds will bring up the HOME screen.  This isn't a problem at all in game and is just an fyi for anyone purchasing this adapter, as this is the way it has to be.  With that said, this is a great controller and is highly recommended if you prefer your Gamecube controller and plan on picking up Smash Bros and or Mario Kart next year.  This adapter works for any and all things from Wii U games supporting the Classic Controller to Wii mode on the Wii U and everything supporting the classic controller there.  Also works well on the original Wii, should you simply need to have the controller used in a location that is further than the cable would reach the Wii.

Pros:
-Fun game for up to four girls who enjoy Barbie between the ages of 3 and 7.
-Nine activities in varied dollhouse locations plus a slew of finding the hidden item games.
-Most activities are fairly easy, yet some can be challenging * see below
-Dress Barbie and her friends in the outfits you unlock during any game (can be a con for older kids, but my young girls don't mind someone changing outfits mid gameplay).
-My 9 yr old son enjoys this with my daughters 3 and 5, but only in short gameplay sessions.
-Great visuals on the Wii U, characters are animated and cutscenes are great.

Cons:
-Only the Gamepad player can play as Barbie, and other players are only selected by the order in which their controller pairs with the Wii U.
-*Some activities are not explained well enough to understand, which may require an adult to intervene and figure out how to play. Case in point, the bedroom level where you collect packages dropping from the sky. If you don't press "A" on the gamepad (or I believe "2" on the Wiimotes) other characters will step in front of you to collect packages you were about to catch. Pressing "A" makes you step forward and isn't explained.
-Difficult gameplay on some levels for the target age group. My daughter's biggest frustrations are the applying makeup level and washing the dog levels. The gameplay on these levels for the Gamepad player is NOT a problem and is enjoyed by both as these stages involve touch screen gameplay, yet the Wiimote play involves pointing the Wiimote at the screen. Even my five (soon to be six) year old who enjoys games like Skylanders, Mario 3D World, NintendoLand, Rayman Legends and others has a difficult time pointing the Wiimote at certain places on the screen when these levels require a lot of precision pointing.

In conclusion, as a budget title this game is a hit with younger girls. Even though the gameplay is fairly easy, and at times more difficult, most games have a bit of strategy involved in them for older players (older siblings, parents) to get involved and enjoy at least in small doses.

I think the character Dune Bug is overlooked, but I find him to be one of my all time favorite magic type Skylanders.  His ability to summon a large globe of energy that medium to smaller enemies stick to absolutely great.  It's pretty enjoyable rolling around a huge ball of energy rolling up a half dozen enemies in it and then tossing it aside.
Bought this game for our son who has enjoyed it.  The included code to download a bonus character and level is now expired, but available for purchase from the 3DS eShop for $2.

Originally played through a few hours of this game on Xbox One X, and then repurchased on Switch after hearing that improvements were made and additional content added.  The game plays well enough on Xbox One but freezes and stutters for no apparent reason.  On Switch I have had zero issues with the game with playing much further than I ever had on Xbox One.  Features like the camera seem to have been refined as well.  Visually the game looks great with no big compromises apparently having been made.  All around I highly recommend this game even if you've played it before.
Call of the Wild is way better.

I played the original Mafia more than a decade ago, and it was enjoyable. This remake brings back nostalgia, under great graphics. Story, as good as it was, is tweaked a little and added a few more things here and there. Cars look gorgeous. Character models can't be better. Good job from the devs.

However, as a remake especially in 2020, I don't think it's good enough. The gunplay, animation, and control are outdated. Most of the time I felt like I was playing Mafia 2 under the glorious graphics. Hell, I even beat the whole game on classic mode but it was lots of frustration and anger. I would say the game is worth it at $30 or less. I'm still grateful we got a remake after all, but the game needed more effort from Hangar 13.

I played the original Demon's Souls and it was great, but this remake brings it to another level. I can say it's one of the best Souls games I have ever played (I've played them all no kidding). My dog agreed with me too!. Get it and you won't be disappointed.
I'm lucky to get one. Nothing to not like about it. Amazing console.

Good game for stealth and puzzle lovers. Ignore the haters.

The game looks and runs amazing on the PS5. There are some bugs and crashes here and there as of Feb 2021, but they are tolerable by me and the devs are working hard to fix that. You can also play H1 and H2 levels if you own them. Just launch H2 and redeem it, then you're good to go. Basically this is the most complete Hitman game and it's the last one in the trilogy. There are new 6 levels. There are good ones and bad ones, depending on how you look at them, but to me most of them are good and some are on par with Hitman 2016's maps.

If you are the type of gamer who plays games once and move on, this will probably not the game for you. Some people complain it's short. That is laughable. Hitman is a puzzle game at its core that's designed to be played multiple times with different experiments and outcomes. There is no other game like it, it's the only one of its kind.

I like it a lot.

What we have here is a perfect tribute to Kirby for Kirby fans. It is also a great way to get into the original Kirby games if you have never played them before, since you get the entire collection of the original Kirby platformers in one convenient package. The included collectors extras are nice, and the addition of challenge stages, which are very similar to Kirby's Return to Dreamland, is a great way to add new worthwhile content to fans who have already been there and done that.

Now, as to the reason why I rated this 3 stars. As someone who has played these games before, you will quickly find how there isn't much to do. The only way I could recommend this game to someone who has already played most of the games included in this collection is if you already own Return to Dreamland and Kirby's Epic Yarn. Heck even if you haven't played the classic games on this collection before I would still recommend purchasing Return to Dreamland and Epic Yarn over this since they are simply the better games to own, and generally easier to enjoy.

What we have here is a special treat for the fans. It isn't for everyone.

The stealth aspect of this game is sadly nowhere near as good as it should have been due to some terrible enemy design decisions, as well as a generally flawed execution of the alarm system.

Basically, what we have here is a game that claims to be Splinter Cell, that in reality plays like a third person Call of Duty with a blend of Metal Gear Solid 4 without all the lengthy forced cutscenes and without the polished gameplay.

I want to like this game, but to be honest I am having an awfully hard time enjoying this game like I feel like I should. It is one of those "stealth" games where you try to play it stealthy, and it can be fun when that works, but more often than not your attempts at stealth can be all too easily ruined by any number of stupid design problems, such as the way enemies react (or don't react) to being shot, how overpowered some enemies are in this game (they now have these heavily armored enemies who can withstand multiple headshots), the way alarms can be unpredictable and far too sensitive at times (going off when there's nobody around who could have caught on), as well as the way the game just poops large numbers of overly aggressive enemies with terrible AI at you from out of nowhere whenever an alarm goes off.

Basically, the entire experience is brought down by the way the enemies were designed. It is like this game tried so hard to present you with a realistic or at least engaging approach to stealth, yet when it comes to actually engaging your enemy it seems like that is where everything got all screwed up. You eventually find yourself becoming frustrated with the game and wind up running and gunning COD style due to the problems that surround the enemy design. It is quite a shame really, and I am truly finding it hard to like this game.

I am giving it 3 stars because there is something appealing about this game, and many aspects of it is technically well made. It is just the way the enemies can suck the fun out of the game as well as the way the stealth can be ruined by technical and design issues truly brings this game down. The enemies generally feel outdated when it comes to the way they were designed and I had higher expectations for a game supposedly designed around stealth, so it's a real shame that the game seems to punish you for trying to be stealthy.

I would give it a shot if you are really big on this type of game, but just don't be expecting anything too deep in the way as stealth as it more or less becomes a third person Call of Duty deathmatch at times.

A great concept, and I am a huge fan of snowboarding games, have been since I played games like Cool Boarders and 1080, so trust me when I said that I really wanted to give this game a solid 10.

What we have here is a game that does about as many things wrong as it does right. For example the environments look great and the character animations look really smooth and respond appropriately, the snowboarding and skiing is well represented and easily the reason to get this game, even the wingsuit and paragliding is well done, and as you explore the game you can really get a sense that the developers just wanted you to be able to go out and explore sort of like you would in Skate and just find ideal lines to repeat or new spots.

Now I have played this game a lot, pretty much unlocked most of what there is to unlock, seen what there is to be seen, and progressed through the challenges. It's satisfying for that winter games itch if you are like me and also a big fan of snowboarding games. Thing is it isn't perfect... far from in fact.

To start lets talk about the snowboarding/skiing, pretty much the entire reason to buy this game. Best way to describe it is somewhere between 1080 for the N64 and Skate for the PS3/360. You sort of have that sim/arcade kind of balance that those games had and a lot of the gameplay seems to be inspired by both games. For example it has that same damage mechanic that 1080 had for landing big jumps and going over rough terrain, but here it's a bit different. What they have done here is give you what they call a "G meter." Now this g meter sort of acts like the COD recovery mechanic, where when you take damage you will hear your character react and the screen will start to go black and white until your character finally gives up or recovers after a few seconds of not taking any damage.

Sounds like a good idea right? Well I would have to agree... if it worked right. Problem is it is inconsistent, and inconsistency is a subject that generally rules my disappointment with this game. For example sometimes it will react appropriately, sometimes it seems like it doesn't react at all, and other times it seems hyper sensitive and goes off seemingly at random putting you on the verge of death when you feel like that shouldn't have happened. Now this is a problem that brings down my score in the end as it leads to a lot of frustration due to the ragdoll effects that happen when you exceed the g meter. When this happens you will literally just watch your character flip, flop, and flail around helplessly and without any attempts to regain composure as if they have gone completely unconscious. This would make sense if the character truly did go unconscious, but the problem is that apparently they don't. The game has an entirely different reaction for when you go unconscious, which is when you endure too much punishment for your character to get back up.

This is pretty bad as you will often watch your character flop around helplessly for what can seem like over half a minute at times. It can be pretty funny or entertaining if you aren't trying to do something, but when you are trying to race or need to go somewhere and your character just keeps flopping around it works like an instant death maneuver. For me this has led to a lot of frustration due to the issues with the g meter mentioned earlier, but this isn't the end of what is wrong with the snowboarding skiing, as I still need to get into the controls.

Now the controls are a real mixed bag. The scheme seems simple enough and at the best of times it is, but the problem is that feels terribly inconsistent at times to the point to where you can sometimes feel like you are merely suggesting what you want your character to do as opposed to controlling them directly. For example, take the freestyle trick controls. You use the right trigger to jump, the left analog to spin and flip, but you can only perform your spin and flip actions on the controller after you have jumped, so in other words there is no "pre-load" like you have in games like SSX. This can be fine, but it doesn't always seem to respond correctly. Sometimes you will perform the maneuver you desires, and other times you will watch your character just do nothing at all. That is right, for some reason, if the game decides you didn't move your analog stick in the spin or flip direction you wanted you will just watch your character stubbornly refuse to do anything. This also works for the jumping, which seems like it has a delay. So not only do you need to jump before you think you would, but the game doesn't even seem to allow you to jump at times as it will cancel out or not even register for some weird reason.

Anyways I think that is enough about the snowboarding and skiing. Oh, there is also some wingsuit and paragliding stuff in this game. It's alright, but I wouldn't get the game for it. Serves best as a means for exploration.

I give this game a C+, could be much better as it is.

First off I want to comment on the hardware, which is fantastic for what you are paying. I love how they gave it a 4:3 screen, a rarity in this day and age, and it's picture quality is fantastic, I honestly didn't expect it to look so good. The size is also just about right, if was any smaller it would be too small to really enjoy using and if it was bigger it would be taking up too much room and probably become some far more expensive real arcade style machine. The controls are also surprisingly good, the arcade stick isn't the notchy 8-way arcade sticks we grew up with in the arcade, it has far more of an analog stick feel to it, but it works very well in action and I was able to play the demanding fighting games without any issues, something that I was also surprised by. As for the buttons I have nothing to complain about, once again they lack the feel of a real arcade cabinet but I was able to use them effectively without any issues, and the placement feels perfect for that old school arcade feel. My only complaint about the hardware has to be lack of range for the sound adjustment, you only have about 4 different settings, and I found the minimum setting to be a bit too quiet and the louder adjustment to be a bit too loud.

Now I feel it is appropriate to get into the games. While the selection is rather good considering how it is limited to 40 games, these all appear to be for the most part the AES versions of the games (in other words the home console versions, not the arcade versions). How these differ from the arcade versions is the lack of the customization options that you get with the arcade emulation found on ACA games for the Switch for example, which includes freeplay credits, a full range of difficulty and time adjustments, as well as censorship options among other adjustments. Yes, sadly what we have here is the censored versions of these games with limited credits and often fixed difficulty, and there is no way to adjust them, the only settings menu offered is just a simple one for the hardware. This means the Metal Slug games for example have censored white blood and you are limited to only about 5 credits for the games which makes them significantly harder. In fact most games seem to have limited credits, which makes it so you either gotta be amazing at these games or call it quits when the games get really tough, and considering how these are classic arcade games that we are talking about, that can happen rather quickly (as these games were meant to eat your quarters after a while).

So would I recommend it? At this price, with this excellent take on the hardware being downsized, most definitely. Just keep in mind how you aren't getting the full arcade experience with the games, but then again this is significantly cheaper than most options for collecting these games. The fact that you can attach a mini-HDMI to this and use it as a game console on your TV with the optional controller (which is very well made I might add) is just a great bonus that sort of makes this a real bargain AES console if you want to play it on your TV.

This is overall a well made controller. I had a Neo Geo Pocket Color so I know what the original microswitches were like and this is honestly just as good to use and a lot quieter. If you are a hardcore purist I could see the complaints on that and the different button placement, but this stays true to the revisions they made with the mini arcade console and it delivers on adding the functionality needed to turn this into a home console for your TV. The cord is generously long and it gives you that authentic AES home console feel at a small fraction of the price it would cost to get the real deal. For what you are paying for the overall package I see no reason to complain.

I love this product. I bought this primarily for my Switch, but I can use it with a multitude of devices in my house including the NES/SNES classics and a couple of other 8bitdo receivers.

What I love about this remote over the Switch's actual Pro is overall the price. I have 2 of them. They are fine. A little over priced in my opinion. Don't let the price of this controller fool you though. It is not cheaply made or cumbersome to use. It very much earns the right to call itself a Pro controller.

After that what I love is the design, and colors. As you can see I got the Game Boy design one, because it looks awesome. There's also a SNES colored one I would have gotten but I have their original Pro in that color and I wanted to change it up a bit. The black is nice but it uses Xbox colors for the button letters and I personally don't like it as much as it clashes to me with the SNES inspired controller design.

Also I like that the sticks have more resistance than the Switch Pro controllers. The Switch Pro sticks are super loose so precise controls are a little harder to accomplish. Also for me personally I hate how far the face buttons stick out from the Switch Pro casing and this is more in line with the near perfect SNES controller. This controller also to me has a much better, more responsive D-pad. Keep in mind this controller uses the Dualshock style of having the sticks be at the bottom and not off set like and Xbox controller. If you don't like that or can't get accustomed to it, then the Switch Pro may be more for you as that is offset.

Now what is great is being able to customize the buttons and the new back buttons from an app on your phone! It's so much better than having to connect it to a PC, which works but is more cumbersome. You can assign them any way you like and even save 3 configurations onto the controller itself. Easy to switch between with a press of a button. Which also reminds me they made the ability to change from working on a Switch, Android, PC, and Mac from a button combination to a simple toggle located at the bottom of the remote which is a nice touch.

The difference between this and the Pro 1 is the back buttons. Me, as I am now spoiled from the Xbox Elite Series 2, if I can have a controller with back buttons, I want that one. I have mine set up to act like thumbstick presses. If I never have to click in sticks again, I will be a happy man. You can however customize them to be anything even a macro for a set of button presses if you want.

Like every 8bitdo controller I own, it works well, is responsive and they have good battery life. The best thing about this version is it has an included battery pack, but you can remove and put regular AA batteries if you really want to do that. It just gives you so many options. For the price, there isn't anything better.

Oh before I forget, yes it does have motion inside if you use it on your Switch for games that support it like Borderlands Legendary Collection, Splatoon 2, Mario 3D Land among others.

Did you want better graphics? Did you want a better shooter interface? Well, Bioware delivered...no question.
So Bioware has made a lot of changes to the game (too many to count perhaps), but one things for sure, they created a winner.

NEW COMBAT SYSTEM:

Much more like a first person shooter now; defiantly fun to shoot people and pop the head off of someone. Also doesn't matter as much what abilities you upgrade or what weapons you have; if you can aim then you can kill a bad guy.

NEW UPGRADE SYSTEM:

Can't really decide if I like this or not. There's a part of me that enjoys how much simpler everything has become and how much time I save, but I think I kind of enjoyed the in depth upgrade and weapons in the first game. This opinion may or may not be shared. Regardless, I was a little to overwhelmed by the greatness of this game to care that much.

INTERFACE WITH PREVIOUS GAME:

You'll hear little reminents of things you did in the past and you'll definitely get the feel that you had an impact, but it's not as dramatic I had expected. They hyped it up so much that your last game would have such a big impact on this one, but I haven't seen much to back that up. I was a level 55 in the first game so I got to start a few levels up in this one and they gave me a little extra cash for being rich in ME1, but it wasn't that significant. Guess I just expected a little bit more, but I have to admit that any interface with the previous game must have been hard and it's groundbreaking, so they get my respect.

HACKING/CODE BREAKING: The new system they designed for unlocking items and hacking systems is a lot more fun. Actually feels a little bit challenging and regardless of your level or path you've chosen, you'll be able to do it.

VEHICLE: Good news! There really isn't a vehicle; you'll pick where you want to go and then you'll go there. The vehicle from ME1 felt like a shopping cart with one bad wheel to me and I'm glad to see it's gone.

PLANET EXPLORATION: Pretty cool system they came up with. You'll use a radar device to explore a planets surface and then deploy pods to check for what you're looking for. This is a much improved system from just driving around in my opinion. Be ready to spend a lot of hours looking around. There's an amazing amount of land to cover in the universe. They really worked hard to give you a lot to explore and it shows. Doesn't have that empty pointless feeling that the first ME had when I was checking planets. If they weren't related to the primary objective, every planet felt the same

THE GOOD:

1) Story is great and managed to integrate with the first game to include your actions taken

2) Graphics are on par with competitive titles from this gen; really stunning to just look around at your surroundings

3) Lots of glitches fixed and too many improvements to count; some things they did were almost to small to even notice, but you can feel they're there

THE BAD:

1) New dumbed down RPG elements feel easy to use but a little empty. If you hated the monotony of upgrading too many small aspects and customizing every weapon for proper ammo and best fit then maybe you'll like it. But, I couldn't help but feel that it was a little bit too easy and boring compared to the first game

2) You'll have to do a long mission to gain the loyalty of every one of your 10 squad members; it's kind of cool at first, but it gets a little old. Really? I have to complete a mission to get Garus on my side? Pretty sure I proved my loyalty fighting the Geth and Saren already

3) The new planet scanning system is cool and I'm glad to be rid of the vehicle, but it starts to get really old searching for minerals. After about 4 hours of it I got tired and decided I had enough uprades. Searched about 60 planets and found 6 side missions, so that feels like there's probably a lot out there. I didn't make it to level 30 so I must have missed a lot, but I just got so sick of scanning planets. Not a big complaint though; I don't know how they could have done it better so I was pleased.

OVERVIEW:

GRAPHICS: 10/10
DIALOGUE: 10/10
AUDIO: 10/10
COMBAT SYSTEM: 10/10
UPGRADES: 8/10
STORY: 10/10
INTEGRATION OF PREVIOUS GAME: 7/10

Whether you liked the first ME or you didn't, this game is a winner. I have my share of complaints, but the game is an amazing edition to the trilogy and you can just sense the effort Bioware put into this. Everyone will have complaints, but I've never seen a developer listen to the feedback and put forth this much effort.

Two days ago I would have told you ME1 was almost perfect, but this game has shown be the light and really set the bar.

Thanks Bioware

I realize that it's a little early to be reviewing such a complex gaming universe that is "Fallout," so I'll just let you know what my first impressions are and how this compares to the last game so far. Hopefully I can help someone to make a decision to purchase or not purchase this game.

First of all, if you didn't like Fallout 3, don't buy this game. It's essentially the same game in a different place. That's not to say that it doesn't have a long list of improvements and it's own innovations, but they certainly kept the same formula from Fallout 3, so if you hated that, you're probably not going to enjoy this.

Let's talk about the improvements over the last game:

1) Graphics are improved; still not great compared to some of the other games out there, but considering the massive interactive environment given to you, they're pretty impressive. And they do seem to be substantially better than the last game (glitches are prevalent though...hopefully a patch will alleviate that issue soon. I haven't had any glitches freeze the game or ruin anything for me yet, so they're minor in my opinion).

2) Weapon systems are improved in my opinion. I like the new aiming system and weapons. I think that they captured something closer to COD than before, and that aint a bad thing.

3) Character interaction and dialogue are great. They really went all out in this one. I couldn't stop laughing at some of the voice work, and it's amazing how many people have a ton of information. You'll find some old man hidden in a discrete building who happens to know the meaning of all existence....I'm exaggerating of course, but there is some crazy information out there for you to find that you wouldn't expect.

4) Environment interaction is really great. If you see it, you can probably destroy it or kill it. I like the idea that you can destroy anyone who stands in your way or just plain "pisses you off." That's not to say that there won't be serious consequences for you actions, but if you want to do it, you can.

Some other notes:

I think that the difficulty level is surprisingly hard. I don't remember having much of a challenge with the last game, but now I'm playing on "medium" and getting killed quite a bit. I guess you could say I'm a newb; of course I did play the last game a lot and I play other FPS and RPG games, but I'm finding it pretty hard. Then again, I chose to invest my upgrades in science and intellect, so if you have a character designed as a "warrior" you may have an easier time early on.

Save often! The auto save feature will screw you again and again. The game doesn't seem to save in the right places; it either saves too early before you die or it saves right when you're in a bad situation. I walked into a house and decided to steal a pack of smokes and beat an old man to death....I guess I was having a bad day. Anyways, the towns fold weren't having it, and I got my ass handed to me by some rangers. Of course, the auto save was right when they started shooting at me, so there was nothing I could do except go back to my last save.

All in all, so far this game seems to have the same winning formula that I loved about Fallout 3, with a long list of small and large improvements.

If you enjoyed FO3, you'll want to pick this up as soon as you can

I'm not going to go into too much detail since I've seen that other reviews have already covered a lot, but so far the game seems to be a huge improvement over MW2. Part of the reason might be just because I got bored of MW2, but I do believe that this game makes improvements.

I've seen people posting that it's the same game as MW. Well first of all, it's a completely different game: different maps, characters, story, weapons, perks, challenges, killstreaks...etc. I don't know how that's the same game as MW, but let's just say that it is the same game...is that a bad thing? MW is one of the best games in the genre and looking like MW and playing like MW isn't a bad thing. To say that Treyarch didn't make something unique is just stupid.

They've kept similar core concepts to the game with a few exceptions:
1) They've balanced the weapons more fairly
2) They've made the killstreaks a little less devestating. They're still cool, but they don't allow you to completely dominate the other team as easily as in MW2
3) They added cool new perks; camera you can leave is really cool idea

The graphics are could be considered inferior to MW, but I actually think that in some ways they're better. The framerate and some of the smooth textures seem to be lacking, but the level of details and the overall look of the maps is really intricate and just awesome I think. If you played WAW then you know that Treyarch has a different way of doing the visuals, but they're still pretty sweet. So, I'd say that they're different but not necessarily inferior to IWs visuals.

I haven't played enough of this game to say that it's the game of the year yet, but my first impressions are that it's an improvement on MW2 and it's definatly the game I've been waiting for. If you read the one star reviews and decide not to pick this up then you're really missing out on a fun time. If you loved the other COD games and you like the old Vietnam error weapons and themes, then this game should be a lot of fun for you

UPDATE:
I've played a lot more of the multiplayer now so I'd like to make a few comments:
1) The contract system is really cool. You'll have to stay on top of your contracts to maximize your potential for earning upgrades, but it really makes the matches a lot more fun. I've always got three different contracts going on, so I can earn extra points towards weapon and perk upgrades. (contracts are a way of gambling to complete tasks with your virtual currency and you can make extra cash if you complete the challenges in a set amount of game time.)

2) I'd like to touch on the graphics again. Most of the levels are just stunning to me. If anything, I think they look and feel better than previous MW games. The level of detail and lighting effects are fantastic. There's also a lot of interactive things happening in the maps that can cause enemies to die or give you advantages. In one of the stages, a rocket launches...pretty fun to watch if your enemies aren't giving you too much of a challenge.

3) Being able to upgrade your weapons and choose your perks is awesome. I've made my SMG and assault rifle really sweet now using the virtual currency and it's great to earn extra doing contracts.

4) They have a world map similar to the one that was in Halo that shows you all the lights on the globe where people are playing...there's no one playing in Madagascar...that's too bad

Cons:
Matchmaking is severely broken as of now. I'm sure they'll fix it as soon as possible, but right now if you have a party bigger than three people, you'll probably have trouble joining games. Some of these issues may be related to moderate or strict NATs, but since it doesn't tell you what your NAT settings are in the game, we weren't 100% on that. You can always check through the Xbox network settings and if your NAT settings are not open, you may need to enable DMZ or port forward...just do a google search.

Also, connections are showing up 3 or 4 green bars, but there still seems to be significant lag in some of the levels. This varies from match to match and I'm confident that they should be resolving it soon.

The more I play this game, the more I love it. I'm really shocked to see so many negative reviews. I guess expectations were really high for this and there's a lot of haters out there.

XCOM doesn't hide the fact that it's a remake of an old PC game. With regards to certain topics, it should consider doing so.

PROS:
-Distinct soldier classes allow for a wide variety of strategies.
-The support class can hold its own against enemies, unlike most support-type characters in RPGs.
-The strategy game is easy to pick up, but hard to master, even for an experienced resource-manager from the glory days of RTS's.
-Alien and environmental designs are interesting, especially for the latter being semi-randomized.

CONS:
-The sniper class is excessively overpowered, seemingly for no reason besides first-person shooter players think snipers are cool. It quickly becomes clear that the best strategy is to create a team centered around protecting and supporting a pair (trio?) of snipers.
-Voice acting and plot are near-abysmal. The fake German accent of the scientist particularly grates.
-Art style feels a little too quirky, ala Team Fortress 2, for an end-of-the-world scenario.
-Glitches cause system crashes occasionally.

BIGGEST CONCERN:
As it stands, the interaction between the enemy AI and the fog-of-war system rewards a gameplay experience that is a bit too slow for my liking. Ultimately, settling in at choke points fails because you have to spot enemies for them to fight you, but running a blitzkrieg from choke point to choke point is asking for your last unit to spot some silly enemy that hid in a corner while its brothers threw themselves at you. The balance is awkward and ruins the game, because the solution is to creep forward at an absurdly slow pace of four or so tiles a turn, even when no enemies are in sight. The fog-of-war levels in Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn were harrowing because the enemies threw themselves at you as if they weren't hampered by the fog, but I'd prefer that to a slow creep.

I like this game both as a member of the SMT: Persona series and as a 2D fighter.

PROS:
-Learning curve is logarithmic (shifted cubic, maybe?) rather than exponential, meaning you can get up to speed quickly, but mastery takes a lot of practice.
-Character art, music, and voice acting are great
-Characters are lovable and feel very distinct gameplay-wise.
-Excellent online play, from a system perspective.
-Good for new and esteemed fighting game players, and everything in between.
-Lightheartedness is a major plus

CONS:
-Backgrounds leave something to be desired.
-Story is entertaining and worth playing through, but drags on at times... hard to finish 100%.

This game is easily the tactical RPG with the best replay value of all time. Let's see why.

PROS:
-Storyline is better than Path of Radiance, even without knowledge of the first one. (I went back and played it afterwards!)
-High level of difficulty for first-time players, especially those not used to permanent character death and limited resources such as gold and experience; eases out after the first playthrough.
-Soundtrack is excellent, exceeding the best of Final Fantasy.
-Very deep gameplay system which must be mastered in its entirety for advanced play, such as "hard mode" runs or performing the side events required for certain ending scenes.
-Huge amount of replay value; see "biggest highlight" section below.
-Great 2D art, good 3D art.

CONS:
-It's hard. This was my first Fire Emblem, and I got a game over like five times on one of the earliest levels. But I'm masochistic, so this isn't a con in my book.
-Art is awesome, but the actual execution in the 3D graphics could be better.
-No voice acting, barring the pre-rendered movies with mostly terrible voiceover.

BIGGEST HIGHLIGHT:
Differences in unit usefulness not necessarily clear to first-time players entice the return player to challenge him/herself to build strategies around the high-potential but hard-to-level characters... the game has a built in risk/reward system in that way. You know it's beautiful, and you know it's linear. What it seems no one has an opinion on is its new battle system. Here's the scoop:

Back in the good ol' days of SNES (through PS2), if you wanted to play a game with a decent storyline, you had to sit through at least 35 hours of mindless character-statistic checks and waiting for a bar to fill. For some reason, developers decided there was something wrong with that, so tactical and action RPGs have become more prevalent than what we now refer to as "traditional" (or "menu-based") RPGs. Square Enix has stuck to its guns, but finally innovated on a long-stale formula.

In Final Fantasy XIII, specialization--the heart of any system that requires thoughtful gaming--is key. You must use pure damage dealers, pure support casters, and pure "tanks" (damage absorbers). You're literally forced to. And you can only use them in predetermined (by the player) trios. This means, at the very least, you'll have to set up a trio for offense, one for emergency healing, and a balanced trio.

But the game has also (finally!) brought status ailments and buffs to the place they belong: at the crux of a player's stratagem. Buffs and ailments are so critical that it's often, if not always, preferential to "debuff" the enemy rather than deal direct damage. So you'll need some character trios that protect and heal a debuffer, or buff while attacking, or...

...you quickly see where this is going. And you're only allowed six different trios ("paradigms", in game). And the buffs and debuffs don't last long, and you need to heal very frequently, so you're switching paradigms constantly.

And then there's the ever-decreasing "chain counter", a bar that fills when you go on the offensive and drains over time. This means you're rewarded for staying on the offensive as much as possible, moreso than in previous traditional RPGs.

The net result? A game that pits you against time, not your enemy's arbitrary stat numbers (your level is kept rigorously controlled, since the game is so linear). You have to keep the chain counter up, your enemies debuffed, your allies buffed, and your allies at high health at all times. That's at least four things to do, and there are only three characters. That means constant attention must be paid to the ebb and flow of battle. In the end, it puts the player where they should be: in CONTROL of the game. In previous Final Fantasy games, the enemies (particularly bosses) told you when to heal, when to cure your ailments, and when it's okay to attack. Now you can say the same to them.

As a stand-alone game, "Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch" (NnK) is really not bad. As a symbol of a trend in gaming, it's an atrocity.

Lots of gamers nowadays are asking for a return of "the good old days" of role playing games. In other words, they want to regress all the advancement the current generation has made and play 100+ remakes of Final Fantasy 6/7. They want to take away the trend of moving towards more action-oriented or tactical games by returning to the real-time, menu-based paradigm of ages past. Even RPGs which have stuck to that route (e.g., FF13) have been criticized as ruining their battle systems by making changes which are, in my opinion, highly innovative. NnK was touted as the "solution" to the problem of innovation. It provided a poorly scaled world map. There were oodles of relatively unrewarding side quests and minigames. The battle system waited a few seconds while animation restrictions of unknowable length played out before performing the action you selected. How wonderful!

In the end, though, the game wasn't so bad. The story, art, characters, voiceover, and Pokemon-like monster raising systems were all fairly enjoyable. I still hold issue with the return of the world map and delay-ridden, real-time battle system... these are tedious aspects which don't provide a whole lot to the game. Nevertheless, as much as I hate what the game represents, I can't give it fewer than three stars.

-The art is pleasant
-The story takes some unexpected directions, and has a sequence of pure gold in the middle
-The final boss is absurdly hard compared to the previous challenges in the game, which makes for an epic conclusion.
-2D cutscenes by ufotable are off the chain; what a great studio!

CONS:
-Very unbalanced characters. Until every character becomes broken (around the level cap), using a character besides Jude and to a lesser extent Milla really cripples you, even if you're more familiar with another character.
-The music is identical to every other Motoi Sakuraba game. If you've played one, you won't be hearing anything new here.
-Story length is below average and side content is very lacking. The number of "post-game" challenges is limited, unless you force yourself to play them on the hardest difficulty ONLY, in which case they seem insurmountable.
-The story climaxes way too early. After that, it kinda glides in to its conclusion.

Overall, this is a good game and worth the time. Unfortunately, between the weak post-game and the drawn-out segment between the climax and the ending, it just leaves a bad taste in your mouth.
