After Sonic Boom Shattered Crystal was released I was thrilled, finally a really great Sonic game that wasn't all about running through a level as fast as possible, and I was really hoping the next installment would solve the biggest issues with that game, namely it was too short, too easy, and too unrewarding to go for full completion. However, this game fails to deliver on all fronts. I'll break the game down into parts for this review:

Length - Short. While it may claim to be double the length of Shattered Crystal, the stages which feature the Sea Fox or Hovercraft don't really deserve to be called levels, as they are less than a minute long each. Discounting boss, tunnel, Sea Fox, and Hovercraft stages, there are only 20.

Difficulty - On a scale of 1-5 where 1 is "A 12 year old could beat it in their sleep" and 5 is "Battletoads", this game scores between -1 and 0. Seriously, there is no difficulty to this game. Most of the enemies in the levels are only there to be targeted to jump over spikes, and the boss fights are a joke. It's like they thought Shattered Crystal was too hard (and it was easy) and took away anything that would make it challenging.

Plot - It plays about like a Sonic Boom episode, worse than Shattered Crystal in originality.

Graphics - Worse than Shattered Crystal, almost to the point where the cutscenes look as if they superimposed a moving mouth over a still image.

Gameplay - Linear stages, no point in not using your favorite character for 90% of the game, the other 10% are for completion items and boss fights. The fire and ice concept is very underused and almost look as if they were put in as an afterthought. The bot races are an interesting concept, but there are no AI racers, and no internet connectivity, so it's effectively useless for most people.

Overall he developers should be ashamed about putting out such a game so terrible the only game which keeps it from ranking dead last in the hierarchy is Sonic Generations. I sincerely hope the next installment will be much better, though it couldn't be worse,

I'm not impressed. Sure there are some new features such as underwater racing, gliding, and collecting coins to upgrade your kart (which is maddening to say the least, as you only get a max of 10 coins per track, and every hit takes 3 away), but they removed traps and replaced it with the bombomb, which also takes you out if you happen to be hit while carrying it. Sadly they also kept the Mario Kart standard of being able to finish where they want you to finish instead of where you deserve when doing Grand Prix races. For instance, you can be on lap 3, finish line in sight, decent margin to 2nd, and amazingly you'll get hit by a blue shell which costs you 3-4 places, or you'll be racing up to a gliding ramp and as soon as you hit it, you'll get slammed by lightning and fall off the track, costing you 3-4 places. My favorite is on Rainbow Road (SNES) you'll get lightning and spin off the track only to come back on and immediately be hammered by another racer or a shell which knocks you right back off, causing you to finish 7th instead of 1st. Also amazing is how often, when in 5th place or worse, you'll get something fairly useless, like a green shell or banana while the CPU racers get blue shells, bullet bills, lightning bolts, or three red shells. Also they kept a limited number of tracks, and they did not allow amiibo to be used, which would have been great so that you could have actual great AI competitors to race against.

All in all it's not any better than its DS predecessor, and not worth $30. Highly disappointed that Nintendo didn't take advantage of the 3DS's increased game size limit to add all tracks from previous Mario Kart games, and the lack of Amiibo functionality is disappointing.

I bought this digitally on the Nintendo eStore. There are a lot of "challenges", but many of the "challenges" are either very easy or very quick, and most of them are focused on the Mario franchise. For example, "Defeat the Goomba", or "Collect 10 coins", and they are all so short they have very little replay value, ranging from 6 seconds to a little over a minute. Nintendo missed a real opportunity with this game, and should have included fewer challenges but made them longer and actually more challenging. For instance, "Clear Super Mario Brothers World 5 without losing more than three lives", or "Clear Kid Icarus Stage 1 without falling to your death". As a time waster it's alright, but it could have been much greater, especially if you were given the full game when you completed all the challenges.

Update: Having completed the game in about 10 hours (all stages 3 rainbow stars), I will say it is not worth more than about $10, decidedly not the $25 I paid or double that I see on Amazon.

I want to give this game 5 stars, but I can't. There's nothing major wrong with it, but there's a lot of little things that add up to a negative star in my opinion.

The graphics are nice. They don't have the 3D depth that I was expecting, and the difference between 2D and 3D is quite minor, it's not like, say, Kid Icarus Uprising, where 3D makes it into a completely different game. There are times when stuttering is noticeable, even on the New Nintendo 3DS which has slightly more power. Thankfully these are limited to cutscenes.

The combat is simple, and that's not really a bad thing. It's a lot like Legend Of Zelda Ocarina Of Time style combat, all about pattern recognition, but this really isn't a combat oriented game. The little negative in combat is that they're a bit -too- predictable and give you plenty of time to react, so much so that sometimes it's not even necessary to dodge an attack, you can swing away, or even use the mechanics like the game tells you to, such as knocking flying enemies down before attacking. It's nothing like Monster Hunter Generations, no fighting that Hyper Shagaru Magala for half an hour only to die due to a lapse in concentration. I will add in here that this game does utilize the New Nintendo 3DS C stick so you can strafe and turn the camera at the same time.

The story is short, in essence, but it is spread out. Think the spirit stone quests of LoZ:OOT but spread out by other quests in between, so it ends up stretching to a decent length. For instance, after the first dungeon you have to stock hundreds of dewgems (currency) worth of items in your shops, which will take many days (in game time) to do since you cannot stock their inventories as much as you want, only a little at a time, and each item is a very small amount. All told it takes about 15 hours to clear the story if you rush through it. There is a post game of sorts, but it is about completion, maxing out your stores and oasis, fighting enemies in the labyrinths, etc.

The dungeons themselves aren't particularly challenging, about as difficult as the LoZ: OOT spirit stone dungeons, perhaps easier. The puzzles in them are usually very simple, and seem like they were put in just to make the dungeon take an extra few seconds rather than having to figure out an actual logic puzzle. In other words, it's nowhere near as maddening as any dungeon in LoZ: OOT, I'd say most are not even on the same level as The Great Deku Tree. It's also worth saying that many "dungeons" you encounter are not actually "dungeons" in the dungeon crawler sense, they are only a few rooms and only serve to connect two areas or serve as a meeting place, so they are much more like the caves of Legend Of Zelda Link To The Past (or Link Between Worlds). The later dungeons do get long, made even longer by "puzzle rooms" which often require you to go back to the oasis and swap one or both of your party members for other members just to use their skills, such as pellet or paraflower.

Building up your oasis is frustrating in that you can't just build everything, you have to look at what is selling and who is interested when it comes to building and keeping shops. Money is slow to get at first until you get at least 6 shops, but even then it accumulates very slowly. You don't need a lot of money at one time, although there are always things to buy, but shops are the only way to actually get money, enemies and objects in the world only drop materials you use for crafting or stocking your shops, and of course to build a shop you need the money. Leveling up the oasis is based on your progress through the story and secondary story quests, since it depends on population and the way to get population is to do quests. Thankfully it does not depend on Streetpass, but I think it would have been nice if they included a feature like the one in Bravely Second End Layer where you could net invite people, much like an online Streetpass, so you could generate extra income, use them as visitors to your oasis to buy items, much like Noots (non speaking penguin looking NPCs that buy stuff but otherwise do nothing) do, or so that you could trade materials, some of which are only obtainable by chance, such as Monster Bones which are only found in the Woodsea Labyrinth and only there if you are lucky enough to get into a treasure room which has digging places.

It's not a BORING game in that there's no "Let's sit around for a few hours while time passes", you're always going on some quest to gather materials and find people, so it is in your best interest to kill every enemy, bash everything you can bash, and move every pile of sand you can as you come across it, you never know when you will need what you get, and will save you some frustration later on when new recipes for stronger items are received and you need those items. Speaking of gathering materials, people you meet in the game and later can form a party with have certain abilities, such as being able to mine or dig, which you can use to harvest certain items in dungeons, which to me would have been much better served like a traditional dungeon crawler or RPG game would, with items (picks, shovels, etc) instead of having to use specific characters, especially considering if those people are running a shop, when they're out with you, their shop is closed, generating no income, so you're not able to form a party of people you will always use so you can focus on only them to maximize equipment and levels, about every dungeon has a specific character you must use to navigate it. This is another gating technique ensuring you cannot go everywhere at any time.

All in all it's a nice game, but it could have been a great game.

Update: After playing it for a good 30 hours, one major problem become apparent: The AI which controls the party members you are not controlling is extremely daft. They will not attack at regular speed, members with distance weapons (wands and crossbows) will try to run to melee range before attacking, they will literally run into charging enemies for no reason, and if they are brought down to critical health levels they will run back out of combat until you heal them. They will also run into walls without going around a corner, and will walk off heights and not be able to get back up because they cannot figure out elevators. I sincerely hope there is a second patch which fixes these issues, because it makes gold level labyrinths effectively single player ventures.

I preordered the game (still have not received my codes from Amazon, though it looks like that's pretty common right now, will update if and when they send them), and have to say I'm pretty impressed. It arrived September 8th and I am at 20 hours of playtime. Previous Monster Hunter games were pretty tedious, having to repeat the same quest over and over in order to get enough materials (or, if you have my luck, to get that one specific monster part), but had no real story. This game does have a fairly predictable story, but there isn't much tedium (yet, at least, as I type this I am at the Felyne island), and the ability to stack multiple quests cuts down on that, whereas in MHG you couldn't, say, go kill a monster, slaughter several weaker monsters, and gather all at one time (unless they were subquests). The amount of loot you receive from a battle is determined on how well you do during that battle, though it is a bit annoying to kill an enemy in one hit but only score a C rank.

Now, for the negatives. Yes there is lag in many parts, even on the New Nintendo 3DS XL, which is very annoying but it doesn't make the game unplayable. The subquest display is a single display, there aren't tabs for "Complete", "Turn In", and "Accepted", meaning the display gets very crowded very quick. It also isn't sorted (e.g. all Turn In quests always moved to the top, active quests next, and completed at the bottom) so you will scroll through completed quests to get to active ones. There aren't client markers for completed subquests, which is annoying as many come from random people in towns and you might not remember where they were. There is no way to sort and search in your inventory, making it annoying to know how many more of a specific item you need to a weapon or armor upgrade. The graphics are very simplistic and flat compared to previous MH games. MHG, for instance, had lush forests and detailed textures whereas MHS looks much like an anime. And finally, the biggest annoyance, is that determining which types of attacks enemies will use is often a mix of intuition and luck. All monsters, yours and the enemies, have tendencies to use certain moves, but there's no way to determine what the enemy will use for certain. For example, a Yian Kut Ku has a tendency to use technical attacks, which are countered by power attacks, but there is no way to know if it will use a technical attack, or if it will flip and use a speed attack which counters power attacks.

All in all it's a very good game, but there are a lot of annoyances which I hope will be attended to with a patch. Better inventory management, subquest displays, and a good stab at tackling the lag issues would go a long way, especially considering that previous MH games, especially MHG, had none of these issues despite being faster paced and more visually complex.

Overall: 4 stars
Story: 4 stars. Predictable, sometimes cheesy, sometimes makes you want to yell GET ON WITH IT!
Gameplay: 4 stars. Finding certain monsters, especially variants (such as Blue Yian Kut Ku or Black Diablos) overly annoying. Finding a specific monster's egg, even in their lair, not guaranteed.
Graphics: 2 stars. Flat, simplistic, far cry from previous MH games. 3D effects add little. Lots of areas with lag, even in the inventory, even on the New 3DS XL.
UI: 3 stars. Better inventory and quest management needed. Pointers on where to turn in completed quests needed. Map needs a third, area wide view option. Items not explained where they are found (e.g. Might Seed in the volcano).
Battles: 3 stars. Requires a good memory, intuition, and luck. Rewards are based on badly explained points system. Paintballs work too rarely. .
DLC: 1 star. Yes it's a new release game, but there are no item packs or host of quests the way there are with MHG. Amiibo add nothing as you get those monsters anyway.

Update - The Japanese version is getting another patch which adds a second story line and doubles the number of monsties you can have, but our version still hasn't been patched to fix the lag issues...Capcom, why did we expect anything better?

When I first started playing I was tempted to write a review when I was about halfway though, but I decided to wait until I was through, and I'm glad I did. I played the original on Game Boy when it was released, and it was a great game, albeit very short. This version increases that length considerably, though it still encourages speed running as, unlike Metroid Fusion, there is no time irrelevant 100% completion specific ending, which I think is a great shame. Also unlike the original game, this one continues the theme of backtracking to previous areas to collect previously unavailable power ups once you obtain new capabilities. The different areas are definitely inspired by the original, but they are also vastly different, and do not feature some of the annoyances as the original game (no "honeycomb" which blocks your missiles, for instance). The Metroid fights are also considerably more difficult than the original (the new alpha Metroids are harder than the original's Omega Metroids). That's not to say they are hard, they went old school and made then powerful but completely pattern based, rewarding attention and punishing randomness. The graphics and sound are good, but they stripped out the "iconic" Metroid II music which plays through all the transition areas, instead limiting it to a single small part of Area 1. The Space Jump is MUCH improved from the original, no more having to time your jumps exactly or fall out of it. Metroids are not limited to the 5/10/20/50 missiles to kill arrangement of the original, and some of the Metroid fights are also not limited to just one room. The new Aeion features are nice additions, especially the scanner which reveals the map in sections as well as powerup locations and breakable blocks.

So why the 3 star review? Well for one, as many have mentioned, you have to buy the baby Metroid Amiibo to get the New Game +, which at current prices makes this near a $70 game which you will spend -maybe- 20 hours on. Playing through my first time to 100% clocked in for me at a bit more than 8 hours, but I backtracked too early (don't until you get the baby Metroid). and had to then backtrack again, so with the Amiibo second mission, you're paying $70 for easily less than 30 hours of playtime, and that's if you go through Normal at 100%, and then speedrun and 100% the Amiibo mission. The 3D graphics also do not add a heck of a lot, sadly. The 360 degree field of fire sounds good in theory, and is a welcome addition as you can pick off enemies through obstacles when you get the wave beam and don't have to jump to line up missile shots, but it is imprecise compared to the precision you need with some hits, especially against Metroid. Some of the combat mechanics, especially the big fight against the Diggernaut (guardian of the Power Bomb), are unclear. And finally, perhaps the biggest disappointment of all, there is nothing about SR388's past revealed in the game despite being stated in the promotional material.

I bought this to protect my New 3DS XL Galaxy edition from the wear and peeling my previous system had. It is two pieces of plastic yes, but they are fairly thick and will protect the finish from scratches.

Bowser's Inside Story is one of the great Nintendo DS games, and it is nice that Nintendo has remade and enhanced it for the 3DS. Sadly it doesn't feature 3D graphics, but it does have enhanced graphics, making it look more polished, and the speed has been altered so it runs slower, yet smoother. This slowdown also extends to some enemy attacks, making them much easier to dodge, and therefore decreases the difficulty of the game.

The difficulty has been lessened to a degree also. In the original getting an excellent attack could be quite difficult due to the narrow window of opportunity, such as with the hammer or with some bros attacks, but in this version that window was expanded -slightly- making it possible to routinely get excellent attacks, but it's not so long that it's button mashing easy, although there is an "easy mode" in the options menu. This also affects Bowser's minion attacks, making it much easier to, for example, launch every Goomba and hit gold ranking in the massage parlor.

The annoyance factors are still there as well. Battles with Mario & Luigi will still take an annoyingly long time due to the low damage dealt outside of Bros Attacks, yet easily avoided enemy attacks. Boss battles still take ages. Enemy health is not visible, which adds to the feeling that boss battles will never end. Some of he bros attacks, such as the bouncer, still seem to be overly complicated and included just to have another special attack. Things like this work themselves out in the later part of the game when star and shine ranks are hit for the better gear and the better bros attacks are obtained, but it makes the first half of the game really drag. The Energy Hold stage, for instance. Speaking of leveling, a new feature to this version is that when you rank up, you get to choose a bonus effect that will affect them from then on, such as an additional +1 power or increased healing from items.

Sadly they did not include a temporary checkpoint feature in this version either, a system where a temporary save point is created so the system can be shut down or game switched which is restored then deleted when the game is launched again. Save points are still plentiful, but some of them have longer stretches between them.

Bowser Jr's Journey is a welcome addition as well, akin to the Bowser's Minions in the Superstar Saga remake. I won't delve deeply into it as to limit spoilers, but I will say that, like Bowser's Minions, it leaves you disappointed, feeling more like a minigame tacked on, which it essentially is, instead of a full companion game.

All in all it's a worthy purchase even if you own the original. I wish there were more new content, such as new minigames and expanded quests, but that is limited to just Amiibo scanning.

I bought this game on New Year's day 2005 as part of my resolution to learn to play chess. I read all the review and weighed the good and the bad, and bought the game new at a video store.

The good thing about the game is that you really do learn to play chess. From the main menu you click on "tutorial" and then you are directed through screen after screen which explains each chess piece in detail, teaching you the legal moves for each piece. After a while I got a little impatient and went to the Battle Chess when I hadn't finished the tutorial, but after 2 moves I got my (...)kicked so I'm back in the chess school!

The bad thing is that this game is hopelessly boring. I have to admit that I thought the game would be like the front cover of the disc case but you will see nothing like that. While you're going through the tutorial, low-register easy listening music plays in the background while a male voice reads from the instructions on the screen. Also, what the other reviewers said about the mini chess board is true. I thought it wouldn't matter to me since I have a large TV screen but it's set up so that half the screen is the chess board, the other half is taken up by the on-screen instructions. Why couldn't they put the instructions as a moving caption below? In the battle chess, you can barely see the pieces -- as if the figures are extremely fuzzy and once they start moving, you don't know which figure corresponds to what chess piece.

This being said, I would still recommmend this if your goal is to have an intelligent and intimate knowledge of the game. You learn different strategies, how to gain a holistic perspective of the board and it is easy to navigate. I admit I've only done the tutorial and Battle Chess so far, and I might even buy that cartoony looking chess game designed for kids (Fritz and something?) just to make it a bit more fun for me to play. There is no doubt that you will learn, but like me, you may fall asleep a few times in the process!

I agree with the second reviewer - if you liked the other Harry Potter games, this latest one is sure to disappoint. However, unlike another reviewer, I won't be so callous as to completely spoil a book's surprise ending.

One of the more disappointing features of this new game is the inability to see more than a few feet in front of you. That is, whereas in the other game you had control of the camera with the joystick you didn't use to run (by the way, Harry cannot duck or jump in this game either); in other games you used the joystick to look up, down and all around the town! When Harry ran through the game, you saw where he was going because the view was from behind. Here, the view is aerial and you have no idea what's ahead.

The card system is indeed confusing and the booklet doesn't explain much. I miss roaming around the entire school, entering into the classrooms, running through Diagon Alley and looking for secret items. You can't go roaming anymore, you must follow an prearranged order. The Bertie Botts Beans you uncover for points now fly away from you, and you must chase them down if you want points. If I had the chance to offer an opinion to the game designers, I would say "do over".

I write this review not from the perspective of the traditional gamer (whatever that is) but from an older grad student who apparently has time for this and not her work! I loved to play Monopoly before I bought this video game so I was excited to see my pieces moving around. There are things I like and don't about this game.

I was hoping that I would be able to immediately play as my Mii but this feeling was rectified on many levels. First, you can't beat the original pieces, and now they're hilarious! For example, I chose that little terrier dog piece, thinking I would be given a little silver terrier that moves around the board. What I was given was a very stylish young woman, asymmetrical hairstyle, sunglasses, dangerously high heels, and then her little doggie is your terrier piece. The wheelbarrow is a barefoot country girl named Natalie who pushes the wheelbarrow. Each piece you select is accompanied by a person (each person has a name except for the terrier-woman who is just called "dog" in the Streets Monopoly board. I don't like that). You don't have access to all the pieces, you have to win money and unlock them. The funniest thing is, the Miis you have created for your Wii are the city folk who walk around town. I attend school far from home, so my Mii people are members of my family. My stylish woman was walking the dog around the corner of Free Parking and there was my sister, waiting to cross the street. A few minutes later, there's my mom walking down the sidewalk. Later, I found out that by winning games and thus earning money, you can "buy" your Mii so that you can play him or her in the game.

The graphics are pretty cool. When you build on a property, a nice house or hotel goes right up. Naturally the hotel that gets built on Baltic Avenue is nothing compared to the ones built on Park Place or Broadway! Cars and trucks drive by on the street. The Banker reminds me of Lenny Briscoe from Law & Order because he always has these one-liners. If you have never played before, he walks you through the whole game, explaining every little detail. There are a lot more boards you can play, but most of them are locked. It only makes me want to play more, earn more money and unlock those boards. I can't wait to see what they look like.

What I don't like is that it seems to be fast-moving, to the point where I think it may be buggy. Before I buy a property and especially before accepting or rejecting a trade, I like to get a bird's eye view of the board to see who owns what first. This is not possible. You may see the entire board before you roll your dice, but once you land on a property this feature is unavailable. Also, in the corner are all the cards/colors of the properties I own, but they are so darn small that I can barely make sense of them. It would be nice if there were a button to temporarily amplify this view. When I played my first game, I would periodically be led to a screen that displayed the players' net worth, but I the screen went by so fast I kept thinking, what was that? Then about 15 minutes into the game, Mr. Banker stops at that screen to explain it. Later when I declared bankruptcy and was taken back to that Net Worth scene, the screen just went black and stayed there until I pressed "2" to fast forward.

I've only played the game a couple of times. I haven't played online yet but I'm looking forward to it and will be sure to come back and update when I do. I love playing this game by myself with a cup of tea, curled up on the couch but playing online against a stranger seems fun!

UPDATE: Although the above description says that you can play online, this is not possible with the Wii. I've looked and looked for it in my game, until a comment by a reader led me to the EA.com page. Online play is only available with the PS3 and Xbox. Yes, I feel duped.

I hemmed and hawed about purchasing this game and finally I went to Target and just went for it. I'm sorry to say I'm a little disappointed.

Two things made me hesitant to make the buy: I didn't know if the leg strap would be big enough and I wasn't sure if I could take advantage of doing the online feature. I won't go into what others have already said, but I'll just give my perspective.

I have a lot of weight to lose. With the first EA Active, the leg strap was so short for heftier legs that there were even online tutorials on how to make your own strap. I was happy when I put the leg strap on over legs and it fit, but just barely. In fact, it squeezes and pinches my leg and when I do the squats, the girth from my tummy turns off the leg-strap unit. I have to put it so high up on my leg that it's right where my thigh connects my torso in order for it not to pinch so much. Still, when I wear it this way it does register and I can do the exercises. I just have to be careful during squats. Also, the Wii Balance board and the Wii Remote tend to shut themselves off during the program. You are obligated to stop exercising and reset these devices; this happens many times during a single workout.

I live in a 2nd floor apartment building that has "free" wireless internet. The signal is so weak that my Wii could not pick up the signal, however, I am paying for internet through the cable company since my computer speed was so slow. I simply purchased what is called a "wireless router". I hooked up my computer to the router and the router to the cable box and voila, wireless internet in the whole apartment. I was online. I was so excited; I was going to be able to have weight loss competitions with my friends and family. However, you can only share your weight (that you enter yourself online, it doesn't come from the game itself); not how much weight you've lost. This would have been such a great feature!! They are probably waiting for the next generation in order to make me buy it again.

Lastly, I mentioned that I live on the 2nd floor. I need to be able to turn off the cardio exercises because my grumpy downstairs neighbor will throw a fit. I was hoping that for the 9-Week Program I could, for example, tailor the entire course to do "all but cardio", but I am not able to do this, the program is fixed to easy, medium or hard and that's it. Once I start the Program for the day, yes of course I can delete certain exercises from the day's workout, but by the title sometimes I can't tell which are cardio. I already go to the gym and do cardio in the morning anyway so I was hoping to tailor the 9-Week Program to my needs, but this is not the case. Apart from the 9-Week Program there is a part called "Custom Workouts" where I can tailor it exactly to my needs. These workouts do record themselves online but not with the details that the other program offers.

Also - there is no yoga program and you still have to do the awkward grip where you hold the Wii remote in one hand and hold two of the straps of the resistance bands in the same hand. Even with the free weights option, you still hold the Wii remote in one hand and the hand weight in the same hand. Not all of the exercises of course, but a couple of them.

I must first say that I agree with a previous poster; why is it so expensive all of a sudden? It's an awesome game but over one hundred dollars? I found it for a low price at my local used video game seller.

I have Wii Fit, EA Active, Zumba and a couple of titles for the PS3, and so far this is my favorite. I admit that I put off buying it for a very long time because I saw a child on the cover, leading me to believe that this was a game for children. But looking for a new exercise program for the New Year, I reread the reviews and decided to go for it.

Yes, you really do forget that you are exercising. You walk on a dirt track around a mythical island ("Rhythm Island"), and there are over four thousand floating bubbles that say "palm tree" or "street light" or "music" or "rainbow" or any variety of things, those are event bubbles. Each bubble also has a point value attached. You must stay in step with the music, because that is the way to get points! Stop walking and you LOSE points. So, the more rhythm you have, the higher your points, and the more you can build up your city, unlock songs and build rainbows. You're so focused on pointing the Wii remote at the screen while watching the step meter to make sure that you're in step, that you forget that your legs are burning. At first I would stop walking to click on the screen (while you walk it's difficult to steady the remote!) but now I just wait until I have about 200 points and then just click indiscriminately at the screen.

I admit that I am disappointed that you cannot set the game in the beginning to do so many miles in one session, or so many steps, or so many minutes. However, your trainer pops up on the screen to say that you've walked 3000 steps, or that you've walked .7 miles, so you can decide for yourself when to stop.

There are mini games; I thought they were within the walking game itself but once you stop the game, you can chose to play a game. I have only played one and not very well, so I will go to the Konami site to download the manual and see exactly how to play.

The music is great and the beat varies. On one song you are walking at a moderate pace, and suddenly the next song is so fast that you are practically running, working up a great sweat! Plus the music is by the original artists, which is a big plus!

I can't wait to walk again so I can continue to build my little island!

I've been buying the JD video games since they first came out, I even had the dance game that had that awful mat, and I'm a fan of the Zumba on Wii as well.

The choreography is difficult but don't be discouraged! It only makes you want to do it over and over again because when the steps are too repetitive, it's too much like an exercise video and not a dance video. However, I do use this game strictly for exercise. At first you won't sweat at all because you'll be learning the steps, missing steps and getting frustrated. Don't give up! There is not too much repetition since it's dance, so by the time you learn the steps well, imagine how fun it'll be! This is truly DANCE, and not just American pop either. I love the Latin music and especially the Bob Marley song, "Could This Be Love". Oh! And I like that once you learn the dance for the song, you can download other dances for the same song!

What I don't like: I'm the only one playing this game in the house, but a lot of the music is for two or more people. Of course I can still play those songs, but it just feels funny! (2) The figure that shows the upcoming dance moves with the arrows is so tiny! It's almost better to just watch the main figure, anticipate the moves and learn from that. (3) The on-screen instructions are way too tiny, are you kidding us? I can't even review what is says to tell you all because I cannot see it. (4) I don't feel like it tracks my moves very well at all. I mean, I got "perfect" points just by waving the wiimote from the sofa. Then again I really don't care about the points, just the exercise.

None of those "bad" things make any difference to the game play, it's still fun fun fun!

I personally found this to be one of the best games I have played and for the current price it is a killer deal.  Have fun!

So, I have been playing games for a long time and really love PC gaming.  One of my favorite genres is the old west and the game being open world.  When Red Dead Redemption came out it fit both of these bills perfectly along with one major caveat, it was not offered on the PC (arrggg....).  So, I waited and waited...and finally gave up on Rockstar ever porting one of the most desired games to the PC.  I can tell you up front that I hate using controllers since they are no where as precise as a mouse, but to play I would have to make this compromise.  So, I purchased the GOTY edition and have had a wonderful time - it is an awesome game and one of the best games ever made!  The one item that almost drove me nuts was the inability to turn off the skinning & looting animations (it almost challenges the definition of insanity), disabling the animations should have been an option.
My daughter looked into many of the PC RPGs and asked for this for her birthday.  So far she is enjoying it and thinks it is a great game.

Oh Crysis how sadly you have fallen! I loved Far Cry as one of my all time favorite games. I also really enjoyed Crysis 1. When Crysis 2 released you could really start to see the shift Crytek was starting to make. I don't know if this was for the console market appeal or because EA "helped" with their decision. It greatly saddens me to say this will be the last Crysis game I will ever buy or play! I totally understand why people are irked about: 1) linear play 2) it's is dumbed down - it's laughable to compare Crysis 3 with the original Crysis and compare the controls 3) quick time events (QTE) I honestly couldn't believe it when this happened in the game 4) A never ending story that drones on and on while being so ridiculous that it gets old fast and you just don't care anymore.

I really do enjoy open world sand box games as my favorite genre. I will always be disappointed that Rockstar did not bring Red Dead Redemption to the PC! This leaves me with my favorite two standouts: 1) Ubisoft with Far Cry 2 & 3 (which also adopted QTE oh the maddness) and 2) Avalanche Studios with Just Cause - Let us hope Just Cause 3 releases this year and doesn't have QTEs!!!

So, off to Amazon to find the game my daughter has such found memories of growing up...  Well the DVD arrived and I gave it her, she was very excited and has spent countless hours indulging herself creating Zoos.  What is excellent about this game is that it stands the test of time and proves that current generation graphics are not as important as something that is fun and inspires the imagination.

I really like Arkane Studios and thought Dark Messiah of Might & Magic was a lot of fun!  This game has a great style and unique setting.  The controls are very fluid and the powers make this quite diverse.  Overall a great game (I just finished the Dunwall DLC and it is a lot of fun).

I tried Saint Row III and just could not get past the crude nature of the game and abandoned it. If I had not gotten such great deal from Amazon on this I would have never tried it. I really enjoy open world games and the super hero aspect of this had appeal to me.

So major props here since the game is REALLY a lot of fun - it totally surprised me!

We decided to go ahead and upgrade our console to the XBox One this year from our 360. Set it up today to discover the family timer we relied on ALL THE TIME on the Xbox 360 was not included in the XBox One and STILL isn't there after several years of the console being out.

Why do I care so much? This is a daily struggle for parents. The Family Timer allowed us to give our children the freedom to play the Xbox without fighting about it every day.

What does this mean for our family? We will set the same limits we had before, but now every time they play I will have to track it (makes my life worse), then when their time is up, I will have to fight with them about it. EVERY DAY.

Hmm, let me think about what that does to the XBox brand in my mind as a parent? Do I want my children to own more games? On this thing we fight about every day? NO! In fact I really wish I could just return the thing RIGHT NOW, given that we nearly only bought it so the kids could play Lego Dimensions, since all the reviews say the Xbox 360 version doesn't work.

Seriously Microsoft, do you not care about your brand? Or do you not care about whether or not parents buy kids XBox One games or accessories? I can't imaging its a negligible part of your customer base. Shame on you.

Pre-ordered from Amazon, and I very much am enjoying it over all. It is a nice nostalgia trip and a pretty good stand alone game all by itself. I've only had time to go through the first 1/3 or so but will happily tackle the rest.

Most people have already covered the important bits, so I'll add a few of my own based on comparing the new game with the old SNES days:

Good:
-Old style game play - most of the gameplay is highly reminiscent of the old game. You'll find yourself picking it up really fast and smiling at the old memories.
-Inventive new game dynamics - there is a lot of new stuff. Many of the levels have unique dynamics (a level where you are running from an Octopus, one with giant waves that crash down) as well as incorporating some of the fun old dynamics from older games (rotating platforms, lots of verticle climbing (grass instead of ropes mostly). Seems like the developers had fun coming up with new stuff.
-Nostalgia levels - some levels just scream "look! I'm supposed to remind you of a level from the old game!" The first level is especially true. It's called jungle hijinx. It's not entirely the same but has much of the same landscape and enemy placement. You can go back in the banana cave and back up to Donkey Kong's hut for bonuses just like in the original.
-Lots of stuff to collect - moreso than the old games even. I don't know if there's a percentage tracker for completionists though...I haven't seen it yet.
-Lives = candy - depending on your viewpoint this might be bad instead of good, but this game gives away free lives right and left. You will probably never run out. Clearly they decided to make it so that you would not be worrying about it much...just enjoying the game and having opportunity to do the levels as many times as you need to complete them.
-Heart meter - on the old game if you hit something you lost your character (Donkey or Diddy or the girl or the baby depending on which game). In this one both of your characters have two hearts. So you keep them around longer. The game sort of depends on it. I've found a couple of situations where it's incredibly difficult if you cant take at least one hit (but it's always possible if you want to try).
-"Super Kong" - I'm not really a fan, but if you fail hard enough, you get the option to watch super kong do the level (basically it just shows you a level run through) and then the level is complete and you can move on. I guess they didn't want anyone getting stuck. I'm ambivalent about this one. I checked it out but have vowed not to do it again. With all the other things mentioned, it's almost like they're afraid of making the game too challenging. I WANT to spend time being frustrated and thinking the game is hard...that's how you get that glowing sense of achievement when you DO manage to do it.
-Boss levels - they seem more involved and fun than in the old games to me. The creatures you fight are interesting, sometimes even cute and they're fun to take on in their different incarnations.

Bad:
-Controller: there are two options - wiimote and nunchuck or just holding the wiimote sideways. I found the first to be okay, but didn't like it since the controls are really designed to be simple and using both just feels like its not necessary. The wiimote alone feels a lot more intuitive if you've played the old games. You hold it sideways like in some of the Mario games for wii (Paper Mario, New Super Mario). This is not the best since it only has 2 buttons on the right hand side instead of 4 like the SNES controller so some of the old functions are assigned off to "shaking the wiimote." Also the d-pad on the new wiimote is a lot smaller and more squared off so it makes your thumb hurt pretty fast if you don't have the old Nintendo (original system) calluses still in place. The other bad thing is that the game refuses to acknowledge the wii classic controller. I don't know why not...it would be nice to play with. My understanding is that if you purchase the original games from the wiiware store, you can use it with them. There is no reason why this game shouldn't support it.
-Shaking the controller - you have to shake it a lot to do things like blow (new to this game), pound the ground, roll and so forth. I don't play with a wiiplus wiimote, but with the old style the shaking doesn't always recognize if you have to do it multiple times in a row which can lead to some unhappy deaths.
-Character respawning - the old games did a good job of recognizing when you'd already killed enemies. This time around they will almost always come back if you go so much as two screenswidth away and come back. It's minor, but still pretty annoying since it seems like the wii should have so much more capability to remember stuff like this.
-Kremlings/Plot - there is a new plot involving these tikihead things stealing the bananas (instead of Kremlings). That's okay I guess (even if the new ones look kind of...stupid and boring) but most of the enemies are just regular animals and whatnot, not the tikis. Makes it feel like you're mostly just going for a jungle stroll instead of fighting an evil Tiki/Kremling empire like in the original game.
-Pigs - what is up with the pigs? They are in every level (halfway points and so forth).
-Lack of old characters - most of the old characters are missing. Kranky runs the store and also fills his old position of giving random advice. In the store you can buy an additional level for each world, squawks (who points out where stuff is in the levels by squawking from the left hand corner of the screen but not doing much else), a couple of other bonuses for defeating hard levels, and extra lives. Rambi is around every now and then. But other than that, none of the old characters seem to have made the jump.
-Lack of barrels. The old game relied HEAVILY on barrels. I miss them. Now they are there, but you almost never use them and when they are there you almost never need them anyway (maybe just for busting open a bonus level or something).
-Diddy Kong - this is my NUMBER ONE complaint. In single player mode, he really isn't playable. When you get him he's just an extra buff that sits on your back and gives you a jetpack ability (for long range jumping) plus extra health (he has 2 hearts as well as your two hearts). This sucks...in the old days it was really fun that both characters had different abilities...made the game completely different depending on which you have.
-Looking around- the screen is FIRMLY locked on Donkey Kong. In the old games if there was something interesting below you, you could crouch down and the screen would scroll down a bit to see it. Same with looking up as far as I remember. You can't do that anymore. Which sucks...there's a lot of stuff that you just barely see below you sometimes. It'd be nice to look down and I keep finding myself trying.
-Wii Update-when I first popped in the game, it asked me to update my wii before playing it (pretty sure it was specific to the game since it didn't show up the way normal updates do). I don't know what the update consists of, but I can see this being a problem for some if you have modified your Wii. If you have hacks, you may have to choose between losing your hacks and possibly your wii or not playing the game. That's unfortunate.

Might edit this review with more stuff as I find it, but that's it for now.

I love the lego games, and this is another great one.

The good (for me): this one is much like the star wars and the (original) Indiana Jones ones. Very easily playable by all levels of players but with cute funny cut scenes, lots of adventure, easy puzzles, and a whole lot of fun smashing legos to get coins and buy stuff. I love the ease and sense of accomplishment and shear fun of these games! By contrast, I actually did not like the Harry Potter version...it had a lot less smash and grab and fight scenes and more puzzles. I like thinking games (Portal, Safecracker, etc), but I don't really want to mess with it in the lego games which to my mind are a whole other kind of fun. This game is much more a return to the previous philosophy.

The bad: Some glitches (on the Wii version at least). I've found some objects fly off where they are very hard to get to (some of the hats) even though I don't think the developers intended that. Also, I've occasionally gotten characters into locations they can't jump back out of and had to either keep jumping until chance popped me out or I gave up and restarted the level. In a similar way, I had an enemies (particularly in the fight in the cave at the end of the first story) get stuck in the scenery, their little legs flashing as they ran in place. I had to jump on them until my character superimposed and got them out. This bothers me. I loved the care that went into Lego star wars and the original Indiana Jones (for the wii). I'd bought the Lego Indiana Jones II for the DS and found it almost unplayable as did most other people whose reviews I've read due to very poor care on the part of the game developers. Lots of glitches, control malfunctions etc. This game (Pirates) has good controls and is very playable...but the number of glitches makes me a little sad that they still aren't showing the earlier level of care.

Like a lot of the other reviewers, mine is getting used with the PS4. It's great because there are two of us and we aren't always on the same sleep schedule. So not only does this provide a handy mic option, but lets one of us game with as much volume as we want while the other person gets to sleep uninterrupted.

It's not perfectly wireless - there is a box you have to plug into one of the ports of your PS4 which seems to prevent using this if you are using two controllers (though presumably if two of you are playing, you probably have the volume over the TV's speakers so that's okay), and you have to plug the headset into the controller, but neither of us finds that the cord gets in the way at all.

Battery life - Good. Was able to use for several hours before needing a recharge. Which is fine because we don't usually play all day and if one of us did, they wouldn't need to use the headphones the whole time anyway.

Ease of setup - Below average. Enclosed instructions were not wholly clear. Had to go to get documentation from the company website in order to complete the bluetooth receiver setup properly.

Comfort - Good. Lighter weight than expected. Ear cups are soft and headset is not too tight. Might become too loose over the life of the product, but this is speculation based on build quality (mentioned later). It's actually a nice balance on the weight - I prefer a light weight headset whereas my partner prefers the heavier sound isolating monsters. We're both okay with this set that's somewhere in the middle.

Sound Quality - Good. Not going to win any awards, but better than expected from a bluetooth device. Incoming sound is clear and distinct over the sound range put out by games. Bass was nothing to write home about though.

Mic quality - Serviceable. Did not use this feature too much, though because frankly when it comes to playing Call of Duty or other online games, neither one of us is much of a talker...mostly we just mute the other players too and enjoy the game. The mic position is adjustable, which is a plus in my book; mic is also detachable, which is good for me, as I don't use it to often for console gaming.

Build quality - Seems average. It FEELS a little less than durable, but time will tell whether or not this is true. So far it has held up well to reasonable use. Audio controls on the headset itself are useful, and add to the device's functionality.

Look is good - the overall black and blue scheme with the blue LEDs looks like a made for PS4 accessory.

I don't play games that often, but when I do...I either stop after 30 minutes or play the hell out of them!

And I definitely played the hell out of this. A as others have said, it's EXACTLY like playing an episode of South Park. I'm so glad the collaboration went well because the humor/storylines/characters/animation style are all perfectly spot on. And for South Park fans, you'll see a lot of little reminders from episodes past that feel like in jokes. It's perfectly wonderful and crude with a the wit and subtle intelligence that I expect from the show. This is a game that actually represents a TV show perfectly well.

It's not a hard RPG exactly, but the main quest is easy enough to follow, the menus are straight forward, and controls masterable. Lots of little side quests also. On the whole, there isn't much skill needed...but that's okay because it lets you sit back and enjoy the story.

Some folks complain about the length of the game, but if you're a completionist, there's still a good 20-30 hours at least you can get out of it. Though that said, I think the replay value is low. Still, not a bad value for the money if you compute that it's just a couple of bucks per hour of entertainment. Speaking of, I definitely recommend playing as a Jew. As far as I can tell there are a few little things available that you can't get any other way. (some quests I hadn't found otherwise and achievements also) Otherwise it's pretty similar though.

The one reason I'm knocking off a star is that the game mechanics are kind of limited. It becomes pretty obvious (and to me annoying) how little of the environment is interactable and some of it just gets redundant. Every bathroom has a toilet with a not very fun "poop" game for instance. And you pick up all sorts of random stuff (mostly stuff from old episodes) into your inventory, but most of it you can't do anything with.

And, while it's fun to dress up your character, there was one really obnoxious thing for me: you can't play as a female. I'm not much of a feminist, but still...I am a girl and if I'm not playing a set character (if I were playing Kyle or Stan or whatever, I wouldn't care) but since one I make myself, I'd like to be able to make the character like me. It wouldn't have been THAT hard for them to change the few little bits of dialog and whatnot and allow a female character to be a thing. But nope...you can make yourself look like a girl, but you'll still be called "he" and "son."

So on the whole I love the hell out of this game, but there's just a few things keeping it from getting all five stars.

Very lightweight headset for the size which is great when sitting on the couch for gaming. It's hard to tell about build quality. It seems almost flimsy because of the weight, but I'm not sure. I haven't beaten up on it, but it's done just fine - no signs of any damage or wear after almost 2 months use, so it's holding up alright.

The sound quality is...decent. It's not going to blow you away but it's not terrible and at least as good as the TV speakers even if I feel the gaming headset that I'm used to using on my PC is better/richer.

Mic seems great. No one has complained about my voice when using it anyway, haha.

The control switches and dials are okay. Mostly it feels a bit crowded. You have to take a minute to identify what you want most of the time.

Ha, honestly the hardest part about this was for some reason it felt intimating to take it out of the box and hook it up to play. Can't blame the game for that...that's all on me.

Really glad when I finally did though. Used the old guitar laying around (which was bought to learn on and then never played) and booted it up.

First thing, there is a WIDE variety of activities which all seem pretty easy to jump into. It was a pretty good intro to the instrument for someone (like me) with Zero skill. I'm not sure how quickly more experienced players would "outgrow" it though...haven't gotten there yet. I really do think this is probably best for total beginners or at least intermediates that have some idea how to play but need some improvement.

It does do a good job of telling you what you should be doing next, but it may take some time to really hone in on your skill level.

It seems like it'll take patience to master, but that's expected...that's part of why it took so long to open the box. But hey, you gotta start some where if you're serious about this and a video game is easier than taking personal lessons (or cheaper anyway).

Two issues:

1) It was not always picking up sound from the guitar. This may have been the guitar used though...just some drop outs.

2) The voice over, while not TOO obnoxious was a bit grating. But oh well.

Pretty small. Fits the hand okay, but might be too small for some.

The Textured surface is pretty good. Grippy without being rough, and doesn't seem like it would slip out of your hands.Multiple lights options are nice for those who want it, and the ability to have them off completely is appreciated.The braided cord is pretty nice, and there is plenty of it. The break-away section is seated well, but looks like it will separate like it's supposed to. The lack of rumble might turn off some people, but the inclusion of a headphone jack is very welcome.

Buttons are just clicky enough that you can feel them, don't feel like they have a ton of travel. The sticks seem to move very easily. Time will tell if they get too loose over the course of using them. As with the controller overall, the buttons and sticks also feel really small. That said, the sticks seem to sit a little higher than on the regular pro controller, which is a plus, but the buttons seem more tightly spaced, which some won't like. The presence of the paddle-style buttons on the back will be appreciated by those who use them. Didn't try programming them, but the option is nice to have.

Would be nice if it could be used on the Switch in handheld mode (if it was on a stand or somesuch), but this can be solved with an inexpensive adapter (which is a solution that was tested and does work). Overall, if you are going for a wired controller, have smaller hands, and don't mind losing the rumble function, this controller is a fairly solid choice.

Season 1 & 2 is Hitman at its finest. Hitman is a "sandbox" stealth series developed by IO Interactive, previously published by Eidos Interactive and Square Enix. Due to cutbacks and layoffs, things took a turn for the future of the Hitman series, but in this rare case, it's all for the better. Square Enix allowed IO Interactive to keep the Hitman IP. Most other companies would have retained the rights to the franchise and later sourced another developer to reboot it. Instead, IO Interactive now acts as an independent studio with the full departure of Square Enix.

Season 2 delivers six additional sandboxes to play in, bringing the total amount to levels to 12 if you include Season 1. I have always been a big fan of the series, and started playing Hitman with the original on PC, and then played the rest of the series up util now. Each game is great and carries its own strengths and weaknesses, with Absolution being the most unorthodox on the list do to its more linear approach.

This new take on the series is what I would call a "true fans dream come true". Everything is greatly expanded upon and levels now feature the scope and detail the series has always deserved. Season 1 had a bit of a slow start being episodic, and it took a while to make a disk version. The game was around, but it was more like a ghost, few even knew about it. As good as Season 1 was, it never felt 100% complete because it only had 6 mission. Even with the missions being large in size, it still felt like half a game, and that is because it was.

Season 2 is the second half we needed, but its greatness doesn't end there. Season 1 lacked only a few things that held it back from being perfect, and Season 2 not only addresses such impediments, it also reprograms the original Season 1 missions with much needed features. Season 2 brings back the six locations from the previous Season, as part of the Hitman Legacy Pack, but it is only a free download for owners of Season 1. The new levels in Season 2, do not take part in the Season 1 levels, they are all new locations.

The new missions from Season 1 have been remastered and enhanced to support new gameplay features found in Season 2, including a new progression system, higher-fidelity crowds, picture-in-picture mode, and new gameplay items such as your briefcase, dart gun and flash grenades. There are new difficulty modes and the A.I has been reworked from the ground up. The A.I will no longer stand around and let you go gun happy, they will now move around tactically, flank and run into cover, so it is now a blast to play it both ways, stealth and as a shooter.

A.I can now see you in a mirror and respond accordingly. Cameras also now serve a purpose. Guards will now run to investigate, like they should with guns ready. No longer do they hide in the back eating Doritos, or whatever it was they have been doing for the past 15 or so years. It is now safe to say that all of the old guards have officially been "let go" do to a lack in job performance, and have now been replaced with guards who are more actively motivated by some kind of new payroll system.

Final Verdict:

Season 2 delivers more needed content, as well as polishing up its Season 1 content. The only feature I would like to see return is the "Human Shield", which for whatever reason is not an option, but does not hinder the great experience. If you have been holding out on buying Season 1 then now is the time. This will now give you 12 large sandbox stages to play around in, but just keep in mind, the Season 1 stages are not included on this disk, they are downloaded only as part of a DLC Legacy Pack, and only free to owners of Season 1.

No need for too much details here, this is the same great game that was released 2 years ago, but with an exclusive key chain, new art book, reversible cover, and it includes the “Rise of the Giants” DLC on the disk. For those who don't know, Dead Cells is a side-scrolling game with an old school Castlevania style presentation that is superbly polished, insanely challenging and very addictive.

The game is littered with items, secrets behind destructible walls, unlockable tools and features more than fifty weapons and spells. Dead Cells is very punishing, and its forever changing do to its generated stages. Death means starting back at square one with everything on your person having vanished, but as you claim cells from fallen enemies, you can use them to purchase new weapons or upgrade your existing arsenal, if you can keep them until the end of the stage. Death is kind of like playing Dark Souls and Bloodborne, only side scrolling this time around.

Over time, you'll find that you're able to push just a little bit further where increasingly nice goodies wait, as well as special items that allow you to activate shortcuts and skip the early stages entirely. Its really hard to say how long the game is because it varies greatly depending on skill, maybe 10-35 hours. After completing the game, there are lots of features to master, such as unlocking the hard, very hard, expert and nightmare mode, and many variables are changed from one setting to the next.

Final Verdict

Dead Cells is one of those games that can be easy to play but hard to master. Its definitely not for everyone, it takes lots of practice and dedication, as well as an inner drive for perfection. As long as the player can except these harsh realities, then Dead Cells is more than worth the price of admission.

NBA 2K20 wants you to spend more money than one should, and it’s more than willing to constantly frustrate you with poor game balances that force your hand in making you pay your way through it. If I had to say anything good, there are noticeable graphical improvement done to the series. The lighting, renders, tattoos, hairstyles, neighborhood and MyCareer cutscenes are delivered with more quality and style than previous versions. This "casino gambling" system is what is going to kill it for everyone, as even governments are looking to pass laws that limit its abusive tactics. I do not recommend this product.

The single player is slam pack with tons of content. The graphics and effects are really nice, missions are challenging and there is a nice history of each mission. Games likes this are rare but this is one of the better tactical games to come around with only a few picky things to say. The tutorial could be much better as it only teaches you the very basics. The story mode seems to have a very open structure in the order many missions can be played, but this can cause the player to go down the path of playing missions that may require the use of more advanced tactics the player has not yet mastered.

The AI is good but can feel like it always knows exactly where you are. Some of the missions are very long and others are not, so the balance between the two can feel a little off. Even with a few faults its still a very enjoyable single player campaign, there are no timers or endless waves of invincible troops and you can even save even without checkpoints. The game does feature online multiplayer, but do to the fact that RTS games are an acquired taste, don't expect to find tons of people, and the few you will find will more than likely be pros. Its a good game but it does not have base building, its more so of a game about tactics.

The career mode opens by placing the player into three different scenarios as well as showing you the variation of the cars on offer. After that, you’ll be testing your skills against various different series of races. There’s no predefined method of completing the career mode, allowing you to concentrate on working through one class at a time, though the invitational series will focus around classes.

You also have the ability to order teammate around with varying results, fans of "Need for Speed Carbon" will feel right at home here. Your options are to ask them to push foreword or hang back and defend their current position more aggressively. Based on the difficulty you choose, the AI will either be a walk in the park or absolutely ruthless. Racers can hold grudges, and introduces a system that sees opponents for who they are and what they may have done, and they aren’t shy about break checking you or being downright aggressive. They can even get a temporary boost to their driving skills as they become extra motivated to get back at you.

Graphically the game looks very well done. Grid features 12 racing locations, a mix of real and fantasy circuits with multiple layouts with a few returning tracks featured in the original GRID. There is also varied lighting and nice weather effects implemented throughout the duration of the game as well as the returning rewind feature. The cars all have nice sounds and handle very well all around, the player can tell there was lots of attention payed to even the smallest of details.

Final Verdict:

GRID is a worthy racing game that offers a perfect blend of arcade racing and simulation-based racing. At first it seemed like Codemasters was simply remastering the original GRID and slapping a $60 price tag on it, but in reality its much more than that. This is a "reboot" of the series that still pays homage to the original series. GRID knows what it was and what it wants to be, and has simply used those assets to reshape such a great racer into what it has now become.

It's hard to even sum up all the charm and wonder of Baldur's Gate in a review.. There is already a countless amount of information surrounding these game and most people are already aware of what they have to offer, so I wont be writing a long winded review. Baldur’s Gate was released in December of 1998 with its sequel appearing in September of 2000. The Enhanced Edition returned to PC once again in 2012 & 2013, and includes the DLC, new companions, small enhancements to the Infinity Engine, as well as many added improvements that are built into the interface.

For those that have not played the series, at its core, this is a giant role-playing game with a very large world as well as an extraordinary and at times, overwhelming amount complexity and strategy. BioWare’s take on Dungeons & Dragons is represented here to the finest. Both games are great, with the original focusing more on exploration, and the sequel focusing more on quality of life improvements while still obtaining the depth and originality of the original.

Baldur's Gate is isometric, which means the player gets a a top-down view of the world. You move your characters by selecting them and clicking where you want them to go. You can recruit up to five allies for a total party of six to follow you around, do your bidding and fight for you. All of the characters in Baldur's Gate have their own goals, personalities, and ambitions, and depending on your actions some might get mad and decide to leave you forever.

Combat in Baldur's Gate is very interesting, it's a mixture of real-time and turn-based combat. You can pause combat at any time to give orders to your party members, just like Pillars of Eternity and Dragon Age Origins, which was actually a spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate. Both games can get outlandishly difficult but you can always change the difficulty settings. If you have played Pillars or Dragon Age, you will more than likely enjoy this, but think of them as a much "lighter" version, while Baldur's Gate is far more complex and requires much more time and dedication to master.

Final Verdict:

Baldur's Gate is a timeless classic and this PC port carries the fun over to consoles, but rather or not how well the games have aged really depends on the player. The deciding factor will be if the player values gameplay over graphics. From a gameplay and narrative perspective the games have aged like fine wine, but players spoiled by the HD games of our time may find them hard to tolerate. It's also worth noting that PC games are always more "ahead of the times" when being compared to consoles, and while the gap is much more narrow these days, it was a very large factor in the earlier years of gaming.

Many people are not aware, but in 2012 a PS3 version was considered and they wanted to create this port. Unfortunately, even during that time the project proved to be to complex, and would require far to much rework and fixes in order to keep a steady performance, so even for consoles in 2012 it was simply to complex to be fully implemented. Just the RAM requirements alone demands 512 MB when the PS3 only ran with 256 MB and the XBox 360 maxed out at 512 MB. In other words, don't let the age of the games fool you, this collection is still a pure joy and real treat to play.

Today is a great day for console gamers, not only are we getting two great classic here, but the Baldur's Gate collection has also been released separately. If your like me and played these classics on the PC but still spend most of your time on consoles, then there is no questions about it that both collections are well worth the price of admission. If you are deciding between this or the Baldur's Gate collection and have never played either one but are stuck trying to decide, I would say it really depends on what your looking for, as both collections offer an entirely different experience all together. I will only be covering a few details considering how many reviews there already are for these classics.

Unlike Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale does not seem to have much story or character interactions, it's pretty much all combat but still loads of fun. The story is alright but is simply not the star of the show, and if you enjoyed the combat in Baldur's Gate you'll probably enjoy Icewind Dale. Icewind Dale is linear, and all side quests are accomplished in the same locations of the main quest with no optional dungeons, but there are some optional sections in the main quest dungeons. It has good art, music and atmosphere, and great customization of the party.

Dialogues and story elements doesn't really make a difference in the game, and are mostly an excuse for you to go dungeon crawling. Baldur's Gate on the other hand is non-linear with branching side quests and optional dungeons and fights, has far more dialogue with a richer story and far more replayability. Baldur's Gate is the RPG Black Isle wanted to do at first, but Icewind Dale was launched later do to the success of Baldur's Gate. In my opinion, Icewind Dale is a good game but not great, it simply eviscerated the idea of good exploration and character building, which is one of the biggest tenants of a great RPG. In Icewind Dale, the combat is what makes the game.

Planescape Torment is an entirely different beast all together, and the game shouldn't be confused with Tides of Numenera which is not nearly as good. Torment is a game with 800,000 English words and 75,000 lines, so it may not sit well with players that don't like reading a huge amount of text. The writing is however very well done and makes the player want to read everything, and can often cause reloads after a conversation just to see what other directions it could take the player.

Planescape Torment while promising, has weaker gameplay, UI and inconsistencies. Combat can be nearly non-existent and most combat can even be avoided through conversations. While there is combat in the game, there is not much opportunity to use tactics in battle because the enemies are much weaker. Planescape is more about story than actual combat. While you have way more freedom in expressing your character than in Baldur's Gate, the course you take is pretty much set and predetermined, without much opportunity to set forth to roam and explore the lands.

Planescape Torment does at times have combat that can be fun, as each party member has at least one thing about them that makes their gameplay stand out and has an awesome selection of spells. However, the game seems to lack enemy variety, and as noted before, complex challenges. What Torment has in spades is your alignment really does make a difference, and it's much deeper and more convincing than in Baldur's Gate. Planescape Torment in my opinion is once again a good but not great. In Torment, the writing is what makes this game.

Final Verdict:

I tried to speak a little about both game and cover a few main differences regarding both collections for players that have not played them. When being compared to the Baldur's Gate series, there is no such thing as "which game is better" because each collection is vastly different from one other. As for which collection I would recommend more would greatly depend on the players needs. The Baldur's Gate series I feel is the better package that seems to hit all the right notes in a great RPG, but such greatness comes at a price, and that's a level of complexity and lack of hand holding that may turn some players off.

Icewind Dale is great for those looking to have a more simplified and linear form of fun while still having a challenging experience, while Planescape Torment offers fun from a completely unique and novel like presentation. I would probably recommend this collection be played before the Baldur's Gate collection in order to learn the way these games are structured. Then if you complete them and enjoy yourself, you could then try moving onto a more complex experience. If you have both the time and money, my definite response would be both collections are worth owning, just go into the experience knowing that each game excels in different areas.

I'm a big fan of the Ace Combat series. I've played 4 (with controller on PS2) and 5 (with the flight sticks on PS2). AC 5 is still my favorite; mostly because of the lack of primary character development, third person storytelling point of view and cheesy dialogue used in AC6.

As any veteran of Ace Combat knows, the missions can be very challenging. The lack of sufficient checkpoints (not enough of them at all) means you may end up playing the first 10 minutes of a mission multiple times. I do this all too often; I make a minor error or end up getting shot down and have to start the mission all over again.

Another complaint I have is getting a plane suited for a ground attack (eg:A-10) as the mission pre-brief describes, and then finding out after the mission is "done", that enemy fighters are closing in and the player must defeat a given amount of them (without dying) before the mission can be done "for real". As you may imagine, defeating 3 or 4 Su-33's using a slow old hog like the A-10 is not ideal.

With those issues out of the way, this is an amazing game, both play-wise, visual-wise, and as an all around flying sim/arcade experience. The Flight sticks and cockpit-only-view are a *MUST* if you intend to fully appreciate everything this game has to offer.
