I'm a casual gamer, playing games that might interest me only, not really on the lookout for the latest and greatest. I'm also a big Harry Potter fan. In past years, I avoided the Harry Potter games merely because of some of the other movie tie-in games that I've played were basically on the intelligence level of an eight year old and rather silly indeed. But with the new book coming out this week, and the movie as well, I was sucked into purchasing this game, and have been pleasantly surprised.

Order of the Phoenix follows very closely the book and the movie, starting with a quick Dementor attach, to learning spells in Grimmauld Place, to quickly landing at Hogwarts. In the game, you are required to assemble the new D.A. by performing tasks, and to train the army with Defence spells. Along throughout the castle, you are asked to use your wand to repair things, clean up things, and discover many secrets hidden in the castle to earn more magical power for Harry.

Now, as a serious, challenging game, this isn't it. I've been finding it fairly easy to complete the tasks. In some occasions which the game required magic to complete a task, I found it easier to hold the controller with one hand while operating my wand with another. It was great fun to use spells to make things fly across the room, make carpets shake, and set lights on fire. Again, not challenging, but fun.

Let me say that the visual representation of Hogwarts is magnificent. It really is very complex, many leveled and layered. The details put into each room is just like being on the movie sets. The Grand Hall is beautiful, the Gryffindor Common Room has lots of little details, and even the journey to Hagrid's Hut is long and breathtaking. It really does simulate Hogwarts beautifully, and with the amazing ability of having NO load times between rooms, you really feel like you are there!

The pitfalls I've found are thus. You do bump into Ron and Hermione frequently., especially if you are in a small room and need to get out. In several of the rooms. In one occasion, a student was stuck partially through the ground. The biggest issue is the sound. In several rooms, I keep hearing this grating, grinding noise that doesn't seem to have any part in the story. In some cases, it is so loud, I cannot hear the characters speak. Occasionally, characters voices would cut out or sound fuzzy or buzzy. I would restart the game, and most of the problems were solved.

But overall, I do feel like I'm really getting my money's worth. Just by feeling like you are in Hogwarts is an amazing feat. This will be one game, after I've finished the tasks, that whenever I feel like visited the old magical school, I'll return to time and time again.

I'm a 42 year old man, who just received "Lego Indiana Jones" for his birthday. Now, I'd been hearing about Lego Star Wars for a long time, and how much fun it was. But I just didn't buy it. I mean, how could having a Lego experience compare with [[ASIN:B0001NE48U Star Wars Battlefront]] or [[ASIN:B0009O7HVM Star Wars Battlefront II]], which was extremely realistic and fun to boot? Well, the truth is, in a campy and fun way, the Lego series takes what you love about the movies, and makes it truly a fun, interactive experience.

Lego Indiana Jones follows the plots of the three movies faithfully (with a few minor plot detail changes that totally don't detract from the enjoyment). Each "movie" has six missions in it, and your goal is to make it through each level. The process of making it through the level is not at all challenging, but really is smart in it's intuitiveness and manor. You instinctively know what to do in each level, and sometimes the challenge comes from trying to figure out how to do it. Embedded in each level are ten "treasure chests" filled with an artifact piece. Find all ten, and you get an artifact from that mission. Normally, I'm not into the side missions, or extra bonus things that some video games have, but finding these treasure chests became an obsession of mine!

All through the game, Lego has embedded some wry humor and playful puns that only enhance the game. For example, in the min-movie that opens "Temple of Doom", Willie's opening dance number is hilarious for her coughing. Since the Lego people don't actually talk but grunt at each other, it makes it even more funny. And Elsa Schneider's greeting at the Venice pier is one for the record books!

I'm throughly loving this game, and as soon as I am finished (I'm purposefully playing it slow to get the most enjoyment out of it over the longest period of time), it's off to Lego Star Wars for me! Highly recommended for all ages, and all Indy fans!

I'm a big fan of the first Godfather game on PS2, and played it through about three times. While repetitive, I did love the immersive environment, the 1940's look, and the vast expanse of NYC and it's surrounding boroughs. It captured the spirit of the movie, and integrated a new story into the existing movie very expertly with a few changes. When I heard that Godfather II was coming out for the PS3, I knew that I would have to get it.

My first reaction was a bit of disappointment. You start in New York, which is a very small area, instantly reminding me of a Hollywood set. Not even needing a car, you could run from business to business to overtake them, which, with a crew, is a fairly simple task. The fights for the compounds offer more of a challenge, but upgrading your crew makes it very easy to overpower.

However, going to Miami improved my attitude with the game, and a bit bigger "set". The makers did maintain some of the elements of the first game that I loved; robbing banks, bombing businesses, going on special missions, the open world to explore. The places of business you go to vary from location to location, so overtaking businesses isn't as repetitive as the first game. You also have to take out major members of the rival families, which adds a new, fun element to the game. I also enjoyed having certain "influence" as a Don, being able to help out my cause.

I haven't had any problems, so far, with the graphics or the game play. I've found the visual look of the game impressive, but not as deep as 1940's New York. Rival families bombing and taking over your businesses is an improvement from the last game, but you can easily retake them. The crew, once upgraded, seems too powerful, making success in missions almost guaranteed.

So, I'm happy with Godfather 2. I don't play thousands of games, so I'm not comparing this to other games, but for a casual gamer, and a Godfather fan, it's a winner.

One of the things that I most loved about [[ASIN:B000OLWBR0 Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix]] was being able to wander around Hogwarts at will, visiting classrooms, Hagrid's Hut, the Owlery, even to Harry's bedroom above the Gryffindor Common Room. Based heavily on the sets from the movie, the immersive three dimension atmosphere charmed and made for a truly fun experience. Fortunately, the makers of "Half-Blood Prince" retained most of the Hogwarts from the game, and gives you yet another in-depth experience in "Harry Potter and the Half Blood Prince" for PS3.

Sometimes, with games such as these, the makers try to change too much of a game that was well loved, removing some elements that a player would truly love for something different (the awful game Spiderman 3 comes to mind). Electronic Arts knew better. This game appears to follow the plot of the movie quite well (since it hasn't been released yet, it's hard to actually judge this, but it does follow the book). Harry is back at Hogwarts. This time, along with the plot of the movie, you have three different tasks: join the dueling club, the potions club, and a fun ride with Quidditch games and practice. As Harry wanders around the castle, he must also collect shields and mini-shields, upon which additional powers and abilities are awarded.

If you didn't play the "Order of the Phoenix" game, you will love the vast expansive Hogwarts. One of the selling points of that game was the fact that there are no "load times", which is still true about this game. You wander around the castle at will, and really never have to wait while entering a classroom or transitioning from inside to outside. While you are constantly given "tasks", important to the plot, you can delay the task and roam around, which I found myself doing. Once of the skills that I quickly developed was dueling, which you grow through joining different house dueling clubs and defeating the people. If you get lost in Hogwart, a quick button push and Nearly Headless Nick comes and will escort you to your next task.

Another aspect I liked from the first game is the ability to complete magic spells. You have spells you learn to be used during dueling and fights, and then you have other spells to use as you wander around the school. While the spells are few, you really do feel like you have some fun control over them. You mostly use "wingardium leviosa" to make things fly, like benches, flower pots, and chairs. Still, great fun!

One of the downsides to the game is the fairly wooden aspect of how some of the people look, especially the girls (and their plasticine looking hair!). And is the game challenging? I wouldn't say that. But I don't buy a game like this to be challenged, but to get a chance to "experience" Hogwarts as if I were in one of the movies. And with that, it's very successful.

I'm anxiously anticipating seeing "Half Blood Prince" after a six month wait from last year. Until then, you'll find me roaming the halls of Hogwarts in my new game.

The last great game that I played on my PS3 was [[ASIN:B001E8VB6O Batman: Arkham Asylum]]. In fact, thinking about it I still smile a bit. I loved every minute of the adventure, and still recall climbing to the top of the clock tower, leaping off, and seeing how long I could soar. I didn't think that another game could come close to this adventure, but it turns out, I was wrong. I'm enjoying "Red Dead Redemption" just as much as Batman; for the graphic quality the shear adventure of the game, the ability to roam, the mini-games, and the total submersion of life in a Western town.

The first time you get a chance to head out into the wilderness, you'll be impressed with the high quality realism of the game. Animals roam freely and are ripe for the hunting, but be careful of some angrier animals. I've been attacked by a cougar (and survived the tale) but didn't after a wolf pack attack. The missions John goes on are of the usual caliber, but they are fun, if not a bit repetitive. The bounty hunting pays a good price, especially if you get to lasso the criminal and hogtie him to carry him back alive. You can play a variety of western games , my favorite is poker where, with the right clothes, you get to cheat.

Overall, I found this game to be very easy to use. The design of the game is very intuitive, and you don't have to learn a bunch of fancy button moves to make things happen. Most importantly, it's just a lot of fun to slip into the old west for a hour a day, and ride my horse into the sunset, or rope a wild horse, or even chat it up with the saloon ladies.

I've been a big fan of the Lego games since playing my first "Star Wars" video game a few years back. At first, I really thought as an adult that the Lego games were just for kids, not challenging nor fun. Boy, was I wrong. The Lego video games are an engaging series infused with what I call a "Lego" sense of humor that permeates through the game. From Star Wars to the challenging Batman game, to my personal favorite, Indian Jones, they all have been pleasurable experiences. When I heard about Harry Potter coming out as a video game, I was elated. And truth be told, this game is as good as all of the others in the series. At first it seemed as if Harry Potter and Lego have somehow parted ways. There weren't any Lego sets released with the last movie, and nothing much on the Lego website about Harry Potter in general. However, the two have united again in a very fun video game, "Harry Potter: Years 1 -4".

Since I'm a casual adult gamer (I play video games but won't spend days playing a game straight without a break), my review comes from that perspective. First, the creators of the game have gotten so much right about this game. From the infusion of the magical components of the game to the story to the characterization of the people, it all works brilliantly. The game starts as Harry is whisked from his sad existence at Privet Drive to Diagon Alley, accompanied by a lovable Hagrid. This section is designed to teach you everything there is to know about the game. However, if you've played any of the Lego video games before, it's all very instinctive and natural. There are some specific controls that you need to learn to move things and cast spells, but it all feels very natural. Just in the first level alone, you can make things fly, move, and animate with a flick of the wand. It's all very entertaining!

When Harry reaches Hogwarts, I was impressed with the both level of detail in the design of the game, as well as Lego components that are infused in the place. It feels very natural and yet very Lego! For those of you like me who adore the coin collection part of the game (it's rather an obsession of mine), Lego has that back and allows you to collect to your hearts content as you smash your way to wealth! Another one of the better additions to the game is also the use of "Polyjuice Potion" to be able to change characters through the game play to make your way through the levels. The challenge of the game isn't too great (I made my way through the first movie on the first day, which was approximately six levels), and you are given spells to use as you need them. I like the gradual release of these spells because you actually remember them.

What are the drawbacks? For one thing, there doesn't seem to be an "area to explore" as in, an area to wander around. You are pretty confined to the "sets" to explore. While in Hogwarts, you can definitely not follow your ghost guide and try to accomplish other tasks, but it definitely isn't an open range. Another drawback is the broom flying feature is a bit weak and hard to get used to. You don't ride from the front on perspective, but from the side, making depth perception a bit tricky.

NEW SECTION: I've been reading the comments from players who are stuck in Professor Flitwick's dungeon. I just played that level in my game, and got out of the room without any problem. After I assembled the dragon, it threw my character up in the air and back into the classroom without any issues. However, I understand the frustration from others who haven't been able to leave that room. (It happened to me once in another game that wasn't working properly on my system, and when I wrote a negative review about the game, I was hammered with unhelpful feedback.) However, because I didn't have the glitch in my game, my review score will stand.

If you are a Harry Potter fan, you'll be purchasing this game immediately. I've played the other games and loved them for their realism and attention to detail. This one? It's just plain fun!

Buying this was a no-brainer for me. Lifelong Disney fan, owner of most of the Disney flicks, Mickey Mouse watches, artwork, stuffed animals. Once I saw this game was coming out, I knew it would be a must-buy for me, even without checking any of the reviews. Upon searching for the game on my iPhone, I saw that I had two choices to make. For an extra few dollars, I bought the collector's edition (even being the Disney fan that I am, I'm not always prone to do). My review mostly about the game, but I'll mention the few extras that came with this set.

First, the game. It kicks. I love it. Mickey is sucked into an alternate Disney universe where the park has become possessed by the Blot, an evil creature designed to wreak havoc on all that is loved. Mickey must fight the park, different creatures, and Walt's first creation Oswald in order to make everything right. Armed with a trusty paintbrush, Mickey controls thinner and paint to make his way through the levels. And the levels are quite fun. Challenging? A bit, but not terribly so.

What makes this game so entertaining is the riff of the Disney parks with a slightly dark side and a bit of humor that make for surprise as you make your way through each level. I knew I was in for a treat when the "Small World" ride features prominently in one of the early levels and you must battle in it as well as outside of it to make is through. I love it. Also, the familiar characters that appear in the story, from the aforementioned Oswald, a mechanical Capt. Hook, and some early Disney characters that haven't been seen in a while (Pete!). For any Disney fan, it's a treasure trove of inside jokes.

A couple of gripes. First, Mickey proceeds through many of his levels by leaping, which, until you get the hang of it, is challenging. The leaping increases in difficulty as you progress through the game, but sometimes it was a pain more than fun. Secondly, as previous reviewers have mentioned, there are camera issues. There are times when you cannot look at where you are needing to leap, or times when all you can see is a close-up of a wall. Mickey has fallen off ledges and walked off swinging chandeliers because of the issue.

As part of the collector's edition, you get a bevy of bonus materials. Honestly, I was so excited to play the game that I spent a grand total of less than a minute looking at them (in fact, they are still sitting in the box). However, I did take the Mickey figurine and place in right next to my Wii. Unlike other reviewers, my Mickey came fully intact, nothing broken.

So, this is a great game, and would make a great gift for any Disney enthusiast, or anyone looking for a fun game to play. Highly recommended!

When I first heard of the Lego video game franchise, I was dubious. I am a middle aged (I hate to admit that) gamer, who plays a variety of video games because of my teen years in the 1980's was spent in front of Donkey King, Asteroids, Pac-Man and my personal favorite, Galaga. While a lifelong Lego fan, when I first learned that Lego was putting out games, I thought it was a video building set. What fun could that be? However, I began to hear tales of [[ASIN:B000R3BNDI Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga]], and quickly fell into the trap. After playing [[ASIN:B00104KJ4M Lego Indiana Jones]], [[ASIN:B000ZK9QC8 LEGO Batman]], and my personal favorite [[ASIN:B002BRZ712 LEGO Harry Potter: Years 1-4]], I was officially hooked. So it was with great anticipation that I heard about this game. After playing it for a few hours, I have to say, Lego has done it again.

Taking the very successful movie franchise "Pirates of the Caribbean", Lego has crafted a game the whole family can love. Starring all of the main characters from the first three movies, as well as new characters from the soon-to-be released "On Stranger Tides", Lego Pirates is a great mashup of the story. One of the things that sets these Lego games apart is the wicked sense of humor that is placed in the sometimes too long cut scenes. The jokes in the scenes somehow manage to poke fun at the movies, while honoring them at the same time. The end result is wanting to watch the movies again! It's a fine line between mocking and funny, and Lego wins every time.

As far as the game play, the game is similar to the others. Lots of fairly easy puzzles to solve, lots of destruction to earn studs. In fact, the breaking of things happens to be one of my favorite parts. It's a great stress reliever, especially when the item explodes into many hundreds worth of studs (not to mention the multipliers!) and you not only get to break things, but get rewarded for doing so.

The Pros:
- Engaging swashbuckling fun!
- Ability to play many different characters in "Free Play" Mode
- Creative, if not challenging, puzzles to solve
- Multiple rewards encourages replay of the levels
- Lots of trophies to earn, lots of hidden areas to explore

The Cons:
- Sometimes the cut scenes run a little long
- The "puppet theater" load time screen video gets a little old
- Some minor camera issues make jumping more of a challenge

While I'm not totally done with the game, I have to give it a great thumbs up. This is a game that could easily be enjoyed by the whole family. Gear up for the summertime, and spend a little time on the high pirate seas, with this soon to be classic game from Lego!

If you enjoyed playing Ghost Recon you will find Island Thunder to be an even better game. The new weapons maps are just a small part of the expansion. The graphics have improved dramatically, the game is visually more crisp with more colors (unlike the usual green tint that overshadowed the original Ghost Recon), and the sounds have also improved (both voices and environment).
The environment completely comes alive, the clouds move and darkens the terrain when they cover the sun, the rain and lightning is extremely realistic (both visually and sound), and the terrain offers so many hidding places (great for snipers).
The AI has also improved, making the game that much more challenging (as if the realism of 1 shot kill wasn't challenging enough already).
The new maps are HUGE and extremely detailed. The new weapons are very impressive and accurate.
The multiplayer split screen mode offers a new game type, Defend (those of you who have played Ghost Recon on Xbox Live ought to be familiar with it).
With all these new improvements, this game makes the original Ghost Recon seem like a Nintendo 64 game. I don't see why anyone would go back to playing the original Ghost Recon (for the exception of a particular map that is not on Island Thunder) after playing Island Thunder.

This is truly a facinating game. I was never really into racing games until I saw the trailer for Burnout 2. As the other reviews have mentioned the incredible crash mode and crash physics, however, no one has mentioned mutliplayer (split screen) pursuit mode (similar to that in Driver 2). This mode adds another twist to the game, instead of just racing to see who finishes first, it's all about trying to ram the other person's car on a high speed chase before they "get away" (reach the finish line). This mode of course has to be unlocked by completing certain objectives/races (Pursuit 3) in the game. Aside from the awesome graphics, game play, great contols, and phenominal cars available in this game, the custom soundtrack is the icing on the cake.
I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a fast and fun racing game. If you are looking for a "driving" with "open" ended maps and various modes/features other than just racing from point A to point B, then this is not the game for you, you may want to consider Midtown Madness 3 (which will be my next purchase).
I only gave this game 4 stars due to some very minor glitches and flaws, I have listed them below:
Sometimes you will run full speed into another vehicle but won't crash, you will only "bump" the other vehicle.
When causing a Log truck to crash the logs stay on the truck and don't roll off, even though the big rig jack-knifes.
Same with the oil rigs, they will crash but no explosion, even in the midst of all the sparks and collisions from other vehicles crashing into the truck.
The game has a replay of each race, pursuit, or crash, but does not offer the option to save the replay, or rewind/fast-forward, or replay in slow motion.
For those of you who have Xbox Live and want to race against other XBL gamers online this is not the game for you. Burnout 2 only offers online scoreboards no online play.
If all these things were fixed in Burnout 3, then the game would be perfect.

I got this game after purchasing a PS3, thinking that even if this game wasn't all that great, I could use the two microphones (which came with a USB adaptor) for Karaoke Revolution games. I was wrong. Because the microphones are not actual USB mics and have to plug into a USB adaptor, Karaoke Revolution games do not detect these "SingStar" mics.

Secondly, SingStar does not give you the option to remove the lead vocals from the songs. This defeats the whole purpose of Karaoke. Even on Karaoke mode, the lead vocals are still there.

Lastly, The game has a very small selection of songs, and there are a handful of tracks that are "medleys", which are basically a medley from choruses of the same songs that are already on this game.

Conclusion. This is NOT a Karaoke game, as it does not give you the option to strip the lead vocals, and the microphones included with the game are not compatible with any other games for the PS2 or PS3. If I was given the option, I would give this game ZERO stars.

I was never a fan of Fight Night games, nor any type of boxing games. The last boxing game I owned was Mike Tyson's Punch Out. However, after purchasing a PS3, I did some research to locate a game that would best show case the power of the PS3. My conclusion was FNR3. I had very high expectations of this game and I must say that most of my expectations were met.

Pro's:

Amazing graphics (skin texture, and sweat).

Great customization to creating your own boxer.

Great Soundtrack (hip hop).

Con's:

Occassional frame rate issue.

Load screens take a very long time.

Customization takes a long time to load, especially when browsing through the different hair styles.

Soundtrack library is too small, only about 10 songs. But this will change once Sony releases a Firmware that allows for custom soundtracks.

Overall, I was very pleased with this game, and enjoy it. Learning curve is about an hour. The various game modes are fun. Split Screen "Get in the Ring" is a cool feature if you want to go up against a buddy. But I personally don't like the "Get in the Ring" mode, although, it's a nice feature exclusively for the PS3.

As of right now I have clocked over 60 hours into Odyssey and I feel like I have barely scratched the surface. This is THE best AC game to date. The changes that were made from Origins are very welcome and the swing to a full on RPG is done perfectly. I hated naval sections in Origins but in Odyssey I spend almost equal time sailing as I do on land. I have been playing as Kassandra (honestly who wouldn't?) And she is by far my favorite main character in the series, there is nothing unlikable about her. Being a mercenary is a breath of fresh air, you can basically act freely and it really makes you feel the part. Having a full armor system is great too making me actually care about looting chests and enemies.  I was worried cultists would be tedious to deal with but I actually enjoy hunting them. Mercenaries are a nice touch too and provide an entertaining way to farm gear. After 60 hours I have only a couple small issues: 1. Legendary gear cannot be sold, disassembled, or dropped. So if you have a piece you don't want or a duplicate you have to just drop it in storage- pretty lame. 2. Keeping your gear up to your current level and upgrading your ship takes a TON and I mean a TON of gold and various resources, it's actually crazy the numbers you will need. This review is getting long and I'm itching to get back to ancient Greece so take my advice and BUY. THIS. GAME.

I still have not played this PC version much yet, and I unfortunately still haven't gotten around to finishing even the original PS1 version of the game yet (though I would like to, eventually). That is part of the reason I got this PC version. I go to college and take my laptop with me but not my PS3 because I play more MMOs than PS1/2/3 games and don't like having more than I need to have with me, so having FFVII on my laptop means I have it with me all the time and can (hopefully) get around to playing it more often and eventually finish it. Also, I am not thrilled that the new PS4 and other new gaming consoles are moving towards dropping backwards compatibility, which means many good older games on them (such as FFX or FFXII, and possibly even the PS1 FF titles eventually) won't be playable on the new versions. With the PC, games have to be made to be playable on a wide variety of computers, so you do not have to worry about backwards compatibility, so I would love it if all the PS titles were released for the PC, too, especially the FF titles, and then if new games were also released on the PC, as well, once more especially new FF titles (though I was not thrilled with FFXIII or the bit I played of FFXIII-2).

Finally, one immediately noticeable improvement that is the main reason I wanted to write this review is the crispness of the graphics on the PC game compared to the PS1 game. The graphics are the same kind of blocky, older graphics used in the original game, but as you can sort of see in the pictures, the blocky, older graphics on the PC are much crisper on the PC while on the PS3 they were fairly fuzzy. So, not only do you get the game on the PC, but you also get slightly improved graphics, which is nice.

Recommended if you are a fan of FFVII and the FF series, and who would like their old PS games on their PC so they do not lose their old, loved titles due to newer versions of gaming consoles losing backwards compatibility. Also recommended if you just want crisper, slightly improved graphics for the game.

P.S. It is a bit weird using the controls. You are able to change them in settings, which helps slightly, but it is weird because they essentially decided to try to recreate the PS3 controller on the keyboard, instead of letting you control things how you do in most PC games. It was also mildly annoying having to create a Steam account (one more account I have to keep track of) to play it, but not a huge deal.

Update 02/17/2014: First of all, in the last few days, I purchased GTA IV and Final Fantasy VIII for Steam from Amazon, so while it was, as I mentioned above, "mildly annoying having to create a Steam account," Steam is actually quite useful and it is well worth having a Steam account, especially if you are like me and would like to have your old games all on the more universal computer rather than stuck on old console systems that are being abandoned. Secondly, while the controls on Final Fantasy VII (and Final Fantasy VIII and even somewhat on GTA IV) feel like they are trying to mimic a PS1/PS2/PS3 controller on the keyboard, I realized that there are controllers for the computer that can be purchased. I haven't played much of the story-line (I got this game primarily for free roam), but I'm really liking the free roam so far. My PC is far more mobile than my PS3 and goes with me far more places, so recently I've been buying some similar games to what I have for my PS3 for my PC. I wanted a Spider-man PC game, but the two new Amazing Spider-man digital downloads were both considerably expensive, so I decided to go with this game, instead, and I'm glad I did. The first Spider-man game I had was Ultimate Spider-man for the PS2, and I really liked the game. It had some pretty cool costumes, let you play as Venom, had great free roam ability, and Spider-man had lots of witty lines in story mode. A year or two ago, I "upgraded" to the first Amazing Spider-man for PS3 to get better graphics, but was disappointed in the web-slinging on it. Ultimate Spider-man had more interactive web-slinging, forcing you to press the web sling button every time you wanted to shoot out a new web, but the Amazing Spider-man let you just hold down the web sling button and he would keep web-slinging (though one could roughly simulate the other style of web-slinging by re-pressing the web sling button instead of just holding it down). Anyway, I did not really like the web-slinging mechanics of the first Amazing Spider-man, and the camera was positioned at a funny angle, though you get somewhat used to it after a while.

I rented the PS3 version of The Amazing Spider-man 2 game from Family Video, and found the web-slinging was only slightly improved, with a large cut to the quality of the graphics. After noticing the first Amazing Spider-man PC download was still $50 or so after being out two years, I realized the second Amazing Spider-man PC download was unlikely to drop from $40 (though I think Steam had a sale a bit ago, so it might have). Anyway, there were not many other Spider-man PC games, and no other PC downloads that I saw, so I went with Web of Shadows, and I am considerably pleased. The web-slinging feels much more like the web-slinging from the Ultimate Spider-man, which makes me the happiest about the game, and you can play a red suit and black suit Spider-man, which is almost like being able to play Venom, as well. Crawling up walls was a bit strange at first because it lets you actually battle enemies on walls, but I got used to it pretty quickly. The game also has some great graphics, despite it being six or so years old.

Some of the negatives about the game is that, from the bit of the story-line I've actually played, Spider-man does not seem as enthusiastic or witty as in the Ultimate Spider-man or even the Amazing Spider-man. I always prefer it when Spider-man is shooting off witty lines at his enemies, and that is one of the reasons I enjoyed the new Amazing Spider-man series of movies more than the first Spider-man trilogy. Another negative is that the city somehow doesn't seem as bright or vibrant as in the Ultimate Spider-man, though that might have something to do with my settings or perhaps where I am in the story-line. Thirdly and lastly, I wish this came in a PC download, especially since it takes up 8gb on my computer and STILL requires the disk!

Anyway, in conclusion, I would highly recommend this game. Of all the Spider-man games I have played, this is my second favorite, right after The Ultimate Spider-man. There are some minor negatives, but they are pretty insignificant, especially if you're like me and are just looking for a free roam game that will let you swing around NYC when you're bored. If you like Spider-man, this is a worthwhile game to get, and is cheaper and (in my opinion) better than the newer Amazing Spider-man games being released.

This is quite a good game! This was on clearance at a local store for $5, and I decided it was cheap enough to try it out. The only other Call of Duty game I have played is the first Black Ops. I have only had this game for the last few days and have just played the multi-player, but the multi-player tends to be the focus of Call of Duty games. So far, while Ghosts does not seem as polished as Black Ops, it seems so far to be essentially the same game with different skins, as I have heard of the Call of Duty series in general. While some people may view this as a criticism, I don't think that this is a bad thing. For Ghosts, if you have played Black Ops (and probably other Call of Duty games), and are bored with all the maps offered in the game having played them too many times and want something different but similar, then I would recommend Ghosts. Even on Amazon it is only about $7, so it is hard to go wrong with a game at that price, and you get a bunch of new maps to play.

One feature that I rather enjoy with this game compared to Black Ops is that there are a lot more fun little add-ons for this game on the PSN store than there was for Black Ops. Being a bit of a space nerd, I definitely had to buy the awesome astronaut costume they had available for your character as well as the space nebula camouflage they had. It is so awesome to be able to play Call of Duty in a space suit with a space gun! It is easily one of the best $6 I have spent on the PSN store.

So if you want to play new Call of Duty maps and enjoy creatively decorating your character, then Call of Duty: Ghosts is for you! Even if you are uncertain about it but think you might enjoy it, for the only $7 max that this game currently costs, it is definitely worth a try. I highly recommend this game! If I ever get around to playing the campaign or make any new observations about this game, I will update my review. Enjoy if you decide to get it!

The location of Egypt intrigued me and I had never seen another game (especially a PS4 game with amazing graphics) set there, so I pre-ordered it and it was probably one of the best gaming decisions I ever made. This game is amazing.

I think the best part about this game is the setting in Egypt. The developers did a fantastic job recreating ancient Egypt. It is absolutely stunning. The pyramids are the main part they are pushing in advertising for the game, and indeed one of the most enjoyable activities in the game is climbing the Great Pyramids and looking out over all of Egypt from their peaks, and then sliding down the sides once you've had your fill of sight-seeing. However, there are many other places to go and breath-taking sights to see in Egypt. My favorite place to go is Alexandria. I love going to the Great Library and being surrounded (in the game at least) by the vast collection of ancient wisdom and having the great statue of Zeus (which reminds me of Zeus Olympios, one of my favorite Wonders of the Ancient World) towering over me. I'm also not sure how realistic it is, but it is also possible to look from the doorway of the Great Library in the game and see the Lighthouse of Alexandria, another Wonder of the Ancient World, towering in the distance. Overall, Alexandria in particular is a shining example of one of my favorite parts of the game: being able to essentially visit cities that are now lost to history. If you've ever wanted to see the Library of Alexandria or the Lighthouse, or see the pyramids before they were too weathered, playing Origins will get you as close to those experiences as it is now possible to get (and hopefully a PSVR update at some point may get you even closer!). Also, in addition to Alexandria, there are many other beautiful sights to see, including lush green areas, sprawling deserts, swamps (watch out for crocodiles and hippos!), and large seas and rivers. All of it rendered with beautiful grahpics, as well - the sunlight glinting off the water I think is especially well done, and how realistic the water looks both when swimming on top and when diving is incredible. There are also many other little things that make the game seem rather realistic, such as when you whistle for your mount it seems to often come out from behind some corner or obstacle instead of just appearing out of thin air, and if you whistle for it when you are already really close (but maybe it is down a cliff it can't climb or something) it won't just port to where you are and you have to go maybe a few 10s of meters up further before you can whistle again and it will port a little behind you and appear to come out from behind a corner, as if it had found some way to navigate the cliff or something that you hadn't found when riding it. Lastly, I think you also get a better perspective on just how old Egypt is and how long ancient Egyptian society actually lasted. Before playing this game, I grouped ancient Egypt into essentially one time period, but this game takes place around 2000 years ago during the time of Cleopatria, and yet there are still many ruins in there day and the pyramids are considered ancient even by the people in the game, being built almost another 2000 years before then. Also, before playing this game, I thought that the Sphinx was about the size of the pyramids, however the game shows that it is much smaller than the pyramids (Bayek even comments that it "is smaller than I expected"). Overall, I think the Egyptian setting is one of the best parts of the game and it makes me excited for what technology may be able to do with historical simulations in the future. I am definitely excited for the release of Discovery Tour mode.

As far as other aspects of the game, it took me a little bit to get use to the movement and combat of the character but once I did I think both are really enjoyable mechanics. I at first disliked how you could not have Bayek jump on flat land, but after a while I got used to being able to make him jump or climb whenver there was an obstacle. Also, there are a variety of different melee and ranged weapons Bayek can use, all of which give a different feel when using, so you are likely to find your favorite. My personal favorites are regular swords, sickle swords, and heavy weapons for melee, and warrior bows and hunting bows for ranged. There are also many cool costumes you can get in the game which make Bayek look really cool.

As for the story, I have gotten all the way to level 40 but have not done any of the main quests beyond The Snake quest, which is essentially among the beginning story quests. I was not overly drawn into the main storyline initially and was more interested in exploring Egypt, so I have not done much with the main storyline and cannot comment on that yet. I plan to eventually finish it and will update this review when I did. As far as stories with the sidequests, many of which I have completed, I have found the sidequests to be rather interesting so far. They aren't the most interesting quests I have ever done but they aren't the worst, either. There is also a ton of content in the game. I have explored most of the map and done a bunch of sidequests and got all the way to 40, and there are still many locations I have not completed and many quests I have not done, so you should have no trouble getting to level 40 and it should be a while before you are bored or have nothing to do in the game. I also like that after you get to level 40, you can still earn more experience and just get ability points for the "levels" you earn without the additional level increase. In most games they stop you from earning levels and ability points. Even if you put enough time into the game to finsih everything, there is a bunch of stuff you can just do exploring Egypt to have fun. There is an ability you can get in the ability tree that lets you tame sleeping animals - I tamed a hippo and led it all the way to the Library of Alexandria (though for some reason it wouldn't go in), then I untamed it and watched the chaos unfold as it attacked citizens and guards had to come and fight it. There are also daily quests from a merchant named Reda that you can get to get really good weapons every day, and Ubisoft has been running Trial of the Gods events which let you fight Egyptian gods in epic showdowns. You need to be level 40 or close to it to participate in them, but so far they have released Anubis, Sekhmet, and Sobek (I will now be calling all crocodiles "children of Sobek" after playing this game...) for players to fight. Overall, there are hours and hours of content to keep you busy for a long time, and Ubisoft has much more content it plans to release, especially if you own the Season Pass. You are likely to never get bored with this game.

To conclude, this game is one of the best I have played. It has a massive amount of content and its recreation of ancient Egypt is absolutely beautiful and lets you come as close as possible to experiencing lost wonders of the world for yourself. I do not yet have the Season Pass but plan to get it soon, and it sounds like the Season Pass unlocks even more great content for this great game. Playing it definitely gives you a new perspective on ancient Egypt. If you haven't gotten this yet, I highly recommend you get this game, and the deluxe edition gives you a pretty cool costume, horse, and weapons in addition to the base game.

Update May 13, 2019: I finished this game a while ago and wanted to confirm that the entire story is indeed very good and it is worth completing it. I have also completed the expansion content and think it is definitely worth getting the season pass for. The Curse of the Pharaohs is very fun - you get to fight four famous pharaohs of Egypt, and you get to enter their tombs which take you into a part of the afterlife. I thought the new afterlife areas were very interesting to explore. I wasn't as impressed with The Hidden Ones expansion, but it still opened up a new area of Egypt to explore. It wasn't the most interesting being a mostly rocky area of Egypt, but it was interesting nonetheless and you get to see how Bayek is doing a few years after the end of the main game. Overall, I recommend both playing both Origins' main story and also getting the season pass for the expansion stories and to explore the new areas.

I was debating between this case and the Co2Crea PSVR headset case, which seemed more spacious. I don't travel with the PSVR headset much and was initially intending to get the Co2Crea case, but then it became (and still is as of writing this review) currently unavailable. Now that I have had this case for a couple days, I'm very glad I got this one, instead. It looked like one of the sturdiest and most protective cases online, and in person it seems equally, if not more, protective. You do need to make sure the PSVR headset is as small as possible if you don't want to risk damaging it, but once you have pushed it in all the way, the PSVR headset fits nicely into the foam. That the foam also covers up the lenses is a nice addition, since most of the other PSVR cases don't seem to have this and it helps a lot with not scratching the lenses. I was also pleasantly surprised to find that the Move controllers also fit in the case, at least when the cords and box aren't in the case. As I said, I don't frequently travel with the PSVR so mostly will use the case for protection when it is sitting next to my TV, and I normally keep the box and the camera connected so being able to fit the headset and Move controllers in the case means that I can store everything I previously kept in the box in this much more protective case. I haven't tested whether the camera and box could fit in the case for traveling while the Move controllers are in there (the cords definitely won't), but I was comparing them next to each other and I think there is a good chance that at least the camera or the box could fit with the Move controllers, if not both. The cords and the box seem to be the most durable components of the PSVR bundle, so I am happy that at least the Move controllers and probably the camera could fit in there for traveling and I could put the box and cords in another bin. I will update this review when I get the time to unplug everything and test how much I can safely cram into this case.

Overall, I am very happy with this case so far. It seems very durable and protective, and I was happy everything that I used to store in the white box the PSVR came in can now be stored in this case. It seems like I might also be able to get the black box and/or the camera into this case as well for the occasional times I might travel with the PSVR. This is a great case and I highly recommend it!

Update (02/10/2019): I tried putting both the PSVR camera and the black box into this case as well as both individually. As long as the PSVR camera is attached to the stand, both don't seem to fit at the same time. I didn't try taking it off of the stand since if I was traveling it wouldn't be worth it to me to remove the stand to try to get both to fit when the black box is pretty sturdy and could travel elsewhere, but the stand seemed to occupy the space where the black box was so I imagine if you took the camera off the stand then both would fit. However, if you put either the black box OR the camera in along with the headset and controllers, the case seems to fit one of them fine. Since the camera and controllers seem considerably more fragile than the black box, I will likely put the camera in the case in addition to everything I will normally keep in there (the headset and controllers) when traveling with the PSVR. I h ave added more pictures showing the camera, the black box, and both in the case, as well as pictures of how it closes (or doesn't close in the last case). Being able to fit the controllers and the camera in this case as long as the less fragile cords and black box are left out of it makes me very happy with it. I recommend this case even more now that I have tested the PSVR camera fitting in the case in place of the black box.

While I played the original Assassin’s Creed game years ago, I never got into it very much and ended up never finishing it. I ended up purchasing Origins when it came out because the location sounded so interesting, and I was blown away by the quality of the game and the graphics. I greatly enjoyed wandering around a beautiful recreation of a country I may never get to visit, during a time I will definitely never visit it in. When I saw the next game was set in Ancient Greece, a location and time period I was even more interested in than Egypt, I pre-ordered it almost immediately. I have not been disappointed.

The graphics and story are equally as amazing as Origins, if not more so. The graphics are incredible, and just as in Origins, the water looks particularly realistic. Taking a little boat out on the lakes and rivers in Egypt was always one of my favorite things to do in Origins, so I am glad there is so much more water in Ancient Greece. Taking your ship sailing is quite fun, and I love “parking” it and going swimming in the deep. You can even see whales! The first time I saw whales I thought the game might be inaccurate, but I was surprised to learn how large the Mediterranean sea actually was in comparison to the lakes of Egypt. So large that many ocean creatures live in it – this is one of the many educational points Ubisoft sneaks into the Assassin’s Creed games, even though it is primarily entertainment. In addition to the water, there are also many beautiful rendered Ancient Greek landscapes and architecture. There was one disappointment, though, and that was when I went to find the Statue of Zeus Olympios. After seeing the statue of George Washington designed after this sculpture in the Smithsonian museums, I couldn’t wait to see this Wonder of the Ancient World, but I was disappointed because the statue wasn’t much different than the statue of Alexander the Great in the Library of Alexandria in Origins (which was just one of several statues exactly like this). I found the massive, if crude, statue of Zeus on the initial island to be much more impressive, and I also found the towering statue of Athena in Athens to be another of my favorite architectural pieces in the game. I feel the Statue of Zeus Olympios should have outshone both of those given that it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. However, other than this slight disappointment, I can’t say enough good things about the quality of the recreation of Ancient Greece that Ubisoft has done here. It is far more massive than Origins’ Egypt was, and it took me far longer to explore everything and go to all the points of interest. Also, there is a quest series near the end of the game you should definitely do which has you going after epic, mythical Greek monsters such as the Cyclops and Medusa. These were very fun quests and battles.

The story was also very interesting and well-written. I like how you can choose to be Alexios or Kassandra, and then the other actually appears in the story as well. I don’t want to give any of the plot away, but there are many surprises as you continue along. The gameplay is also very good. It is similar to Origins but just different enough that I was thrown off at first and kept dying and wasn’t very impressed with the gameplay. However, after getting more used to it the gameplay grew on me. The combat is similar to Origins, except where you had to block a lot of attacks as Bayek, basically trading off between blocking and attacking, you do not have a shield in Odyssey and so Alexios/Kassandra has to dodge and parry between attacks. That said, I have not gone back to test this, but I think even if I knew what I was doing better that progressing would seem harder at first than Origins was. I also purchased an extra drachmae and experience boost from the store for about $10, but I think even if I hadn’t purchased it you could still progress pretty quickly once you got to a high enough level, but it would basically shorten the beginning part where you seem very weak to all enemies. The one other complaint I have about gameplay is that all the regions auto-level. You can adjust the difficulty, and this controls how far below everything you have out-leveled is below you, but they still all change their levels as you level up. I preferred how Origins worked and had all the regions at a set level, and you had the option to go in and set all regions to your level. This made going back and completing bases and other points of interest easy as you grew in level, since lower-ranked regions went very fast. In this game, that isn’t the case, since everything is always your level or only a few under, at least. One last gameplay point to mention is the store. I made the mistake of buying gear from the store early on, and it costs a lot of money and resources to level up gold gear. While by the end of the main story I had a lot saved up, if you want to save a lot of resources and know you want the look and the stats of certain pieces of gear from the store, then you want to wait to buy them later. Note that I specifically said “and” the stats. This is because I ended up saving a lot of resources because I found gear with better or preferable stats as I went through the game and used these, but I still liked the look of the gold gear I had bought around level 5 (the Pegasus armor) and luckily Ubisoft fairly early on added a way to change the look of your armor to other gear, so I put on the armor with the stats I wanted and then changed it to look like my Pegasus gear, an option I would not have had if I had not purchased it. So if you want a look, you can purchase something from the store and just change the look of your armor, but if you want the stats and you buy it very early on, then you will be paying a lot of drachmae and resources to level up your gear.

Lastly, in regards to the season pass and expansion quests, I have not gone very far into that yet, though will update it with more information if I do in the future. I finished the main quests and then started on some of the Lost Tales of Greece quests and stopped there a few months ago. I was not impressed with the two Lost Tales of Greece that I played – they seemed like mostly fetch quests. They had many running around collecting random objects with a thin story-line between. I have not played any of Legacy of the First Blade or Fate of Atlantis quests, though I would imagine and hope they would be more interesting than these Lost Tales of Greece. I am generally a completionist, and while I might go back to finish these, I wouldn’t feel bad about skipping what I have so far seen as very boring Lost Tales of Greece quests. I will update this review if I explore any more of these and find one to be interesting, or if I start on the other two expansions.

Overall, this is a wonderful game and just as good, if not better than, Origins. If you enjoyed Origins then you will definitely enjoy Odyssey. For $60, I think the new Assassin’s Creed games are wonderful ways to explore beautiful recreations of real places many of us may never get to see, and even better they are set during a time all of us will never get to visit those places during. While the games are primarily entertainment, Odyssey continues to spark my imagination about how we may be able to improve education using technology and simulations, as well. I also found the music in Odyssey to be very good, even better than Origins, and encourage you to check out the soundtrack in addition to the game. I highly recommend this game and look forward to the next massive and beautiful Assassin’s Creed game that Ubisoft has in store for us.

Since seeing this game was coming out, I thought it looked interesting. However, many of the trailers and gameplay videos made it look like the game was almost exclusively focused on combat with a bow and arrow, and I never liked using the bow and arrow as my main weapon in games. Luckily, even though I waited about a year after the original release, I decided to give it a try. I found out that it wasn’t just the bow and arrow that was used, but also the spear, so my combat gravitated towards mostly using the spear. I sometimes do use the bow and arrow though, too, but the mechanics of the bow and arrow are better than in other games. In addition to the combat being better than I expected, I am also glad I got this game because the graphics are incredible and there are so many different environments to explore. There are both grassy and snowy terrain to explore, and they are rendered in superb detail. Also, the story is very well written. The Final Fantasy series of games are some of my favorite games and I consider them to have some of the most well written stories, and Horizon Zero Dawn is nearly on par with the Final Fantasy series in terms of its story. The Frozen Wilds expansion is also worth getting, giving you a whole new frozen landscape to explore, new creatures (including both ice and fire bears, which give some pretty epic fights!), and also, for those such as myself who primarily use the spear, new spear upgrades! Overall, this game has beautiful graphics, great gameplay, and a wonderful storyline, and I highly recommend it. If you aren’t a bow and arrow fan and are worried that you won’t like this game because of the combat, don’t be worried because the bow and arrow mechanics aren’t that bad and also you can use the spear both a lot like a sword and as your main weapon. This game is absolutely worth getting.

This is a great new Spiderman game with awesome graphics. My favorite Spiderman game is still Ultimate Spiderman from the PS2, but Spiderman PS4 comes very close to this game. I don’t remember the storyline of Ultimate Spiderman being overly deep, but the main reason I like playing Spiderman games is just to swing around New York City, so let’s discuss web-slinging mechanics first. The Ultimate Spiderman still has my favorite web-slinging mechanics. It felt more like you were actually web-slinging because pressing R2 essentially had you shoot out a web, and if you held it Spiderman would just keep hanging onto his current web, and you had to let go of R2 to make him drop the web. Hitting it again would make him shoot out another web. My first attempt to get an “upgraded” Spiderman game was with the first Amazing Spiderman game on the PS3, but the web-slinging mechanics was horrible. You essentially just pressed R2 and he would auto-web-sling. The camera was also in a weird position, essentially just over his left shoulder instead of in the middle. With this new Spiderman PS4 game, it is a bit like a cross between those two games. You can just press R2 and have him auto-web-sling, but if you want to press and let go of R2 like in Ultimate Spiderman, doing so feels much more natural than the Amazing Spiderman on the PS3 felt. The camera is also back in an appropriate spot behind Spiderman with him in the middle. Since it wasn’t designed to press and let go like in Ultimate Spiderman, I don’t think Spiderman PS4 has quite as good of web-slinging mechanics as Ultimate Spiderman, but since you can recreate this feeling pretty closely with the built in web-slinging mechanics, I like it much better than the Amazing Spiderman and overall think the web-slinging mechanics in Spiderman PS4 are closer to Ultimate Spiderman than to Amazing Spiderman. Another area that Ultimate Spiderman does better with gameplay than both Amazing Spiderman and Spiderman PS4 is that if you fall from a tall building and don’t double jump or web-sling away, then you die. This seems more realistic than Spiderman not taking any damage regardless from how high he falls from in both Amazing Spiderman and Spiderman PS4. I have somewhat rationalized this by thinking that Spiderman is a superhero and can maybe do a small “mini-jump” to avoid hurting himself (and in Spiderman PS4, there is the Iron Spider suit from the Avengers and other similar suits, which all could likely absorb the impact damage), but I still like the more realistic mechanic of Spiderman dying if he falls too far like in Ultimate Spiderman. One area Spiderman PS4 does better than both the previous Spiderman games is combat. I don’t remember the Amazing Spiderman combat very much, but the Ultimate Spiderman combat was pretty good with lots of acrobatic moves. Spiderman PS4 brings a bunch of fun, acrobatic moves like Ultimate Spiderman has, but also gives you a bunch of fun combat gadgets to use. Also, in terms of the graphics Spiderman PS4 is the best of the three, and I love that they included the Avengers tower in the game. You can even swing by the museum from Night at the Museum. I also love that you can take pictures in Spiderman PS4, and they even have a challenge to take pictures of different locations. Lastly, in regard to the story, I never made it far enough in Amazing Spiderman to get a good gist of the story and I don’t recall the story in Ultimate Spiderman to be overly deep. In Spiderman PS4, the story will definitely keep you interested, and it is much deeper (and even darker in parts) than Ultimate Spiderman was. I definitely think Spiderman PS4 has a much better storyline than most Spiderman games. I also recommend getting The City That Never Sleeps expansion, since it adds some new interesting stories about Black Cat and Silver Sable that are worth playing, and also includes a number of cool new suits. Overall, while I still ultimately (haha…) think Ultimate Spiderman did a better job than Spiderman PS4 with the web-slinging, Spiderman PS4 has better graphics, better combat, and a better story than Ultimate Spiderman, so it definitely is one of the best Spiderman games out there. If you have a PS4 and want a current-gen Spiderman game, then I highly recommend Spiderman PS4.

I've been a fan of God Eater since I first played Burst in PSP. Now, I'll admit that I hated games like this until playing Burst for the first time. I think it was the story that made me love it so much.
So when I saw 2 was coming to the US, I nearly wet myself with excitement. And I preordered that sucker in full the next day. Such a good decision.
The graphics are great, the gameplay has been amped up since Burst, and the operator can be set to talk via your controller instead of the TV. That last part alone was mind blowing.

Day 1 edition came with the collection DLC. This includes crossover costumes, unique heads, and came with the remastered version of Burst (renamed resurrection). All of this in one nice and neat package means I'll be busy for a few weeks.

If you're looking for an alternative to Monster Hunter or even just looking for something to keep you occupied until your next big score, I strongly recommend God Eater 2 Rage Burst.

I'm not a huge soulsborne fan, and the whole... genre, i guess is a close enough word... it spawned isn't hugely my thing. Like I have DS2:SotFS edition for PS4, and I've played a bit with it, but it just wasn't a game I dove into. The Surge though, with the DS meets robots aesthetic, I really do enjoy. I tried the trial version, played that to the point that I either needed to buy the game or drop the game entirely, and then saw the game was $22 on here. I jumped on it without thinking twice.

The Surge has some clunkiness to it, and for all the other minor complaints I have, it's not a disaster of a game. Where in DS2 I stopped before the first boss, The Surge threw me headlong into the first boss and I felt amazing trashing the bastard. I'd say it's not the same difficulty as a DS game, but you can see the influence through and through with this game and the agonizingly punishing way it treats you if you make a mistake. Though there's some trophy glitches I ran into, like the trophy for dying the first time didn't register for me, but that's minor when compared with the fun I have playing it.

On the one hand, really liked the story. Ont eh other hand, the controls were sometimes a little wonky and would turn a nearly perfect non-lethal level into an "oh sh** I killed that guard, didn't mean to- an there's his buddy. If I can just- no I didn't want to warp there damn it!"
All in all, decent game and okay DLC on disk.

It is nice getting a cameo from one character of Star Ocean 1, but not enough to redeem the game. It's kind of a sad entry, seeing as Star Ocean is normally amazing.
I got about 2/3 of the way through the game and just... had to stop. It's a cult classic, but it's not as fantastic as I had hoped.

I don't particularly like golf, but I really quite enjoy HOT SHOTS GOLF 3. It's easy enough to learn, but tricky enough to take some time to master. Instead of offering up another "realistic" interpretation of sports, HSG3 delivers a fun parody that's really enjoyable.
The characters and caddies are funny, though eventually repetitive. The animation and character design is humorous. It's not all beautiful to look at, but I do appreciate the design and effort made into including as many stereotypes as possible.
Combine that with 4 player versus, some in game booing, and some chips and drinks, and you've got yourself a really fun few hours of play for that afternoon get together.
HSG3 is one of the more enjoyable games I've played recently.

I must first admit that I haven't spent a weekend playing HERDY GERDY. I tried it for a few hours and here's my reaction:
The art direction on this game is really great. CORE should be really proud of themselves. Particularly the cinematics...I'm impressed with the amount of facial animation they put into lil' Gerdy.
The person who says this game has the worst graphics ever has no idea what he's talking about. This game has a great, traditional animation feel without the obligatory toon-shaded lines. I was really impressed.
I found the gameplay, however, to be a bit frustrating. The herding aspect proved tricky, and I found myself getting more disinterested than compelled to keep on going.
In fact, I was more interested in just watching than playing. But maybe that's because I'm a little bit older. The mixed reviews are probably going to kill this game, but if you're an animator or art director worth your salt, you'll be sure to pick up this game and give it a good look.

I was used to playing UNREAL TOURNAMENT prior to SOCOM, and because of that, I was turned off by the controls. I had the keyboard/mouse combination down, and mentally, that seemed like the only way to play. In fact, I was so turned off by the controls that I let this game sit for a couple of weeks before really spending any time with it.
Then I took a deep breath.
Instead of complaining, I just played the first mission over and over again for any evening until I got the hang of it...and I have to say it's not that bad. It took a little getting used to, but I'm a big boy with a two-sided brain, so I was able to adapt. And if you give it a couple of hours, which isn't a lot to ask after spending (money), I think you'll find it all okay, too.
I also find myself really enjoying all the stealth, sneaking around, and team work. A great change from UNREAL TOURNAMENT.
My recommendation is edit your controls so your sight moves slower than the default and you'll find yourself able to adapt to the control switch.

I can't say that I completely share the enthusiasm of other reviewers...
ZONE OF THE ENDERS 2 is a good game with beautiful, stylized graphics. It's fast, with lots of combat action and gorgeous special effects. Unfortunately, I find the combat to be repetitive and somewhat obvious.
I don't think the story is great. It's convoluted and choppy, and the constant interruption of anime cinematics gets aggravating. There's a lot of watching in this game...it makes for more of an interactive experience, I suppose, but it gets tiresome.
The art direction is top notch, without a doubt, but the mech-element is hardly integral. You in no way feel like you're in a lumbering behemoth...instead, you're super-fast and flying in zero gravity. It's all good fun, I suppose, but if you're a mech enthusiast and you're looking for some MECH ASSAULT type of experience, look elsewhere.
ZOE2 is basically a beautiful 3D shooter, physics be damned. Perhaps if some kind of online or multiplayer option where included the experience would be more rewarding. Better than the first game and definitely worth renting, if not to experience the look alone.

I'm a big fan of SOUL CALIBUR, having played the heck out of both the original DreamCast version as well as the PS1's SOUL BLADE. SOUL CALIBUR 2 for the PS2 is a nice follow up, with updated characters, arenas, and graphics.
In all honesty, gameplay isn't too different from SOUL CALIBUR 1, but it's been a while and I don't really seem to mind. They've made tossing someone out of the ring more difficult, and they've added walls to the arenas. I haven't noticed any control lag, as suggested by other reviewers, and you can change the voices from english back to japanese in the options menu. That reviewer is right, however, when he points out how insufferable the english dialog is.
Here are the negatives: The game lacks online play, which is really too bad. Almost unforgivable, in my opinion. Some of the new character designs (Charade, Necrid) are really lame. The addition of Heihachi, from Tekken, doesn't add anything to the game, either, and Yoshimitsu is tired. Finally, being asked to play through "Weapon Master" mode a second time is downright tedious.
On a picky note, some of the character re-designs fall a little flat. Xianghua, Seung Mina, and Astaroth seem to've lost something with their updated graphics.
Now that I'm older and don't live at home, I depend on online play to compete against my brother, who now lives across town. Not including it in SC2 is really too bad.
SOUL CALIBUR 2 is a nice follow up. Fun, fast, and full of special moves and effects. It's a great fighter and a lot more engaging than TEKKEN 4 was.

SHADOW OF THE COLOSSUS is a lot of fun. Very entertaining. It looks really good, it's cinematic, expansive, the gameplay is original and exciting, and it's not frustratingly difficult. No button mashing or complex combinations. It's more timing and ingenuity.

The landscape is immense and varied, and it's a pleasure to roam about. My one wish is that, outside of the colossi, there were something else to do. Call them mini-games, or whatever. Even just a few extra diversions hidden in the great landscape could've been exciting.

My real score would be 4.5, but I'm rounding up, as I feel this original, artistic game deserves it. Both ICO and SHADOW OF THE COLOSSUS are must-have games for the PS2.

I'm somewhat surprised by the disparity in reviews of TOMB RAIDER: LEGEND. I've played through half of it so far, and I think it's a solid game. Not perfect, but a lot of fun.

I haven't played TOMB RAIDER since the very first PS1 game, so I missed the downward spiral of previous games.

The environments are great, and I think the controls are really good. I like the additional "second chance" grabs lifted from GOD OF WAR, and the interactive cinematics. In fact, I wish there were more of them. Every time I see an action cinematic I want to participate.

The puzzle solving is just tricky enough, and searching for the "gold rewards" on each level is -really- hard... but fun. Admittedly, I need the internet's help to find most of the gold prizes. I guess I'm losing my skills.

The motorcycle sequences are lame. I understand the desire to mix it up, but I'm not sure this was the way. If the driving controls were better, if the track environments were more exploratory, and if the shooting element was removed, I think it would be far more enjoyable.

I'm surprised that people are harping on the costume changes. They're non-essential, but they're fun enough. A harmless, entertaining addition, and I like it. Exploring Croft Manor, however, is a little tiresome. The climbing room was boring... I would've enjoyed more secret tunnels and riddle solving instead.

Three final gripes... 1) I wish the camera view were wider. I'm playing WideScreen on an NTSC monitor and I still wish I could see more. Another 10 degrees would've been perfect. 2) As I said, I'm halfway through the game... so it's feeling a little short. If it reported I was at the 33% mark, I would feel better. And finally, 4) I wish that Lara looked better. Given the models in games like Rumble Roses from -years- ago, I think Lara could've been a bit more refined.

In short, I'm glad I picked up LEGENDS.

PSYCHONAUTS is a mixed bag. The story is fun and imaginative, and they made a serious attempt to freshen up the traditional platforming activities (finding, collecting, etc.). The dialog is also pretty funny. My problem with the game, however, is with the art direction and character design. Both were clumsy and disappointing.

Usually I'm all about gameplay, and the gameplay in Psychonauts is satisfactory. After that comes things like design and graphics. Great design doesn't cost more to model or animate... it just demands talent on the front end. You need a great designer with a sharp pencil, and there, I think, is where Psychonauts really drops the ball. Given the creative environment, I wish they spent as much time putting together a worthy cast. These players are, well, just plain ugly.

If the characters even approached, say, THE NIGHTMARE BEFORE CHRISTMAS, this game would be far stronger. Far more engaging. As it stands now, I don't like Raz, the main character. And I can't stand looking at many of his playmates. Who wants to sit and look at ugly design hours on end?

As an owner of the HTC Vive and Oculus Rift, I have to say I really prefer these controllers over the Vive wands. These essentially feel like console controls in terms of how they feel in your hands and button placement. Add in motion control, and you've got something pretty awesome.

As is writing this, they do work on Steam. For room scale and SteamVR, I had a lot of issues getting it setup. I ended up just using the quick setup with SteamVR in which you just place the Rift and controllers on the floor in the middle of the play area and click OK. Setup in the Oculus software (required) was fine though, and didn't have issues with tracking like I did with SteamVR. The tracking issues during setup appear to be related to the Rift headset turning off while it sits unused in setup (or so that was my experience.)

While I love these and gave the Rift 5 stars as well, I still recommend the HTC Vive ever so slightly for being easier to setup, the sensors don't need to be wired to the PC via USB 3.0, and you don't need to install the Vive software for it to work (you do NEED Oculus software installed for Rift.) There's also the fact HTC Vive users can use Revive to play Oculus games.

If you have the Oculus Rift, you owe it to yourself to get these.

Installing all of the compressed data onto your hard drive may take a long time, but it's small price to pay to have all of the content on disc.

So I want to personally thank "Firaxis Games" and "2K Games" for showing that ALL games can hold all of it's DLCs, Updates, Expansions and the Base Game content on a single disc... Now we can know for sure when a company is being lazy or greedy for not putting all of the content on disc.
